title: Israelis and Diaspora Jews are donating more since Oct. 7, says JGive founder
body: Charitable giving to and within Israel has not fallen since the surge that followed October 7, but has kept rising, JGive founder and CEO Ori Ben-Shlomo said on The Deep Dive this week.Ben-Shlomo said the platform expects to finish this year at more than four times its pre-war volume, with over 250,000 Israeli and Diaspora donors giving about NIS 500 million."It changed society," he said. He added that Israelis now see civil society organizations as a "must-have" rather than a nice extra. Ben-Shlomo, a lawyer who was general counsel at a major Israeli media group, founded JGive after serving in Gaza as a reservist during Operation Protective Edge in 2014. There, he said, he saw how much donated goodwill was lost to poor coordination.On October 7, as calls came in from New York, Los Angeles and London, JGive helped thousands of charities raise emergency funds. It also set up a national emergency fund whose leadership included a former Israel Air Force commander and a former Supreme Court justice. The fund began with basic needs, such as food, clothing and medication for evacuees from the kibbutzim, including Holocaust survivors, before moving on to education and rehabilitation.The way Diaspora Jews give has also changed, Ben-Shlomo said. Their grandparents' generation wrote checks to large institutions. Younger donors want to give "without the middleman," to specific causes they have researched themselves, and increasingly alongside Israelis rather than simply to them. "Israel is not a young state," he noted. "We're close to 80." He said young people are now among JGive's top donors, the same group that major charities had once told him they could not reach.Israeli elections two weeks awayWith Israel's elections two weeks away, the conversation turned to Diaspora Jews who feel tied to the country's future but cannot vote. Ben-Shlomo argued that giving is "the best way" for them to have a say, and said it does more to shape the country than politics does. "Politics divides people, and giving connects people," he said. He also addressed the strain that rising antisemitism has placed on Jewish communities abroad, which must fund their own security while still supporting Israel. He said those donors have shifted the balance toward their own communities without stopping their support for Israel, and argued that the Israeli government and Israeli donors should now help Diaspora communities in return.Ben-Shlomo described working with Israel's Tax Authority to introduce donor-advised funds, a tool familiar in the US, and to allow donations of stocks and other assets, which he called "a game changer." He said further reform is still needed, including ceilings on tax benefits for major donors. He framed the larger task as building what he called Israel's "fourth power." After defense, the economy and technology, he said, the country now needs the strength of a society "that makes sure no one is left behind," built from the ground up, much like the start-up nation.Asked whether he is optimistic about the next generation, he answered with the story of a reserve officer badly wounded in Lebanon who, while still in rehabilitation, organized a campaign for a fellow patient.

title: China will keep speaking up for Palestinian cause, supports two-state solution, FM Wang Yi says
body: China's foreign minister voiced support for Palestinians on Thursday, saying China will continue to speak up for the Palestinian cause, according to a ministry statement."The Palestinian issue should not be marginalized," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Palestinian counterpart, Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, in Baku, the statement said.Wang urged "all peace-loving countries" to support the two-state solution, according to the statement.Wang's remarks came as he also met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of the CICA Summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, according to a statement from the President's Office.The meeting focused on Israel-China bilateral relations and the broader situation in the Middle East.Herzog highlights Israel-China ties in meeting with Wang YiHerzog welcomed the meeting and highlighted the importance of strengthening bilateral relations, particularly in the areas of "economic, trade, and cultural ties, among other areas," according to the statement.President Herzog's Meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on the sidelines of the CICA Summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, October 15, 2026. Itay Beit-On (GPO) / Sound credit: Ben Peretz (GPO)The two also discussed regional developments, with Herzog emphasizing the strategic threats facing Israel, particularly those posed by Iran and its terrorist proxies.China says Israel should stop its 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlementsWang Yi told Herzog that his country should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements, China's foreign ministry said in a statement on Friday.China has consistently held that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century, Wang told Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan, the ministry added.

title: Why Azerbaijan, Bahrain's Baku meetings with President Herzog are important - analysis
body: Israel's President Isaac Herzog met in Baku on Wednesday with Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Bahrain's Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani during his attendance at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).These meetings, of importance for Israel, come amid a number of diplomatic and other recent successes, such as Colombia inaugurating its embassy in Jerusalem. Colombia's Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar came to Israel for the event. Additionally, on October 8, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with Paraguay's Vice President, Pedro Alliana, in Jerusalem.These are historic days for the Jewish state. Three years after the October 7 attacks, Israel is increasing its engagement with several countries. This comes as the media discusses whether fighting will resume against the Islamic Republic. In this context, the meetings between Herzog and the president of Azerbaijan, as well as Bahrain's foreign minister, are important. Azerbaijan is a rising power in the Caucasus, with influence that extends to Europe, Central Asia, and beyond. It also borders Iran.Bahrain is an important Gulf country. It joined the Abraham Accords in 2020. About the Wednesday meeting between Herzog and Aliyev, the President's Office, in a statement distributed by Israel's Government press Office, noted that Herzog had attended the summit “at the invitation of President Aliyev” and that he “thanked President Aliyev for the warm welcome and noted that Azerbaijan is a model of stability and an important and respected voice in the international community.”Azerbaijan is an important country for many reasonsThe leaders looked at “ways to deepen the strategic relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan, which is rooted in mutual respect, shared interests, and the deep historical ties between the two peoples. They also discussed recent regional developments and their countries' shared commitment to stability and security in the region.”Azerbaijan is strategically important: It has been reaching out to Syria recently, and it is a close friend of Turkey's. Turkey has tended to be critical of Israel; and Israel has concerns about Turkey's role in Syria. Baku can potentially play an important role in reducing tensions between the two.Herzog's office noted that “President Aliyev thanked President Herzog for his words of appreciation regarding Azerbaijan's chairmanship of CICA, and emphasized that his country continues to work to strengthen mutual trust among CICA member states and to advance practical cooperation between them.”Herzog said, “Israel and Azerbaijan share a unique relationship, one that has been developed over many years and has proven its importance in complex times as well. I thank President Ilham Aliyev for our partnership and for the open dialogue between us, and I believe we have much more to achieve together: strengthening the ties between our peoples, expanding our cooperation, and creating new opportunities for generations to come.”In the meeting with Bahrain, Herzog also brought up the importance of strengthening the Abraham Accords. The October 7 massacre and the ensuing Israel-Hamas War created a backdrop against which it was difficult for expansion of the accords to take place. Currently, though, there are many opportunities.“President Herzog emphasized the great importance Israel attaches to its relations with the Kingdom of Bahrain and commended the courageous leadership of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and the Government of Bahrain. The President conveyed his warmest wishes to His Majesty the King and the Bahraini people,” Herzog's office said.The important relationship between Israel and AzerbaijanIt is worth recalling the important relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan that has developed over the last decades. They established diplomatic relations in April 1992, shortly after Azerbaijan gained independence, following the collapse of the Soviet Union.The relationship expanded over the years: Energy trade and defense sales have been important building blocks. Azerbaijan has become a modern military power and has showcased Israeli defense technology during events in the past. In 2023, Azerbaijan opened an embassy in Israel. George Deek played a key role as ambassador to Azerbaijan from 2018 to 2025.Bahrain-Israel ties are also important, though less in the spotlight than Israel-UAE ties or even Israel-Morocco ties. However, Bahrain is an important part of the Abraham Accords. It is a cautious country, and this caution means it is not often in the spotlight in the Gulf. However, it has also suffered from threats during the recent Iran conflict. Israel opened an embassy in Manama in 2021, following the signing of the Abraham Accords. Its first ambassador, Eitan Na'eh, was a former ambassador to Azerbaijan and Turkey – as well as Israel's first envoy to the United Arab Emirates in 2021. (He died of a heart attack in January.)There has been cooperation between Israel and Bahrain in recent years.The meetings in Baku are important in terms of the larger regional context. Israeli defense companies also had a major role at the Marrakesh Air Show this week in Morocco. As such, there is a growing perception that Israeli ties with various Muslim countries are now improving and have become more public than they were in the past several years.

title: Istio 1.31 拥抱 AI 智能体，却先宣布“告别”Google Cloud
body:
8 月 31 日发布的 Istio 1.31 允许团队使用新的 istio-agentgateway-waypoint GatewayClass，在 ambient 网格中将 agentgateway 作为七层 waypoint 代理运行。
同一版本停止向 Google Cloud 发布容器镜像和 Helm Chart。仍在使用 gcr.io/istio-release 、registry.istio.io 或由 Google 托管的 Helm 仓库的团队，应在 10 月 13 日下一次计划内断供测试之前完成迁移，这些服务将在 12 月退役。Istio 1.31.0 支持 Kubernetes 1.32 至 1.36。
这项 waypoint 支持以 1.30 中新增的实验性纯网关集成为基础。 Agentgateway 是一个面向智能体流量构建的 Rust 数据平面，由 Solo.io 捐赠给 Linux 基金会，除了普通 HTTP 外，还能处理 模型上下文协议 等协议。Istio 1.31 还修复了 agentgateway 后端的 ListenerSet 处理和 mTLS 连接问题。 Waypoint 之间的流量迁移 目前处于 Alpha 阶段，维护者警告称，其标签、注解和行为都可能发生变化。
这种流量迁移机制也是新增功能。服务或命名空间可以通过 use-waypoint-canary 标签，在主 waypoint 之外指定一个金丝雀 waypoint，然后使用 use-waypoint-canary-weight 注解，将可配置比例的新建网格内连接发送到金丝雀 waypoint，而不需要修改客户端。已经建立的连接不会迁移，因此长连接可能会延迟流量拆分效果的显现。
9 月 21 日发布的 Istio 1.31.1 修复了一个问题：仅被引用为金丝雀的 agentgateway waypoint 无法获得引用它们的服务所对应的路由和策略，导致迁移过去的连接被拒绝。该补丁还包含安全修复，并修正了 ALLOW_ANY_DYNAMIC_DNS 在纯 IPv6 集群中的转发问题。
对于大型网格，两项流量管理新功能尤为突出。DestinationRule 和 MeshConfig 新增的 zoneAwareLbSetting 字段允许 Envoy 将请求路由到下游代理所在可用区内的端点，并且仅在本地容量耗尽时才将流量溢出到其他可用区。这一决策由 Envoy 自动完成，不再需要 localityLbSetting 所要求的静态百分比配置。ALLOW_ANY_DYNAMIC_DNS 出站模式会在请求发出时，根据 HTTP Host 标头解析主机名，从而无需为每个外部目标编写 ServiceEntry。
在安全方面，COMPLIANCE_POLICY 环境变量新增 fips-140-3 值，可将 TLS 限制为 1.2 或更高版本，并仅允许使用符合 FIPS 标准的密码套件以及 P-256 和 P-384 曲线。 变更说明 明确指出，Go 组件必须使用 Go 1.24 或更高版本构建，并采用 GOFIPS140=v1.0.0 或更高的已验证版本；仅设置运行时策略并不足够。AuthorizationPolicy 新增的 trustDomains 和 notTrustDomains 字段，可以根据从对等端证书中取得的信任域匹配或排除请求。
这次托管平台变更要求仍在使用现有仓库的团队采取行动。Microsoft 的 Steven Jin 和 Solo.io 的 Keith Mattix 于 8 月 21 日在 Istio 博客 中写道：“由于资金模式发生变化，今年 Istio 正在将全部基础设施从 Google Cloud Platform 迁移到 Amazon Web Services。”下一次计划内断供测试将在 10 月 13 日 15:00 至 18:00（UTC）期间停用旧端点；最终测试将从 12 月 8 日 15:00（UTC）持续至 12 月 9 日 15:00（UTC）。验证镜像签名的团队还需要考虑密钥轮换：迁移指南列出了适用于 1.31.0 的 istio-key.pub，以及适用于 1.31.1 及后续版本的 istio-key-v2.pub。在 跟踪此事的 GitHub Issue 中，有人询问该项目为什么选择 Docker Hub 而不是 GHCR，Jin 回应称：“GHCR 存在一些未公开的限制。”他还补充道：“按照我们目前的使用量，我认为我们很容易就会超过那些限制。”
原文链接： https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/10/istio-1-31-agentgateway/

title: Europe distinguishes Iranians from Iran. Why not Israelis from Israel? - opinion
body: Europe knows how to condemn a government without condemning everyone it governs.When Iranians take to the streets, European leaders do not tell them they are responsible for the Islamic Republic. They condemn the regime and express solidarity with the protesters. Europe sanctions North Korea while speaking of North Koreans as victims of repression. It condemns Hezbollah without pretending that Lebanon and Hezbollah are the same thing.The distinction has been particularly clear in the Palestinian case. After the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led massacres in Israel, the European Union (EU) repeatedly separated Hamas, the Palestinian Authority, and the Palestinian people. Josep Borrell, then the EU's foreign policy chief, warned against collective punishment and reminded Europeans that “not all the Palestinian people are terrorists.”Russia complicates the picture. Even before the invasion of Ukraine, the European Parliament distinguished “between the Russian people and President Putin's regime.” After the invasion, ordinary Russians faced visa restrictions and exclusions from sports and culture. Still, European leaders continued to talk about Russian President Vladimir Putin's war and Putin's regime.None of these comparisons is exact. Iran, Russia, and North Korea are authoritarian states. Hezbollah is a terrorist organization whose weapons answer to no electorate. Hamas won Palestinian elections in 2006 and has not faced voters in two decades.Israel is different. It is a democracy. Israelis choose their governments.And this is where things get uncomfortableAcross parts of Europe, Israeli universities are treated as extensions of the state. Israeli artists and cultural institutions face calls for exclusion. Broadcasters withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest because Israel's public broadcaster, KAN, was taking part. There is growing pressure to keep Israeli athletes out of international competitions.Official Europe is more careful. When European Council President António Costa supported proposed measures against Israel in September 2025, he stressed that they were “not aimed at the Israeli people,” but were a response to the government's actions in Gaza and the West Bank.Outside Brussels, that distinction is less secure. In debates over universities, culture, broadcasting, and sports, the categories slide into one another. The Israeli government becomes Israel. Israel becomes its institutions. Its institutions become its citizens.Why? The obvious answer is democracy.ISRAELIS VOTE, pay taxes, and elect the politicians who govern them. Many serve in the military. Perhaps Europeans are, therefore, entitled to hold Israelis responsible in a way they would hesitate to hold Iranians responsible for the ayatollahs.There is something to that argument. Israelis cannot have democracy both ways. We cannot celebrate democratic choice when it produces governments we like, and then pretend that governments we dislike have nothing to do with the society that elected them. The death, displacement, and destruction in Gaza resulted from decisions made by an elected Israeli government. European anger at Israel did not come from nowhere.But there is a long distance between political responsibility and collective guilt.Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested against the judicial overhaul. Israelis have demonstrated for the hostages and demanded accountability for October 7. Israel's research universities went on strike against the judicial overhaul in 2023. Supporting a war does not mean supporting everything done in its course.And what about the roughly one-fifth of Israeli citizens who are Arab, many among the government's strongest critics? If responsibility follows automatically from an Israeli passport, where do they fit?Citizens in a democracy have a relationship with state power. But they are not the state.Still, democracy is not the whole explanation. Israel occupies a peculiar place in the European imagination. It is not European, but neither does it feel entirely foreign.Much of its early political leadership came from Europe. Its universities, political parties, trade unions, legal traditions, and public culture were deeply influenced by European ideas. The Holocaust sits at the heart of both Israeli political memory and Europe's understanding of its postwar self. Israel participates extensively in European research, culture, trade, and sports.That closeness does not always work in Israel's favor.When many Europeans look at Israel's rule over Palestinians, they see things they recognize from their own history: a powerful state ruling another people, settlements, contested land, and a profound imbalance of power. Much of the language now used to describe Israel comes from Europe's arguments about its past: colonialism, occupation, settler colonialism.Europe spent centuries ruling other peoples, building settlements, drawing borders, and calling domination civilization. Much of postwar Europe was built around the determination not to be that Europe anymore.Israel, therefore, does something unusual. It does not confront Europe only with the Middle East. It confronts Europe with Europe.Perhaps that is part of what makes Israel so difficult for Europeans to discuss. It is familiar enough to be judged by European standards, yet different enough to carry meanings beyond the country itself. Arguments about Israel become arguments about colonialism, nationalism, war, memory, and Europe's own past.The settler-colonial argument takes this further. If the problem is understood not as the policy of one government but as something built into Israeli society itself, the Israeli citizen becomes part of the structure being condemned. The distinction between government and people begins to disappear.THIS DID NOT begin with Gaza. Before October 7, an EU Agency for Fundamental Rights survey found that 75% of Jewish respondents felt people held them responsible for the Israeli government's actions because they were Jewish. The war did not invent this tendency. It intensified it.Government becomes country. Country becomes citizens. Citizens become Jews.Yet democracy should push us in the opposite direction. Elections create responsibility, but they also reveal disagreement. A democracy contains those who voted for the government and those who voted against it, majorities and minorities, supporters and protesters.None of this means Israel should be shielded from criticism. Israeli governments should answer for their decisions. Israeli institutions should be judged for what they do. Israelis who commit crimes should be held responsible.But responsibility should be attached to conduct.That should also guide European decisions about “Horizon Europe,” cultural programs, universities, and artists. If an Israeli institution is complicit in wrongdoing, make the case and act accordingly. If an individual has done something that warrants exclusion, demonstrate it. Nationality itself should not become the evidence.And Israelis cannot demand this distinction only for themselves.Palestinians are not Hamas. Criticism of Israeli policy is not necessarily hostility toward Israel. Hostility toward Israel is not automatically antisemitism. If we insist that Europeans distinguish between Israel and Israelis, we must be equally serious about distinguishing between Palestinians and those who claim to act in their name.Otherwise, this is not a principle. It is simply an argument we use when it suits us.Europe knows how to make these distinctions, imperfectly but deliberately.It should be able to make them with Israel too.The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

title: Palestinian farmers petition High Court over three years of blocked access to West Bank land
body: Six Palestinian farmers have petitioned the High Court of Justice to restore access to agricultural land around Nahalin in the West Bank, saying soldiers and settlers have prevented or severely restricted their work since October 2023 without presenting orders authorizing the restrictions.The Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI), which submitted the petition on their behalf, is seeking an urgent hearing as the olive harvest begins. The farmers say they face a fourth harvest under restrictions that have damaged crops, deprived families of income, and left cultivated land vulnerable to encroachment.The petition, dated Wednesday, targets the IDF commander in the West Bank, the head of the Civil Administration, and the commander of the Israel Police's Judea and Samaria District.Its central argument is the no legal basis for the restrictions has been disclosed. Rather than asking the court to overturn a particular closure order, the farmers say no such order has been shown to them, their lawyers, or local Palestinian authorities despite repeated requests.They describe overlapping obstacles: agricultural roads blocked with earth and stones, soldiers ordering farmers off their plots, settler threats and violence, and a checkpoint where passage allegedly depends on an unexplained list of approved residents.Petition says criteria for inclusion on Etzion checkpoint list left unexplainedAccording to the petition, farmers have been turned back at the Etzion checkpoint since April 2024 because their names were absent from that list. They say neither the criteria for inclusion nor the legal authority for denying passage has been explained, and attempts to add names through Palestinian liaison officials have failed.The land comprises olive groves, vineyards, fruit trees, and seasonal crops around Nahalin, southwest of Bethlehem. Some petitioners claim ownership through family holdings; others cultivate leased land, including property belonging to the Muslim religious trust Wakf.One farmer says he worked a plot for approximately 50 years before worsening harassment and military instructions prevented him from continuing. The petition acknowledges that access varies: Cultivation has stopped on some plots, while farmers continue trying to reach others despite the threat of expulsion or violence.In one incident described in the filing, on June 23, a farmer said settlers brought sheep into his olive grove, damaging trees. He called the police, who he said did not arrive. Soldiers who subsequently reached the site allegedly detained him, threatened him at gunpoint, and ordered him to leave, instead of removing the settlers.The petition also describes a September 14, 2025, visit accompanied by the farmers' lawyer, during which soldiers allegedly claimed a closure order existed but did not produce it.The filing includes photographs and mapped locations of roadblocks and cites affidavits, land records, and police complaints. It lists four written approaches to the authorities between October 2025 and August 2026, which it says received no response.High Court ruling from 2006 says Palestinian farmers should not be kept off landThe legal argument draws on the High Court's 2006 Morar ruling, which held that keeping Palestinian farmers off their land to protect them from attacks was disproportionate. Authorities should provide protection and act against those responsible for the threats. The ruling nevertheless preserved narrowly limited emergency powers to impose temporary closures.ACRI argued that such exceptions cannot justify restrictions continuing for years without a disclosed order. It also said that the damage extends beyond missed harvests: Trees and soil require regular care, and prolonged absence exposes plots to takeover and threatens the farmers' interests in the land.“The state and the army are obligated to protect Palestinian residents, their property and their livelihoods,” ACRI attorney Reut Shaer said in the accompanying statement.The petition asks the court to order the removal of unlawfully placed barriers, ensure access wherever no valid, duly published restriction applies, and instruct troops not to demand prior coordination without legal authority. It also seeks passage through the checkpoint for residents accessing their farmland, a short deadline for the authorities' response, and an urgent hearing.

title: Iran tells Hezbollah to increase readiness, prepare for potential conflict - report
body: The Iranian regime told Hezbollah leaders in Lebanon to be prepared for the United States to resume the war with Iran, following Wednesday's report that Iran currently estimates that "an American attack is only a matter of time," two diplomatic sources told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.Iran's message to Hezbollah, according to the sources, was: "We estimate that an American attack is a matter of time - you should also be prepared."According to Lebanese security and military sources mentioned in a report by the Emirati site Erem News, all full-time Hezbollah members who receive monthly salaries were summoned, although it was emphasized that these directions were only preparations for a near-term scenario and not a final decision to go to war.One prominent change in Hezbollah's strategy, according to the sources, was adopting elements of Iran's "mosaic defense" doctrine, which decentralizes military responsibilities and reduces reliance on a central command hierarchy.A source told Beirut-based independent news outlet Al-Modon earlier this week that Hezbollah is preparing to rearm and rebuild its terror capabilities in the event of an escalation with the IDF amid rising regional tensions."If a large-scale war breaks out, it will reach Lebanon. Israeli is waiting for any opportunity for military escalation against Hezbollah, as it is working to convince Washington of the need to renew the war against Iran. Just as Tehran is anticipating the possibility of war against it, Hezbollah is preparing and equipping itself," the report said.Hezbollah anticipating, preparing for warSources told the outlet that Hezbollah is "anticipating" war and "has succeeded in taking advantage of the extended ceasefire period to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon, both south and north of the Litani River."Sources also linked Hezbollah's rebuilding of militarist terror capabilities to the interception of a truck that was transporting explosive materials from the Bekaa Valley to Beirut.The Jerusalem Post reported on Sunday that the Lebanese Armed Forces seized a truck at a checkpoint in the Bekaa Valley, which was carrying hundreds of kilograms of explosives belonging to the terror group, including TNT and C4.Ziad Hawat, a member of the Lebanese Forces party and the former mayor of Byblos, insisted the state investigate the origins, destination and purpose of the explosives and “if Hezbollah's involvement with the state is proven, the judiciary must expedite the adoption of deterrent legal measures against the party, the arrest of the involved leadership and members, and the banning of all its activities, including political activity.”Defense Minister Katz threatens to seize Lebanese territory in retaliation to aggressionDefense Minister Israel Katz threatened on Wednesday that Israel would seize additional territory in southern Lebanon should Hezbollah launch attacks in coordination with Iran.“If Hezbollah joins Iran in an attack on Israel, it will be dealt a heavy blow and lose additional territory in southern Lebanon, in the areas of Nabatiya and the Litani [River], which will become part of a permanent Israeli security zone – the IDF is prepared to launch a [new expanded] invasion,” Katz said during a visit to the IDF's buffer zone.James Genn, Danielle Greyman-Kennard, and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

title: Strike looms as NLC rejects FG response to 14-day ultimatum
body: …Insists on petrol price cut, tax relief, others By Victor Ahiuma-Young The Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, has rejected the Federal Government’s response to its demands for urgent economic relief and the commencement of negotiations for a new national minimum wage, raising concerns over a possible escalation of industrial tension as its 14-day ultimatum runs its course. The Congress, in a letter to the Minister of Labour and Employment, Dr Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi, faulted the government’s position that negotiations for a fresh minimum wage review would be premature before June 2027, insisting that preparations for a new wage agreement should begin immediately. The NLC in the letter by its President, Joe Ajaero, also insisted on a reduction in petrol prices, the implementation of tax relief measures agreed upon in 2023, immediate wage awards to cushion the rising cost of living, and the implementation of agreements with the Joint Health Sector Unions (JOHESU) and the Joint Public Sector Negotiating Council, JPSNC. Although the NLC in the letter did not expressly declare an imminent strike, sources within the NLC told Vanguard that its rejection of the government’s response to NLC’s ultimatum and insistence on urgent action by government is an indication of a looming industrial confrontation if the dispute remains unresolved before the ultimatum expires. FG response to NLC Ultimatum In the federal government response to the NLC’s communiqué, the minister of Labour and Productivity maintained that the current national minimum wage of N70,000, signed into law on July 29, 2024, would become due for review on June 1, 2027. According to the minister, the law provides for a review of the national minimum wage every three years, making an earlier review premature. “Commencing a fresh review exercise barely two years into the implementation of the current wage, which represented an increase of over 133 per cent from the previous minimum wage of N30,000, would be premature, inconsistent with the law, and disruptive to the orderly industrial relations system envisaged by the Act,” the minister stated. The government also cited its efforts to cushion the effects of economic hardship, including the Presidential Compressed Natural Gas, CNG, Initiative, food security interventions and other social support programmes. It assured the NLC that the Ministry was engaging relevant Ministries, Departments and Agencies, MDAs, to address other demands within the Federal Government’s jurisdiction. The minister noted that the government would convene the National Minimum Wage Tripartite Committee “at the appropriate time” to commence negotiations for the next review. The Federal Government reiterated its commitment to tripartite engagement, decent work and workers’ welfare, while urging the NLC to sustain cooperation in the interest of industrial peace. The minister added that his office remained open to constructive dialogue and appealed for the Congress’s continued understanding and collaboration. NLC rejects govt’s response In its letter dated October 13, 2026, and addressed to the minister, the NLC acknowledged the Ministry’s prompt response to its communiqué but argued that the government’s position failed to address the substance of workers’ grievances. “The Congress notes that, for the first time in recent history, the Ministry has responded with relative speed to our resolutions. We acknowledge this departure from the usual culture of bureaucratic silence,” the letter stated. “However, while we appreciate this prompt acknowledgement, we are constrained to observe that speed without substance may amount to an empty gesture.” The labour centre further argued that the Federal Government’s position was “fundamentally incorrect in law, economics, and social justice.” The dispute centres on the interpretation of the National Minimum Wage Act, 2019, as amended in 2024, and the appropriate time to begin negotiations for a new wage agreement. However, the NLC rejected the government’s interpretation of the law, arguing that the statutory timeline for reviewing the minimum wage should be calculated from the commencement of the 2019 Act. “The National Minimum Wage Act, 2019, which the 2024 Amendment Act amended, was signed into law on 18 April 2019. Under the clear provisions of that Act, a review was statutorily due by 18 April 2024,” the Congress argued. It further maintained that the 2024 amendment did not extinguish the original statutory timeline for wage negotiations. “The 2024 Amendment Act did not abrogate the 2019 Act,” the letter stated. The NLC also claimed that, during negotiations for the 2024 minimum wage, organised labour agreed to a reduction in retrospective arrears following appeals by the Federal Government to reduce the financial burden on government and employers. “This patriotic gesture cannot be construed as a forfeiture of the statutory timeline for implementing the National Minimum Wage,” the Congress said. The labour centre argued that negotiations should commence at least six months before the proposed implementation of a new wage to prevent the accumulation of arrears. “Under this scenario, effective negotiations should commence by 17 October 2026,” it stated. The NLC insisted that it was not demanding the immediate implementation of a new minimum wage but the commencement of the necessary administrative and negotiation processes. “The Government is not being asked to implement a new wage immediately, but to commence the negotiation process,” the letter stated, listing the call for nominations, inauguration of the tripartite committee and setting of the negotiation agenda as preliminary steps. Beyond the legal dispute, the Congress said the economic realities facing workers had eroded the value of the current N70,000 minimum wage, despite the increase from N30,000. The NLC argued that the nominal increase had failed to translate into a corresponding improvement in workers’ purchasing power because of inflation, the depreciation of the naira and rising living costs. “The Federal Government must understand that a wage increase immediately eroded by inflation is not a meaningful improvement in workers’ purchasing power; it is merely a statistical illusion. While the nominal wage increased by 133 per cent, real wages have actually declined ,” the Congress said. The NLC blamed the rising cost of living partly on the government’s macroeconomic policies, particularly the increase in petrol prices, which it said had pushed up the cost of transportation and other essential goods and services. According to the Congress, workers are increasingly unable to afford basic necessities, including food, shelter, healthcare, education and transportation. It also questioned the effectiveness of the CNG initiative, alleging that inadequate infrastructure and shortages of gas supplies and conversion kits had undermined its intended benefits. “Workers cannot feed their families with an initiative that has yet to deliver the promised relief, especially when their children are hungry today,” the letter stated. The Congress consequently called on the government to provide immediate tax relief and wage awards rather than continue to demand sacrifices from workers. On the outstanding demands, the NLC asked the Federal Government to implement tax relief measures agreed upon in 2023 and introduce immediate wage awards to cushion the impact of rising living costs. It also demanded that petrol prices be reduced to the level prevailing when the current national minimum wage was signed into law in 2024. In addition, the Congress called for the implementation of the terms of settlement with JOHESU and the resolution of demands raised by the JPSNC. The labour centre warned that further delays in addressing the issues could worsen workers’ hardship, insisting that the government had the capacity to provide relief if it demonstrated the necessary political will. “Procrastination is no longer a policy choice; it constitutes a direct threat to the survival and well-being of Nigerian workers,” the letter stated. It also cautioned that dialogue without definite timelines and immediate relief measures would amount to rhetoric. “We acknowledge your assurance that your office remains open to dialogue. However, dialogue without concrete timelines and immediate relief measures amounts to mere rhetoric,” the Congress said. The NLC, however, maintained that urgent intervention was necessary to avert further deterioration in the living conditions of Nigerian workers, declaring that it remained “resolute, organised, and uncompromising” in its struggle for a fair and equitable Nigeria. With the two sides holding divergent positions on the timing of the next minimum wage negotiations and the immediate measures required to ease economic hardship, attention is expected to focus on whether further engagement will produce a resolution before the labour centre’s ultimatum expires. The post Strike looms as NLC rejects FG response to 14-day ultimatum appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Flydubai hijacking attempt exposes major gaps in Israel's aviation security, experts warn
body: A bomb scare aboard a Delta Air Lines flight at Ben-Gurion Airport on Tuesday morning prompted a security search that found no explosives, less than two weeks after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv exposed serious questions about Israel's aviation security arrangements.Passengers were evacuated after the Delta flight arrived from New York, and the aircraft was moved to an isolated area for inspection. Authorities found no explosives, and preliminary assessments suggested the anonymous threat might have been a hoax.The September 30 flydubai incident presented a different and potentially more dangerous threat: An airline employee allegedly attempted to turn the aircraft into a weapon.According to prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates, a co-pilot aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 attacked the captain with an emergency axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. Investigators said he intended to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben-Gurion Airport, causing mass casualties.The aircraft plunged thousands of feet before the wounded captain, passengers, and other crew members managed to subdue the attacker. Two additional pilots aboard the flight helped bring the aircraft safely to an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.Brig.-Gen. (res.) Dr. Mena Bacharach, an international aviation security expert and former senior aviation security official with Israel's Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), said the attack demonstrated the need for additional technological safeguards inside aircraft cockpits.Bacharach proposed installing remotely activated, Wi-Fi-based cockpit cameras that would allow authorized personnel on the ground to observe what was happening during an emergency. The cameras would remain off during normal operations and activate only after a distress signal had been triggered, potentially allowing ground personnel to assess a crisis and coordinate a response.Such a system would require careful consideration of operational reliability, secure communications, privacy, and protection against unauthorized access.“A serious problem needs creative solutions, and there is need for a whole range of them,” aviation commentator Aharon Lapidot told The Media Line. “Any solution, especially the technological ones, brings with it a host of new challenges, such as privacy issues and vulnerability to cyberattacks.”The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, had passed professional and security checks before joining flydubai in January. UAE investigators said he had developed extremist views years earlier and had deliberately pursued a career in aviation to carry out an attack inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.The disclosures have intensified scrutiny of how airlines assess their employees and whether existing safeguards adequately address threats originating inside the cockpit.“In professional terms, this is an 'insider threat,' and it forces us to re-examine the fundamental beliefs that aviation security is built on,” Yossi Amrusi, a former senior officer in the Shin Bet security agency and a researcher at the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy, told The Media Line. “It highlights the importance of having additional protection mechanisms in case one of the crew members, not necessarily the pilot, turns out to be a threat.”Security screening must include ground crews, non-pilot flight personnelHe said security screening must extend beyond pilots to include other flight personnel and ground crews responsible for maintaining and servicing aircraft.“This is a major earthquake,” Lapidot told The Media Line. “It opens a whole new perspective and a wide range of possibilities for terrorists to carry out attacks.”UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said on October 9 that the co-pilot's radicalization began in 2017 while he was studying in Australia. Investigators said he had consumed extremist material, adopted beliefs advocating violence, and made preparations for an attack.The suspect had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc before joining flydubai. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal, his employment history included concerns about extremist interests that had affected his prospects at those airlines. Flydubai reportedly did not consult his former employers about those concerns before hiring him.The revelations have raised questions about whether airlines should be required to share more information about employees whose conduct or expressed beliefs have prompted security concerns.“You can check a person's history, his training and his professional abilities, but it is much harder to predict his future intentions,” Amrusi told The Media Line.The incident recalls the March 2015 Germanwings disaster, when co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately flew a passenger aircraft into the French Alps, killing all 150 people aboard.French investigators subsequently found that Lubitz had experienced serious mental health problems and had concealed information about his condition from his employer.Although the Germanwings crash was not a terrorist attack, both incidents demonstrate how dangerous it can be when a person entrusted with operating an aircraft deliberately endangers those aboard.“There are far more terrorists than people with suicidal tendencies who wish to commit suicide while killing other people,” said Lapidot, explaining why the flydubai incident is being viewed as a turning point in the aviation industry.Bacharach said the flydubai incident exposed weaknesses in Israel's aviation security arrangements that had already been highlighted in a 2024 State Comptroller's report.The report called for a comprehensive examination of civil aviation security, including flights departing Israel, Israeli aviation operations abroad, and foreign aircraft entering Israeli airspace. It recommended that the National Security Council work with relevant government and security agencies to reassess responsibilities, oversight, and the allocation of resources.Following the report, the security cabinet ordered an interagency review of security arrangements for international commercial flights to Israel. The National Security Council was tasked with coordinating the work of the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad, and Finance Ministry.According to subsequent Israeli media reporting, disagreements emerged over which agency should bear responsibility for security checks on foreign airlines and whether the Transportation Ministry had the personnel and resources to carry out the task.The ministry ultimately retained responsibility, but reporting following the flydubai attack indicated that important screening requirements had not been consistently enforced.Bacharach said the attempted attack illustrated the need to translate security recommendations into practical safeguards.“Israel spends billions of dollars on security; it shouldn't be left to the hands of a brave pilot, courageous civilians and a miracle to thwart attacks,” said Bacharach. “Someone didn't do their job and fell asleep while on guard.”Omani co-pilot allowed on flight to Israel despite lack of diplomatic relationsOne of the most immediate questions concerned how the Omani co-pilot was allowed to operate a flight to Israel.Oman does not maintain formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Israeli security regulations restrict the participation of crew members holding citizenship in certain countries on flights to Israel, including countries without diplomatic relations.According to an internal security directive reported by Israeli media, foreign airlines were responsible for checking crew members against a list of restricted nationalities. However, the Transportation Ministry had not consistently enforced those requirements or verified crew lists.Following the attempted hijacking, the ministry tightened restrictions on foreign airline crews, barring people holding citizenship in countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel from operating or traveling aboard Israel-bound flights, according to Channel 12.The change has already affected airline operations.Israeli media reported that an Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight traveling from Addis Ababa to Tel Aviv was forced to turn back overnight Sunday after Israeli authorities discovered an Indonesian national among the crew.Indonesia has no diplomatic relations with Israel. According to reports by Channel 12 and The Jerusalem Post, the crew member was a pilot.Channel 13 reported that the crew list was transmitted to Israeli authorities only after the aircraft departed Ethiopia. The plane subsequently resumed its journey after the crew member was replaced.The incident illustrated the operational difficulties of enforcing restrictions when authorities do not receive and check information about flight crews before departure.But Bacharach warned against treating nationality as a sufficient measure of risk.“The problem is not only pilots from hostile countries,” Bacharach told The Media Line. “With the massive migration waves into Europe in recent years, even a pilot from a country that has relations with Israeli could undergo radicalization.”Israel has also established a legal framework to collect and analyze passenger and crew information to help identify potential security threats.A 2023 law provided for the establishment of the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis within the Israel Tax Authority. The legislation authorizes the creation of a database containing passenger and crew information and specifies how authorized agencies may access and use that information.The legal framework is intended to support aviation security, counterterrorism, border control, and other authorized activities. However, the current operational status of the center, and whether it played any role in screening the flydubai crew, has not been established.The attempted attack has raised broader questions about whether existing information systems are adequately integrated with airline screening procedures and whether relevant intelligence reaches officials responsible for approving foreign flight crews.“This isn't just an Israeli problem,” Amrusi said. “An 'insider threat' is relevant to all airlines. A person's nationality isn't necessarily the main motivator once someone has decided to use their position in order to target the plane.”Aviation security has changed significantly since the September 11 attacks, with tighter passenger screening, reinforced cockpit doors, and stricter access controls.Those measures were largely designed to prevent unauthorized individuals from bringing weapons aboard or gaining control of an aircraft.The flydubai incident demonstrates the different challenges posed by an authorized crew member who already has access to the cockpit and the aircraft's controls.“Airlines have to conduct much more thorough and frequent background checks and psychological evaluations,” Lapidot said. “Peer reviews must also be more frequent.”Such measures could help identify concerning behavior, changes in circumstances, or information unavailable during initial hiring.Expanded screening would require clearer guidelines on information sharingBut expanded screening raises questions about privacy, employment rights, the reliability of intelligence, and the possibility of unjustified suspicion based on nationality or personal beliefs.Airlines also operate across numerous jurisdictions, each with different legal requirements governing background checks, professional licensing, and the sharing of security information.Establishing a coordinated approach would require clearer rules governing what information should be exchanged, who may access it, and what action should follow when a potential warning sign is identified.Lapidot warned that additional security requirements would also carry financial consequences.“All of this is going to raise prices for the consumers,” Lapidot added.Amrusi said screening improvements alone would be insufficient because no system can reliably predict every person's future behavior.“We need to be honest though - there is no test that can predict with certainty the malicious intentions of a person,” Amrusi said. “Therefore, we need a system that can handle the situation once a person has managed to evade the testing.”That approach would place greater emphasis on safeguards capable of limiting the damage if an authorized crew member attempts to seize control of an aircraft.Flydubai suspects Tel Aviv flights, Miri Regev declines resumption of serviceThe flydubai incident has already produced operational consequences. The airline suspended its Tel Aviv flights following the attack, and Transportation Minister Miri Regev subsequently declined its request to resume service pending further scrutiny of its security procedures.According to published reports, flydubai has conducted an internal investigation, dismissed several employees, and sought discussions with Israeli authorities about measures needed to restore service.The case has renewed pressure on governments and airlines to reconsider how they identify potential insider threats and how aircraft can be protected when prevention fails.Any new safeguards will have to balance security requirements with the realities of international aviation. Yet the questions raised by the attack extend beyond screening technology or the nationality of individual crew members to the effectiveness of coordination among airlines, regulators, and intelligence agencies.For the passengers aboard flight FZ1073, the existing defenses were insufficient to prevent a violent cockpit attack. Their survival ultimately depended on the wounded captain, other pilots, and passengers who intervened before the aircraft could be brought down.

title: Russia, US can establish joint sports working channel — Trump’s special envoy
body:
WASHINGTON, October 15. /TASS/. Russia and the United States could establish a joint working channel for cooperation in sports, US Special Envoy for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli said in an interview with TASS.
"The first steps should be practical: establish a joint sports working channel, develop the proposed hockey series, explore a FIFA international friendly between our national football teams, restore youth and coaching exchanges, support university competitions, invite retired champions to serve as goodwill ambassadors and create clear pathways for eligible athletes to return under transparent rules," the diplomat within both the White House and the US State Department suggested.
According to him, "[US] President [Donald] Trump believes in peace through strength and in agreements that produce visible results." "Sport offers exactly that kind of opportunity. We do not need to agree on everything before athletes and fans are allowed to meet. Perhaps sooner rather than later, the first whistle on a football pitch can begin a new conversation. Sometimes the handshake after the match is what makes the next diplomatic step possible," the US leader’s special envoy emphasized.
The full text of the interview is available on the TASS website: https://tass.com/world/2202537 .

title: Kamala Harris criticizes Biden administration's failure to curb Israel's conduct during Gaza war
body: Former US vice president Kamala Harris criticized former US president Joe Biden's administration's response to Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza during the 2026 Asan Memorial Lecture in Seoul on Wednesday.Harris said that the United States needed to uphold its obligation to international law and that the Biden administration's response to Israel's war was a failure in that regard.The former vice president called out the "failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government's horrific conduct in the war in Gaza," saying that the Biden administration should have acted "sooner and more fully."Harris also criticized the current US government under US President Donald Trump, saying that it "offers Netanyahu a blank check."She also discussed the modern development of American foreign policy, saying that the "orthodoxies of old" were insufficient for current challenges.“Coming out of world wars, and into the Cold War, military might was the primary source of power,” she said. “But now more than ever, economic innovation, markets and minerals, chips and computers, have greater influence.”Kamala Harris plays coy on 2028 presidential runShe also said US relations and alliances must be strengthened. “The growing relationship between, for example, China and Russia and Iran and North Korea is something we have to pay attention to, and it should be the reason that within our alliance that we are committed to strengthening what must, without any question, happen in terms of deterrence," she said.Harris also expressed confidence that Democrats will win the upcoming US midterm election, though she avoided directly answering whether she was considering a 2028 presidential run. "2028, from my perspective, doesn't matter if we don't win 2026."

title: Petrol price cut: Filling stations shut in Kebbi
body: By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi The reduction in petrol pump price announced by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) has been followed by the closure of several filling stations in Birnin Kebbi, leaving motorists and commuters struggling to access the product. A survey by our correspondent revealed that a day after the NNPC announced a N66 reduction in the price of petrol, several filling stations in the Kebbi State capital had shut their gates, with motorists facing difficulties buying the product. The development reportedly followed decisions by some independent marketers to suspend sales, leaving many residents without easy access to petrol. The closure also reduced vehicular movement on major roads in the state capital, as some motorists stayed off the roads amid high fuel prices and limited availability. A filling station manager, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said his station had petrol in stock but was directed by his employer to suspend sales. According to him, the product in stock was purchased at a higher price, making it difficult for the station to sell at the newly announced lower rate without incurring losses. A civil servant in the state, Aminu Muhammed, lamented that the scarcity had disrupted workers’ daily activities, with some staying at home and commercial drivers parking their vehicles because of the high cost and unavailability of petrol. Some kabu-kabu operators, who provide informal commercial transport services, also expressed frustration over the situation. They said the price reduction had not eased their difficulties, alleging that some stations that opened for sales charged as much as N1,500 per litre after motorists had waited for hours in long queues. The situation has left residents grappling with limited access to petrol despite the announced price reduction. The post Petrol price cut: Filling stations shut in Kebbi appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Europe shuts US out of Russian assets conversation
body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Multiple EU leaders on Oct. 15 firmly rebuffed the idea that the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of immobilized Russian assets held in the bloc would be handed to the U.S. as a bargaining chip in peace talks.
The idea was floated by U.S. officials when they met with European counterparts on Oct. 9, and was first reported on the next day by the New York Times.
The proposal surfaced in the media again as EU leaders meet for a two-day summit in Brussels, where several countries are set to raise the issue of using Russian assets to support Ukraine.
"It cannot be viewed positively in any way. Absolutely not," said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, in response to questions from journalists.
"These are frozen Russian assets held in Europe, belonging to Russians who are destroying Ukraine and killing people there every day... the idea of releasing these assets is completely out of the question," Orpo said.
"On the contrary, a proposal will be put forward today to continue exploring ways to ensure that these frozen assets are used to support Ukraine," he added.
Likewise, Austrian Prime Minister Christian Stocker said he is "not convinced of the idea of imprisoning these assets under U.S. control in view of the volatility in U.S. policy and how quickly things are changing there."
"The assets are frozen in Europe, and they shall remain frozen in Europe. That is a matter for us, and we will decide it," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters.
"All these things that they (Russia) are interested in, the frozen assets, the lifting of sanctions, it is up to Europeans to decide," said the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas.
The EU's draft conclusions for the summit were also updated on Oct. 14 to say that leaders "will revert to the issue (of financing Ukraine) in a timely manner," supporting Orpo's comment that the bloc will continue working on possible ways to use Russia's immobilized assets to support Ukraine.
Even if some EU leaders might have supported placing Russian assets under U.S. jurisdiction — and none have said so — the idea was a non-starter, given that the bloc would need unanimous agreement.
The chances of that happening have never been slimmer, after recent U.S. moves against Ukraine have provoked widespread condemnation from European leaders.

title: Trump’s envoy says Russian athletes’ participation in international contests important
body:
WASHINGTON, October 15. /TASS/. US Special Envoy for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli said the participation of Russian athletes in international competitions was important for the Americans.
"American and Russian athletes have elevated one another for generations. Real competition creates respect, and respect is one of the few diplomatic currencies that never loses value," Trump’s special envoy noted in an interview with TASS.
According to him, "the best champions want to beat the best." "When major athletes are absent for reasons unrelated to their individual conduct, the competition loses something and the public knows it. That does not take away the medals earned by American athletes, who compete under the rules placed before them, but the greatest victories are the ones achieved against the strongest possible field," the diplomat within both the White House and the US Department of State said.
The full text of the interview is available on the TASS website: https://tass.com/world/2202537 .

title: Nigeria’s fiscal crisis forced us to be creative, look beyond oil revenues – Cardoso
body:
Olayemi Cardoso, the governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria , said on Thursday that Nigeria’s fiscal crisis forced the monetary and fiscal authorities to be creative in revenue generation and stabilisation efforts.
Mr Cardoso spoke on Thursday while featuring on a high-level panel themed “Debate on the Global Economy: Forging Resilient and Dynamic Economies for the Future”, held on the sidelines of the World Bank/IMF meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
Moderated by Lisa Abramowicz, co-host of “Bloomberg Surveillance”, the debate was put together to explore how countries can build resilient and dynamic economies in an increasingly fragmented and uneven global landscape, using resilience as the common thread across the three segments.
Speaking on the panel, Mr Cardoso said the fiscal reality of the Nigerian state when the new administration came into power forced policy makers to be creative in their solution ideas.
“When you are going through a crisis, it forces you to be creative,” Mr Cardoso said.
Nigeria’s gross external reserves stand at $55.1 billion, with net foreign reserves at about $46 billion, according to recent updates from the Central Bank of Nigeria, amid relative stability in the foreign exchange market.
The CBN governor explained that the government inherited a situation where external reserves dropped to about $3 billion and the nation was owing about $7 billion in sundry obligations.
The orthodox monetary policy helped to pay the debt and stabilise the economy, Mr Cardoso said, adding that it was clear to the CBN that reliance on oil revenue was not a sustainable model.
“We had to be creative as to how we diversify,” he said, adding that the apex bank looked at the diaspora and international remittances to remove all the bottlenecks and ease capital flow.
Mr Cardoso said the CBN embraced how to do things differently, and changed from ways that were not sustainable, as part of measures needed to create value.
“It seemed impossible to everybody and people laughed,” he said of the degree of scepticism the CBN leadership faced, adding that the policy decisions paid off.
The Central Bank Governor added that the nation is now looking in the direction of value addition, while making reference to the Dangote Refinery and its potential contributions to growth and foreign exchange stability.
Participants looked at how economies, firms, and institutions can preserve stability and withstand recurrent shocks despite more limited policy space, how they can sustain balanced growth amid widening global divergences, and how they can harness AI, innovation, and productivity-enhancing reforms to expand opportunity and growth.
The debate featured Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kyriakos Pierrakakis, the Minister of Economy and Finance of the Hellenic Republic, and other experts.
Oladeinde Olawoyin reports Business & Economy, Development and Lagos Metro at PREMIUM TIMES. A First Class graduate of Mass Communication from the University of Ilorin, Ilorin, he was nominated in the journalism category of The Future Awards Africa in 2017. Aside maintaining a column titled ‘SATURDAY SATIRE’, he also writes art and culture pieces on weekends. Twitter : @Ola_deinde

title: AI could deepen rural-urban inequality without better connectivity – Sam George
body: The Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Sam George, has warned that Ghana’s adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) could deepen existing inequalities between rural and urban communities unless deliberate investments are made to improve digital connectivity across the country. He says while AI presents enormous opportunities for economic growth, education and improved public services, communities without reliable internet access risk being left behind as the country embraces the technology. Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology & Innovations, Sam George. “If we do not take specific steps to avoid it, I’ve always said AI will not just mean artificial intelligence, it will mean advancing inequalities,” he cautioned. Speaking in an interview ahead of the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, the minister said the government recognises the danger and is considering measures to ensure that the benefits of AI are not concentrated in major cities. “As a ministry, we’re very minded about that. It’s part of the reason why for me, again, I’m pitching to cabinet that we should have a phase three of the rural telephony project. And I’m not looking to just roll out new sites,” he explained. Mr. George disclosed that Ghana has nearly 3,000 rural telephony sites operating largely on older 2G and 3G technologies, which he believes are inadequate to support the level of digital participation required in an AI-driven economy. He is therefore proposing an upgrade of existing rural telecommunications infrastructure to provide faster internet connectivity rather than focusing exclusively on expanding the number of sites. “What I’m looking to do is to upgrade all the existing sites. Then they need to be able to use 4G and 5G technology because that’s where you can stream. That’s where you can learn using 4G and 5G,” he explained. The minister argued that without such investments, rural communities could remain disadvantaged in accessing digital education, developing technological skills and participating in emerging economic opportunities. “So we want to do an upgrade of our existing infrastructure to be able to make sure that even our rural telephony sites, just like our main urban and peri-urban networks, provide 4G and soon 5G services,” he added. The proposal is currently being pitched to Cabinet as part of a possible third phase of the rural telephony project. Lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic The sector minister pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic as evidence of how unequal access to technology can disadvantage children in underserved communities. He recalled that when schools closed and teaching moved online, many children in rural Ghana were unable to continue learning because they lacked the necessary digital access. “We saw what happened during COVID, when the country shut down and kids in remote areas could not go online,” he said. The Ningo-Prampram MP noted that children in major cities, including Accra, Kumasi and Takoradi, had greater opportunities to participate in online learning, while their counterparts in remote communities faced significant disruptions. The minister believes Ghana must avoid repeating this experience as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly important in education and other aspects of everyday life. Ghana’s national AI strategy identifies education, healthcare, agriculture and government services as priority areas for the adoption of the technology. The communications minister explained that better connectivity could allow rural communities to benefit from AI-supported learning, improved agricultural services and remote healthcare delivery. He cited the possibility of using community information centres and 5G connectivity to connect patients in underserved areas with medical professionals based in regional hospitals. “With 5G, I should be able to do telemedicine with a midwife in there or a nurse in there taking the vitals and getting services of a doctor in a community where there’s no doctor,” he said. Equal opportunities for rural communities Beyond education and healthcare, the minister said rural communities must also be supported to participate in the growing digital economy. He rejected the notion that technological innovation and digital content creation are activities limited to urban centres, insisting that young people in rural Ghana are already engaging with digital platforms and should have access to the same opportunities. “We can also have that in our rural communities because don’t get it twisted. There’s a lot of content creation going on in our rural communities today. The kids are on TikTok and they need to get the same opportunities that those in our urban areas get,” he indicated. For the minister, expanding connectivity is therefore not simply about providing faster internet services. It is also about ensuring that where a Ghanaian lives does not determine their ability to benefit from technological advancement. Despite the challenges, Mr George remains optimistic that deliberate investment in digital infrastructure and the successful implementation of Ghana’s AI strategy could ensure that communities across the country benefit from the technology. He says his ultimate ambition is to build a digital economy in which technology improves the lives of all Ghanaians, irrespective of their location. “I want to leave this ministry with a legacy that we’ve left a digitally inclusive and data-driven economy. That, for me, is the focus,” he said. The question of whether AI will create opportunities for all Ghanaians or deepen existing inequalities will feature in the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, under the theme “AI and the Ghana Economy: Opportunity or Disruption?” The forum, held in partnership with Hubtel , will feature Sam George; Technical Advisor at the Finance Ministry, Dr Theo Acheampong; Founder of AI for Ghana, Adam Watkins; Head of Engineering at Hubtel, Augustine Adjei; and Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons. It will air live on JoyNews and Joy 99.7 FM on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8 p.m.

title: Full list: 45 countries Nigerians can visit without visa as passport climbs 92nd globally
body: Nigerian passport holders can access 45 countries without obtaining a visa before travelling, according to reports on the latest Henley Passport Index, which places Nigeria 92nd in its October 2026 global ranking.
