title: What are Saudi Arabia's options to deter the Yemeni rebels?
body: Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar problem in Yemen: having the military resources to strike the Iran-backed Houthis hard, but no guarantee that a campaign will stop the heavily armed militant group from threatening the kingdom again. The latest wave of missile and drone attacks has brought that dilemma into sharper focus, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi airports and threatening critical energy infrastructure, including Saudi Aramco ’s headquarters in Dhahran. While Saudi Arabia ’s challenge is restoring deterrence, analysts say Riyadh’s options are narrow. They include intensifying air strikes, bolstering Yemeni government forces on the ground, strengthening air defences and seeking renewed diplomatic engagement. “Saudi Arabia should apply military pressure on the Houthis inside Yemen to deter further attacks,” Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre, told The National . “A key priority is to limit their ability to launch cross-border attacks, particularly by degrading their missile capabilities.” Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to escalate in July, when an air strike hit Sanaa International Airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia. Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government claimed responsibility, saying it had hit the runway to prevent an unauthorised Iranian aircraft from landing. The strike tested a fragile period of calm that had largely held since a truce took effect in 2022. The Houthis subsequently launched missiles towards Saudi Arabia, while fighting between the group and Yemeni forces intensified. Mr Sager said that the kingdom had accepted the principle of a ceasefire with the Houthis and remained committed to de-escalation. “However, renewed military pressure may be necessary before agreeing to another ceasefire, to secure credible commitments that attacks will stop,” he added. The Houthis have been fighting the Yemeni government since seizing Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 at the head of a coalition of regional allies to support the government against the rebels. Beyond air power Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s largest military budgets and a sophisticated arsenal, including American warplanes, missile-defence systems and other advanced weapons. However, Aziz Algashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said defeating the Houthis militarily would require more than air power. The kingdom has demonstrated its ability to conduct air operations, but he explained that a successful campaign would also require effective ground forces capable of changing the balance of power in Houthi-held territory. Maritime forces would be needed to restrict the movement of supplies reaching the group through the Red Sea and from the Horn of Africa, he added. That combination could be difficult to assemble. Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis have improved their capabilities, but continue to face problems of competence and political fragmentation. “The reason why the Houthis may hold what they have is not because of their strength, but really the weakness of the other ground operation,” said Mr Algashian. “A state-building approach would also be needed.” The Houthis, once regarded as a relatively poorly equipped militia, have developed into a formidable fighting force. Their arsenal includes missiles and drones that can strike targets more than 1,000 miles away. Since the war in Gaza erupted in 2023, the group has launched hundreds of drones and missiles towards Israel . Most were intercepted, but some reached their targets, including a drone strike in Tel Aviv that killed a man in 2024 and a missile strike near Ben Gurion Airport last year. The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Washington and Tehran have not yet reached a lasting peace agreement . In recent weeks, they have exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy shipments, but negotiations have not resumed. Some observers argue that a broader agreement between the US and Iran offers the most viable path to ending Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Under such a deal, the US could seek Iranian commitments to rein in the Houthis and secure an end to their attacks as part of a wider regional settlement. But whether the group would comply with such an arrangement is not known. US assistance The US supports Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthis through arms sales, military advisers, intelligence sharing and targeting assistance, though it has avoided direct military combat operations. President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining strikes against the Houthis, as the rebels attack a US ally and threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have warned that any US strikes could prompt them to attack American personnel and interests across the Middle East, potentially drawing the US deeper into the wider war. But a senior US official has told The National that the Trump administration has “no announcements to make regarding US support for new military operations” in Yemen. The official added that the administration remains in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. “We will always fulfil our commitments to our partners." Mr Algashian believes American firepower could deter the Houthis, at least initially. But he cautioned that the rebels may be prepared to absorb the strikes and wait for US resolve to weaken. “The Houthis feel they will try to weather the storm. Their calculation seems to be that they have withstood many storms before,” he added. “The Saudis still need their allies and still need to focus on alliances for defence.” Mr Trump ordered a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but declared a swift victory after the US expended weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone. “Saudi Arabia should also mobilise the international community to respond to this aggression against the kingdom. Strengthening Saudi defensive capabilities and securing support from regional and international partners are essential to protecting its territory and deterring further attacks,” affirmed Mr Sager.

title: Military cleared over September air traffic meltdown
body: The disruption to air traffic on 8 September was caused by a software defect in the National Airspace System flight data processing software, and not by incorrect actions by military or civil operators, according to an answer given in Parliament. Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what assessment had been made of the impact of military flight plan data entry on the NATS flight processing system that day. Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government has been clear that the disruption caused to passengers and industry was completely unacceptable. Following the incident, NATS was instructed to undertake a rapid investigation, and the Civil Aviation Authority has been commissioned to conduct an independent review of the findings and wider resilience arrangements. “NATS’ investigation into the incident concluded that the disruption was caused by a software defect within the National Airspace System flight data processing software. NATS has stated that the incident was not caused by any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators. “The Government will continue to work with NATS, the Civil Aviation Authority, airports, airlines and other stakeholders to ensure lessons are learned and that any necessary improvements are implemented to strengthen the resilience of the UK’s air traffic management systems.” Obese-Jecty had asked specifically about the entry of military flight plan data into the NATS system, and the department ruled that out as a cause. The post Military cleared over September air traffic meltdown first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
body: The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries. The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO , within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command . This will enable “risk assessment of military service members who are exposed to blunt impacts resulting from acceleration of the body, blunt injury from a ballistic strike to the helmet, or effects from blast pressure produced by a weapon system or explosion,” the RFI reads. BIRCO is seeking a variety of information that can help formulate standards for assessing mild traumatic brain injuries, or mTBI. The information could include existing criteria, standards and models for brain injuries, as well as identifying experts on the topic. The Pentagon is also seeking input from manufacturers of protective gear that can be “highly relevant to understanding human tolerance limits and predicting blast injuries.” The RFI uses a broad definition of blast injuries, including the effects on the body of blast-wave overpressure, fragments, the human body being thrown against hard objects, collapsing buildings and burns, as well as the effects of toxic gases and radiation. “The standards can range from simple dose response curves and injury thresholds that address single components of blast insults, such as blast pressure wave magnitude, or address multiple components of blast insults, such as pressure magnitude over time,” the RFI said. These standards will be used for “health hazard assessments, survivability assessments, and protection system development aimed at producing safe weapon systems, survivable combat platforms, and effective protection systems.” The effects of traumatic brain injuries on military personnel have become better known in recent years. There is evidence that exposure to the blast of firing artillery, tank guns and handheld missiles , as well as being thrown around while riding small boats used by special operations forces, leads to brain trauma, or even TBI. Department of Defense data from the Iran war shows a relatively high proportion of head trauma from Iranian missile and drone strikes. The RFI was published after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide baseline cognitive assessments to troops. Across the services, the Defense Department is hampered by staff shortages and a lack of technology needed to conduct the assessments, the GAO found. The Pentagon announced in April that it will begin a one-year pilot program to test a new cognitive assessment tool, an app that service members can use to complete assessments. DoD officials said the app will be less resource-intensive than current assessments and will help improve the services’ ability to track exposures. Veterans who have suffered traumatic brain injuries are more than twice as likely to die by suicide, according to a 2019 study .

title: The global water conversation is changing – now the UAE and the world must act
body: One of the defining characteristics of UN conferences is the opportunity to bring together perspectives and stakeholders whose paths might otherwise rarely cross. During the high-level week at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, I engaged to technology leaders on artificial intelligence, investors on infrastructure, policymakers on climate resilience, business leaders on opportunity, and researchers and development institutions on sustainable development. These conversations reflected different priorities, yet increasingly converged around a common question: how can we build a future that is more resilient, more prosperous and better equipped to withstand disruption? Time and again, the conversation came back to water. This was not simply a matter of increased attention to water as a standalone issue. Rather, it reflected a growing recognition of its fundamental role in addressing the interconnected challenges facing communities, countries and economies. Food security depends on water . The energy transformation depends on water. Economic strength depends on water. And thriving communities require reliable access to safe water. For many years, those working to advance the global water agenda have emphasised the importance of integrating water into discussions on climate, food, energy, infrastructure, economic growth and development. Increasingly, however, water is being recognised as an integral part of these discussions in its own right. This shift reflects an important evolution in how the international community understands the relationship between water and sustainable development. We are increasingly recognising water not only as a resource we need to conserve, but also as a strategic asset we need to invest in – one that underpins resilience, enables opportunity and supports long-term prosperity. The scale of the challenge is clear. Agriculture accounts for about 70 per cent of global freshwater withdrawals, while millions of livelihoods depend on water-intensive sectors. When water becomes unreliable, the consequences extend well beyond the water sector, affecting food prices, employment, businesses, communities and investment. Yet the human impact is even more significant. When water is scarce or unsafe, women and girls often carry a disproportionate burden. Globally, women and girls are responsible for fetching water in more than 70 per cent of households. Instead of receiving an education, learning a new skill or joining the workforce, women and girls are collectively spending 200 to 250 million hours every single day collecting and hauling water. Water security is fundamentally about people. It is about peace, stability and human dignity. When water systems are disrupted, livelihoods are disrupted. When scarcity puts pressure on communities, resilience is tested. And when countries share rivers, aquifers and water systems, co-operation becomes essential . Water can be a source of pressure. But it can also be a reason to co-operate and collaborate. That matters even more at a time when faith in international co-operation is under increasing pressure. We are living through a period of profound global change, when trust between countries and confidence in multilateral institutions cannot be taken for granted. Yet there are challenges that no country can solve alone – and water is one of them. Every country depends on water, every economy depends on it, and every family needs it. We have spent years talking about climate, energy, food, technology and water as separate agendas. But those boundaries are disappearing That gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that international co-operation can still deliver something tangible: solutions that improve lives, strengthen resilience and create opportunity. Here in the UAE, we understand this connection particularly well. We live in one of the world’s most water-scarce regions . For us, water has shaped how we think about our cities, our economy and our future. This understanding also informs our approach to international co-operation. At Cop28, hosted by the UAE in 2023, the adoption of the historic UAE Consensus by 198 Parties demonstrated the importance of collective action in addressing interconnected climate challenges. It reinforced the need to advance climate ambition through practical solutions, international co-operation and implementation. Beyond that event, we have spent years talking about climate, energy, food, technology and water as separate agendas. But now those boundaries are disappearing. Climate change is intensifying droughts, floods and water variability around the world. Extreme weather is placing greater pressure on economies, infrastructure and communities. At the same time, the world is rapidly electrifying, investing in new technologies, expanding digital infrastructure and seeking pathways to sustainable growth. Water systems require energy. Energy systems require water. Food production depends on both. And the rapid growth of AI and digital infrastructure is creating a new set of demands on these interconnected systems. This is why we recently launched the Crosscurrents Report , examining the growing relationship between AI, water and energy. The report highlights a dual challenge. As digital infrastructure expands, its demand for energy and water will grow. But there is another side to the story: AI is also helping us manage water better – from detecting leaks and improving irrigation to forecasting drought, optimising infrastructure and strengthening decision-making. The significance of this extends beyond AI itself. It points to a broader truth: the systems that underpin our economies can no longer be planned in isolation. Decisions about energy affect water. Decisions about water influence food production , industry, communities and economic growth. Climate adaptation affects all of them. The future will not be built by solving one issue at a time. It will depend on how effectively we understand these connections and plan for them together. What gave me optimism during our discussions in New York was the scale of the coalition engaging with these challenges and opportunities. The most encouraging discussions were not confined to governments or traditional water stakeholders – instead, they involved investors, technology companies, financial institutions, entrepreneurs, researchers, young leaders and development organisations. There is growing recognition that resilience is a shared responsibility. But awareness alone will not close the gap. We know many of the solutions. We have better technologies , better data and better tools than we did a decade ago. We know more about reuse, storage, loss reduction and efficient desalination. The challenge is getting those solutions out of the pilot phase – to translate ideas into impact. How do we connect capital to projects? Innovation to deployment? Technology to communities? And international commitments to action on the ground? These are the questions I heard often in New York . And they are the questions that will matter most at the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi in December. The conference, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal, will bring these conversations together. The event will hold special significance as the first UN Water Conference to be co-hosted by two nations from the Global South, reflecting their role as active partners in shaping solutions and driving international action on water. It is also the first UN conference focused on accelerating the implementation of SDG 6, which addresses clean water and sanitation services. Our ambition is to build momentum around investment, international co-operation, innovation and implementation – and to keep that momentum going long after December. That means bringing governments together with investors, development institutions with the private sector, technology companies with communities, researchers with policymakers. And, critically, giving youth a seat at the table – not simply asking them to listen to the decisions of today, but empowering them to help shape the solutions of tomorrow. We understand that the future of water will not be solved by one government, one institution nor one technology – it will be solved by what we do together. The strongest lesson I took away from the General Assembly last month was that for the first time the global conversation is truly changing. Water is moving from the margins to the centre – of economic planning, climate and humanitarian resilience, sustainable development, technology, food and energy transformations, and international co-operation. At a time when global confidence in international co-operation is being tested, water gives us a practical opportunity to prove what it can achieve. If we get water right, the benefits will be boundless – healthier communities, greater opportunity for women and girls, stronger economies, more resilient food and energy systems, stronger digital infrastructure, and greater peace and stability. The conversation has shifted. Now, the water conference will turn that momentum into action. Together, we invite everyone, no matter where they may be in the world, to join us in reimagining water’s role in creating a better future for all, driving co-operation, growth, resilience and opportunity.

title: Ukraine’s hobbit-named robot fired on targets up to 1.3 km away in a demo for border guards
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s six-wheeled Frodo ground robot fired on targets during a demonstration in Kharkiv Oblast for the Pomsta (Revenge) Border Guard Brigade, a border guard detachment posted on Facebook. Frodo made its public debut only on 30 September. Ukraine had contracted more than 22,000 ground robots for 2026 by July, mostly logistics carriers, with combat models the smallest group, the Defense Ministry said . Frodo’s first reported mission was an evacuation . The demo shows its armed version to a fighting brigade, the kind of robot Ukraine has ordered least. What the armed version carries The platform completed its tasks at a training ground in near-combat conditions, said the 3rd Border Guard Detachment named after Hero of Ukraine Colonel Yevhenii Pikus. The Buria turret mounted on Frodo can fire either a Mk 19 automatic grenade launcher or a Browning M2 heavy machine gun. It engaged targets at up to 1.3 km (0.8 mile), the detachment said. Frodo ground robotic vehicle (UGV). Screenshot from a video by the 3rd Border Guard Unit The 47-kg (104-lb) module has a ballistic calculator, stores up to 256 targets, aims in three seconds, and has a stated autonomous run time of up to 48 hours, the post said. Frodo is rated for up to 150 km (93 miles) on paved roads and 75–80 km (47–50 miles) over rough terrain, the post added. A Frontline Robotics Zoom reconnaissance drone flew reconnaissance during the test. The developer, Frontline Robotics, describes its core philosophy as arriving fast, doing the job, and leaving very fast—hit and run, the detachment’s post said. Familiarizing the brigade’s soldiers with such systems aims first and foremost to preserve personnel’s lives and health, the detachment said. A robot first reported as a medevac Frontline Robotics told Militarnyi at the unveiling that Frodo had passed Defense Ministry codification and was built for logistics, evacuation, and strike missions. The robot reaches 40 km/h (25 mph) and carries up to 200 kg (441 lb) of payload, or 400 kg (882 lb) at most, the company said . A single soldier can swap its batteries. Frodo ground robotic vehicle (UGV). Photo: Frontline Robotics The 92nd Assault Brigade used an early test unit to evacuate a wounded soldier, Frontline Robotics told Militarnyi. An operator, callsign Tango, named the robot’s speed and its ability to handle complex maneuvers as its main advantages, Militarnyi reported. title: Corps Member Death: Senate To Probe State Of Health Facilities At NYSC Camps Nationwide
body: The Senate has ordered a holistic investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of an NYSC Corps member, Etimbuk Daniel, who died at the NYSC Orientation camp in Enugu State, as well as the state of health infrastructure in NYSC camps across the country. The probe will be carried out by the Senate Committees on Police Affairs, Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters, Ethics, Code of Conduct and Public Petitions, Youth Development and Health, in conjunction with the Nigeria Police Force and the Department of State Services (DSS). The resolution followed a motion of urgent public importance on the urgent need for a review of medical services in NYSC camps nationwide, sponsored by Sen. Aniekan Bassey. Lawmakers noted with concern the sudden and untimely passing of the corps member, describing him as a vibrant, patriotic young Nigerian and a shining light of his community who had only set out to serve the country. Lawmakers expressed concern over reports indicating that Daniel died from complications arising from a minor headache after allegedly experiencing a delay in obtaining timely and adequate medical attention at the camp clinic. The Upper Chamber further expressed worry that the incident is not isolated, but highlights a recurring pattern of systemic negligence, poor medical infrastructure, and absence of qualified emergency personnel and rapid referral protocols across NYSC camps, underlining that the government owes a duty of care to young graduates mobilized away from their homes to serve the nation. The Senate thereafter observed a minute of silence in honour of the late Corps member. The post Corps Member Death: Senate To Probe State Of Health Facilities At NYSC Camps Nationwide appeared first on Channels Television .

title: One of six inmates who escaped from Konongo police cells rearrested
body: One of the six inmates who escaped from the Konongo Police cells in the Asante Akyem Central Municipality of the Ashanti Region has been rearrested, while efforts continue to track down the remaining five who are at large. The escapees reportedly escaped through a hole believed to have been dug toward the station’s detached washrooms, then jumped down and fled. Police immediately launched a manhunt following the incident, leading to the arrest of one of the escapees in a suburb of Kumasi. Efforts are ongoing to apprehend the remaining five. Asante Akyem Central Municipal Chief Executive, Dr Ebenezer Ekow Aidoo, who confirmed the incident to Accra-based Citi News, said the Municipal Security Council was taking measures to strengthen security at the facility. He said plans were underway to reinforce the walls of the police cells to prevent similar incidents. Dr Aidoo also outlined longer-term measures, including the construction of a new police station and increasing the number of police officers deployed to the area, particularly during the night. Additional security measures will include improving lighting at the station and installing surveillance cameras to help monitor activities and prevent future escapes.

title: EU afraid Russia, US might resolve Ukrainian conflict on their own — Russian envoy
body:
VIENNA, October 15. /TASS/. European nations are concerned that Moscow and Washington could resolve the Ukrainian conflict without their involvement, Russia’s Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) Dmitry Polyansky said.
"Over the past week, the most acute phobia of our European neighbors has once again become particularly evident: the fear of a scenario in which Russia and the US - without them - might reach a long-term and sustainable solution to the Ukrainian conflict," he said at a meeting of the OSCE Permanent Council.
The diplomat noted that US President Donald Trump had previously come to the clear conclusion that Vladimir Zelensky is not interested in peace and is simply doing all he can to retain his grip on power in the country. In Europe, however, there have been "attempts to prove his commitment to peace, while simultaneously reaffirming an unwavering stance toward confrontation with Russia."
"One cannot help but notice that whenever signs of a respectful and mutually beneficial dialogue emerge between Russia and the US, and as soon as the untouchability and infallibility of the leader in Kiev are called into question, European states invariably panic and take steps aimed at derailing that process," Polyansky stated.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 17, injure 67 across Ukraine, as drone waves wreak havoc in central, western oblasts
body:
At least 10 people were killed and 66 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as hundreds of Russian drones struck targets across the full width of the country, regional authorities said on Oct. 15.
Kirovohrad Oblast experienced the most massive attack the oblast has seen since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion overnight, as Russia killed three people and injured six others, said regional governor Andrii Raikovych . The casualties are the result of Russian attacks on Kropyvnytskyi, he added.
Russia struck critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities, and residential buildings with almost 360 drones across 26 locations, Raikovych said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated the attacks, having received a relaxation of sanctions and seeing attempts to put pressure on Ukraine. Russia uses every such moment and must be responsible for what it does," President Volodymyr Zelensky said, referring to the attack.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight from 06:00 p.m. with 580 Shahed-type and other drones, as well as with two Kh-59 guided aircraft missiles. The Air Force said it neutralized 536 of the Russian drones across 31 locations.
Zelensky said that Russia used a total of 850 Shahed-type drones during the day since 09:00 a.m. on Oct. 14.
"There were constant waves, and our sky was not clear of them for a single hour," he said.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, killed three people and injured three more, authorities said. Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported two people died in Novooleksandrivka and two others injured. A third person was injured in a Russian strike on a private house in Pavlohrad, Hanzha added. Zelensky raised the number of people killed in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast to three.
In western Volyn Oblast , wreckage of a Russian drone fell on the city of Lutsk , killing six people and injuring 12 others, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. A large-scale fire broke out in the 'Eurogroup' warehouse as a result of the Russian attack, killing five people at the scene, and injuring a sixth person so heavily they succumbed in hospital, Romaniuk said.
In Rivne Oblast , a Russian drone crashed into the city during the day on Oct. 14, injuring eight people, including a child born in 2012, according to regional governor Oleksandr Koval . The oblast also experienced several attack waves overnight, but no people were injured, he said .
In Kyiv Oblast , Russian attacks over the past day injured four people across Bucha, Obukhiv, and Fastiv districts, the regional military administration said. In total, Russia struck across 26 locations in the oblast, damaging private houses, infrastructure, warehouses, and cars.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , three people were killed and eight others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin .
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks injured nine people, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. The explosion of an unknown object in the village of Spodobivka also killed one man and injured a 15-year-old boy, the governor added. Russian attacks damaged private and commercial buildings, as well as parts of the power grid, Syniehubov said.
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person and injured five other people over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Many settlements in the oblast, including the city of Kherson, were under Russian artillery, drone, and air attacks throughout the day, he added.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , seven people were injured as Russia attacked over the past day, with almost 200 artillery strikes, 734 drones of varying types, and two missiles, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov .
A Russian attack on Ternopil Oblast injured five people, as a Russian drone struck a manufacturing enterprise in Chortkiv, according to regional governor Taras Pastukh and Ukraine's interior ministry .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , Russian attacks did not lead to casualties or injuries but damaged a numer of private houses and civil infrastructure, as the air raid alert lasted for more than 18 combined hours, the Sumy military administration said.

title: How Toluwanisings died – Singer’s PA
body:
Babadunni Gbolabo, the personal assistant (PA) to late gospel singer Olayemi “Toluwanisings” Bolaji, has revealed that efforts to save the singer’s life took them to between seven and eight hospitals.
The revelation offers further details about the singer’s final hours after his family confirmed his death on Wednesday.
PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the singer’s family didn’t state the cause of death or explain the circumstances surrounding it.
Speaking to the BBC at the late singer’s residence in Alakia, Ibadan, Oyo State, on Thursday, Mr Gbolabo said Toluwanisings slumped in the early hours of Wednesday.
He said he was away when the incident occurred but received a call about the singer’s condition. He later arrived at the residence and joined others who tried to rescue him.
He said: “They carried him and tried everything to save him. At every hospital he was taken to, some said the doctors were on strike, some said the doctors weren’t on the ground, and some said they couldn’t admit him.
“That is what happened. We tried our best to save him, with prayers and everything. We took him to seven to eight hospitals in Ibadan, Oyo State. But God said it was his time.”
Mr Gbolabo further said Toluwanisings showed no signs of illness before he suddenly slumped, adding that the singer was in good health.
He said the singer’s band members and others were waiting for his family to arrive before deciding on the next course of action.
“The next step is for the family members who are already here, so we are doing everything together. He is in the mortuary once the family finishes its meeting.
“We will do whatever they agree on. Some of them are not here yet, and they have not done the necessary things,” said Mr Gbolabo.
This newspaper earlier reported that news of Toluwanisings’ death emerged on social media on Wednesday afternoon, leaving fans worried and uncertain until his family confirmed the reports.
Following the confirmation, colleagues, friends and fans took to social media to express their grief and pay tribute to the late singer.
Toluwanisings was a gospel singer, songwriter and music minister known for his energetic praise sessions and worship songs infused with Yoruba influences.
Some of his well-known songs include “Kabiyesi Olorun Ayo”, “Unreserved Praise”, “A Very Big God”, “Onibuore”, “Eleda” and “I’m Not Alone”.
He developed a passion for music early on and began singing in church choirs before taking further steps toward a career in gospel music.
Throughout his career, he collaborated with gospel artistes, including Tosin Bee and Adeyinka Alaseyori.

title: Death toll unknown after intense fire in fatal Highway 401 crash: OPP
body:
Ontario Provincial Police say an intense fire has prevented investigators from determining how many people died in a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 401 Tuesday.
OPP said officers were called around 4:03 p.m. on Oct. 13 to the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Mill Road in the Township of Southwold for reports of a multi-vehicle crash.
Police said traffic had slowed because of an earlier collision in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Colonel Talbot Road in Middlesex County. A second crash then occurred west of the initial scene and involved two transport trucks and a passenger vehicle.
The vehicle and one of the transport trucks caught fire and quickly became engulfed in flames, police said.
Police described the collision as fatal but said investigators had not determined the total number of occupants or deaths because of the intense fire involving the passenger vehicle.
“The driver of the transport truck was able to exit the vehicle and was not injured. The second transport driver was taken to hospital to be treated for minor injuries,” police said in a news release Wednesday.
Highway 401 was closed for approximately 11 hours while emergency crews investigated.

title: Kernel, NASA Harvest complete testing of satellite crop rotation monitoring technology on 87 fields in Ukraine
body:
Agroholding Kernel and the international scientific initiative NASA Harvest have announced the completion of testing of a satellite crop rotation monitoring technology, carried out on 87 Ukrainian fields.
According to a Kernel press release, a research team involving the University of Strasbourg, the EBRD and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has completed testing of the technology, in which the agroholding provided data on 87 Ukrainian fields that are a pilot of its own carbon project and are undergoing independent international validation.
It is noted that scientists analyzed the company's fields in Sumy and Chernihiv regions, reconstructed the history of crop rotations over several years and recorded the use of sustainable practices.
The agroholding explained that the aim of the project is to create a digital tool that will make it possible to remotely confirm compliance with sustainable agricultural practices over several years.
Among other things, this approach will simplify attracting financing from international partners and operating in the EU market.
Separately, the agroholding presented data showing that the share of cases in which the same crop was grown on one field two years in a row fell from 16.5% in 2017-2020 to 0.8% in 2021-2025. In addition, a consistent rotation of different crops has formed on most of the fields studied.
Kernel stressed that such regular rotation helps maintain soil fertility and reduce the risks of soil health deterioration.
"We know from our own experience how difficult the process of confirming sustainable agricultural practices can be. Ukrainian agricultural producers need simple and reliable ways to confirm compliance with market requirements and European standards. This is where we see the practical value of such cooperation," Marta Trofimova, head of sustainable development at Kernel, is quoted as saying in the press release.
In addition, the company said the next stage will cover determining soil tillage methods and the areas under green manure and cover crops.
In the future, the developers plan to scale the satellite analysis system across the whole of Ukraine, the statement said.
NASA Harvest is NASA's consortium on global food security and agriculture, within which the program implements satellite observations and develops analytical tools to assess yields, crop structure and the sustainability of agricultural production.
Agroholding Kernel is one of the world's largest producers (about 6%) and exporters (about 10%) of sunflower oil, Ukraine's largest grain exporter, the operator of an extensive network of logistics assets and a leading producer of grain and oilseed crops in Ukraine. It is one of the largest producers and sellers of bottled oil in Ukraine. The company grows agricultural products and sells them.
Its land bank totals 530,000 hectares. The holding has Ukraine's largest private network of grain storage facilities with a one-time storage capacity of 2.1 million tonnes and the largest private fleet of grain railcars, at 3,300. Its sunflower seed processing capacity is 4 million tonnes per year.
In the nine months of fiscal 2026, Kernel's net profit decreased by 5% to $208 million, revenue rose by 0.4% to $3.092 billion, and EBITDA rose by 1% to $403 million.

title: Tinubu sends NDLEA, NSIB, school of government bills to Reps
body: By Gift ChapiOdekina, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has transmitted three executive bills to the House of Representatives for consideration, including proposals to reform the country’s drug law enforcement framework, expand the mandate of the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) and establish a National School of Government. The three bills were contained in separate letters dated October 12, 2026, which Speaker of the House, Tajudeen Abbas, read during plenary on Thursday. In the letters, marked “Restricted” and received by the Office of the Speaker on October 13, Tinubu said the bills were forwarded pursuant to Section 58(2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended. The bills are the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Bill, 2026; the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (Amendment) Bill, 2026; and the National School of Government Bill, 2026. NDLEA Bill The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Bill seeks to repeal the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Act, Cap. N30, and the Indian Hemp Act, Cap. 16, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. It proposes a consolidated legal framework for enforcing laws against the cultivation, processing, sale, trafficking and use of hard drugs. The bill would also empower the agency to investigate persons suspected of involvement in drug-related activities. NSIB Amendment Bill The Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (Amendment) Bill seeks to amend the NSIB (Establishment) Act, No. 35 of 2022, to reposition the bureau as an independent, multimodal safety investigation authority. The proposed amendment would expand its mandate beyond aviation to cover rail, maritime and other transport-related incidents. It would also transfer supervisory oversight to the Presidency and strengthen the bureau’s institutional, operational and administrative powers. National School of Government Bill The National School of Government Bill seeks to repeal the Administrative Staff College of Nigeria Act, Cap. A4, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004, and establish the National School of Government, Nigeria. The proposed institution would serve as a national centre for leadership development, policy delivery and executive capacity building. Tinubu urged the House to give the three bills “expeditious consideration.” The post Tinubu sends NDLEA, NSIB, school of government bills to Reps appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Sam George cautions ministers against reading unverified AI-generated speeches
body: The Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Sam George, has cautioned government ministers against delivering speeches generated by artificial intelligence (AI) without verifying their accuracy, revealing that some directors are already using the technology to prepare speeches for their ministers. He is concerned that the growing reliance on AI-generated content could result in government officials presenting inaccurate or unverified information, particularly when adequate background research and fact-checking are overlooked. Speaking in an interview ahead of the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum, Mr. George disclosed that he had raised the concern during an AI retreat for Cabinet ministers. “Ministers must be careful about the speeches they read, because right now we’re seeing directors use AI to prepare those speeches for ministers,” he cautioned. He explained that although AI tools can significantly reduce the time required to prepare documents, their output may contain information drawn from sources that have not been properly verified. “Now, what that means is there’s little background research that’s been done. But don’t forget that the AI tool that’s writing that speech is pulling from a number of multiple sources online, verified and unverified,” he said. The minister warned that the ability of AI systems to produce convincing responses within seconds should not be mistaken for a guarantee of accuracy. “And that’s the danger of AI. Because AI is unable to tell what is verified information and what is not verified information, because it’s basically pulling from the entire web anything related to the subject matter and the prompt that you’ve given to it,” he explained. His concerns raise questions about how government ministries and public institutions are integrating artificial intelligence into their daily operations, particularly in the preparation of official communications and other documents used to inform the public. AI changing the future of journalism Beyond government communications, the minister also expressed concern about the implications of AI-generated content for journalism, arguing that media professionals must develop new skills to distinguish accurate information from potentially misleading material. He believes journalism training institutions must reconsider how they prepare students for a media industry in which AI can increasingly perform tasks traditionally undertaken by reporters and editors. “So our academic institutions, GIJ, for example, needs to begin to look at what kind of journalist are you training in an AI world?” he questioned. He explained that journalists would increasingly require skills in verifying, editing and critically assessing AI-generated material before it is published or broadcast. “A journalist who is able to then pick what the AI has generated and proofread it and fact check it before pushing it to the newsroom. Because if you’re not careful, you have the newscaster reporting news that is not 100 percent verified,” he said. The minister’s concerns come as Ghana seeks to accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence across government institutions, businesses and other sectors of the economy. He disclosed that the government has already organised AI training for Cabinet ministers and appointed AI focal persons across ministries as part of the implementation of its national AI strategy. The ministry is also working with UNESCO and the United Nations Development Programme to build the capacity of civil servants, including chief directors and directors, to support the responsible deployment of the technology. Human intelligence remains critical Despite his concerns about misinformation and the potential displacement of certain jobs, Mr. George maintains that artificial intelligence presents significant opportunities for Ghana if workers and institutions learn to use it responsibly. He argued that AI should be seen as a tool to improve productivity rather than a substitute for human judgement and critical thinking. “So, yes, AI is fantastic. AI gives you speed. It gives you scale. But what AI cannot replace is human intelligence. So the AI tools are only as good as they’re structured to be,” he added. He consequently urged workers, including those already established in their careers, to acquire new skills that would allow them to remain relevant as AI transforms their professions. The Ningo-Prampram MP pointed to the government’s One Million Coders programme as one of the initiatives intended to help Ghanaians acquire the skills required to participate in an AI-driven economy. “We have multiple AI programmes in there. It’s for everybody. I keep saying that the One Million Coders programme is for skilling, reskilling and upskilling,” he said. The opportunities and risks associated with AI adoption will be examined in the second episode of the Digital Economy Forum , under the theme “AI and the Ghana Economy: Opportunity or Disruption?” The forum, held in partnership with Hubtel , will feature Sam George; Technical Advisor at the Finance Ministry, Dr Theo Acheampong; Founder of AI for Ghana, Adam Watkins; Head of Engineering at Hubtel, Augustine Adjei; and Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons. It will air live on JoyNews and Joy 99.7 FM on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 8 p.m.

title: Gov Sani Signs Executive Bill Establishing Specialist Nursing Hospital In Rigasa
body: Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani has signed into law an Executive Bill establishing the Kaduna State College of Post-Basic Nursing Sciences in Rigasa, Igabi Local Government Area, as a major step towards addressing shortages of specialist nurses and improving medical services across the state. The Kaduna State Commissioner for Information and Culture, Ahmed Maiyaki, disclosed this in a statement, describing the legislation as a strategic investment in skilled manpower development under the Governor’s ongoing health sector reforms. The institution is expected to expand advanced nursing training, produce specialists in critical fields, and improve maternal and child care, emergency response, and intensive care services across Kaduna State. Under the Kaduna State College of Post-Basic Nursing Sciences, Rigasa Law, 2026, the institution will operate as a specialised tertiary training college, with its main campus in Rigasa and provisions for additional campuses, schools and training centres, subject to regulatory approvals. Maiyaki explained that the College will offer programmes in midwifery, psychiatric and mental health nursing, perioperative nursing, paediatric nursing, accident and emergency nursing, intensive care nursing, public health nursing, as well as nursing education and administration. He said the Governor’s assent represents a significant investment in developing the skilled workforce required to address critical personnel shortages, strengthen clinical expertise and improve patient outcomes. Beyond professional training, the College will promote research, continuous professional development and partnerships with teaching hospitals, universities, specialist facilities and other accredited institutions. The law also establishes a Governing Council to provide strategic direction and institutional oversight, alongside an Academic Board responsible for academic standards, research and professional training. All programmes will be subject to the accreditation and regulatory requirements of the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria and other relevant authorities. The Commissioner noted that the legislation complements Governor Uba Sani’s broader reform agenda, including the upgrading of 255 primary healthcare centres, rehabilitation of 16 general hospitals and sustained investments in workforce recruitment and development. He emphasised that investments in medical infrastructure must be matched by qualified professionals capable of delivering specialised services, particularly in underserved communities. Maiyaki added that the College would help build a sustainable pipeline of specialist nurses, enhance institutional capacity and contribute to better health outcomes for generations to come. He reaffirmed the commitment of Governor Uba Sani towards developing the institution into a centre of excellence for specialist nursing education, research and clinical training, further advancing the Governor’s vision of accessible, quality and people-centred medical services. The post Gov Sani Signs Executive Bill Establishing Specialist Nursing Hospital In Rigasa appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Injury toll after Russian strike on store in Odesa region rises to four
body:
According to Ukrinform, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) announced this on Facebook .
"A large-scale fire broke out in a supermarket building following a Russian strike in the Odesa region. Preliminary reports indicate that four people were injured," the statement said.
Firefighting efforts were complicated by repeated air raid alerts. Rescuers were forced to suspend their work and move to safe locations each time an alert was issued.
Vehicles parked nearby were also damaged in the strike.
As Ukrinform previously reported, on October 15, Russian forces struck a store in the Odesa region with a drone. Three people had initially been reported injured.
