title: 'You have to keep fighting': Former Dubai resident gives first interview after five-year detention in Iraq
body: A former Dubai resident detained for five years in Iraq over a contract dispute will take time to adjust to freedom and is determined to fight for vindication after the “dark times” he endured. Australian engineer Robert Pether was released from prison in Baghdad in June last year but was barred from leaving the country due to financial claims linked to a case over a contract dispute between his employer and authorities in Iraq. “The concept of freedom is still kicking in for me because it's been a long time and I'm still adjusting,” Mr Pether, 50, told The National in his first interview since returning to Dublin on Monday. Spending time with family who now live in Ireland will be his main priority. He will soon have surgery to treat high-risk skin cancer, which deteriorated while he was in prison. “I'm having surgery in the next few days,” he said. “But it will be fixed, there's no doubt about that. We caught it in time.” 'No innocent person should suffer this' He will consult lawyers over the next few months to address the “huge injustice ” he suffered. Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, both of whom lived in Dubai, travelled to Baghdad in April 2021 and were locked up four months later. They were fined $12 million over a contract dispute between their employer CME Consulting and the Central Bank of Iraq. “I'm looking for accountability,” he told The National . “I was innocent when I was arrested. We did nothing wrong. “What was done to us was not reasonable, was not justice. So there does need to be accountability. I'm not at a stage where I'm going to identify who we're looking at for that accountability. I will let lawyers keep working on that.” Mr Pether did not share details of the legal case he plans to pursue and is aware of the challenging road ahead. “It will all be made known when the time is right. What we went through, no one, no innocent person should have to be subjected to … that is not something that you can just snap your fingers and say it's finished. “There needs to be some balance and that's where we're seeking accountability among the people who caused this, the people who are truly responsible for it … so that we feel more vindicated.” 'Don't give in' Mr Pether sought to give strength to others who have been wrongly incarcerated and their families. “Do not give up. That's really all I could tell them. Do not give in. You have to keep fighting,” he told The National . “There is an end. There is a way through … arbitrary detention is completely unjust but unfortunately it still happens. It will continue to happen. You just have to be strong enough to get through it.” The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention in 2021 deemed that Mr Pether’s detention breached international law and said he was being used as leverage in a commercial dispute. Mr Pether said his pursuit of justice also aims to deter those who consider detain innocent people unjustly. “The fact that we did suffer a huge injustice … it's going to be a long path but it's one that needs to be crossed,” he said. “This is not just for me, this is for other people … because it will happen again. I will not be the last … if we do bring in some measures of accountability and a way to achieve accountability, it will help the next person. And perhaps give people thought, to not put people into arbitrary detention.” His first priority is his family and he will then set aside time with lawyers. “In terms of actually making something happen, it will take months or years,” Mr Pether said. “I'm prepared for that, as is my wife. We've already discussed it, this is part of the healing process for us.” Not if but how to survive prison Conversations with his wife, Desree, and children, Flynn, Oscar and Nala, gave him courage . Speaking to former hostage Terry Waite, the Archbishop of Canterbury's special envoy kidnapped in Beirut in 1987 and held in captivity for five years – four of those in solitary confinement – helped him make crucial choices to draw on his inner resilience to survive his prison ordeal. “Terry and I started talking soon after my incarceration,” Mr Pether said. “The very first discussion we had, he said that I needed to make some hard decisions, and I had to decide how I was going to survive. There was never any question of if, it was always how.” Building mental fortitude, distancing himself from other prisoners and trying to keep tight control of his emotions proved to be his lifeline. “I personally decided I'd be better off isolating myself, relying on myself and my own internal strength,” Mr Pether told The National . His wife Desree and the embassy sent over books and immersing himself in reading took him away from the prison walls. After his release from jail last year, Mr Pether lived in a secure compound and his reading continued to give clarity of mind. “Reading books was a form of escapism that helped me build up my strength,” he said. “Basically that was how I got through the years in prison and the last 12 months when I was hidden away somewhere quietly and I had a few people I would speak to daily and catch up with … “I’m a fairly voracious reader, so anything I could get my hands on, I was reading. It was a way to fill in time and also a way to keep my brain moving, so that I could think about things more clearly.” Family lifeline The Pether family have spoken about being robbed of sharing personal milestones, from graduations to birthdays. “There were a lot of dark times but we got through them,” he said. “My wife used to prop me up when I was really down. There were times it was a roller coaster … each time it went down, it went further down and that was hard because then you had to drag yourself back up from there.” He initially thought the case would be resolved quickly, then as months and years passed there were times he lost hope. “I'll be honest, there were times when I did question that – 'will I actually go home?’” Mr Pether said. “It was a matter of trying to avoid the really dark patches, keeping the mental strength to know I would go home. It was just a question of when.” Conversations with his wife and children encouraged him to keep going. “My family was always on my mind, my wife especially, and there was never any question of not getting back,” he said. “What she was doing was not just fighting for my freedom. She was also propping up myself, our children, holding our family together. And it was her strength, sharing her strength with me, that helped.”

title: Violating oil tanker catches fire in Sea of Oman
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – A violating oil tanker that had switched off its tracking systems caught fire in a prohibited zone in the Sea of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Army Navy said.
An oil tanker caught fire in a prohibited zone in the Sea of Oman after switching off its tracking systems in an attempt to cross the area, Iran's Army Navy said.
Monitoring teams from the Army Navy detected the violating tanker while on patrol and controlling the east of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Army Navy's public relations office.
The tanker had turned off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through the prohibited area in the Sea of Oman, the statement said.
The Army of the Islamic Republic of Iran said the Strait of Hormuz is under the full control and surveillance of its forces and the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy.

title: The Bridges We Build Become the Roads Others Walk
body: There are moments in life when recognition does not feel simply like an award, but like a mirror. It asks you to look backward at the road you have traveled, the people you have encountered, the convictions you have defended, and the moments when you chose to speak even when silence would have been easier. Being named one of The Jerusalem Post and Jewish National Fund-USA's 25 ViZionaries is such a moment for me. I receive this recognition with gratitude, but also with a profound sense of responsibility, because it reminds me why I began this journey and how much work still lies ahead.I was born and raised in Marrakech, Morocco, a city where the Muslim call to prayer rises from minarets not far from neighborhoods where Jewish families lived for centuries. I grew up Muslim, Arab, and Moroccan, and these identities remain deeply rooted in who I am. But growing older taught me something important, loving our identity does not require us to inherit every prejudice that has become attached to it. For much of my childhood, Jews and Israel existed more in stories than in reality. Like many young people across the Arab world, I inherited conclusions before I was old enough to question the assumptions behind them. Then I began meeting Jewish people, traveling to Israel, listening, reading, and asking questions that challenged some of what I thought I knew. Slowly, the human being replaced the story, and that transformation became the foundation of my advocacy.When I founded the Moroccan-Israeli Friendship Association, I wanted to create something that went beyond political normalization. Governments can sign agreements, diplomats can shake hands, and airplanes can cross borders, but genuine peace asks something more difficult of us, people must also cross the borders they carry within themselves. Morocco taught me that this is possible because Jewish history is not foreign to Moroccan history, it is part of it. Our music, cities, language, food, traditions, and collective memory carry the fingerprints of generations of Moroccan Jews. Strengthening the relationship between Morocco and Israel is therefore, for me, not simply about creating something new, it is also about remembering and restoring something old.My writing grew from the same conviction. Through my book, Arab Identity Syndrome, my articles, speeches, interviews, and public advocacy, I have tried to ask questions that are sometimes uncomfortable in Arab and Muslim societies. Why should hostility toward Israel be inherited as part of Arab identity? Why should a Muslim who stands against antisemitism or defends Jewish people be considered somehow less Muslim? Why should recognizing Jewish history, suffering, and connection to Israel require us to abandon compassion for anyone else? Over the years, I have come to believe that identity should be a home from which we encounter the world, not a prison that prevents us from seeing it.My answer has never been to abandon where I come from. On the contrary, this journey has made me return to my Moroccan and Muslim identity with greater honesty and confidence. I can be deeply Moroccan, proudly Muslim, culturally Arab, and still extend my hand to the Jewish people and stand for Israel's right to exist in peace and security. I do not see a contradiction between these convictions. I believe that when our identities are secure enough to make room for another person's story, they become stronger rather than weaker. Peace begins when we stop asking people to choose between their identity and their humanity.That philosophy also inspired Abrahamic Voice, the nonprofit media and educational initiative I recently founded. Its mission is especially close to my heart because it seeks to speak directly to Arabic-speaking audiences about Jewish history, Israel, antisemitism, coexistence, and Muslim-Jewish relations. I want young Arabs and Muslims to encounter these subjects through something other than slogans, propaganda, and inherited hostility. I want them to read, question, travel, meet people, and think for themselves, because I know from my own journey that sometimes one genuine encounter can accomplish what a thousand political speeches cannot.This is why being recognized among the 25 ViZionaries carries a meaning far beyond seeing my own name on a list. I am grateful to The Jerusalem Post for recognizing the value of this work, and I am equally grateful to Jewish National Fund-USA for helping create a platform that recognizes people who are willing to build, educate, speak, and lead. There is something deeply meaningful to me, as a Moroccan Muslim, about being included among people working in different ways toward a stronger Israel, stronger communities, and a more hopeful future. It reminds me that friendship does not demand sameness and that some of the strongest bridges are built by people who begin their journeys on different shores.I also receive this recognition with humility because the work is far from finished. Antisemitism continues to poison conversations and communities, Muslims and Jews are still too often taught to encounter one another through fear, and social media has given hatred and misinformation a speed our ancestors could never have imagined. Every day, another generation is being handed stories about people they have never met, and those stories can either become walls or invitations to seek the truth. That is where I believe my work must continue, particularly among Arabic-speaking audiences, where courageous conversations about Jews, Israel, identity, and peace remain urgently necessary.Recognition is meaningful, but it cannot become a destination. Its greatest value is the responsibility it creates for what comes afterward. Years ago, I began this journey by questioning stories I had inherited, and today I find myself encouraging others to question theirs. Perhaps this is how lasting change happens, through conversations, friendships, uncomfortable questions, acts of courage, and the willingness to see another human being before seeing a label. If being called a visionary means anything to me, it means believing in a future that does not yet fully exist and then accepting the responsibility of helping to build it. For that recognition, I am deeply grateful, and for the work that still lies ahead, I am ready.This article was written in collaboration with Jewish National Fund USA

title: Uzbekistan Delivery Drivers Under Police Scrutiny: Why Tashkent Lacks Space for Mopeds
body: A delivery courier in Tashkent says police confiscated the electric bicycle he used to deliver orders after demanding a driver’s license, leaving him unable to work. In an early October video appeal , the man said his bicycle could not exceed 25 kilometers per hour and that he did not ride on roads used by cars. Economist Otabek Bakirov published the video amid increasingly frequent police inspections of moped and scooter riders, including delivery workers. Police have justified the inspections by pointing to traffic accidents. Figures released in early October put the number of accidents involving mopeds and scooters in Uzbekistan this year at 563, leaving 89 people dead and another 488 injured. But how well are Tashkent’s streets equipped to accommodate the vehicles used by thousands of delivery workers every day? Thousands of Violations and New Regulations According to the Road Traffic Safety Service of Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, inspectors recorded 4,312 violations involving moped and scooter riders in 2026, about 14 times the number recorded throughout 2025. The agency attributes accidents partly to riders lacking driver’s licenses and having insufficient knowledge of traffic rules. However, the sharp increase in recorded violations also coincides with new requirements for riders and more frequent police inspections. In early October, Tashkent police publicly explained another incident involving a motorized two-wheeler. On the night of October 2, inspectors stopped a man on Amir Temur Street because, according to their account, his vehicle was obstructing traffic. It had a homemade attachment that restricted visibility, while the rider’s clothing lacked reflective elements. He also did not have the required documents. Since October 2025, Uzbekistan has required mopeds and scooters to be registered. In January 2026, the country introduced a simplified A1 driver’s license subcategory for mopeds and certain other low-powered vehicles. This can be obtained by passing theoretical and practical exams, without compulsory driving-school training. Drivers who hold Uzbekistan’s national licenses in categories A, B, C, or D do not need a separate A1 license. A vehicle’s legal classification depends on its technical specifications. For example, ordinary electric kick scooters are classified as personal mobility devices and do not require a license. Couriers and Delivery Services In 2025, the People’s Democratic Party of Uzbekistan estimated that there were approximately 130,000 couriers across the country making deliveries on bicycles, mopeds, and scooters. For students, people from other regions, and those without steady employment, delivery work can offer a way to earn money quickly. However, couriers often have to cover vehicle expenses, documentation costs, and fines themselves. Amid the police inspections, Sardor Kadyrov, vice president of Yandex Uzbekistan, presented his own figures. According to his estimates, couriers have received fines totaling nearly 4.7 billion soums, approximately $390,000, since the beginning of 2026. Missing documents accounted for only about 8% of the violations he cited, which covered motorcycle, scooter, and moped riders. Kadyrov also claimed that mopeds were involved in fewer than 6% of all recorded traffic accidents. His figures cover mopeds alone, while the Road Traffic Safety Service’s figures include scooters, making a direct comparison difficult. Yandex has a commercial interest in the debate because restrictions affecting couriers also affect delivery services. In June 2025, the company began offering Tashkent couriers rental electric bicycles that automatically limit their speed depending on the area. The initial rollout involved 100 bicycles, with plans to expand the fleet to 500. Bike Lanes Are Being Built, but Mopeds Cannot Use Them By the end of 2030, Tashkent plans to improve 100 streets designated for tourism, dining, and round-the-clock activity. The decision was adopted by the city’s Council of People’s Deputies, its local representative body. The project includes upgrading sidewalks and building bicycle lanes . These improvements are good news for cyclists, but couriers riding mopeds must travel on the roads alongside cars . The problem is particularly noticeable around restaurants and cafes. A courier arrives to collect an order, parks for a few minutes, and then returns to the road. There may be dozens of such stops during a shift. Yet published summaries of the street improvement plans do not specify short-term parking spaces for delivery mopeds near businesses. The situation is complicated by cars parked on sidewalks and near building entrances. Tashkent has previously announced smart parking plans and began testing an integrated management system for private parking facilities in April 2026. However, the pilot project description does not mention dedicated spaces for delivery vehicles. For a courier, searching for somewhere to stop means losing time and potentially income. Designated parking areas near restaurants could reduce conflicts with motorists and pedestrians without requiring extensive street reconstruction. Road Safety Requires More Than Enforcement A lack of convenient routes does not justify dangerous riding. In February 2026, a courier riding a scooter collided with a bus in Tashkent. According to the preliminary account provided by the city’s bus operator, Toshshahartransxizmat, the courier ran a red light. In another incident, a scooter rider traveling against traffic crashed into the hook of a mobile crane parked by the roadside. He died at the scene, according to Tashkent police. The same police report described accidents in which motorists driving at high speeds struck pedestrians, including after running red lights. In a collision with a bus or truck, a moped rider has virtually no protection. That makes enforcement of speed limits, vehicle safety standards, and traffic rules essential. But safety also depends on how streets are organized: whether couriers can reach pickup locations, stop without obstructing pedestrians, and safely rejoin traffic. The case of the courier whose electric bicycle was confiscated has yet to receive a publicly reported legal resolution. Nor has a technical assessment been released to establish whether he was required to hold an A1 license. For the courier himself, the answer will determine whether he can return to work.

title: Will Georgia’s new media regulations lead to widespread website censorship?
body: New media regulations in Georgia have led to the issuance of fines to broadcasters. This could soon be rolled out to the digital realm and involve website blocking. Media freedoms in Tbilisi are shifting somewhat. Once a fairly liberal sphere, recent changes have seen fines levied for biased language, and specific phrases on broadcast television have been banned. While regulatory battlegrounds have typically been on television, there is a possibility this could now shift to the online sphere. This could have a huge impact regarding what can and can not be said online. How website blocking occurs Website blocking can occur in several different ways. Generally, it is done as a tool to promote positive working environments. Many people choose to use a website blocker to increase productivity. By restricting sites and apps during working time, it prevents workers from scrolling the web and going off track. This is a perfect tool for those who work remotely. They can also be used to prevent people from accessing harmful content. Minors could be blocked from sites that contain adult content. People who are at risk of problem gambling can use them to exclude themselves from online betting facilities. Yet they can be used by governments, who want to block certain sources of information. Internet service providers in Georgia may be asked to use them, possibly through DNS tampering and IP address blocking. In this way, websites can be targeted in minutes, and newsrooms can be cut off from their audience overnight. From airwaves to firewalls The Georgian National Communications Commission (GNCC), colloquially referred to as ComCom , has recently fined several high-profile companies. One of these was Formula TV, which was made to pay ₾10,000 (USD 3,900) over claims of impartiality, citing that broadcaster footage included personal views. TV Pirveli has also been issued with formal reports. Certain words and phrases have been banned from use in broadcasts, with the independent body Transparency International (TI) Georgia noting that there are 101 words and phrases which are forbidden. These are easily translated to the digital realm, and it could see web servers, text archives, and content providers fined for their use of them. Currently, the penalties for this are financial. Yet it could go one step further for digital companies, running to domain seizures and ISP-level URL blocking. Website blocking around the world The blocking of websites is not necessarily a bad thing. It can shield a country from harmful influences, particularly those of foreign actors or threats. It does this through multiple methods, and one of the most common is DNS filtering. This is where a particular website name is blocked. When a device tries to look up the website’s numerical internet address, a not-found message is returned, or the request is redirected. Another is URL filtering. This inspects a specific path or requested page. This can be more nuanced, as it can allow specific pages on a domain but not others. One other is IP blocking. Each device has an IP address, which stands for Internet Protocol. It is a digital mailing address, so information can reach the right place or request. A server can block a numerical IP address, so that any data transfer from that server, either to or from, becomes impossible. Much of this can be done by people on their own device, allowing for parental controls. The best control to block websites will attach neatly to a browser. They can then block pages and websites by category, keywords, and other criteria. For those looking to use them to boost productivity, they can also block messages from messaging and work apps like Slack. Changes to Azerbaijani website access If Georgia does decide to follow this route, it will not be the only country in the region to have chosen to censor the internet. In July 2026, Azerbaijan decided to adopt major amendments to the laws on Information, Informatization and Information Protection. Particularly, this focused on being able to block internet resources with judicial authorisations. Before this, website blocking was restricted to emergencies. These were defined as situations in which state or public interests were under threat. Now, a range of broad criteria define what can be blocked. These include films or games lacking age-rating disclosure to defamation or insult of individuals. Yet it also contains many very sensible suggestions, such as adult content and information that could endanger mental health. According to data by the World Bank group, 84% of Georgia’s population now has access to the internet. This figure has risen sharply over the last ten years. Its internet penetration rate is 83.80%, up 2.3% from 2023. The government will now have to manage this carefully, treading a line between using internet blocking to protect its citizens and making sure not to infringe on their freedoms. Written by Sophie Bennett, a geopolitics writer who explores finance, communications, and more. Her background in international studies has shaped a particular interest in how technology, social expectations, and geopolitical boundaries influence the modern world. She approaches sensitive subjects with warmth, curiosity, and an unbiased perspective. _____________________________________ Paid for by: Bazoom Group

title: Call of the Wilde: Jakub Dobes struggles continue as the Montreal Canadiens fall to the Capitals in Washington
body:
Back-to-back games for both the Washington Capitals and Montreal Canadiens on Wednesday night. The Capitals lost to the Carolina Hurricanes while the Canadiens edged the Buffalo Sabres in a shootout. It was another strong defensive game for the Canadiens allowing only 17 shots through 65 minutes.
In Washington, the Canadiens played well, but it was another rough night for Jakub Dobes in net as they fell 5-4.
When the Canadiens finish building their team, they will have three lines that are going to be formidable. The top line is the Nick Suzuki connection with Juraj Slafkovsky and Cole Caufield. The second line will be Ivan Demidov with likely Michael Hage and, perhaps, Zachary Bolduc.
The third line is the shocker, and what a pleasant shocker. Alex Newhook has turned into a quality centre with Josh Anderson and Chris Kreider. What a tremendous development for the sum of the parts of these three players to be so much better than the actual parts.
Anderson is rejuvenated. He scored two goals on the night on identical plays. Newhook set up Anderson for tap-ins from three feet. Kreider did excellent dirty work on both goals winning the puck. This is a line that should stay together. It’s excellent that a home has been found for Kreider already.
Kreider had another strong night. On the fourth goal, he executed a perfect screen on the Suzuki shot. Lane Hutson with the assist to go with his tally for another two-point night. Hutson is scoring at better than a point-per-game clip.
Late second period, Slafkovsky was hit in what looked like a dirty play but actually wasn’t. However, the Canadiens went straight to getting even led by Kaiden Guhle and Alexandre Carrier. The Canadiens have been intimidated a lot in this moment over the years, but they seem to have decided that it will happen no more.
Guhle is aggressive and plays with attitude, and Carrier always backs up his teammates. A couple minutes after the exchange, Arber Xhekaj also looked to get even. When this type of moment hits, a team has to make the point strongly that they will be not backing back down but will respond angrily.
Owen Beck has been trusted with only limited minutes in his first two games with the Canadiens this season, but he’s impressed in his limited time. Beck is never going to be an offensive player in the league. If he becomes an NHL regular, it will be as a fourth liner.
However, he could be a very good fourth liner. From a fourth line, the hope is to be able to compete just in case the match-up gets unfavourable against the other club’s top players. It’s also desired that the fourth line is tough and can wear down the opposition physically.
Beck is never going to be the second part of the equation, but as a centre, he can drive the first part of the equation. If Beck can play solid and smart hockey at centre, there’s a spot for him in the league. He is smart. He chooses the defensive side of the puck when unsure.
Jakub Dobes is struggling mightily to begin the season. Regression from the best goalie in last year’s playoffs was expected, but this is a lot of difficulty.
Dobes is trying too hard. He wants so much to do well that he can’t keep his body still, because he is not keeping his mind still. He is overplaying every shot. When he slides across to make a save, he is so anxious to get there that he gets beyond his target, then is out of position for a second shot.
The technical issue begins the difficulty, then losing confidence takes it from there. On a Capitals shorthanded goal, Hutson played a two-on-one well forcing the shot. It’s what the goal is for the defender, but Dobes couldn’t stop the off angle shot from Alex Tuch. Not a good goal.
The winning goal for the Capitals was scored on the Canadiens achilleas heel this season. It was a 55-foot shot that seemed to have eyes. or was deflected on the way in. All three goals were of this variety against Buffalo, and the key goal in Washington was scored in the same manner.
Head Coach Martin St. Louis spoke of his players not boxing out after the Buffalo game, but on this one, it was simply a bad goal as it wasn’t deflected late at all. Dobes made himself small on the shot. He tucked his shoulders in. All he had to do was spread his wings to make the save.
Dobes is an imposing figure. He is a giant in the net, so he needs to just let his size do the work for him. Dobes doesn’t need to move much to make saves, if he makes himself large. Before the night began, he was 59th of 64 goalies in Goals Saved Above Expected.
After this contest, he added a negative value of 1.86 and now he is 62nd among 64 goalies with a negative 5.86. The old-school numbers are equally grim. Dobes had a save percentage of .792 on the night and .842 for the season.
No one could have seen that coming. He will figure it out. Until they do, they should ride the hot hand of Jacob Fowler.
It feels like a changing of the guard is coming on the blue line for the Canadiens. The depth chart is definitely changing from last season. Sometimes it can take time for an established hierarchy to rotate.
On the first pair last season, Mike Matheson was often logging 28 to 30 minutes of ice with Noah Dobson. Lane Hutson was on the second pair logging big minutes as well, but his defensive partner always logged a lot less.
It often felt like the Matheson minutes were pushed to the limit. To accommodate Matheson, Hutson even found himself on the right side of the ice to defend, just so the hierarchy could remain intact.
This season, it’s early, but the winds of change have definitely blown in. Head Coach Martin St. Louis seems comfortable with the new first pair of Dobson and Hutson. This top pairing makes sense: Dobson is the best defender on the right side and Hutson is the best on the left side.
However, there seems to be a bigger shake-up on the horizon. Kaiden Guhle is 24 years of age. Mike Matheson is 32. Guhle still has ceiling in front of him to be a better defender. He logged 25:25 against the Sabres. He was a beast on the penalty kill.
Guhle is soon to be the second-best left side defender on the team and a natural coupling with the second best on the right-side Alexandre Carrier that has begun should stick for the long haul.
This leaves Matheson to drop all the way down to the third pair where he belongs as he begins to age. Matheson’s contract expires in 2031. To get strong years out of him, it’s not in the team’s best interests to be playing him into the ground as he heads to age 37.
Matheson dropping from 28 minutes to 16 minutes would serve his longevity well, and the team well to have him with easier match-ups. He and Arber Xhekaj would make a strong pair. Eventually, a pairing of Matheson and David Reinbacher would be interesting as well.
Reinbacher was called up on Wednesday to Washington, but he did not play.
Brian Wilde, a Montreal-based sportswriter, brings you Call of the Wilde on globalnews.ca after each Canadiens game.

title: Services drive 7.4% expansion in Ghana’s economic activity
body: Ghana’s economic activity expanded by 7.4% year-on-year in July 2026, up from 4.9% in the same period last year, driven by strong growth in services and a recovery in industry. The latest Monthly Indicator of Economic Growth (MIEG), released by the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), shows that the index rose to 121.6 in July from 113.2 a year earlier. Services remained the main driver of the expansion, growing by 12.2% year-on-year, compared with 6.7% in July 2025. The sector accounted for 63.8% of the growth recorded during the period, with information and communication leading the expansion. Industry also recorded a recovery, growing by 5.4% compared with 0.4% in July last year. Mining and quarrying provided the main impetus for the sector’s improved performance. Agriculture, however, slowed, expanding by 3.7% in July, down from 8.2% a year earlier. Crops and livestock were the main contributors to the sector’s growth. The figures point to stronger overall economic activity, but also highlight differences in performance across the three main sectors. While services continue to drive expansion, the slowdown in agriculture raises questions about how to sustain growth across the wider economy. The GSS data highlights the importance of maintaining momentum in services while strengthening agriculture and broadening the contribution of other productive sectors to economic growth.

title: Opposition Alliance Announces Rallies on October 25, November 28 Amid GD’s Bid to Ban Parties
body: Opposition Alliance, which unites nine Georgian opposition parties, announced an October 25 rally in Tbilisi titled “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better,” protesting, among others, the ruling Georgian Dream party’s efforts to ban several opposition parties through the Constitutional Court. The Alliance invited supporters to gather at the Tbilisi State University campus at 7 pm on October 25, with the event meant to kick off a major protest campaign to culminate in a larger rally on November 28, which falls on the second anniversary of the non-stop anti-government protests sparked by Georgian Dream’s announcement on halting EU integration. The rally announcement came two days after the Constitutional Court said it was starting to review the ruling party’s lawsuit on its merits. Representatives of opposition parties targeted in the case reported receiving calls about first hearings being scheduled on October 21, 22, and 23. Speaking at a press briefing on October 15, Gvaramia said that the party-ban initiative was not about depriving opposition politicians of their positions, but “about depriving the country of democracy.” “It is about depriving our great ancestors and Georgia’s great history of their greatest aspiration: full membership in the European family,” he said. “[…] It is all about all the emptied regions and cities, about depriving Georgians of the opportunity to live in their ancestral homeland and forcing them to leave the country.” Gvaramia vowed to continue challenging the ruling party in court and through street protests. “We will be everywhere: in courtrooms, in Batumi, and, most importantly, on the streets of Tbilisi,” he said. “We will protest everything fearlessly and forcefully, with one central demand – Georgia without Ivanishvili.” Gigi Tsereteli, chairman of European Georgia, further said that the planned demonstration was not solely an initiative of the opposition alliance, but was intended to bring together political parties, civic groups, and individuals who view free elections as essential to Georgia’s democratic future. Speaking at the briefing, Tamar Chergoleishvili, leader of the Federalist Party, which was added to the party-ban lawsuit in April, said that the October 25 rally would mark the beginning of a broader protest campaign culminating in a major demonstration in Tbilisi on November 28. “With this desperate move, Ivanishvili is merely revealing that he does not trust the Georgian people or their choices,” Chergoleishvili said. “If these parties are bad, then, logically, the Georgian people should not be voting for the very parties he is seeking to ban.” She said that the proposed party bans would not change the opposition’s strategy. “Our plan is to expand peaceful and principled protests until we force Ivanishvili to make concessions,” she said. Georgian Dream initially filed the constitutional lawsuit in November 2025, seeking to outlaw the United National Movement (UNM), Lelo/Strong Georgia, and Ahali/Coalition for Change. The lawsuit was subsequently expanded in April 2026 to include the Federalists and again in September to add For Georgia, the only opposition party still represented in Parliament. Each expansion required Georgian Dream to resubmit the lawsuit, resetting the court’s nine-month deadline to issue a ruling. While the resubmissions initially fed perceptions that GD was deliberately dragging out the process, the premature resignation of Manana Kobakhidze, one of the Court’s judges, ahead of the start of proceedings sparked worries that the ruling party may be seriously considering using the Court to have its opponents declared unconstitutional. title: Cardoso: Nigeria to replicate remittance reforms to diversify FX earnings
body: *Says Nigeria must lead Africa’s investment drive through reforms By Babajide Komolafe The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Olayemi Cardoso, has said Nigeria will replicate the reforms that boosted diaspora remittances to diversify its foreign exchange (FX) earnings and reduce dependence on crude oil exports. Cardoso stated this while speaking at a debate on the ‘Global Economy: Forging Resilient and Dynamic Economies for the Future’ during the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings, Bangkok, Thailand. Speaking alongside the Managing Director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, the President of the Eurogroup, the Minister of Economy and Finance of Greece, Kyriakos Pierrakakis, the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister of Thailand, Ekniti Nitithanprapas, and the Minister of Economy of the Argentine Republic, Luis Caputo, Cardoso said the CBN would apply lessons from the growth in remittance inflows to other sectors, including commodities and oil, to unlock additional sources of foreign exchange. He also said Nigeria must lead Africa’s investment drive by sustaining macroeconomic stability, implementing reforms and demonstrating through concrete results that the economy had changed. Explaining how the country responded to a crisis that depleted its external reserves and left it with substantial outstanding foreign exchange obligations, Cardoso said the situation forced Nigeria to explore alternative sources of FX. “When you are going through a crisis, it forces you to be creative, and that was the situation Nigeria faced,” he said. “We went through a crisis in which our net external reserves fell to about $3 billion at one point, despite having a population of over 200 million people. In addition, we had outstanding foreign exchange obligations of more than $7 billion. “That situation forced us to be creative. We were able to take the right measures through an orthodox monetary policy approach, which helped to stabilise the economy. Believe it or not, we were able to pay off those obligations and attract investment.” Cardoso said Nigeria could no longer rely on oil revenue, particularly given production challenges that constrained earnings. “We were also clear that relying on oil was not a sustainable model. At the time, we had challenges with oil production, and we were not generating what we considered a sustainable level of revenue,” he said. Remittances rise to $950m monthly. Cardoso identified diaspora remittances as a major opportunity to increase FX inflows, saying the CBN engaged Nigerians abroad, international investors and other stakeholders to identify and remove obstacles to regular remittance transfers. He said the bank drew lessons from countries such as India and Egypt, where international remittances provide significant financial inflows. “One of the areas we focused on was the diaspora and international remittances. “When we started looking at this, we were in a desperate situation and had to ask ourselves, how could we generate the revenues we needed? We identified international remittances as an important opportunity,” he said. “Once we understood the problems, we moved quickly to remove the bottlenecks preventing capital from flowing into the country.” According to him, monthly remittance inflows rose from about $200 million when the initiative began in 2025 to $600 million by the end of the first year. “When we started, monthly international remittances were about $200 million. We said we would double that figure before the end of the year, and people laughed. They did not believe it was possible. “In actual fact, by the end of the year, we had reached $600 million a month,” Cardoso said. He added that inflows subsequently rose to approximately $950 million monthly by July this year, against a target of $1 billion. “We then said that, this year, we would take the figure to $1 billion a month. Happily, by July, we had reached about $950 million,” he said. Cardoso attributed the growth partly to digital solutions and the removal of outdated practices that hindered financial flows. “I do not have enough time to explain all the measures we implemented to achieve those results, but much of the progress was related to digital solutions and an understanding that certain outdated ways of doing things were no longer sustainable,” he said. He disclosed that he chaired a CBN committee established to coordinate the initiative and ensure banks were involved. “That is the approach we intend to apply in other areas, including commodities and the oil sector,” he said. Dangote Refinery to boost value addition Cardoso also identified domestic refining as an opportunity to reduce the foreign exchange burden associated with importing petroleum products. He said the Dangote Refinery was beginning to support a shift from exporting crude oil and importing refined products to retaining more value within the domestic economy. “On the value-addition side, we now have the Dangote Refinery, which is beginning to contribute to economic diversification. It offers an opportunity to move away from a model in which we export crude oil, import refined products and lose money in the process,” he said. Nigeria must lead Africa’s investment drive. On Nigeria’s role in attracting investment to Africa amid global efforts to diversify supply chains and create employment, Cardoso said the country must demonstrate leadership through sound economic policies and sustained reforms. “The role of a country like Nigeria, which is obviously a large economy with a large population, is to lead by doing the right things. “This brings us back to an issue that has been discussed frequently here: getting your house in order and staying the course,” he said. He said macroeconomic stability had helped restore investor confidence, citing Nigeria’s return to the FTSE and J.P. Morgan bond indices, as well as improved assessments by rating agencies. “We have had macroeconomic stability over the past couple of years. As a result, Nigeria has returned to the FTSE index and the J.P. Morgan bond index. Rating agencies have also been improving their assessments of the country at every stage. “Confidence has returned,” he said. Cardoso stressed that sustaining the gains was essential to changing international perceptions of Nigeria and attracting investment. “We need to sustain that progress and demonstrate to the world that change is possible and that things are different from what they were in the past. “It is not enough to say that things have changed. We must demonstrate it through our actions. In my view, the numbers speak for themselves,” he said. The post Cardoso: Nigeria to replicate remittance reforms to diversify FX earnings appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: US ‘economic supremacy’ key in the Western Hemisphere, top US Army general says
body: The U.S. Army’s top commander for the Western Hemisphere described American “economic supremacy” as an overarching goal of Washington’s regional security strategy, outlining plans to expand its military footprint in Central and South America on Monday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting . The 2025 National Security Strategy prioritizes economic dominance in the Western Hemisphere through national security, Gen. Joseph Ryan, the commander of the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said during a panel discussion with Gen. Luis Cardozo, Colombian attaché, and Vice Adm. Jo-Ann Burdian, the U.S. Coast Guard’s Atlantic Area Commander. “The end state is economic supremacy for the United States,” Ryan said, later adding, “We have ceded control of that economic terrain in this hemisphere to the People’s Republic of China over at least the last two decades, and that is a major threat to our national security.” Ryan pointed to Panama as an example, explaining how a high percentage of trade to and from the United States passes through the Panama Canal. He said the Panamanian government saw a mutual benefit in the partnership. It also allows the U.S. to “keep an eye on those states that are aligned with other adversaries in the region,” he said, such as Cuba, Nicaragua and formerly Venezuela. Lebanese Hezbollah has a presence in the area, he added. Recently, the U.S. military co-led PANAMAX, a massive multinational exercise hosted in Panama for the first time since 2012, where forces practiced defending the Panama Canal . During the exercise, which included personnel from 19 countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Colombia, troops drilled command post and field exercises. Countering cartels In addition to countering China, the Defense Department has railed against cartels, prioritizing counter-cartel operations in the Western Hemisphere. Burdian said the cartels are trafficking people, narcotics and bulk cash. She characterized them as “multi-billion-dollar organizations that operate globally and are unconstrained in the ways we are — they are unconstrained financially,” she said, adding, “and they demonstrate extraordinary agility, and they certainly are unfettered by rules or basic human decency.” Cardozo said his country — Colombia — has seen how cartels can build diverse, enormous economies. “In Colombia, it’s not only using the drug trafficking as a main source of income, they also use illegal mining,” he said, which can destroy the environment and people’s homes, but reap huge financial rewards. “I think that’s their Achilles’ heel: the illegal financing. If we take that money away from them, they’re going to asphyxiate.” With the Army’s logistics assistance, Burdian said the Coast Guard is working to establish an Expeditionary Cutter Squadron with two ships in Panama to conduct interdiction operations. Ryan said officials recently approved a capacity increase for Joint Task Force Bravo — a forward-deployed task force based at Soto Cano Air Base in Comayagua, Honduras — to expand the footprint over the next few fiscal years. Ryan said the task force would receive more rotary-wing aircraft and personnel to “address some of the natural disasters and threats in the region.” Those additional resources, he said, “become absolutely critical when you’re talking about moving supplies, moving people to the point of need, and making assessments.” Command restructure In a major force restructure, the Army stood up the Western Hemisphere Command in December 2025, combining U.S. Army North, U.S. Army South and Armed Forces Command under a single headquarters. As its focus shifted, the Army revived its jungle school in Panama’s “Green Hell” and approved service-wide wear of the Jungle tab. In August, U.S. Southern Command activated Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, a new headquarters to unify operations with allies and partners, including the 18 partner nations of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. The new task force replaced Operation Southern Spear , which has destroyed scores of sea vessels as part of what the Trump administration characterizes as a counternarcotics campaign. More than 210 people have been killed in the attacks . The strikes have drawn controversy, and the Trump administration has offered little evidence of drug-trafficking activity. The Defense Department’s inspector general launched an investigation into whether U.S. Southern Command followed protocols with the strikes, but the White House has emphatically defended the attacks. Ryan said that joint exercises with partner forces in the region will increasingly center on counter-cartel operations. “We are going to focus our exercise programming going forward to be really focused on those things that contribute to the counter-designated terrorist organization threat and cartel threat in the region,” he told the crowd. Publicly available technology is fueling the cartel’s economy, the panelists emphasized. “Make no mistake, you know, Starlink is great as long as you’re using it on your side. When it pervades to the adversary side, it becomes very difficult to counter,” Ryan said, emphasizing that the military cannot stop cartels from accessing publicly available technology. Ryan said the intelligence is showing an increase in unmanned aerial systems for human trafficking operations, and Burdian said the Coast Guard is used to seeing homemade submersibles from the cartels coming out of riverine terrain off the coast of Colombia. But now, as the markets grow, they are seeing them move across the Atlantic. “The greatest threat I face — the most persistent threat, frankly — is the commingling of illicit traffic or threats or another nature with legitimate traffic,” Burdian said. Only completely closing a port can eliminate all illegal traffic, she said, but that is economically destructive. “So, how do you know what to let in? How do you know what to keep out?” she asked. “How do I enable those commanders on scene to allow the legitimate commerce to pass in and out while at the same time, identifying and neutralizing threats before they damage the U.S. economy or kill Americans?”

Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users into Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending. The Universal Cart tool Google previewed at its I/O event in May is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search, with the aim of making it easier to stay organized and save money when shopping online.
As the name suggests, it’s a “universal” digital cart that lets you save products from multiple retailers in a single unified space, and works across different Google platforms. That means you can find and add a bunch of products using the Gemini app and Google Search AI Mode, and they’ll all be saved to the same cart. There are also plans to integrate Universal Cart with Gmail and YouTube, but Google hasn’t announced a timeline for that yet.
Google will send you notifications about price drops and restocks for items saved in your cart, which spares you from having to check each retailer’s website individually, and can display any relevant promotional codes it finds besides the products you’ve saved. You can choose to pay for items from the cart using Google Wallet, or transfer them to the merchant’s own cart so you can checkout with the retailer directly. Together with Google Wallet, Universal Cart can also analyze the perks provided by each of your saved credit cards and help you choose the best payment method when purchasing.
The launch comes as competition in the AI-assisted shopping space is heating up, with Google rivals including OpenAI and Meta having launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user’s behalf. Shopify also recently announced that it’s opening its platform up to allow more AI agents to browse and purchase from Shopify listings. Big Tech players are entering this race on the bet that the future of online shopping involves having a robot do most of the work for you.

title: Quick question: Who exactly is iPhone Handoff for?
body:
Last month, Apple announced a feature called iPhone Handoff. Not to be confused with that Handoff; this is a new one.
iPhone Handoff allows you to keep your number active on two iPhones at the same time so you can easily switch between them. According to Apple’s support website, you pick one phone as your main phone and set up Handoff on the other as your secondary phone. When you unlock one of them, your number becomes active on that phone — that’s where you’ll get calls, and that device will be used for Find My.
The idea is that your secondary phone will be something you pick up on weekends, for example, with apps and settings configured to your needs, and Handoff means you can use it with your existing phone number. Apple is pitching it as a totally seamless way to use your number on two phones, but that convenience comes at a cost. T-Mobile is the first US carrier to support the feature, and it’s an extra $5 on your monthly phone bill to use it. Verizon is also planning to support Handoff by the end of the year. If you’re on AT&T you’re out of luck, it seems.
As someone who uses a lot of different phones, this all sounds handy. But the more I considered how it would actually work, the more I wondered: Who is this feature really for? Why not just switch your eSIM? As I read up on it, the wilder it seemed. And so I present my short list of potential iPhone Handoff users, ranked from least to most speculative.
You want to live the Duo lifestyle but you don’t want to give up your slab phone
Given that Apple announced Handoff when it unveiled the Duo, this is likely a scenario that Cupertino had in mind. You want the benefits of a medium phone that turns into a giant phone, but you also want to use your regular iPhone sometimes. Seems reasonable, I guess. Photo quality could be one motivator here since the Duo comes with downgraded camera hardware. Or maybe you just don’t want to carry the heavier, bulkier Duo on weekends. Maybe you just like gadgets and you want to switch between phones on a whim. The heart wants what the heart wants!
[Image: If you want a Duo but don’t want to carry this chunk around all the time, maybe iPhone Handoff is for you. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/268734_iPhone_Duo_handson_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
You have a work phone and a personal phone
I don’t know a lot of people who live the dual work/personal phone lifestyle, and I haven’t had a work phone since my BlackBerry Curve, rest its soul. But this could be a genuinely nice feature for someone who needs to keep two phones around but doesn’t want two phone numbers. But that’s the key — if your work phone already has a phone number through an account that’s managed by your employer, then Handoff as it works now isn’t an option. T-Mobile specifies that the secondary iPhone you’re using with Handoff “should not have any other service attached to it,” and that it can’t be used with a T-Mobile business account at launch. Kinda seems like a niche use case.
You have a small, fun iPhone that can’t hack it as your main phone
Do I have a personal bias here? Yes. But I don’t think I’m totally alone. Maybe you love your iPhone Air or you’re holding on to an iPhone Mini for dear life, neither of which has great battery life. So maybe Handoff lets you get a newer phone with better battery and cameras while still holding on to the smaller phone to use on lighter days or weekends. Could I set up my 13 Mini as a more minimalist phone without social media and switch back to it when I want to take a break? Totally. Do I have the self-discipline to actually do that on a regular basis? Uh, I plead the Fifth.
You work at Apple
Sometimes the ideas that come out of Cupertino seem to solve problems only an Apple employee could have. This feels like one of them. Do you read a lot of PDFs in business class? Do you have the disposable income to keep another iPhone around rather than trading it in to offset the cost of a $2,000 phone? Do you insist on elegant solutions even when they create unneeded complexity? Congratulations, you probably work for Apple.
But… why?
Realistically, I think very few people will want or need Handoff, and that’s fine. Did Apple engineers with multiple iPhones invent a feature to make their own lives easier? Maybe! They get to do that! But I have a theory for the rest of us who like the idea of a secondary iPhone and don’t work in a big glass circle: Try a cellular Apple Watch and see if that doesn’t do the trick.
An always-connected smartwatch remains the best minimalist phone, and I grow more convinced of this every year. You get access to messages, calling, music, and navigation. It already shares your phone number. And you can customize what notifications you’ll get so that it doesn’t bother you with Instagram pings if that’s the freedom you’re looking for.
But if you truly need two phones and you don’t want to pay your carrier for the privilege of having your line active on both, I have more good news: Swapping eSIMs between iPhones is reliable and free, and it only ruins your life if you’re a professional phone user.

title: Zelensky arrives in Brussels
body:
The head of state announced his arrival on Facebook , Ukrinform reports.
"Already in Brussels with my team to attend the European Council meeting and hold talks with our partners. Important meetings are scheduled for today with the NATO Secretary General, the President of France, and the prime ministers of Poland, Denmark, and Belgium. I will also have an audience with King Philippe of the Belgians. Tomorrow, meetings are planned with the presidents of the European Council and the European Commission, as well as the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland, and Sweden," Zelensky said.
He noted that everyone in Europe wants the war to end. To achieve this, the president said, strong signals are needed — including greater practical pressure on Russia and increased defense support for Ukraine.
"It is especially important now to act together to protect lives," the head of state said.
As previously reported, at the Ukraine–EU Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on October 13, Clusters 2 and 3 of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations were officially opened.
Cluster 2, Internal Market, forms the economic foundation of the accession process. It covers nine technical chapters governing a candidate country's integration into the EU single market.
Cluster 3, Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth, concerns the driving forces behind socioeconomic development during the EU accession process.
Ukraine's EU accession negotiating framework is divided into six thematic clusters, covering a total of 33 negotiating chapters.

title: 7 sailors missing as two ships off Romanian Black Sea coast catch fire amid drone incursion
body:
Seven sailors are missing from one of two tanker ships that caught fire in Romania's Black Sea overnight amid drone incursions into the country's airspace, Romanian officials said on Oct. 15.
The San Marino-flagged "Wine Trader," a chemical tanker, reported a fire aboard and eight people missing at 07:00 a.m. local time near the Romanian city of Sulina, a press release by Romania's naval authority said . The authority has since updated the numbers to seven missing.
Search and rescue operations were continuing, it added.
On the evening of Oct. 14, Romanian defense minister Radu Miruta said the country's authorities were also investigating a reported drone attack on an chemical tanker, the "Yara J," Romanian media Digi24 reported.
The Romanian Agency for the Rescue of Human Life on the Sea (ARSVOM) received a call for a rescue mission for the Comoros-flagged ship after it had caught fire.
The sailors from Syria, India, and Iran were all safe aboard, but said the ship was hit by a drone at about 08:25 p.m. local time, Digi24 said.
The leader of the Romanian Seafarers' Free Union, Adrian Mihalcioiu, considered the incident an intentional attack of a ship in Romanian territorial waters en route to Ukraine, Digi24 said.
Miruta said that no drone was seen approaching the ship on the defense ministry's radars, but at the same time pointed toward two drones that entered Romania's airspace at 10:26 p.m. local time, according to Digi24.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," he said. "It is a matter of significant gravity, as long as such incidents occur in Romanian territorial waters."
On Oct. 13, two cargo ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast overnight, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Radev called the attacks " absolutely unacceptable " and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union. Sofia is seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and improve its response capabilities.
Attacks by Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea intensified over the summer.
In July, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, a campaign targeting Russia's shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea .
Turkey called on Moscow and Kyiv in August to impose a moratorium on attacks against vessels, following a series of strikes in the region that involved Turkish-flagged ships.
While Kyiv has said it is ready to accept a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, Moscow has shown no interest in de-escalating the situation.
Ukraine established its own Black Sea maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia withdrew from a U.N.- and Turkey-brokered grain deal. Since then, Russia has regularly targeted ports and civilian shipping.

title: Canada will ‘end up being US 51st state’ – Trump
body: United States President Donald Trump has renewed his controversial suggestion that Canada could become the country’s 51st state, citing trade disputes and what he described as unfair treatment of the US by its northern neighbour. Trump made the remarks on Wednesday during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, where he listed several grievances against Canada, including tariffs on American goods and car manufacturers relocating production to the United States. “Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not anymore. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town,” he said as quoted by CTV News. The US president accused Canada of exploiting the American economy through tariffs on dairy products, claiming the restrictions applied to “anything past two bottles (of milk).” “They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” Trump said. “We don’t need them, but they need us.” He also questioned why the United States should lose billions of dollars supporting a country he said was not part of America. Trump further compared his remarks about Canada to his interest in Greenland, saying, “They’ll be doing something just like Greenland.” He added that the prospect “just adds to our beautiful plate,” referring to the United States, before declaring: “Our plate’s getting larger all the time.” The president also brought up the idea of renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” while discussing his longstanding complaints about Canada. Trump’s latest comments come amid escalating trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa, with Canadian officials repeatedly rejecting suggestions that the country could become part of the United States. In September, following Canada’s announcement of additional retaliatory tariffs on American goods, British Columbia Premier David Eby said the province would install signs at US border crossings declaring that it would “never the 51st state.” Lutnick also made a similar remark about Ontario last month, saying the province would be the “last out of our 51st states.” His comment followed Carney’s call for the Trump administration to take trade negotiations seriously. Trump revived his proposal in June, when Canada faced economic challenges that some economists said met the definition of a technical recession. The suggestion drew criticism from Canadian officials across the country. Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded at the time by saying the US president was “back on his high horse” and insisting that Canadian sovereignty was not for sale. “I can tell President Trump that will never, ever happen.” Vanguard News The post Canada will ‘end up being US 51st state’ – Trump appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Raul Daza, longtime congressman of Northern Samar, dies
body: MANILA, Philippines – Statesman Raul Daza, the longtime legislator from Northern Samar, has passed away, his family announced on Thursday, October 15. “He peacefully passed away at 91 years old. He was a devoted husband, loving father, grandfather, great-grandfather, son, brother, colleague, mentor and friend,” read the statement of his widow Teresita Ruiz and their family. “He leaves a legacy of integrity, courage, humility, empathy and commitment to democracy. He was a man who genuinely put himself in the shoes of others,” it added. Daza served seven non-consecutive terms in the House of Representatives between 1969 and 2019, and was, at the peak of his political career, speaker pro tempore from 1992 to 1998. He was also governor of Northern Samar from 2001 to 2010. He served as deputy minister of the Presidential Commission on Good Government, the agency tasked with going after the Marcos family’s ill-gotten wealth. “A steadfast defender of democracy, justice, and the rule of law, he stood firm in his convictions through the Martial Law years and political exile. He was a member of the Liberal Party (LP) for 61 years, beginning in 1965, and served as its president from 1994 to 1998,” the family’s statement reads. “Despite the many colors of politics, he firmly believed that we have only one flag and we have only one country,” it added. Daza was a certified public accountant and a lawyer who graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law. His family said he placed 11th in the Bar exam. After retiring from politics in 2019, he was succeeded in Congress by his son, Paul, and later his grandson, Niko. Details of his memorial are as follows: October 17 to 19: 3 to 10 pm, The Chapels at Heritage Park, Taguig October 18: 7 pm, Tribute by LP, The Chapels at Heritage Park, Taguig October 19: 10 am to 12 pm, Necrological Service, House of Representatives, Batasan Hills, Quezon City October 21 to 22: 1 pm (October 21) to 12 pm (October 22), Daza Residence in Daganas, Catarman, Northern Samar October 22 to 24: 1 pm (October 22) to 12 pm (October 24), Provincial Capitol Gymnatorium, Dalakit, Catarman, Northern Samar October 24: Funeral Mass at 1 pm, Our Lady of Annunciation Cathedral, Catarman, Northern Samar “Please omit flowers. Instead, kindly consider supporting God’s work through the Foundation for the Diocese of Catarman FDC, Inc. Metrobank Account No. 7346502823 ,” the family said. – Rappler.com

title: Trump’s envoy says he would welcome friendly between Russian, US national teams
body:
WASHINGTON, October 15. /TASS/. US Special Envoy for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli said in an interview with TASS he would welcome an international friendly between Russian and US national football teams.
"Football is the world’s game, and with FIFA and the relevant national federations, I would also welcome an international friendly between our two national teams," said the diplomat who works both in the White House and the US State Department.
"Perhaps sooner rather than later, our great nations can meet again on a football pitch - not to pretend that one match can resolve every disagreement, but to show that competition can reopen conversation. Football unites the world because it belongs to everyone. My role in Global Partnerships is to help turn good ideas into practical conversations. Hockey and football can both remind us that rivalry does not have to mean hostility," Zampolli stressed.

title: The New Foot Soldiers of Espionage: How ISI is Weaponizing Indian Social Media
body:
From Instagram Direct Messages (DMs) to digital wallets, how Pakistani intelligence is recruiting vulnerable youth for pocket-money espionage.

By Jai Kumar Verma 
Introduction - The Paradigm Shift
New Delhi. From Instagram DMs to digital wallets, how Pakistani intelligence is recruiting vulnerable youth for pocket-money espionage.

In a quiet town in Uttar Pradesh, an unemployed youth scrolls through Instagram, seeking validation and quick cash. He receives a friendly message praising his profile, followed by a seemingly harmless offer to take photos of a local railway station for a small fee. He accepts, unaware that this casual online connection is an Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) handler operating from Karachi. A quick UPI transfer drops a thousand rupees into his digital wallet, sealing his entry into a dark web of low-cost treason.
This chilling reality marks a structural shift in Pakistan’s ISI operations against India. Moving away from highly trained cross-border infiltrators and heavily armed foreign militants, the agency has embraced the modern "gig economy" of espionage. By weaponising popular social media platforms, the ISI now systematically targets and exploits vulnerable, ordinary Indian youth. It manipulates their economic anxieties, transforming unsuspecting smartphone users into decentralized, low-cost assets executing pocket-money treason from their own neighbourhoods.
ISI - Genesis and History 
The Directorate for ISI was established in 1948 as a direct consequence of the 1947–48 Indo-Pakistani War. During that initial conflict, Pakistan deployed armed tribal lashkars as a frontline vanguard to mask the direct operational involvement of its regular military troops.
There were serious coordination breakdowns between Pakistan’s Military Intelligence (MI) and the civilian Intelligence Bureau during this campaign, exposing critical gaps, prompting the state to centralize its apparatus. The resulting entity was structurally weaponized to unify tri-service military intelligence with a core, institutionalized mandate centred on countering India.
The classic modus operandi of this era relied heavily on high-cost, high-risk operations defined by massive financial investments and weapons smuggling pipelines. To execute these operations, ISI systematically infiltrated trained foreign nationals across the Line of Control (LoC) and other porous borders. These assets primarily included Pakistani operators, battle-hardened Afghan Mujahideen, and mercenaries recruited from Central Asian nations like Uzbekistan. Supported by heavily armed, centralised sleeper cells, these cross-border networks were strategically deployed to destabilize regional security and sustain long-term insurgencies within Indian territories.





High-Cost, High-Risk Operations: This phase demanded massive financial investments to bankroll sophisticated weapons smuggling pipelines and heavy ammunition stockpiles across the border. By establishing centralized sleeper cells within urban centers, the agency accepted extreme operational exposure, banking on high-impact sabotage and logistical longevity to tie down Indian security infrastructure. ISI also generated and used drug money in financing the terrorists outfits and their operations. 
The Strategic Pivot - Why the Old Model Failed
India’s strengthening of the Line of Control (LoC), through fencing, surveillance technology and layered counter-infiltration measures, has made traditional cross-border infiltration increasingly difficult and costly.
Simultaneously, international scrutiny raised the diplomatic and financial costs of Pakistan-linked terrorism. Pakistan was placed on the FATF grey list in 2018, while inadequate progress on its action plan created the risk of escalation to the FATF’s public statement, commonly described as the “black list.”
India has actively exposed and highlighted Pakistan’s terror-financing concerns in international forums.
The Strategic Shift
These constraints have increased the attractiveness of methods that require less physical infrastructure. Digital platforms, encrypted communications and online propaganda can facilitate recruitment, radicalisation, financing and coordination at comparatively low logistical cost.
For India, this has expanded the counter-terrorism challenge beyond the LoC into the digital domain. The emerging contest therefore increasingly combines physical border security with efforts to detect, disrupt and attribute online radicalisation and Pakistan-linked influence operations.
Recruitment Beyond Demographics and Religion





Modern digital subversion operates as an equal-opportunity threat. Recent investigations by India’s National Investigation Agency (NIA) and various state Anti-Terrorism Squads (ATS) reveal that digital traps do not discriminate by religions.
Arrests across India show Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs alike falling prey to hostile handlers. This indicates a paradigm shift where adversaries prioritize vulnerability and access over a target's religious or cultural background.
To cast this secular net, handlers deploy divergent recruitment pathways tailored to specific psychological profiles. The Ideological Route exploits domestic grievances and hyper-communal narratives to radicalize targets. Conversely, the Apolitical Route is entirely transactional. Handlers prey on widespread unemployment, poverty, or sheer financial greed, turning vulnerable citizens into insider threats through monetary rewards. For instance, several low-income youths and contract workers have been arrested for photographing sensitive infrastructure simply to earn quick digital payments.
Honeytraps
Finally, the Honey-Trap Route utilizes fake female profiles on social media platforms to manipulate lonely youths, defense hobbyists, or low-ranking security personnel. A prominent example includes the multi-state espionage cases where Indian Navy personnel were compromised via social media and blackmailed for leaking sensitive information.
Similarly, high-profile arrests of defense handlers and researchers, such as cases involving DRDO scientists and border-state residents, underscore how emotional manipulation and psychological grooming are weaponized to bypass national loyalty, proving that the digital threat environment is defined by strategic exploitation rather than ideology.
Anatomy of the Modern Cyber Trap - Step-by-Step Modus Operandi
While traditional intelligence operations historically relied on highly trained, deeply embedded espionage operatives, the digital age has democratised state-sponsored subversion. The shifting landscape of cross-border infiltration no longer demands physical crossings or complex deep-cover identities. Instead, hostile intelligence agencies have weaponized everyday technology, turning smartphones, digital payment apps, and algorithms into tools of warfare.
To understand how ordinary citizens, local labourers, and unsuspecting social media users are weaponized against their own country, it is critical to dissect the highly structured, predatory pipeline that defines modern hybrid warfare.





Step 1 - The Initial Digital Footprint: ISI-backed syndicates (like the notorious Shahzad Bhatti network) map Indian youth using automated tools to scan profiles showing financial distress, job searches, or specific geographical location tags near cantonments.
Step 2 - The "Engagement" Hook: Fake profiles approach targets by liking their reels, sending casual DMs, or offering small online gigs (e.g., data entry, local photography, freelance journalism). The recruiters also analyse the comments and through comments adjudge their anti-system, anti-government views and then these sentiments are exploited. 
Step 3 - The Odd Jobs Economy: The recruit is initially asked to perform completely legal or seemingly harmless tasks—taking photos of a crowded railway station, checking out a public park, buying a local SIM card, or putting up physical posters. For instance, operatives hire ragpickers and daily-wage labourers for ordinary labour tasks that mask sinister motives, such as fixing solar-powered, internet-enabled CCTV cameras on highways near military cantonments to stream live troop movements overseas.
Step 4 - The Micro-Payment Loophole: Recruits are paid paltry sums (ranging from ₹500 to ₹5,000) directly via UPI apps or cryptocurrency. These micro-transactions slip under the radar of traditional anti-money laundering monitoring systems.
Step 5 - The Escalation & Blackmail: Once the person accepts money, the handler demands sensitive information (like army convoy movements or coordinates of vital installations). If the recruit hesitates, they are blackmailed with their financial transaction history, leaving them trapped in treason. The network even extends to digital amplification, dragging in local social media influencers like Jyoti Mehrotra to distribute propaganda, inadvertently turning ordinary citizens into national security liabilities.
Centre bans Shahzad Bhatti Network under UAPA
The government unleashed a massive multi-state crackdown in August, which exposed the sheer scale of the network's hybrid operations.
Security agencies registered over 80 FIRs and arrested more than 200 operatives across 14 Indian states. The investigations uncovered that the network had graduated from organized crime to full-scale terrorism, acting as a crucial proxy for ISI. The syndicate has been linked to high-profile violent incidents across India, including grenade attacks in Punjab, an IED blast near Ambala's Baldev Nagar police station, and facilitating cross-border smuggling of drone-dropped weapons, explosives, and narcotics.





The legal landscape of Indian counter-terrorism reached a critical milestone on 16 September 2026.The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) issued a historic Gazette Notification formally declaring the Shahzad Bhatti Network (SBN) a banned terrorist organization under Section 35(1)(a) of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). Home Minister Amit Shah reiterated that the ban aligns with the government's strict "zero-tolerance" policy against cross-border terrorism. The ruling formally identifies the ISI-backed network, operated by gangster-turned-terrorist Shahzad Bhatti from abroad, as a direct threat to India's communal harmony, democratic structure, and internal security.
