title: Flying Wedge Defence Unveils India’s First AI- Piloted Fighter Jet Full-scale Prototype
body:
FWDA showcases India’s first AI-piloted fighter jet programme, with 1,500 kg-plus aircraft, 350 kg payload and autonomous combat architecture
 	The full-scale prototype was unveiled by the esteemed defence representative from the Ministry of Defence, India
 	The FWD Supreme programme positions India on among the top 4 programs that are parallel running in the globe
 	The company is looking to integrate the Manik Turbo fan developed by India’s DRDO to make it completely indigenous and remove any dependency or delay because of foreign components
 	FWD Supreme Lite, the smaller version said to be made for the Army is 90% indigenous and is running on a made in India engine manufacture by UMS, Coimbatore













































New Delhi, As the global defence industry moves towards artificial intelligence, autonomous aircraft and new models of combat aviation, an Indian AI warfare company, raised the curtain on its vision to give India its first AI-Piloted Fighter Jet.

Marking a historic milestone in the advancement of Indian defence and aerospace industry, Bengaluru based Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA), a defence tech company, unveiled the nation's first AI-piloted fighter jet programme, FWD Supreme, showcasing its full-scale static prototype, on Tuesday Oct 12.






















The event, held at Le Meridien, was graced by Mr A.Anbarasu (IAS), DG Acquisition; Air Marshal Prem Kumar, DG Weapon Systems; Lt. General Puneet Ahuja, Chief of Staff, Western Command and Major General Tarun Aggarwal, ADG Acquisition Tech. Mr Miguel Abreu, CEO of SketchPixel and Director of KEYDEF has also joined.

Being developed as an AI-powered autonomous fighter jet, FWD Supreme Heavy is specified to a 1,500 kg-plus class, with an approximate payload capacity of 350 kg. The aircraft is designed to feature a 5 kN propulsion system, a maximum speed of Mach 0.8 - 0.85 and a cruising speed of approximately 500 - 600 km/h. Expected to have a range exceeding 1,500 km and an endurance of more than two hours, the platform is supported by satellite communications (SATCOM).





















The aircraft will follow a flying-wing configuration incorporating an internal weapons bay, with approximate dimensions of 10 metres by 10 metres.
While speaking during the conference, Suhas Tejaskanda, FWDA, said, “FWD SUPREME represents our commitment to building advanced defence capabilities through Indian design, engineering and manufacturing. Our ambition is to develop a family of AI-piloted fighter aircraft that combines operational relevance with affordability. Through Operation 777, we aim to bring together international partners around an India-led development and manufacturing programme, while strengthening our country’s indigenous aerospace capabilities”.
“We are looking to integrate a DRDO engine to make it completely indigenous, reducing any delay and dependency on foreign components. FWD Supreme Lite which has already passed the taxi trials, is 90% indigenous, annd for now equipped with a Made in India engine manufactured by UMS, Coimbatore.”
The programme is being developed in phases. The lite version, said to be designed for the Army, is a 250 kg-class demonstrator, which also serves as a test bed. It has already completed taxi trials and is now being prepared for its first flight in the next two months











The Team
The event also introduced the esteemed team behind FWD Supreme, who have also designed Tejas Mark1 and AMCA and are now designing FWD Supreme.


The programme is being led by Mr Sr Girish Dixit , Secretary ADA and Control systems expert (former DRDO scientist), and is joined by distinguished aerospace scientists including Mr. V. Subba Rao, Outstanding Scientist (OS), Scientist ‘H’, Project Director, LCA Tejas programme; ⁠Mr. G. Radhakrishnan, Outstanding Scientist H Airframe & Structural Systems; ⁠Mr. Mahesh Prabhakar Padwale, Outstanding Scientist H, Propulsion & Engine-Integration; ⁠Mr. R.S. Rao, Outstanding Scientist H, Avionics and weapon integration collectively bringing decades of experience in military aviation, fighter aircraft development, aerospace engineering, and advanced defence technologies.












Giving heartiest congratulation for the unveiling at the event, chief guest, DG Acquisition, Mr A.Anbarasu said, “It makes us happy to see that the Indian defence ecosystem is growing at a stellar pace. We are living in an extraordinary situation. The war between Russia and Ukraine has continued even as





















years have passed. The conflict in the Middle East began earlier this year, and we do not know what trajectory it will take.”
He observed: “In this context, looking at the way forward put forth by Prime Minister and Defence Minister, today’s event fits very well within the policy enunciated by the Government of India. It amplifies the concept of ‘Owned by India’, producing and owning in India, and this is the direction in which we have to move forward in the coming days.”
Built and manufactured entirely in India, the programme positions India amongst the top 4 programs that are parallelly running in the globe and envisions to make advanced combat aviation more affordable through indigenous development, AI-enabled systems and scalable aircraft production.











Swarm of Jets 










At the core of FWD Supreme platforms is FWDA’s Mobbing Doctrine, an approach to air combat built around AI-piloted aircraft operating as a coordinated force. Instead of relying on a small number of high-value platforms, the doctrine envisions multiple autonomous aircraft working together like a swarm of jets, sharing information and making coordinated decisions in real time.
The objective is to change the economics of air combat by deploying capable, networked aircraft at scale, absorbing losses without losing the mission, and creating an operational advantage through numbers, autonomy and coordination.
The event progressed with a briefing on the programme's development, intended applications, affordability-led approach to combat aviation and future roadmap. The next phase of FWD Supreme will focus on technology development, testing and integration, alongside the development of the wider Supreme family of aircraft.
FWDA also plans to build international aerospace and manufacturing partnerships through Operation 777, with the aim of developing an India-led ecosystem for advanced combat aviation.

title: Destroying Jimi River for gold could cost us our lives – Asantehene
body: Asantehene Otumfuo Osei Tutu II has warned that illegal mining driven by unemployment could cost communities their lives if rivers like the Jimi are destroyed. Speaking after inspecting the heavily degraded Jimi River and the Jimi Dam near Obuasi, the Asantehene said he understands why many young people turn to galamsey, but cautioned that irresponsible mining will leave lasting consequences. “I understand illegal mining has become an option because many young people have no jobs. But we cannot continue to do that because the river is also relevant to our lives. If we destroy the river, what happens to us then? We will give birth to deformed babies,” Otumfuo said. The Asantehene was visibly distraught after seeing how illegal miners at Tasliman had diverted the course of the Jimi River with heaps of sand, causing siltation and threatening the Jimi Dam which treats water for over 200,000 people in Obuasi and Adansi. He was accosted by some youth at the dam during the inspection, which is part of the 153-hectare Jimi Land Reclamation and River Watercourse Rehabilitation Project, a pilot under the Green Ashanti Initiative which is being led by Oheneba Nana Kwaku Dua with support from AngloGold Ashanti. “I understand unemployment is a challenge, but we must also think about the damage we are doing to the river. We may get the money, but we will die after the environment is destroyed. I know that if there is no employment, the youth will always go and mine. But we should also know that the river cannot be destroyed,” he stressed. The King called for a balance between job creation and environmental protection, urging responsible mining practices. “We can find ways of mining responsibly. Because of gold, many are also felling their cocoa farms. We may end up destroying ourselves and the environment. I will plead with you, if you turn to galamsey due to unemployment, it must be done responsibly, without destroying the environment,” he appealed. Otumfuo said he will take the matter before his chiefs to deliberate on lasting solutions. The Jimi reclamation project is expected to restore degraded lands in six steps and provide alternative livelihoods through kenaf and other tree farming. Two Ministers, the Lands and Natural Resources Minister, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah and Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs Minister, Mahama Ayariga, joined the Asantehene on the tour, which started with briefings at AngloGold Ashanti and tree planting at Lot 1 of the project.

title: Could Israeli technology aid Saudi Arabia's struggles to stop Houthi missile attacks? - analysis
body: Houthi attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 8, 10, and 11 killed at least 16 people. The deadliest strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309 others. On October 13, another attack damaged an administrative building at Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran. Saudi forces have intercepted numerous incoming weapons, but others have reached their targets despite the billions of dollars the kingdom has spent on air defenses.Why are missiles and drones still getting through, and could Israeli technology help Saudi Arabia stop them?Israel has spent decades developing defenses against different types of aerial threats. Some have already been supplied to the United Arab Emirates. In May, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help defend the UAE against Iranian attacks.There have also been reports of Saudi-Israeli discussions about sharing intelligence through American military channels. Neither government has confirmed such an arrangement, but it raises the possibility of cooperation that would have been politically difficult to imagine only a few years ago.Why are Saudi defenses struggling?Saudi Arabia operates American-made Patriot missile batteries and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), which is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitude. The kingdom's first THAAD battery became operational in July 2025, according to the Saudi Press Agency.These systems provide substantial protection, but the Houthis have weapons designed to exploit different weaknesses.Ballistic missiles climb high into the atmosphere before descending at high speed toward their targets. Cruise missiles fly more like pilotless aircraft, sometimes close enough to the ground to escape radar detection until late in their flight. Drones can be smaller, slower, and much less expensive than the missiles used to shoot them down.A defender facing multiple weapon types at once must identify each threat, choose the right interceptor, and respond before the weapons reach their targets.A 2020 study by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, The Missile War in Yemen, documented the Houthis' growing arsenal of missiles and drones, developed with Iranian assistance, and their repeated attacks on Saudi territory.The Houthis have since improved their capabilities. Regional officials told the Associated Press that investigators believe drones were launched ahead of cruise and ballistic missiles during the recent attack on Riyadh's airport. If confirmed, the sequence would suggest an attempt to stretch Saudi defenses by presenting several threats in quick succession.The kingdom has faced similar problems before.After the September 2019 attacks on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities, Washington Institute for Near East Policy researchers Michael Knights and Conor Hiney examined gaps in Saudi radar coverage and weaknesses in the coordination of its defenses.The weapons appeared to approach from the north, while much of Saudi Arabia's defensive posture was oriented toward threats from the east. Low-flying missiles and drones could take advantage of radar blind spots created by terrain, the curvature of the Earth, and the limitations of individual sensors.The researchers recommended better coordination among existing radars, command systems, and interceptors, rather than relying solely on additional missile batteries.Saudi Arabia's geography presents another problem. The kingdom covers nearly 2.15 million square kilometers, approximately 78 times the combined land area of Israel and the West Bank. Its cities, airports, refineries, oil fields, military bases, and ports are scattered across enormous distances.Israel's much smaller geographic area lets some defensive systems cover several population centers or installations. Saudi Arabia needs far more widely distributed equipment, even though large stretches of sparsely populated desert do not require the same protection as major cities or oil facilities.Cost is another concern. An inexpensive drone can force defenders to fire an interceptor worth hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars.Dr. Sidharth Kaushal of Britain's Royal United Services Institute discussed the depletion of Gulf interceptor stocks and the difficulty of replacing them quickly in an April 2026 BBC interview. The Financial Times reported this week that Saudi Arabia was struggling with interceptor shortages and ongoing gaps in radar coverage.Interception does not always prevent casualties. On October 13, debris from intercepted cruise missiles injured four people and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to Saudi Civil Defense.Which Israeli systems could help?Israel's air defenses rely on several systems that operate at different ranges and altitudes. Iron Dome is the best known, but other Israeli weapons may be better suited to some of the threats Saudi Arabia faces.Iron Dome was developed to intercept short-range rockets. Its radar tracks incoming projectiles and calculates where they are likely to land, allowing the system to focus on threats to populated areas or key installations.Upgrades have expanded its ability to engage drones and cruise missiles. Iron Dome batteries could protect individual Saudi sites, but their coverage is too limited to defend much of the kingdom's territory.David's Sling, developed jointly by Israel and the United States, is designed to intercept cruise missiles, certain ballistic missiles, aircraft, and drones. Tests conducted in February 2026 included improvements intended to address newer aerial threats.Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 are intended mainly for ballistic missiles. Arrow 3 can intercept suitable targets outside the atmosphere, before they descend toward the ground. Israel has used Arrow-family defenses against missiles launched from Iran and Yemen.Such systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia's ballistic-missile defenses, but they would not solve the problem of detecting and intercepting a small drone approaching an airport at low altitude.Two less familiar Israeli products could be especially useful for defending individual installations.Rafael's mobile SPYDER system is designed to engage aircraft, drones, and cruise missiles. Israel Aerospace Industries manufactures Barak MX, which uses different interceptors against aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, and some ballistic threats.Either could potentially complement Saudi Arabia's existing defenses around oil facilities, airports, or military bases, provided the equipment could be integrated into the kingdom's command and radar networks.Iron Beam offers a different approach. Instead of firing an interceptor missile, it uses a powerful laser to destroy certain short-range threats. Israel delivered its first operational system to the military in December 2025.The attraction is partly financial: Firing a laser can cost far less than using a missile against a relatively inexpensive drone.Its limitations are substantial, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Lasers need a clear line of sight, and dust, haze, clouds, and distance can reduce their effectiveness. They cannot replace longer-range defenses against ballistic missiles.Israel also operates C-Dome, a naval adaptation of Iron Dome that could help protect ships and offshore installations.Which systems would be most useful to Saudi Arabia would depend on the targets it wanted to protect, the weapons it expected to face, and the equipment it already possessed.How has Israel helped defend the UAE?The United Arab Emirates offers the clearest example of Israeli air defense technology being used by an Arab country.After Houthi attacks on Abu Dhabi in early 2022, Israeli defense sources told Breaking Defense that an agreement to supply Rafael's SPYDER system was nearing completion. The publication subsequently reported that an Israeli-made Barak air defense system had been deployed in the UAE, although the precise model was not identified.The two countries had established diplomatic relations under the 2020 Abraham Accords, removing a major obstacle to military purchases.Their cooperation reportedly expanded during the 2026 war involving Iran.On May 12, Huckabee publicly confirmed that Israel had sent Iron Dome batteries and personnel to help operate them in the Emirates, according to the defense publication Janes.The Financial Times reported that Israel had supplied additional equipment, including a version of Iron Beam, surveillance technology, and real-time intelligence about Iranian missile launches.Those details have not all been independently confirmed. An October study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies discussed the reported laser and surveillance deployments but did not independently verify that they took place. Janes also noted that Huckabee's remarks did not confirm those specific transfers.There is no public accounting of how many incoming weapons were intercepted by Israeli systems operating in the UAE.Still, the deployment of Iron Dome batteries and personnel establishes that the Israeli-Emirati defense relationship has moved beyond ordinary equipment sales. That experience may offer lessons for Saudi Arabia, although Riyadh has not normalized relations with Israel.Could Saudi Arabia obtain Israeli assistance without normalizing relations?Intelligence sharing would probably be easier to arrange than a weapons sale.Information about missile launches and flight paths could potentially be relayed through American military channels, giving Saudi crews more time to prepare an interception without requiring Israeli launchers or personnel on Saudi territory.Regional arrangements already support this kind of cooperation. In January 2026, US Central Command announced the establishment of a multinational air- and missile-defense coordination cell at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. It aims to improve information sharing, joint planning, and coordination among regional military partners.Israeli media reports suggest that Saudi-Israeli intelligence cooperation may already be taking place.In September, The Jerusalem Post reported, citing a regional diplomat, that the two countries had discussed intelligence assistance through US Central Command. Ynet and Israel Hayom also reported, citing diplomatic and security sources, that Israeli intelligence was reaching Saudi Arabia through American channels.Neither government has publicly confirmed those accounts, and it is unclear what information, if any, is being shared.The Media Line reported in September that senior military commanders from Israel, Saudi Arabia, and six other Middle Eastern countries had attended a US-organized security meeting in Germany. US Central Command confirmed the gathering, but it did not establish a formal military alliance.Saudi political analyst Abdulaziz Alshaabani warned against assuming that such contacts would lead to open military cooperation.“Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” Alshaabani told The Media Line.Purchasing Israeli missile defenses would raise additional problems.Israel would have to authorize the export, and Saudi Arabia would need arrangements for training, maintenance, software, spare parts, and replacement interceptors. Some Israeli systems would also require American approval because of US involvement in their development.Germany's purchase of Arrow 3, for example, required Washington's consent.Political considerations could be harder to overcome than the technical requirements.Saudi Arabia has repeatedly insisted that diplomatic relations with Israel depend on the establishment of a Palestinian state. Its Foreign Ministry reiterated in February 2025 that it would not normalize relations without an independent Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.A publicly acknowledged purchase of Israeli weapons would be considerably more difficult for Riyadh to explain than intelligence cooperation conducted through American military channels.Saudi Arabia has not publicly announced an agreement to purchase Israeli missile defense systems, nor has it officially confirmed that negotiations for such a deal are underway.Would Israeli technology solve the problem?Israeli missile defense systems could strengthen Saudi Arabia's defenses, but acquiring and deploying them would take time.Saudi Arabia would need its own launchers, radars, trained crews, and interceptor supplies. Iron Dome batteries stationed in Israel are too far away to protect Riyadh. Any new equipment would also have to operate alongside the kingdom's existing Patriot and THAAD systems.Israel has its own shortages to consider after prolonged fighting with Iran and the Houthis. Its military needs to replenish interceptor stocks, which could limit the equipment available for export.Saudi Arabia is also seeking assistance from established defense partners, including the US, Britain, France, Turkey, and Pakistan. Those relationships offer alternatives without the political complications of buying weapons from Israel.Protecting civilians remains important even when interception fails. Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent attacks after September 29, leaving residents without official alerts before the deadly airport strikes. Warnings later resumed, including alerts issued by Saudi Civil Defense for Riyadh and Al-Kharj on October 14.For Saudi Arabia, earlier warning of incoming attacks may be more immediately useful than new missile batteries. Better intelligence could help its existing defenses respond sooner, while new equipment would require procurement, deployment, and training.A Saudi purchase of Israeli missile defenses would be a much bigger step, requiring decisions in Riyadh, Jerusalem, and possibly Washington. In the meantime, Saudi forces must defend widely separated cities and installations against missiles and drones that can approach from different directions, often with little warning.

title: Nigerian authors gain global distribution channel as Spotify launches audiobooks
body:
Nigerian authors and publishers have gained a new channel to reach international audiences after Spotify launched its audiobook service in the country.
The service, available in Nigeria on Wednesday, lets local publishers and self-published authors distribute audiobooks to listeners in more than 180 markets through Spotify for Authors.
Spotify said its audiobook partnerships are non-exclusive, meaning writers and publishers can distribute their works through other platforms.
The platform also provides audience information that can help authors and publishers understand who listens to their books and how audiences engage with them.
Spotify disclosed the development in a statement sent to PREMIUM TIMES, adding that its Nigerian catalogue contains more than 350,000 titles at launch.
The company said the collection would continue to expand as more local publishers, distributors and independent authors joined the service.
However, it did not disclose how many Nigerian-authored books were available at launch or provide details on the revenue-sharing arrangement for local authors and publishers.
Audiobooks offer authors an alternative way of reaching readers who may not have the time or inclination to engage with printed books.
The format also gives Nigerian writers a potential route to audiences outside the country without relying solely on physical distribution networks.
Through Spotify for Authors, publishers and self-published writers can upload their audiobooks and make them available alongside titles from international publishing markets.
Spotify’s Vice President of Audiobooks, Owen Smith, said the expansion was intended to connect writers and publishers with audiences they had previously been unable to reach.
He also noted that audiobooks could help people return to reading by letting them follow books during commutes, walks, and other daily activities.
Spotify said both Free and Premium users in Nigeria can access its audiobook catalogue. However, audiobook listening is not automatically included in an existing Premium subscription.
Users can purchase Audiobooks+, a monthly add-on providing 15 hours of audiobook listening for N2,300.
Only time actively spent listening is deducted from the monthly allowance. The allocated hours will reset at the end of every billing cycle, meaning unused listening time will not be carried into the next month.
Listeners who exhaust their monthly allowance can buy a 10-hour top-up for N2,700.
Listeners can also purchase individual audiobooks separately for continued access without relying on the monthly allowance.
Spotify did not provide a uniform price for individual titles, noting that pricing and access arrangements may differ by market and book.
The 15-hour monthly allowance may cover some books in full, while listeners choosing longer titles may need additional hours or more than one billing cycle to complete them.
Spotify has added a dedicated audiobook section to its app, where users can search for titles, browse categories, and get recommendations.
The recommendations will draw from a listener’s activity across audiobooks, music and podcasts.
One feature introduced with the rollout is Page Match, intended for people who alternate between printed or electronic books and audio editions.
Users can scan a book’s International Standard Book Number barcode and enter a page number to locate approximately the same point in its audiobook version.
Spotify said Page Match works in more than 30 languages and has been used by over one million readers.
The platform will also save a listener’s progress across compatible devices. A book started on a mobile phone can therefore be continued through a vehicle’s sound system, smart speaker or another connected device.
Other features include offline downloads and a sleep timer that automatically stops a book after a selected period.
Spotify said its service is accessible through more than 2,000 types of devices.
The Nigerian launch forms part of Spotify’s plan to expand its audiobook service from 22 countries to more than 180 markets by the end of 2026.
The company introduced audiobooks to Premium subscribers in selected countries three years ago as it continued expanding beyond music and podcasts.
Spotify said the number of people listening to audiobooks on its platform rose almost 40 per cent over the past year, while total listening hours rose more than 30 per cent.
It added that Audiobooks+, introduced just over a year ago, had attracted more than one million subscribers.
Spotify currently reports 777 million monthly users, including 300 million paying subscribers, across more than 180 markets.
Nigerian users must update the Spotify app and open the Audiobooks section, or search directly for a title.

title: Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ new Dubai hub highlights bold plans for regional growth
body: Dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical giant Pierre Fabre Laboratories Group has underlined its ambitions for growth in the Middle East and beyond with the opening of a new regional hub in Dubai. The company is a global player with its dermo-cosmetics brands Avène, Ducray, A-Derma, Klorane, and René Furterer, as well as its entire medical division specialising in oncology, dermatology, and rare diseases. Eric Ducournau, chief executive of Pierre Fabre Laboratories, officially inaugurated the new premises in the Landmark Group building near Dubai Marina. It is the headquarters of the French company’s Middle East, Africa, Russia, Turkey (MEART) subsidiary and will play a central role in its strategy to double its sales in six years. Ducournau said the move confirmed Pierre Fabre Laboratories’ bold expansion route, which also involves leveraging local expertise. “This investment clearly illustrates our desire to expand in this region, and Dubai is ideal for recruiting international talent from the UAE,” he told The National. Ducournau also said the country’s political stability, its investment in science, and its strong commitment to health care were the main reasons for choosing Dubai as the regional centre. Pierre Fabre Laboratories aims to continue its research into “the medicines of the future” while potentially adapting existing medical treatments and dermo-cosmetic products to regional needs. “We work closely with healthcare professionals to understand patients’ needs,” Ducournau said. “Here, the country invests in its hospital infrastructure, equipment, and training for doctors to treat patients. Our expertise, combined with that of healthcare professionals, will enable us to provide medicines and dermo-cosmetic care tailored to the needs of the local population.” Ducournau said: “What is important for a pharma company is to develop products, and to develop products you need scientific partnerships. “And in this area, countries are really investing; the level of hospitals is very high … the equipment, the training, the presence of highly experienced doctors. “The country is investing in good facilities to treat the population…that’s very important because you can’t develop the company more in the field of oncology or dermatology or rare diseases without this footprint in science.” A proud history Founded in 1961 by pharmacist Pierre Fabre, the group expanded from its initial activities in the field of pharmaceuticals to include dermo-cosmetics, investing heavily in research and development - as it continues to do today - particularly in the fields of oncology and dermatology. Upon his death in 2013, Pierre Fabre finalised the donation of his majority stake to the Pierre Fabre Foundation, which he had created. The foundation, recognised by the French government, works to improve access to essential medicines and doctors, particularly in Africa and East Asia. In Lebanon, for example, it has helped Syrian refugee populations in camps by providing them with care. Ducournau said the company is fully committed to caring for patients and its employees, as well as for the environment. Also a botanist by training, Fabre had a strong desire to respect nature, minimise his footprint, and support local communities. Pierre Fabre Laboratories invests in CSR (corporate social responsibility) initiatives and sources many of its active ingredients from plants. Today, the company operates directly in 44 countries and markets its products in all geographies. It is the world’s second-largest player in the dermo-cosmetics market and France’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical company, with an already significant presence in the Middle East. “We have grown significantly in Europe in recent years,” explained Ducournau. “Today, we are continuing our development in this region, as well as in China, Asia at large, and the United States. These regions are very important for the medicines of tomorrow.” In the Arabian Peninsula, Pierre Fabre Laboratories is renowned for its Avène brand - in sun protection and anti-ageing care - and for A-Derma in eczema care. The same is true for Ducray and René Furterer in the field of hair and scalp care, dandruff and hair loss, where the brands rank first in sales. Pierre Fabre Laboratories said it wants to forge scientific partnerships with key healthcare professionals and hospitals in the region to understand the needs of patients here and offer dermo-cosmetic care addressing their specific skin issues. It is also committed to supporting research in oncology and dermatology and wants to support clinical programmes in these areas with innovative partners. “To establish our brands, we seek to build long-term relationships with dermatologists and dermatology clinics, in particular by showing them how these formulas are formulated to be highly tolerable and clinically proven through clinical trials,” said Ducournau. He also confirmed digital technology as another priority area for investment. “We need to develop the online presence of our products and brands,” Ducournau continued. “To do this, we need to recruit talent with real digital and international expertise. “Dubai is an international city with a mix of different cultures. This is a real strength when we want to develop our presence across an entire region such as MEART. “You have a lot of people not from this area, but living in Dubai. And that creates a sort of international framework, which is very important, because we have a different culture mix here, and you want to reach very different parts of the population.” The chief executive said Pierre Fabre Laboratories plans to raise its revenue from €3.1 billion (Dh13.37 billion) in 2024 to a minimum of €5 billion (Dh21.8 billion) by 2032, ensuring a balanced split between its dermo-cosmetics and pharmaceutical activities. The company is investing heavily in developing new, increasingly targeted treatments for patients with cancer or rare diseases requiring targeted therapy. The same applies to dermo-cosmetic care. Ducournau said: “Each region has its own specific characteristics, whether in terms of skin types, lifestyle, or climate. “To establish ourselves, we need to understand these specific characteristics so that we can commercialise products locally that are tailored to them. “Patients in Europe or in the Middle East are not the same as those in America or Asia. So we really need to combine global scale and local grasp to do what’s right for patients, consumers and customers everywhere we operate.” While Ducournau has ruled out developing new brands locally for now, the Pierre Fabre Laboratories boss acknowledged need for localised manufacturing in the future. “Today, we are doing 71 per cent of our revenues internationally, but still manufacturing 95 per cent in France,” he said. “Tomorrow, we will have to manufacture closer to the area where the products are sold and consumed.” Ducournau highlighted that Pierre Fabre Laboratories has been present in this region since the 1980s, and its growth trajectory will continue to be deployed on the basis of the strong regional ties it has built. “I want to emphasise that we found good partners to establish our business here…we believe that this chain of distribution will extend in the region,” he said, re-confirming the Dubai hub’s role as part of the broader strategy to dramatically increase global footprint and revenues. Ducournau added: “We took 40 years to establish a certain level of revenue…and we want to double this in only six years. So, that’s the objective of this opening and this presence here.” This page was produced by The National in partnership with Pierre Fabre Laboratories.

title: Several countries, not just US, interested in purchasing Russian diesel
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. A number of countries, not just the US, are interested in purchasing Russian diesel fuel, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
"Russian diesel is demanded all over the world. Other consumers are also interested, of course," he said when asked whether other countries had shown interest.
Russian oil companies are ready to start supplying diesel fuel to global markets at any moment, with commercial terms being negotiated now, the official said.
Novak told TASS earlier that Russia would begin to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule immediately, being one of the key suppliers of this fuel to the global market. Moscow is ready to supply additionally 300,000 tons of diesel to the US market and to all partners in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons in December, while monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons, he added.
The Russian Energy Week (REW) International Forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16. It is being held with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Energy of the Russian Federation, and the Government of Moscow. The Roscongress Foundation organizes the forum. TASS is the information partner of Russian Energy Week.

title: Court adjourns Mohbad’s son’s DNA case
body:
The court handling the paternity dispute over Liam, the son of late Nigerian singer Ilerioluwa “ Mohbad ” Aloba, has adjourned the case until 16 November.
PREMIUM TIMES gathered that an Ikorodu Magistrates’ Court approved three DNA tests in February following renewed demands by the singer’s father, Joseph Aloba, for a court-supervised examination to establish his grandson’s paternity.
The court directed two facilities in the United Kingdom and another in the United States to conduct the tests. Representatives of the Aloba family and Wunmi, Mohbad’s widow, were present during the collection of samples.
In a video that went viral on Thursday, the family’s lawyer, Oladayo Ogungbe, appeared alongside Mr Aloba to explain the latest developments. He said the court postponed the proceedings after the family raised concerns about the proposed testing arrangements.
Mr Ogungbe said the court had assigned a newly appointed officer to address the family’s objections to the selected testing facility.
He also questioned the testing centre’s suitability, particularly because its director had allegedly featured in an earlier request relating to DNA testing.
Mr Ogungbe said: “What came up in court today is not the regular DNA; it is the reportedly secret DNA that was found by the other party while our own was still ongoing.
“We have filed a motion to be joined as an interested party, and the motion has now been adjourned to 16th of November 2026.”
Mr Ogungbe said the court had appointed another officer, who heard the family’s concerns and pledged to look into the matter before reporting back to them.
He added that the family would hold off on further action until it received her response.
According to him, the officer had clarified certain issues, but her explanations had not allayed the family’s concerns.
“However, the court has now appointed a new welfare officer. I don’t want to mention her name for private purposes. We met with her; she made a good impression, and she explained several things to us.
“And we made it known to her because a centre was picked in Lagos for the DNA. We have our reservation with respect to the director of that centre, who was the same person who conducted Mohbad’s former autopsy
According to the lawyer, the family sought clarification on the centre’s role in the process, particularly whether it would conduct the test or transfer the collected samples to another laboratory.
He added that they wanted details about the sample collection location, how the samples would be handled and how long it would take to deliver them to the laboratory.
“If the welfare officer at the centre can guarantee us, one, the procedure for taking the sample, the chain of custody, because it is clear they don’t do tissue-based DNA. They are merely a collection centre. They merely collect samples. So we want to be sure which particular laboratory overseas they want to transfer the sample to. What is the timeline for taking the sample and sending it?
“Because during the coroner inquest, it took more than six, eight months before the sample that was taken was transferred to the purported place that was used to conduct the autopsies. And unfortunately, Aloba wrote to them, and they said they never received any sample related to Mohbad”, Mr Ogungbe said.
Mr Ogungbe also called for openness in the process, emphasising that the samples must be handled appropriately and the test’s reliability protected.
The singer died on 12 September 2023, aged 27, and was laid to rest a day later. His body was exhumed nine days after his burial for an autopsy intended to help determine the cause of death.
However, three years later, questions surrounding his death remain unanswered. Outstanding issues include a paternity dispute involving his son, Liam, and disagreements over control and administration of his properties.
These unresolved matters have held up his final burial. The singer’s father has repeatedly said he will not bury his son until the cause of death is determined.
He continues to demand justice and answers about the events that preceded Mohbad’s death.

title: Former MP seeks independent bid, urges inclusive elections
body: Former South Sudanese lawmaker David Aruai De-Dau has called for greater political inclusion and protection of civic space ahead of the country’s planned December 2026 elections, as he seeks to contest a seat in the National Legislative Assembly as an independent candidate representing Twic East County in Jonglei State. De-Dau, who represented Constituency No. 10 in Twic East County under the 2018 peace agreement, told Radio Tamazuj on Thursday that he would run independently, citing divisions within his party and the wider opposition alliance. He said he had served in parliament since 2020 representing the South Sudan National Movement for Change (SSNMC), a member of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA). “I have been an MP since 2020 representing a party, South Sudan National Movement for Change, but not my people,” De-Dau said. “I thought it worth running as an independent candidate because my own party and SSOA as a whole suffered division, and that division is not good for my own or family legacy.” De-Dau, who previously served on parliament’s Specialized Standing Committee on Regional Integration and East African Affairs, said he is seeking a five-year term to pursue development projects without party bureaucracy. His priorities, if elected, would include improving peace and security, controlling floods through the proposed Bor-Khorfulus highway dyke project, promoting land-use planning and resettlement, and developing self-contained administrative units known as bomas . De-Dau said he is confident of his support among grassroots communities but questioned whether the broader electoral process would be inclusive. “The fact that there may be election in December is something to be responded to. As for its fairness, it depends on the level of participation because, as an MP, I will be elected by my people whom I trust,” he said. He also raised concerns about the presidential race, citing what he described as restrictions on the movement of presidential aspirant Kornelio Kon Ngu. “For the presidential election, of course there is unfairness, as we saw with the barring of presidential aspirant Kon Ngu from travelling,” De-Dau said. “I will not conclusively say that the election will be free or fair. But what I can confidently say is that it will not be an inclusive one,” he added. South Sudan is scheduled to hold general elections in December 2026, a vote expected to test the country’s political transition amid continuing concerns over political participation and the conditions required for a credible electoral process. The post Former MP seeks independent bid, urges inclusive elections appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
