title: Ukrainian Navy Strikes 6 Russian Su-34M Bombers Using Neptune Missiles
body:
Ukraine’s navy said on Thursday, Oct. 15, that an overnight Neptune missile strike hit six Russian Su-34M bombers at a military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.
The attack targeted Borisoglebsk airfield and also destroyed equipment used to support flight operations, the navy said in a statement posted on social media.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Secondary explosions and a fire were recorded at the airfield. The navy said information about the consequences of the strike was still being clarified.
“On the night of Oct. 14-15, the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ navy struck the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region using the Neptune coastal missile system,” it said.
The navy reported that six Su-34M aircraft had been hit without specifying the extent of damage – whether destroyed or simply damaged.
The Su-34M can carry multiple guided and unguided aerial bombs, as well as missiles of various types. It is described as one of Russia’s principal platforms for launching guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian defensive positions and communities near the front line.
The navy said hitting the bombers would weaken Russia’s aviation capabilities and reduce its ability to conduct tactical air operations in the affected sectors.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russia moves to enlist foreign influencers to convey viewpoint to blocked audiences
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The Russian Foreign Ministry has proposed forming a network of foreign bloggers and opinion leaders who can convey Russia’s viewpoint to the world, International Organizations Department Director Kirill Logvinov said at a meeting of the Federation Council’s Commission on Information Policy and Media Relations.
"To reach end consumers of information abroad, especially in unfriendly countries, in addition to major news outlets such as RT and Sputnik, it is necessary to form networks of foreign bloggers and opinion leaders who can convey messages from key Russian media outlets to their audiences," the diplomat said. "An audience that Russian media cannot currently reach under the conditions of the current Western information boycott," he noted.
According to Logvinov, this is facilitated by the fact that today "there is an increasingly noticeable shift from a predominantly Western-centric model of information dominance to a more complex system in which the nations of the Global South and East are asserting more and more loudly their right to independently determine priorities and strategies for advancing their sovereign interests."
"For decades, major Western news agencies, broadcasters, technology corporations, and think tanks have enjoyed significant advantages," the diplomat pointed out. "Their influence was supported by a well-developed infrastructure for funding the media, non-governmental organizations, and educational initiatives abroad. This allowed them to disseminate information and, to a large extent, set the parameters of the international agenda, impose their own discourse, and promote narratives that serve globalist interests," he stressed.

title: Parliament passes law on taxing international parcels worth up to €150
body:
According to Ukrinform, Danylo Hetmantsev, head of the parliamentary committee on finance, tax and customs policy, said on Telegram that 252 lawmakers supported draft law No. 16051‑1.
Yaroslav Zhelezniak, an MP from the Holos party, added that the document includes a provision reducing personal income tax from 18% to 5% for individuals renting out residential property. “The amendment by Shuliak was included in the parcels bill (No. 16051‑1): PIT for those renting out housing is reduced from 18% to 5% (the 5% military levy remains). The argument: ‘more opportunities for bringing the real‑estate market out of the shadows,’” Zhelezniak said. (Olena Shuliak is chairperson of the committee on state governance, local self‑government, regional development and urban planning — ed.)
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada previously twice rejected bills that would have abolished the tax exemption and introduced VAT on international parcels worth up to €150.

title: Five Questions for a General: Brigadier-General Pascal Godbout
body:
Welcome back to Five Questions for a General , a production of the Modern War Institute at West Point. This series features specially selected cadet hosts who are given an incredible professional development opportunity—to sit down with senior military officers and ask carefully crafted questions about everything from leadership to their unique experiences while serving to their expectations about the future of war.
In this episode, Cadet Olivia Hanson sits down with Brigadier-General Pascal Godbout, commandant of the Royal Military College of Canada, to discuss leadership, professional military education, and lessons learned from his thirty-six-year career in the Canadian Armed Forces. General Godbout reflects on his unlikely journey from a small town in Quebec to senior military leadership, explaining how a career initially motivated by educational opportunity became a lifelong commitment to service. He discusses the similarities and differences between Canadian and American military academies, emphasizing the importance of joint education, bilingualism, and developing leaders of character. Drawing on his experience at the North American Aerospace Defense Command, he highlights the importance of preparation, disciplined decision-making, and maintaining composure under pressure. He also shares lessons from commanding Joint Task Force North in the Canadian Arctic, where he learned the value of listening, respecting Indigenous communities, building trust, and understanding the human and environmental dimensions of military operations. Turning to leadership development, General Godbout stresses that technical competence must be complemented by emotional intelligence, ethical judgment, and the courage to confront misconduct. He also discusses ongoing reforms at the Royal Military College, including the need to challenge outdated traditions and strengthen accountability. Throughout the conversation, General Godbout emphasizes humility, adaptability, and lifelong learning, encouraging young officers to embrace unexpected opportunities, nurture professional relationships, and recognize that mistakes are an essential part of becoming an effective leader.

title: France’s detention of tanker requires international condemnation — Russian diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. France’s detention of the DF Peak tanker off the coast of Reunion is an act of piracy that should be condemned by all countries, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko told reporters.
"This is a blatant violation of international law and an absolutely unacceptable practice, which requires condemnation by the international community. Put simply, this is an act of piracy on the sea lanes," he pointed out.
The deputy foreign minister specified that "there were no Russian nationals on board, but that fact does not change our attitude toward such acts of piracy at sea." "This goes far beyond the bounds of international law; in particular, this is a blatant violation of the 1982 Convention. This is absolutely unacceptable," he stressed, adding that "no international conventions account for such actions."
"No matter how France frames this, I reiterate that this can only be classified as a flagrant violation of all the existing maritime regulations," the senior diplomat concluded.
The French Navy detained the DF Peak oil tanker over 450 nautical miles south of Reunion Island on the morning of October 12, President Emmanuel Macron wrote on X. He claimed the move was part of efforts to combat Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
The Russian embassy pointed out that France violated international law by detaining commercial vessels on the high seas, seeking to justify piracy by citing a UN convention.

title: High Court sets November 4 for ruling on Wontumi’s bail application
body: The Accra High Court has set November 4, 2026, to deliver its ruling on a bail application filed by former New Patriotic Party (NPP) Ashanti Regional Chairman, Bernard Antwi Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi. The application seeks his release from custody pending an appeal against his conviction and 20-year prison sentence for illegal mining-related offences linked to a concession at Samreboi in the Western Region. Mr Boasiako’s lawyers are seeking bail while the appeal process continues. The application was initially scheduled for hearing on August 19 but was adjourned after Mr Boasiako and his lead counsel, Samuel Atta Akyea, failed to appear in court. The matter was subsequently rescheduled to today. The Attorney-General has opposed the bail application, arguing that the former NPP regional chairman poses a flight risk. The court is expected to determine whether Mr Boasiako should be released on bail pending the outcome of his appeal when it delivers its ruling on November 4.

title: Two dead in Istanbul as torrential rain floods Turkish city
body: Torrential rainfall has killed two people and caused chaos across Istanbul, as the Turkish city recorded its highest rainfall in more than 80 years. Istanbul Governor Davut Gul instructed the city’s 16 million residents to stay at home unless outings were absolutely necessary, closed schools and banned motorbikes as 8,000 emergency service workers were sent out to deal with the effects of days of downpours. “Rainfall in Istanbul will continue for another two to three days. Do not go outside unless absolutely necessary,” Mr Gul told a press conference on Thursday morning. He said it was “the highest level of precipitation recorded in Istanbul since 1942”, when records began. Many areas of the city had received more than 100kg of rain per square metre, equivalent to 100mm, since early on Wednesday, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said. Rainfall in the Beykoz area of north-eastern Istanbul had reached 242kg per square metre, the authority said. An investigation has been launched following the death of a 14-year-old boy who died from electrocution after he stepped into a puddle in the Fatih district, the Istanbul governorship said. He was taken to hospital unconscious but could not be saved, the statement added. A 34-year-old died after slipping and hitting their head on a pavement. Footage published by state media showed cars drifting down streets, flooded homes and mosques, and passengers trapped in a bus with dirty flood water up to their knees. “Roads turned into lakes in many parts of the city,” state broadcaster TRT reported. At Istanbul Airport, 51 flights were diverted to alternative airports and another 19 flights were cancelled, Mr Gul said. The unusually heavy rain began on Tuesday and continued into Wednesday. Streets began to flood as drainage systems were overwhelmed. Istanbul residents received text messages from disaster management services on Wednesday evening warning them to stay away from riverbanks and flooded roads. Residents of basement apartments were told they “should take precautions”, while power cuts halted water supplies to homes and businesses in parts of the city, despite the torrential rain falling outside. Emergency services received more than 1,200 reports of flooding, 15 of landslides, 47 of people trapped and two of roofs blown off, the governorship said. Heavy flooding also made streets impassable in the city of Antalya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The state meteorological service issued warnings for more heavy rain and wind across the country on Thursday. Turkey has been experiencing an unusually wet 2026, the service said in a climate report released in September. Rainfall between January and August was 54 per cent higher than the 30-year average between 1991 and 2020. A third of the extreme weather events in the first eight months of the year were heavy rainfall and flooding.

title: Why American doctors travel to Israel for Magen David Adom training
body: The call was for a young man having a heart attack in an apartment near Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv.Dr. Michael Block, an American anesthesiologist, was riding with a Magen David Adom ambulance crew alongside his son, Evan, an EMT. The team started an IV, called ahead to Ichilov, and rushed the patient to the hospital.They didn't take him to the emergency room. He went straight to the catheterization lab.“He would have died had we not gotten there so fast,” Michael said. “The way that it was organized was just incredible. It doesn't happen in [the US].”Jeff Covitz had a similar reaction when he came to Israel.A paramedic captain with the San Francisco Fire Department, Jeff has spent years working on mass-casualty training and policy. He knew Israel handled major emergencies differently. He wanted to see how.“We run out of ambulances in San Francisco on your average Tuesday,” he said. “How do they get 30 ambulances to the scene in 10 minutes? That's amazing.”He was particularly struck by the speed. In an incident with 20 casualties, Jeff said, Israeli teams can sometimes triage, treat, and transport everyone from the scene in under 15 minutes.“In San Francisco, it would take us the better part of an hour,” he said.“I always knew the Israeli way was better, but I just wanted to know exactly why it's better and how they do it. What's their secret?”Jeff went looking for the answer through Magen David Adom's International Seminar on Emergency Response, which brings doctors, paramedics, and other medical professionals from around the world to Israel for an inside look at the country's emergency medical system.MDA will hold its 11th seminar from December 13 to 18, with a new group of medical professionals training in mass-casualty response, disaster preparedness, and search and rescue. They will participate in simulations, meet Israeli medical teams, visit MDA facilities and communities in southern Israel, and spend a day on MDA ambulances.Jeff found plenty that was different from home.In the US, EMS is largely local, and hospital care is highly specialized. Israel has a national emergency medical service that can move personnel, ambulances, and equipment quickly. During a mass-casualty event, hospitals can also shift their operations to take on large numbers of patients.This year's participants will also take part in a simulation at Jerusalem's Shaare Zedek Medical Center, offering a firsthand look at how an Israeli hospital prepares for a sudden influx of casualties.Some of that would be difficult to replicate in the United States. Other ideas, Jeff thought, were worth bringing back.But some of the most memorable lessons came from simply talking to the people who had been there.During a visit to southern Israel, Jeff met MDA paramedics who responded on Oct. 7. They told him about handling casualties at seven or eight locations at the same time, with terrorists still on the ground.“An MCI [mass casualty incident] on a good day is finding order in chaos,” Jeff said. “They were doing it across seven to eight different locations while there were roving bands of terrorists murdering everyone they encountered. “There's no training for that. They just made it up as they went along.”This year's program will include lessons from Israel's recent wars, mass-casualty simulations, and visits to MDA's Sderot station and sites in southern Israel.For Michael, who first attended the seminar in 2019, the experience ended up leading somewhere he hadn't expected.His son later volunteered with MDA, and the two eventually worked ambulance shifts together, including the heart attack call near Ichilov.Then, after Oct. 7, Michael came back.His parents were Holocaust survivors. His father was the only member of his family to survive Auschwitz, Dora, and Bergen-Belsen. Michael felt strongly that, as a Jewish physician, he should use the skills he had.He traveled to Israel three times to volunteer as an anesthesiologist at Ichilov while Israeli doctors were being called into military reserve duty.“As a Jewish physician, my parents were Holocaust survivors,” he said. “I really wanted to be in a Jewish state in Israel and just work side by side and take care of Israelis, Jews and non-Jews and everybody. “MDA really gave me that connection.”Michael thinks emergency physicians and trauma surgeons are obvious candidates for the seminar, but says they aren't the only ones who would benefit.“It could be anybody who's a doctor,” he said. “If you have an interest in prehospital care and emergency medical services, that's who should go.”Jeff apparently agrees. A Jewish affinity group he helped establish for San Francisco firefighters and other city employees is already funding another participant this year, with the goal of sending one or two people annually.Magen David Adom's 11th International Seminar on Emergency Response will take place Dec. 13-18, 2026. The $1,750 fee includes five nights of hotel accommodation, two meals per day, transportation, and program activities. Airfare and health insurance are not included.For information or to apply, contact Vicki Angel at vickia@mda.org.ilWritten in collaboration with MDA

title: RMB Nigeria Asset Management Wins Excellence Award
body: RMB Nigeria Asset Management Limited has been honoured with the Excellence in Investment Management award at the 2026 Banks and Other Financial Institutions (BAFI) Awards, celebrating the firm’s exceptional performance and dedication to delivering superior investment solutions. This prestigious category win recognises RMB Nigeria Asset Management’s rigorous investment expertise, disciplined risk management, and steadfast commitment to generating sustainable, long-term value for its clients. Commenting on the recognition, Chief Executive Officer of RMB Nigeria Asset Management Limited, Kike Mesubi, said: “This recognition reflects our commitment to disciplined investment management, informed decision-making and a clear understanding of our clients’ objectives. In a market shaped by changing economic conditions, our focus remains on applying rigorous analysis and sound risk management to deliver investment solutions aligned with our clients’ needs and long-term goals. We are proud of this recognition and remain committed to creating lasting value for the clients that place their trust in us.” Operating in a dynamic financial landscape, the firm offers a diverse suite of tailored investment solutions spanning money market, fixed income, bespoke solutions, access to offshore investments and alternative investment solutions. title: Depesha robot turns ‘deadly mission’ into routine work in special op — Rostec
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The risky evacuation of the wounded and the delivery of cargo during combat operations have become safer thanks to the Depesha ground robotic system developed by the High Precision Systems Holding Company (part of Rostec), the state corporation reported.
"The Depesha platform reduces risks to personnel. This robot is a true, highly maneuverable ‘unmanned taxi’ for ammunition and other cargo. It forges its own path even on broken roads and can haul about 100 kilograms of cargo over a distance of more than 20 kilometers. On the return trip, the vehicle is capable of evacuating a wounded person from under fire, either by carrying them directly or using an evacuation sling. The Depesha turns logistical support from a deadly mission into routine operations," the statement reads.
Rostec noted that this ground drone is also suitable for reconnaissance missions.
The Depesha was designed as a multifunctional system that can be adapted to various tasks thanks to its modular design. It can transport cargo, ammunition, provisions, and other supplies to the front, as well as evacuate the wounded from the battlefield. It is an independently sprung platform with enhanced maneuverability that can develop speeds of up to 30 km/h.

title: Gaza rebuilding efforts gain German support as Israel reportedly blocks international troop base
body: The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) and the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on Wednesday to establish a framework for cooperation on the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip.The MoU outlines the framework for cooperation as consisting of GIZ providing technical expertise and specialized consultations to the NCAG's Planning and Implementation Unit for the purpose of enabling Gaza's economic and municipal recovery.The signatories of the MoU were Dr. Ali Shaath, General Commissioner of the NCAG, and Dr. Alexander Zuliga, Country Director of the GIZ.At the signing ceremony, Shaath thanked Germany and the GIZ for their support and emphasized the importance of international partnership in enabling the NCAG to fulfill its mission of rebuilding Gaza.Also in attendance at the signing ceremony were Board of Peace Director-General Nickolay Mladenov; Martin Maute-Keiter, Head of Development Cooperation at the German Representative Office in Ramallah; Valerie Koppelle-El-Naji, Foreign Affairs Advisor at the German Embassy in Cairo; and the commissioners of the NCAG.Israel bars international military outpost construction in GazaThis comes after The Guardian reported on Wednesday that Israel has yet to allow the construction of a military outpost for international troops in the Gaza Strip, according to a source familiar with the matter.The outpost was the subject of the first construction contract issued in Gaza by US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace in August 2026. However, two months later, the source said Israel still hasn't allowed the project to move forward.“Israel won't open the border,” the source said, adding that contractors and trucks have been prevented from entering Gaza to begin construction.Sarah Moskowitz contributed to this report.

title: Kremlin Says Russia Restarts Diesel Exports After Deal With Trump
body:
The Kremlin said on Thursday that Russian diesel had begun to reach global markets following an agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, while Moscow partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from Oct. 10 following the agreement.
"The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call.
LSEG data showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk.
According to the shipping data, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on Tuesday and was heading towards Morocco.
Under the terms announced by Trump last Friday, Russia agreed to immediately release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel onto global markets, followed by an additional 500,000 metric tons in November.
The initial 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) is less than a day's supply for the U.S. transportation sector alone, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued a license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The deal has sparked pushback from European and Ukrainian officials, who argued that unlocking Russian energy revenues directly fuels the Kremlin’s war effort.
Russia has rejected European criticism of the diesel deal as "cynical," given that Europe continues to buy some Russia n oil and liquefied natural gas.
Peskov's comments came a day after Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the diesel supply deal with the U.S. would boost Russia’s economy and include direct exports to the U.S. market.
“Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy,” Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum in Moscow, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
“In accordance with the agreements, supplies will go to world markets, as well as the U.S. directly,” he said .
He added that Russia aims to restore monthly diesel exports to 3.5 million metric tons by the end of 2026, bringing its share of the global market above 10%.

title: Tetteh Kwetey files nomination for NDC Greater Accra Regional Chairmanship
body: Michael Tetteh Kwetey has officially filed his nomination to contest the Greater Accra Regional Chairmanship position of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), taking a significant step towards his ambition of leading the party in the region. In a statement announcing the development on Thursday, October 15, 2026, Mr Kwetey said he had submitted his nomination forms at the NDC Greater Accra Regional Office, marking an important milestone in his quest for the position. “One step ahead of a dream to be fulfilled soon, the hard work continues,” he stated, expressing optimism about his ambition and his determination to continue working towards its realisation. title: The Clear Corridor to Oke Mosan: How Ogun’s Political Calculus Shifted After the INEC Ballot Shake-Up
body: By Kunle Somorin History, as the venerable English historian Thomas Carlyle once postulated, is ultimately shaped by the interplay of persistent preparation and the sudden, unyielding turns of fate. In the fastidious arena of Nigerian democratic contestation, where political careers are routinely made or unmade at the stroke of an administrative pen, the electoral landscape of Ogun State has just witnessed a seismic reconfiguration. The release of the Independent National Electoral Commission’s final candidates list for the upcoming February 6 poll did not merely refine the contest; it fundamentally altered the gravitational laws of the Gateway State. With the dramatic administrative disqualification of the Peoples Democratic Party flagbearer, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu – whose campaign foundered upon the unyielding rocks of statutory compliance – the long-anticipated battle for Oke Mosan has dissolved into what looks unmistakably like a clear corridor for Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola, universally known as Yayi. To observe the swift collapse of the opposition’s vanguard is to witness a classic lesson in political vanity. For over two decades, the Adebutu political machine operated under the comfortable delusion that inherited wealth and periodic electoral vanity projects could substitute for systemic party building and rigorous legislative stewardship. His endless quest for the governorship had long assumed the tragicomic quality of Sisyphus rolling his boulder up the rocky heights of Olumo Rock, only to watch it inevitably slip from his grasp. Adebutu’s protracted struggle was defined less by ideological conviction than by an entrenched sense of elite entitlement – a belief that the governorship was a family birthright waiting to be claimed. Yet, as the proverb wisely admonish: one does not gauge the readiness of meat merely by its outer appearance. While Adebutu spent years navigating internal party squabbles, procedural blunders, and endless litigation, he failed to erect a resilient, legally watertight institutional apparatus capable of surviving the basic rigours of electoral regulation. His ultimate undoing by the fine print of the Electoral Act is not an act of political sabotage; it is the natural culmination of a long, chaotic campaign built upon shifting sand. In stark, deliberate contrast stands Senator Olamilekan Adeola, whose trajectory reads like a masterclass in pragmatic political investment and calculated expansion. Long before the INEC guidelines excised his chief antagonist from the ballot, Yayi had already redefined the parameters of representation across Ogun State. Critics and political opponents once sought to tether him to a catalog of whispers, weaponising regional parochialism and dredges of past legislative disputes to question his lineage and motives. Yet, in politics as in life, performance is the ultimate antidote to prejudice. Rather than engaging in the toxic mudslinging that so often characterises sub-national politics, Yayi adopted the philosophy of Niccolò Machiavelli, who observed that true authority is preserved through tangible virtue and visible beneficence. His systematically executed strategy was disarmingly simple: weaponise development. Across the length and breadth of Ogun State – from the industrial hubs of Ado-Odo/Ota to the agricultural stretches of Yewa, through the historic precincts of Abeokuta and down to the coastal fringes of Ijebu – Yayi unleashed an infrastructural and human capital intervention of unprecedented proportions. Transformers were planted in long-neglected rural corridors, primary health centres were rehabilitated, tertiary scholarships were distributed by the thousands, and massive road interventions were facilitated through legislative appropriations. He treated non-constituents with the same administrative urgency as his immediate constituency in Ogun West, effectively building a cross-zonal movement that transcended traditional senatorial fault lines. By the time the political establishment began to take stock of his ambitions, Yayi had entrenched himself in the daily livelihoods of the common folk. Consequently, the lingering inquisitions regarding his past and the tired campaigns of calumny simply evaporated under the heat of his sheer productivity. The voter on the street of Sagamu or Ilaro is rarely persuaded by abstract political philosophy; they care deeply about illuminated streets, functional clinics, and economic empowerment. Yayi provided all three in abundance. As the old Latin maxim goes, Res ipsa loquitur – the thing speaks for itself. As the political machinery prepares for the February 6 election, the road to the executive house at Oke Mosan appears remarkably unobstructed. The opposition front lies in a state of irreversible fragmentation, reduced to post-mortem legal gambits that arrive far too late to sway an electorate that has already moved on. The traditional fault lines that once split Ogun politics along rigid regional lines have been softened by Yayi’s broad-based, inclusive coalition, which seamlessly unites the political interests of the East, Central, and West. Senator Solomon Olamilekan Adeola is not merely riding a wave of political good fortune following an opponent’s administrative error. He is harvesting the yield of years of deliberate, calculated, and generous political investment. When the voters turn out on February 6, they will not be participating in a tense, nail-biting thriller. Instead, they will be ratifying a process whose conclusion was written months ago in the concrete, asphalt, and human lives transformed by a politician who understood that the shortest path to power is paved with genuine service to the people. Yes, Oke Mosan awaits its master builder. *Somorin is a veteran journalist

title: Injured in Kyiv's Pecherskyi district rises to 6 – mayor
body:
The number of people injured in Kyiv's Pechersk district, where an unmanned aerial vehicle crashed between residential buildings, has risen to six, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.

"The number of injured in Pechersk district has increased to six. Medics hospitalized three of the wounded," Klitschko wrote on his Telegram channel on Thursday.

Earlier, the mayor reported that due to the UAV crashing in an open area between buildings, the facade, part of the roof, and window glazing of a five-story building were damaged. Additionally, the facades of two three-story residential buildings near the crash site sustained damage, and a car caught fire in the courtyard. Five injuries had previously been reported.

According to police information, four of the six injured—a 68-year-old man and three women aged 24, 49, and 64—have been hospitalized.

title: N’Delta: Group Demands Equitable Distribution of Oil, Gas Pipeline Surveillance Contracts Among Stakeholders
body: *Says Urhobo, Isoko, Ilaje, Opobo, Bakassi, Ibibio, Efik, Ogoni communities should demand fair share of contracts As the debate for even distribution of oil and gas pipeline surveillance contracts in the Niger Delta region continues, the Initiator of “Guard Your Pipeline I Guard My Own Movement”, Fejiro Oliver, has urged the federal government to lay emphasis on the decentralisation of pipeline surveillance contracts which was originally driven by demands for fairness and equitable distribution of opportunities among oil-producing communities, rather than ethnic considerations. He listed the Urhobo, Isoko, Ilaje, Opobo, Bakassi, Ibibio, Efik and Ogoni communities among those he believed should be demanding a fair share of the contracts. He argued that the Eastern corridor, currently handled by PINL under Osahon Okunbo and, reportedly, the Olu of Warri, already provides opportunities for Edo and Itsekiri interests and should remain with them. At a media briefing in Abuja, Fejiro stated that he sought to clarify his position amid renewed controversy over the allocation of pipeline surveillance contracts and allegations concerning the amounts paid to contractors. He said the movement, which began in March, gained national attention and prompted the federal government, through the National Assembly, to convene what he described as an emergency town hall meeting to discuss the campaign’s demands. He said his group, the United Niger Delta Congress, was invited to the meeting and participated despite concerns that the process might not produce meaningful results. According to him, the central argument of the campaign was that Tantita Security Services and Maton Engineering should not exercise control over contracts worth about N2.1 trillion to protect pipelines passing through communities where other capable local contractors could perform the job. He said the campaign drew part of its justification from the Petroleum Industry Act, which he argued supported a more equitable approach to opportunities in oil-producing areas. Oliver also questioned the composition of the contractors initially engaged for the surveillance work, noting that two of the major contractors were associated with Ijaw interests, while PINL was led by Okunbo, whom he said was from Edo State with the Olu of Warri, an Itsekiri traditional ruler, serving as the company’s chairman. He said his concern was that “communities across the Niger Delta should have a fair opportunity to participate in pipeline surveillance activities, rather than allowing contracts to remain concentrated in the hands of a few interests”. The activist, however, said he was disturbed by recent media reports and social media discussions that, in his view, had distorted the original objectives of the campaign and turned the issue into a confrontation involving ethnic and commercial interests.

title: Zelensky announces resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries
body:
He made the remarks in an interview with the Financial Times , Ukrinform reports.
Zelensky stressed that, at Washington’s request, Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries for three days, while Russia continued to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“The ban [on strikes against oil refineries – ed.] is lifted. We’ve had enough,” the head of state said.
He emphasized that Ukraine had been ready to observe an “energy truce,” but Russia continued to attack Ukrainian businesses and energy facilities. Russian strikes had left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without electricity.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine would agree to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure only if the United States provided more missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
Commenting on the prospects for restoring relations with Washington following last week’s events, the Ukrainian leader stressed that this was not in his hands.
“We did not destroy any relations,” Zelensky said.
As Ukrinform reported, US President Donald Trump said on October 11 that an energy truce in the war between Russia and Ukraine would allegedly take effect on Sunday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had not known about such an arrangement, while confirming that Ukraine was ready for a truce if Russia also halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelensky said the Armed Forces of Ukraine had received the relevant orders following the US President’s statement.
On October 14, Zelensky reported that overnight Russia had used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against energy facilities and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the surrounding region and Kharkiv.

title: Moscow Court Places Prominent Economist Under House Arrest in Bribery Case
body:
A Moscow judge has placed prominent establishment economist Sergei Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest on bribery charges, the RBC news outlet reported Thursday, citing law enforcement sources.
Sinelnikov-Murylev, 66, is a senior researcher at the Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy and the former president of the Economic Development Ministry’s Russian Academy of Foreign Trade.
He received state awards and a presidential commendation in 2018 for contributing to Russia’s 2018-24 national development strategy. He also joined the government’s expert council in December 2022.
The Zamoskvoretsky District Court reportedly granted the investigation’s request to place Sinelnikov-Murylev under house arrest for two months.
The 66-year-old economist faces up to 15 years in prison if found guilty of receiving a large-scale bribe.
Specific details on the alleged bribe amount or the involved parties have not been disclosed . The Interfax news agency reported that the case material is available on the court’s website.
This is Sinelniov-Murylev’s second criminal prosecution in recent years. He was arrested in April 2023, and in March 2025 convicted of large-scale embezzlement and abuse of power, receiving a suspended prison sentence of five and a half years.
Sinelnikov-Murylev served as president, or rector, of the Russian Academy of Foreign Trade from 2007 to 2024, continuing there as chief researcher while also holding senior research roles at the Gaidar Institute.
According to RBC, Sinelnikov-Murylev in 2017 ranked third among Russia’s wealthiest university rectors with an annual income of 53.4 million rubles ($638,700 at the current exchange rate). He attributed the earnings primarily to research and teaching activities at the time.

title: ‘Deadly consequences’: How lack of proper prison in Abkhazia leads to further crimes
body: The recent murder of a Russian tourist has exposed problems with prison sentences in Abkhazia . Edgar Abukhba , who stands accused of murdering Amina Bikbova , received a nine-year sentence for a previous serious crime. In practice, however, he served only half that time. This proved fatal for his next victim. Amina’s murder prompted Abkhazian society to take a closer look at how courts enforce their rulings. It emerged that in Abkhazia, a sentence tells you very little about how long someone will actually spend in prison. The republic has no proper prison, and a complicated system of “penitentiary arithmetic” determines how much time a person spends behind bars. Even those who apply the rules struggle to make sense of them. One last coffee Amina Bikbova’s family had a rule: call her mother every evening. The 26-year-old followed it without fail when she travelled to Abkhazia with her friend Adila for a holiday in September 2026. But one evening, she did not call and failed to answer her phone either. The next day, her phone remained silent. Her family then realised that something serious had happened. Amina Bikbova The circumstances surrounding Amina’s final day are known from accounts given by her family and witness testimony reported by Abkhazian and Russian media. Amina and Adila met Edgar Abukhba, a 25-year-old fruit seller. A couple of days later, he invited Amina for coffee. Adila says she tried to talk her friend out of going, but failed. Amina went to meet Edgar and never returned. During his initial questioning, he denied any wrongdoing. He claimed that he and Amina had simply had coffee, after which she got into someone’s car and drove away. Investigators quickly disproved this account, and Edgar admitted that they had argued, that he had strangled Amina and left her body in bushes beside the road. Man who killed Russian tourist in Abkhazia could face life sentence but serve just eight years Edgar Abukhba is accused of murdering 26-year-old Amina Bikbova in Abkhazia. He previously served time for a brutal rape, and lawyers say the court will take this into account. A familiar name Edgar Abukhba For Abkhazians who follow local crime reports, the surname Abukhba sounded familiar. In July 2019, a 24-year-old Russian tourist suffered a brutal attack in central Sukhum. Her assailants beat, raped and robbed her. Everyone familiar with the case said they had rarely encountered such brutality. Authorities arrested Edgar Abukhba on suspicion of the crime. The case took more than two years to reach court, and in 2021 a judge sentenced him to nine years in prison . If the nine-year sentence is counted from 2019, when Abukhba entered pre-trial detention, he should not have been released before 2028. Yet by the summer of 2026, he was already selling fruit in Gagra. Sentences without a prison Court rulings specify the regime under which a convicted person must serve their sentence, and this affects the time they spend in prison. But Abkhazia has no prison colony with different security regimes, which creates confusion. Officials recalculate sentences differently depending on how much time a prisoner has spent under various conditions. The final figure depends on the coefficient they apply and can differ significantly from the court’s verdict. Got that? No, of course not. For anyone unfamiliar with the system, it is almost impossible to understand. Even staff at the relevant institutions struggle to explain on the spot how they calculate a particular sentence, how long a specific prisoner will serve and when they will be released. Perhaps this explains why a man who, on paper, received a nine-year prison sentence attacked another woman long before that term had expired. Juvenile crime in Georgia: Why is it so high — and what can be done about it? Statistics point to a growing trend in juvenile crime, with the number of offences doubling over four years. Leniency vs prudence There is another legal complication in Edgar Abukhba’s case. He was still a minor when he committed his first crime, and under Abkhazian law, courts must not take juvenile convictions into account in the future. There are two opposing views on this rule. The logic of juvenile justice holds that a teenager’s actions should not determine the rest of their life. But this approach conflicts with public safety concerns, which suggest that authorities cannot simply ignore a proven threat posed by an individual. Many countries face this dilemma, but they also assess risks before releasing offenders and supervise them afterwards. They may also restrict where former prisoners can work or live and impose other measures. Abkhazia, however, has no such safeguards in place. A tarnished reputation Cynical as it may sound, Abkhazia’s tourism sector — and, consequently, its budget — can also be counted among the “victims” of this tragedy. Abkhazia effectively lives off Russian tourists, who provide the republic’s main source of income. Its reputation as a safe holiday destination is vital to its survival. Now, Amina Bikbova’s murder has left a major black mark on that reputation. This is particularly troubling because it is not the first attack on tourists. Russian tourist shot in Abkhazia over bare torso – why are local authorities covering it up? Social media claims high-ranking official involved in shooting of Russian tourist in Abkhazia Tourists may forgive reckless taxi drivers or poor service. But they are unlikely to accept the idea that killers who have not served their full sentences can freely walk the streets in search of new victims. Many Abkhazian lawyers believe the authorities should publish a breakdown of Edgar Abukhba’s first sentence, including the coefficients they applied and his release date. In other words, they should at least explain why he regained his freedom so quickly. Perhaps the authorities should also review the system for calculating prison sentences. Better still, they should finally build a proper prison colony so that no one has to perform these calculations in the first place. The public, meanwhile, wants an open trial in this case. People are waiting for an explanation of how this mysterious coefficient can allow rapists and murderers to walk free earlier than petty thieves. title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
body:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham says goodbye to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after their meeting at 10 Downing Street in London, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Alberto Pezzali/AP hide caption
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

title: Ukraine destroys 4 Russian Su-34 bomber jets, damages 2 with Neptune missile, Zelensky says
body:
An overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
"The Russians used them (the Su-34Ms) to terrorize our people. These aircraft were ready for new strikes on Ukraine and were equipped with aerial bombs," Zelensky said .
"Russia is dragging out the war, therefore, our long-range operations will continue," he added.
The attack was carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system, Ukraine's naval forces said on Telegram . Ukraine's General Staff said that explosions and a fire were recorded on the airfield territory.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev warned several times of a drone attack. Online footage of the attack filmed by local residents showed explosions and a large fire at the airfield. The Borisoglebsk military airfield is about 370 kilometers (about 230 miles) from the front line.
Neptune is Ukraine's ground-launched, domestically produced anti-ship cruise missile with a maximum range of several hundred kilometers which it used in April 2022 to sink Russia's Black Sea flagship, the Moskva.
In 2025, Ukraine unveiled an upgraded version of the missile, which had already demonstrated a range of 1,000 kilometers (620 miles). In March 2025, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system had successfully completed testing and would be deployed for combat use.
The Su-34M is a heavily modernized, upgraded variant of the baseline Su-34 fighter-bomber. The Russian Su-34 is a Russian medium-range fighter-bomber. Ukrainian forces have targeted the warplanes in attacks on Russian military airfields and have reported downing the jets on several occasions.

Big Walk ’s co-op multiplayer walking adventure has proved popular since launching in August, but Xbox players have been excluded from the fun — and now the game’s creators have explained why. Developer House House said in a blog post that it decided not to release Big Walk on Xbox consoles in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which has called to boycott Microsoft, including products under the company’s gaming division.
Microsoft was named a priority BDS target in June last year over contracts it has with the Israeli military and government , with the boycott specifically calling out Xbox consoles and Game Pass subscriptions, gaming franchises owned by Microsoft, and any gaming accessories produced by the company. Microsoft’s involvement with Israel has also been protested by its own employees , and the company has fired staffers for participating in pro-Palestine demonstrations.
Here’s what House House said regarding its participation in the boycott:
It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions. This decision means that some people will miss out on playing Big Walk with their friends, and we understand the disappointment we’re causing. We are disappointed too.
We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.
We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free.
Big Walk is playable on Microsoft’s Windows operating system, however, as it’s available to download via Steam . We’ve asked House House why it hasn’t excluded Big Walk from Windows and will update if we hear back.

title: Microsoft Defender for Linux
body:
As more developers begin to use Linux desktops, they become more attractive to attackers: high-privilege, high-value, and easy for admins to overlook. A developer using Linux for day-to-day development may interact with source code repositories, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, cloud infrastructure, container environments and internal development platforms. If their workstation is compromised, an attacker doesn’t just gain access to a laptop, but a foothold in the pipelines that build and ship the organization’s software. As Linux adoption expands beyond the data center, organizations need a consistent approach to protecting Linux wherever it is used.
That’s why we’ve extended our industry-leading endpoint protection in Microsoft Defender, bringing enterprise-grade protection, detection, vulnerability management and response capabilities to Linux workstations.
Defender support for Linux workstations spans all three key areas of endpoint security:
The result is broader Linux protection, delivered through the tools and processes security teams already trust.
With Defender on Linux desktops, organizations can:
Defender protects Linux desktops with the same deployment organizations already use to protect Linux servers. There is no separate desktop-specific agent to deploy or maintain, and existing deployment packages, deployment methods and security capabilities on Linux servers extend directly to Linux workstations.
Defender automatically identifies whether a Linux device is a server or a workstation, so devices appear correctly within inventory and security workflows without any additional administrative effort. With Microsoft Defender, security operations teams can gain visibility into Linux workstations alongside the rest of their enterprise endpoint estate. They can respond through a single portal, whether Linux is running in the data centre, in the cloud, or on an engineer’s desk.
Defender support is based on the underlying Linux distribution and kernel version, regardless of the desktop environment running on top of the distribution. Every distribution currently supported by Microsoft Defender on Linux servers is supported on Linux desktops as well — including RHEL, CentOS, Ubuntu, Debian, SLES, Fedora and Oracle Linux, running GNOME, KDE or other desktop environments.
Defender on Linux desktops requires the standalone Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 or Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 .
If your organization runs Linux on developer, engineering or security desktops, now is the time to close that visibility gap. To join the public preview, onboard eligible Linux workstations using any of the existing deployment methods. Before you begin, review what’s new in Defender and complete the pre-requisites .
This is another step towards our vision of helping organizations secure every endpoint, no matter which operating system or platform.

Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters.
