title: Hormuz matters but UAE has more than one gateway, economy minister says
body: The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism. “ Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai . “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.” It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years. Before the Iran war , roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28. But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said. The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains. It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah , outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman. If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said. Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added. However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy. With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”. Tourism rebound anticipated In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity. The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict. With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year. The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”. Economic football The International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted. The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.” For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital. On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”. As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

title: KOSOVO: Major General Roberto Vergori took the helm of the NATO-led KFOR mission
body: PRISTINA . Major General Roberto Vergori, from Italy, yesterday, took the helm of the NATO-led KFOR mission, at a change of command ceremony held at KFOR Headquarters, in Pristina. He succeeds Major General Özkan Ulutaş, from Türkiye. The Commander of Allied Joint Force Command Naples, Admiral George M. Wikoff, presided over the ceremony The Commander of Allied Joint Force Command Naples, Admiral George M. Wikoff, presided over the ceremony. Representatives of the institutions in Kosovo and of the international community were in attendance. Admiral Wikoff paid tribute to Major General Özkan Ulutaş’s leadership and service during the KFOR change of command ceremony and welcomed his successor, Major General Roberto Vergori. Major General Roberto Vergori, new KFOR Commander He praised Major General Ulutaş’s commitment throughout two tours as KFOR Commander, highlighting his engagement with communities across Kosovo and his work to strengthen relationships with the Kosovo Police and the EU Rule of Law Mission (EULEX). “He did so with initiative, adaptability, and selfless commitment to the mission and to those under his charge,” Admiral Wikoff said. The Admiral also recognised the sacrifices of KFOR personnel and their families. Reflecting on KFOR’s continued contribution to a safe and secure environment for all communities in Kosovo, Admiral Wikoff highlighted the ongoing optimisation of the mission to maximise its effectiveness. He expressed confidence in Major General Vergori’s leadership and reaffirmed the support of Allied Joint Force Command Naples. “Roberto, thank you for accepting this responsibility,” Admiral Wikoff said. Major General Ulutaş pointed out: “Throughout, KFOR stood laser-focused on the pursuit of a single goal: contributing to lasting security for all people and communities living in Kosovo, and freedom of movement, in accordance with our long-standing UN Mandate; KFOR also continued to support the EU-facilitated dialogue between Belgrade and Pristina.” Major General Vergori emphasised that KFOR personnel “remain deeply committed to fulfilling our UN mandate, in contributing to create the right conditions for a future in which new generations can enjoy the full benefits of lasting peace, democracy, and prosperity.” The security situation in Kosovo has remained generally stable and has continued to improve. In June, NATO announced that it would optimise KFOR’s posture, to ensure that the mission remains fit for purpose. This process is ongoing. It entails a gradual and calibrated adjustment of KFOR’s posture and strength, over the following year. It is conditions-based and can be reversed, if security developments require it. The Western Balkans is a region of strategic importance for NATO. The Alliance’s commitment to regional stability is steadfast, and KFOR continues to contribute to lasting security for all people and communities living in Kosovo, and freedom of movement, in accordance with our long-standing UN Mandate, based on UN Security Council Resolution 1244 of 1999, at all times, impartially, and in close coordination with the Kosovo Police and the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX), in their respective roles as security responders. ©RIPRODUZIONE RISERVATA L'articolo KOSOVO: Major General Roberto Vergori took the helm of the NATO-led KFOR mission proviene da Report Difesa .

title: Zamfara Govt To Distribute Dangote Shares To 36,176 Residents
body: The Zamfara State Government says it has approved a plan to provide 36,176 residents with shares in Dangote Group as part of efforts to promote financial inclusion and economic empowerment. The initiative, according to the State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Relief Matters, is designed to enable residents to participate in investment opportunities and benefit from the country’s business sector. Under the programme, each beneficiary is expected to receive approximately 20 shares through the Dangote Initial Public Offering, in collaboration with the state ministries of Humanitarian Affairs and Finance, as well as the Zamfara Investment Company. The programme will be coordinated by the Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs, Salisu Musa Tsafe Kainuwa. According to the ministry, the beneficiaries will be drawn from the state’s 14 local government areas, with 2,261 beneficiaries allocated to each of 13 local government areas, while Gusau, the state capital, will have 4,522 beneficiaries. The ministry also said the programme would accommodate persons with disabilities as part of efforts to ensure inclusiveness. It added that the initiative was approved by Governor Dauda Lawal to expand residents’ access to investment opportunities and promote financial independence. The state government says the investment scheme forms part of its broader humanitarian and economic empowerment agenda, with additional programmes targeting women and young people expected to be announced. However, the ministry’s claims about the number of shares, expected returns and payment to the company could not be independently verified at the time of this report. The statement did not provide details of the share price, the total investment involved or the mechanism for distributing the shares to beneficiaries. The post Zamfara Govt To Distribute Dangote Shares To 36,176 Residents appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Korle Bu appeals for more doctors, nurses as A&E Centre struggles under pressure
body: Management of the Korle Bu Teaching Hospital has appealed to the government for additional doctors and nurses to address persistent staffing shortages and ease pressure on its Accident and Emergency (A&E) Centre. The hospital’s Chief Executive Officer, Dr Yakubu Seidu Adam, said the recruitment of more permanent medical personnel was critical to improving emergency care and strengthening services at the country’s leading referral facility. Speaking during an engagement with Parliament’s Health Committee, Dr Adam disclosed that the hospital’s 64-bed Accident and Emergency Centre was struggling to cope with the growing number of accident victims and other emergency cases referred from different parts of the country. He noted that the limited number of permanent medical staff was placing additional pressure on critical departments, particularly the A&E Centre and the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). According to him, although the hospital has a significant number of doctors, a large proportion are medical trainees who leave after completing their training, creating challenges for the facility’s long-term staffing needs. “This is a training institution. We have a number of doctors, but when we look at our numbers, most of them are not our staff. It’s a training institution; they come, we train them, and they go,” he said. Dr Adam stressed that the hospital needed to recruit more medical officers who could provide sustained support for emergency and intensive care services, rather than relying heavily on doctors undergoing training. He said management had already brought the staffing concerns to the attention of the hospital’s Director of Human Resources and the Minister of Health, but the meeting with Parliament’s Health Committee provided another opportunity to highlight the urgent need for additional personnel. The Chief Executive Officer also called for more nurses to complement the efforts of existing medical staff and ensure patients receive timely and effective treatment. The appeal comes as the hospital continues to face pressure on its emergency care services due to the volume of cases it handles from across the country. Beyond addressing the shortage of personnel, management has also advocated the construction of a new facility to ease congestion and improve the hospital’s capacity to manage emergency cases. The proposed intervention, alongside the recruitment of additional doctors and nurses, is expected to help strengthen emergency care delivery at the country’s premier referral hospital.

title: AFCON 2027Q: ‘I’m optimistic Black Stars can turn things around’ – Agyemang-Badu
body: Former Ghana midfielder Emmanuel Agyemang-Badu is confident that the Black Stars can recover from their poor start and secure qualification for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON). Ghana made a disastrous start to their Group C campaign, losing 2-0 away to Côte d’Ivoire before falling to a humiliating 4-2 defeat against The Gambia at the Accra Sports Stadium. With zero points from their opening two matches, the team now sits at the bottom of Group C, with four matches left to play. However, Agyemang-Badu, a key midfielder in Ghana’s historic 2009 FIFA U-20 World Cup-winning squad, believes the team can still bounce back when they face Somalia in a decisive double-header in November. “I’m optimistic that the Black Stars might win their next games,” Agyemang-Badu told Ahenfie Sports. “Let’s give local players the chance they deserve,” he added. Agyemang-Badu’s comments come shortly after the Ghana Football Association (GFA) and head coach Carlos Queiroz mutually agreed to part ways following the disastrous start to the qualifiers. A five-member committee has since been set up to interview candidates and recommend a permanent replacement. In the meantime, an interim technical team is expected to lead the Black Stars in their upcoming fixtures against Somalia.

title: Africa buys and makes weapons, but who controls them?
body:
At the height of some of the most consequential military campaigns the Nigerian Air Force had against Boko Haram in 2016, some of Nigeria’s Franco-German Alpha Jet aircraft, acquired decades earlier, were close to being grounded in the middle of the war. The reason for this was not a missing missile or a failed engine; it was something as mundane as a brake assembly. Combat aircraft central to the counter-insurgency campaign were about to become unusable because we didn’t have the capacity internally to manufacture the required brake assemblies. This may seem shocking to many, but it is a normal occurrence for many countries that rely on external military equipment and support and are not conscious about building internal capacity, which in turn builds sovereignty.
The solution to this dilemma for the Nigerian Air Force did not arrive in the form of another multibillion-dollar aircraft purchase, a foreign military package, or a televised arms delivery. It came quietly through Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing; the Nigerian company was brought in to adapt and overhaul brake assemblies, including work associated with the MB-339 brake system, helping return Alpha Jets to service. It was a small industrial intervention with a large strategic meaning: a locally available solution helped restore combat availability where foreign dependency had created a vulnerability.
A fighter aircraft, even when purchased fully and handed over, is not sovereign simply because a government owns it. Without the ability to repair, sustain and adapt it, the platform remains only as useful as the supply chain behind it.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), military expenditure across Africa is rising: $58.2 billion in 2025, up 8.5 percent in one year and 45 percent since 2016. Conflicts are also becoming more technologically intensive, and governments are acquiring drones, attack helicopters, surveillance systems and precision munitions from an expanding range of suppliers. At the same time, African firms are beginning to manufacture airframes, batteries, vehicles, components and autonomous systems.
Yet the most consequential parts of military power are often the least visible: the sensors, encryption keys, software, datalinks, munitions, technical documentation, spare parts and maintenance approvals that determine whether a weapon can actually operate.
Nigeria’s Alpha Jet episode exposes a distinction that is becoming more urgent across African defense: possessing a platform is not the same as controlling the capability it represents. A state may own an aircraft, drone or helicopter, but still depend on outsiders for the parts, software, encryption, sensors, maintenance approvals, munitions and export permissions that make it operational.
Africa is buying more weapons and beginning to make some of them. The harder question is where the decisive bottlenecks sit, and who has the power to close them.
Africa as a combat market, not simply an arms market
Africa’s wars are no longer only places where weapons are used. They are increasingly places where the value, credibility and consequences of modern military systems are established in real time. Take Sudan: Al Jazeera’s analysis of ACLED data recorded more than 1,000 drone attacks from April 2023 to January 2026, devastating & displacing the civilian population, showing how quickly externally supplied drone capability has become central to the conflict.
In 2025, Amnesty International identified China’s GB50A guided bomb in Sudan, describing it as the weapon’s first documented use in an active conflict. The Sudanese Armed Forces have used Turkish and Iranian systems, while the Rapid Support Forces have obtained increasingly sophisticated Chinese-origin weapons and drones through external supply networks; Sudan is therefore not only a civil war. It is an arena in which networked, externally supplied military technologies are being operationalized and assessed.
The Sahel reveals a related shift. Burkina Faso acquired Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones for counterinsurgency operations, while Human Rights Watch documented civilian deaths from several strikes in 2023. At the same time, armed groups are using commercial quadcopters, modified first-person-view drones and improvised munitions for reconnaissance, propaganda and attack. The barrier to launching an aerial strike has fallen, but the institutions required to use force responsibly, accurately and accountably have not kept pace.
A drone that performs in Sudan or the Sahel does more than alter a battlefield. It produces operational evidence, commercial visibility and demand from governments confronting similar threats. But battlefield visibility should not be mistaken for sovereign capability. The strategic question is not merely whether an African state can buy, fly or assemble a drone. It is whether it can sustain, modify, arm, secure and operate it when a supplier, software vendor or export-control authority no longer agrees.
The platform is only the visible layer of military power
A drone operator may sit in Abuja, Bamako or Khartoum while directing an aircraft hundreds of kilometers away. That control depends on a datalink carrying commands to the platform and imagery back to the operator. If that link is insecure, unavailable, or hacked by a third party, the operator may be holding the controls at that moment without truly owning the system; at any point, his operations may be compromised or even undermined. A country should always ask itself: Who owns encryption keys? Can the military change mission software? Can our engineers connect a different camera, local radio, or new weapon systems? Does the supplier control updates or diagnostic access? Where is mission data stored, and are we the only ones with access? Because it is increasingly becoming obvious that in the digital age, sovereignty is the right to control & debug your own weapon.
When a country does a military parade, people mistake the visible layer – weapons and machinery – as the most important layer of their defense platforms, but it truly isn’t; it is only the visible layer of their military strength, easier to photograph for propaganda and also the easiest layer to buy. But these platforms are only the outer shell. Its real power sits in less visible places: the camera that finds a target at night, the encrypted link that carries orders, the software that controls its mission, the foreign factory that makes a replacement part, and the government that can approve or deny its export. To put simply, a country may own the machine while somebody else controls its eyes, voice, brain, ammunition, or heartbeat.
Türkiye’s Bayraktar TB2 has become a symbol of an indigenous drone industry, but it also demonstrated the vulnerability of the supply chain beneath its airframe. In 2020, Canada suspended export permits connected to military goods and technology for Türkiye after allegations that Canadian-made sensors had been fitted to Azerbaijani drones in the Nagorno-Karabakh war. After its review, Canada canceled permits after saying the use of the technology was inconsistent with Canadian foreign policy and Türkiye’s end-use assurances. Canada’s report did not present the matter as a simple, conclusively proven case of diversion; it said the available information could be interpreted as inconsistent with those assurances.
The more important lesson is what happened next. Türkiye moved to integrate ASELSAN’s domestically developed CATS electro-optical system into TB2 deliveries, reducing its exposure at that particular bottleneck. Dependency, then, is not permanent. It can trigger substitution, investment, and learning. The question for African defense industries is whether local production is reducing dependence at similarly critical points, or merely relocating final assembly.
Even when a platform is assembled in Africa, the chain of permission may still pass through several capitals: the country that licenses the engine, the company that supplies the sensor, the owner of the software, the satellite provider carrying the signal, and the state that regulates a critical material or component.
Military sovereignty is not a purchase receipt; it is the degree to which a state controls, or has reliable alternatives for, the decisive parts of its capability chain: the platform, sensors and software, communications and data links, munitions, sustainment, technical data and political permission.
The point is not autarky, i.e complete self-sufficiency with zero need for external trade. No modern military makes or controls everything it uses. The test is narrower and more demanding: where are the bottlenecks that could ground a fleet, disable a system, block an upgrade or halt a sale, and who has the power to close them?
Some of these dependencies are technical, embedded in software, sensors, intellectual property and engineering access. Others are contractual and political, embedded in maintenance agreements, export licenses and continuing supplier approval.
Control can also fail even when the technology itself is fully functional. Maintenance contracts, export permissions and supplier support can determine whether an owned platform remains operational. South Africa offers a particularly clear example.
South Africa possessed a world-class fighter force on paper. In practice, a break in the support chain made ownership of part of that force largely ceremonial. The country did not lose its Gripen fighter jets in combat. No enemy destroyed them on the runway. The country still owned them.
Yet in 2021, its Gripen fleet was grounded because support arrangements with Saab and GKN, the original airframe and engine manufacturers, had lapsed amid funding and contractual problems. Support was subsequently restored under new contracts, but the episode remains glaring: ownership does not guarantee operational availability.
A newer aircraft does not automatically guarantee a more sovereign capability. Nigeria’s A-29 Super Tucanos arrived through a United States Foreign Military Sale; that deal was never just about the twelve aircraft; it bundled munitions, training, spare parts, infrastructure, contractor logistics and maintenance support into one operating system. Then, in October 2024, the Nigerian Air Force had to engage the United States Office of Security Cooperation as the existing contract extension approached its end, seeking a seamless transition for maintenance and sustainability. The purchase was completed years earlier; the capability, however, remained an ongoing negotiation that ended up leaving our Military capability as a subscription that needs to be periodically renewed.
The dependency chain does not disappear when a country becomes an exporter. It can simply move deeper into the weapon. Nigeria operates Türkiye’s T129 ATAK attack helicopter, a platform marketed as part of Türkiye’s growing defense-industrial rise. But its CTS800 engine was developed by LHTEC, a joint venture involving Honeywell and Rolls-Royce. That meant export permissions tied to the engine, which incorporates US-controlled technology, became a strategic issue for Türkiye and potential export customers. In the exact same light, Pakistan’s proposed acquisition of 30 T129 helicopters was delayed for years because the required United States export license for the engines was not granted.
Nigeria could buy a Turkish helicopter, but the ability to manufacture and export that helicopter was still shaped partly by decisions beyond Türkiye. Supplier diversification matters, but it is not always independence. Sometimes dependency has simply been pushed deeper into the bill of materials.
Africa’s emerging defense manufacturers, including Paramount Group, DICON and Terra, matter for more than the symbolism of local production. Their strategic value lies in whether they reduce reliance on the bottlenecks that determine operational availability, adaptation and political freedom of action. The degree of sovereignty lies not in how much of a weapon is manufactured locally, but in which decisive dependencies remain externally controlled.
African-made is not yet sovereign: manufacturing, procurement and the struggle for control
Africa has an emerging defense-industrial base, which changes the equation for the continent because it can move expertise, production, maintenance and adoption closer to users, but a locally assembled platform is not automatically a sovereign capability; what makes the difference is control of critical bottlenecks and whether governments procure not only weapons but also the right skill, infrastructure, software, spare parts and long-term funding that makes the weapons usable and readily available. Dependency is often designed across international supply chains, but it is also reproduced by domestic procurement decisions, weak sustainment planning, and political preference for visible acquisitions over invisible readiness.
“African-made” is a great starting point; Terra closed its $52 million seed round in August 2026 after raising an additional $18 million in strategic funding. It has framed itself around autonomous systems and ArtemisOS, its AI-powered operating system; its significance is not that Nigeria has found a local company to print a Nigerian label on imported equipment. Its significance lies in whether the partnership can transfer control over the capabilities that determine availability, adaptation, and operational independence.
Terra illustrates both the promise and the limits of the new model. Its proposition combines autonomous systems with software through ArtemisOS, while its DICON partnership formally includes local production, R&D, training and technology transfer. That potentially moves more than final assembly into Nigeria: it could build a domestic base of engineers, maintainers, system integrators and users capable of adapting equipment to Nigerian conditions. But the strategic test remains unresolved. Can Nigerian personnel service the platform without external approval? Can they modify mission software, integrate another sensor, extend or modify, access diagnostics, retain critical mission data, and replace a restricted component? The answers reveal where localization ends, and meaningful control begins.
“African-made” should therefore be treated not as a marketing claim, but as an auditable supply-chain question, where important questions can be verified, such as: What share of the system is manufactured, designed, and tested locally? Who owns the IP and software? Which components require external export approval? Can Nigerian engineers independently repair, modify, and upgrade it? Can the country sustain production during a diplomatic rupture or supply interruption? The answers reveal where localization ends, and meaningful control begins.
South Africa offers the historical warning. It built one of the continent’s most substantial defense-industrial bases, Denel, with capabilities accumulated over decades; it was intended to preserve a sovereign defense-industrial base spanning artillery, ammunition, missile technologies, aerospace maintenance and design authority over locally developed systems. South Africa did not merely import defense equipment: through the industrial ecosystem Denel inherited and later managed, it developed indigenous competence in weapons production, aerospace support, testing and systems integration.
The problem, however, is that much of this capability has since been allowed to erode. Years of governance failures, particularly during the state-capture period, undermined Denel’s credibility with customers, suppliers and financiers, while skilled engineers, artisans and programme managers departed and infrastructure aged. The consequence is larger than the decline of a state-owned company: it risks the loss of strategic skills, intellectual property and the local ability to maintain, upgrade and adapt critical defense systems without deeper dependence on foreign suppliers. The lesson is severe: sovereignty is not acquired once. It must be funded, staffed, ordered from, and continuously exercised.
A Nation’s defense vulnerability rarely arrives with a warning. It appears when a platform needs a part that cannot be sourced, when a weapon needs a software update its operator cannot access without external authorisation or validation, when a weapons system cannot be modified without permission from a company or government thousands of kilometers away. In those moments, the difference between possessing military hardware and controlling military capability becomes impossible to ignore.
Africa’s defence future will not be decided only by the size of its procurement budgets or the number of platforms produced locally. It will be decided by whether its states can repair, adapt, secure, arm, and sustain the systems they depend on, on their own terms and when circumstances demand it.
No country can produce everything. But every country can identify the dependencies it cannot afford to lose. Until that becomes the measure of defense policy, Africa may continue to own the machines while others retain control over their limits.
Babatunde Fatai works at the intersection of emerging technologies, strategy, innovation and defence in Africa. He writes about emerging tech, defence-tech policy, dual-use technology, venture capital dynamics, and the systems that shape how innovation succeeds or fails on the continent.
He can be found on YouTube, Substack , LinkedIn , and X .

title: Kenora residents applaud ‘fantastic’ move to permanent daylight time
body:
Whether it’s watching NHL games, appointment scheduling or just less confusion, some residents of Kenora, Ont. say permanent daylight saving time is a “fantastic” move.
Scott Green, owner and operator of Lake of the Woods Marina and Service Centre, said Wednesday he loves that the community will stick to the same time zone as Manitoba going forward.
“I love it as long as we’re still matching with Winnipeg and Manitoba,” he said in an interview with Global News.
Green added his marina also has a restaurant and bar that hosts Winnipeg Jets watch parties during the season. He said with the permanent change, watching the game “just times out better.” He added it will also make it easier if travelling to Winnipeg for a Jets game.
The Ontario government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian would stop the twice-annual clock changes and stay on daylight time year-round.
Kenora, along with communities like Dryden, Sioux Lookout and Pickle Lake, currently observe Central daylight time, the same time zone observed by Manitoba.
That means come Nov. 1, it will be the same time in Manitoba and all of Ontario. But when the clocks tick forward an hour in March for much of Ontario, people in the province’s northwest and Manitoba won’t have to adjust their time.
Tuesday’s announcement from the Ontario government came after what MPP for Kenora-Rainy River Greg Rickford says was “unanimous consensus” across the region.
“Through the collective efforts of communities and First Nations across the northwest, we’ve led a process to build consensus the right way, with detailed and nuanced considerations,” said Rickford in a news release on Tuesday.
Several communities conducted surveys from residents to see if there was support for a change.
In Kenora, about 6,000 of its approximately 16,000 residents responded to the survey and Mayor Andrew Poirier told Global News 93 per cent supported keeping daylight time.
“So we listened to the people of Kenora and we stand by what we did as a council to pass a resolution that we would look at aligning ourselves with Manitoba, and so did lots of our neighbouring communities, which was very important in this whole process,” Poirier said Wednesday.
The mayor said though in Ontario, Kenora is “much more linked” to Winnipeg or Manitoba.
He said whether during much of summer or winter, travel between the Ontario and Manitoba communities is “like the 401” highway that runs through Toronto.
“That’s how much economic activity, tourism, visiting back and forth occurs between the two jurisdictions,” Poirier said.
But it’s not just economic activity, it’s also logistical aspects like medical appointments or tourist bookings.
“So when somebody makes an appointment for a boat taxi or a tour and we are on the same page for a time frame (or) often Zoom meetings if people are calling out of Toronto you have to definitely make sure that you’re on the same time,” said Green. “So this will really make things efficient and a lot easier for bookings and communications.”
Northwestern Ontario is not the only region to observe a different timezone than the majority of the province it is in.
The Kootenay Region in B.C. is on Mountain Time, Nunavik and Lower North Shore in Quebec are on Atlantic Time and parts of Labrador are also on Atlantic Time unlike the rest of Newfoundland and southeastern Labrador.
Golden, B.C., Coun. Wesley Routley said his community last month originally planned to shift to Mountain standard time permanently on Nov. 1, but after hearing from hundreds of residents, council reversed course.
He said people felt they wanted to be aligned with other communities like the Regional District of East Kootenay to the south and other communities on Mountain daylight time.
He added a large share of visitors to Golden are from Alberta, so it could limit confusion for people visiting the community.
British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba have each announced they will remain on daylight time starting Nov. 1, with Saskatchewan having observed central standard time year-round. The remaining provinces have said in recent months no changes are expected though discussions and analyses are ongoing.

title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
body: Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation. But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both. At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements NVIDIA is joining the campaign , providing: Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources Skills, training and technical support Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent Support for startups and ecosystem development “Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.” Open Models NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology. NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub. Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit , NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences. Skills and Training Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute. The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline. Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs . Access to Compute NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France , Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services. The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education. AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results. The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe. Sweden AI Factory , one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets. As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing , the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre , the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY . AI Infrastructure Expansion To top it all off, NVIDIA is powering Europe’s most ambitious expansion of AI infrastructure to date, with 35 supercomputers currently in development across the continent — the largest single-year buildout of supercomputing capacity Europe has ever seen. Together, these systems will equip over 3 million researchers with next-generation infrastructure, accelerating discovery across domains from climate science and drug development to materials research and beyond. Explore NVIDIA technologies for science and open source courseware , and find hands-on training through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute . Follow the European Commission’s RAISE Pledging Initiative . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: Press review: Ukraine, EU push peace away and US blacks out Kiev's missile sight
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Ukraine and the EU continue to show that they are not peace-minded; the US is no longer warning Kiev about Russian missile attacks; and Germany’s authorities face mounting pressure over the Nord Stream blast investigation. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
The course of action pursued by Kiev and its European allies is doing little to bring talks on Ukraine any closer. The European Union is discussing a new package of sanctions on Moscow and may try to undermine the recently agreed diesel deal between Russia and the United States, moves that Moscow sees as contradicting its claims that it is ready to join peace talks, Izvestia writes.
There is no basis for negotiations with Britain, Germany and France at this point as they seem content to speak to Moscow through a series of ultimatums and meaningless sanction packages, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told the newspaper.
The EU is set to continue its policy of maximum military and diplomatic support for Kiev, regardless of the cost. Besides, European elites will keep strengthening ties between Ukraine and the EU in various ways, European studies expert Mikhail Kucherov noted.
Meanwhile, efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict remain at a standstill. It's worth noting that the US appears to have adopted a different approach than Europe, resuming partial pressure on the Kiev regime. First, media reports surfaced that Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing with the Ukrainian armed forces, followed by reports from the Ukrainian military of disruptions and restrictions affecting satellite internet services.
Oleg Karpovich, department head at the Diplomatic Academy of the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, pointed out that this pressure on Kiev was aimed primarily at ending strikes on Russian oil refineries and stabilizing diesel prices. Still, the parties remain too far apart to reach a settlement. The US has repeatedly flip-flopped on who it supports, but this has never led to any long-term solutions, the expert stressed.
If Russia and the US develop a joint peace plan, the EU is unlikely to accept it because the bloc’s interests are now totally opposed to those of Moscow, Kucherov said. Europe may instead seek to strengthen the Coalition of the Willing and draw up its own peace initiative.
A shift toward a really effective settlement process would require the US to put pressure on its allies in Europe. It’s the Europeans that are showing no willingness to engage in dialogue with Russia, seeking to increase support for Kiev and prevent the normalization of relations between Moscow and Washington.
Kiev hasn't received any US data on Russian ballistic missile launches for at least two days, the Ukrainian authorities claim. On October 14, Ukraine also reported disruptions to Starlink services, Kommersant writes.
Reports emerged on October 9 that the United States could suspend weapons supplies and intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kiev halted strikes on Russian refineries. On October 12, the Ukrainian armed forces reported that they had not received US early-warning data on ballistic missile attacks. As a result, air raid sirens in Kiev were not activated until after the strike. The next day, the same thing happened.
Ilya Kramnik, a research fellow with the Center for North American Studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, explained that the early-warning data in question allows air defense systems to be readied by identifying the direction of the attack and its potential targets.
"If early-warning data is unavailable, enemy missiles can be detected only once they enter the range of air defense radars, which significantly complicates defensive operations. Radars must remain on permanently, which increases the risk of their being destroyed. Besides, continuous operation wears those systems down," the expert said. This will further aggravate Ukraine’s already existing air defense problems, he added.
Talking about Starlink disruptions, Kramnik said they will affect the Ukrainian army’s strike capabilities. A speed limit of 160 km/h means that Kiev will not be able to use Starlink terminals on drones. This would reduce Ukraine’s ability to strike targets within its 1991 borders, Kramnik explained, as Starlink services are not available in Russian territory.
"This is a fairly powerful way to hint at the need to accept certain conditions for participating in the peace process. However, it remains to be seen if this works as intended," the expert concluded.
The Alternative for Germany party plans to send further inquiries to the German government regarding the investigation into the explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a Bundestag member told Izvestia . Meanwhile, the trial of the first defendant in the case has begun in Hamburg. According to the prosecution, the act of sabotage was carried out on orders from Kiev.
The trial has drawn unprecedented attention for several reasons. First, the case concerns one of the largest acts of international sabotage in modern history. Second, the defendant is a citizen of Ukraine, a country that Berlin has been actively supporting for several years, by providing both funds and weapons.
However, even if evidence is found of government involvement in the attack, Germany is unlikely to change its policy on assistance to Kiev, said Fyodor Basov, a senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations. In his view, the attack against the Nord Stream pipelines could be classified as an act of self-defense. Still, the trial has just begun, and it is too early to assess its potential political consequences, the expert added.
The German authorities have found themselves in a difficult situation. Acknowledging Ukraine's involvement in the attack would confirm Moscow’s assertion that the Kiev leadership poses a security threat to all of Europe. On the other hand, concealing the investigation’s findings would undermine Germany’s key principles of the rule of law and judicial transparency, Denis Denisov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, pointed out. As long as Berlin tries to sit on the fence, its official policy toward Kiev will not change.
Nevertheless, European authorities will eventually have to choose which way to go, Denisov said. They will have to officially acknowledge that Ukraine is to blame for undermining the competitiveness of European manufacturers and creating systemic energy security problems for Europe. Alternatively, European politicians could once again turn a blind eye to the issue, disregarding the enormous damage inflicted on their own citizens, the political scientist emphasized. The latter scenario could trigger a further collapse in the approval ratings of Germany’s ruling coalition.
The case is of great political importance for Berlin, and there are serious doubts about whether the court will be able to remain impartial, Rossiyskaya Gazeta notes. Earlier, the court barred the pipeline operators, Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2 AG, from taking part in the proceedings. Even Germans don’t believe that the truth will emerge. Experts doubt the trial will establish that the attack was authorized by government officials.
Yemeni Houthis are threatening further attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities, while strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue. Attacks on the Middle East’s largest oil producer will further hurt the global outlook, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes.
Saudi Arabia’s economy is important both for the region and the entire world, which is why the current developments could affect everyone, without exaggeration, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned. "If further strikes target oil pipelines, processing facilities or export terminals, it will become harder to offset supply shortfalls. This could drive fuel prices and transportation costs up, accelerate global inflation, and slow the global economy," Freedom Global analyst Vladimir Chernov specified.
As for Russia, the International Energy Agency estimates that the country’s total oil export revenues rose by $3.58 billion in September amid increasing global oil prices. However, these gains may turn out to be short-lived. "A prolonged crisis will weaken global demand. In the current situation, Russia may benefit from a temporary increase in prices but it would be wrong to view further tensions as a beneficial factor," Chernov said.
Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure have given Russia a short-term windfall, agrees Oleg Abelev, head of analytics at the Ricom Trust investment company. However, the advantages are being offset by discounts, sanctions, Ukrainian strikes and structural economic problems, the expert added.
Meanwhile, Finam analyst Nikolay Dudchenko does not rule out that Houthi strikes could trigger a further escalation of violence and draw the United States into the conflict. "If the Americans intervene, US ships and facilities in the Red Sea region could come under attack, which would also keep oil prices high," the expert said.
Russia’s agricultural trade gained significant momentum in the January to August period of 2026, with food exports rising faster than imports. However, the increase stems largely from favorable global prices, while serious damage to export terminals sustained at the end of the summer raises questions about whether the current trend will persist, Izvestia writes.
According to the World Bank, average food prices were 6.7% higher in the first eight months of the year compared to 2025. That said, the rise in dollar-denominated revenues does not necessarily mean a corresponding increase in actual export volumes, Alexander Firanchuk, leading researcher at the Presidential Academy’s Laboratory of International Trade of the Presidential Academy, observed.
Southern Russia’s transport infrastructure suffered a serious blow at the end of the summer. Darya Snitko, head of Gazprombank’s Department for Economic Forecasting, confirms that agricultural exports have declined considerably since August due to disruptions to shipping through Black Sea ports.
The disruption of the usual and cheapest sea route is forcing traders and producers to look for alternatives. Shipments are being redirected to rail transport and ports on the Baltic and Caspian seas. The forced redirection of flows is increasing transportation costs and reducing profits, even amid high global prices. Food exports are unlikely to return to previous levels until port operations in the country's south are fully restored and shipment processes normalize, Firanchuk said.
In short, Russia’s agricultural sector is currently in a state of uncertainty. On the one hand, rising fertilizer and energy prices driven by the Middle East crisis have prepared the global market for high-priced Russian exports. But on the other hand, damage to port infrastructure presents an obstacle that cannot be fixed through financial measures alone. Russia’s ability to resume profitable food exports will depend largely on how quickly Black Sea terminals are restored and whether transport companies can optimize more expensive alternative delivery routes.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: US Army to address parents’ blocked access to teen medical records
body: To military parents who are frustrated because they can’t get access to their teenagers’ medical records , the U.S. Army Surgeon General has a message: “We share your concern,” and are working to address it. Currently, parents don’t have access to a child’s medical records from the time they turn 13, “based on current departmental policy,” Lt. Gen. Mary K. Izaguirre said Tuesday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army. In addition, children don’t have ID cards to sign in to the Defense Enrollment Eligibility System (DEERS), she said. Children must be at least 18 to log in to the system. The question of parents’ access came up during a family forum at AUSA. Izaguirre said the issue is one of her husband’s favorite topics, and “I share his passion for it,” she said. For now, parents must go to the patient administration offices at their military treatment facilities and have their teenage children sign consent forms to give parents permission for access to their medical records. “That’s a barrier,” Izaguirre said, adding that “we’ve been working with the [Defense Health Agency], and the [Department of Health and Human Services]” to address the hurdle. The issue stems from privacy laws and has come up in various settings with military families. Researchers with the organization Feedback were “surprised at how often this came up, not just one parent at one base,” said Erin Domagola, the research director at the organization. Feedback analyzed comments received in the Federal Register, following a Defense Department solicitation in March for comments and suggestions from military families on how DoD could improve their quality of life. Feedback uses applied anthropology, behavioral science and digital ethnography to understand what people experience and why. The company independently analyzed Federal Register military family comments from 2024 to 2026 about quality of life. While there were a relatively small number of comments overall —117 in 2026 — it does provide a window into some of the concerns and suggestions, the researchers said.

title: US Army to address parents’ blocked access to teen medical records
body: To military parents who are frustrated because they can’t get access to their teenagers’ medical records , the U.S. Army Surgeon General has a message: “We share your concern,” and are working to address it. Currently, parents don’t have access to a child’s medical records from the time they turn 13, “based on current departmental policy,” Lt. Gen. Mary K. title: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses
body: September’s 7.2% inflation rate was bad enough on its own. For businesses, the bigger concern is that price pressures could spread beyond the food and fuel shocks that first pushed inflation higher. Seasonally adjusted inflation accelerated to 1.1% month on month in September from 0.5% in August. In what National Statistician Dennis Mapa described as a relatively “rare” broad increase, 11 of 13 major commodity groups posted faster inflation, while 16 of 18 regions saw inflation pick up. Core inflation also climbed to 4.7%, its highest in three years. Nerve spoke with three economists to understand whether this is turning into a more persistent inflation problem and what businesses should prepare for heading into 2027. None sees a prolonged second wave as inevitable, but the risk is becoming harder to dismiss. The September uptick comes as several price increases have yet to fully work their way through the economy. Among them: Recent jeepney, bus, and taxi fare hikes were barely captured by the Philippine Statistics Authority in September and should show up more clearly in October. Passenger transport by road carries a 3.5% weight in the inflation basket. Meralco has won approva l to raise its average distribution rate from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, its first increase after a rate review in 15 years. Once implemented in November , that increases energy costs for households and businesses. The P60 minimum wage increase in Metro Manila took effect only on September 26, which means possible cost pass-through could be reflected in later months. El Niño could add another supply shock into early 2027, with economists warning that a strong drought could cut rice and other food production across the Philippines and the region while also putting pressure on power supply and electricity costs. The weakness of the Philippine peso is another source of inflation, as it raises the peso cost of imported fuel, food, raw materials, and equipment and could keep feeding into domestic prices. Mapa pointed to energy, transport, and housing rents as some of the harder pressures to unwind. Electricity inflation was already 14.6% in September, while rents rose 4% and carry more than a 12% weight in the consumer price basket. READ: [READOUT] What Philippine borrowing tells businesses ahead of 2027 SM Investments Corporation group economist Robert Dan Roces expects inflation to remain a concern, but said much will depend on food and energy prices over the coming months. “Some businesses may feel the pressure, but demand should remain relatively resilient,” he told Nerve. RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort told Nerve that inflation may pick up further in the coming months “in view of second-round inflation effects or higher prices of other affected goods and services, or pass-through effects, especially due to higher minimum wages.” Meanwhile, Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said a second, stickier wave becomes more plausible if higher food, fuel, electricity, and transport costs begin feeding into other prices and keep inflation expectations elevated. Agriculture, transport, food businesses, and energy-intensive manufacturing face the most direct exposure, while smaller firms have less room to absorb higher costs. Manufacturing may be especially vulnerable given that the sector was already weakening before the latest inflation pressures intensified, with employment falling to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July and 3.46 million in June. “Small businesses, meanwhile, have less room to absorb higher costs, and retailers could suffer as households spend more on necessities and cut back elsewhere,” Punongbayan told Rappler. Even as the “ber” months go by, retailers may need to temper expectations for the usual consumption boost. Consider that inflation among the bottom 30% of households reached 9% in September, compared with 7.2% nationally, leaving lower-income consumers with even less room for discretionary spending. Forecasts vary considerably on how quickly inflation will ease in 2027, with Ricafort taking the most pessimistic view while institutional forecasts generally cluster between 4% and 5.4%. Source 2027 inflation outlook RCBC Chief Economist Michael Ricafort Around 7% until February, then 5% to 6% from March onward Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) 5.4% average Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) 4% to 5% average ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) 4.6% average Asian Development Bank (ADB) 4.4% average International Monetary Fund (IMF) 4.1% average World Bank (WB) 3.9% average High inflation also creates a second problem for businesses through interest rates. Here’s how economists think the BSP will react: Roces expects the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to be more cautious in putting too much additional pressure on growth. Ricafort is more hawkish, seeing scope for further tightening while inflation remains far above the 2% to 4% target. He also noted that the BSP could partly match future US Federal Reserve hikes to manage interest rate differentials and help stabilize the peso. Punongbayan said further hikes are possible and easing could be pushed into 2027 depending on how core inflation and expectations go, though higher key policy rates risk further straining borrowing, investment, and growth without fixing supply-side pressures. The next BSP policy decision is scheduled for October 22, with another Monetary Board meeting set for December 17. We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve , bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters. title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training
body:
They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.
"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.
"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.
"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."
The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.
As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."
Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.
