title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
body: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants. Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on? Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33. But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again. Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment. Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded. The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019. Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes. Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times : “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.” Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal. A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant. Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032. It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that. Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors. This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: Messi’s Inter Miami Beat New York City, Book Playoffs
body: Lionel Messi set up a Rodrigo De Paul goal and German Berterame snapped his scoring drought as Inter Miami booked their place in the MLS playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday. Victory gave Cristian ‘Kily’ Gonzalez his first back-to-back wins since taking over as head coach last month, guaranteeing second-placed Miami at least a place in the wild card round, with five games left to play. “I’m leaving happy. Obviously, there’s a lot to improve, but we’re making progress little by little,” Gonzalez said. Messi — who had scored twice on Saturday after returning to his club side from last week’s emotional Argentina send-off — was again a dangerous presence, playing a hand in both first-half goals. In the 20th minute, Messi trapped the ball just outside the penalty area and passed it to De Paul, who found Suarez on the byline with a diagonal looping ball. Suarez rolled it flat across the face of the goal, giving Berterame a simple finish for his first goal since May. De Paul grabbed Miami’s second on a quick counter with the final kick of the first half. Berterame brought the ball across the halfway line and was slightly fortunate to find Messi to his right with a mishit pass. Messi drew in three defenders then laid it off with the outside of his left foot to De Paul, who slammed it high to the keeper’s right. In a goalless second half, Messi sent a curling effort from just outside the box over the bar. As the game clock hit 90, Messi played a short corner to De Paul, who unleashed a shot from outside the box toward the far top corner. United States national team goalkeeper Matt Freese made a superb diving save, tipping the ball onto the post. New York City, on a dire streak of just one win in their last 11 MLS games, at least had a chance for a consolation deep in stoppage time with a penalty. Ian Fray brought down fellow substitute Talles Magno, who turned sharply away from goal and ran into the defender’s trailing leg. But Dayne St. Clair made a brilliant save, flinging himself low and right to palm the ball around the bar. It was Inter Miami’s second straight clean sheet, after none in their previous 10. “I really liked how we handled dropping back into defensive shape. We didn’t get caught out on the counter and were very aggressive, breaking up plays whenever a sudden transition from them looked likely,” said Gonzalez. “Perhaps our ball circulation was a bit too slow at times, but that’s just how the game played out.” Even with first-place Nashville out of sight this year in the Eastern Conference, the win consolidated Miami’s grip on second, and home-field advantage into the playoffs. AFP The post Messi’s Inter Miami Beat New York City, Book Playoffs appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Digital innovation could widen Africa’s inequalities if people are left out – Sam Jonah
body: Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has warned that digital innovation could widen inequality in Africa if its benefits are concentrated among people who already have access to technology, education and economic opportunities. He said governments, universities and businesses must ensure that digital policies and platforms do not exclude people who lack reliable internet access, electricity or the resources to participate in the digital economy. “Every digital policy, every new platform, must ask a simple question: who is left out?” he said. Sir Sam was speaking at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, where he delivered the keynote address for the university’s 25th anniversary celebrations. He argued that a child in Dansoman with a laptop and reliable internet access has substantially different opportunities from a child in a village without electricity. “If digital innovation only serves the connected, it will not close our inequalities. It will widen them,” he said. Sir Sam also called attention to barriers facing women in accessing credit, owning land and attaining senior positions in institutions across Africa. Drawing on his experience as patron of the Executive Women Network in Accra, he said women had demonstrated what they could achieve when given opportunities. “An economy that underuses half its talent is running on one leg,” he said. He argued that inclusive development required businesses and institutions to open up access to finance, markets, technology and decision-making. The business leader also called for greater respect for technical and vocational education, saying not every young person needed a university degree but every young person needed a skill. He said Africa’s industrial development depended on technicians, artisans and engineers, and urged the continent to give practical skills greater recognition. Sir Sam further emphasised mentorship, describing the opportunity to learn from experienced people as one of the most valuable contributions leaders could make to the next generation. He said his own career had benefited from managers at Ashanti Goldfields who recognised his potential early on. “The greatest gift we can give the next generation is not money. It is a chance,” he said. His address called for digital innovation, education and economic development to be accompanied by deliberate efforts to ensure that opportunities reach people who are often excluded.

title: CSTO peacekeepers practice repelling enemy attack on humanitarian convoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) peacekeepers have repelled an attack by a simulated enemy on a convoy carrying humanitarian aid as part of the Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 exercise in Belarus, Vladislav Shchegrikovich, press secretary for the CSTO Joint Staff, reported.
"At the Losvido training ground in the Republic of Belarus, during the Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 command and staff exercise involving CSTO peacekeeping forces, peacekeeping units repelled an attack by a simulated enemy on a convoy carrying humanitarian aid. The exercise focused on organizing the safe transit of vehicles and ensuring the unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid to the population. Particular attention was paid to the escorting of humanitarian cargoes, which required coordinated action among various units and the use of specialized equipment," the statement reads.
According to the exercise scenario, a simulated sabotage and reconnaissance group attacked the humanitarian convoy while it was in transit. "Motorized rifle units from a Central Military District formation, supported by BTR-82A armored personnel carriers, practiced repelling an attack using the standard weapons of their combat vehicles and AK-12 assault rifles. The BTR-82A crews used 30mm 2A72 automatic cannons and coaxial 7.62mm PKTM machine guns to provide fire support for the motorized rifle units and suppress the simulated enemy’s firing positions," Shchegrikovich reported.
"Mobile reserve groups were promptly deployed to provide fire support, successfully eliminating the remnants of a sabotage and reconnaissance group. "A damaged armored personnel carrier was successfully recovered by repair units using a REM-KL wheeled repair and recovery vehicle, which underscored the readiness of the collective forces to handle complex tasks in the field," he said.
The CSTO press secretary noted that during this phase of the exercise, the peacekeepers demonstrated determination and professionalism, while an electronic warfare (EW) system successfully neutralized several explosive devices, thereby minimizing casualties. "Although one vehicle sustained damage, the rest of the convoy quickly moved out of the line of fire and continued its advance," he added.
He pointed out that the movement of the mixed convoy was carried out under heavy, reinforced protection. "The airspace was monitored by a pair of Mi-35 helicopters providing air cover. The route was scouted using an unmanned aerial vehicle. To protect the convoy, a security detail was organized, comprising armored personnel carriers, a mobile fire support group, and electronic warfare systems," he noted.
Shchegrikovich emphasized that an electronic warfare system mounted on an all-terrain vehicle played a key role in ensuring security. "The automated electronic warfare system, capable of operating at a range of up to 500 meters, effectively suppresses radio emission sources--a capability that is critical for preventing the detonation of radio-controlled explosive devices," the press secretary said.
On October 11, the CSTO command and staff exercises Indestructible Brotherhood 2026 and Barrier 2026 began in Belarus. They involve over 1,500 military personnel and 300 pieces of weaponry, military hardware, and specialized equipment. Taking part in the exercises are troop contingents (Collective Forces) from the CSTO member states: Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan. These include military contingents, units of internal affairs bodies and national guard, as well as task groups of the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian military contingent is primarily composed of units from a combined arms army of the Central Military District.

title: Azerbaijani activist who organised tutoring for child hijab ban protesters reportedly missing
body: . Photo: personal archive" /> Baku-based activist and artist İlkin Huseynov has been unreachable since yesterday, shortly after he set up the ‘Let Leyli Go to School’ project, which sought to organise tutoring for those boycotting school amid hijab ban protests . It is not clear whether any pupils have received tutoring from the project yet. The initiative’s website and Instagram page were inaccessible on Thursday morning. According to a X post from another activist Javid Agha, unidentified individuals arrived at Huseynov’s home on Izzat Nabiyev Street at around 16:00 and the activist left the house with them. His phone has reportedly been switched off since then, and his whereabouts remain unknown. Agha also noted that he received a notification indicating that a new device had been added to Huseynov’s Facebook Messenger account. ‘I had sent him a message on Facebook Messenger, and a short while ago I saw the notification: “Huseynov Ilkin added a new device to this conversation”. It appears that his account may have been compromised. We are worried about Ilkin’, he wrote. There has been no official information so far confirming whether the activist has been detained. According to Agha, Huseynov is associated with the ‘Let Leyli Go to School’ initiative, which seems to have been established earlier this week following the latest restrictions on wearing hijab in schools. The initiative aimed to provide a platform for teachers to offer lessons to students affected by the hijab ban, helping ensure that they are not deprived of their education. The initiative briefly operated an Instagram page under the username ‘qoy mektebe getsin,’ which now seems to have been deleted . ‘I suspect that he has been arrested, and I believe this is the reason’, Javid Agha said. As of now, it remains unclear whether Huseynov has been detained by law enforcement authorities. There has been no official information about his whereabouts or the identities of the individuals who arrived at his home. The incident comes amid ongoing protests in Azerbaijan over the hijab ban in schools. Explainer | Why are schoolchildren protesting a hijab ban in Azerbaijan? The protests against the hijab ban in schools appear to be some of the largest public demonstrations in years. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov Who is Ilkin Huseynov? Ilkin Huseynov is an Azerbaijani artist, photographer, musician, and cultural activist known for his contribution to the development of independent art and cinema in Baku. His work focuses on urban life, memory, social issues, environmental concerns, and visual culture. One of his most notable projects is Salaam Cinema Baku, an independent cinema and arts space established in Baku, which also became associated with the preservation of Baku’s historical architectural heritage. In 2019, concerns arose about the possible demolition of the historic building in which Salaam Cinema was located. Huseynov and other members of the community advocated for its preservation.

title: Galamsey is an economic, health and moral problem – Sam Jonah
body: Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has described illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, as an economic, health and moral problem, warning that the pursuit of wealth without responsibility is damaging Ghana’s natural resources. He said discussions about sustainability must confront the effects of illegal mining on rivers, forests and farmland. “Rivers that fed our grandparents now run the colour of chocolate milk,” he said. Sir Sam was delivering the keynote address at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, as the university marked its 25th anniversary. Drawing on his career in the mining industry, he said mining companies and individuals must consider what they leave behind after extracting resources from the earth. He posed the question of whether mining would leave communities with damaged land and polluted rivers or with lasting benefits such as schools, skills, roads and businesses. “This is not only an environmental problem. It is an economic problem, a health problem and, in the end, a moral problem,” he said of galamsey. Sir Sam said the principle of sustainability should also guide how public money and human talent are managed. He criticised the use of borrowed funds for consumption instead of investment and pointed to abandoned public projects as examples of poor stewardship. He argued that incomplete projects represent wasted resources, particularly when successive governments begin new projects instead of completing existing ones. He also expressed concern about skilled young people who struggle to find opportunities after receiving an education, saying a sustainable Africa should provide conditions that allow its talent to contribute at home. Sir Sam said digital tools could support efforts to improve environmental and public-sector accountability. He cited satellite data as a means of tracking illegal mining, digital land registries as a way to reduce longstanding land disputes, and digital public procurement systems as a tool for showing citizens how public funds are spent. “The technology exists. What we need is the will to use it, even when transparency is uncomfortable for the powerful,” he said. He linked responsible resource management to ethical leadership, arguing that economic gain should not come at the expense of communities and future generations. His address called for enterprise and innovation to be pursued alongside responsibility for the environment, public resources and society.

title: Opinion: The DoD has a funding crisis – the ANC has made it an accountability crisis
body:
Deputy Minister Bantu Holomisa is right to warn that Treasury bureaucracy can delay constitutionally authorised military deployments and jeopardise national security.
The South African National Defence Force (SANDF) has been chronically underfunded for years. A country cannot authorise military deployments and then expect soldiers to wait while departments argue over budgets. Rebuilding South Africa’s defence capability will require substantially greater and more predictable investment.
But funding alone will not rescue the SANDF.
The Department of Defence and Military Veterans also suffers from a profound accountability crisis after decades of ANC governance. Until that changes, every request for more money will be met with a perfectly reasonable question: can taxpayers trust the Department to spend it responsibly?
Treasury is entitled to ask whether Defence needs more money. It does. But Treasury and taxpayers are equally entitled to ask whether Defence has demonstrated that it can responsibly manage significantly larger budgets.
Indeed, a position paper on defence acquisition and procurement published by DefenceWeb last month identifies serious weaknesses inside the system itself. It describes Defence supply-chain management as fragmented, ineffective and inefficient, with unclear ownership of processes, cumbersome procedures, poor integration and systems that remain largely manual and difficult to trace.
It argues that the SANDF requires far more agile procurement and that unnecessary bureaucratic bottlenecks must be removed. That is correct. But crucially, it advocates “legality with agility”: retaining PFMA compliance while removing duplication and unnecessary delays.
The solution cannot simply be to loosen Treasury controls and pour more money into a procurement environment in which accountability is already difficult to assign. South Africa needs both faster procurement and stronger accountability.
The consequences of failing at the latter are already before Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Hawks and Special Investigating Unit (SIU) detailed investigation after investigation into procurement failures, fraud and corruption across the defence portfolio.
Within the Department of Military Veterans alone, the Hawks are investigating approximately R215 million in alleged procurement irregularities, including the Hatfield contracts, the R100 million travel management contract, security training, drone procurement and the notorious walk-behind roller and rammer project.
The SIU is simultaneously investigating matters including the R257.5 million Microsoft licensing contract, R922 million in asset-management contracts, the R217 million Cuban Interferon procurement and R273.5 million in PPE procurement.
Together, investigations across the defence portfolio involve between approximately R2.1 billion and R2.5 billion.
Former Defence Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula is currently standing trial on corruption charges. Procurement decisions from the same broad era remain under investigation. Former senior officials left the Department before disciplinary processes could run their course.
And one of those former officials, Tsepe Motumi, now serves as Special Advisor to the current Defence Minister.
Many of the Military Veterans matters under investigation arose while Motumi served as Acting Director-General. More importantly, the Supreme Court of Appeal found that he had unlawfully committed the Department to expenditure beyond his legal authority in the Zeal Health matter. The Constitutional Court subsequently upheld the essential findings.
Yet Minister Angie Motshekga continues to retain him as one of her closest advisers.
I have repeatedly asked her in Parliament how this can possibly represent consequence management. Those questions have never been properly answered.
That is precisely why calls for more defence funding struggle to gain public confidence.
The contradictions extend beyond procurement.
While pleading poverty, the Ministry maintains an extensive programme of international travel. Military diplomacy matters, but diplomacy cannot become a substitute for leadership at home. Deputy Minister Holomisa himself has participated in many of these engagements.
Defence has also found money for luxury vehicles for senior generals and golf days. Just last month, it took delivery of 20 new Haval vehicles for military chaplains.
Meanwhile, when serious concerns arose about conditions at Fort iKapa and later at De Brug, where soldiers returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo were quarantined, the response from ANC parliamentary leadership was too often to defend the Department rather than demand answers.
That is the credibility gap Holomisa must confront.
He is right that Treasury bureaucracy can undermine operational readiness. He should therefore support reforms that make defence procurement quicker, more agile and better suited to military requirements.
But reform cannot stop at Treasury’s door.
Defence also needs transparent procurement systems, clear lines of responsibility, proper parliamentary oversight and real consequences when officials abuse public money.
If Holomisa believes Defence deserves more funding, he should join us in demanding both: adequately funded armed forces and an accountable Department capable of spending that money effectively.
That means confronting unnecessary expenditure, supporting genuine consequence management and persuading Minister Motshekga to part ways with a Special Advisor whose conduct has already been declared unlawful by South Africa’s highest courts.
South Africa spends too little on defence. The Democratic Alliance has said so consistently.
But additional funding cannot become a substitute for accountability. If the Department wants South Africans to support billions more for Defence, it must demonstrate that corruption will be punished, political protection has ended and every additional rand will strengthen the SANDF rather than disappear into another investigation.
Nicholas Gotsell MP is a Member of the Joint Standing Committee on Defence (JSCD).

title: Yemeni armed forces reject Saudi claim of attack on Medina
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree rejected Saudi Arabia's claims of an attack toward Medina, calling it a big and blatant lie.
Yemen's armed forces spokesman Yahya Saree rejected on Thursday that any attack was launched toward Medina, calling the Saudi claim a big and blatant lie.
In a statement carried by Al-Masirah, Saree said the Yemeni armed forces did not carry out any targeting operations toward Saudi territory today.

title: Africa must create AI technology instead of paying to use it – Sam Jonah
body: Business leader Sir Sam Jonah has warned that Africa risks becoming a mere consumer of artificial intelligence and other digital technologies unless it invests in the skills and capacity needed to develop its own solutions. He said the continent must avoid a situation in which it imports technology, exports its data and pays foreign companies to access the resulting products and services. Delivering the keynote address at Methodist University Ghana’s international conference in Accra on Thursday, October 15, Sir Sam said Africa must learn from its history of exporting raw materials while buying back finished products. “We must not do it again with data,” he said, referring to the risk of repeating that pattern in the digital economy. The conference was held as the university marked its 25th anniversary under the theme “Excellence, Morality, and Service at 25: Advancing Digital Innovation, Equity, and Sustainability in a Transforming World”. Sir Sam called on African universities to produce graduates who can develop digital technologies, rather than only use applications created elsewhere. “Our universities must produce people who can write the code, not just use the app,” he said. He argued that countries that had made significant progress had invested in building their own technical workforce. He also urged entrepreneurs to focus on solving problems in African sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, logistics, energy and finance, particularly for people who remain underserved by formal systems. According to him, Africa’s opportunities lie not simply in replicating products developed in places such as London and San Francisco, but in creating solutions suited to the continent’s needs. Sir Sam cited mobile money as an example of innovation that emerged from a practical problem: millions of Africans had mobile phones but lacked access to bank accounts. He said the development of mobile money demonstrated Africa’s capacity to create solutions that respond to local conditions. He warned, however, that the next wave of technologies—including artificial intelligence, data and automation—could deepen the continent’s dependence on external providers if it failed to build local expertise. Sir Sam also called for enterprise to be treated as a respected career path, arguing that Africa needed more young people who created businesses and jobs rather than focusing only on securing government employment. He said the continent had the people, resources, and ideas needed to advance, but required the habits and investments that would turn its potential into prosperity.

title: Anthropic's Q3 revenue hits $16.8B but growth slows ahead of planned November IPO
body:
Slowing growth and a tough market are hurting Anthropic's valuation ahead of its planned November IPO.
Anthropic shared its quarterly numbers with potential investors at a private meeting in San Francisco, according to multiple US media reports. Third-quarter revenue hit $16.8 billion. That marks a roughly 45 percent jump from the second quarter and is more than 3.6 times the company's total annual revenue for 2025.
Growth has slowed, though. In the second quarter, surging demand for the developer tool Claude Code had pushed revenue up by more than 140 percent compared to Q1. Anthropic is far from that pace now, though a summer slowdown is one likely factor since people typically work less during those months and burn through fewer tokens. OpenAI also launched a strong competitor with Astra in September, which Anthropic only successfully countered in late September with Opus 5.5 . Ad
According to The Information , Anthropic reported an adjusted operating margin of 11 percent for the year through Q3. That number leaves out major costs like stock-based compensation, but it shows the company is moving toward profitability. Ad
The Financial Times reports this was the second straight quarter of adjusted profitability for the AI lab. The company is cash-flow positive, too. During the third quarter, Anthropic generated $1.70 in revenue for every dollar it spent on compute.
This is good news for the AI industry because it shows trained models can turn a profit despite months of price wars. Plenty of caveats remain, though, including steep training and staff costs and the risk that open-weight alternatives start replacing proprietary models like Claude. Ad
Anthropic also estimates that 5 to 7 percent of its revenue comes from distillation. In this process, other companies use Anthropic's AI to extract data about how it works and train their own models.
Anthropic has repeatedly accused Chinese AI labs of copying its models this way. Still, the company recently rolled out effective countermeasures , raising questions about why Anthropic spent so much time lobbying against distillation if it had the tools to stop the practice all along. Ad
That said, distillation revenue will likely drop now and weigh on the current quarter's numbers, Anthropic told investors. Over the long run, blocking distillation should pay off by making it harder for rival model makers to match Claude's quality. Ad
The planned IPO, which The Information says is set for November before Thanksgiving, will be the biggest test yet of investor appetite for the AI boom. Anthropic's private valuation jumped to $965 billion in May, up from under $20 billion just two years earlier. Some bankers even floated a $2 trillion IPO.
But the now presented revenue numbers reportedly disappointed some potential investors. Several now expect Anthropic's banking advisors to lower valuation expectations to possibly under $1.5 trillion, especially since the company did not discuss its September annualized revenue rate or a full-year outlook. In July, that rate was reportedly $65 billion .
The timing for an IPO is hardly ideal. Inflation stays high, borrowing costs are rising, public sentiment toward AI remains more negative than positive, and unsolved cybersecurity risks pose a real operational threat . Moreover, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others have been locked in a brutal price war for months while open models keep closing the performance gap. Still, people will almost certainly use more AI in the future rather than less as improving model capabilities work their way into more everyday office jobs.

title: Navigating nautical confusion: In pursuit of a common maritime lexicon
body:
From “chokepoints” to “freedom of navigation,” the world’s headlines have been replete with maritime terms in recent years, and navigating that terminology has become a challenge for policymakers and maritime professionals alike, not to mention the general public. The maritime world is niche, with many archaic terms and concepts that have no terrestrial equivalent. Furthermore, it is often difficult to differentiate between terms that are colloquial versus technical. The term “shadow fleet,” for example, has graced newspapers around the world, but has no official definition and no legal significance. And while it may seem a pedantic or even trivial matter to try to clarify the terminology such that everybody is on the same page, there is an increasingly critical need to do so. As security threats, accidents at sea and climatic events disrupt maritime commerce in more frequent and significant ways, global supply chains of critical goods, including food and energy supplies, continue to break down. The resulting economic turbulence and life-threatening situations mean that maritime policy has become more important than ever. If leaders do not first understand how to articulate maritime matters in a way that is mutually intelligible to all actors, setting clear policy and resolving these critical issues (in some cases of existential concern) become all the more difficult, if not impossible. The time for a universal maritime lexicon with clear, commonly understood definitions has arrived.
Four main challenges inhibit the ability of the maritime space to be governed in as clear a fashion as is currently necessary:
All four of these issues encumber the ability of maritime professionals to be able to recognize and respond to the panoply of threats and challenges currently facing the domain that carries 90% of world trade, 99% of telephonic and internet communication, and more than 20% of our dietary protein intake. We need the maritime domain to function, so we need to be able to talk about it with clarity and precision.
The first problem is that different terms mean different things to different maritime actors. What navies, coast guards, and marine police forces care about is very different than what the shipping industry, the offshore oil and gas industry, the fishing industry or any other aspect of the maritime sector would care about. This means that there is incredible variation and, in fact, mismatched language between different portions of the maritime world itself. When the Houthis began to attack ships in November 2023, the need for interaction between navies and shipping lines became critically important. Within minutes, however, it became evident that the two portions of the maritime world that had to be working together spoke very different languages, despite the common operating environment.
As a simple example, naval officers and political leaders kept talking about the needs of “shippers.” But shippers are the people who put goods on ships. Shipping lines or common carriers are the ones that actually bring the goods from Point A to Point B. At a time when clarity was of critical importance, that level of inexactness and disconnect was a problem as it created confusion among those who were already facing unprecedented challenges. It also eroded trust, as imprecise language in the ears of someone who recognizes the imprecision can translate into serious concerns as to the competency of that person or entity.
Then, as ships started getting hit by missiles and drones, political leaders would talk about “marine insurance” as if it was a singular phenomenon, not understanding that there may be five or more marine insurance policies on a single voyage, all of which conflict with each other. Comments about how “marine insurance” would want to avoid a vessel sinking betrayed a lack of knowledge that, while the hull and machinery policy would certainly want to avoid the loss, the protection & indemnity policy would not want to risk the lives of salvors amid a perpetual missile and drone barrage. Terminology matters, as it is what allows us to understand the same situation in the same way. When seafarers’ lives, the marine environment and the global economy are all on the line, that understanding is vital.
This is not just a phenomenon, however, that is problematic in times of unusual security crises. As in many professional environments, the maritime sector has a tendency to use acronyms in place of lengthy expressions. The acronym “SAR,” for example, is used frequently. To maritime operators at sea, it typically means “search and rescue.” To those running the technical side of a maritime operations center, however, it may instead mean “synthetic aperture radar.” Knowing that disambiguation is important to ensure that conversations – particularly at critical moments – do not lead to life threatening confusion.
Beyond the intra-maritime lexical diversity, regional and national diversity also play a part in creating challenges for establishing a consistent, and common understanding of maritime phenomena. To work on countering illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, there are a lot of terms that need to be understood. “IUU fishing,” as an acronymic term itself, has a tendency to blur the important distinctions between illegal fishing versus unreported fishing versus unregulated fishing. All of those matters need to be distinguished from other phenomena like fisheries crime. But even just within IUU fishing, regional variation can be vital. For example, it is impossible to talk about IUU fishing in Ghana and not understand the concept of Saiko. Saiko is a form of transshipment at sea whereby industrial vessels and artisanal canoes exchange catch, taking advantage of what each other can legally land. The practice occurs elsewhere, but under a different name.
And while Saiko is a technical term in Ghana, colloquial terms are used throughout the world, often as if they were legally-based. “International waters,” for example, is not a legal term of art, yet many believe it is. It is a colloquial term to describe both the High Seas and the areas where High Seas freedoms apply. Generally, that means anywhere outside of the 12 nautical mile territorial sea – the sovereign jurisdiction of the coastal state. Location is critical for understanding what can be done about a maritime situation, and not being precise in identifying that location can be catastrophic. While there is no problem with using a colloquial term in certain circumstances, in other cases, it may obscure the path to resolution.
Similarly, the use of maritime terminology for political purposes can create real problems. In the span of less than a week at the end of April 2026, amid a ceasefire, the United States Secretary of Defense accused the Iranian Navy of being “ a gang of pirates ,” and the Iranian government accused the United States of “ acting like pirates .” Ironically, the President of the United States went on to describe his own Navy’s blockade enforcement by claiming “ we’re like pirates ,” seemingly validating the Iranian accusation. While this political rhetoric may seem appealing to both sides from a public perception standpoint, as a matter of law, neither party could engage in piracy for failing to meet the “private ends” requirement under international law. In other words, states can’t legally engage in “piracy” in general, and they certainly can’t do so in the territorial sea of a state, which is where the incidents at issue were taking place. At a time when maritime claims are holding 20% of the world’s energy supply hostage, using technical maritime terms colloquially can add to the confusion and, once again, complicate the processes of resolving key issues.
Whether addressing a real-time crisis, communicating critical information, reporting an incident, or developing new laws and policies, if we do not have a common understanding of the terms we are using, we run the risk of serious harm to human life, the marine environment, and the global economy that sustains us all. We often say, “No shipping, no shopping.” But if we do not understand the difference between a shipper and a shipping line, for example, we may not be able to formulate sufficiently clear and sound policies to keep global maritime trade functioning in a way that benefits everyone.
Recognizing this challenge, the Signatory States to the Djibouti Code of Conduct /Jeddah Amendment (DCoC/JA) are developing a Common Maritime Security Lexicon, with the support of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) through the European Union-funded Crisis Response Project for the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean (CRP-RedWIO). The initiative gives effect to decisions taken by DCoC/JA States at their High-Level Meetings. At the Seventh High-Level Meeting in Dar es Salaam in November 2024, States agreed to develop a standard lexicon of terminology for use within the DCoC Information Sharing Network (ISN). This mandate was reinforced at the Eighth High-Level Meeting in Mauritius in November 2025, where Resolution II on Information Sharing called for the development of a Common Lexicon to establish a common operational language across the network.
While originating as a DCoC/JA initiative, the Lexicon is intended to support maritime security cooperation across the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and Red Sea Area, providing States, maritime security agencies, practitioners and regional and international partners with a shared understanding of key maritime security terminology and concepts. In doing so, it will strengthen communication, information sharing, interoperability, policy development and operational cooperation.
Given its comprehensive scope and the breadth of maritime security issues and terminology it addresses, it is hoped that the Lexicon will extend beyond the DCoC region and ultimately provide the basis for adoption as a global maritime security lexicon. Such a common framework of terminology and understanding would represent an important contribution to international maritime governance, enabling States and organizations to communicate and cooperate more effectively at a time of increasing maritime complexity and turbulence, and helping to address disorder and discord in the maritime domain for the benefit of the global community.
Dr Ian Ralby is president of Auxilium Worldwide , a charitable nonprofit that, among other things, works on issues of ocean governance, supporting regional and international organizations in their efforts to advance the safety, security, stability, and prosperity of the world’s maritime spaces. Ralby is a globally recognized expert in maritime law and security who has worked on maritime matters in more than 100 countries around the world.

title: Zelensky: Russia unleashes 850 Shahed drones as Ukraine faces restrictions on its defenses
body:
The Ukrainian President wrote this on Facebook , Ukrinform reports.
“Emergency services are still providing assistance in dozens of our cities and communities. Repair crews and rescuers are working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks. For practically all of yesterday and throughout last night, a massive Shahed attack was underway. The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them. From midnight yesterday through 9:00 today, there had already been more than 850 Shaheds – and this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted. We managed to shoot down some of the Shaheds. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelensky stressed.
He noted that Kirovohrad region had suffered one of the largest attacks. Strikes were also reported in Kyiv and the surrounding region, the Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Rivne, Kharkiv and Donetsk regions, as well as the Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Poltava and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Three people were killed in Kropyvnytskyi and another three in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such opportunity and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, the previous day, Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, a technology adviser to the President of Ukraine, said that SpaceX had introduced restrictions overnight on the operating speed of Starlink terminals while in motion, without giving Ukraine’s Defense Forces advance notice.
The Ministry of Defense reported that, as of Wednesday evening, SpaceX was maintaining a speed limit of 161 km/h for Starshield terminals (the “military package”) while in motion. During the day, the actual restrictions were considerably stricter.
The Ministry of Defense stressed that the Starlink restrictions detected overnight had complicated the operation of the Defense Forces’ unmanned systems, logistics and middle-strike capabilities.

title: Sharjah Police arrest 33 in crackdown on $2.4bn global money-laundering scheme
body: Sharjah Police have arrested 33 people from 12 countries accused of cyber fraud , digital wallet theft, money laundering and violent assault. Police said they were members of an organised criminal network who targeted individuals and companies through cyber attacks, stolen data, cryptocurrency transactions and physical intimidation. The arrests were the result of an international operation and carried out in the UAE and abroad. The suspects are accused of operating as four separate gangs, each specialising in one area. The first group carried out cyber attacks and stole customer information and databases, police said. The second gang specialised in laundering money through virtual assets and other financial channels, and the third used social engineering to manipulate victims and steal digital wallets. Members of the fourth group are accused of violent assaults, allegedly targeting victims to force them to disclose passcodes to their digital wallets. Sophisticated layers of encryption Lt Gen Abdullah Mubarak bin Amer, commander-in-chief of Sharjah Police, told a press conference on Thursday that more than 30 companies and institutions were targeted by the criminal network, with the operation securing the assets of companies worth Dh65 billion. More than Dh200 million in cash was seized, with about 3,000 digital wallets audited and verified. “What distinguished this gang was that it did not rely on a single type of criminal activity,” he said. View this post on Instagram The Sharjah Police Digital Crime Combat Department “uncovered the highly complex and concealed infrastructure of the organisation, whose members had made the deepest reaches of cyberspace a home for their activities”, he said. The suspects are accused of hiding their activities behind sophisticated layers of encryption, moving through closed networks. In public, they “cultivated an image of wealth, travelling between world capitals and displaying a lavish lifestyle that concealed a framework managed secretly, and they appeared to be legitimate businesspeople and investors, while their illegal activities extended across countries”. Teenage suspect Sharjah Police said initial inquiries alerted them to one suspect in particular, a 15-year-old boy. “We traced the networks and their locations until we reached the teenager,” said Brig Dr Khalifa Balhai, director of Sharjah CID. “He had a digital wallet with huge amount of cryptocurrency. We traced all the suspects through the teenager.” It was discovered the gang had set up a group on social media, which was locked by a code that changed every eight hours. “What has been achieved in this case is the result of integrated institutional work, continued security efforts, and close co-operation and co-ordination with federal, local and international authorities,” Lt Gen bin Amer said. “These efforts led to the dismantling of these networks and groups, the arrest of their members and the thwarting of their plans. “This confirms the efficiency of the UAE's national security system and its ability to handle various cases, regardless of their complexity or whether they extend beyond its geographical borders, and to keep pace with security challenges efficiently and competently.” The security operation, called End of Battle, has also served to protect interests and assets, he added. Anwar Al Harmoudi, Attorney General of Sharjah, said the investigation “revealed a cross-border criminal organisation with integrated criminal roles, beginning with seizing victims’ funds through fraud and hacking”. The suspects are accused of converting stolen assets into property and other investments to give the appearance of legitimacy.

title: 2026 U-17 WWC: Black Maidens to face Norway, Brazil and Canada in Group C
body: The Black Maidens of Ghana are set to embark on their FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup Morocco 2026 campaign, with their Group C fixtures now confirmed. Head Coach Joe Nana Adarkwa’s side will open their tournament against Norway on Sunday, October 18, at the Mohammed VI Football Complex – Pitch 3 at 18:00 GMT. Ghana will then face a stern test against Brazil on Thursday, October 22, at the same venue and time, before concluding their group stage campaign against Canada on Saturday, October 24, at the Mohammed VI Football Complex – Pitch 1 at 15:00 GMT. The Black Maidens arrived in Morocco in early October to begin a two-week training camp in Casablanca, where the technical team has been assessing the players’ readiness. During their preparations, the team played two international friendlies, suffering a 3-0 defeat to China before bouncing back with a 2-1 victory over Kenya on October 14. Returning to the U-17 Women’s World Cup after missing the previous edition, the Black Maidens will be looking to build on their rich history in the competition, which includes a bronze medal in 2012 and three quarter-final appearances.

title: Morning attack on Kyiv region injures woman, damages private houses – official
body:
A 66-year-old woman sustained shrapnel wounds as a result of a hostile morning attack on Kyiv region, with buildings damaged and fires breaking out, Head of the Regional Military Administration Timur Tkachenko reported.

"In Bucha district, a 66-year-old woman with shrapnel wounds to her face was hospitalized. Also, a private residential building was damaged in the district, and fires broke out in two outbuildings," he wrote on Telegram on Thursday.

According to the Regional Military Administration, a private house caught fire in Vyshhorod district due to the enemy attack, while another house was damaged.

"Rescuers extinguished the fires. Fortunately, according to available information, there are no other casualties," Tkachenko added.

title: Jeepney drivers vow to continue Tatay Elmer’s fight for good
body: MANILA, Philippines – As late jeepney driver and activist “Tatay Elmer” Cordero ‘s memorial services come to a close, his peers at Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahan ng Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON) have promised to continue the calls for justice that he has long fought for. Cordero died on October 7 at 78 years old after suffering a heart attack during a protest. In this series of interviews with Rappler at his cremation on October 14, family and friends look back on their fondest memories of Cordero, sharing how they plan to honor his life. – Rappler.com Must Watch Tatay Elmer honored with final caravan

title: Agbodza, Sam George move to curb fibre optic cable cuts during road works
body: The Minister for Roads and Highways, Kwame Governs Agbodza, has engaged the Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, and other key stakeholders to address recurring damage to fibre optic cables during road construction and rehabilitation works across Ghana. The meeting focused on strengthening coordination between road agencies, contractors and telecommunications service providers to prevent cable cuts and minimise disruptions to communication services. The engagement comes amid concerns over the damage to critical digital infrastructure during road projects. Participants highlighted the need for improved communication, early planning and closer collaboration among the institutions involved in road construction and telecommunications infrastructure. Effective coordination, they noted, would help ensure that fibre optic cables are identified and protected before excavation and other construction activities begin. The engagement forms part of efforts to safeguard essential infrastructure while ensuring the smooth implementation of road projects. Improved cooperation between the roads and communications sectors is expected to reduce avoidable damage, limit service interruptions and support the country’s broader digital development objectives.

title: US, Iran have weeks to avert food crisis, UN official warns
body:
NEW YORK, October 15. /TASS/. Iran and the United States should agree on an effective mechanism to ensure fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz in the coming weeks, or parts of Asia and Africa could face a food crisis, Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services, told Reuters .
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," said Moreira da Silva, who also heads a UN task force on humanitarian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. "If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," he added.
According to the UN official, the issue of fertilizer transit requires an immediate solution. The United States and Iran should not make it conditional on a comprehensive agreement, which the parties may reach later. "What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," Moreira da Silva said.
"Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea - the world's most widely used fertilizer - and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input," the news agency noted.

title: 2026 U-17 WWC: Black Maidens unveil 21-player squad for competition in Morocco
body: Black Maidens Head Coach Nana Joe Adarkwa has named his final 21-player squad for the FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup Morocco 2026. The squad announcement comes with a major boost as forward Jessica Appiah Asamoah makes a remarkable return after recovering from injury. Adding to the excitement, three U15 talents – Christiana Ashiaku, Mavis Koah and Belinda Kpentey – have successfully transitioned to the U17 side, bringing fresh energy to the team. Goalkeepers: Belinda Maku Aklie, Rahima A. Napari and Josephine Nyanufule will man the posts for Ghana. Defenders: Matilda A. B. Amoah, Hajara Adam, Latifa Musah, Mavis Koah, Rafia Osman, Juliana Gyekyewaa and Seraphina E. Esse will marshal the backline. Midfielders: Coach Adarkwa will rely on the creativity and tenacity of Belinda Kpentey, Christiana Ashiaku, Benedicta D. Nkietah, Seidatu Wahab, Zeinab Shani and Sekinatu Amadu. Forwards: Priscilla Mensah, Linda Achiaa, Jessica A. Asamoah, Cynthia Obinsrewuo and Gloria A. Adomako will lead the attack. With a blend of experience, returning talent and youthful exuberance, the Black Maidens are set to intensify preparations for a strong campaign in Morocco.

title: Integrating Ukraine into EU a powerful response to Russia's attacks, says Irish PM
body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin doubled down on his country's push to move forward Ukraine's EU accession bid as much as possible by the end of the year, in comments made at the Oct. 15 EU leaders' summit in Brussels.
Ireland is chairing the EU's Council Presidency until the end of 2026, meaning it is responsible for the bloc's agenda during that period. One of Dublin's oft-stated priorities is to unblock and make serious progress on EU enlargement.
"Now is the time to be ambitious over the next months to open all clusters in respect of Ukraine and Moldova," Martin said, referring to the six to-do lists of reforms that Kyiv is partway through unlocking.
"The people of Ukraine need that as a very strong signal given the extraordinary pressure they are under from Russian attacks on civilians and civil infrastructure," Martin said, reiterating that he aims to have all six clusters open by the end of the year.
Russia has upped its attacks across Ukraine with extensive use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones against civilian targets.
The draft conclusions for the EU leaders' summit refer to these developments, but lack new concrete measures to help Ukraine fend off Russian attacks.
What Russia is doing is "appalling and... horrific, and it illustrates that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin is not interested in peace. That's why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways that we can," Martin said.
For him, advancing Ukraine's EU membership bid is one of those things.
Ukraine unlocked a third and fourth of the six enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, leaving two still to go.
Despite Hungary and Bulgaria attacking ambitious words on enlargement in the draft conclusions for the ongoing leaders' meeting, it seems there are no public objections to Ukraine being able to open the remaining two.
Lithuania's President Gitanas Nauseda said he "does not see any big obstacles to opening the remaining two clusters" and echoed Martin's message that "Ukraine has to receive some positive signals."
"One of the strongest signals is the chance and the light at the end of the tunnel regarding the integration of Ukraine into the EU," Nauseda added.

title: A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Debris from a Russian drone damaged Cosmogony , a painting that set a national record in Ukraine, the Korsaks Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, where the artwork was exhibited, reported on 14 October. A fire destroyed part of the painting’s final section, titled The Future , according to the statement. Russian drones continue to attack Ukraine. Overnight into 15 October alone, Ukrainian air defense forces downed or suppressed 536 Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). In recent days, Lutsk, a city in northwestern Ukraine, has been among the cities damaged by Russian attacks. Russian UAV attacks set fire to an oil depot , a wholesale warehouse , and a shopping center . At the museum, located on the shopping center’s premises, the fire damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, which covers a canvas of more than 2,000 square meters. Russian attack damages museum in Lutsk A fire broke out at the Adrenalin City shopping and entertainment complex, where the museum is located, Suspilne Lutsk reported . The blaze damaged the last of the painting’s six sections, according to the report. “By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians,” Tetiana Repnytska, director of the Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, told Suspilne Lutsk. A section of Petro Antyp’s painting Cosmogony before a Russian drone attack on Lutsk on 13 October 2026. Photo: Korsaks Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art/Facebook Museum staff also had to evacuate more than 300 works by Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska, which were exhibited alongside Cosmogony , Oles Tomakh, the museum’s chief curator, told Suspilne Lutsk. Some works could not be removed in time, resulting in shattered glass. However, the museum’s other exhibition halls were unaffected, the chief curator said. The museum is weighing whether to fully restore the damaged fragment or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war, and will decide after consulting the artist, Petro Antyp, and restoration specialists, it said. Repnytska told Suspilne Lutsk that the painting’s authors could also create a new section. “Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said. Cosmogony—Ukraine’s largest painting Artist Petro Antyp began working on the painting in November 2022, Suspilne Lutsk reported, and it took almost two years to complete, according to the museum’s website. The painting covers an area of 2,086 square meters. In September 2024, the project set a national record as Ukraine’s largest painting. The artwork explores the evolution of the universe, Earth, nature, humanity, society, culture, and science. Its six sections combine myths, legends, scientific theories, and symbols from different cultures, according to the museum’s website. A section of Petro Antyp’s painting Cosmogony. Photo: Taras Luchko The project extends beyond the canvas, as the museum presents a multimedia performance that combines light, sound, and art. Civilians killed and injured in Russia’s latest attack on Lutsk Around noon on 14 October, a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone attacked Lutsk. Drone debris damaged a wholesale goods warehouse and a residential building, Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration, told Suspilne. Falling drone debris sparked a large fire at the Yevrohurt wholesale warehouse. A nine-story residential building on Sobornosti Avenue was also damaged, Romaniuk later reported on social media. Six people were killed in the strike on the warehouse: five were found at the scene, and another person died in the hospital. Eleven more people were injured, Romaniuk said. Aftermath of Russia’s attack on Lutsk on 14 October 2026. Photo: Volyn Regional State Emergency Service Two other people, including a child, were injured in the residential building. Twelve people remained hospitalized, one of whom was in serious condition, according to the report. title: Military Starlink Service Restored in Ukraine, Defense Sources Say
body:
Starshield satellite connectivity while in motion has been restored for Ukrainian forces following restrictions a day earlier, sources in Ukraine’s defense ministry told Kyiv Post on Thursday morning, Oct. 15.
Reports from military units confirm that the service has resumed and remains operational.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The ministry is continuing communications to establish the reasons and circumstances behind Wednesday’s restrictions. The sources did not specify what restored connectivity or whether any speed limits remain.
The update follows disruptions affecting the military satellite service that complicated Ukrainian drone operations and frontline logistics.
On Wednesday, defense ministry sources told Kyiv Post that SpaceX had imposed restrictions overnight without advance warning to Ukraine’s defense forces.
They described a speed limit of 160 kilometers per hour, or about 100 mph, although units reported losing connections at different speeds, ranging from approximately 72 to 161 km/h, or about 45 to 100 mph.
The restrictions hampered drone missions, including interceptor and medium-range strike operations, and reduced capabilities for logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay, the sources said.
On Wednesday, the ministry said that it was contacting the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners, collecting reports from units, while also checking and activating backup communications channels.

She explores the secrets of Ukraine's intelligence services and shows the hidden side of global events. Her passion is uncovering secrets that change history. Born and lives in Kyiv.

title: New autonomous system provider debuts in Italy
body:
Sentiq Defence has announced the start of operations as an Italian integrator of autonomous and remotely operated maritime systems for defense, security and the blue economy.
Founded by a former Italian Navy mine warfare officer, Antonio J. Belfiore , the company debuts with a complete offering of uncrewed surface, underwater and aerial systems and sonars for port and infrastructure protection to address evolving naval and maritime security requirements.
Monitoring underwater areas is increasingly important for navies, energy operators, port authorities, telecommunications companies and coast guards, which must cover large areas with limited resources. Autonomous systems can extend monitoring coverage while reducing personnel requirements, operational risks and costs. However, integrating platforms, sensors and software from different suppliers can present challenges due to incompatible interfaces, support arrangements and export restrictions.
Sentiq addresses these challenges by adapting and integrating commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) platforms and payloads to specific mission requirements. The company plans to provide these systems, including training and through-life logistical support, through a single point of contact in Italy.
Specifically, Sentiq’s offering covers three domains: surface, underwater and air. The SQ family of modular USVs will be configurable for hydrographic survey, environmental monitoring, offshore asset inspection and persistent surveillance, as well as defense missions such as mine countermeasures (MCM) and anti-submarine warfare (ASW).
In the underwater segment, the firm plans to supply sonars for detecting intruders, in fixed (SQ DDS) and portable (SQ PDDS) versions, and long-range (SQ UDS) to protect ports, naval bases, coastlines and critical infrastructure, supported by inspection-class ROVs. It will also work on tactical aerial drones that extend the surveillance reach of surface assets beyond the horizon.
“I spent most of my career at sea, in mine warfare, and later training the people who do this job,” said Antonio J. Belfiore , Founder and CEO of Sentiq Defence.
“I learned that technology rarely fails on its own: what fails is integration. Sentiq was created to give anyone who works at sea – navies, coast guards, port and energy operators – full control of their domain: mission-focused solutions developed with our international partners, tailored here in Italy and supported by people who have done the job themselves. That, for us, is why we operate under the principle of 'Command your space'."

title: South Africa evacuation and the minority’s half-truth
body: Read before you comment! The Minister for Foreign Affairs is not against accountability; he has voluntarily put out the FACTS since the end of the evacuation exercise. Passenger manifests. Receipts. Signed sheets and other relevant records were all made available to the Minority in an RTI response. The Minister also invited the public, the Minority and the Auditor-General to use their microscopes to obtain an even clearer view of the GHc49.72m expended on the evacuation of our compatriots from South Africa. The Minority is justified, just like every Ghanaian, in demanding accountability from every public office holder. But when legitimate scrutiny extends into the realm of personal attacks, unfounded allegations and the deliberate concoction of half-truths, it must be called out. The Minister for Foreign Affairs voluntarily rendered accounts even before anyone asked for them. First of its kind for any Foreign Minister in Ghana. If he had any intention of concealing the use of public funds, that would have manifested through opaque and dodgy mechanisms shrouded in secrecy. In fact, he wouldn’t have even announced the GHc16m contribution from businessman Mr Ibrahim Mahama. He would’ve collected MTN’s donation and sat on it. Now, let’s go to the substance of the Minority’s claims. The commercial flight figures The Minority alleged that, after reviewing more than 200 pages of documents, they discovered that only 247 passengers arrived on commercial tickets. What is fascinating is that the airlines are known. Ethiopian Airlines, Air Tanzania, ASKY and EgyptAir are not occult organisations. For the avoidance of doubt: A) Ethiopian Airlines brought in 260 passengers on commercial tickets. B) Air Tanzania brought in 598 passengers. C) ASKY brought in 130 passengers. D) EgyptAir brought in 20 passengers. TOTAL: 1,008 PASSENGERS. This clearly defeats the false claim that only 247 commercial tickets were accounted for. This is verifiable information provided as part of the RTI response. (Receipts attached) A Minority seeking to conduct proper due diligence would have contacted these airlines to confirm the receipts submitted by the Ministry. At the very least, they could have authenticated whether the receipts were genuine and then proceeded to establish whether the total number of passengers and the amounts presented by the MFA tallied. That is what scrutiny means. The Minority could not even take the pains to count the 1,008 commercial-flight receipts. I understand that could be tedious work, but there are party boys or even colleague MPs who could sit at a table and count them to arrive at the total number of passengers who came in on commercial tickets. When you abandon this simple and basic counting or tallying exercise and concoct imaginary figures to suit your mischief, one is tempted to conclude that you are deliberately being economical with the truth merely to drag the Minister for Foreign Affairs through the mud. The GH¢5,000 and GH¢500 allowance The Minority again concluded, based on their own analysis, that only 824 passengers received both the GH¢5,000 reintegration allowance and the GH¢500 transportation allowance. They then deducted that figure from the 1,964 total evacuees and concluded that 1,140 returnees received no packages and demanded answers for GH¢6.27 m funds. And in another twisted claim, the Minority alleged that 1,100 people signed for only the GH¢500 transportation allowance, while only 1,508 signed for the GH¢5,000 reintegration allowance. So, where do we draw the line? People who signed and received both amounts are 824; hence, the Minister must account for (1964-824 = 1,140 evacuees) Then you turn around and also allege that those who received only GHc5,000 are 1,508 and those who received only GHc500 are 1,100. The above, from your own analysis, clearly points to the fact that those who received the GHc5,000 package or the GHc500 package exceed the 800 you conveniently put out. Do we conclude that only those whose signatures appear in corresponding positions on both sheets received the monies? NO! In fact, it took more than 10 hours for MFA officers to count and cross-check each signature. They initially arrived at 1,955 people who had signed both sheets. The Minister asked for a recount, and after another thorough exercise, they identified the nine-person difference. The TOTAL NUMBER OF EVACUEES who signed and received the GHc5,000 reintegration and the GHc500 transportation allowances were 1,964, not less, not more. It requires patience and a little meticulous work to arrive at the right conclusion. The 442 Minors The Minority again alleged that the Ministry/Minister could not account for some 442 minors and, therefore, the Minister must account for GH¢2.43 million. They arrived at this lame conclusion by asking how a two-year-old child could have signed for or received GH¢5,500, forgetting that the minors arrived with parents or guardians who signed on their behalf. This also addresses the allegation of duplicate signatures. You do not expect a parent who signed on behalf of one, two or three minors to suddenly produce a different signature for each child. In a worst-case scenario, it should also be appreciated that some signatures could appear similar because of fatigue, stress and trauma. But because the Minister wanted to satisfy our curiosity about the Minority’s claims, we went back to interrogate the records. We discovered NO duplication of pages or names as alleged, except for parents who signed for their wards. At the press conference held by the Majority, which also received and interrogated the records, we arrived at the same conclusion. Someone may ask: should we expect the Majority to discover anything different? No. When the facts on record corroborate the attached affidavit given to all stakeholders. The Minority and Majority received the same data. If both sides, in their usual political elements, choose to pick and choose what they want to put out, that does not, in any way, impute culpability to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or the sector Minister. The basic conclusion should therefore be straightforward: It should not be difficult to contact the airlines to ascertain what they charged and authenticate the receipts they issued. It should not be difficult, with diligence, to ascertain the names of those who signed for the transportation and reintegration allowances. Even simple random sampling through phone calls could have cured the false claims. Hon. Asafo-Adjei Ayeh, there are no alarming discrepancies in the report you received. What is alarming is that basic arithmetic appears to have been glossed over while performing such an important oversight responsibility. If this important role is reduced to who shouts the loudest in the media, the figures you are seeking could be sitting right before you, yet remain difficult to see. Why do the names not always appear in the same order It is obvious that part of the Minority’s confusion stems from its inability to appreciate why Kofi Mensah (for this analysis) could be No.1 on the GH¢5,000 reintegration sheet and also No. 1 on the GH¢500 transportation sheet for the commercial flights, while Ama Kumi may not appear in the same position on the chartered-flight lists. Ama, who is No.1 on the GH¢5,000 list, could appear as No.8 or even No. 700 on the GH¢500 list. The explanation is simple. During phase one of evacuations, the GH¢500 transportation allowance list was coordinated by NADMO at a separate desk, while the MFA coordinated the GH¢5,000 reintegration allowance list on another desk. You don’t need spiritual powers to confirm this from NADMO unless you have a different agenda. Don’t forget: this was a multisectoral national exercise. NADMO, RED CROSS, GHS, NATIONAL SECURITY, SECURITY SERVICES, GACL, AIRTELTIGO, MFA, etc. No one received an allowance for this exercise. After the first phase involving three chartered flights, it was resolved that all payments would be handled on one desk during the commercial-flight evacuation. That is why the names on the commercial-flight lists aligned, while those on the chartered-flight lists varied in sequence. That difference in sequence does not mean people disappeared. It does not mean money disappeared. And it certainly does not, on its own, establish wrongdoing. So where’s the alleged “massive discrepancies?” As the Ranking Member on the Minority side on the Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Jinapor admitted in several interviews, they are not accusing the Minister of any underhand dealings, YET! Nothing stops the Minority from writing to the MFA seeking explanation for the so-called nonexistent anomalies. Running to hold a press conference on a holy Sunday without due diligence is incompetence. It’s simply a desperate attempt to look for scandals where there’s none. Accountability is necessary. Scrutiny is necessary. Questions must be asked, and every pesewa of public money must be accounted for. But accountability must be driven by facts, evidence, arithmetic rigour and due diligence. Not conjecture, selective interpretation of data or political sensationalism. Finally, the 200-page RTI was scanned and sent by mail, as requested. If the receiver noticed anything unusual, it’s fair to ask. MFA has invited the Auditor-General to audit the numbers. Nothing stops the Minority from engaging an independent audit firm they listed and paying for it. They should remember to task those auditors to do thorough work on the GHc44m taxpayers’ money spent on COVID-19 quarantine, even though people were charged for it. Let’s stop the unnecessary shouting and do some reading comprehension under this post.

title: Ukraine Renews Oil Blitz on Russia, Strikes Ryazan Refinery as Zelensky Ends Pause
body:
Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries early on Thursday, Oct. 15, striking the Ryazan refinery as explosions and fires were reported at a military airfield in the Voronezh region.
Ryazan Region Governor Pavel Malkov confirmed a fire at the refinery, as well as a strike on a warehouse and vehicles at another industrial site in the city. No casualties were reported, and authorities were assessing the damage.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Drone attacks also prompted officials to cancel classes at schools and kindergartens in Ryazan’s Oktyabrsky district, where the refinery is located, and parts of the Sovetsky district.
The attack came after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had paused strikes on Russian oil refineries for three days at Washington’s request, but was lifting the restriction because Moscow continued targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview in London.
The Ryazan refinery is Russia’s third-largest by processing capacity, handling 17.1 million metric tons (18.8 million US tons) of crude oil annually.
Owned by Rosneft, it produces more than 2 million metric tons (2.2 million US tons) of gasoline and over 3 million metric tons (3.3 million US tons) of diesel fuel each year, making it a key supplier to Moscow.
The facility was last attacked on Sept. 6, following which it halted operations .
Also overnight, Ukrainian forces reportedly struck a military airfield in Borisoglebsk, in Russia’s Voronezh region.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Supernova+ and Exilenova+ published eyewitness footage showing the reported strike and a glow from a fire .
According to reports circulated by Ukrainian monitoring channels, the airfield was targeted with Neptune missiles, damaging six Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers. The claims have not been independently verified.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev confirmed an attack on the region, saying air defenses had destroyed 33 drones and “several jet-powered aerial targets.”
Falling debris damaged outbuildings at several private homes and one vehicle, but caused no casualties, Gusev said. He did not mention the reported strike on the military airfield.
Russia’s defense ministry claimed that its air defenses had intercepted 166 drones over 14 regions overnight, including the Moscow, Ryazan, Voronezh, and Rostov regions.
