A Russian drone struck the plant on Feb. 14, 2025, punching a hole through its roof and igniting a fire in the cladding. The fire smoldered inside its layers for two weeks before it was extinguished. The strike damaged the ventilation system and the structure’s seal, allowing moist air to enter and raising the risk of corrosion in the steel arch.
In May, the EBRD said that radiation was not escaping the confinement, but warned that corrosion could undermine the structure if repairs are delayed. Engineers also face difficult working conditions: the site’s radiation levels limit how long workers can remain inside.
The extent of the damage is still being assessed, and the final repair estimate could change. More detail on the damage to the confinement and the repair work shows why the British contribution is one part of a much larger funding effort.
The UK has previously donated €8 million ($9 million) to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account, which supports nuclear safety at the site. It announced another £54 million ($72 million) in winter support last week, including £20 million ($26 million) for energy assistance. The government says Britain has provided nearly £25 billion ($33 billion) in total support to Ukraine.
During a meeting in London, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told President Volodymyr Zelensky that Britain was “behind you and that will not change,” The Guardian reported .
The pledge comes as European support for Ukraine faces political pressure.
Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally party and a potential contender in the 2027 presidential election, said France “cannot keep financing Ukraine,” citing the country’s economic situation. Le Pen has said she would end French financial aid to Kyiv if elected, while leaving military assistance and training open.
Her comments raise questions about future French policy, but do not signal an immediate change in France’s current support. The Guardian said current polling predicts Le Pen could win next year’s vote. Her position also comes as European governments debate how to finance further support for Ukraine.
In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany and the leftist BSW party backed a motion in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament calling for Berlin to end military support for Ukraine. The measure is symbolic: state parliaments do not set Germany’s foreign policy, so it does not change the federal government’s aid. It does, however, show how opposition to military assistance is entering regional political debate.
The political debate coincides with a disruption to military satellite connections. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials said restrictions had affected Starshield terminals, the military-grade service associated with SpaceX’s satellite network. Some units reported losing connections while moving at speeds ranging from about 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45 to 100 miles per hour), according to Ukrainian defense ministry sources .
The disruption affected drone missions, including interception and medium-range strike operations, as well as frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relays. Ukraine’s defense ministry said it was gathering reports from units, contacting the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners, and checking backup communications channels. The cause of the restrictions had not been established. The timing added to concerns over strained US-Ukraine relations, but did not prove the restrictions were politically motivated.
Reuters reported that Europe has no ready-made satellite system Ukrainian soldiers could attach to drones as an immediate replacement. Eutelsat’s OneWeb network does provide connectivity in Ukraine through partners, but consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp said its terminals’ capacity, weight, size, and power requirements make them less suitable for frontline use.
Starlink and OneWeb terminals also use different technology, meaning Ukraine could not simply connect existing Starlink equipment to OneWeb – thousands of terminals would need to be replaced.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defense technology company Buntar Aerospace, told Reuters the disruption showed that users “can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off.” European governments and companies are working on longer-term options, but those plans do not offer a quick fix. The dependence extends beyond communications. Ukraine and European countries rely on US satellite systems for early warnings of ballistic missile attacks.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Starlink service in Ukraine 'restored,' Defense Ministry source says
body:
Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
SpaceX, the owner of Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning , limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
" As of now, (Starlink military package) Starshield service while on the move has been restored and remains operational. We have confirmed this through reports from our units," the source said.
"The Defense Ministry is also continuing its engagement to clarify all the reasons and circumstances surrounding yesterday’s restrictions."
The source did not say if all restrictions had been lifted or if some speed restrictions still applied.
Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to Fedorov who was one of the first to report the restrictions, also said on Oct. 15 that "Starlink (Starshield) service has been restored."
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
The source of the disruption has yet to be confirmed, but Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
The speed restrictions that were put in place on Oct. 14 were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.

title: Everyone is doing Git on S3 wrong
body:
tl;dr: At Enroute, we have built a new kind of git server that is based on modern database principles, written in Rust and backed by object storage. In our testing, we’ve been able to achieve 7,600+ concurrent pushes per second on a single repository at millisecond latency; more than an order of magnitude faster than existing solutions, while delivering clone/fetch performance on par with exclusively disk-based architectures. We are making this available as open-source, programmable git infrastructure to unlock new possibilities for agentic coding at scale as well as bringing version control to more platforms and products.
While database technology has seen a massive wave of cloud-based innovation in the past few years, Git hosting hasn’t changed much. Up until now, the typical production Git hosting (probably the most famous of which being GitHub's Spokes architecture) has relied heavily on SSDs as the primary storage mechanism. This only makes sense, since both the Git client but also the Git data model virtually assume fast random access storage.
However, in a hosting context, this does not come without cost: Disks can fail, so one needs RAID and/or backups. Servers can fail, so every repository needs replicas to be highly available. And any disk eventually fills up, so repositories must be sharded and rebalanced across a fleet of file servers.
Object storage has become much better in the last few years, and so rewriting databases to run on object storage has been one of the hottest trends in infrastructure engineering lately, perhaps most famously turbopuffer who did it for vector search, as well as Neon for Postgres. The advantages are obvious: a bucket is durable, replicates itself and it never fills up.
Following this, it is only logical to want to put Git repositories into object storage too. Especially in this day and age, this matters particularly for agents: hundreds of clients pushing to a monorepo at once, or kicking off a large fleet of CI runs, is no longer a problem that is limited to just Google, Microsoft or Meta.
So it is not surprising to have seen more innovation coming for Git hosting solutions lately. Most prominently, in August, Cursor/SpaceX described Continuity, their S3-backed Git storage, in Git at any scale . What followed were many open source implementations copying the same approach of an S3-backed write-ahead log (WAL) for Git.
While these implementations have been successful in moving the burden of scalability and durability into object storage, they fall short in two ways: Firstly, while they perform well when scaling out reads, they typically falter under write-heavy traffic. And secondly, they still rely on the canonical Git CLI which memory maps files on disk, which means that they need to have each repository fully loaded on disk before they can begin serving it.
To understand why Git is hard to put on object storage, we first need to look at how Git actually stores data. There are three kinds of objects:
Each object is addressed by the hash of its content, so it never changes. On top of that there are refs. A ref is just a name that points to an object. Branches are refs: main is stored as refs/heads/main and holds the hash of the latest commit on that branch. When you commit or push to a branch, Git writes the new objects first and then moves the ref to the new commit. Refs are the only thing in Git that changes, everything else is immutable.
So in a sense, Git is a content-addressed storage with mutable pointers layered on top. However, Git is not just a content-addressed storage system. It is also a graph database: Any object can point at, or be delta encoded against, any other object.
If Git wants to answer a query, it typically starts at a ref and follows the pointers from commit to tree to blobs, and it only knows the next key to fetch once the previous read has come back. On top of this, an object may be delta encoded, and so it may also need to follow its delta chain to the base object. On a local disk this is basically free.
If one were to treat Git as just content-addressed storage on object storage, every one of these steps would be a 30-40ms round trip.
This is why treating Git on object storage as just a content-addressed storage problem doesn’t work. Instead, the key to Git on object storage is maintaining data locality: Keeping the set of objects that are frequently used together close so they can be covered with a small number of reads.
Incidentally, this is exactly what the Git CLI does when your repository on disk gets large enough: It bundles objects into a packfile, writing a single monolithic file that it can map into memory for fast access. So you might be wondering: Why not just put those packfiles on S3?
Recently made famous by Cursor Origin, this newer design keeps Git's packfiles and makes the bucket a log. Each push is stored as an immutable packfile plus a log entry. Packfiles become visible through conditional PUTs against a WAL index, which records a pointer to the new entry, once the push's ref transaction is prepared on a local copy. Once committed this way, any machine can serve any repository by rebuilding a local copy from the log.
On the read path, the log is a real win. Any server can rebuild a local copy from the bucket and serve fetches from it, so reads scale out with replicas: Cursor reports linear read scaling up to 100 of them. Durability and failover, the hardest parts of running Git on disks, come with the bucket.
The write path however still depends on a single linearizable sequence of packfiles. This brings two problems: In effect, write operations to one repository compete for the same WAL index object and are then applied by one machine in sequence.
To their credit, Cursor have worked hard to make WAL updates fast:
With these improvements, Cursor reports up to 120 pushes/s on S3 Standard and more than 300 on S3 Express One Zone, where they find it is "effectively bottlenecked by the speed at which Git can compact the on-disk data."
At the end of the day, no matter how fast the WAL is, every push still has to land in one repository on disk. This means that Git’s single repository write throughput remains the shared limit for all pushes and repacking/garbage work on a repository. However many servers you run, a repository can only ingest as fast as one machine can apply and compact.
The Continuity design has significantly raised the ceiling for git hosting. However, it stops short of making Git fully scalable: Not only is this effectively a single-writer system, but while the bucket stores the log and the data, reads aren't served from it. Instead, every replica still has to keep a full copy of the repository on disk, no matter how large and how long it takes to download, to serve it.
While building Enroute, we’ve been asking ourselves the question: What if Git worked more like a modern distributed system backed by object storage, rather than a file on a disk? The answers we came up with rely heavily on proven distributed systems principles that we adapted to Git.
The results speak for itself: Running in the cloud on EC2 and S3, we have achieved a sustained peak load of more than 7,600 concurrent pushes per second on a single repository!
Like many modern databases, Enroute separates compute and storage. Our storage tier consists of replicated log for low-latency operations and an object storage backend for scalability and long-term durability. Compute is fully stateless and holds nothing but cache. In contrast with the WAL-on-S3 design, we made three key design decisions that result in higher throughput and lower latency:
Enroute is optimized for scale. Following the principle of separating compute and storage, we replaced the traditional git server with two dedicated tiers:
1. Ledger tier: A small cluster of nodes that keeps one replicated log per repository using Raft consensus. The log holds the repository's refs and the list of layers that make up its data. A layer is an immutable file of Git objects with its own index, much like a Git pack.
2. Compute tier : Any number of interchangeable nodes that do the actual Git work: building layers, serving clones and fetches and compacting. Compute nodes keep nothing that can't be rebuilt from the ledger and the bucket.
Let’s step through how this helps repo-level scalability by following a single push request:
You might wonder where the bucket comes into play? In practice, most pushes tend to be small, so there is a fast path that allows them to initially travel inlined into the log, deferring object storage writes until the log is flushed. Only layers larger than 1 MiB are uploaded directly to the bucket and then committed as a ledger entry.
Compared to the WAL approach, the log is no longer written in the bucket, but it is not the only thing that helps us keep throughput on a single repository fast:
We want data to eventually end up in object storage and keep the ledger lightweight, so inline layers can't stay in the log forever. Only refs and the layer list remain on the ledger nodes in the long run.
However, uploading layers one by one would bring back the object storage request cost we just avoided, so layers move in batches to the bucket. About once a second, a compute node flushes the layers from the log: It takes the recent inline layers, merges them into a single file, uploads it to object storage, and swaps out the layers in the log. If you’re familiar with LSM trees, this is similar to a memtable flush.
The same compute node also runs compaction jobs by merging small layers into bigger ones. Merges only copy bytes without recompressing them, so they are relatively inexpensive to run. Once about eight layers of similar size pile up, they are merged into one layer roughly eight times larger. This way, a byte is rewritten only a handful of times as the repository grows, and the largest layers are merged rarely.
Stateless compute and a cache that removes the read penalty
To keep typical read accesses to a repository fast, Enroute caches parts of layers locally in memory and on disk via a buffer pool abstraction which pages data from object storage as needed.
In turn, compute nodes hold no state. On the first request for a repository, it downloads only what’s required to serve the request from the ledger and object storage, typically the repository and layer metadata as well as the first few chunks of the most recent layers. To keep its data up to date, the compute node subscribes to log updates for the repository and gets updates on refs and the layer list.
When a request needs more data that isn't on disk, the node fetches just the chunks it needs, with parallel ranged GETs. But even a cold cache costs less than you might think. In our tests, a node with an empty disk served a full clone of linux.git in 128.6 seconds, against 126.0 seconds warm.
The secret to serving repositories from object storage lies in optimizing for access patterns: It turns out that with only a few exceptions, a Git client never asks a server for random objects. Instead, a clone or a fetch negotiates what it needs based on the commit history: The set of commits the client wants to fetch, and what it already has locally.
The server's job is to send everything reachable from the requested commit without sending data already available. In practice, these are the objects from a consecutive run of commits. Canonical Git uses the object graph at read time to answer these questions and that assumes the full repo is on a local disk. We already learned that this does not work on object storage, but there is another way!
To fix this we developed a new storage format. Every commit is recorded in a segment . Each segment holds the set of objects representing the delta to the commit’s parents. Multiple consecutive segments are grouped into layers, which are immutable files with a table of contents at the end. The segment of a commit in combination with its ancestors holds all necessary data that is reachable from a commit. So to catch the Git client up on recent changes, Enroute can simply serve it from the respective segments, knowing that the common ancestry between client and server contains all dependencies to properly resolve the packfile.
This works because Enroute restricts Git’s object graph in two ways:
Of course, as with all things in engineering, there are trade-offs. While for us, this format has shown massive benefits not just for speed but also simplicity, it also comes with some caveats:
To put Enroute’s design to the test and push its limits, we used forgemark , which is capable of simulating large numbers of concurrent agents pushing to branches of one shared repository. In these tests, Enroute demonstrates a peak performance of more than 7,600 pushes per second into a single repository.
Put into perspective, this is roughly 18 times what Entire.io reports and more than 1,000 times what GitHub is currently able to handle (the numbers come from slightly different setups but give a good sense on the order of magnitude).
We’re not saying everyone needs a repository that supports 7,600 pushes per second today, but we are excited about what becomes possible when pushing to a Git repository is no longer a bottleneck:
To get a better sense of performance under load, we also compared Enroute with the most famous open-source Git server on object storage, walgit. Using the same benchmark, we gradually scaled from 1 to 512 concurrent pushes, while keeping a close eye on latency:
However, pushes are only half the story. A forge spends most of its time serving clones and fetches, and that is exactly where git hosting on object storage needs to close the gap against purely disk-based architectures. We compared Enroute with a warm and cold cache against stock Git 2.56.0, served by git http-backend behind Apache, using a repacked copy of linux.git, and measured the wall time as the client sees it, from starting the command until it returns.
The results are close, and in one case clearly better: Enroute managed to shine on the shallow benchmark, with its clones being more than 2x faster. This showcases Enroute’s raw server performance.
Partial clones are on par, full clones are about 17% slower and incremental fetches about 13% slower. Interestingly, this difference mostly happens on the client side: While Enroute’s server is faster than stock git, the deltas it serves are currently more computationally expensive for the client to decode.
The results show that a warm cache mostly improves shallow clones and incremental fetches, whereas the cold start penalty for the other scenarios is less relevant.
What we built shows that you can scale Git hosting based on modern database principles on top of object storage. But it is only the start, and there is still a lot we want to improve and find out:

title: Russian ambassador rejects Japan’s complaints over Chinese delegation’s visit to Iturup
body:
TOKYO, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Ambassador to Tokyo Nikolay Nozdrev rejected Japan’s complaints over a Chinese delegation’s trip to Iturup Island, the embassy reported.
Following Wednesday's meeting between Nozdrev and Japanese Foreign Ministry’s European Affairs Bureau Director General Kimitake Nakamura, the diplomats said in a statement: "The Russian ambassador to Japan firmly rejected Tokyo’s complaints regarding <...> the visit by representatives of the Heilongjiang Provincial People's Government and business community to Iturup Island."
"The ambassador noted that practical cooperation and interregional exchanges within the framework of the comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation with Beijing will continue to grow steadily, including in the context of socioeconomic development programs in Russia’s Far East," the embassy added.
Earlier, the press service of the Sakhalin Region government reported that businesspeople from China’s Heilongjiang Province had expressed interest in developing the hotel industry and cultivating marine biological resources on the Kuril Islands. Specifically, Chinese entrepreneurs visited potential sites for tourism infrastructure construction on Iturup Island and discussed mariculture cooperation prospects. In response, the Japanese authorities lodged a protest with the Russian ambassador, who was summoned to the Foreign Ministry.

title: First diesel supplies to US possible in at least 2-3 weeks — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The first supplies of Russian diesel to the US could take place in at least 2-3 weeks, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"To carry out the shipments, it is necessary to conclude a contract and load the fuel, charter a vessel and dispatch it to the consumer, which takes 2-3 weeks. Therefore, it is probably necessary to conclude an agreement as soon as possible," he said on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
Russian and US leaders, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, held a phone call on October 9, during which they discussed, among other things, petroleum product supplies. The Russian president said that Moscow had reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global market.
Novak told TASS earlier that Moscow would lift its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule, being ready to supply 300,000 tons of diesel in October, increasing the volume to 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons in December. Monthly supplies could subsequently reach 3 million tons.
The Trump administration, in turn, has issued a general license authorizing Russian diesel supplies to the global market until April 7, 2027.
The Russian Energy Week (REW) International Forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16. It is being held with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Energy of the Russian Federation, and the Government of Moscow. The Roscongress Foundation organizes the forum. TASS is the information partner of Russian Energy Week.

title: Air Chief Marshal Aman Preet Singh’s Garba Moment Goes Viral
body:
Vadodara, The ever-smiling Air Chief Marshal AP Singh’s appearance at the United Way of Baroda Navratri Garba Mahotsav in Vadodara has became one of the most talked about moments of the 2026 Navratri season. This video of IAF chief participating in Garba Mahotsav and trying a few traditional moves alongside other Officers and Families has gone viral.



The Air Chief attended the festival’s third night, arriving in navy blue traditional attire with a matching turban and scarf, blending seamlessly with the festive dress code required at the venue. What began as a polite gesture soon turned into a moment of pure spontaneity: he smiled, matched the rhythm, and even slipped in a few playful, Bhangra tinged steps that delighted the crowd.

It was a rare glimpse of the Air Chief in a relaxed, celebratory mood just days after his final Tejas fighter sortie was in the news
The event also saw the presence of senior defence officials including Air Marshal PV Shivanand, Air Commodore RS Bhandari, and retired Air Marshal Sunil Kashinath Vidhate who joined him for the prayers.

The United Way of Baroda Garba Mahotsav is known for its popularity, record setting participation and massive crowds.

title: CIS Defense Ministers Council meeting centers on organizing troop combat training
body:
CHOLPON-ATA (Kyrgyzstan), October 15. /TASS/. At a meeting of the Council of Defense Ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) member countries held in Kyrgyzstan, officials focused on organizing operational and combat training for troops, Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov said.
"Great attention was paid to the organization of operational and combat training for troops. This area of cooperation is the main theme of our meeting," Belousov said, closing the session.
According to the minister, the meeting included discussions on how to plan combat training and defining priorities for this work under current conditions. The meeting participants also analyzed methods and techniques for employing unmanned aerial vehicles and robotic systems in modern combat operations.
"Ways of incorporating combat experience gained during the special military operation into troop training were determined. Issues regarding enhancing the combat capabilities of the troops and conducting joint military exercises were also considered," Belousov said.

title: Zelenskyy: important that everyone in America stands not with aggressor but in defense of our lives
body:
Russia has escalated and increased the intensity of its strikes against Ukraine after benefiting from relaxed sanctions and deciding to take advantage of the situation, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized.
"It is obvious that Russia went for such an escalation of strikes specifically after receiving a relaxation of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia uses every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Thursday.
He noted that overnight the occupiers launched over 850 "Shaheds," coming precisely at a time of artificial speed limitations on Ukraine's defense capabilities. Three residents of Kropyvnytsky and three others in Dnipropetrovsk region were killed. According to the President, it was one of the largest attacks against Kirovohrad region, with impacts also recorded in Kyiv and 14 other Ukrainian regions.
"Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Stable support for Ukraine is needed, first and foremost in defending the skies. Honesty from partners regarding the war is required: it is important that everyone in America stands not on the side of the aggressor, but on the side of our defense of life and our attempts to end this war and guarantee security," Zelenskyy stressed.

title: Essential items to stock in your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season
body:
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Is your household ready if you get hit with a stomach bug tomorrow? Sniffles on Saturday? The flu in a month or two?
In the United States, cold and flu season occurs in the fall and winter, starting in October and stretching all the way through May, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The combination of dropping temperatures and drier climates makes us more susceptible to common respiratory viruses like the common cold, the flu, RSV or COVID-19, and "back-to-back illnesses," says pediatrician Mona Amin .
Get ready now by creating a cold and flu prep kit. "Have things readily available so that you're not scrambling or depending on someone else to run to the drugstore for you when you become sick," says pharmacist Alisha Reed . That includes fever and pain relievers, hydration supplements and monitoring tools to help manage symptoms.
Many viruses and fevers can be managed at home, says Amin. And the common cold and the flu are viral infections, so they can't be treated by prescription antibiotics anyway.
Below, you'll find a list of items for the whole family, recommended by Amin and Reed. Put the products in one designated place, like a shelf in your medicine cabinet or a handy "sick day" box.
You'll also want to take preventative measures like disinfecting frequently touched surfaces, getting vaccinated, wearing masks and washing your hands. But remember, says Reed, no prevention strategy is foolproof.
When you're dealing with cough, congestion, sore throat, fever, fatigue or other common cold and flu symptoms, you may be tempted to reach for a medication that hits multiple symptoms.
But those meds often include extra unnecessary ingredients that can sometimes put you at risk of accidentally overmedicating yourself, says Reed. Instead, opt for medications that target individual symptoms.
These items all come with a price tag, of course. So if you don't have something like a flexible spending account to help cover costs, consider purchasing your personal sick day must-haves to start, then building from there as you're able.
Reed and Amin suggest these medications:
Pain relievers. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help relieve pain and discomfort from headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation, says Reed.
Fever reducer. Medications like acetaminophen and ibuprofen can safely reduce body temperature, though acetaminophen is usually the better choice for fevers .
You might be wondering about other common cold and flu medications. Reed and Amin walk through a few of them and explain how they work. They say it's important to make sure you understand what they really do and why you're using them.
Decongestant . Pseudoephedrine pills or nasal spray, the type you have to ask the pharmacist for behind the counter, can relieve a stuffy nose or sinus pressure by restricting blood vessels and opening airways in your nasal passages. Using decongestants longer than recommended can cause serious side effects, so use only as directed.
Cough suppressant for a dry cough. Dextromethorphan – often referred to as "DM" on the cough syrup box — may temporarily suppress the signal in the brain that triggers your cough reflex, says Reed. However, various studies have found its effectiveness to be minimal at best. And because it's frequently combined with other medications like sedatives and pain relievers, it can put you at higher risk for overmedicating and adverse side effects.
Cough expectorant for a congested cough . Guaifenesin may help relieve chest congestion by thinning mucus in your airways, says Reed. But before you buy, try just staying hydrated first. "Water is a natural expectorant," she says.
Now keep in mind — while antihistamines, cough suppressant and cough expectorants are safe and reliable options, and can offer some mild symptom relief, research suggests the benefits are marginal and should be weighed against their potential risk of side effects. That's according to pharmacist Candy Tsourounis, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of California, San Francisco.
Read the label on the box or bottle of OTC products carefully to make sure that what you're taking isn't expired and will treat the ailment it's intended for. And always stick to the recommended dosage and usage to avoid unnecessary risks or side effects, says Reed.
Honey is a great sick day remedy for all ages, but is especially helpful for small children not yet old enough for cough medicine, says Amin. "Honey is an anti-inflammatory that also helps with coating the throat, which can help with that cough trigger that children will have."
Note: honey isn't safe for children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
This is a basic, must-have tool to check your temperature on those days you suspect you or your little one are running a fever, says Amin.
Rectal thermometers are preferred for children 3 and under; oral and digital infrared thermometers are both fine choices for anyone older than that. (But oral thermometers are usually more accurate.)
The dryness of winter can dehydrate your nasal passages and make it easier for viruses to attach and replicate in your nose and throat.
One easy solution is to irrigate your nose with a saline spray or rinse, says Amin. This can be both preventative by helping to keep the mucous membranes in your nose moist, as well as symptom-relieving by loosening thick mucus if you have a cold.
Research even suggests that using saline drops at the first sign of a cold can reduce symptoms in small children by up to two days .
Chest rub. Vapor rubs containing combinations of camphor, eucalyptus and menthol oils may provide some relief for nighttime cough and cold symptoms when applied to the chest and neck.
Use with caution, says Amin. Though a lot of families use this homeopathic remedy, there's not a lot of research supporting its effectiveness, and it can be harmful if used improperly. Vicks VapoRub , for example, should be applied only to the chest and throat and never heated up. And be sure to check age restrictions before using any products on children — baby and child chest rubs will be formulated with gentler ingredients.
Disposable vomit bags. These are useful to have, easy to store and a great replacement for sitting by the toilet if the stomach flu should hit your house this year, says Amin.
Humidifier. A humidifier adds moisture to the air, which can help loosen mucus stuck in your sinuses. Reed suggests using a cool-mist humidifier when sick, which can help ease stuffiness during a cold.
Pedialyte, apple juice, water, Gatorade. Diarrhea or vomiting, common symptoms of the flu or COVID-19, can sometimes lead to dehydration. Make sure to have a few favorite drinks handy, like Pedialyte, that can help replace those lost liquids for you or your little one, Amin says. If you're going to drink juice, make sure to dilute in a 1:1 ratio with water.
As long as your symptoms are improving — and responding to treatment — many viruses can be dealt with from the comfort of your home.
However, if you're seeing these concerning symptoms, reach out to your doctor.
These aren't the only signs to look for, so when in doubt, reach out, says Reed. "Don't be afraid to call your doctor or talk to a pharmacist about what's going on. It doesn't hurt to double check," she says.
This digital story was edited by Malaka Gharib. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.
We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify , and sign up for our newsletter .
Clarification: This web story has been updated with information about the efficacy of antihistamines, cough suppressants and cough expectorants. Although they are safe and reliable drugs, research suggests the benefits are marginal. Additionally, some portions of this story, including an illustration, were removed and then later reinserted after additional reporting was done. Oct. 22, 2026

title: Iran may not order every Houthi attack, but backing Yemen's rebels carries consequences
body: Attacks by Yemen 's Houthi rebels on Riyadh 's international airport and Saudi Aramco have exposed the strategic threat posed by a militia whose growing missile and drone capabilities have become a key part of Tehran's regional reach. The attacks have brought the war in Yemen directly into Saudi Arabia's capital and its oil-producing heartland, raising the stakes for the world's largest oil exporter and testing its ability to protect critical infrastructure. A weekend attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said. A further strike on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. On Tuesday, an attack targeted an administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran, causing a fire but no reported casualties. Debris from intercepted missiles injured four people in Riyadh. The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi targets and threatened further strikes after Saudi-led coalition forces bombed an oil facility in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa . These latest exchanges mark a sharp escalation in a conflict that had increasingly become intertwined with the wider confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the US. The immediate question is how the Houthis have acquired the capability to threaten major airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links across Saudi Arabia. UN investigators and American military assessments have documented extensive links between Iranian military technology and Houthi weapons systems. A February 2024 report by the US Defence Intelligence Agency identified similarities between Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones. UN experts have also investigated foreign weapons supplies, technical assistance, training and procurement networks supporting the organisation. Such evidence does not establish that Tehran ordered every attack. But it makes Iran's role in strengthening the Houthis' military capabilities central to understanding the threat now facing Saudi Arabia. The militia has its own political leadership and domestic objectives. It emerged from Yemen's internal conflicts and seized Sanaa in 2014, before the Saudi-led military intervention began in 2015. Its independence in decision-making, however, does not negate the strategic importance of external assistance. For Iran, the Houthis offer a partner positioned near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a vital shipping corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Their ability to threaten Saudi infrastructure and disrupt maritime traffic gives Tehran an additional source of pressure on regional adversaries without requiring publicly demonstrable Iranian command over every operation. The attacks also carry consequences beyond the immediate damage. Disruption to Saudi aviation, heightened risks to oil facilities and uncertainty over regional security threaten not only the kingdom's efforts to establish Riyadh as a centre for international business but also the global economy that relies on Saudi oil flows. It also threatens the millions of Muslim pilgrims who go to Saudi Arabia as a key tenet of Islam. Tehran has repeatedly rejected the characterisation of the Houthis as a proxy force, despite evidence to the contrary Saudi Arabia has responded with further strikes on Houthi-held targets in Yemen, including fuel infrastructure in Sanaa, increasing the danger of a wider cycle of retaliation. Tehran has repeatedly rejected the characterisation of the Houthis as a proxy force, despite evidence to the contrary, and it repeats rhetoric that Yemen's crisis requires a political settlement. But the latest attacks sharpen the question of whether Iran is prepared to use its influence to restrain an ally whose military operations have direct consequences for Gulf security. The issue is no longer simply whether the Houthis take orders from Tehran. It is how Iranian assistance has helped build a military capability that can threaten Saudi Arabia's most important economic and transport assets – and whether diplomacy can prevent that capability from driving a wider regional conflict.

title: Pope Leo XIV’s diagnosis highlights importance of lung cancer screening
body:
Pope Leo XIV is making progress in his recovery after undergoing surgery for lung cancer , as his diagnosis puts a renewed spotlight on the disease and the importance of screening.
Vatican officials say the pontiff has been walking in his hospital room and eating normally following surgery.
For MaryAnn Bradley, a lung cancer survivor in St. Catharines, Ont., the Pope’s diagnosis carries special significance. Bradley said she underwent the same surgery after being diagnosed with adenocarcinoma.
“So the Pope and I have something in common. I had the same surgery,” Bradley told Global News. “I had a right upper lobectomy and it was diagnosed as an adenocarcinoma, which is the same as the Pope.”
Dr. Natasha Leighl, a medical oncologist at Toronto’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, said the procedure involved removing one of the five lobes of the Pope’s lungs. “There’s three on the right, two on the left,” Leighl said.
Leighl said lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada, with almost 33,000 Canadians expected to be diagnosed this year.
Signs and symptoms can include a persistent cough, shortness of breath, coughing up blood and chest pain, according to public health information cited in the script.
Doctors say early screening is the best way to improve a person’s chances.
Dr. Rosalyn Juergens, president of Lung Cancer Canada, said lung cancer screening involves a low-dose CT scan, which is performed to reduce the risk of radiation.
Juergens said screening currently focuses on people considered at high risk based on their smoking history, including whether they have smoked and how much they smoked over a period of time.
Bradley urged people who are concerned about their health not to put off speaking with a doctor.
“Please don’t wait,” she said. “Women have a tendency to wait because we have children. Our lives are busy, because we’re working full-time. Please don’t ignore (the signs).”
Bradley said she hopes the Pope’s openness about his diagnosis will help raise awareness about lung cancer around the world.
Bradley added that she believes the Pope’s lung cancer diagnosis is helping save lives by drawing attention to the disease.

title: For some Christians, Hegseth's plan for public execution fits a biblical mandate
body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
President Trump has cancelled the livestreaming of the execution of the man behind the Fort Hood attack. A U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution told NPR that Trump was persuaded that such an event would run counter to American values and also could fan recruitment for radical, Islamist terrorist groups — further putting U.S. forces in the Middle East at risk. Nevertheless, some religious scholars worry that damage was done the moment that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared that a public execution would take place.
"I think one of the most worrisome parts of this development is that … it pushes the boundaries of what's acceptable," said Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religion at the University of North Florida who specializes in the religious right and Christian Reconstruction. "Just saying it out loud moves the boundary."
The last time the U.S. government conducted a high-profile public execution was 90 years ago. But Hegseth suggested that livestreaming Nidal Hasan's death by firing squad would deter future, similar attacks. Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and violent Islamist extremist, killed 13 people and injured 32 in a 2009 attack at Fort Hood. His execution is set for Dec. 3 .
"We'll make sure that people are able to … watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that … there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.
For Ingersoll and some other religious scholars, Hegseth's promotion of an idea that has largely fallen out of favor with the American public ties in closely with his religious background. Hegseth affiliates with the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, or CREC, whose leader identifies as a Christian Nationalist, envisions a theonomous America where women are denied the right to vote and has defended the institution of slavery.
"These are extreme ideas and these are extreme leaders, and I don't have a better way of phrasing it than to just note that Pete Hegseth is a religious extremist," said Matthew Taylor, a visiting scholar at the Center on Faith and Justice at Georgetown University. "He holds ideas that are far outside the mainstream. He is trying to implement those ideas within the U.S. military structure within the Pentagon."
Hegseth's announcement of a livestreamed execution elicited reactions of disgust and condemnation from some faith leaders and politicians. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who serves Catholics in the U.S. military, issued a statement of disapproval on the proposal and instructed any Catholics who may be assigned to the firing squad to request an excusal. Taylor said he believes Hegseth's idea represents "an outlier position within American Christianity," including, he said, within right-wing Christianity.
But Ingersoll said that within Hegseth's church, it is not an outlier.
"The religious community from which Hegseth comes is very comfortable, shall we say, with the death penalty. There's a pretty much unanimous endorsement of it," Ingersoll said. "The crimes discussed in the Hebrew Bible or the Old Testament that carried the death penalty are understood by them to still carry the death penalty. So execution, and even public execution, is very much a part of the way they see the punishment for crime in general."
But some are also asking whether Hasan's religion may partly account for a public proposal that is, to many Americans, abhorrent.
"The question is, why is he being punished differently than everyone before him?" said Joshua Salaam, president of the Association of Muslim Chaplains. "And the answer that most people from my community will say is it has something to do with his religious beliefs, his religious identity."
Indeed, Ingersoll said that the CREC goal to enact Christian governance, and Hegseth's own apparent animus toward Islam, are key factors in this discussion.
"I think he sees himself as engaged in a battle on behalf of God against the infidels," she said.
When Hegseth was nominated to head the Pentagon, his tattoos drew national attention. At the time, he had tattoos of the Jerusalem Cross and of the phrase "Deus Vult" on his body. At some point later, he also added another tattoo in Arabic script of a word that means "infidel." Taylor said all this, plus his authorship of a book titled American Crusade , point to a clear worldview.
"Hegseth is, for lack of a better term, obsessed with the Crusades," Taylor said.
Within the context of the CREC's goals, this history of civilizational conflict between Western Christendom and Islam holds particular importance, said Ingersoll.
"There is an idealization of the Christendom of the medieval period," she said. "Because that was a Christian society, it was the theocratic kind of world that they wanted built. So, much of the viewpoint that seems medieval, actually is."
Today, Ingersoll said, a term often used to describe this project is "dominionism." It is a concept that extends beyond the CREC to other strands within the Christian nationalist movement. It holds that Christians have a Biblical mandate to assert their version of religious governance over every aspect of society. In the U.S., concern over the growth in Christian Nationalism over the last decade has largely centered on the fundamental conflict between dominionism and American principles of inclusive democracy.
Perhaps among the most concerning aspects of the discussion around a livestreamed execution, said Taylor, is the possibility that Hegseth may be instrumentalizing the U.S. military in pursuit of his personal religious goals.
"What Hegseth is trying to do is consolidate the military around a particular ideology – an ideology of Christian nationalism, an ideology of Christian supremacy, an ideology of Western supremacy, that also has racial undertones and patriarchal and misogynistic undertones and anti-LGBTQ undertones," he said.
NPR reached out to the Pentagon for comment, but did not hear back by the publishing deadline.
But the idea of reviving public executions has, in fact, been openly discussed in more mainstream right-wing circles, beyond the CREC. In a 2024 podcast , the late hard-right activist Charlie Kirk argued in favor of it, saying, "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised." Kirk even suggested that large corporations might underwrite the televising of executions to raise money for public coffers.
"Part of what is underneath Christian nationalism and the coalitions that Christian nationalists have made with … the 'tech bros' and the 'podcast bros' and that whole world is this interest in being transgressive," Ingersoll explained.
The name of the podcast where Kirk floated these ideas was Thoughtcrime .
Even if a livestreamed execution of Hasan does not take place, Taylor said the proposal serves as a warning sign of how someone in a position as powerful as Hegseth's can reorient government and society toward what he calls extremist goals.
" Somebody like Hegseth presents an opportunity for them to test some of these ideas, to enact them on a more shortened timeline, and to create precedence within American culture, within the U.S. military, for the ultimate vision that they hope for," Taylor said.
Amid all the discussion, Salaam said it is important also to reflect on the potential damage that public executions do to the moral fiber of the country.
"It does something to all of us to have to watch something like that publicly," he said. "This is not normal for us to promote something like that for our children, for men and women and community members to watch this."

title: These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices
body:
A person walks past a voting sign at the East Point Library on Tuesday, the first day of early voting, in Atlanta. Megan Varner/Getty Images hide caption
📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App
Some key voters say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.
NPR observed two online focus groups Tuesday night with 12 Georgians who voted for President Biden in 2020 and then supported Trump in 2024.
Almost every voter — 11 out of 12 — said they were disappointed with the overall job Trump has been doing. And 10 said they regret voting for him.
"I've been disappointed," said Charles P., 43, who identified as a Democrat. (The voters participated under the condition their last names would not be used.)
"I just don't feel like there's any positive to this administration at all," he continued. "Inflation has only gotten worse, there've been more wars. The tariffs haven't done anything. It seems like we have more enemies now than ever. I just don't see anything positive with his tenure."
Richard A., a 56-year-old Republican, said he's been out of work for 10 months and there is a long list of problems he sees with the direction of the country under Trump.
"Food crisis, starting the war with Iran, inflation," he said. "ICE immigration has just torn families apart, has caused deaths. ... It just seems like everything has gone downhill."
The comments align with Trump's faltering approval rating and a darkening midterm outlook for Republicans . Trump has picked up his campaign travel in recent days, touting his record and arguing for the GOP to retain control in Washington.
These focus groups with swing voters are conducted every month in battleground states across the country. They are run by messaging firm Engagious and market research recruiting firm Nelson Recruiting . NPR partners with them each month as part of the Swing Voter Project .
Focus groups are not scientifically significant like polls, but they do provide insight into what voters are thinking. And in this case, they provide some insight into how voters are deciding who they are supporting this fall.
Rich Thau, president of Engagious, moderates these focus groups. He said for the first time this year, a majority of swing voters said Trump was going to influence their midterm decisions.
"In previous months, when we asked people whether President Trump would influence how they vote, they would say things like, 'Well, I'm looking mainly at the candidates themselves,' or 'I'm looking at the overall sort of environment in the country,'" Thau said.
"This month, seven out of 12 said that he would influence them to vote for Democrats. And that was new."
Karla S., a 49-year-old Democrat, was one of those seven.
"I did vote Republican for 2024," she said. "I made up my mind. I've been so disappointed that I'm just going to go straight and just do Democrat, Democrat, Democrat. Because I'm so disappointed with how this administration has been doing."
Cedric, a 41-year-old independent, said he won't be voting for any politicians that are closely aligned with Trump.
"I think we're not going in the right direction, so I don't want to vote for a candidate that's not going to stand up to him or they're going to go along with his policies," he said. "I'm looking for something different."
Ten out of the 12 participants said they plan on voting for Georgia incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Some voters said they wanted to keep him in office specifically because he wouldn't be aligned with Trump.
Thau said some voters felt that if Democrats take control of Congress, it could provide some needed stability to the country — and the economy, in particular.
"There was some sense that Democrats could restore some semblance of order, and that they'd be able to control a bit of what the president is trying to do or has been doing, to the point where that might restore some of their confidence in the economy," he said.
That's what Thomas M., a 65-year-old independent voter, said is his expectation of a Democratic-run Congress.
"I think there would be more controls placed on Trump with people who are not afraid to stand up to him," he said.
In contrast, if Republicans retain power, Thau said "some respondents told us they thought that the president would have even more control over what goes on because Republicans are afraid to stand up to him."
Jennifer W., a 43-year-old Republican, said she worries "Trump would have free rein."
