title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
body: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. EDDIE GUY Head transplant White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed. The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life. Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One , all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily. Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.” “There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email. Mindclones Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities. While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.” Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality. What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered , “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone. Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar. Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you. But at some point it might be good enough for me. Brain in a jar So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood. The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers. Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ. Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation. While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity. That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues. What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours. That wouldn’t be much of a second life. Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems. Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks. EDDIE GUY Gradual brain replacement On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function. Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging , that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones. We don’t want to lose our identities. That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue. Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach. While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied. Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories. What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab. One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids. Imagine, if you will, a human cortex grown in a lab dish without a body. We know that the agency has an aggressive timeline: Over the course of five years, it wants researchers to lay the foundation for the first human tests of replacement cortex. The aim, it says, is to “take the ‘permanent’ out of brain damage.” And maybe out of old age, too. Brain upload Scientists are already mapping this wiring in simpler animals. Two years ago, Seung took part in analyzing a fly brain that had been cut into paper-thin sheets and imaged with an electron microscope. Then he and his colleagues used image-analysis software to trace 139,255 neurons and about 55 million synapses. The fly map could lead to energy-efficient software that computes the way real brains do, Seung says. Others believe the ultimate outcome of “connectomics” research will be what’s called “whole-brain emulation,” or sometimes just “uploading.” It’s the idea, popular in some quarters of Silicon Valley, that a simulation created from a sliced-up brain could become so detailed that it would reproduce not only a generic intelligence but a particular one, like yours—complete with memories and opinions, and able to live again in a data server somewhere. Setting aside the question of whether a simulation would really be you, everyone agrees that this technology isn’t coming in time for those of us alive today. A survey of 312 neuroscientists, published in 2025 in PLOS One , estimated that human whole-brain emulation wouldn’t happen before 2125. That long and unpredictable tech horizon helps explain why two US companies, Nectome and Sparks Brain Preservation, are offering to preserve human brains (or bodies) today by infusing them with the same potent chemicals used to “fix” the brains of fruit flies for connectome mapping. The idea: If the fine details of a brain’s structure can be preserved, one day in the far future it might be reanimated. But there’s a startling twist. Because brain tissue needs to be preserved quickly after a person’s death, both companies say they want to work with people taking advantage of medical aid in dying, now legal in 13 states and Washington, DC. In that procedure, doctors supply a lethal dose of drugs, but it’s the patient—someone with a terminal prognosis—who pushes the plunger. For a fee, the companies say, they can have a preservation team at the ready. So far, the service is not popular. The companies each say they are still awaiting their first aid-in-dying customer. EDDIE GUY Synthetic neocortex That’s right: an extra brain. Recently, we’ve seen inklings of how this might come to pass. In 2024, Science Corporation, in California, unveiled a “biohybrid” brain-computer interface featuring nerve cells grown on a digital chip. Placed on an animal’s brain, these cells sent out long, thin axons that integrated with the animal’s own neurons. The result: two-way communication from computer to brain, in the brain’s language. The technology could permit new types of medicine, like an implant that directs brain cells to produce dopamine and thereby treat Parkinson’s. But Max Hodak, the company’s CEO, says it also might count as a new brain part, which he likens to a “big, externalized cranial nerve.” Such a device could serve as the connector to Kurzweil’s computerized neocortex in the cloud, giving a living person unlimited extra processing power. Still other entrepreneurs believe if you kept adding biohybrid components to a brain, eventually you could morph it into an immortal machine. Daniel Burger, founder of the venture-­funded stealth startup Eightsix Science (its name refers to the 86 billion neurons in a human brain), says this dream could require mixing several of the brain-saving techniques on this list. He thinks we might need brains in vats, affording neuro-­engineers easy access, so they can gradually replace brain parts with biohybrid neural grafts. The ultimate goal is to migrate your mind into your extra, engineered brain, without ever breaking the continuity of self. “It’s not the typical ‘scan, store, simulate,’” says Burger. “I don’t think simulations will be conscious.” He adds, “We’re saying it’s going to be way more complicated, and it’s probably going to look like gradual brain replacement into a hardware brain.” Once your mind is hardware, you won’t need a biological body. Instead, you could take up residence in a data center somewhere and perhaps even have backups distributed around the globe. “From that point on,” Burger acknowledges, “stuff becomes really crazy.”

title: Cedi depreciates by 7.11% against dollar in August 2026 – BoG report
body: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) Monetary Policy Report for September 2026 has shown that the cedi depreciated by 7.11 percent against the dollar on a year-to-date basis in August 2026 — on the interbank market. In the same period, the cedi depreciated by 7.78 percent, and 6.09 percent, against the pound, and euro, respectively. This is against an appreciation of 28.95 percent, 19.49 percent, and 14.08 percent, against the dollar, pound, and euro, respectively, during the same period in 2025. The report however pointed out that, the cedi was less volatile during the first 185 transaction days in 2026 than in the last four years. “On the international market, the US dollar strengthened in September due to the Fed’s recent policy rate hikes and, as a result, EMDE currencies came under pressure. On the local FX market, pressures on the cedi were muted in August 2026 due to moderated demand pressures and BoG’s support to the market. In the outlook, seasonal demand pressures coming from energy and commerce sectors may weigh on the cedi”, it added. Reflecting exchange rate movements with other major trading partners, the cedi depreciated by 6.80 percent and 7.58 percent, respectively, in nominal trade weighted terms and nominal forex transaction weighted terms, on a year-to-date basis, in August 2026. This is compared to an appreciation of 14.22 percent and 21.60 percent, in nominal trade weighted terms and nominal forex transaction weighted terms, respectively, over the same period in 2025. In real bilateral terms, the Ghana cedi depreciated by 8.47 percent, 8.15 percent, and 6.97 percent against the dollar, pound, and euro, respectively, on a year-to-date basis, in August 2026. Comparatively, the Ghana cedi experienced an appreciation of 20.51 percent, 15.91 percent, and 16.94 percent, respectively, against the dollar, pound, and euro, over the same period in 2025. “In terms of the real effective exchange rate, the Ghana cedi depreciated by 7.27 percent and 8.35 percent, respectively, in real trade weighted terms and real forex transaction weighted terms, on a year-to-date basis, in August 2026. This compared with an appreciation of 17.34 percent and 20.15 percent, respectively, in real trade weighted terms and forex transaction weighted terms, for the same period in 2025”, the report said.

title: Rada abolishes VAT exemption for parcels valued up to EUR 150
body:
The Verkhovna Rada, on its third attempt, has adopted at second reading and in general bill No. 16051-1 on amendments to the Tax Code regarding the taxation of e-commerce transactions with VAT, which abolishes the tax exemption for international postal shipments valued up to EUR 150.
As reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, deputies began reviewing amendments to the bill on Wednesday, October 14, with the vote taking place on Thursday, October 15. The decision to adopt the document in general was supported by 252 MPs against the required minimum of 226 votes, with three voting against.
During preparations for the second reading, deputies submitted 1,935 amendments. The second edition of bill No. 16051-1 was amended during the vote to include a provision on the lifetime status of former politically exposed persons (PEPs), establishing at least 12 months of enhanced oversight following resignation, coupled with individual risk assessments by banks. This measure is intended to help unblock the signing by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy of another law—No. 15111-d on taxing income from digital platforms (adopted in June of this year as a structural benchmark under the IMF program).
During Thursday's voting, the Rada rejected amendments concerning the presumption of innocence for businesses regarding the cancellation of advance payments on corporate income tax for retail fuel traders, as well as provisions concerning the placement, installation, assembly, and construction of wind power plants in the Carpathian mountainous areas.
However, an amendment to reduce the personal income tax (PIT) rate on apartment rentals from 18% to 5% was supported on the floor.
Implementing the provisions of the law alongside Customs Code amendments (bill No. 15460) is a condition for Ukraine to receive the third tranche under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) program, totaling approximately $0.7 billion, and the second tranche of macro-financial assistance from the European Union of EUR 3.7 billion under the Ukraine Loan facility of EUR 90 billion. Under the updated IMF memorandum, Ukraine was required to adopt this law by July 2026, while the original timeline was the end of March alongside other tax norms, though this structural benchmark was missed.
The law introduces special VAT taxation rules for remote sales of goods (excluding excisable goods) imported into Ukraine via international postal and express shipments addressed to individuals valued up to EUR 150, making e-commerce interface operators or their intermediaries responsible for calculating and remitting the tax.
At the same time, VAT exemptions are preserved for small non-commercial consignments valued up to EUR 45 sent between individuals free of charge, as well as for goods in unaccompanied baggage valued up to EUR 150 and security and defense goods (energy equipment and supplies for the defense forces).
Prior to the first reading, presenting the document, Minister of Finance of Ukraine Serhiy Marchenko noted that implementing these norms will generate an additional estimated UAH 10 billion annually for the state budget.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada adopted the respective bills in the first reading on September 16, 2026, following previous unsuccessful attempts.
During the consideration of the documents, Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko stated that the provisions of the laws will begin to apply from July 1, 2027, following the technical implementation of automated tax payments by international marketplaces.

title: Russian oil companies ready to start exporting diesel any moment — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Russian oil companies are ready to start supplying diesel fuel to global markets at any moment, with commercial terms being negotiated now, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"Our companies are ready to [start] shipments immediately, at any moment," he said on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
Asked whether supplies have started, Novak said: "Negotiations on commercial companies are currently underway."
Novak told TASS earlier that Russia would begin to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule immediately, being one of the key suppliers of this fuel to the global market.
The Russian Energy Week (REW) International Forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16. It is being held with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Energy of the Russian Federation, and the Government of Moscow. The Roscongress Foundation organizes the forum. TASS is the information partner of Russian Energy Week.

title: Ukraine’s Navy says it hit six Su-34 bombers at a Russian airbase with Neptune missiles—the jets that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian towns (updated)
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s Navy hit six Su-34M bombers at Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield in Voronezh Oblast with Neptune missiles overnight into 15 October, the Navy said . Residents filmed a large fire at the base after a missile alert, and the Navy’s count has not been independently confirmed. The facility is about 400 km from the frontline. Glide bombs are now central to how Russia’s army fights, used to pin down Ukrainian defenders, including drone teams, before small infantry groups move in. They also hit frontline cities and the civilians who live in them. Six bombers and flight equipment hit, the Navy says The Neptune coastal missile system also hit technical equipment that supports flights, the Navy said. It recorded secondary detonations and a fire on the airfield and said details were still being clarified. The Su-34M can carry several guided and high-explosive aerial bombs at once, along with missiles, the Navy noted. It called the jet one of Russia’s key tools for glide-bomb strikes on Ukrainian positions and frontline towns. In September, a Ukrainian Neptune missile reached a Russian warship at its own pier. Smoke over Borisoglebsk in Voronezh Oblast, Russia, during the fire at the town’s military airfield, 14 October 2026. Photo: Supernova+/Telegram Fire over the airfield late on 14 October Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev declared a missile alert across the region shortly before 22:00 local time on 14 October. Within an hour, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported explosions and a fire, preliminarily at the Borisoglebsk airfield. It later wrote that the airfield had come under missile attack and a fire was burning there. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ posted footage from the town showing the blaze. A large fire is raging at the site of the missile strike. https://t.co/l4aqVvNJIg pic.twitter.com/JYjhM57GYh — Exilenova+ (@Exilenova_plus) October 14, 2026 On the morning of 15 October, Gusev claimed that 33 drones and several jet-powered aerial targets had been downed over the oblast overnight. He did not mention the airfield. A base Ukraine has hit before The airfield hosts the 783rd training aviation center and units of the 105th composite aviation division of Russia’s Aerospace Forces, which flies Su-34, Su-35S, and Su-30SM jets, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported . In summer 2026, it had no permanently based combat jets, and Russia used it mainly as a stopover to refuel and rearm aircraft striking Ukraine, the outlet said, citing satellite observation. Ukrainian drones hit the airfield overnight on 8 July, starting a fire, and satellite images later showed its fuel and lubricants depot destroyed. Drones also attacked the base’s pilot training center in July 2025. The same night, Ryazan Oblast Governor Pavel Malkov reported a fire at an oil refinery in Ryazan. It came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was resuming strikes on Russian refineries. Update: Satellite imagery confirms the strike New satellite images show damage at Borisoglebsk airbase and six Su-34 bombers positioned in the affected area two days earlier, although the extent of the aircraft losses remains unconfirmed. Satellite image shows the aftermath of Ukraine's strike on Borisoglebsk airbase in Russia's Voronezh Oblast on 15 October 2026. Image: Airbus Defence and Space / AviVector. Satellite image from 13 October shows six Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers parked in the area later struck at Borisoglebsk airbase. Image: Exilenova+. The monitoring channel Exilenova+ reports that 4 airframes were completely destroyed, while 2 others sustained significant damage. Read also Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. No refinery strikes reported since Trump’s “energy ceasefire”

title: FSB Arrests Swede in Pskov Region Over Border Crossing and Sabotage Allegations
body:
Russia’s FSB security service said Thursday it has arrested a Swedish citizen in the northwestern Pskov region on allegations of illegally crossing the border to carry out sabotage attacks against military facilities.
An FSB video published by the state-run news agency TASS showed the man identifying himself through an interpreter as 35-year-old Freddy Michael Stålkrantz Lindholm.
In a statement on its website, the FSB said it had detained Lindholm in the Sebezhsky district near the border with Latvia and Belarus. It did not indicate from which country he crossed into Russia.
The FSB claimed he crossed into Russian territory under the guise of enlisting in the Russian military, with the alleged intent of committing “sabotage and terrorist acts at military facilities.”
The FSB said Lindholm served as a contracted service member in Ukraine from February to June this year as a squad commander operating drones.
In the interrogation video, Lindholm said he had signed a military contract with the Aidar battalion, which Russia has banned as a terrorist organization.
He also said he signed the contract in the western Ukrainian city of Ternopil, where he underwent training to operate reconnaissance drones and later instructed other recruits.
The FSB reported that Lindholm was charged with illegally crossing the state border and added that he also faces charges of participating in a terrorist organization and mercenary activities.
The Swedish Foreign Ministry said it was aware of media reports about the detention, but was not currently involved in the case. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

title: Merz: We must do everything to increase support for Ukraine
body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is urging European Union leaders to do more to support Ukraine.

He stated this in Brussels on Thursday upon arriving for a two-day meeting of the European Council.

"Tomorrow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy will join us. The Sunday before last, I was in Kyiv and saw the situation there with my own eyes. We are witnessing an increasingly brutal wave of Russian attacks against Ukraine. This morning, during several smaller meetings, I emphasized that we must do everything possible to help Ukraine, both through the winter and next year," the German Chancellor reported.

In Merz's view, the European Union "will have to increase funding to provide long-term assistance to Ukraine."

"I am firmly convinced that we are defending not only Ukraine's territorial integrity, but also the political order of Europe—an order that Russia is pressuring in every possible aspect. That is why we intend to continue supporting Ukraine, and I am glad that Zelenskyy will join us …

title: Lavrov to hold series of meetings on sidelines of CICA summit — diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to hold a series of meetings on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"The minister will hold numerous meetings, as usually happens on the sidelines of multilateral events," she noted, commenting on media reports about Lavrov’s possible meeting with top Turkish diplomat Hakan Fidan.
On Wednesday, Lavrov arrived in the Azerbaijani capital of Baku to take part in the CICA summit. He has already held a bilateral meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. The parties reaffirmed the two countries’ similar or converging positions on international issues and expressed hope that a planned meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of an informal Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen would give the two leaders an opportunity to exchange views.

title: Bay of Plenty Army engineer helping communities in Indonesia
body:
Unfortunately you are viewing this website on an outdated browser which does not support the necessary features for us to provide an adequate experience. Please switch to a modern browser such as latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge.
A Combat Engineer Officer says working with a local community during Humanitarian Aid and Disaster Relief (HADR) training underscores her reasons for joining the New Zealand Army.
Lieutenant Teagan Andrews-Paul, 2nd Engineer Regiment, was a troop commander leading combat engineers during Exercise Trident Resolve in Banten, Indonesia recently.
Trident Resolve focused on cyber-security, HADR and Military Medicine, with about 2,200 personnel from 19 militaries and civilian agencies working together to prepare for natural disasters.
As part of the exercise a group of 13 NZ Army engineers controlled a site and assisted in renovating a medical facility.
At the conclusion of the exercise the facility was handed over to the Tentara Nasional Indonesia, the national armed forces of Indonesia.
“Working with the local community has been my highlight of the exercise,” she says.
“We had a school very close to our work site and the children would come down every day to watch and hang out with us.”
She was born in Canada but grew up in Masterton and Ōhope in the Bay of Plenty and attended both Wairarapa College and Trident High School.
Both of her parents served with the NZ Army. Her mother was a transport officer and her father was a chef while also a professional athlete.
Members of the Australian Defence Force, Tentara Nasional Indonesia, New Zealand Defence Force and United States military work together to renovate a medical clinic during Exercise Trident Resolve in Banten, Indonesia.
Growing up she spent a lot of time outdoors, which contributed to her decision enlist in 2021.
“Anything involving mental and physical perseverance has always been a huge draw for me and that is why the Army felt like the right choice.
“The Army offers some great opportunities while also continuously providing new challenges.
“Just when I think I understand my job, there is always something new I get to learn about.”
She was also drawn to being able to support communities during times of crisis.
“I was very interested in being able to provide HADR support to countries during times of crisis and that is why I wanted to join the Corps of Engineers. It’s a big part of our role.”
“Exercise Trident Resolve was my first real opportunity working in a HADR capacity overseas and it was very rewarding.”
Her advice to those thinking of joining the New Zealand Defence Force is to be prepared as much as possible.
“The work and training is rewarding but it can be hard – it’s designed to push you.
“If you want to be challenged, learn new skills and have experiences you cannot get in any other job, the military could be the right pathway for you.”
Members of the New Zealand Defence Force hand over a renovated medical clinic as part of a multinational effort during Exercise Trident Resolve in Banten, Indonesia

title: Ukraine destroys six Su-34M bombers at airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region using Neptune missiles
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Navy said this on Facebook .
Overnight on October 15, the Ukrainian Navy struck the Borisoglebsk airfield.
The strike destroyed six Su-34M bombers.
Technical equipment used to support aircraft operations was also destroyed.
Secondary detonations and a fire were reported at the airfield. The information is being verified.
The Su-34M can carry several guided and high-explosive bombs simultaneously, as well as various types of missiles, and is one of the key assets of the Russian Air Force used to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian defense positions and frontline settlements.
The destruction of the Su-34Ms significantly weakens Russia’s air capabilities and reduces the intensity of tactical aviation operations along the relevant sections of the front, the Ukrainian Navy said, adding that it continues to strike Russian military targets, systematically degrading Russia’s combat capabilities.
As reported by Ukrinform, explosions were heard at the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.

title: Put women and youth at the centre of mineral resource governance — ActionAid
body: ActionAid Ghana has called for a fundamental shift in natural resource management, insisting that women and young people must be placed at the core of all decisions regarding the governance of Ghana’s mineral wealth. Speaking on Wednesday in Goaso, Kwame Afram Denkyira, Programme Manager of ActionAid Ghana for the Ahafo, Bono, and Bono East regions, stated during a regional consultation on mining that host communities bear an unequal share of environmental and economic burdens, making inclusive governance an urgent necessity. “The impacts of mining are not experienced equally. Women and young people must be at the centre of conversations about the future of Ghana’s mineral resources.” The initiative forms part of the Uplifting the Voices of Mining Communities (VOICES) project, a two-year regional effort funded by Comic Relief and implemented by ActionAid across Ghana, Malawi, and Senegal from June 2026 to May 2028. In Ghana, ActionAid is focusing its intervention on four heavily impacted mining districts, including Asutifi North in the Ahafo Region, Mfantseman in the Central Region, Ahafo Ano South in the Ashanti Region, and Talensi in the Upper East Region. Through citizen education, artistic activism, and community-led research, ActionAid is equipping populations in localities with tools to document environmental abuses, labour concerns, and human rights violations to drive policy advocacy. In 2024, mineral production generated 9.5 per cent of Ghana’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), pushing total mineral export earnings up by 52.7 per cent to 11.9 billion dollars. Gold alone contributed 11.6 billion dollars, representing over 97 per cent of total mineral export revenue, solidifying Ghana’s position as Africa’s top gold producer. While the sector sustains approximately 1.14 million livelihoods, more than 1.1 million of these jobs are in artisanal and small-scale mining. Over the last two decades, small-scale extraction has degraded upwards of 78,000 hectares of forest and agricultural land, polluting vital water bodies and threatening food security for host families. To counteract these deep-seated challenges, ActionAid’s VOICES project relies on a mineral justice model geared toward gender equity, youth empowerment, and corporate accountability. Over the 24-month project timeline, ActionAid will train 80 women and youth leaders to head civic campaigns and community mobilisation efforts. Simultaneously, four Community-Based Monitoring Committees will be established to collect grounded, verifiable data on local environmental and social conditions. Data gathered by these committees will be converted into actionable policy briefs to engage traditional authorities, District Assemblies, regulatory agencies, and mining companies.

title: "Six hours is absurd" — Patients describe long night-time waits on Finland's A&E wards
body:
A patient visiting an emergency room between 10pm and 7am in many parts of Finland can expect to wait for an average of between five and six hours.
Patients seeking care at an accident and emergency (A&E) ward during the night in Finland face average waiting times of between five and six hours.
That's according to information obtained by Yle from several regional healthcare authorities, otherwise known as wellbeing services counties, about the average waiting times during the month of August.
The data reveals that patients who arrive between 10pm in the evening and 7am in the morning could spend an average of up to six and a half hours waiting to receive treatment.
The worst waiting times during August were found to be in Turku, where they averaged 6 hours and 29 minutes, while the shortest were in Jyväskylä, at 4 hours and 49 minutes.
Based on the information Yle received from the wellbeing services counties, the situation regarding waiting times during the night appears to have remained almost unchanged for several years.
Yle visited the A&E ward at Jorvi hospital in Espoo — where the wait for night-time care (6 hours and 4 minutes) was among the longest in the country in August — to speak to patients about the waiting times.
Marcos Wichert , a Brazilian who has lived in Espoo for six years, injured his arm while dismantling a trampoline in his yard. He told Yle that he suspects his arm is broken, but at the time of his interview he had been waiting to see a doctor for more than two hours without any pain medication.
"I thought I'd get help faster," he said.
Espoo resident Heini Nurmi was also surprised by the length of the waiting time at Jorvi.
She told Yle that she came to the emergency room with chest pains just before 10pm.
"I can't wait five and a half hours, which is the estimated visit duration shown on the screen in the waiting room. I need to go to my children," she said, adding that the absolute maximum length for an emergency room visit should be four hours.
"Six hours is an absurd amount of time to wait for urgent care," Nurmi noted.
Kimmo Suojanen , regional chief physician responsible for the Jorvi emergency room, told Yle that only a small proportion of the hours a patient spends in a waiting room is wasted time — as much of the care takes place out of the patient's sight.
"For example, X-rays are being analysed, specialists are being consulted, or blood test results are being awaited," Suojanen said.
He added that the conditions of patients arriving at night are often more demanding to treat than those arriving during the day, so treating them requires several time-consuming examinations and procedures.
This naturally lengthens waiting times, Suojanen noted, adding further that the situation at Jorvi has improved considerably compared to a number of years ago, when waiting times of up to 10 hours were possible.
"There are far fewer completely unreasonable waiting times than just a few years ago," he said.
Maaret Castrén , former chief of operations at HUS and professor emerita of emergency medicine, meanwhile noted that studies have shown the detrimental impact lengthy waiting times can have on patients, particularly elderly people.
"This hasn't been taken seriously in Finland, even though we, as representatives of emergency medicine, have said that patients should be moved on from the emergency room within four hours," she said, adding that hospitals should focus on shortening waiting times in the emergency room as a matter of priority.
"This should be a priority for the entire hospital, not just a goal for the emergency department," Castrén said.
Castrén is currently serving as a member of parliament for the governing National Coalition Party, and she also intends to stand as a candidate in next spring's elections. In this article, she comments on the topic based on her previous professional experience.
Yle caught up with the interviewees — Marcos Wichert and Heini Nurmi — before they left Jorvi to hear how long they had to wait.
Wichert left around midnight, meaning his visit lasted four hours and 40 minutes. An X-ray revealed that his arm was not broken, but it remained swollen and sore.
Nurmi meanwhile grew increasingly frustrated with the waiting time and opted to go home after an hour and a half — despite not seeing a nurse or doctor during that time.
The next day, she told Yle that her chest pains had eased and she would not require medical attention, at least for the time being.

title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
body: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs. The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.” “Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.” Buying time Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years . But there’s plenty of room for improvement. One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs. People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer. The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand. “With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger. Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder. Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through. Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field. When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C. The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023 . Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats. Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs. Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar. Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100. It hasn’t been easy. The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.” Deep-freezing kidneys The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig. Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab. There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure. Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects. It takes around two hours. The next step is to infuse the organ with the iron oxide nanoparticles, which are pumped through the organ for around seven to eight minutes, says Finger. Then it’s time to cool the organ by pumping cold nitrogen vapor into a chamber housing it. It’s a delicate process, and the team must ensure that the organ is cooling all the way through. At the same time, they must lower the kidney’s temperature as quickly as possible to prevent ice from forming. “Oftentimes there are multiple people doing different things to make sure that things don’t go awry,” says Bischof. Once the organ reaches the vitrified state at around -120 °C, it “behaves like a glass,” says Finger. “At that point, you can stay stable for long periods of time—we think indefinitely.” The team then pauses the cooling process to ensure that the organ is glassy throughout. Otherwise, it could crack. After the pause, if everything goes well, the kidney is ultimately cooled to -150 °C. Once it’s in the freezer, it can stay there for days, weeks, or even months. The team has kept a small number of kidneys banked for over a year. Pink right up The real test of these kidneys comes when they’re taken out of the freezer, rewarmed, and flushed of their chemicals and nanoparticles. Can they support life? So far, the team has tested some of them in a couple of different ways. In one set of experiments, the researchers put rewarmed kidneys on perfusion devices —systems that are already used in transplant surgeries both to provide organs with nutrients and to help doctors assess them while they’re out of the body. In another set of experiments, Finger and his colleagues transplanted rewarmed kidneys into pigs and monitored them for two hours. In both experiments, the rewarmed kidneys seemed to recover, says Finger. “They pink right up,” he says. The team see blood flow into the rewarmed, transplanted kidney, allowing it to “pink up.” COURTESY OF THE RESEARCHERS There are lots of ways to measure the function of a kidney, but one key test is whether or not the organ can make urine. By this measure, the rewarmed kidneys did well, although they produced around two-thirds of the amount that would normally be expected. “They produce urine … within a minute or so,” says Finger. “We know that they work.” Most of the rewarmed kidneys had been banked for days or weeks. But one had been in the freezer for just over a year. When Finger and his colleagues rewarmed it and put it on a perfusion machine, they found that it produced urine “immediately.” “It actually looked better than many of the [other] kidneys,” says Finger. “We’re comfortable now saying we can store them for a year and rewarm them with excellent function.” “It’s a very big deal to go a year,” says Kevin Myer, president and CEO of LifeGift , an organ procurement organization based in Texas. Being able to store organs for that length of time would transform organ transplantation. He envisions banks of organs that could be used on demand in emergency cases where people can’t wait, such as for some drug overdoses or gunshot wounds. Final hurdles But the procedure isn’t ready for prime time just yet. As well as producing less urine than expected, the rewarmed kidneys also showed signs of injury. The damage seems to be caused by the cryoprotectant chemicals, say the researchers. “This is one big breakthrough that solves half the problem,” as Kilbride puts it. The team has shown that the rewarmed kidneys can regain blood flow, which is “very important,” says Greg Fahy, a cryobiologist who is considered a pioneer in the field. But he’s worried about the extent of the damage to the organs. “We can’t tell from these experiments whether these kidneys might have supported life or not.” But Fahy, who is chief scientific officer at the biotech companies Intervene Immune and 21st Century Medicine (where he is also executive director), acknowledges that it’s not clear how these kidneys might fare once they’re inside a living animal for the long term. Finger also hopes to find ways to repair the damage seen in the kidneys. Other research has shown that the health of transplant organs can improve while they’re on perfusion machines . And damaged kidneys might undergo some level of self-repair once they’re in a body. At any rate, human kidneys may cope better with the process than pig kidneys, says Finger. The next step will be to test the kidneys in pigs over longer periods of time. The team, along with many other researchers in the field, will continue the search for less toxic cryoprotectants, too. Finger, Bischof, and their colleagues are also planning experiments with human kidneys. Finger is optimistic. “We’re going to see that there’s injury, and it’s not perfect … but now we’ve got to the point where it works,” he says. “These are big, historic milestones in our field, and we’re excited about it.”

title: Moscow Arrests Swede Accused of Planning Attacks
body:
Russian security services said on Thursday they had arrested a Swede they accused of fighting for Ukraine, “illegally” crossing into Russia and plotting “sabotage and terrorism” attacks on military infrastructure.
Russia has arrested Western citizens throughout the Ukraine war, which has pitted Moscow against the West.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The powerful FSB did not name the man but said he was detained in the north-western Pskov region, near the border with Lithuania.
It said he had “illegally crossed the state border of the Russian Federation from the territory of a neighbouring state”.
It specified he was arrested in the Sebezh area, close to the borders of Lithuania and Belarus.
The FSB said it had “documents” it alleged showed the man “took part in combat acts against our country within the Ukrainian army”.
“Under the pretence of joining the Russian armed forces, he travelled to the Russian Federation with the intention of carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on military facilities,” the FSB said in a statement.
It said a criminal case was launched against the Swede on charges of crossing the border illegally, organising “terrorist” activities and being a mercenary.

title: The hijab issue and spontaneous protests in Azerbaijan
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – Public protests against the hijab ban in the Republic of Azerbaijan have been entirely spontaneous and represent a natural reaction to the violation of fundamental civil rights.
The recent wave of protests against hijab restrictions in the Republic of Azerbaijan—sparked by Cabinet Ministers decree regarding school uniforms—has become the starting point for on-the-ground demonstrations and the initial focal points of spontaneous domestic unrest.
The first signs of public protest emerged after officials at School No. 9 in the Jalilabad district barred girls wearing the hijab from entering classrooms; these protests quickly spread to other cities, including Baku. Subsequently, Azerbaijani authorities defended the Ministry of Science and Education’s decree of September 21, 2026—which prohibits any attire inconsistent with the "principle of secular public education"—asserting that it aligns with the country's secular constitution. Although the specific phrase "hijab ban" does not appear in the text of the decree, it declares any attire inconsistent with the official uniform to be unauthorized—a clause effectively amounting to a ban on the hijab. In this context, the following points are significant:
1.Public protests against the hijab ban in the Republic of Azerbaijan have been entirely spontaneous and represent a natural reaction to the violation of fundamental civil rights. In this context, even teachers and students who do not wear the hijab stepped forward; in a spontaneous social movement, they demonstrated their solidarity with the expelled schoolgirls by participating in marches and class boycotts. Religious communities and Islamic activists within Azerbaijan also viewed the Ministry of Education’s anti-hijab decree as a clear violation of the constitution, freedom of belief, and the right to education. Meanwhile, figures and media outlets close to the Azerbaijani government have attempted to portray this spontaneous movement as alleged foreign ideological interference by Turkey and Iran, using it as a pretext to crack down on hijab advocates. This is despite the fact that there is no evidence of Iranian or Turkish involvement in the matter; the primary cause of the protests and unrest was the Azerbaijani Ministry of Education's anti-hijab decree.
2. Efforts by Zionist media, as well as officials and media outlets aligned with Israel, to accuse Turkey and Iran of interfering in Azerbaijan's internal affairs and inciting protesters are seen as reflecting Tel Aviv's strategy to undermine Baku's relations with its two key neighbors and to discredit the spontaneous actions taken by the Azerbaijani people against the hijab ban.
Many political and media analysts believe that Israel is the force behind the scenes—or at least the primary beneficiary—of this situation. Friendly relations between Baku, Ankara, and Tehran have long been a source of concern for Israel; media outlets aligned with the Zionist regime aim to weaken Azerbaijan's regional ties with its Muslim neighbors by highlighting anti-Islamic stances in Azerbaijan and deliberately pitting Baku against Muslim public opinion in Turkey and Iran. Some also view Israel's approach as part of a broader scenario aimed at steering the Republic of Azerbaijan toward a strictly secular identity aligned with Tel Aviv's strategic interests in the Caucasus.
3. There is no doubt that the entirely spontaneous popular movement opposing the ban on the hijab in schools occurred without foreign interference; while the country's Muslims welcome moral support from Muslim nations, they oppose any action that would highlight foreign involvement in this event—a stance that demonstrates the political maturity of Muslim political parties and groups. Furthermore, the secular constitution of the Republic of Azerbaijan recognizes the freedom of worship for followers of various religions, including Islam, as a fundamental right of citizenship.
Accordingly, reason dictates that the country's authorities—by upholding the constitution, adhering to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and observing the standards of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation—should not oppose the hijab itself, which is a religious ruling and a fundamental tenet of Islam, nor should they further position themselves in opposition to the people.

title: At least 32 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse
body: At least 32 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said. Most of the students killed were under 13 years old, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department. At least ​45 people ⁠suffered major and minor injuries, ‌he added. Rescue workers spent hours pulling children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of ⁠their loved ones. The incident took place at 8.48am local time, and the rescue operation lasted four to five hours, Mr Khattak said. Victims of the collapse were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesman Mohammad Asim. “The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher,” Mr Asim said. Three children remained in critical condition, with head injuries, he said. Most of the injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home. A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor had collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in. Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said excessive weight from construction on the school roof had caused the collapse. “It was a weak building structure,” he ​said. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, ‌which caused the collapse.” Mr Saeed said ⁠the school's owner had been arrested ​and authorities had opened an investigation. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in. Distraught relatives accused the ​school of ‌ignoring safety concerns about the building's condition and demanded accountability. “Make an example of them, a lesson ⁠for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make ⁠money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif promised “a thorough investigation” into the incident. “My heart is with the families grieving the loss of their children and a teacher in the tragic roof collapse at a school in Peshawar. No parent should have to endure such pain,” he wrote in a statement on X. “I extend my deepest condolences and pray for strength for every family affected. I have directed that the injured receive the best possible care. We will ensure a thorough investigation into this tragedy and take every necessary step to protect the safety of children in schools across the country,” he added. Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse. “In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the President’s office posted on X.

title: Ukrainian Drones Spark Fire at Ryazan Refinery as Zelensky Vows to Resume Attacks
body:
Ukrainian drone attacks set fire to a Rosneft oil refinery in the Ryazan region overnight, officials said Thursday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed to resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in response to Moscow’s continued strikes.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the region had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
“The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene,” he said.
Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday that Ukraine had paused attacks on Russian refineries for three days to comply with U.S. President Donald Trump’s surprise announcement of an “energy ceasefire.”
He said Kyiv was now resuming the attacks because Moscow continued to hit the Ukrainian power grid and fuel depots over the same period.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told FT.
Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, Zelensky said he could only agree if in return he was given more U.S.-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the “minimum” that would be acceptable.
The Kremlin said Thursday that Moscow did not perceive that Kyiv had ever complied with the ceasefire and said that the fact that it had struck another Russian refinery was "nothing new."
"The Ukrainian regime in Kyiv continues to strike these facilities, thereby, of course, coming into serious contradiction with the peace efforts of the United States and of the American negotiators who are indeed making very vigorous efforts to somehow initiate the peace process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"But so far, these vigorous attempts have been thwarted by the unwillingness of the Kyiv regime — and of Zelensky personally — to make peace," he said.
The Rosneft-owned Ryazan oil refinery supplies fuel for Moscow and accounts for 5% of Russia’s total crude refining capacity.
The plant previously suspended operations following drone attacks in May, July and September.
On Wednesday, 24 hours before the confirmed attack, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak claimed Ukrainian forces had hit refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions. At the time, Ukrainian officials dismissed Novak’s claims as false.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. Ukraine’s air force said 580 Russian drones attacked the country overnight, of which 536 were shot down.
Three people were killed and six wounded in an attack on critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities and residential homes in central Ukraine’s Kirovohrad region, said the local governor.

title: Ex-NPA MD, Aminu Dabo, resigns from APC
body: A former Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), Arc Aminu Dabo, has resigned his membership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) with immediate effect. Dabo, who served as the APC caucus chairman in Dambatta Local Government Area of Kano State, announced his resignation in a letter dated October 7, 2026, addressed to the party chairman of Dambatta Gabas Ward. In the letter, Dabo said his decision followed careful consideration of personal reasons and his future endeavours. He confirmed that he had formally submitted his resignation to the appropriate party officials in Dambatta for necessary action. NSCIA calls for national unity, peaceful coexistence as CAN marks 50th anniversary Ondo crash: Aiyedatiwa orders river fumigation, emergency water supply in Igbokoda The former NPA managing director expressed appreciation to the APC leadership for the opportunity to serve, as well as the support and confidence reposed in him. “I remain grateful for the cordial relationship I enjoyed and appreciative of the experience gained during my time of service,” he said. He also thanked the party leadership for allowing him to contribute to its development and progress. Dabo was a governorship aspirant in Kano State and previously served as the state’s Commissioner for Land. He is also the proprietor and chief executive officer of Aminu Dabo College of Health Sciences and Technology and Aminu Dabo College of Nursing Sciences, both located in Kano.

title: Aldar enters Sharjah with Dh1.1bn residential acquisition
body: Aldar , Abu Dhabi ’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio. The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion. Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community. “Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio. The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi- Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island. Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria. Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE . The new project, with an undisclosed value, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London this week. The move comes as the UAE property market continues to perform strongly despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. The Emirates was ranked as the world’s leading real estate investment destination in a property market league table released in June. Arada’s UAE Property Investment Index – conducted on behalf of the Dubai developer by US-based Penta Group – found that 56 per cent of global investors have serious interest in the UAE’s property market. The latest acquisition will broaden Aldar’s geographic exposure while adding residential rental assets aimed primarily at end users and long-term tenants seeking housing at accessible price points, the company said. Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said Aldar’s decision to make its first investment in Sharjah at Aljada reflected confidence in both the development and the emirate’s residential market. “To have a developer of Aldar’s calibre and track record choose Aljada as its first investment in the emirate reflects the quality of what we have built here, and the scale of the opportunity that Sharjah represents,” he said. Aljada spans 2.2 million sq m and is expected to comprise about 25,000 homes at full buildout, with an anticipated gross sales value of Dh35 billion. Residential handovers at the development began in 2021, with more than 8,800 homes delivered across multiple districts, according to the statement. The community also includes schools, hotels, student accommodation, retail space and the Madar family entertainment district. Aldar said the acquisition adds to its strategy of expanding its portfolio of income-generating properties, as the developer seeks to diversify its revenue streams. The Abu Dhabi developer, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, is expected to hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company’s launch, with the deliveries going up to 4,500 next year, according to Mr Emery.

title: Seaspan Shipyards lays keel for Canada's new polar icebreaker
body:
Shipbuilder Seaspan Shipyards has held a keel-laying ceremony for the Canadian Coast Guard's polar icebreaker, CCGS Imnaryuaq.
As maritime activity in the Arctic grows and the region experiences unprecedented environmental and geopolitical change, the Government of Canada’s strengthened presence and capability in northern waters has never been more important.
The CCG’s new polar icebreakers represent a major step in advancing Canada’s leadership, security, and ability to continue delivering critical services to Northern communities. The keel laying is a significant step in the construction of the polar icebreaker, marking the moment when the first constructed section on the vessel is put in place, and the ship begins to take form.
This milestone builds on the official start of construction for the future CCGS Imnaryuaq in April 2025, marked by the cutting of steel for the vessel’s first polar block. Less than two years later, the vessel is taking shape at an accelerating pace, bringing Canada one step closer to welcoming its next heavy polar icebreaker in the early 2030s.
CCGS Imnaryuaq is designed to operate self-sufficiently in the high Arctic year-round. Once delivered, it will play a critical role in enabling the Canadian Coast Guard to transit and operate in more than 162,000km of Arctic coastline.
The future polar icebreakers will be 158 metres long and 28 metres wide, with a design displacement of 26,036 tonnes, and will accommodate a crew of up to 100 personnel and feature diesel-electric propulsion with Polar Class 2 icebreaking capability.
“Canada’s Arctic sovereignty depends on our ability to be present, to operate, and to respond. The keel laying of CCGS Imnaryuaq marks a major step toward strengthening that capability. Built by skilled Canadian workers, this polar icebreaker will reinforce our year-round presence in the North, support Northern communities, and ensure the Canadian Coast Guard has the tools it needs to protect Canada’s interests in a changing Arctic," David J. McGuinty , Minister of National Defence, said.
“This milestone underscores the Government of Canada’s commitment to taking concrete action to support a safe, secure, and prosperous Arctic. Investments in modern, Arctic-capable vessels like the CCGS Imnaryuaq will provide the Canadian Coast Guard with enhanced capabilities needed to operate effectively in challenging environments, respond to evolving needs, and support communities throughout the North," Jill McKnight , Minister of Veterans Affairs, commented.
Seaspan has previously designed and built three offshore fisheries science vessels currently in service with the Canadian Coast Guard and delivered an offshore oceanographic science vessel to the CCG in 2025. The company is also involved in the construction of up to 16 Polar-class multi-purpose icebreakers.
The Canadian Coast Guard is acquiring two polar icebreakers, with one being built at Seaspan’s Vancouver Shipyards and the other at Chantier Davie Canada. Once complete, these vessels will bolster the Canadian Coast Guard’s presence in a rapidly changing Arctic.

title: Theovision provides free healthcare to 2,500 rural residents and Ejura prison inmates
body: Theovision International has provided free healthcare to about 2,500 residents of rural communities in the Ashanti and Bono East regions, as well as inmates and officers of the Ejura Prison. The week-long medical outreach covered communities in the Anyinofi and Watoro areas, offering screening and treatment for various health conditions. During the exercise, 401 residents, mainly women and children, registered with or renewed their membership of the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS). The annual campaign forms part of the organisation’s efforts to provide healthcare and support to underserved communities in Ghana. It also offers counselling and Christian support to beneficiaries. Health conditions identified during the exercise included rheumatism and joint pains, malaria, upper respiratory tract infections, gastritis, skin diseases, conjunctivitis, hypertension, peptic ulcers, cataracts and otitis media. Other conditions included diabetes, typhoid, insomnia and arthritis. The Atebubu District Director of Health, Kwadwo Osei Sarfo, commended Theovision International for the outreach, saying the findings would help guide healthcare planning and interventions in the district. “On behalf of the management of the Ghana Health Service, I would like to express our heartfelt appreciation to Theovision International for this kind gesture. Our health is what keeps us going, and I must say all our people who turned up in their numbers for the health screening are satisfied,” he said. He added that the data collected reflected prevalent health conditions in the area and would help the district plan its resource allocation and interventions to improve healthcare delivery. The President of Theovision International, Theodore Philip Asare, reaffirmed the organisation’s commitment to improving access to healthcare in rural communities. “At Theovision International, bringing hope to the hopeless, supporting especially all the vulnerable is key, and we are always delighted to contribute our quota to society,” he said. He thanked the beneficiaries, staff, partners, volunteers and other stakeholders who contributed to the success of the week-long exercise, adding that the organisation would continue its medical outreach programmes. Theovision International is a Christian non-profit organisation that records the Bible in audio formats to make it accessible to people in their mother tongues. It says it has recorded the Bible in more than 500 languages across Africa.

title: Turkish Navy Deploys MALAMAN Smart Bottom Mine at Nusret 2026 Exercise
body: Türkiye’s domestically developed MALAMAN smart bottom mine was deployed during the multinational Nusret 2026 mine warfare exercise, marking another operational milestone for the system. Hosted by Türkiye from October 6 to 16 in the Gulf of Izmir and off Karadeniz Ereğli in the Black Sea, the Nusret 2026 Invitation Exercise provided the operational backdrop for the demonstration. During the exercise, a MALAMAN mine was seen being laid from the Turkish Navy’s Tuzla-class patrol boat TCG Karabiga (P-1205). Wrapped in artificial grass camouflage designed to mimic seabed vegetation, the mine was launched into the water from the ship’s stern. MALAMAN was developed through a joint defense industry effort involving KoçSavunma, MKE, and TÜBİTAK SAGE to address the Turkish Navy’s modern mine warfare requirements. According to details released by the Turkish Ministry of National Defence, Nusret 2026 brings together 20 naval vessels, five aircraft, and various unmanned systems. Turkish Naval Forces, Air Force, and Coast Guard units are participating alongside NATO and partner nations. Key participant groups include NATO’s Standing Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2)—with assets from Germany, Greece, Italy, Spain, and Türkiye—and the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, featuring ships from Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye. Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) and Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) teams from the United States, Belgium, the Netherlands, Kuwait, Romania, and Oman are also participating, alongside 32 international military observers. The exercise focuses on the planning, execution, and evaluation of mine warfare operations, emphasizing interoperability in multi-threat environments. Previous deployment from MARLIN USV MARLIN USV fitted with a mechanism to dploy MALAMAN smart bottom mines (Photo courtesy of Anadolu Agency) MALAMAN’s deployment at Nusret 2026 follows mine-laying trials involving MARLIN , reported by Naval News in August. Those trials included mine releases in both remotely controlled and autonomous modes. The integration scope included designing a custom mine carriage and release apparatus, alongside mission-planning software algorithms tailored for autonomous mine-laying operations. MARLIN was jointly developed by Sefine Shipyard and ASELSAN under the coordination of Türkiye’s Presidency of Defence Industries (SSB). As the Turkish Navy’s flagship operational USV, MARLIN has also been configured for anti-surface (ASuW), anti-submarine (ASW), and electronic warfare (EW) operations. About the MALAMAN Smart Mine A mockup of Malaman Smart Sea Mine exhibited at DSA 2024 in Malaysia MALAMAN is a seabed/bottom mine equipped with acoustic, magnetic and pressure sensors for target detection and classification. Its electronic module and smart firing mechanism process these inputs to determine whether a passing vessel meets programmed engagement criteria. According to information previously provided to Naval News by KoçSavunma, the mine can be programmed using ship counters to engage a selected vessel among others passing through the same area. Its casing and camouflage are designed to blend with the seabed, while its construction also incorporates measures to reduce acoustic detectability. The mine is designed for deployment from surface vessels, submarines and aircraft. Its 533 mm diameter allows deployment through submarine torpedo tubes, and earlier activities have included fit checks aboard the Turkish Navy’s REIS-class submarines. The MARLIN trials subsequently demonstrated deployment from an unmanned surface platform. MALAMAN was first displayed at IDEF 2023 and later exhibited at DSA 2024 in Malaysia . At DSA, KoçSavunma representatives told Naval News that the system had completed a functional demonstration in February 2024, including a live detonation at sea, and was undergoing final acceptance procedures. Specifications presented at that exhibition listed a weight exceeding 600 kg, a length exceeding 1,800 mm and a plastic-bonded underwater explosive charge. The system was presented in both combat and exercise configurations. The post Turkish Navy Deploys MALAMAN Smart Bottom Mine at Nusret 2026 Exercise appeared first on Naval News .
