He said, “It follows that our party has no excuse not to win. Victory is guaranteed when we are united, committed and work as a focused team. So we must jettison any misgivings we have against each other.” He warned that a party that controls every tier of government can easily grow comfortable and begin to mistake the size of its structure for the depth of its support. Wike promises to deliver Rivers, FCT The Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Minister, Nyesom Wike, promised to ensure President Tinubu wins in Rivers State and FCT and urged APC governors to work hard to deliver their states for the president. He said any governor who did not win his state for Tinubu should not join to say “we have won,” if the president is reelected. The minister said he was happy to see his name as the coordinator in charge of Rivers and FCT. “My job is already simple. As coordinator of Rivers State and the FCT, by the grace of God, the people will vote massively for President Tinubu,” Wike declared. Tinubu’s campaign council a confession of fear – Atiku Former vice president and African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar has described the APC’s revised Presidential Campaign Council as “a crowded confession of Tinubu’s fear.” Atiku, in a statement by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said the length of the list revealed a president more eager to count politicians than be accountable for what Nigerians have endured. He also condemned the decision to inaugurate the APC Presidential Campaign Council inside Aso Rock Villa. The statement read, “Only a man afraid of his record would think he could bury it under hundreds of names. Tinubu can gather every governor, minister and political defector in Nigeria. None of them can erase the hunger in people’s homes, bring back those killed by violence or free Nigerians still held captive. Their families are waiting for answers, not another campaign list. “Tinubu has room for an army of ministers and a stadium full of campaign officials, but no room in his plans for Nigerians crushed by the cost of living. “He feeds his political machine and tells hungry families to sacrifice. He may surround himself with elite friends and fill his campaign schedule with endorsements, but the list of Nigerians determined to vote against him is much longer. On January 16, Nigerians will answer with one question: Are we better off under Bola Tinubu? “When the first list drew criticism, Tinubu had a chance to show that he understood the country’s anger. Instead, he returned with an even longer list, reaching into other parties for more names. He is collecting politicians like shields against public judgment. Let him collect them all. Not one of them can cast a vote for the mother who can no longer feed her children or the family still waiting for a loved one taken by kidnappers.” APC-PCC inauguration a ‘rape of democracy’ – ADC campaign Similarly, the African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has condemned the inauguration of the APC-PCC in Abuja, describing it as a calculated attempt to impose a one-party dictatorship on Nigeria. The ADC-PCC Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, alleged that the ruling party was undermining Nigeria’s multiparty democracy by “coercing” opposition governors into its fold or incorporating them into its presidential campaign council despite their refusal to defect from their respective political parties. “What we are witnessing is not politics but political abduction. You cannot claim to be a democrat while using state power to force opposition governors into your party and then drafting them into your campaign council. This is political banditry,” he said. He accused the APC of pursuing a political agenda that could concentrate power in the hands of one individual, alleging that key national institutions, security agencies and the judiciary were being deployed to weaken opposition forces. The ADC-PCC spokesman urged Nigerians to resist what he described as the emergence of an immoral political order driven by the desire to retain power at the expense of citizens’ welfare. A coalition council heading for the rocks – APM campaign The Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has described the APC-PCC as a “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition” heading for the rocks. APM also declared that the APC is on a collision course with the will of Nigerians. The MDPCO described the council as a haven of internationally discredited and politically inconsistent characters, adding that this “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition is headed for the rocks as it cannot whitewash the failures of the present administration.” Richard Ihediwa, Director of Strategic Communications of MDPCO said with the confidence that President Tinubu reposed in this alliance of “governors, yes-along legislators, and discredited politicians, some of whom are fleeing from corruption investigations; even as his administration presides over an unprecedented economic crisis, worsening insecurity and a devastating collapse of public confidence, we see in the APC Presidential Campaign Council imminent political humiliation.” He added, “History is replete with the humiliation of those who mistake transitory power for permanence while reinforcing their illusions by surrounding themselves with compensated loyalists and sycophants, who do not command the loyalty or followership of the people, rather than confront the stark reality of failures. “What explanation will the “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition” offer Nigerians for the 140 million citizens (63% of the population) now trapped in multidimensional poverty according to the World Bank Report and the 113 million experiencing deprivation in health, education and other basics occasioned by President Tinubu’s misrule?”

title: Oil transfers off India's west coast surge as Gulf shipping congestion worsens
body: Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack . Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. " Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm Vortexa The expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs. Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict. "The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said. A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes. Transfers move east The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale. South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa. In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data. Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally. "The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst. The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed. Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east. Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island. Security versus cost Moving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf. "The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said. Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said. Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata. Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers. A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said. "If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil. Discounts deepen The disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply. Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad. The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict. Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase. QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document. “In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said. Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz. "Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it." The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad. For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa. The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing. Beyond price Gulf producers are increasingly taking on transit and security risks themselves to keep Asian customers. Adnoc, Aramco, Iraq and Qatar now offer STS deliveries outside Hormuz, and Kuwait has adopted the same approach to attract buyers, according to Mr Choudhary. These arrangements let buyers receive cargoes without sending their own tankers through the strait. The UAE has also moved to lock in Asian demand. Adnoc agreed in May to explore raising its crude storage in India to as much as 30 million barrels, from about 5.9 million at Mangalore. Aramco, which sold more than 60 million barrels for transfer off Sohar for September and October deliveries, is negotiating term contracts for next year involving loadings outside Hormuz, Mr Choudhary said, signalling that buyers and sellers alike expect the arrangement to last.

title: Bandits fleeing Zamfara kill 5, burn houses in Niger
body: Five farmers have been killed, 18 people abducted, and houses and shops burnt in a series of attacks by suspected bandits in communities in Niger State. The attacks occurred between October 9 and 12, 2026, in Fanga community in Mashegu Local Government Area (LGA), as well as Kigbere and Kokani communities in Borgu LGA. The latest attack occurred in Fanga on Monday after the bandits allegedly demanded millions of naira in levies from residents who could not meet their demands. A resident, who spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity, said the attackers invaded the community in the afternoon, setting houses and shops on fire and killing five people. Ondo crash: Aiyedatiwa orders river fumigation, emergency water supply in Igbokoda Dankwambo’s loyalist, PDP stalwart for APC “They set one of our trucks ablaze, broke into many shops and stole food items. They also abducted 18 people, including women and young children. Fanga has been completely deserted,” he said. The resident said the bandits had imposed levies on the community five times, but continued to attack it despite previous payments. “Even after we have paid, they still come to attack us. This time, we have not been able to pay what they demanded, and they have insisted that if we want peace, we should raise the money and pay. “Our children no longer go to school because of insecurity. We can no longer access our farms. We need government intervention,” he added. Meanwhile, residents of Rukukuje community in Rijau LGA fled their homes on Monday following reports of the movement of suspected bandits in the area. A resident said some of those fleeing had moved to Rijau, the local government headquarters, while others crossed into neighbouring Zamfara State for safety. He said the suspected bandits entered the area through a forest in Zamfara State in the afternoon. Another resident said farmers fled after the armed men were sighted advancing towards their community. A video circulating on social media showed women, children and elderly people wading through a river towards Shambo in search of safety. They were seen carrying food items and other personal belongings as they fled the reported threat. Some residents were also seen pushing their motorcycles through the water as they made their way out of the community. Local sources said the reported movement of the suspected bandits triggered panic, forcing families to abandon their homes over fears of an attack. The Rijau axis of Niger State has faced growing security concerns, with suspected bandits operating across the border from Zamfara State, which has battled persistent banditry for years. Despite repeated security operations aimed at flushing out the armed groups, rural communities continue to face threats that disrupt farming and force residents to flee their homes. The spokesperson for the Niger State Police Command, SP Wasiu Abiodun, did not respond to a message sent to his phone seeking comment.

title: ‘We’re Done’: Zelensky Says Ukraine Will Resume Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after Washington pressured Ukraine to halt attacks, warning that the US has endangered Ukrainian lives by restricting access to intelligence and Starlink satellite communications.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview in London.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Zelensky said Ukrainian military officials had been warned by their US counterparts that Washington would restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian energy facilities.
The comments mark a further deterioration in relations between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump , who has pushed Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil infrastructure as Washington seeks to lower fuel prices.
Last week, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “ simple victory ” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side,” he added. “This is not the right side of history.”
The dispute escalated after Ukraine reported restrictions on military Starlink services, which Ukrainian forces rely on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
Zelensky warned that the restrictions could lead to significant casualties as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“It’s a big mistake,” he said. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses… People will die.”
He urged Elon Musk, whose SpaceX operates Starlink, to restore the service, saying he hoped the disruption was the result of a technical problem.
Musk said on Wednesday that Starshield, the military-grade satellite system, is owned and controlled by the US government , which determines restrictions on its use.
He added that Starlink is a commercial service intended for civilian and defensive purposes and should not be used for offensive military operations.
The reported Starlink restrictions came amid concerns that a reduction in US intelligence sharing could weaken Ukraine’s ability to detect incoming Russian missile attacks and protect its cities.
Ukrainian officials told CNN that the loss of intelligence could give Russian forces an advantage on the battlefield, while a European official questioned Washington’s explanation that weather had caused gaps in missile-warning information.
For two consecutive nights, the air raid warnings that normally give Kyiv residents precious time to seek shelter came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the Ukrainian capital.
On Monday and Tuesday, Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, striking civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Ukraine received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners , President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The Trump administration has previously warned that it could suspend intelligence sharing and halt European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to stop deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
The dispute comes as Russian forces continue attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Zelensky said Russian strikes had left more than 600,000 people without electricity.
Moscow has also intensified aerial attacks as battlefield advances remain limited, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure.
Zelensky has sought to strengthen European support amid uncertainty over Washington’s commitment. During his visit to London on Wednesday, he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III .

title: Retired police officers, wives protest over pension bill
body: Retired police officers and their wives on Wednesday staged a protest at the National Assembly in Abuja, demanding that President Bola Tinubu assent to a bill seeking to exempt the Nigeria Police Force from the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS). The protesters, under the Police Retired Officers Forum of Nigeria, accused the federal government of delaying action on the bill, which they said would address the poor retirement benefits paid to former police personnel. The protest was part of an indefinite demonstration that resumed on September 29, 2026, following what the group described as the failure of previous engagements with government officials to resolve the matter. The forum’s leader, CSP Raphael Irowainu (retd.), said the National Assembly passed the bill on December 4, 2025, and transmitted it to the president on March 16, 2026. He accused the National Pension Commission (PenCom) and police management of opposing the proposed exemption, alleging that their actions had contributed to the delay in the president’s assent. Irowainu said the retirees were no longer satisfied with assurances that their welfare would improve, insisting that their main demand was the removal of the police from the scheme. The protest followed a demonstration at PenCom’s headquarters in Abuja on Monday, where the retirees reportedly spent about seven hours demanding that the commission stop opposing the bill. According to Irowainu, PenCom’s secretary and legal adviser, Mohammed Sani, who represented the Director-General, Omolola Oloworaran, appealed for calm and assured the protesters that efforts were being made to improve their retirement benefits. The retirees, however, insisted that they wanted an exemption rather than improved benefits under the existing arrangement. Irowainu said the military, Department of State Services, National Intelligence Agency and National Assembly had been exempted from the contributory pension system, introduced in 2004. He said retired Assistant Superintendents of Police received lump-sum payments of between N2.1 million and N2.5 million, with monthly pensions of about N25,000. According to him, retired superintendents received between N2.5 million and N2.8 million, with monthly pensions of N35,000 to N40,000, while retired Commissioners of Police received between N7 million and N9 million, with monthly pensions of N90,000 to N100,000. He said the payments were inadequate to meet retirees’ basic needs, including medical expenses. The forum’s leader further alleged that more than 20 members had died in the preceding six months because they could not afford medical treatment. Irowainu said the group had protested at the Presidential Villa in April and engaged the Inspector-General of Police, the Ministries of Justice and Police Affairs, but had yet to secure a satisfactory resolution. He vowed that the retirees would continue their protest until Tinubu assented to the bill or the government took concrete steps to address their grievances.

title: NSCIA calls for national unity, peaceful coexistence as CAN marks 50th anniversary
body: The Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA) said the 50th anniversary of the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN) serves as an opportunity to reflect on the responsibility of religious leadership in strengthening national unity and promoting peaceful coexistence. A statement by the Secretary-General of NSCIA, Prof. Is-haq Oloyede, said the Council considers the 50th anniversary of CAN a significant milestone not only for the Christian community but also for the Nigerian nation. It said that throughout this period, Nigeria has passed through various challenges and difficult moments. “Through these periods, religious leaders and institutions have continued to play an important role in promoting peace, dialogue, mutual understanding and peaceful coexistence among the diverse peoples and faith communities of the country,” it said. It said the NSCIA recognises the importance of the relationship between Muslims and Christians in Nigeria as the two communities constitute the overwhelming majority of the Nigerian population and share a common responsibility to promote peace, entrench justice, advance security, contribute to responsible citizenship and the development of our dear country. “The challenges confronting our nation, particularly injustice, insecurity, poverty, unemployment, social inequality and the need for accountable and responsive governance, require the collective efforts of all Nigerians. “It is in this regard that the NSCIA attaches great importance to sustained inter-faith dialogue and cooperation. “The Council particularly appreciates the platforms that have enabled leaders of the two faith communities to engage constructively on issues affecting the peace, unity and development of Nigeria, including the Nigeria Inter-Religious Council (NIREC). “The 50th anniversary of CAN is therefore an opportunity to reflect on the responsibility of religious leadership in strengthening national unity and promoting peaceful coexistence. “The NSCIA believes that religious differences should never be allowed to become sources of division, hatred or violence. Rather, our respective faiths should continue to inspire us towards justice, compassion, peaceful coexistence and service to humanity,” the statement said. The Council congratulated the President of CAN, Archbishop Daniel Okoh; the National Executive Committee (NEC), the various Christian denominations and Associations under its umbrella as well as Christians across the 36 states of the Federation and the Federal Capital Territory.

title: Saudi Pro League's big money signings: Who's shining and who's struggling?
body: The 2026-27 Saudi Pro League season is now well under way and the latest influx of talent is already influencing the title race. This summer’s recruitment was concentrated on investing heavily in established internationals still in their prime. Several of the most expensive arrivals have wasted little time in justifying their price tags while others have faced criticism. Al Hilal lead the standings on 21 points, two clear of Al Qadsiah and defending champions Al Nassr. Below, we take a look at how the competition’s latest wave of imports have performed. Gabriel Martinelli (Al Hilal) English Premier League side Arsenal recorded their record sale when Martinelli signed for Al Hilal in September for £60 million, with the Brazilian highlighting his pride at joining a club that countryman Neymar played for. Martinelli, though, will clearly be hoping for a far more successful stint at Hilal than the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain attacker, who had his contract terminated after an injury-ravaged 18 months in Riyadh. After a subdued debut off the bench against Al Shabab , Martinelli conceded he might need “some time to adapt” to his new surroundings having been with the Gunners since 2019. The story of that Gabriel Martinelli goal 🔥 pic.twitter.com/gvCnUWzh6q — Roshn Saudi League (@SPL_EN) October 10, 2026 Those concerns appeared to be unfounded as the 25-year-old bagged a hat-trick little over a week later as Hilal demolished Al Taawoun 6-0, ending his seven-month goal drought. He then opened the scoring in the Saudi Clasico win over Al Ittihad on Saturday, taking his league tally to four in four appearances. “He’s a big player and we are lucky to have Martinelli,” manager Simone Inzaghi noted after Tuesday’s 2-0 AFC Champions League win at Al Sadd . Tijjani Reijnders (Al Qadsiah) Reijnders was honest about his motives after completing a £52m move from Manchester City . “Me a money grabber? I can't deny that,” he said. “By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?” Qadsiah manager Brendan Rodgers has given him the box-to-box role he prefers and he responded by scoring in his first start in the 2-0 win over Neom. The 28-year-old then scored a double in the 3-2 defeat of Al Ahli at the beginning of September and opened the scoring in Friday’s 5-0 victory over Al Kholood. Three of his four league goals have come from outside the box, more than any other player in the SPL this season. Tijjani Reijnders maakt zijn eerste goal in de AFC Champions League Elite 🤩🔥 UEFA Champions League ✅ AFC Champions League Elite ✅ pic.twitter.com/kHDAizjLf6 — ESPN NL (@ESPNnl) October 12, 2026 Crysencio Summerville (Al Hilal) Summerville joined in a £60m switch from West Ham United who had just been relegated to English football's second tier. The 24-year-old's first goal arrived against Al Khaleej in his third appearance when he scored the fourth goal with a dinked finish as Hilal ran out 5-1 winners. Summerville also supplied his first two assists in that game. He was on target again the following week, this time driving home a low finish from a tight angle and also scored a fine winner against Al Ittihad. Summerville has registered three goals and three assists in eight league appearances. 🎬 Surrounded, but it’s done by Summerville 🤷‍♂️🎯 pic.twitter.com/XTcISdvYST — AlHilal Saudi Club (@Alhilal_EN) October 11, 2026 Samu Costa (Al Nassr) Al Nassr signed Costa from Mallorca for €22m at the request of new coach Ange Postecoglou, with the 25-year-old Portuguese midfielder recruited to replace Marcelo Brozovic. He was bought to give the reigning champions greater energy in midfield but his early performances have attracted criticism. Speaking on TV, former Al Nassr defender Hussein Abdulghani called the signing of Costa “disastrous”, and dismissed comparisons with Brozovic, claiming Cristiano Ronaldo had encouraged management to sign his countryman. But it has not all been bad with Costa scoring three times in seven SPl appearances, including Friday's 3-0 win over Diriyah, while it was his cross that Anvar Gofurov turned into his own net to seal a 3-1 Champions League win over Neftchi on Monday. ⚽️ SAMU COSTA 🇵🇹 POUR LE 2-0 ! Magnifique corner de João Félix. 35’ | Al Nassr 2 - 0 Al Diriyah pic.twitter.com/ZEtK3UphE9 — SPL 🇸🇦 (@ActuSPL) October 9, 2026 Francisco Trincao (Al Ahli) Former Barcelona attacker Trincao insisted “the passion of Al Ahli supporters was one of the main reasons” he moved to the Jeddah club in a €40m deal from Sporting. But passionate fans are also demanding and the player tasked with replacing the much-loved Riyad Mahrez has struggled at times as Marino Pusic’s side lost three of their opening six games. But the 26-year-old Portuguese appears to be finding his feet, scoring four times in his last four SPL matches, including a double against Al Fateh on Friday that earned him the man-of-the-match award. Trincao then scored one and supplied another as back-to-back Asian title winners Al Ahli defeated UAE outfit Al Wasl 3-1 in Dubai in the Champions League three days later. GOAL | Francisco Trincão restores Al Ahli’s lead against Al Wasl in the 58th minute, making it 2–1 in their AFC Champions League Elite clash. #AlAhli #AlWasl #ACLElite pic.twitter.com/rc4l55WrZb — Alkass English (@alkassenglish) October 12, 2026 Ollie Watkins (Al Hilal) Al Hilal forked out £50m to Aston Villa for England striker Watkins who the club had been monitoring since last season, according to Inzaghi. The 30-year-old scored on his debut against Al Ahli and was delighted by the reception he was given. “The fans were calling my name. From minute one, it was amazing,” he said. He later described Saudi football as being of “Premier League quality”. Watkins has already registered five goals and four assists from his six appearances for Hilal and played a role in all three goals in their 3-2 win over Al Ittihad. He was on target again on Tuesday after opening the scoring in Tuesday's win away to Qatari side Al Sadd. Ollie Watkins opens his RSL goal count on his debut for Al Hilal 🔵 pic.twitter.com/T9KWKlZc09 — Roshn Saudi League (@SPL_EN) September 1, 2026

title: Fire, sinking and reported scramble for cargo: what we know about ship lost in Strait of Hormuz
body: A Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by an unidentified projectile. All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were evacuated safely and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority has said. The sinking was confirmed on Wednesday, after the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the attack on Tuesday. A sister ship, the GFS Giselle, was damaged in the same wave of attacks but made its way to anchorage. Singapore condemned the strikes as a breach of international law. The incident highlights how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies. What do videos show? Photos and videos on social media appeared to show a container ship listing heavily under thick black smoke, with containers and their contents floating nearby. Pakistan’s maritime authority warned mariners of floating containers in the area. Other clips added a stranger note. Posts on X suggested small boats converged on the scene to scoop up cargo, and one described sellers doing business on the spot, calling out offers of phones and perfumes. Another post said paying Iran’s unilaterally declared transit toll, which has faced international opposition, would beat losing everything on board. The footage is unverified. It could not be confirmed where or when any clip was filmed, or whether it relates to the GFS Pride. AI-generated images were also widely shared around the sinking, including claims that thousands of iPhones were found floating in the water. What was the ship carrying? The GFS Pride had the capacity to carry 2,824 standard containers, it was reported. It was not clear how many it was carrying when it sank and no manifest was published. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the ship had more than 2,500 containers, including alleged contraband. The claim could not be substantiated. The IRGC also warned local vessels and fishermen to avoid the floating boxes. Why does it matter? Quoting two senior Iranian officials, Reuters reported on Wednesday that Tehran was changing its tactics against shipping to keep oil prices high and influence the November 3 US midterm elections. One warned such vessels “would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz”. Another said a complete closure of the waterway would come soon. The IRGC claimed the ship struck a naval mine while using an “unauthorised” route. Tehran has described the US-backed route hugging the Omani coast as dangerous. Maritime security firm Marisks said there was no independent evidence that a mine sank the vessel and described Iran’s claims as consistent with a psychological operations campaign. The available evidence does not establish that the southern route near Oman has been mined.

title: What Gulf economies need to watch out for as potential bond crisis looms
body: Much has been heard recently about the risk of a bond market crisis, with US government bond yields this month reaching their highest levels since 2002, and some warning of 6 per cent US Treasury benchmarks. Yields in several advanced economies globally have also hit multi-decade highs on the back on inflation fears amid soaring energy costs. However, a crisis related to investors losing confidence in governments’ ability to control inflation and debt levels is only part of the story. The next bond-market crisis could start with more technical factors, an increase in issuance, a wave of selling that pushes prices lower, sparking further losses and forcing more investors to sell. Investors demand higher returns when inflation threatens to persist, governments borrow heavily or interest rates are expected to remain elevated. But markets can also move for reasons that have little to do with a sudden deterioration in economic fundamentals. When bond prices fall, leveraged investors can face margin calls or tighter financing conditions. Funds may need to sell assets to raise cash, while institutions managing interest-rate exposure adjust their hedges. Those transactions can put further downward pressure on prices, pushing yields higher and generating new losses. In a sufficiently stressed market, even investors who believe government debt will ultimately be repaid may sell simply because they cannot afford to hold their positions. The US Treasury market is particularly important because its securities underpin global borrowing costs, provide collateral for financial transactions and serve as a benchmark for corporate debt. A disorderly sell-off can therefore spread well beyond Washington. The market has already demonstrated its vulnerabilities. During the disruption of March 2020, US Treasuries experienced severe dysfunction despite their status as one of the world's safest and most liquid assets. Meanwhile, the OECD's Global Debt Report 2026 estimates that governments and companies will borrow $29 trillion from markets this year. The growing role of price-sensitive investors, alongside the retreat of central banks from bond holdings, adds to concerns about the market's capacity to absorb shocks. The AI boom could also complicate that equation. Technology companies and infrastructure developers are competing for capital rapidly. Bloomberg reported this month that major AI-related borrowers had issued nearly half a trillion dollars of debt in 2026. The Dallas Federal Reserve estimates that AI-related investment-grade bond issuance could reach about $300 billion this year, adding significant long-term borrowing to US financial markets . If borrowing rises sharply to finance data centres and other AI infrastructure, investors may demand higher returns, particularly if future revenues appear insufficient to justify the investment. A deterioration in profitability expectations could also undermine the value of AI-related debt, reduce financing and force companies to postpone projects, with losses and tighter credit conditions spilling into other markets. The interaction with government borrowing matters. Heavy Treasury issuance, substantial corporate financing needs and a reassessment of AI investment returns could coincide, putting pressure on all borrowing costs. If that happened alongside leveraged positions being unwound, an initial repricing could become more disruptive. A sharp reversal in the yen carry trade could amplify this dynamic for example, while higher Japanese bond yields may encourage domestic investors to repatriate funds rather than buy US Treasuries. For Gulf economies, the implications extend beyond investment portfolios. US Treasury yields influence international borrowing costs, and a sustained increase can make it more expensive for regional governments and companies to issue debt, refinance obligations and finance infrastructure and economic diversification projects. The effect is direct for Gulf economies whose currencies are pegged to the US dollar, because their monetary conditions are closely influenced by US interest rates. Gulf governments and investors are committing resources to data centres, computing capacity and digital infrastructure. If markets begin to question the returns on AI investment, financing conditions could tighten just as regional projects require more capital. That would not necessarily derail these ambitions. Strong sovereign balance sheets and long investment horizons provide resilience. But higher funding costs and a more selective investor base could change the economics of specific projects. AI could also generate substantial productivity gains, while higher bond yields can attract buyers and eventually stabilise prices. Neither heavy borrowing nor market volatility alone signals a systemic crisis. But the real concern is the possibility that several pressures coincide: heavy government issuance, rising corporate borrowing, doubts about AI returns and leveraged investors forced to unwind positions. For policymakers and investors, the priority should be to monitor market functioning as well as headline yields. Are transactions becoming harder to execute? Are funding pressures rising? Are investors demanding larger premiums to hold assets that would ordinarily be considered liquid? The next bond-market crisis, if and when it comes, may not begin when investors decide governments are insolvent. It may begin when a crowded financing cycle meets a sudden reassessment of risk, and investors who believe in the underlying assets still find themselves forced to sell.

title: Shoga: Tinubu’s Revenue Reforms Creating Greater Fiscal Breathing Space
body: Director-General of City Boy Movement, Hon. Oluwatosin Shoga, in this interview, defends President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, saying his government is correcting several years of structural distortions and laying a solid foundation for Nigeria’s emergence as a $1 trillion economy. He also speaks about Nigeria’s growing foreign reserves, proposed Gateway Deep Seaport and increased revenues to state and local governments. Folalumi Alaran brings excerpts. States and local governments are now receiving higher allocations. What should Nigerians expect from them? This is an important aspect of President Bola Tinubu’s reforms that deserves greater attention. By July 2026, monthly federation revenues available for distribution had risen to around N3 trillion. That means more resources are available to states and local governments for infrastructure and public services. Governors and council chairmen must therefore take responsibility for delivering visible improvements in schools, healthcare, rural roads, water supply and agricultural development. It would be unfair to attribute every difficulty in local communities exclusively to the President when subnational governments now have greater resources and constitutional responsibilities. President Tinubu is creating additional fiscal opportunities. States and local governments must demonstrate what they are doing with them. Citizens deserve accountability at every level. How can the administration ensure that development reaches every geopolitical zone? President Tinubu’s vision must be understood as a national development agenda. Every zone possesses economic advantages. The North-Central has agriculture, minerals and logistics; the North-East has livestock, agriculture and cross-border commerce; while the North-West has textiles, leather and food processing. The South-East possesses formidable entrepreneurial and manufacturing capacity. The South-South offers petroleum, gas, petrochemicals and maritime industries, while the South-West remains strong in finance, manufacturing, technology and aviation. The administration’s challenge is connecting these strengths through transportation, electricity, industrial infrastructure and digital development. A genuinely prosperous Nigeria cannot leave any geopolitical zone behind. You are enthusiastic about President Tinubu’s economic achievements, yet millions of Nigerians are struggling. How do you reconcile this? We must be fair to President Tinubu and honest about the condition of the economy he inherited. Nobody disputes that Nigerians have experienced hardship. Fuel prices increased, transportation became more expensive, food prices rose and household purchasing power suffered. But the fundamental question is whether Nigeria could have continued indefinitely with the economic arrangements that created those problems. President Tinubu inherited an economy burdened by unsustainable fuel subsidies, distorted foreign-exchange arrangements, weak government revenues, enormous debt-servicing obligations and infrastructure deficiencies. These were not problems created overnight, and they could not be solved through political convenience. What distinguishes President Tinubu is his willingness to confront challenges that had been postponed for years. Leadership sometimes demands taking difficult decisions today to prevent a much bigger crisis tomorrow. The encouraging development is that the reforms are beginning to produce measurable results. Our responsibility now is to ensure those gains translate into jobs, affordable transportation, stronger businesses and improved living conditions. What concrete evidence supports your claim that the economy is recovering? The figures are increasingly speaking for themselves. Nigeria’s real Gross Domestic Product grew by 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 4.23 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. That represents progress in an economy undergoing substantial structural adjustment. We are seeing improvements in revenue mobilisation, foreign reserves, domestic refining and investment opportunities. Critics should acknowledge that these developments are occurring because the administration chose reform over the temporary comfort of maintaining an unsustainable system. Of course, GDP growth alone is insufficient. But you cannot create sustainable prosperity without first building a productive and stable economy. President Tinubu is laying that foundation, and the next task is translating growth into employment, industrial expansion and stronger purchasing power. Why does the Dangote Refinery feature so prominently in your assessment? Because it illustrates the industrial transformation Nigeria desperately needs. For decades, we produced crude oil, exported it and spent enormous foreign exchange importing refined petroleum products. That was an economic contradiction which deprived Nigeria of industrial opportunities and employment. Today, the Dangote Petroleum Refinery is changing that narrative. Seaborne petroleum-product shipments from Nigeria averaged approximately 561,000 barrels daily in the second quarter of 2026, with about 350,000 barrels going into exports. Consider what that means for a country previously heavily dependent on imported petroleum products. Beyond refining, the opportunities extend to shipping, storage, engineering, petrochemicals, transportation, logistics and thousands of associated businesses. President Tinubu’s vision of economic diversification is about creating an environment where Nigeria increasingly processes what it produces and exports finished products rather than raw materials. That is how serious economies develop. But Dangote Refinery is a private investment. Why should the administration receive credit? Nobody is suggesting that government built or financed the refinery. Credit belongs to the entrepreneur who conceived and invested in it. However, no major industrial enterprise operates outside the policy environment created by government. Crude supply arrangements, foreign-exchange policy, the naira-for-crude framework, regulatory decisions and infrastructure support all matter. President Tinubu understands that government does not have to own every factory to drive industrialisation. Its responsibility is to create conditions that encourage investors to commit capital, expand production and generate employment. That partnership between government and private enterprise is precisely what Nigeria requires. You have also highlighted the proposed Gateway Deep Seaport in Ogun State. Why is it particularly important? Because it demonstrates the enormous investment opportunities that can emerge when government policies encourage productive partnerships. In September, Ogun State signed agreements with DP World for the proposed Gateway Deep Seaport and Blue Marine Special Economic Zone. The envisaged investment exceeds $7 billion, including a 10,000-hectare economic zone designed to accommodate manufacturing, logistics and export-oriented industries. The proposed port is expected to have approximately four kilometres of berth and an 18-metre draft, with projections of more than 50,000 direct jobs at full development. These are substantial economic opportunities. What President Tinubu’s administration is encouraging is a development model in which federal and state governments cooperate with credible international investors to expand Nigeria’s productive capacity. Of course, agreements must translate into construction and completed infrastructure. That is the next important responsibility. There is also a separate Dangote-backed proposal around Olokola. How do the projects relate? Publicly available information indicates that Dangote Industries is pursuing a proposed deep seaport and industrial development covering more than 10,000 hectares within the Olokola Free Trade Zone corridor. There is also the Gateway project involving Ogun State and DP World. Whether these eventually become separate facilities or components of an integrated maritime development remains to be established. But look at the bigger picture. Ogun is already one of Nigeria’s strongest manufacturing centres. Providing modern maritime infrastructure along that coastline could fundamentally strengthen its industrial competitiveness. That is the kind of investment-led transformation President Tinubu wants across Nigeria. How would a modern deep seaport benefit the national economy? A seaport is not merely a place where vessels discharge cargo. It is an engine of economic development. Major ports attract industries, warehouses, logistics companies, financial institutions, shipping businesses and commercial activities. Ogun already hosts significant investments in cement, pharmaceuticals, steel, food processing, packaging and consumer products. Many of those manufacturers currently depend on Lagos ports. Modern maritime facilities in Ogun could reduce logistics costs, improve access to production inputs, expand exports and relieve pressure on Apapa and Tin Can ports. The important point is that President Tinubu’s economic agenda recognises infrastructure as a catalyst for production, competitiveness and employment. Nigeria cannot become an industrial powerhouse while manufacturers struggle with avoidable logistics bottlenecks. How does the proposed maritime corridor connect with the administration’s $1 trillion economy ambition? President Tinubu’s $1 trillion economy ambition is not merely a political slogan. It represents a vision of a more productive, diversified and competitive Nigeria. But such an economy cannot emerge without reliable infrastructure. We need modern ports, railways, roads, electricity, industrial estates and efficient financial systems. Imagine Nigerian manufacturers exporting directly through modern maritime facilities, agricultural products from northern states reaching international markets and solid minerals being processed locally before export. That is how value is created. The Gateway Inland Dry Port at Kajola, proposed Ijebu-Ode Inland Dry Port, Lagos-Ibadan railway, Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and Gateway International Agro-Cargo Airport could become important elements of an integrated logistics network. The administration’s ambition must be supported by this kind of productive infrastructure. What difference would these investments make to agriculture and farmers outside Ogun State? This is where the wider economic benefits become obvious. Nigeria produces cocoa, sesame, cashew, rubber, fruits and vegetables with substantial international demand. But inadequate storage, processing facilities, transportation and export infrastructure frequently limit farmers’ earnings. Modern ports connected to warehouses, cold-storage facilities, processing centres and efficient transportation networks can open international markets to agricultural businesses. More importantly, we must stop exporting so much of our agricultural wealth in raw form. Why export raw cocoa or cashew when processing them locally creates additional jobs and income? President Tinubu’s economic diversification agenda offers an opportunity to connect agriculture with manufacturing and international trade. That is how farmers across different geopolitical zones can participate in national prosperity. Nigeria’s foreign reserves have reportedly exceeded $54 billion. Why is that significant? It is one of the encouraging indicators of the administration’s economic management. External reserves exceeding $54 billion provide greater protection against international shocks, strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to meet external obligations and can improve investor confidence. Stronger reserves also support efforts to achieve greater foreign-exchange stability. We should remember the difficult foreign-exchange conditions President Tinubu inherited. The administration has taken difficult decisions to address those distortions, and improving reserve levels are an encouraging development. Naturally, the ordinary Nigerian wants to see a more stable naira, predictable prices and reduced business costs. That is precisely why these reforms must be sustained until macroeconomic improvements produce broader benefits. What about Nigeria’s debt burden and the substantial cost of debt servicing? Nobody is claiming that Nigeria’s debt challenges have disappeared. But we must recognise that stronger government revenues have improved the country’s fiscal position relative to the extremely difficult circumstances inherited by this administration. President Tinubu’s revenue reforms are creating greater fiscal breathing space. The responsibility now is to sustain fiscal discipline and ensure borrowing increasingly supports productive investments. Nigeria needs resources for electricity, roads, education, healthcare, security and agriculture. The solution is not to abandon reforms but to consolidate revenue improvements, strengthen accountability and invest more strategically. Critics argue that GDP growth, reserves and investment announcements mean little when Nigerians struggle to afford food. What is your take on this? I understand those concerns, but we must distinguish between the hardship associated with correcting longstanding economic distortions and the long-term benefits of reform. President Tinubu did not create Nigeria’s structural economic weaknesses. He inherited them and demonstrated the courage to confront them. The easy political option would have been to postpone difficult decisions and allow the problems to deepen. Instead, he chose a path intended to secure Nigeria’s economic future. We recognise that families need affordable food, young people need employment, businesses need electricity and farmers need access to markets. That is why the reforms must continue to focus on food security, transportation costs, industrial expansion and job creation. The President’s $1 trillion ambition is achievable, but its real value will be measured by improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians. As Director-General of the City Boy Movement, why do you believe Nigerians should support the continuation of these reforms? Because sustainable economic transformation requires consistency and political courage. President Tinubu has demonstrated his willingness to take difficult decisions in the national interest, even when those decisions carry immediate political costs. At the City Boy Movement, we believe Nigeria must not return to the cycle of postponing essential reforms because they are politically uncomfortable. We support the President because we believe his economic programme offers a foundation for long-term stability, industrialisation and prosperity. That does not mean denying hardship or suggesting that every challenge has been resolved. It means recognising the progress already made and supporting the continued implementation of policies capable of producing enduring results. The sacrifices Nigerians have made must not be wasted. What concerns do you have about the implementation of major infrastructure projects? Our support for these investments is accompanied by a strong expectation of delivery. Projects such as the Gateway Deep Seaport require transparent financing, environmental safeguards, proper engagement with host communities and effective road and rail connectivity. Signing agreements is an important first step, but Nigerians ultimately want completed infrastructure. President Tinubu’s development vision must be matched by disciplined implementation from every participating institution. That responsibility extends to federal agencies, state governments and private investors. What do you consider the greatest challenge facing President Tinubu now? Consolidating the reforms and translating economic recovery into prosperity that Nigerians can experience. The President has taken courageous steps to address longstanding weaknesses. The task now is ensuring that improving indicators produce jobs, stronger businesses, food security and better public services. Higher revenues must translate into infrastructure. Stronger reserves must support currency stability. Domestic refining must strengthen energy security, while modern ports must expand manufacturing and exports. Nigeria has the resources, population, entrepreneurial capacity and geographical advantages to become a $1 trillion economy. What we need is policy continuity, implementation, accountability and national commitment. At the City Boy Movement, we believe President Tinubu has demonstrated the leadership and determination required to move Nigeria towards that ambition. The reforms are laying the foundation. The next phase must consolidate the gains and deliver prosperity. That is why we believe the President deserves the opportunity to complete the transformation he has begun.

body:

title: Slightly warmer temperatures expected towards the end of the week
body:
Parts of Finland may even see some sunshine on Thursday, before the weather turns slightly wetter on Friday.
After a colder start to the week , milder air will move into Finland over the coming days as southerly winds strengthen.
Thursday afternoon will be mostly cloudy and dry, with some sunshine possible in eastern Finland and along the west coast.
Rain is expected in the northwesternmost part of Lapland, while drizzle is possible elsewhere in the north. By Thursday evening, rain will spread more widely across Lapland, while elsewhere in the country conditions will remain mostly dry.
By Friday, scattered showers will also reach southern and central Finland, although some areas will see only light drizzle.
A more widespread and heavier band of rain will move into central Finland on Friday evening.

title: Global Village reopens in Dubai: What’s new for the 31st season?
body: Global Village has reopened in Dubai for its 31st season, with new restaurants, live shows and a rollercoaster added to the popular multicultural festival park . The outdoor destination welcomed visitors back on Wednesday and will remain open until May 2027. Running under the theme A More Wonderful World, the season features 29 pavilions representing more than 90 cultures, plus more than 3,500 shopping outlets and more than 250 dining options. Opening-night celebrations included a choir performance, the Parade of the World and the destination’s signature confetti shower at the Gate of the World. A display featuring 600 drones also marked the season's start. New attractions and cultural experiences Among the additions is Tokyo Rush, a rollercoaster scheduled to open later in the season, featuring sharp turns and a loop. It will join returning attractions including Dragon Kingdom, The Horror Hotel, Secrets of the Lost City and Exo Planet City. The Festival Wheel returns with refreshed carts offering panoramic views of the destination, while the Gardens of the World has also been updated. Across the cultural attractions, visitors will find refreshed experiences at the Sri Lanka pavilion and the Russia and Azerbaijan areas. The Syria and Kuwait pavilions have new facades. A redesigned Season 31 passport and a new passport for children allow visitors to collect stamps as they explore the pavilions. Fernando Eiroa, chief executive of Dubai Holding Entertainment, said: “Global Village holds a special place in people’s lives because of the connections they make here, with their own roots, with other cultures and the people they visit alongside. It has become a much-loved tradition for families and friends, reflecting the welcoming, multicultural spirit of the UAE.” New restaurants and cafes Restaurant Plaza, beside Carnaval and overlooking the Falcon Stage, has several new additions, including Trabzon Turkish Restaurant, Robo Al Sham, Hawawshi Al Rabie and Chicking. New cafes include Vinci Dolci, Emir Bey Gourmet and Uzungol Cafe. Dessert District also returns with a refreshed facade and a selection of sweet treats. The venues join a wider dining offering of more than 250 options, spanning international street food, restaurants and cafes. Live shows and family entertainment Global Village will host 40,000 shows throughout the season, with a programme spanning music, dance, acrobatics and family entertainment. New productions include Fast Live 2: The Police Strike Back , a stunt show featuring driving manoeuvres and action sequences. Bollywood Idol and Bank Heist also join the programme, alongside returning show Slam . For younger visitors, characters from Care Bears and PJ Masks return to the Kids Theatre. Upgrades to amenities include a new VIP parking self-payment system, improved directional signage and expanded ticketing capacity at Happiness Gate. Additional family washrooms have been introduced, including accessible areas for people of determination. Other updates include bilingual signage at the Gate of the World, upgraded lighting at Cultural Gate and a new theme for the Sharjah tunnel. A new WhatsApp chatbot will provide visitors with information and assistance during their visit. Opening hours and tickets Global Village is open from 4pm to midnight on Sunday to Wednesday, with extended hours until 1am on Thursday to Saturday and on public holidays. Tickets cost Dh30, or Dh25 from Monday to Thursday excluding public holidays. They are available through the Global Village website, app and gate counters. Tuesdays are reserved for families, couples and women, except on public holidays.

title: TypeSafe AI Releases Jev 1.14 With Images, Box Type and 262k Context
body: TypeSafe AI has released Jev 1.14 , a new version of its System One decision model. It is live now under the jev-preview alias. It adds 3 experimental ‘danger zone’ features: images, a box type and longer context. For developers, Jev 1.14 pushes a typed decision model toward vision tasks like inspection and localization. TypeSafe shares a note that none of the 3 features are ready for production yet. TL;DR: Jev 1.14 Size: Parameters not disclosed. Context is 64k tokens per request and 32k per question by default, or 262k with an opt-in header. Runs on: TypeSafe’s hosted API only ( POST /v1/systemone ). No open weights. Hardware and quantized variants not disclosed. Performance: Small gains everywhere, largest in multilingual support (TypeSafe’s claim, no public scores). Best: In TypeSafe’s Box test, 4 edge-check questions caught 30 of 36 cut-off crops. Worst: Images and Box are not production-ready, and Box has no “not found” answer. What is Jev 1.14? Jev is a System One model from TypeSafe AI that returns typed decisions instead of generated text. You send a state along with typed questions : Choice, Score or Noul. Jev answers each with a typed value, probabilities and a confidence score. TypeSafe trains it with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) . The new version, jev-1.14.0 , brings small, subtle improvements to almost everything, according to the release post . TypeSafe expects the largest gain in multilingual support. How does image input work in Jev? Images are composable. Each image is listed once in a top-level assets map under a reference string. You then place that reference anywhere in state , instructions or criteria . The API swaps each reference for the image before the model reads it. TypeSafe says jev-1.13.0 was multimodal all along. Per the Images docs , both Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 now accept images. Each request needs the header TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true . Key image limits : PNG or JPEG still images only, up to 16 MiB per file 256 to 1568 pixels per side 32 MiB per request body Images bill as input tokens at the normal price, with no separate charge TypeSafe warns that all models, Jev included, perform worse on images than on pure text. It recommends the simplest possible questions. What is the new Box type? Box is a new question type that returns 1 bounding box per question. The answer gives top , bottom , left and right edges as fractions from 0 to 1. It also returns a confidence score. Box needs jev-1.14.0 or jev-preview , plus the images header. Box always returns a box. A question about an absent object still returns 4 edges. TypeSafe suggests pairing it with a Noul question that checks whether the target exists. TypeSafe also shared a small test on 36 painting crops, each cutting off part of the target. 4 per-edge Noul questions caught 30 cuts. A single “is all of it inside” question caught 26. Drawing the box as an outline and asking about it caught 20. How long is Jev’s context window now? By default, both models keep 64k tokens per request and 32k per question. Sending TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true raises both limits to 262k tokens, per the Models docs . TypeSafe states that Jev always supported longer context internally. It capped context on purpose because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on long inputs. The dev team still recommends short contexts. What do the benchmarks show? TypeSafe published internal intelligence charts in the release post . They compare Jev only against open-weight models. The post does not include a numeric score table. TypeSafe says the measurement is likely biased toward its own models. It tells developers to favor their own evals. title: Russia launches massive drone attack on Ukraine: Air Defence neutralizes 536 of 580 targets
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported the information on Telegram .
From 18:00 on Wednesday, October 14, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with two Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles from the Black Sea and 580 attack drones, including Shahed and Gerbera drones, as well as Parodiya-type decoy drones. The drones were launched from the directions of Orel, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Bryansk, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defence Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8 a.m. on Thursday, October 15, air defence forces had shot down or suppressed 536 drones.
Impacts were recorded at 31 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 11 locations.
As Ukrinform previously reported, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, the interception rate for Russian jet-powered drones has risen to 76%, compared with approximately 60% last month.

title: US aims to destroy Iranian-Islamic civilization
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – The United States aims to destroy Iranian-Islamic civilization, not just overthrow the Islamic Republic, an Iranian Army spokesman said, citing recent remarks by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Iranian Army spokesman said the United States aims to destroy Iranian-Islamic civilization, not merely overthrow the Islamic Republic.
Speaking on the anniversary of the founding of the Army's Political Ideological Organization, Brigadier General Akraminia said Iran's Islamic Revolution is one of the world's few great revolutions, with a cultural nature and an Islamic system rooted in Islamic teachings and the spiritual leadership of Imam Khomeini.
He said the enemy's false narratives in the recent war, aimed at presenting itself as victorious, must be countered, and that cultural figures bear a major responsibility in this regard.
Referring to recent remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Acropolis in Greece, Akraminia said they continue enemy efforts to weaken soft power foundations. Unlike the usual US claim that its enmity is only with the Islamic Republic and not the Iranian people, he said, Rubio's speech removed the mask of US hypocrisy and revealed its anti-civilizational nature and arrogant disposition. The goal of US rulers in the current war is the destruction of Iranian-Islamic civilization, not just the fall of the Islamic Republic, he said.
He also said that for the first time since World War II, the United States has suffered strategic isolation, with its main allies not coming to its aid.

title: RenkuOS: Haiku OS forked with AI-assisted coding and LLM integrations
body:
An open source operating system forked from Haiku OS — built for developers who want to use modern tools to create applications and move the OS forward.
We loved Haiku OS — its speed, elegance, and BeOS heritage. But when we tried to bring modern AI and LLM tools into our development workflow, we hit walls. The ecosystem simply wasn't there yet. So we forked it.
RenkuOS is Haiku with the doors opened wide: AI-assisted coding, LLM integrations, and a community that welcomes every kind of contributor — human or otherwise.
Renku is a form of Japanese collaborative poetry where many voices contribute to a single poem, each verse building on the last. It felt like the perfect name for an operating system built by a community, one contribution at a time.
many voices join — each line builds upon the last, the OS grows whole
First-class support for AI coding tools and LLM integrations. We forked Haiku specifically so developers could use the tools they want.
Everyone is welcome. We accept contributions from developers of all backgrounds, and yes — AI-assisted code is explicitly allowed.
Built on the Haiku OS codebase, which carries the DNA of BeOS — a legendary OS known for its speed, clean API, and responsive design.
Join us on the Desktop on Fire forum and Telegram. A small but growing community of OS enthusiasts and developers.
RenkuOS is built in the open, by people who care about the future of desktop computing.
Browse the source, open issues, submit PRs
RenkuOS is entirely community-funded. Your donation helps keep development moving — server costs, developer time, and tooling.
A fork of Haiku OS built for the modern era.

title: Trump Weighs Easing Shadow Fleet Sanctions to Lower Oil Shipping Costs
body:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to lower shipping costs and increase oil supplies from the Persian Gulf, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The proposal would allow sanctioned vessels to transport “legitimate” fuel, excluding Russian and Iranian oil subject to sanctions, the sources said. Companies seeking to use the vessels would have to obtain authorization from the US Treasury Department.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The move could make a small number of additional tankers available for short-haul trips through the Strait of Hormuz, but is unlikely to lead to a widespread drop in freight rates, maritime industry sources told Reuters. Insurers would still have to comply with European Union and UK regulations.
The US Energy Department said any easing of restrictions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia transport oil or petroleum products.
The latest proposal comes days after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports following an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said lower fuel prices for Americans were his top priority ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Republicans hope to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
The US president has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure for driving up fuel prices.
On Oct. 10, he called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky , saying Kyiv needed a leader willing to reach a deal with Moscow.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Zelensky condemned the diesel agreement, arguing that easing sanctions would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue its war against Ukraine.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelensky wrote on X on Oct. 9. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
In an interview with Axios , Zelensky described Trump’s decision to lift sanctions as “not fair and not honest,” adding that it looked like a “happy birthday present” for Putin.
The Ukrainian president also argued that any halt to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure should be reciprocal, with Moscow stopping its attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities.
The diesel agreement drew criticism from US lawmakers, including some Republicans, who argued that allowing Russian fuel sales would undermine sanctions intended to restrict Moscow’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
The US also temporarily exempted some Russian oil and petroleum product shipments from sanctions in the spring amid the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Kremlin argued at the time that stabilizing global oil markets was impossible without significant volumes of Russian oil. Putin also warned that attempts to damage Russia’s oil fleet would create problems for everyone, particularly those seeking to harm Moscow.
The latest discussions on easing shadow fleet restrictions come as the Trump administration seeks to contain fuel prices amid disruptions to global energy supplies. However, any broader reduction in shipping costs could be limited by insurance restrictions and the continued enforcement of European and British sanctions.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Meet Grok Voice 3.0: SpaceXAI Voice Agent Model Ranks #1 on Artificial Analysis
body:
SpaceXAI just released Grok Voice 3.0 . Grok Voice 3.0 is a SpaceXAI speech-to-speech model that listens, reasons, calls tools and speaks. It now ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. For developers, the endpoint, events and $0.08 per minute price are unchanged from Grok Voice 2.0. TL;DR Runs on: SpaceXAI’s hosted Voice Agent API only. No open weights, no local or quantized variants. Performance: Highest Index score of any model Artificial Analysis currently ranks. Best: 86.9 on the AA Speech-to-Speech Index, ranked #1. Worst: 71.6% on τ-Voice, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. Bottom line: Best: top composite score at 0.81 s time to first audio. Worst: not the leader on agentic task resolution or raw speech reasoning. What is Grok Voice 3.0? Grok Voice 3.0 is SpaceXAI’s flagship realtime voice model, exposed as grok-voice-3.0 on the /v1/realtime WebSocket endpoint . The grok-voice-latest alias already points to it, so existing agents switched automatically. SpaceXAI has not published parameter counts or architecture details. Reasoning is on by default ( reasoning.effort: "high" ) and can be set to "none" for faster turns. Server-side voice activity detection handles barge-in. Tools run inside the session: collections search, web search, X search, remote MCP servers and custom functions. How does Grok Voice 3.0 perform on benchmarks? The AA Speech-to-Speech Index is an equal-weighted average of 4 components. Those are Big Bench Audio reasoning, τ-Voice agentic performance, Speech Agent Arena preference and task success rate. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 86.9. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) scores 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking 82.6. Grok Voice 2.0 scored 81.3. Component results are strong, not uniformly first: Big Bench Audio: 98.5%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 99.7%. Full Duplex Bench: 97.0%, ranked 4th. StepAudio 3 Realtime leads at 98.9%. Task success rate: 94.8%, up from 94.6% for Grok Voice 2.0. Speech Agent Arena Elo: 1070, the highest among the 4 models compared here. τ-Voice: 71.6%, up from 56.5%, but below GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5%. ServiceNow’s EVA-Bench scores enterprise voice agents on accuracy and experience. SpaceXAI reports a top accuracy score of 74%. Is Grok Voice 3.0 fast and cheap? Artificial Analysis measures 0.81 s time to first audio. GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) measures 1.34 s, so SpaceXAI’s “40% lower latency” claim checks out. Grok Voice 2.0 was faster, though, at 0.70 s. On cost, SpaceXAI cites Artificial Analysis cost per Big Bench Audio task. Grok Voice 3.0 costs $0.025 per task, versus $0.030 for GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) and $0.055 for GPT-Realtime-2.1 (High). On AA’s cost per hour of input audio, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking is cheaper: $3.50 versus $4.80. List prices are not directly comparable. GPT-Live-1 costs $0.05 per minute, but backend model and tool usage is billed separately. Gemini 3.8 Live bills audio per minute plus text tokens. Back
