In his remarks, DECAN President, Mr Odita Sunday, said the courtesy visit was intended to express the association’s appreciation to Sam-Sumana for accepting its invitation and participating in the DECAN Conference and Awards 2026.

title: IMF official says Iran war price shock buffers are narrowing
body: A senior International Monetary Fund official has said prewar buffers are helping countries in the Middle East to limit the economic impact of the Iran war, but the region's outlook remains highly uncertain as it faces threats of renewed disruption. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's energy supplies was shipped before the war, has rattled markets, as have Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway and key sites in neighbouring countries. “The impact was more contained than the scale initially suggested,” the fund's regional director, Jihad Azour, told reporters during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand. While the price of Brent crude is 47 per cent higher than its prewar levels, it has yet to hit the $200-a-barrel mark that was previously feared. The IMF this week maintained its 2026 global growth projection at 3.1 per cent and slightly raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. Higher oil prices were partially attributed to the fund lifting its 2026 inflation forecast to 4.7 per cent. The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been exploring alternatives to send their supplies to markets, while International Energy Agency members agreed in March to release up to 425 million barrels of reserve stocks. Output from non-Gulf producers and an adjustment in energy demand have also mitigated the war's impact, Mr Azour said. “These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments,” he explained. Iranian attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz this week. At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the waterway in the past week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. On Wednesday, Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters . Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz , Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said in a statement. The IEA said crude oil exports from Gulf producers, led by Saudi Arabia, jumped by 4.4 million barrels a day in September to reach more than 75 per cent of prewar levels. Iran's escalatory attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker traffic threaten to derail those gains, the agency said. Brent crude rose 0.36 per cent at $106.1 a barrel on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 1.08 per cent at $95.16 a barrel. The IMF said its 2026 forecasts show a sharp divergence for oil exporters and importers, with the latter being assisted by remittances, tourism and government support. Regional economies are forecast to see a sharp divergence in trends due to the war. The IMF projected economic contractions of 11.3 per cent for Bahrain, 16 per cent for Iraq, 16.7 per cent for Kuwait, 15.6 per cent for Qatar , 3.3 per cent for Saudi Arabia and 3.9 per cent for the UAE this year. Growth is expected to rebound in 2027, but the conflict has inflicted a "long-lasting scarring impact" on regional economies, Mr Azour told journalists on Thursday. The economic recovery will take time and will require additional spending on infrastructure to boost resilience. "If we compare to the [growth] trajectory before the war, in 2030, we will be below it," he said. A more prolonged conflict remains the most significant risk for the region's highly uncertain outlook, with further disruptions likely to weaken economic activity, inflame inflationary pressures and place extra strain on fiscal positions across the region, he said. Mr Azour also said tighter financial conditions could deepen vulnerabilities in economies with large sovereign financing needs. He urged the region's economies to prioritise price stability, rebuild their fiscal buffers and build capacity to withstand future shocks. The IMF will release its outlook for the Middle East next week in Dubai. On Wednesday, UAE central bank governor Khaled Balama noted the region's experiences have shown that resilience depends on how quickly economies adapt to changing circumstances while building their fiscal buffers, state news agency Wam reported. Mr Balama was addressing the region's central bankers and finance ministers during a meeting alongside the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok. He also said the UAE economy has shown resilience, supported by its robust fiscal buffers, low levels of public debt and its vast sovereign assets, helping to reinforce investor and market confidence. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening international co-operation frameworks amid geopolitical tension. Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan was due to hold a media conference with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday. The International Monetary Finance Committee, which is the fund's policy advisory panel, announced this week it had extended Mr Al Jadaan's position as IMFC chair by another year after his term ends on January 3, 2027.

title: Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform
body:
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.
The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas, and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.
What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules.
In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it toward more predictable outcomes.
Figma also made its code layers feature available to users in open beta, which adds coding to designs on canvas for more interactive prototypes. The company announced this feature in private beta back in June. At its India event this week, the company is making the function available in public beta to let more users test it out. Users can also ask the agent to turn a design into code or change a part of the code to iterate on a prototype.
“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”
The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Meta Muse, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.
Last year, Figma acquired open source headless CMS Payload . Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.
The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales , partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.
The story has been updated with a new list of MCP partners Figma announced at the event

title: Atiku Urges Nigerians to Collect PVCs, Promises Economic Relief If Elected in 2027
body: • ADC condemns Akpabio’s seven virgin’s remark Chuks Okocha in Abuja Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has pledged to make life more affordable and improve security across Nigeria, blaming President Bola Tinubu’s administration for the rising cost of living. Atiku made the promise in a post on his official X account yesterday, while urging registered voters to collect their Permanent Voter Cards ahead of the 2027 elections. The former vice-president said Nigerians of different ages and economic backgrounds were grappling with financial hardship and insecurity. “Parents go to bed worried about what they will feed their children tomorrow. Pensioners must choose between buying medicine and buying food. Young people work hard, yet transport, rent and basic needs consume what they earn,” Atiku said “And across the country, families live with the fear of kidnapping, attacks and whether their loved ones will return home safely,” he added. Atiku warned that Nigerians should not have to contend with hunger and insecurity at the same time, urging the country to prevent the current challenges from becoming the inheritance of future generations. He called on eligible voters to collect and keep their PVCs, describing the cards as a means of exercising their democratic rights and seeking change through the ballot. “If you are a registered voter, please go and collect your PVC. Hold on to it. It is your voice, your choice and your peaceful power to demand change,” he said. Atiku also accused Tinubu’s administration of making life more expensive and pledged to reverse the trend if given the opportunity to govern. “Bola made life expensive. I will work to make life affordable again and restore the security every Nigerian deserves,” he said. “Let us stand together, across generations, and vote for a Nigeria where every family can live with dignity, safety and hope,” he added. ADC Condemns Akpabio’s Seven Virgin’s Remark Meanwhile, the ADC, has condemned Senate President Godswill Akpabio’s reported remarks on attempted suicide, describing his reference to “seven virgins” as a cynical and offensive comment that potentially promoted religious stereotyping. In a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the party also described the Senate President’s defence of imprisonment for suicide survivors as a disgraceful endorsement of what it called “an outdated colonial relic” that preferred to punish citizens who ordinarily required help. The ADC commented on the National Suicide Prevention Bill which the Senate President had supported via imprisonment as punishment for failed suicide attempts. In a video that went into circulation afterwards, Senator Akpabio could be heard saying, as he laughed, “why death may be attractive to some young people is that they have seven virgins waiting for them.” The opposition party said it took strong exception to the Senate President’s remarks. According to Abdullahi, “We find the ‘seven virgins’ remark particularly disturbing because it introduces religious stereotyping into a discussion that should be about protecting human life. Such a lurid comment is not only careless and insensitive. It also trivialises an issue that is, literally speaking, a matter of life and death.” The party however declared its support for the position that suicide is a mental health issue rather than a criminal act. “The criminalisation of attempted suicide is a colonial legacy. These laws belong to an era when people experiencing profound distress were treated as offenders who, by trying to take their own lives, wanted to deprive ‘the Crown’ of the services they could render and the taxes they could pay, rather than as human beings in need of care. “It is shameful that, when presented with an opportunity to reform this punitive inheritance, the head of the Senate chose to champion its preservation. Nigeria cannot continue to punish people for surviving a crisis that nearly claimed their lives, especially when those who handed us those laws have long abolished them,” the party said.

title: NAF Moves to Prevent Air Crashes as CAS Orders Stronger Flight Safety Oversight
body: • Ondo orders fumigation, water supply as residents fear disease outbreak Linus Aleke in Abuja and Fidelis David in Akure The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, has directed strengthened flight safety oversight across the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) as part of efforts to prevent air crashes involving NAF aircraft. Air Marshal Aneke also reaffirmed the Service’s commitment to personnel safety, professional standards and institutional accountability following the tragic accident involving NAF ATR 42-500 aircraft NAF 931 on 5 October 2026. In a statement, the Director of Public Relations and Information of the Nigerian Air Force, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said the directive was issued during a meeting with branch chiefs, Air Officers Commanding (AOCs), principal staff officers and other senior commanders on Wednesday. During the meeting, the CAS emphasised the need for sustained vigilance, strict adherence to established procedures and continuous improvement in safety management. Expressing profound sorrow over the loss of personnel, Air Marshal Aneke acknowledged the grief of the bereaved families and the wider NAF community. He stressed that operational effectiveness must be underpinned by sound judgement, professional discipline and the highest standards of flight safety. Accordingly, he directed commanders to maintain rigorous oversight of aircraft airworthiness, maintenance quality assurance, operational procedures and aircrew competence. He also emphasised proactive safety monitoring, prompt reporting of potential hazards and the effective implementation of safety measures, noting that flight safety remained a shared command responsibility. Meanwhile, search and recovery operations at the accident site in Igbokoda, Ondo State, continued with the involvement of specialist personnel and equipment from relevant agencies. The Head of the Recovery and Investigation Team, Air Vice Marshal EOE Ebiowe, disclosed that the operation had involved extensive mud excavation and water pumping to facilitate access to relevant areas. Ondo Orders Fumigation, Water Supply as Residents Fear Disease Outbreak In a related development, the Ondo State Government has ordered the fumigation of the river around the crash site following complaints by residents over foul stench and fears of possible environmental contamination. The government also directed the provision of potable water to residents if the river was found to be severely polluted and unsuitable for use, while nose masks and other essential health kits were to be distributed to protect the community against potential health hazards. The directives followed growing concerns among residents over the condition of the swamp where the aircraft crashed on October 5, killing all 25 persons on board, comprising 20 passengers and five crew members. More than a week after the incident, residents said the stench from the crash site had spread to residential areas, with reports of human remains floating in the water. In a statement by the Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Idowu Ajanaku, Governor Lucky Orimisan Aiyedatiwa had directed the Ministries of Environment and Health to commence extensive fumigation of the affected river to prevent a possible outbreak of diseases. According to the statement, the governor also directed the Ilaje Local Government to arrange water tankers for the continuous distribution of potable water if the river was confirmed to be severely polluted and unsuitable for use. The arrangement, it said, would remain in place pending a lasting intervention to address the pollution concerns. The governor further directed the Ministries of Health and Environment to provide nose masks and other essential health kits to residents.

title: Dino Melaye Accuses National Assembly of Surrendering Powers to President Tinubu
body: • Says Rivers emergency rule, electoral law controversies, budget lapses expose weakening legislative oversight Sunday Aborisade in Abuja Senator Dino Melaye has accused the 10th National Assembly of weakening its constitutional independence and failing to hold President Bola Tinubu’s administration accountable, warning that the legislature risks becoming an extension of the presidency. Melaye, who made the allegations at a press conference in Abuja, yesterday, said the handling of constitution amendments, electoral reforms, budget implementation, security matters, and other critical national issues raised questions about the commitment of Senate President Godswill Akpabio and House of Representatives Speaker Tajudeen Abbas to legislative oversight. He described the 10th National Assembly as having become a “department of the Villa”, stating that the legislature is increasingly failing to exercise the institutional independence required to restrain executive power. In a paper, titled, “The 10th Assembly: The Pathway to Tinubu’s ‘Lifetime Presidency’,” Melaye stated that a president did not need to abolish constitutional term limits to accumulate excessive power if the institutions designed to check executive authority failed to perform their duties. He said, “A lifetime presidency does not begin with the abolition of term limits. It begins when the institutions created to restrain a president stop restraining him. “Nigeria’s constitution does not establish an elected monarchy. It establishes a presidential democracy deliberately divided among institutions so that no individual, however popular or politically powerful, exercises the authority of the Nigerian state without constitutional restraint.” According to him, the president possesses extensive executive powers, but the legislature retains independent authority over legislation, appropriation, and oversight, while the judiciary interprets the law. He stated, “Cooperation is different from submission. The president may request. Parliament must scrutinise. The president may propose. Parliament may accept, amend or reject. The president may exercise power. Parliament must ensure that power remains within the constitution.” Melaye acknowledged that the National Assembly had passed legislation, conducted investigations, and held public hearings. However, he questioned whether it had demonstrated sufficient independence when confronted with issues affecting the exercise of presidential power. He cited the March 2025 declaration of a state of emergency in Rivers State, controversies surrounding the passage and gazetting of the 2025 tax laws, disagreements over the Electoral Act 2026, delayed budget implementation, rising Service-Wide Votes, and the handling of constitutional amendments. He also questioned the legislature’s response to the deaths of 37 people in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps in Niger State in September and the constitutional implications of Tinubu’s three-week vacation abroad.

title: N’Delta Group Cautions against Attacks on PINL
body: Olusegun Samuel in Yenagoa The Niger Delta Ambassadors for Good Governance (NDAGG) has warned against what it described as unwarranted attacks on Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL), saying such actions could undermine the interests of Ijaw communities benefiting from the company’s operations. The group commended PINL for its role in protecting critical national infrastructure and assets, particularly oil and gas pipelines, while contributing to employment generation, economic activities and community development across the Niger Delta. NDAGG also said the House of Representatives Committee on Host Communities had cleared PINL and its principal, Osahon Okunbo, of allegations of ineffectiveness and financial recklessness in the management of the pipeline security contract. In a statement signed by its President, Zipamoh Moses, on behalf of the executive council and members, the organisation urged the public to disregard the allegations, insisting that the company’s contributions to pipeline security and host communities should not be overlooked. The group maintained that PINL’s operations had brought considerable benefits to Ijaw communities through employment opportunities, economic empowerment and other forms of support. It noted that the impact of the company’s activities extended beyond individual beneficiaries to community institutions and socio-cultural organisations, including the Ijaw National Congress (INC) and the Ijaw Youth Council (IYC). According to NDAGG, the widespread benefits associated with PINL’s presence in the region made it necessary for stakeholders to carefully consider the implications of allegations capable of damaging the company’s reputation and its relationship with host communities. The organisation argued that attempts to discredit the company without due consideration of its contributions could ultimately affect the interests of the communities that had benefited from its operations. NDAGG stressed that pipeline surveillance and the protection of oil and gas infrastructure were critical to Nigeria’s economic stability, given the Niger Delta’s strategic importance to the country’s petroleum industry. It said effective pipeline security was essential to curbing vandalism, preventing disruptions to oil and gas operations and sustaining economic activities in host communities. The group therefore urged community leaders, stakeholders and members of the public to exercise restraint and responsibility when making allegations concerning pipeline surveillance operations, noting that such issues should be addressed based on verifiable facts and the performance of the companies involved. It further maintained that companies operating in the Niger Delta should be assessed on their contributions to infrastructure security, community welfare and peaceful engagement with their host communities, rather than being subjected to what it described as unwarranted attacks. NDAGG reaffirmed its support for initiatives that promote the protection of national assets, peaceful coexistence and sustainable development in the Niger Delta. It called for stronger collaboration among pipeline surveillance companies, host communities and relevant government institutions to address security challenges in the oil and gas sector while ensuring that the benefits of such operations continue to reach the people of the region.

title: 64 Years After Father, Isiaka Abdulrazaq Inherits Tafidan Zazzau Title
body: Kuni Tyessi in Abuja Sixty-four years after his father was turbaned as Tafidan Zazzau, former Chief Financial Officer of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, NNPC Ltd, Isiaka Abdulrazaq, has been confirmed as the new Tafidan Yamman Zazzau. The Emir of Zazzau, His Highness, Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli, approved the appointment in a letter dated October 7, 2026 signed by the Magatakardan Zazzau, Malam Yusuf Abubakar Hayat. The Emirate Council said the title recognizes Abdulrazaq’s contributions to peace-building, philanthropy and community development, and his service to the Zazzau Emirate, Kaduna State and Nigeria at large. The appointment marks the continuation of a family legacy in the Emirate, as Abdulrazaq is the son of the late Alhaji A.G.F. Abdulrazaq, SAN, a foremost lawyer who held the title of Tafidan Zazzau from 1962 until his death. The Abdulrazaq family has lived in Zaria since the mid-1950s and has maintained enduring relationships with the Zazzau Emirate. A Barewa College alumnus, Isiaka Abdulrazaq is a lawyer and finance professional who rose to Executive Director, Finance and Accounts at NEPA/PHCN and retired as Chief Financial Officer of the NNPC in 2019. Born in Zaria, Abdulrazaq attended Barewa College, Zaria, one of Northern Nigeria’s oldest and most reputable educational institutions. His personal and family connections to Zaria reflect a longstanding relationship with the Zazzau Emirate and its people. Beyond his professional accomplishments, Abdulrazaq is widely recognised for his community engagement and philanthropic activities over the years, demonstrating a sustained commitment to the welfare and development of the people. The Emir and the Zazzau Emirate Council congratulated him, expressing confidence that he would uphold the dignity of the title and discharge its responsibilities with integrity, and prayed that Almighty Allah would guide him and grant him wisdom and strength to fulfil the expectations of the office.

title: Opposition Parties Consult Presidential Hopefuls in Furtherance of G100 Resolution
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja The National Chairmen and National Secretaries of six opposition political parties have met with the presidential candidates of five parties as part of the ongoing strategic consultations and deliberations ahead of the 2027 general election. The participating parties were the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Social Democratic Party (SDP), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and Peoples Redemption Party (PRP). The consultations have involved Alhaji Atiku Abubakar of the ADC, Governor Seyi Makinde of the APM, Mr Peter Obi of the NDC, Prince Adewole Adebayo of the SDP and Mr Donald Duke of the PRP. In a statement by the coordinator of the G100 coalition, Salihu Moh. Lukman, and on behalf of other participating political parties, he said that, “These engagements are being undertaken in furtherance of the resolutions of the G100 Opposition Summit, which called for sustained dialogue, stronger cooperation and a coordinated approach among opposition parties in defence of multiparty democracy and the interests of the Nigerian people.” The G100 coalition said the consultations represented a practical step towards giving effect to those resolutions. “They provide an opportunity for party leaders and presidential candidates to deliberate on the framework for opposition cooperation, identify areas of common ground and consider the steps necessary to advance a shared democratic agenda ahead of 2027. ‘’At the heart of this process is the conviction that the challenges confronting Nigeria demand serious engagement across party lines. Nigerians deserve political leaders who are prepared to place the country’s future, the wellbeing of its citizens and the credibility of its elections above narrow interests. ‘’The consultations remain ongoing. Further engagements will build on the G100 resolutions and the commitment to an opposition that is organised, responsible and capable of working together in the national interest,’’ Lukman stated. He said Nigerians would be informed of substantive decisions and agreed next steps as the deliberations progress.

title: Israel accused of imposing media blackout on occupied south Lebanon
body: UN peacekeepers have been blocked from arranging journalist visits to Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon for weeks, a spokesman told The National, amid accusations of a media blackout. Journalists have embedded with the UN Interim Force for Lebanon ( Unifil ) several times since a June ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Those visits provided one of the few means of accessing the occupied territory, which Israel designates as a buffer zone. The visits allowed journalists to report on the handful of predominantly Christian villages that remain inhabited , as well as the systematic destruction of largely depopulated Muslim villages. “At the moment, we cannot conduct media visits south of the so-called yellow line,” said a Unifil spokesman. “This has been the case for the past few weeks.” He added that Unifil did not know when visits would be permitted to resume. Elsy Moufarrej, president of the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told The National that the union had received several complaints from journalists denied access to the zone in recent weeks. She accused Israel of a “media blackout” that prevents independent reporting on “potential crimes and violations”. “It also deprives these communities of a voice and violates the public's right to know,” she added. Israel occupied an area extending 10km to 12km into Lebanon during its war with Hezbollah, which reignited in March. The Israeli military launched a ground invasion and forced people to leave the south before establishing its security zone. Since then, Israel has severely restricted movement in and out of the occupied area, enforcing control through military positions, strikes, forced displacement orders and restrictions on access. The charity Reporters Without Borders has condemned restrictions on journalists entering the zone, accusing the Israeli military of turning co-ordination mechanisms intended to facilitate safe access into tools of censorship. “It is unacceptable that Lebanese journalists are denied access or prevented from entering Lebanese territory,” said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF’s Middle East office. “Ceasefire agreements and military considerations must no longer serve as a pretext to obstruct the right to information and threaten the safety of journalists.” While some communities such as the Sunni Muslim village of Kfarshouba can still be reached from the Lebanese sid e, predominantly Christian villages deeper inside the territory are effectively besieged, with movement in and out subject to Israeli permission. Travelling with Unifil had offered journalists rare opportunities to reach these communities. The media restriction appears to have begun in mid-September, following visits to the occupied zone by journalists from international news organisations. Téa Ziade, a French-Lebanese freelance journalist, was scheduled to enter the zone with Unifil on September 25 for an assignment with a European news outlet. Her trip was cancelled that morning, just minutes before the convoy was due to depart. “We had submitted all our papers to Unifil. Everything was in order,” she said. “A Unifil lieutenant told us: ‘It’s the journalists. No journalists are allowed in the convoy.’” She was given no explanation at the time. She was later told by Unifil that a proper deconfliction process had not taken place. There have been no Unifil journalist embeds since. The Israeli military confirmed to The National that it had raised the issue of journalist access with Unifil. “Following incidents in which journalists entered the security zone without prior co-ordination and published footage revealing the locations of troops, the issue was discussed with Unifil,” a military spokesperson said. But another Israeli military official went further, alleging that journalists had entered the occupied zone concealed within convoys and “shared photographs, which showed the location of our troops, with Hezbollah operatives or people connected to Hezbollah operatives”. The official did not identify the journalists or news organisations involved, or provide evidence to substantiate the allegation. When questioned about the accusation, an Israeli military spokesperson appeared to backtrack on the claim that journalists had shared information with people linked to Hezbollah, instead saying that publicly available information about Israeli troop positions could be exploited by the group. Pictures of Israeli positions inside southern Lebanon are widely available online. Israel, which has been accused of targeting journalists, has routinely portrayed them as militants. In October, it published a list of 170 people killed in the Gaza war who it said were militants posing as media workers. Israeli forces have killed at least 16 journalists and media workers in Lebanon since October 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Among them was Reuters journalist Issam Abdallah , killed by Israeli tank fire in October 2023 in an attack that wounded six other journalists and which Human Rights Watch described as an apparent war crime. In April 2026, Al Akhbar journalist Amal Khalil was killed in an Israeli strike while reporting from the security zone during a ceasefire, while her colleague Zeinab Faraj was seriously wounded. Tighter restrictions Unifil was not the only means of accessing the occupied territory. Humanitarian and civilian convoys had also offered journalists a route into the occupied zone. Those routes, too, have become increasingly restricted in recent weeks. Sources within Unifil and other organisations say access requires “prior deconfliction arrangements, usually through humanitarian convoys”, Ms Moufarrej said. Deconfliction with the Israeli army usually involves speaking to Unifil or a US and French-led committee established to monitor the ceasefire. The process is intended to arrange safe passage through the area . “However, Israeli forces have reportedly begun preventing these convoys from entering if journalists accompany them,” she added. A humanitarian worker who regularly travels into the occupied territory told The National that Israeli soldiers have significantly tightened checks at checkpoints, inspecting every vehicle to ensure no journalists were on board. Such checks were not previously routine, the worker said. “Israeli soldiers now come out of their base and check every person inside the car to make sure their identity matches the approved list.” An Israeli army spokesperson said the military reviewed journalists’ requests to enter the occupied zone on a “case-by-case basis”, without clarifying what procedures must be followed for approval. “Areas where military operations are taking place pose genuine security risks, requiring measures to protect the lives of journalists on the ground, as well as the safety of [Israeli] troops,” the Israeli army spokesperson added. “This policy is intended to enable journalistic coverage to the extent possible, without endangering human lives or compromising the safety of troops and their operational activities.” However, Israeli military operations are an inherent feature of the occupation, meaning any area could be cut off. Ms Ziade rejected the Israeli army’s security justification. “If we cannot go to the south, how are we supposed to tell the story of the occupation?” she asked. “We lose part of the meaning of this profession, the ability to build trust and intimacy with people. Without journalists on the ground, there is also a question of accountability and impunity.” Access for journalists has always been challenging. In July, a vetted humanitarian convoy, which included The National , was barred at the last minute by the Israeli army, despite having obtained prior approval. At the time, Unifil said the decision was probably made because of media presence. It has now become practically impossible. Since the end of September, no journalists have been allowed inside the security zone. “What worries me is that this justification could come to be accepted by the international community, and that we, as journalists, will simply be expected to accept it too,” Ms Ziade said. “And that is how, little by little, a territory becomes closed to journalists.” Collective punishment The restrictions have also had consequences for civilians living under Israeli occupation. Israeli forces suspended convoys to Debel and Rmeish for three days after journalists entered the occupied zone , according to a humanitarian worker who regularly travels to the area. Residents of both villages confirmed they had been prevented from entering or leaving during the three-day closure. They said Israeli military officials had accused journalists of entering the territory without authorisation. The Israeli military official denied having a policy of punishing civilians or villages for hosting reporters, saying troops had temporarily paused the convoy to investigate the incident. “It is unacceptable that a civilian area is isolated for three days simply for having hosted journalists,” said Mr Dagher from RSF. The suspension temporarily cut off a lifeline for the besieged communities, whose residents depend on the convoys for travel and supplies. The closure sparked fears about speaking to the media. “It was indirect, but the message was received by all the villages: ‘There are a lot of mistakes happening, be careful. If there are more mistakes there won't be any more convoys,'” said a locally elected official from Debel, who requested not to be named to avoid retaliation by Israeli forces. “People got scared. They need these convoys to access hospitals, doctors and supplies.”

title: US Consulate Honours RMD, Kunle Afolayan, Six Others for Strengthening Hollywood-Nollywood Link, Posthumously Honours Olu Jacobs for Driving Global Nollywood Expansion
body: Sunday Ehigiator The United States Consulate General in Lagos has honoured celebrated Nigerian actor Richard Mofe-Damijo, popularly known as RMD, award-winning filmmaker Kunle Afolayan and six other creative industry leaders for their contributions to strengthening professional and commercial ties between Hollywood and Nollywood. The recognition was presented at an event themed, ‘Reel Connections from Hollywood to Nollywood’, which brought together leading figures from Nigeria’s film and television industries, government officials, creative industry stakeholders and alumni of United States government exchange programmes. The event also featured the posthumous presentation of the Creative Industry Legend Award to veteran actor, Olu Jacobs, in recognition of his career spanning more than five decades and his contributions to Nigerian cinema and international filmmaking. Speaking at the event, the US Consul General, Brandon Hudspeth, described Nollywood as a growing source of content, talent and investment opportunities for American companies seeking to expand their engagement with African markets. He noted that Nigerian stories and creative talents were increasingly reaching audiences in the United States and other parts of the world through streaming services and digital platforms, including Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+ and YouTube. According to him, the expanding reach of Nigerian productions was creating new opportunities for collaboration, investment and access to international markets. Hudspeth also highlighted the role of US government exchange programmes in building professional networks and strengthening relationships between Nigerian and American creative communities. He identified the American Film Showcase, Global Media Makers and the International Visitor Leadership Program as initiatives that had connected Nigerian creative professionals with American filmmakers, producers, institutions and other industry leaders. “U.S. government exchange programs are not simply about what happens during the exchange,” Hudspeth said. “Their real impact is what happens when participants return home; the relationships they bring with them, the ideas they put into action, the creative collaborations they build, and the next generation they inspire.” The US Consul General said such relationships had helped establish professional connections that continued to generate creative collaborations beyond the duration of the exchange programmes. Paying tribute to Jacobs while presenting the posthumous award, Hudspeth described the late actor as one of Nigeria’s most celebrated screen personalities, whose career helped shape the country’s film industry and strengthen its connections with international cinema. “Olu Jacobs’ life embodied the kind of creative exchange that continues to connect Nigeria’s film industry with the United States and the world,” he said. Jacobs built a career spanning theatre, television and film, earning recognition for his performances in Nigerian productions as well as international cinema. His contribution to the industry, the consulate said, reflected the possibilities created by exchanges between creative communities across borders. Other recipients of the recognition included Chioma Ude, founder and executive director of the Africa International Film Festival (AFRIFF); Kunle Afolayan; and Bolanle Austen-Peters, both of whom are alumni of the American Film Showcase’s African Film and Television Leadership Initiative. RMD, an alumnus of the International Visitor Leadership Program, was also honoured alongside Zulu Oyibo, co-founder of Inkblot Productions and another alumnus of the programme. The remaining honourees were award-winning producer Josh Olaoluwa, an alumnus of Global Media Makers, and Emmy Award-winning visual development artist Uzoma Dunkwu. The recognition highlighted the contributions of Nigerian actors, filmmakers, producers and other creative professionals to expanding the international reach of Nollywood and strengthening its relationships with global entertainment industries. The consulate said the relationships built through exchange programmes remained important to fostering collaboration, developing creative talent and connecting the Nigerian film industry with international markets.

title: 2027: Peter Obi Not Missing from Policy Debate, Declares Obi-Kwankwaso Coalition
body: • Insists NDC presidential candidate has consistently presented policy alternatives • Cites Obi’s positions on electricity, production, insecurity, healthcare, faults FG’s 30-day fuel price reduction Sunday Ehigiator The Big Tent Coalition for Obi/Kwankwaso has rejected a THISDAY report of October 14, 2026 suggesting that the presidential candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, was missing from the policy debate ahead of the 2027 general election, insisting that he has consistently presented policy alternatives on critical national issues. The coalition also demanded that THISDAY give its right of reply the same front-page prominence and visibility as the newspaper’s October 14, 2026 lead story, titled, “2027 Presidential Poll: Atiku Brings Tinubu into Policy Debate, Obi Missing.” In a statement by its Director of Media and Communications, Charles Odibo, titled, “Right of Reply: THISDAY’s False Narrative on Peter Obi: Nothing Could Be Further from the Truth,” the coalition described the report as misleading and inaccurate. It said, “Peter Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and the leading candidate in this race, has been consistently, publicly and substantively at the forefront of policy discussions and the presentation of concrete alternatives, more than any other presidential candidate. “To suggest he is ‘missing’ from the policy debate is a distortion that does a disservice to Nigerians and to responsible journalism.” The coalition stated that Obi had consistently engaged Nigerians on critical policy issues through interviews, television appearances, and other public platforms, rather than relying solely on press statements or political surrogates. It said, “Obi does not govern by press statements or through surrogates. He speaks directly to Nigerians on the issues that matter.” Describing him as the most interviewed presidential candidate in the history of Nigeria’s Fourth Republic, the group said he had continued to offer policy alternatives and subject himself to public scrutiny. On electricity generation and transmission, the coalition said Obi had repeatedly advocated increased investment in generation capacity, comprehensive reforms of transmission and distribution infrastructure, and decentralisation where necessary. It added that his approach included creating an enabling environment to attract private investment while ensuring accountability and reliability in the power sector. Obi’s focus, according to the coalition, remained ending persistent electricity shortages and making power supply a driver of production and industrialisation. On the economy, the group said Obi had consistently called for a transition from a consumption-driven economy to a production-based system through investment in agriculture, manufacturing, solid minerals, and value addition. It also listed targeted incentives for productive sectors, support for small and medium-sized enterprises, and the removal of structural bottlenecks that made local production uncompetitive among his proposed measures. “He has repeatedly stated that leadership must measure success by what the nation produces, not merely what it consumes or borrows,” the coalition said. On insecurity, particularly in northern Nigeria, the group said Obi had advocated a comprehensive security architecture combining intelligence-driven operations, community engagement, technology, and the political will to protect lives and livelihoods. It maintained that farmers must be able to return safely to their farmlands and resume agricultural activities, adding that insecurity should not remain an unending political talking point while citizens continued to suffer. The coalition also highlighted Obi’s position on primary healthcare, saying he has consistently advocated investment in primary healthcare centres, preventive care and basic health infrastructure. It said the measures were essential to improving human development outcomes, boosting productivity, reducing poverty, and strengthening access to essential services. The statement said, “These positions are on the public record. They are not hidden. They are not absent. They are available for any serious journalist or citizen to examine.” The coalition also cited Obi’s October 11, 2026 criticism of the federal government’s 30-day fuel price reduction at NNPC Retail stations, which he reportedly described as reactive political optics rather than sound policy. According to the group, Obi questioned the reach and potential impact of the temporary intervention, stating that approximately 900 NNPC Retail stations out of an estimated 24,000 petrol stations nationwide would account for less than four per cent of the outlets. The statement said Obi had questioned “what lasting impact a temporary discount of less than five per cent could have on poverty, unemployment, insecurity, or productivity”. It added that he advocated a broader approach to public support, extending subsidy assistance beyond petrol to agriculture, healthcare, education, and infrastructure, while prioritising policies capable of genuinely reducing the cost of living. Further faulting THISDAY’s presentation of the policy debate, the coalition said the report created the wrong impression that Obi had been absent from discussions on the country’s challenges, despite his repeated public interventions. It, therefore, demanded that the newspaper publish its response with the same prominence accorded to the original report. The Big Tent Coalition for Obi/Kwankwaso stated, “We, therefore, demand that THISDAY Newspaper afford this ‘Right of Reply’ the same front-page prominence and visibility that it gave to the original story. Anything less would compound the injury already done to the facts and to the integrity of the public discourse.” The coalition urged the media to ensure that political reporting reflected candidates’ positions accurately, stressing that Nigerians deserve informed discussions based on facts rather than selective narratives. The statement added, “Nigerians deserve accurate reporting. They deserve policy debate grounded in truth, not selective narratives. Peter Obi has never been missing from the issues. He has been leading on them.”

title: By pursuing a big 'win' in Iran, Trump is destined to lose
body:
The war is most likely to end through a minimalistic ceasefire that opens a path to a broader deal
President Donald Trump, seeing the success of the U.S. Navy’s operation in the Strait of Hormuz in blocking most of Iran’s imports and oil exports while restoring some of the non-Iranian oil trade through the strait, evidently does not regard the conflict with Iran as stalemated.
The current situation regarding the flow of oil and distribution of economic pain is actually more complicated and does not constitute a one-sided U.S. advantage, but Trump clearly believes that continuing to squeeze Iran through measures such as a naval blockade — an act of war — will increase U.S. leverage and yield a better result.
Trump always has viewed the world as a zero-sum game . Whether the subject is military conflict, trade agreements, or real estate deals, he regards most outcomes as having a winner and a loser. He also never admits a mistake and certainly will not do so publicly regarding the current war. Thus the conflict continues as a search for something Trump can claim as a “win.”
A book that I wrote more than four decades ago showed how the endings of wars are best understood as negotiated bargains. Even supposed unconditional surrenders are not entirely unconditional and involve bargains in which the surrendering side agrees not to use its continued capacity for resistance in exchange for the other side ending its assault. Other scholars have recently applied the same concept to contemporary conflicts. A lesson is that couching U.S. war-fighting strategy primarily in terms of wins and losses obscures the issues at stake, how those issues affect U.S. interests, and what will be required to end the war and implement a stable peace.
What Trump would welcome as a “win” could take one of two basic forms: either the Iranian regime somehow cries “uncle” and makes concessions that clearly and significantly go beyond anything it offered before, or the regime collapses. A tension between these two possibilities exists, because a regime that believes the U.S. is determined to destroy it has no incentive to make concessions and sees no alternative to continued fighting. Even considered separately, however, each of the two versions of a supposed “win” raises major questions.
For Iranian concessions to play that role, they would have to advance U.S. interests significantly and be what even an Iranian regime under severe pressure could realistically be expected to offer. One difficulty in assessing the value of Iranian concessions is that Trump and his administration never made its war aims clear. They have said different things at different times, including even a demand for “unconditional surrender,” which is unrealistic to expect from any Iranian regime.
Iran’s nuclear program gets mentioned most often, and Vice President JD Vance came closest to a specific demand by stating just last week that “meaningful” reduction in Iran’s enrichment of uranium would be necessary for peace. The Iranian nuclear program is relevant to U.S. interests insofar as it raises the possibility of an Iranian nuclear weapon, and in this regard further continuation of the war is not helpful. Previous attacks already largely disabled the Iranian program, and now intentions matter at least as much as capabilities. Being the target of continued attacks by a foreign power will strengthen voices in Tehran — where there already is talk about withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — that argue that Iran needs a nuclear deterrent.
An exhibit of what is necessary for a meaningful agreement on nuclear matters is the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action , known colloquially as the Iran deal, which entered into force in 2015 and effectively closed all possible paths to an Iranian nuclear weapon until it was abandoned in 2018 by Trump, who was determined to destroy what was widely regarded as President Barack Obama’s most significant foreign policy achievement. The JCPOA is 159 pages long. It was the product of difficult and detailed negotiations that spanned several years and involved numerous nuclear experts and other specialists. It is not the sort of thing that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner could knock out in a couple of negotiating sessions.
Any new nuclear agreement between the United States and Iran would require comparable detail, partly to ensure that reductions would be meaningful, enforceable, and verifiable through international inspections. To make completion of such a comprehensive agreement a condition for ending the war — rather than coupling a ceasefire with a commitment to engage seriously in future negotiations — would mean continuing the war for months and possibly years.
The Trump administration has made the task of negotiating a new nuclear agreement with Iran even more difficult and complex by pursuing its recent nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia , which has justifiably raised concerns among nonproliferation experts because the deal does not require the most stringent form of international inspections and opens the door to Saudi enrichment of uranium, even to the 20% level. Any regime in Iran will resist restricting its own nuclear program to something less than what Iran’s rival on the other side of the Persian Gulf will enjoy, with U.S. approval and assistance.
As for a supposed “win” through regime change, the first thing to note is that Trump already claimed to have achieved such a change after the killings of senior Iranian leaders in the opening days of the war. What happened next is a lesson in being careful what you wish for: Iranian hardliners became more powerful than they were when Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was still alive. Another wartime leadership change might move Iran even further in the hardline direction, such as to a military dictatorship that silences remaining moderate voices in the regime.
Even if a leadership change went in a direction appearing more favorable to the United States, securing wins for U.S. interests requires that whoever speaks for Iran can negotiate agreements that stick. A future government would have to deal internally with Iranian factions that have different views and would not vanish even with a leadership change. But the ability to influence those factions does not necessarily reside with those whose ideologies and orientation might seem friendliest to the U.S.
In this regard, a loss was the killing by an Israeli airstrike two weeks into the war of Ali Larijani, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. Larijani was a creature of the Khamenei regime but also a pragmatist with the political chops and connections to make credible commitments on behalf of the entire power structure in Tehran.
Amid the economic hardship that the Iranian population is enduring, one cannot rule out a popular uprising leading to a more sweeping political upheaval, but several observations about this type of possible regime change are in order.
First, several popular uprisings have occurred during the history of the Islamic Republic but did not lead to regime change.
Second, there currently is no cohesive opposition movement comparable to the one Ruhollah Khomeini led during the revolution that overthrew the shah in 1979.
Third, a popular uprising is less likely during a continued war, which has generated a significant rally-around-the-flag effect among Iranians who unsurprisingly see U.S. military and economic assaults as aimed at Iran as a whole and not just at the regime.
Fourth and related to the previous point, the war will leave lingering and widespread resentment against the United States for the suffering it has imposed on Iranians. Such resentment will be stronger the longer the war lasts. No new regime can ignore this sentiment.
Fifth, policies under any new rulers will illustrate how past Iranian policy has reflected Iranian security concerns and nationalism at least as much as the ideological coloration of whatever regime happened to be in power.
A conclusion is that the United States should not count on major up-front concessions or regime change as the occasion for ending this war. The most feasible way out of the war is a skeletal ceasefire agreement that defers most substantive negotiations, like the Memorandum of Understanding that the parties agreed to in June, but without the ambiguous language concerning the Strait of Hormuz that led the MoU to break down. A president looking for a “win” will have to rely on his rhetorical ability to depict such a ceasefire and the destruction already inflicted on Iranian forces as a victory.

title: War cuts off 800,000 in Taiz, diesel shortages to extend into 2027 and Gaza committee signs development deal
body: In today's episode of Trending Middle East , about 800,000 people in Yemen’s city of Taiz are largely cut off from food, fuel and medical supplies as fighting between the government troops and the Houthi rebels intensifies. As the Iran conflict drags on, the global diesel shortage is expected to continue well into 2027, the International Energy Agency has warned. In Lebanon , private suppliers now provide half of the country’s electricity, leaving households facing soaring bills. A special report by The National reveals how politically connected businesses are profiting from the country's power crisis. The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s development agency, GIZ, to support reconstruction. However, Israel continues to block the committee’s entry into the strip. And the UAE has announced a $1 million prize for a global competition to develop agentic artificial intelligence solutions that improve everyday life. Trending Middle East is AI-assisted, using original reporting published in The National and curated and edited by humans.
