title: Passengers of Egyptian aircraft that landed in Israel before October 7 were businessmen - report
body: Two businessmen on a routine trip were the passengers of the Egyptian aircraft that landed in Israel on September 26, 2023, KAN News reported on Wednesday, citing several sources familiar with the matter.The report comes amid suspicion that Egyptian General Intelligence Directorate Director Abbas Kamel was on board the flight, which was first reported by The Atlantic on Friday.According to the KAN report, the passengers entered Israel through the Fattal Terminal at Ben-Gurion Airport, and QAS provided ground services before the aircraft returned empty to Cairo.KAN noted that the flight was not registered as official or security-related, and that the Transportation Ministry, Fattal Terminal, the Population and Immigration Authority, and an Egyptian charter company are all aware of the passengers' identities. However, the entities refused to publish the names, in line with standard privacy practices.The flight in question has come under scrutiny after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed earlier on Wednesday that an Egyptian aircraft had landed in Israel several days before the October 7 massacre.Netanyahu denied meeting with Kamel in September 2023 and told KAN he didn't know who the Egyptian intelligence chief met during the alleged trip."I want to know who he met. I don't know," said Netanyahu, claiming that whoever had met Kamel was trying to "pin it" on him.On Wednesday, N12 News also reported that Israel's security chiefs were unaware Kamel had visited Israel in September 2023.Netanyahu denies ever meeting Kamel despite PMO statement, photographic evidenceThe prime minister said he had been attending a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers at the time, having further claimed in a Tuesday interview with Channel 14 that he had never met Kamel before."When does an intelligence chief come and speak to a head of state?" Netanyahu asked. "It hasn't happened to me once, OK? There's no such thing."His claim contradicted official statements from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) that Netanyahu had met with Kamel in May 2021."Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met today with Egyptian General Intelligence chief Abbas Kamel and a delegation of senior officials headed by him at the Prime Minister's Residence in Jerusalem," the statement read.Footage of the meeting was also published on the prime minister's official YouTube channel, while an official photograph of Netanyahu and Kamel shaking hands was published by the PMO alongside the statement.Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

title: ‘Putin Is Laughing’ – Zelensky Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal a Victory for Moscow
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky described US President Donald Trump’s Russian diesel deal as a victory for Vladimir Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washington’s decisions to pressure Ukraine into concessions.
In a wide-ranging interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky criticized Starlink restrictions that he said had cost Ukrainian lives.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Morgan ended the interview with a direct appeal to Trump, comparing Putin to Adolf Hitler and warning against appeasement.
The interview took place during Zelensky’s visit to Britain for meetings with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, amid renewed Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
Morgan questioned Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel amid rising energy prices linked to the war involving Iran, arguing that the deal would have little impact on US fuel prices.
Zelensky agreed, describing the arrangement as a tactical victory for Putin.
“Now Putin is laughing,” he said, suggesting that the Kremlin was gaining concessions from Washington even as Russia struggled on the battlefield.
Zelensky said the diesel agreement and restrictions affecting Starlink had handed Putin victories without requiring Russian forces to achieve military breakthroughs.
Morgan suggested Trump might be seeking to deflect public anger over rising gasoline prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
Zelensky acknowledged that domestic political pressures could be influencing Washington, but said Russia was also trying to exploit the situation to force Ukraine into concessions.
He warned that Moscow was looking for ways to force Ukrainian troops out of Donbas without defeating them militarily.
Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.
He insisted that the real cause of rising fuel prices was the conflict in the Middle East and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine’s strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
Asked how he reacted to Trump’s diesel agreement, Zelensky expressed deep disappointment.
“It’s a pity that we are losing. We are losing a strong partner,” he said.
“You think you’re losing America?” Morgan asked.
“Yeah. But not because of us,” Zelensky replied.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Kyiv could not sacrifice its sovereignty to maintain Washington’s support.
“We can’t be weak. Otherwise we can’t survive… We are not selling our country. Look, guys. It’s not about business for us. It’s just our life, and this is our country.”
He described Ukraine as the home of its people and children, rather than something that could be traded in negotiations.
“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelensky said.
He argued that Trump could remain a neutral mediator, but should not move toward Moscow.
“We are okay that he’s in the middle. But if you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side.”
Zelensky questioned the advice Trump was receiving.
“I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side… This is not the right side of history.”
Morgan also quoted Trump supporter Laura Loomer, who questioned why Moscow was not being held accountable for violating the energy ceasefire.
Loomer had described Putin as the “Hitler of our time.”
Asked whether he agreed, Zelensky replied: “Absolutely.”
But he challenged the perception that Putin was overwhelmingly powerful.
“He’s not so strong as [he is] evil, I think. But people are afraid of him,” Zelensky said.
He argued that the United States was stronger than Russia and had the power to stop Moscow’s aggression.
“The United States is stronger... and they have to be on our side.”
Zelensky said Putin’s strength depended on how far other countries allowed him to go.
“He’s strong till the world will stop him.”
Asked what message he would send directly to the US president, Zelensky began by thanking Trump and the American people for their support.
But he warned that Russia was deliberately undermining Trump’s authority.
“He has to understand that Russia wants him to be weak,” Zelensky said.
He characterized Moscow’s continued bombardment of Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s ceasefire announcement as an act directed against the American president himself.
Morgan suggested Russia was openly mocking Trump.
Morgan argued that Russia was demonstrating its disregard for Trump’s demands by continuing to launch missiles and drones against Ukraine.
Zelensky said the Kremlin cared far more about destroying Ukraine than about American political considerations.
“They hate Americans. It’s absolutely clear,” he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine supported Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire even though Kyiv had not been informed before the US president announced it.
“We need our people to live, to go through this winter and to stop the war,” he explained.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine refrained from striking Russian energy infrastructure for three days and did not immediately retaliate when Moscow resumed attacks.
“We didn’t attack during three days any kind of energy objects,” he said. “We didn’t respond.”
He recalled warning American officials that Russia would take advantage of the arrangement.
“They will attack energy. They will do it.”
Russia subsequently launched another massive barrage, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles aimed at Ukrainian energy infrastructure, Zelensky said.
Morgan noted that Ukrainian defenses intercepted only four of the ballistic missiles, leaving dozens to penetrate the country’s defenses.
Zelensky argued that Moscow was exploiting the ceasefire rather than honoring it.
Zelensky also criticized restrictions affecting Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system during Russian attacks.
He said Ukrainian forces lost connectivity around 1 a.m., affecting interceptor drones used to destroy incoming Russian Shaheds.
Morgan asked whether the restrictions had been imposed deliberately.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky replied.
He said Ukrainian soldiers attempted to contact SpaceX, American generals and other US partners after discovering the disruption.
“We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Starlink was not used solely for offensive missions.
“It’s not just about attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s also about defending the lives.”
Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the restrictions as a serious mistake.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said.
But he warned that disruptions to air defenses were already having deadly consequences.
“People are dying because of his decision.”
Zelensky urged the restoration of full connectivity, while acknowledging that a major technical problem remained a possibility.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know,” he said.
He also emphasized that European countries, including Poland, had paid for the Starlink services used by Ukraine.
The operational restrictions have been confirmed by Ukrainian officials, although responsibility for ordering them remains disputed.
Zelensky said Ukraine was facing another serious problem: interruptions in intelligence warnings from the US about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
“It’s two big problems,” he said, distinguishing between Starlink connectivity and advance missile intelligence.
American officials had attributed the intelligence disruptions to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the problems continued during Russian attacks.
Without timely warnings, Ukrainian civilians have less opportunity to reach shelters before ballistic missiles strike.
Trump has denied suspending American intelligence-sharing with Ukraine.
Despite Russia’s continued strikes against Ukrainian cities, Zelensky said Putin was suffering enormous military losses.
“Putin, he’s losing at the battlefield.”
He estimated that Russia was suffering approximately 43,000 casualties each month. Of those, Zelensky said approximately 20,000 to 25,000 were being killed monthly.
Asked how Ukrainian losses compared, he described a casualty ratio of approximately one Ukrainian for every seven to ten Russians.
Zelensky also said Ukraine had approximately five or six wounded soldiers for every soldier killed, while Russia’s casualty ratio was closer to 50–50 between killed and wounded.
“For them it’s nothing, for us it’s important,” he said.
Zelensky maintained that Ukrainian forces had stabilized the front despite continued Russian offensives and argued that Moscow was seeking political victories because it was struggling to achieve decisive battlefield gains.
Morgan played a recording of Trump calling for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with someone willing to negotiate a deal with Russia.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Morgan asked whether Trump was attempting to force Zelensky from office.
Zelensky recalled that Russia had already occupied Crimea and parts of Donbas before he became president in 2019.
He argued that replacing Ukraine’s leader would not resolve Russia’s aggression.
“No Trump, no Musk, nobody in the world can choose the president… in other countries,” he said.
Zelensky stressed that only Ukrainians could choose their president and expressed confidence that whoever succeeded him would continue defending the country.
“I’m sure the new man or woman will defend our country. This is our home.”
Morgan pressed Zelensky on whether a peace agreement could involve Ukraine formally surrendering territory to Russia.
Zelensky suggested that his refusal to recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied Ukrainian territory was one reason powerful figures might want him replaced.
“Some big guys want to change me, because I will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian land,” he said.
He nevertheless acknowledged that avoiding further loss of life was essential.
“I’m a realist, and I understand that people are more important than one kilometer or two kilometers.”
“It’s not about kilometers. I mean, this is about land and homes.”
He distinguished between acknowledging Russian occupation and legally recognizing the territory as Russian.
“Yes, it’s occupied, but this territory is occupied. It’s temporary.”
Zelensky expressed confidence that Ukraine would eventually recover its occupied regions, potentially through diplomacy rather than further military offensives.
“In any way it will come back, but without weapon,” he said.
Asked whether he intended to resign, Zelensky rejected the suggestion.
“No, of course. It’s my responsibility.”
He also said Ukraine could not hold a secure presidential election while Russian missiles and drones continued attacking the country.
“From the point of security, you can’t do elections.”
Zelensky stressed that Ukrainian service members on the front lines must be able to participate in any national vote.
“We can’t choose the president without soldiers, because they give and gave their lives.”
“They are first who have to vote, and I think it’s fair.”
Asked whether Ukrainian citizens supported him, Zelensky emphasized national unity.
“We are all Ukrainian people, and we are all on one side.”
“We have only one enemy: it’s Russia.” ‘We will not lose our independent country’ – even without America
Morgan asked whether Ukraine could prevail without US support.
Zelensky distinguished between preserving Ukraine’s independence and forcing Putin into negotiations.
“We will not in any way lose our independent country,” he said.
But he acknowledged that a diplomatic settlement would become much more difficult without Washington.
“We will have huge problems with how to push Putin to diplomatic way of ending this war – to negotiations.”
He praised European leaders, including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and French President Emmanuel Macron, for their continued support.
Zelensky said Ukraine needed clear commitments from its partners on weapons, sanctions and funding.
“Putin will not win, will not prevail, 100%,” he declared.
Toward the end of the interview, Morgan asked whether Zelensky genuinely believed Ukraine could achieve victory.
Zelensky returned to what he described as Putin’s original objective.
“Putin’s goal is total occupation of Ukraine,” he said.
Asked what Ukraine wanted, Zelensky replied: “To stop this war, make peace, stay where we stay.”
He maintained that occupied Ukrainian territories remained Ukrainian and would eventually return.
“Everything will come back because we are a real country.”
He said that Russian political circumstances would eventually change and could create opportunities for the peaceful return of occupied land.
Morgan concluded the interview by addressing Trump directly, telling him that siding with Putin against Ukraine would place Washington on the wrong side of history.
“It’s what we called in World War II appeasement to Hitler. Don’t be that guy,” Morgan warned. “Give this guy the support he needs to defeat the modern-day Hitler.”
Zelensky thanked Morgan and the British public, praising the United Kingdom for supporting Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He described Britain as a friend that had stood on the right side of history.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played key role in Venezuela, Iran operations - report
body: US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played a crucial role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.The WSJ was granted access to a US Space Force base in Colorado, where it was shown some of the Pentagon's space warfare capabilities, including systems designed to disrupt enemy satellites and detect threats to the US military.Among the weapons demonstrated was Meadowlands, an offensive system that can jam enemy satellites and disrupt their communications.According to the WSJ, these satellites are used for surveillance, communications, and navigation.Meadowlands often operates alongside a defensive system known as Bounty Hunter, which scans the electromagnetic spectrum to detect and locate potential threats to US forces, the report explained. Commanders can then pinpoint the location of a specific threat and order a defensive strike.Transportable jamming system used by US Space ForceThe US Space Force has also accelerated the deployment of a newer jamming system known as the Remote Modular Terminal. The equipment can be packed into a container and transported to locations around the world, allowing US personnel to deploy electronic warfare capabilities quickly.Over the past year, US Space Force soldiers, known as Guardians, have transported and deployed these systems to support US military operations in both Venezuela and Iran.According to the WSJ, “In a sign of how important space systems are, Iran repeatedly targeted US space capabilities, including satellite communications terminals, to try to degrade those advantages.“Satellites help the US detect missile launches, guide weapons, and get a clear picture of the battlefield,” taking high-resolution imagery from above.Tech.-Sgt. Joshua Lomax, who helped counter threats during operations in Venezuela before being deployed to defend against threats from Iran, described the pressure of preparing for the missions.“The threat is real,” Lomax told the WSJ.He recalled having just 72 hours to pack the equipment in Venezuela, load it onto an aircraft, and depart for Iran.“It was incredibly intense,” he told the WSJ. “Everybody was head on a swivel.”Importance of electromagnetic waves in modern warfareThe US Space Force also highlighted the importance of electromagnetic waves, which travel at different wavelengths and frequencies and underpin many of the technologies used in modern warfare. These systems connect military assets ranging from submarines and drones to radar installations.According to US Space Forces' Combat Forces Command, led by Lt.-Gen. Greggory Gagnon, a key mission for the US is to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.“That thing you never see is incredibly important in warfare,” he said. “If we can dominate the spectrum, we can keep our systems, our satellites, our ships, our planes, all connected and working more effectively, but we can also disrupt the adversary's ability to do it.”

title: Why Europe's reading habits should concern the Arab world
body: Even with some of the world's oldest and most prestigious publishing houses, extensive library networks and a celebrated literary culture, Europe is struggling to keep successive generations reading. That was among the takeaways from a presentation by the Federation of European Publishers, which represents national publishing associations across the continent, at Frankfurt Book Fair last week. While the federation reported that print book sales had fallen by about 6 per cent over five years in the markets surveyed, equivalent to a 110 million decline in copies, more revealing was its examination of reading habits. Drawing on Eurostat research from 2022, the report highlighted that 47.2 per cent of European Union residents aged 16 and older had not read a book in the preceding year. Among those aged 16 to 29, nearly four in 10 had not read one. The reasons reported by non-readers warrant attention. Among those aged 16 to 29, a lack of interest was cited by 58 per cent, compared with 21.8 per cent who said they lacked time. Across all age groups, 2.4 per cent identified cost or access as the obstacle. The figures add to gnawing concerns that predate Frankfurt, with research published in February by Britain's National Literacy Trust finding that 46.9 per cent of children aged eight to 11 enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 29.5 per cent of those aged 11 to 14. Among boys aged 14 to 16, the figure was just 18.8 per cent. Europe's experience offers a reminder against taking the Arab world's considerable investment in introducing children to books for granted. As educators and parents know, that desire to turn the page can change as they grow older, with education, social media and entertainment compete for attention, followed eventually by the growing pressures of professional and family responsibilities. Reading habits are not set in stone simply because children were encouraged during childhood. That is merely the first chapter of an ongoing story. The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing the reading bug. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. An impact study conducted in partnership with Unesco reported increased reading frequency and more books completed by participating students. Meanwhile, the Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, is more concerned with encouraging children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested on what they have consumed. Researchers are evaluating its effects and the longer-term affects remain unknown. Beyond the classroom, UAE libraries are also finding ways to keep books part of people's everyday lives. Sharjah's House of Wisdom and Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Library have become places to work, study and attend cultural events, as well as read books. The latter houses nine specialised libraries, including sections for children and young adults. But reading habits cannot develop through osmosis alone and both libraries continue to encourage younger audiences through workshops, holiday programmes and exhibitions. The quality of that content is critical, particularly when young Arabs themselves are questioning the appeal of the cultural content available to them. At the Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi in September, a survey of 4,092 people aged 18 to 25 across 10 Arab countries found that 71 per cent preferred media in Arabic, yet 67 per cent considered much of the available Arabic content outdated compared with English-language alternatives. The findings covered media broadly rather than books specifically, but they should give publishers reason to consider whether their books are resonating with younger audiences. Cairo's Diwan Publishing is one example worth noting, having reintroduced Naguib Mahfouz's novels through contemporary cover designs and graphic-novel adaptations, including The Thief and the Dogs . As previously reported by The National , co-founder Ahmed Qarmalawi said the project, developed with the Mahfouz family, sought to introduce the Nobel laureate's work to a generation familiar with his reputation but not necessarily his writing. At the 2024 Abu Dhabi International Book Fair, a large interactive pavilion dedicated to Mahfouz showcased the new editions. Qarmalawi recalled young visitors responding enthusiastically to the books, suggesting that an author some might regard as a literary cultural heirloom could still speak to a younger generation. And in that regard, social media is also playing a role in building a love of books during adolescence. As The National has reported, BookTok and BookTube communities have emerged in the region, with members recommending titles, sharing punchy reviews and introducing fellow readers to new authors. While the footfall at such events and the viewing figures online deserve to be celebrated, more work is needed to turn that enthusiasm into lasting reading habits and make reading books a normal part of life rather than homework. Authors and publishers must also take risks and create content that resonates. With its young population, eclectic cultural sensibilities and governments that view culture as an investment, the Arab world has a chance to lead in keeping people reading. That would be an achievement for a regional publishing industry still regarded as evolving by some of its European counterparts, provided the same commitment that encouraged children to pick up books in the first place is sustained.

title: Acting US Army secretary creates task force for HVAC repairs
body: HVAC problems, particularly air conditioning breakdowns, are not uncommon for U.S. soldiers residing in barracks. This summer, mechanical problems with a water treatment plant in Hawaii left thousands of soldiers at multiple Army installations on Oahu without central air conditioning . Soldiers at Fort Hood, Texas, experienced five to six weeks of unbearably hot temperatures in their rooms last year before AC was restored. And just last month, soldiers assigned to Fort Carson, Colorado, reported sleeping in their cars to escape hot barracks rooms, Stars and Stripes reported . Now, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle is attempting to do something about it. Telle announced Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting the creation of an enterprise-level Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning Task Force focused on soldiers’ quality of life. The task force includes leaders from facility operations, contracting and military engineering who can “cut through bureaucratic silos,” the Army said in a Monday statement . The announcement follows a directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last year to create another military-wide task force to improve barracks . “Secretary of War Hegseth has said every service member deserves clean, comfortable, and safe housing,” Telle said at the annual meeting in Washington, D.C. “This has never been done before — we’re taking this for the first time to the national level, to deliver results across the country to soldiers.” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a statement that HVAC is the top quality-of-life complaint that leadership hears from soldiers. The Government Accountability Office reported in August that the Defense Department does not request enough funding to fully meet its installation maintenance and major improvement needs, leading to a backlog of deferred maintenance at barracks. Hundreds of thousands of service members live in military barracks, with concerns about poor living conditions and management going back decades, according to the government watchdog. Before the end of the fiscal year in September, the Army directed $15 million toward 44 high-priority HVAC projects across multiple installations, the service said in a statement. “While that effort brought immediate relief to specific facilities, the [task force] leaders recognized that one-time emergency funding cannot replace a comprehensive, proactive strategy,” the Army said. Members of the task force will work directly with garrison commanders to find HVAC projects for 2027 and 2028, the Army said. So far, it has identified more than $100 million in projects to be awarded in early 2027. “This ensures ready-to-award projects are pre-engineered and priced as soon as funds become available,” the service said. “Additionally, the [task force] will utilize regional contracting approaches, utility energy service contracts, and commercial best practices.”

title: Why trust in AI is hard to earn and easy to lose
body: Trust, it is often said, is earned in drops but lost in buckets. When it comes to realising the potential of artificial intelligence , trust is arguably as important as computing power or economic returns. Just how much ordinary people are willing to trust this technology is a critical question – and one that is difficult to answer quantifiably. Nevertheless, it is a pertinent question for the UAE , a country that has positioned itself at the forefront of this technology. Dubai ’s announcement yesterday to offer a $1 million (Dh3.6 million) prize in collaboration with the World Economic Forum for meaningful AI innovation is another expression of that commitment. However, as the technology becomes more capable, its success will depend on more than just the ability to build it. To this point, speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders yesterday in Dubai, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Omar Al Olama suggested AI has to earn trust before being granted broader decision-making powers. His observation deserves to be central to the debate about the technology’s future. It is a future that offers the possibility of a substantial economic prize. Research presented alongside the WEF gathering suggests that AI could unlock more than $1 trillion in value across the Middle East and North Africa by 2030. For a region in which many countries want to diversify their economy, this is an opportunity to be taken seriously. However, projections such as these should not gloss over some important caveats – and the human factor. An AI system that makes a demonstrable contribution to productivity is valuable. One that people feel they cannot trust with their personal data, their finances or important decisions will struggle to succeed. Trust has to be earned through clear accountability and tangible safeguards. When AI makes mistakes, people need to know who is responsible and how errors will be corrected. These protections gain importance in step with the greater authority granted to automated systems. Success will belong to those who give people good reason to trust them Dubai’s gathering of established and emerging leaders is an opportunity to consider these questions in depth and across generations. Future generations will inherit the consequences of the decisions being made today. It stands to reason that they should also have a meaningful voice in determining how AI moves forward. The UAE has demonstrated that early investment and a willingness to experiment can establish a country as a serious player in a new industry. The next stage requires a comparable determination to get the governance right. AI may transform the Middle East’s economy and help prepare it for a rapidly changing world with many challenges. However, its lasting value will depend on whether it improves people’s lives without asking them to surrender their confidence in the technology. In the long run, success will belong to those who give people good reason to trust them.

title: Reconstruction in north-east Syria key to refugee returns from Iraq, UNHCR official says
body: Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National . Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle. “We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added. Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said. Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey. “When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war. Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”. “I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added. However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community. “I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said. He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said. He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees , Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee. “But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees. To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said. Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.” A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said. Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants. "What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said. Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014. Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq. ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces. “I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said. He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas. In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis , with UN support. However, its implementation has largely stalled amid disputes over who should control the area and appoint a mayor. The Popular Mobilisation Forces , an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar. Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK , and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.

title: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons consider leaving UK as tax concerns mount
body: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found. The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth. Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth. The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE , Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US. The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs. CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says. Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai -based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”. “UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National . Tax overhauls intensify debate Under the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains. Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules. The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon. UAE leads inquiry list Enquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds. Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent. Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows. “ Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits. Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon. Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows. For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity. “The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.

title: Russia Exploits Starlink Disruptions to Launch Massive Drone Barrage on Ukraine – Zelensky
body:
Russian forces launched at least 269 drones against Ukraine overnight and throughout Wednesday, Oct. 14, killing six people and injuring 13 in the western city of Lutsk, as President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Moscow was exploiting Starlink restrictions to intensify its attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
Speaking after talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London, Zelensky described the assault as one of the largest in scale.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Russia launched 124 drones overnight alone, and another 145 during the day. And right now, there are still more than 40 ‘shaheds’ in our skies,” he wrote on X.
“They attack energy infrastructure, logistics, and railways.”
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted a significant number of the drones, but some penetrated defenses and struck their targets.
The attacks continued despite US President Donald Trump’s recent announcement of an energy ceasefire.
Zelensky warned that Moscow was taking advantage of disruptions affecting Ukraine’s Starlink-dependent interceptor drones.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things,” he said.
Restrictions affecting SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield system have disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, although responsibility for the changes remains disputed.
“That is why it is especially important right now to strengthen our air defenses and provide Ukraine with everything it needs to protect lives,” Zelensky said.
Following his meeting with Burnham, Zelensky announced that Britain would accelerate deliveries of air defense weapons designed to intercept faster, jet-powered Shahed drones.
“Today, a decision was made to accelerate deliveries of British-made air defense systems to Ukraine to counter jet-powered ‘shaheds,’” he said, thanking Britain for the timely assistance.
In an earlier statement following the deadly strike on Lutsk, Zelensky condemned Russia’s continued bombardment of civilian areas as a deliberate campaign of terror.
“This is intentional, permanent pressure on our people,” he said.
“Russia is once again showing what it really wants. This is a deliberate continuation of the war, in defiance of calls from the United States and the American President.”
He urged G7 leaders and other international partners to increase sanctions and military assistance rather than rely on Moscow’s willingness to negotiate.
“Moscow must not be talked into stopping – it must be forced to stop through increased pressure, sanctions, and assistance to Ukraine that enables us to protect people from these attacks,” Zelensky said.
“There must be action. Because as long as Russia does not feel sufficient pressure, it will continue to sow death.”

title: NZ Army service brings Staff Sergeant back to Penrhyn
body:
Unfortunately you are viewing this website on an outdated browser which does not support the necessary features for us to provide an adequate experience. Please switch to a modern browser such as latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge.
When New Zealand Army Staff Sergeant Tokahaumata Oltaches-Tagavaitau stepped off the aircraft on Penrhyn, a remote island in the northern Cook Islands, the welcome awaiting her was unlike any previous deployment.
Family had travelled across the lagoon to meet her and news of her arrival had spread through the community. “I cried,” she said.
For the first-generation New Zealander, Exercise Tropic Twilight became much more than another deployment – it brought her back to her family’s roots, allowed her to spend time in her father’s village for the first time, and reconnected parts of her own story.
Tropic Twilight is a long-standing annual New Zealand Defence Force-led South Pacific humanitarian assistance and disaster relief effort, supported by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Both sides of Staff Sergeant Oltaches-Tagavaitau’s family have links to Penrhyn. Her parents were born and raised in the Cook Islands before moving to New Zealand seeking greater educational opportunities for their children. Although born in New Zealand, her home life remained distinctly Cook Islands, speaking Cook Islands Māori and maintaining the traditions and expectations her parents and grandparents had grown up with.
“First generation is important, because inside the house you live a Cook Islands life, but outside the house you have to live a New Zealand life,” she said. Growing up between those two worlds was not always easy.
“As a teenager it was confusing. They wanted me to go to school and get an education, but how you lived at home was completely different to what was expected in society.”
Even something as ordinary as water use reflected life on the islands. As a child living in New Zealand, she remembers being taught never to waste water, something that made much more sense when she later experienced how precious freshwater is on remote Pacific islands.
Joining the NZ Army was another departure from her parents’ hopes – instead of university, after taking part in an Army programme through Pakuranga’s Edgewater College, she made her own decision. It did not go down well.
Her parents were, however, at her graduation – and almost 20 years later their view of her career has changed considerably, and her younger sister has followed her into the NZ Army. In 2020, Staff Sergeant Oltaches-Tagavaitau was named both NZ Army Soldier of the Year and NZDF Person of the Year as she thrived in her chosen environment.
When Staff Sergeant Oltaches-Tagavaitau heard Tropic Twilight would return to Penrhyn in 2026, the opportunity was difficult to ignore.
Although she had briefly visited Penrhyn once before, she never imagined her NZDF service would give her the opportunity to return and spend meaningful time in her father’s village.
On Tropic Twilight, she worked primarily as the Contingent Staff Sergeant, with a secondary role as a mechanic. She has also served as a community liaison officer, her cultural knowledge and family connections helping to bridge the gap between NZDF personnel and the Penrhyn community. She has helped personnel understand local customs, the importance of church, family responsibilities and aspects of island life that can be difficult to appreciate without cultural context. It quickly became a significant part of her deployment.
“If you didn’t have someone who understands the community, the contingent could come here, work, and then be isolated back at the centre,” she said. Instead, personnel have been invited into family homes, eaten with local families, and taken part in daily life beyond their work. Some have even gone fishing after work to help provide food for families catering for the contingent.
“That full immersion is important. They might see something, but when they’re living it, they understand it. There’s so much more that we can learn from them, just as much as they can learn from us,” Staff Sergeant Oltaches-Tagavaitau said.
The deployment has also helped her reconnect with parts of her identity that had faded into the background during a busy NZDF career.
“When I joined the Army, I lost some of this. Not my identity – it was just forgotten. Seeing it again gives me clarity and closure on why things were the way they were growing up. I definitely feel like I belong here.”
That sense of belonging made her work on Penrhyn even more personal. From the moment she arrived, her people made sure she knew she was one of them.
As one family member said when news of the deployment reached the island, “She is Penrhyn.”
As Staff Sergeant Oltaches-Tagavaitau puts it – “There’s nothing more satisfying than giving back to your own people.”

title: Chinese J-16 Pilot Recalls How He Defeated French Rafale and Russian MiG-29M Jets While Outnumbered
body: The Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force has disclosed further details of its joint air training exercise with Egypt, including simulated beyond-visual-range engagements in which J-16 fighters faced a numerically greater force of Egyptian Air Force French-supplied Rafale and Russian-supplied MiG-29M combat aircraft. Footage broadcast by Chinese state media on October 11 revealed how the Chinese contingent employed a KJ-500 airborne early warning and control aircraft to coordinate its J-16 fighter operations, while also highlighting the use of electronic warfare and aerial refuelling during the exercise. The training, designated Eagles of Civilization 2026, took place in Egypt from mid-August to early September and provided an opportunity for the two air forces to assess their respective capabilities under simulated combat conditions. Training placed greater emphasis on beyond-visual-range combat, where sensor coverage, electronic warfare and coordinated weapons employment can be more decisive than close-range manoeuvrability. According to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, the third day of the exercise included an engagement involving four Chinese J-16s against six Egyptian fighters, comprising two Rafales and four MiG-29s. The Chinese contingent was therefore outnumbered by a ratio of three to two, prompting the deployment of a KJ-500 airborne early warning aircraft to support the fighters. The exercise was intended to explore how coordinated operations and airborne surveillance could compensate for a numerical disadvantage in a simulated air battle. The KJ-500 is designed to provide wide-area airborne surveillance, track and identify aerial targets, and coordinate the activities of friendly aircraft. Its radar and mission systems allow it to function as an airborne command and control node, providing information that fighter pilots might otherwise have to obtain using their own sensors. By sharing a broader tactical picture with the J-16s, the aircraft can help them coordinate their movements and weapons employment while reducing the need for individual fighters to operate independently. Its contribution is particularly relevant in engagements involving multiple aircraft, where the ability to detect threats early and distribute targeting information can help offset differences in numbers. This complemented the considerable situational awareness and command and control advantages the J-16 already enjoyed over the Rafale and MiG-29. Wei Yuexin described how the Chinese pilots approached the simulated engagement, stating: “When the air battle started, we forgot about the numerical disadvantage and forgot that they might be Rafales. We only remembered the timeline for missile evasion. We just needed to evade their weapons, and through tactical coordination, we made up for the numerical gap.” His account placed particular emphasis on coordination and defensive manoeuvres during the engagement, rather than claiming that the Chinese fighters had defeated the Egyptian aircraft through superior individual performance. The exercise also reportedly prompted extended discussions between the two sides after the day’s training, with Egyptian pilots remaining at the airfield at 9:30 pm to discuss the engagement with their Chinese counterparts. Electronic warfare was another prominent feature of the training. Wei said Egyptian pilots had expressed particular interest in the Chinese use of electronic jamming, commenting: “What impressed me most was how much they appreciated and were interested in our use of electronic jamming. They thought our timing and jamming capability were excellent.” The remarks suggest that the exercise included opportunities to observe how electronic countermeasures could be employed during simulated air combat, although the report did not disclose the systems used, the techniques practised or the effectiveness of the jamming against specific Egyptian aircraft and equipment. Electronic warfare can complicate an adversary’s ability to detect, track and engage targets, but its effectiveness depends on the characteristics of the systems involved and the countermeasures available to both sides. The training also provided a platform for direct exchanges between the two air forces regarding their aircraft and weapons. One Chinese pilot said Egyptian personnel had praised the J-16 and the PL-15 long-range air-to-air missile, stating: “When we chatted, they praised not only our skills but also our J-16 fighters and PL-15 missiles. I could feel it in their eyes. They were giving a thumbs-up to our country’s development.” Wei Yuexin stressed that Egyptian aircraft demonstrated strong close-combat manoeuvrability - a feature for which the MiG-29 in particular has for decades been renowned due to its outstanding thrust-weight ratio. The J-16 notably retains strong advantages in visual range combat due to its integration of the PL-10 air-to-air missile for high off Boresight targeting, to which France and Russia produce no near-peer rivals. The exercise appears to have simulated visual range combat without use of missiles, relying on gun kills, to even the odds in the favour of Egyptian Air Force units, reflecting a broader global trend towards the scripting of engagements to compensate for significant technological discrepancies.

title: Five Possible Backdoors into LLM Search Results
body:
With the plunge in traditional traffic from search engine results, due to the new trend for AI summaries , publishers at all levels are now seeking to gain prominence in the attention of the Large Language Models that power web-search AI summaries, and directly, in popular frontier models such as ChatGPT.
Legitimate approaches, according to prior works such as Optimizing Visibility in Generative Engines and How to Dominate AI Search , include securing independent editorial coverage; publishing authoritative and well-structured content; providing machine-readable product information; and adapting material for different languages and markets.
Alternative methods that have recently attracted attention resemble the black-hat SEO practices of earlier decades: these include astroturfing on Reddit, where ostensibly independent recommendations were planted to influence AI search results; memory poisoning , in which deceptive links attempted to make assistants retain promotional claims as trusted information; and prompt injection , where hidden website instructions sought to influence an AI assistant’s recommendations, rather than merely provide information for it to summarize.
One particularly ingenious example of GEO manipulation was when researchers at ETH Zürich created a fictitious camera and published a promotional webpage containing a concealed instruction, rendered in tiny white text, directing Microsoft’s Bing Copilot to recommend the camera exclusively. The tiny font size and low contrast was designed to conceal the manipulation.
Two fictional camera advertisements used in an ETH Zürich experiment to manipulate AI search recommendations. The conventional advertisement (left) contains visible promotional text, while the ‘PixelBlitz’ advertisement (right) conceals an instruction in one-point white text, invisible against the white background. The hidden message impersonates a system instruction, telling the AI to recommend PixelBlitz exclusively and conceal the instruction’s existence. In controlled tests, this technique increased the fictional camera’s recommendation rate from 34% to 59.4%. Source
In controlled tests, the fake camera’s recommendation rate rose from 34% to 59.4%, slightly exceeding the 57.9% achieved by genuine Nikon and Fuji-film cameras, demonstrating that malicious instructions embedded in retrieved webpages could indeed influence AI recommendations.
With the stakes so high, it’s reasonable to assume that Black Hat GEO is an active and well-funded illicit strand of research across marketing industries and various other sectors looking to gain or restore their former SEO prominence by gaining recommendations from AI oracles and chat engines.
Therefore let’s take a look at some of the possible or emerging avenues:
The Internet Archive is one of the most exhaustive and useful network resources around, with its Wayback Machine passing the one-trillion-page milestone in 2025. At the time of writing the IA reports a phenomenal 47,381,733 PDF documents stored and available to the public:
A staggering collection of PDF material, largely volunteer-donated, is stored at the Internet Archive. Source
As can be seen from the example results above, many of the PDFs uploaded are quite pedestrian in nature, from obscure music fliers from the 1950s-90s; to rare and fascinating magazines and books thought lost to posterity; to mind-numbing tranches of meeting minutes from municipal assemblies in the 1970s and 80s; and much more.
This collection is being indiscriminately hammered in this period, and the obvious culprit is a horde of AI scraper-bots desperate for novel data, or for better or corroborating versions of data they already have.
Clearly it is a trivial matter to amend an uploaded document to support a false statement, false products, false references to people (laudatory or defamatory), false statements about the same, etc.
Such material can be injected into outputs considered ‘authority’ sources by LLMs, such as PDFs of well-respected magazines that happen not to be fully indexed yet in the IA’s collection; in such a case, the ‘doctored’ edition would be seen as ‘filling a hole’, legitimately.
Text style could be simulated by AI itself to match the existing style of a short article or even a caption, and the PDF’s date amended, along with multiple other trivial tricks to make the document appear to be (for instance) something found in an archive from the 1990s – or earlier:
A simple ‘historical amendment’ provided by ChatGPT-5.5, without protest, and easily inserted back into the PDF source document. Thus the ‘Pence Opera House’ exits existence, while the Guthrie Theater’s opening (it is a real theater in Minnesota) is brought forward from its true launch date of 1963, to the much earlier 1867. Source
All one has to do in such cases, it would seem, is wait for the information to be picked up by the avid AI scraper-bots. It’s still too early to know for sure the extent to which any filters or checking systems in dataset curation could catch such illicit amendments; however the scale of such datasets is so enormous as to generally prohibit that particular degree of oversight. At this enormity of volume, one is essentially ‘trusting the data’.
Or, if you’re old enough to remember them, a modern ‘webring’ – the interconnected sites of the early internet, predating Google’s PageRank and Moz’s Domain Authority , which valued the number and quality of inbound links.
However, Synthetic Consensus Networks go further , manufacturing apparent independent corroboration across supposedly unrelated websites . A recent study from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and EPFL broadly demonstrated the principle when the paper’s researchers tested 12 AI models against 225 products in 15 categories, replacing genuine brand references in retrieved search results with fictitious alternatives.
From the paper, an illustration of two routes by which fabricated product information can influence AI recommendations. Above, false content is planted on the live web and enters search results; below, researchers simulate the same process by modifying retrieved pages locally. Both routes can lead an AI assistant to recommend a nonexistent brand alongside genuine products. Source
The effect increased as more results carried the same false information. With three manipulated pages among the leading results, the most vulnerable model recommended nonexistent products in 73.8% of tests. Even a single corrupted first-place result could mislead some models in 27% of cases.
More remarkably, the models sometimes invented corroboration of their own : in one test involving a fictitious screen-protector brand, Claude and DeepSeek added claims about community recommendations and product testing that did not appear in the supplied material.
Though the experiment was conducted on locally-modified search results, rather than a live network of fraudulent websites, it suggests how a coordinated collection of ostensibly independent reviews could manufacture credibility, with AI reinforcing the untruth with additional endorsements.
Citation generation (arguably, ‘citation laundering’) is a variation on synthetic consensus networks, but with greater emphasis on the apparent provenance of information rather than on the number of sources repeating it.
A fabricated claim might first appear in an obscure trade journal; a self-published research paper; or a specialist publication, with little editorial oversight. It can then be cited by blogs, directories and other publications – and each repetition gives the original assertion a little more apparent legitimacy.
Eventually, an AI search engine may encounter the claim several steps removed from its original source , perhaps in an otherwise reputable article that cites an intermediary publication; and what began as an unsupported assertion now has a citation history – even though none of the subsequent references constitutes independent verification.
There are already several documented examples of this process, though most predate the emergence of AI search. In one notorious case, a teenager invented the nickname ‘Brazilian aardvark’ for the coati , and inserted it into Wikipedia.
The invented name propagated to newspapers and at least one academic book. Eventually, Wikipedia itself cited a newspaper article as evidence for the claim it had originally introduced – a near-perfect circle of fabricated authority. The episode was documented by The New Yorker.
A more deliberate demonstration emerged in 2025, when researchers created multiple AI-generated academic papers attributed to a nonexistent scientist . The fabricated publications accumulated 380 citations and an h-index of 19 on Google Scholar, giving the fictional researcher an apparently respectable academic standing. The experiment , published in Nature’s Scientific Reports , illustrates how citation counts can be manufactured without any corresponding body of genuine research.
Neither case demonstrates a successful attack on an AI search engine. However, both establish the underlying weakness, in that once a false assertion has been reproduced by apparently credible sources, subsequent systems may have difficulty distinguishing independent corroboration from the repeated circulation of a single fabrication. The particular danger for AI search is that a model may summarize this chain of references as corroborating evidence, without recognizing that all the apparent authorities lead back to the same unverified claim.
Expired domains can retain the apparent credibility, inbound links and search visibility of their former owners. Acquiring these addresses and populating them with new material can make recently-introduced claims appear to originate from established publications – a practice that goes back 20-30 years . The domain authority of an expired/abandoned domain is often acquired in order for its content to be revamped into ‘related’ but commercialized material.
In 2024, the influential women’s blog The Hairpin , which had closed in 2018, reappeared under new ownership as an AI-generated content farm, with its original articles intermingled with rewritten material and fictitious author bylines, exploiting the reputation and domain authority of a once-respected publication. While this is not a demonstrated AI-search attack, the case illustrates how an established website’s history can be appropriated.
Although archived snapshots can help expose the difference between a domain’s genuine past and its newly-manufactured content, even this kind of evidence is not necessarily permanent: In 2002, the Internet Archive removed snapshots of websites critical of Scientology following copyright complaints from the organization’s lawyers, initially suggesting that the removals had been requested by the website owners themselves.
Until 2017, the Wayback Machine applied website exclusion rules retroactively , potentially allowing new domain owners to conceal their predecessors’ content. Although this practice was discontinued , the Internet Archive still considers requests to remove historical snapshots.
Academic repositories offer another route to apparent authority. Preprint servers allow researchers to publish papers before peer review, while search engines and AI retrieval systems may encounter these documents alongside established scientific literature.
The problem is that publication and verification are not the same thing: in 2024, researchers demonstrated how malicious instructions embedded in academic papers could manipulate AI assistants processing those documents. Their work showed that the apparent legitimacy of a research paper does not prevent its contents from being used to influence an AI system.
A less conspicuous GEO approach would involve depositing plausible but marginal research that repeatedly associates a company, product or individual with particular expertise. Even without explicit instructions to an AI, such material could provide apparently scholarly support for claims that originated with the beneficiary.
Other potential avenues include review ecosystem infiltration (planting favorable assessments on comparison sites and software directories); knowledge graph manipulation (altering structured data to establish misleading associations between companies, products and expertise); and multilingual reputation laundering (placing promotional claims in less-scrutinized foreign-language sources).
Finally, agentic GEO optimization could automate these techniques (repeatedly testing content against AI search engines and refining whichever variations produce the desired recommendations).
First published Monday, October 12, 2026. Amended within thirty minutes to fix Title Case and missing tags.
Writer on machine learning, domain specialist in human image synthesis. Former head of research content at Metaphysic.ai, until its dissolution into DNEG's Brahma.ai. Website: martinanderson.ai Contact: martin@martinanderson.ai

title: HM confers Royal Orders on Omani figures
body:
Muscat: His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik conferred Royal Orders on a number of Omani figures at al Barakah Palace on Thursday in recognition of their dedicated service and commitment to their professional duties. HM the Sultan conferred the Order of Honnour, First Class, on Sayyida Dr Ghalya bint Fahr al Said and Sayyida Dr Mona bint Fahd al Said, Assistant Vice-Chancellor for International Cooperation at Sultan Qaboos University. The Order of Al Rusoukh (Order of Establishment), Second Class, was conferred on Sayyid Loay bin Ghalib al Said, Secretary-General of the Royal Court Affairs, and Sayyid Nader bin Shihab al Said. HM also conferred the Oman Civil Order, First Class, on Anwar bin Hilal al Jabri, Minister of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion, and Sayyid Faisal bin Hamoud al Busaidi, Governor of Musandam. The Order of Commendation, Second Class, was awarded to Mulham bin Bashir al Jarf, Deputy President for Investment at the Oman Investment Authority (OIA), and Munir bin Ali al Muniri, Deputy President for Operations at the OIA. In addition, the Order of Al Numan, First Class, was conferred on Badr bin Mohammed Al Mandhari, Oman’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom, while Dr Aflah bin Said al Hadhrami, Managing Director of Petroleum Development Oman (PDO), received the Order of Commendation, Second Class.

title: King Charles Welcomes Zelensky as Britain Steps Up Military Support for Ukraine
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met King Charles III at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday, Oct. 14, before holding talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as London pledged faster air defense missile deliveries and tougher sanctions against Russia amid strained US-Ukraine relations.
King Charles received Zelensky for a private audience at Buckingham Palace, underscoring Britain’s continued support for Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience,” Zelensky said afterward, expressing appreciation for the monarch’s unwavering support and Britain’s assistance to Ukraine.
Following the royal audience, Burnham welcomed Zelensky to Downing Street with a ceremonial guard of honor involving the Irish Guards.
“We are behind you and that will not change,” Burnham told the Ukrainian president.
Britain announced plans to accelerate a £45 million (approximately $60 million) package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses against Russian drones, including increasingly fast jet-powered models.
The government will bring forward £10 million (approximately $13 million) to meet urgent winter requirements.
London also pledged additional sanctions against Moscow, including restrictions targeting maritime services supporting Russian liquefied natural gas exports.
Burnham said his government would continue providing military and financial support while pressing international partners to increase pressure on Russia.
Before meeting Zelensky, Burnham told Parliament he would seek to “repair bridges” between Trump and the Ukrainian president to restore American support.
Despite criticizing Washington’s recent decisions, Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remained committed to its US partnership.
“We count on our partnership with the United States,” he told Burnham.
“We just want to be very honest, very clear, be strong partners.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan , Zelensky said he believed the overnight Starlink restrictions were not caused by technical problems.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he said.
He warned that Starlink restrictions weakened Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, while separate disruptions in US intelligence-sharing left Ukraine without advance warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, putting civilian lives at greater risk.

title: Presidential Message on the Birthday of President Dwight D. Eisenhower
body: Briefings & Statements Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research On this day, we mark the 136th birthday of President Dwight David Eisenhower—a visionary leader, respected warrior, distinguished statesman, and noble public servant. In command of great armies and in the White House, he met every trial with steadiness, courage, and resolve, earning the enduring trust of the American People and the lasting gratitude of the free world. Born in Denison, Texas, and raised in Abilene, Kansas, President Eisenhower began his legendary life of service to our great Nation as a graduate of West Point. His stellar military career spanned nearly four decades and included appointments such as the Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force during World War II, during which he orchestrated the historic D-Day Invasion of Normandy, and as NATO’s first Supreme Allied Commander Europe. In his first bid for the Presidency in 1952, the celebrated general and political outsider was elected in a landslide victory. After four years, Americans still liked “Ike” and handed him another decisive win in the 1956 election. Eisenhower’s tenure in the White House was marked by peace, growth, economic prosperity, and a remarkable record of foreign and domestic accomplishments. He negotiated an armistice in the Korean War, signed the Civil Rights Act of 1957, created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Small Business Administration, and championed the Interstate Highway System, which connected communities across our country and boosted American commerce. Eisenhower’s commitment to military might and the preservation of our birthright of freedom is reflected in the cautionary words from his 1953 Inaugural Address: “History does not long entrust the care of freedom to the weak or the timid.” My Administration is proudly advancing the ideals that shaped Eisenhower’s Presidency, including economic prosperity, a strong national defense, secure borders, an unwavering commitment to peace through strength, and the tireless pursuit of American exceptionalism. Like President Eisenhower, I believe lasting peace is secured only through unquestioned American strength, and my Administration is rebuilding our military into the most powerful fighting force on Earth. We are upholding the law and order he championed, making our streets and communities safe again, igniting an economic boom unlike anything our country has ever seen, and renewing the strength and spirit of American life at every turn. More than seven decades later, Eisenhower’s example continues to guide our Nation as we restore the peace, prosperity, and confidence that defined his era and usher in a new Golden Age for the American People. As we commemorate the birthday of our 34th Commander in Chief, we honor the extraordinary life and legacy of this patriot, hero, and American icon, whose devotion to duty and country will inspire Americans for generations to come. Happy Birthday, President Eisenhower! The post Presidential Message on the Birthday of President Dwight D. Eisenhower appeared first on The White House .
