title: The Double Headed Stack Allocator
body:
When programming high performance applications, such as video games, you learn neat tricks for writing fast code that makes the most of limited resources.
Memory allocation is a huge topic for performance critical code that needs a variable amount of memory.
When you hear “stack allocator” you might think of “alloca” which lets you allocate memory from the actual program stack. That is super useful in a pinch, but that is not what today’s post is about. Another name for the type of stack allocator we are talking about today is “bump allocator”.
Around 2010 I was working at Surreal Software (Midway Seattle) on an open world game “This is Vegas” which unfortunately was cancelled when Midway went out of business.
On that project, one of my duties was animation programming. Animation worked by having a state machine for sets of bones, where each state was a tree of animation blends. When states changed, they would blend out from the old state into the new state to preserve continuity.
There was a lot of blending going on, and it used a large number of dynamic memory allocations for these animations to be evaluated and blended on the CPU. These allocations were all transient though and only needed to exist for part of the frame. Furthermore, these allocations had to happen per frame, as things could change drastically from one frame to the next, as to which characters were being animated that frame – based on the camera frustum for example. The allocator showed up as a hot spot in profiling this section of code.
To solve this problem, we implemented a “stack allocator” where allocation is just an integer add, and deallocation is even cheaper.
To do this, you allocate and keep some amount of memory that is the maximum amount you will need, like say 1MB. This is your stack. You also keep an integer “tos” variable to know where the top of the stack is.
When you want to allocate memory, your memory is the memory at the top of the stack, and you add the number of bytes you want to allocate to the tos variable so that the next allocation comes after yours:
In a real implementation, you would also want to know how big the memory was, so that you could handle the tos hitting the end of the memory – by returning null, or asserting, or something else.
When you are done with the memory, you just set the tos variable to 0.
In our case, we set the tos to 0 after animation blending was finished and we had copied the results into the buffers that were heading to the vertex shader for skinning. If you were using a stack allocator more generally for all transient memory allocations during a game’s frame, you may set it back to 0 when the frame starts.
The result was night and day. Allocation no longer took any measurable time in the profiler, because allocation was an integer addition, and freeing all memory was a single integer assigment. It doesn’t get faster than that.
One thing to note is that as written, this allocator does not call destructors or destructors. Using placement new for constructors would be easy enough. Calling destructors would be harder, as it would have to be a manual process, which is error prone. You might be able to use some RAII pattern, but stack allocators work best for simpler types.
Another great thing about stack allocators is that they can work in multi threaded environments. If the tos variable uses atomic addition, multiple threads can allocate from the same stack allocator. This can be nice in a fork/join situation on the CPU, or for a complex algorithm running on the GPU.
You can also do “partial deallocations” with stack allocators. For instance, if you had some recursive process where each level needed dynamic allocation, you could remember where the tos was when that level started, and set it back to that value when that level of processing finished.
A few years later, I found myself at Blizzard on the StarCraft 2 team. My boss James Anhalt was (and still is) a really smart dude who introduced me to shader toy, and shared a bunch of really cool techniques that have been previous blog posts. He told me about double headed stack allocators as a solution to a memory fragmentation problem he had hit in the past.
Imagine that you had a streaming world game where as the player ran around the world, old level geometry would deallocate, and new level geometry would allocate and stream in from disk.
At the same time, imagine the player character could shape shift into different forms – and each time they changed forms, the old form was deallocated, and the new form was allocated and streamed in from disk.
A challenge is, when you have these two systems allocating and deallocating random amounts of memory, on their own timelines, your memory is going to get fragmented.
Lets walk through a simple example. Let’s say you have 100 MB total memory for the level (red) and the character (green). The level allocates 20MB, then the character allocates 30MB, then the level allocates 20MB and the character allocates the final 30MB.
Now let’s say that the player runs to a new section, so the old level data memory is freed. The new level data only needs to make a single 30MB allocation. We do have 40MB memory free, but it isn’t in one chunk! We only have two blocks of 20MB. So even though the new level data is smaller, we can’t allocate space for it. This is memory fragmentation, and it’s a big problem in memory constrained environments.
So, James told me what they did in this type of situation was to have a chunk of memory like a normal stack allocator, but the level data had a tos which grew upwards from 0, and the character data had a tos which grew downward from the end of the memory. You knew you were out of memory when they crossed over each other and the level tos was greater than the character tos.
This made it so when the level data needed to change, it could reset the level tos back to 0, and reallocate the memory it needed, without any fragmentation whatsoever. Similarly, when the character freed its memory, it would reset its tos back to the end of memory, and could then reallocate the memory it needed, also without any fragmentation.
Once again, these allocators work fine in multithreaded environments, even when each thread might allocate from either side. Atomic add to the tos indices is all you need.
You might ask “why not have two stack allocators instead of a double headed one?” The main benefit is when you are memory constrained and know that the size of one stack allocator is enough to serve two systems, but the proportion of memory that goes to one side vs the other is flexible. In a game situation like described above, that means some levels could use more memory, but in those situations, the character would need to have reduced memory usage. A bit of a contrived example but hopefully you get what I mean.
There is a variation of this when you are trying to store a number of variable sized objects in a fixed amount of memory, but you want random access by index. An example may be that you want to send network packets of a specific size for efficiency reason, and you want to that memory to encode a variable number of variable sized network commands in it. You want to be able to easily iterate through the messages, but you want to support them having variable sizes too.
What you do is have a double headed stack allocator where one stack is for the dynamic allocations, and the other stack is for an array of integers that are an offset in the memory to the dynamic allocations.
Let me show you what I mean with an example. Starting with an empty double headed stack allocator:
you also have to somehow keep track of how many objects there are. You could have a separate integer keeping count of how many offsets there are in the offset table, or maybe you could have a sentinel value in the offset table to indicate where the end of the offsets are. Perhaps ~0 (all 1s in binary) could be the sentinel value.
Just like the other stack allocators we talked about, this one can also work in a multi threaded environment. You might be tempted to make the two updates transactional – like with a compare and swap loop – but it isn’t needed.
Lastly, this configuration allows you to remove items, or move them around in memory, which is another way of reducing fragmentation – you just need to update the offset table to match reality when you do so.
Another little write up that includes this topic, from the AMD vulkan memory allocator: https://gpuopen-librariesandsdks.github.io/VulkanMemoryAllocator/html/custom_memory_pools.html#linear_algorithm

title: Dubai Police arrest group over fake reviews: Can bad review land you in trouble?
body: Posting a negative online review of a business could land UAE residents in legal trouble if their comments are deemed defamatory or deliberately damaging to the business's reputation, experts have warned. The warning follows the arrest of a group by Dubai Police accused of posting fake reviews on a company’s Google Maps page in an attempt to harm its business. Police said an investigation launched after the company filed a complaint revealed that several commercial shops had formed groups to publish false and damaging comments. While customers are entitled to share their experiences online, their comments must not harm others or their interests, said Maj Yasser Juma Mohammed, head of the Social Media Crimes Section at Dubai Police. He warned social media users that there is a difference between leaving an honest negative review and posting comments that could amount to an insult or defamation. A lasting impact Nikhat Sardar Khan, a litigation lawyer in Dubai, said that insulting, misleading or malicious reviews can expose the writer to legal action. "Online defamation is considered more harmful as it can cause lasting damage because it can be saved, shared and viewed long after it was first published." Ludmila Yamalova of law firm Lylaw said: "Deleting a review does not automatically eliminate legal liability. Once a statement is published, the offence may have occurred. Screenshots, platform records, or other electronic evidence may preserve the original content." For small businesses, a few negative or fake reviews can bruise their reputation and leave a lasting online imprint. For Apple Gawaran, a Dubai-based content creator who runs a personalised 3D-printed gifts business, the issue is personal. "One fake review can create unnecessary negativity and potentially influence people who have never even experienced the business," she said. Ms Gawaran said customers should share honest feedback, positive or negative, but there is a clear difference between genuine criticism and deliberately posting false information to damage a business. Amreen Iqbal, founder of jewellery brand Piece of You, said fake reviews can create doubts among potential customers who rely on online feedback when choosing gifts. "When someone posts a review about an experience they never had, it creates confusion and doubt," she said. The team at Mövenpick JLT raised a similar concern, saying fake reviews can mislead families planning holidays and business travellers booking accommodation, while unfairly affecting the staff behind the service. A bad review is not necessarily illegal Constructive criticism or opinions based on genuine experiences generally do not constitute defamation if they are not insulting or made with malicious intent. However, even factual statements that damage a reputation can be defamatory. Ms Yamalova said: “Negative reviews are not illegal in the UAE. However, the distinction between legitimate criticism and unlawful defamation is not always clear-cut, and is more nuanced.” Simply put, saying a restaurant's service was slow or a product didn't meet expectations is different from accusing a business of fraud or insulting its employees. "These reviews, while critical, aim to provide constructive feedback without making false statements," said Ms Khan. In contrast, a defamatory review contains false statements. Such reviews go beyond mere opinion or criticism, which can lead to legal consequences. According to Ms Khan, "Businesses and individuals can sue for defamation if they can prove that the statements have caused harm or tangible damage. Reviewers must ensure their feedback is honest and not insulting or defamatory, causing reputational harm or tangible damage." UAE cybercrime law Under Article 43 of the UAE Cybercrimes Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 34 of 2021), online insults and statements that expose others to punishment or public contempt can carry criminal penalties. The penalties can include fines ranging from Dh250,000 to Dh500,000 and/or imprisonment. Depending on the circumstances, the affected party may also pursue a separate civil claim for compensation where legally recognised damage can be applied. However, a complaint does not automatically establish an offence. Criminal liability depends on the particular statements, circumstances, and applicable legal requirements. The UAE cybercrime law strictly prohibits spreading false information and imposes severe penalties. Violators may face imprisonment for at least one year and a fine of at least Dh100,000. The penalty increases to two years in jail and a minimum fine of Dh200,000 if the crime was committed during an emergency or crisis. Ms Yamalova's advice to consumers is simple: "Focus on the facts, not accusations. Criticise the product or service, not the individual. Avoid inflammatory language, personal insults and unsupported allegations. Consider whether the review aims to share a genuine experience or cause harm. "Negative reviews are a legitimate part of consumer feedback. But in the UAE, approach them thoughtfully, recognising that even an honestly held grievance does not automatically protect you from legal liability." If a consumer has a bad experience, they can exercise their rights under Consumer Protection law. This law protects consumers and gives them the right to fair treatment, accurate information, and compensation for damage caused by defective products or poor services, holding businesses accountable for their actions. Seeking compensation under this law is more effective than posting negative reviews because it provides a formal process for resolving grievances.

title: Dubai's shared housing rules will lead to better quality of life for those on low incomes, says official
body: Dubai's crackdown on overcrowded and illegally sub-let apartments will result in a better life for residents on low incomes, a senior official from the emirate's municipality has said. The Dubai Municipality's shared housing guide sets standards for building design, occupancy, health and safety, shared amenities and approved locations. It gives landlords until September 1, 2027, to comply with the new requirements across 43 designated areas of the emirate. Nasser Al Shaibani, structural control section manager at Dubai Municipality, said most tenants living in shared accommodation previously did not have any contracts "or any legal backbone to their residential status”. “With this law, tenants can have a one or two-month contract, which gives them the flexibility to change, to go and come back while having legal support," he said. “This will have a big impact on Dubai, as we'll see people moving to better housing and a better quality of life.” The new regulations address unregulated residential practices , prevent rooms from being subdivided, and protect the privacy and rights of owners and occupants. The new law requires buildings to be designated as either individual or family-shared housing. “Each building should be designated only for individuals or only for families; you cannot mix both permits within one building,” Mr Al Shaibani said. “Within this year, we are giving the building owners time to get the necessary approval from Dubai Municipality, Dubai Land Authority, Civil Defence and Rera. “During this time, Dubai Municipality will keep on monitoring those buildings. We will continue visiting and we will do the inspections. This period does not exempt them from unpermitted building modification." The municipality has received six applications for shared-housing permits so far. Three of them have been approved through the Build in Dubai platform. Apartment blocks designated for shared accommodation are close to public transport and workplaces to reduce commuter traffic and encourage people to walk or cycle. A 2025 Dubai workforce report by Edenred UAE found that 60 per cent of workers earned less than Dh5,000 ($1,361) a month, creating strong demand for affordable housing. While the new regulations aim to improve housing standards, industry operators caution that higher costs could make it harder to provide affordable accommodation for all. Rayan Hanna, founder and chief executive of Next House, an affordable housing platform in Dubai specialising in short-term rentals, backed the regulations but said the sector still faces challenges. “Although subdividing apartments into smaller rooms, commonly known as partitions, and operating shared rooms in residential units was prohibited, this type of accommodation has existed across Dubai for years,” Mr Hanna told The National . “A clearer legal framework for shared housing creates opportunities for experienced operators, property owners and institutional investors. “I also believe we will see stronger enforcement against illegally subdivided and overcrowded apartments in premium residential areas, with shared housing gradually moving towards designated locations.” Next House caters to professionals visiting Dubai who are looking for short to medium-term rental agreements. Under the new standards, shared accommodation must include kitchens, sanitary facilities and designated areas for dining, recreation, laundry and clothes drying. Bedrooms must be at least five square metres per person. There must be at least one toilet for every four occupants and one shower for every six people. Kitchen space must provide at least one square metre per person, and buildings must provide bicycle parking for at least 10 per cent of residents. Landlords found in breach of the regulations can be fined up to Dh500,000 ($136,147) for a first offence, with repeat offenders facing a maximum penalty of Dh1 million. Mr Hanna, who has amended his business model to comply with the latest rules, said affordability remained the biggest challenge for many people moving to Dubai for work. He said operators may need to generate about Dh2,000 to Dh3,000 per rentable room per month to make the model financially attractive for investors and property owners. “Many people relying on bed spaces simply cannot afford more than Dh700–Dh900 a month,” he said. “The new regulations introduce minimum space requirements, which are important improvements, but they also increase operating and development costs. “The real challenge is finding the balance between making housing safe and compliant, and making it attractive for investors. I don't think these regulations alone will solve Dubai's affordable housing problem, but they're certainly a step in the right direction.” Dubai is one of the world's fastest-growing cities , with its population of about 4.8 million forecast to increase to six million by 2040. The city's infrastructure is expanding alongside its population, with extensions to public transport networks and existing communities.

title: Michelin Guide Dubai: How come closed restaurants have been awarded stars?
body: This week on Culture Bites , Enas Refaei and Farah Andrews discuss the reaction to this year’s Michelin Guide Dubai , which was not without controversy. The annual list awards highly coveted stars to the most impressive eateries in the emirate. Two new venues have been awarded stars this year, while Orfali Bros has been promoted from one to two stars. But some have questioned how more than 10 restaurants on the list could have been recognised by Michelin, while their operations were paused. Enas and Farah talk about the challenges faced by the hospitality sector since the start of 2026 due to disruption caused by the regional conflict. They reflect on Michelin’s decision, which has given restaurateurs some grace in the face of these difficulties. The hosts also highlight some of the regional films submitted for the Best International Feature category at next year’s Oscars. Enas shares her thoughts on the Algerian horror film Roqia and Farah talks about Lebanon’s heist thriller Furies , which is inspired by the country’s banking crisis. They discuss how Arabic cinema has diversified its genres over the years, presenting submissions that range from romance and documentary to films about mental health.

title: Israel yet to allow Board of Peace first construction contract in Gaza - report
body: Israel has yet to allow the construction of a military outpost for international troops in the Gaza Strip, The Guardian reported on Wednesday, citing a source familiar with the matter.The outpost was the subject of the first construction contract issued in Gaza by US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace in August 2026. However, two months later, the source said Israel has yet to allow the project to move forward.“Israel won't open the border,” the source said, adding that contractors and trucks have been prevented from entering Gaza to begin construction.Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company, is expected to build the outpost. It will measure about 100 meters by 100 meters and will be located on a site previously used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, The Guardian reported.The base would accommodate approximately 150 international troops drawn from a larger group of 500 soldiers already deployed from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the source.Board of Peace plans can't continue without initial outpost built However, the source said the Board of Peace's larger plans cannot proceed without the initial construction project.“You can't get in without an International Stabilization Force (ISF). You can't rebuild,” the source said, as quoted by The Guardian. “There's no security. There's no deliveries of construction equipment. You can't even start putting utilities. You can't start putting in basic life-support facilities, you know, because without the ISF you can't go in.”Despite the delays, the source said the Board of Peace believes the Israeli government will allow construction to proceed after the October 27 Israeli elections.

title: Zelensky Says Starlink Was Switched Off During Russian Attacks – ‘People Are Dying Because of This Decision’
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Starlink satellite communications were intentionally restricted during massive Russian attacks on Ukraine, questioning explanations that the disruption was caused by technical problems.
Speaking in an exclusive interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said the restrictions undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones, defend its energy infrastructure and protect civilians.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The Ukrainian president said the disruption began around 1 a.m., as Russia launched another wave of missiles and drones against Ukraine.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky said when Morgan asked whether the restrictions were deliberate.
“We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added.
His remarks came as Ukrainian officials confirmed speed restrictions affecting military communications and US lawmakers from both parties condemned the disruption, warning that it could endanger Ukrainian civilians and benefit Russia.
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces immediately contacted SpaceX, American military commanders and other US partners after discovering the overnight disruptions.
American officials had attributed the intelligence-sharing problems to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the disruptions reportedly continued during subsequent attacks.
Starlink, meanwhile, plays a crucial role in Ukraine’s defense against Russian Shahed drones, including interceptor drones that use satellite communications to reach incoming targets.
“It’s not about just attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s not about attack. It’s also about defending the lives,” Zelensky told Morgan.
Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the decision as a serious mistake.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said.
He nevertheless warned of the consequences.
“People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said, cautioning that further casualties could follow if Russian attacks continued while Starlink remained restricted.
He appealed directly for the restoration of normal service.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know, but we are asking... to switch on,” he said.
The tightening of Ukraine’s satellite communications access drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, with lawmakers questioning the consequences of limiting critical defensive capabilities during active Russian attacks.
The Congressional Ukraine Caucus, whose co-chairs include Democratic Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Mike Quigley and Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson, issued a joint warning.
“We are alarmed by reports from Ukraine that US intelligence and Starlink support are being withheld, putting innocent civilians and American citizens in Ukraine at the mercy of Russian attacks,” the lawmakers said.
The caucus said Washington must continue providing intelligence to protect civilians and stressed that US allies pay for Ukraine’s Starlink access.
“Restrictions that put civilians in harm’s way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress,” the lawmakers declared.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina also publicly challenged Musk, warning that intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself could be construed as helping a mass murderer.
Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska criticized the administration’s handling of intelligence-sharing and Starlink access, arguing that reducing such support effectively aided Russia’s invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Their objections underscored concern among Ukraine’s Republican supporters that the restrictions could weaken Kyiv’s defensive capabilities at a critical moment.
Democratic lawmakers also raised questions about the humanitarian and strategic consequences of restricting systems on which Ukrainian troops and civilians depend.
Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer of Maryland issued one of the strongest statements, warning that the restrictions could leave more Ukrainian civilians exposed to Russian attacks.
In an official statement , Hoyer said that if Trump administration officials were involved, it would represent a “heinous act of betrayal” of Ukraine and a fellow democracy under attack.
He called for full Starlink access to be restored, arguing that Washington should help Ukraine win rather than tip the scales in Putin’s favor.
European allies also joined the criticism.
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski confronted Musk on X, questioning whether the billionaire was using satellite communications as a political instrument.
“Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski wrote, warning that European customers were watching.
Musk responded by distinguishing between commercial Starlink and Starshield, the military-grade satellite service.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk wrote on X.
He said decisions about operational limits were ultimately made by the US military and the president.
Musk maintained that commercial Starlink service could be used for civilian and defensive purposes but should not support offensive military operations.
A senior US official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration had not been involved in imposing the restrictions. Ukrainian officials remained suspicious that the move was connected to Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil facilities.
The conflicting accounts left unanswered who authorized the restrictions, and why they were introduced without warning.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reported Wednesday evening that Starlink connectivity was being restored at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), although restrictions on the military-grade Starshield system remained in place.
Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connectivity had improved at speeds below that threshold, but the limits continued to complicate efforts to intercept Russia’s increasingly frequent jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said the operating speed would need to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to effectively counter the faster Russian drones.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis
body:
Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.
“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”
While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans to focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.
“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”
The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.
They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.
The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.
“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and biological computing, it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

title: US soldiers must train on ‘new basics’ of unmanned systems, officials say
body: As the U.S. Army trains soldiers for multi-domain operations, like in the multinational exercise Project Flytrap , the service needs to prepare them with “new basics” to establish one standard and baseline, officials said. Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting , titled “ Project Flytrap —Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.” Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations. The most recent exercise, Project Flytrap 5.0, took place in Lithuania and was concluded earlier this year with partner nations, including the United Kingdom and Australia, and was led by the Army’s V Corps . The countries integrated and tested more than 50 industry-provided technologies, launched effects and unmanned ground vehicles and tested against a live opposing force. “The American way of war is centered on maneuver, and counter-UAS cannot remain tied to static defense,” Col. Timothy Price, commander of the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, said in a Tuesday release . “Project FlyTrap ensures we maintain mobility and offensive survivability in a highly contested, opaque operational environment.” The 2nd Cavalry Regiment is expanding Project Flytrap into a battalion-level operational capability, adapting from small-unit field trials into tactical employment connected with operational objectives aimed at breaking through drone-saturated frontlines on Europe’s Eastern Flank. “As we’re training our soldiers for the multi-domain operations, or multi-domain breeds, we talk about the new basics inside of 2CR,” Command Sgt. Maj. Jesse Clark, 2nd Cavalry Regiment senior enlisted leader, said during Monday’s discussion. “With the new basics, we need to focus on sUAS, counter-UAS, camouflage for electromagnetic signatures … and how we’re going to do that so soldiers understand how to camouflage themselves with those spectrum options,” he continued. Officials listed the previous basics to include topics such as marksmanship, map reading and navigation, radio etiquette and UAS and jamming reaction to contact. Clark said the service needs to have disciplined unit training management in which personnel, time and equipment are included to ensure soldiers are proficient at the new basics. One way to complete this is to have a series of expert badges. “Everyone needs to know these basics because it’s going to be required whether you’re on the frontline or you’re back in the rear because we’re going to have UAS all over the place,” Clark said. The U.S. military has strived to incorporate UAS and counter-UAS training across all branches, with new units in the Marine Corps and the Defense Innovation Unit aiming to recruit service members with first-person-view drone experience to participate in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program.

title: Air Force May Buy Land for 120 New Sentinel ICBM Silos
body: The Air Force may wind up buying land to build 120 new intercontinental ballistic missile silos as part of its revamped infrastructure approach for the new Sentinel ICBM. The service revealed that and other new details about its Sentinel plans as it announced the start of an environmental impact analysis meant to supplement the program’s original review, which was completed in 2023. The environmental impact statement released in March 2023 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Air Force’s effort to replace the aging Minuteman III with the Sentinel across three bases in the western U.S.: F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo.; Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.; and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. But much has changed since that EIS—in early 2024, critical cost and schedule overruns for Sentinel triggered a notice to Congress and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act . The program’s issues are not caused by the missile, but rather by the massive infrastructure and civil engineering work needed to build the systems it requires, officials say. The Air Force had hoped to reuse much of the infrastructure that supported Minuteman, but analysis showed much of it was too old or too expensive to upgrade. Eventually, Pentagon leaders certified the Sentinel program to continue. But in an effort to control costs, Air Force officials decided in spring 2025 it would be more effective to build entirely new silos instead of reusing the old ones. There are 450 active Minuteman silos, which the Air Force plans to replace on a one-for-one basis. At the time, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new silos would be “predominantly Air Force-owned real estate, which means reusing the existing missile sites but not the 55-year-old silos.” A new website associated with the supplemental environmental impact analysis, launched Oct. 9, states that just over a quarter of the sites could be on land not currently owned by the Air Force, with the service considering: Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around F.E. Warren Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around Malmstrom Acquisition of land and construction of up to 60 new launch silo sites around Minot Additionally, the service said it is evaluating old sites at Malmstrom formerly operated by the 564th Missile Squadron, now inactive, to reuse for up to 60 new launch silo sites. The Air Force is planning to buy up to 12 acres per silo, according to the supplemental EIS website. Launch Centers Silos aren’t the only ICBM infrastructure getting a refresh in the Air Force’s latest plan for Sentinel. Currently there are 45 missile alert facilities across the three bases where Airmen stay on watch 24/7. The original plan for Sentinel called for building new “launch centers” to command and control the ICBMs at 24 of those facilities and razing the rest. The new EIS website states that the Air Force will reutilize Missile Alert Facility sites for Launch Centers “where feasible,” but at Minot specifically, officials are considering “construction of new launch center sites in previously undeveloped areas,” the website states. Each Launch Center would have a footprint of up to 16 acres. Another new consideration is the construction of a “purpose-built Operations Group Facility” at Malmstrom. Timeline Now that the Air Force has announced its plans to craft a supplemental EIS, there is a 30-day public “scoping” period where federal, state, and local agencies, interested organizations, and members of the public can all provide comments on the proposed actions. After that, the service will release a draft of its supplemental EIS, and there will be another window for public comments. The Air Force plans to release its draft by fall 2027. A final supplemental EIS is scheduled for release in spring 2028, after which the Secretary of the Air Force can sign a Record of Decision, clearing the way for the acquisition of land and construction. After that, it will be several more years before Sentinel is in the ground—the current Air Force estimate is for the new missile to reach initial operational capability by the early 2030s. For now, though, the Air Force and contractor Northrop Grumman are already building a prototype silo for Sentinel at Northrop’s Promontory, Utah, facilities. The post Air Force May Buy Land for 120 New Sentinel ICBM Silos appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole, and army needs $45 billion more on top
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is seeking fresh funding for 2027 and says it is ready to deliver the reforms . Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi says Ukraine’s external budget financing need for 2027 exceeds $52 billion, with more than $32.6 billion still to be raised. That money underwrites the basics of a country at war: the army, pensions, hospitals, and support for business, he notes. Defense and security alone will take almost 44 percent of GDP in the 2027 budget, and the gap comes as Russia keeps hammering the infrastructure that generates Ukraine’s own revenue. “The defense capability of the country, the payment of pensions, the support of hospitals and business depend on these funds,” Koretskyi says. The hole Russia keeps digging faster than Kyiv can fill it Russia’s strikes widen the gap even as Kyiv tries to close it. Russia systematically attacks critical infrastructure, business, production and civilian sites, and the destruction and halted enterprises will leave tax revenues about $1.5 billion below forecast by the end of the year, he warns. For instance, output of Ukraine's steel industry, one of the pillars of its wartime economy, fell 57.3% in August due to Russian strikes. This sector is Ukraine's second-largest foreign-currency earner, employing more than 70,000 people directly and another 250,000 in related industries, and paying close to $1 billion a year in taxes. Beyond the budget itself, the off-budget needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces for 2027 are estimated at $45 billion, or about 40 billion euros, a figure that sits on top of the $52 billion budget requirement, he says. The reforms Kyiv must deliver to unlock the money The money hinges on reforms Ukraine still has to deliver. In the next few days, the government is to approve all the decisions needed to continue financing. “Ukraine continues to work on fulfilling its part of the commitments. This week, the government is expected to approve all the necessary decisions to ensure continued funding,” the Ukrainian prime minister says. Meanwhile, the Parliament plans to consider the bills required under the support programs of the IMF, the World Bank and the EU. title: To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is handing its factories the right to shoot back at the Russian drones hunting them. Nearly 100 companies have joined Ukraine’s experimental program that allows private enterprises to operate their own air defenses, granting them authority to conduct air defense operations and form their own crews, the Defense Ministry says . Russian drones strike Ukrainian factories, warehouses and power sites so relentlessly that the state cannot shield every one, so the Defense Ministry is enlisting the businesses being hit to defend themselves. The program has grown quickly, from 24 companies in April to 81 by mid-September and nearly 100 now, and its crews have already destroyed a substantial number of Russian aerial targets. The companies range from operators of critical infrastructure to state and private firms across the economy. The project is carried out under a Cabinet resolution dated 19 November 2025, which mobilizes enterprise resources to support Ukraine’s defense against air threats. Civilian crews that answer to the Air Force, not themselves These teams do not fire into a shared sky on their own. About 50 air-defense groups have been formed and are operating under the relevant Air Force commands, and crews from six enterprises are already carrying out combat missions, the ministry says. The rest are training or finishing preparation before they join. As of 14 October, the groups have downed more than 60 aerial targets, mostly Russian drones, using interceptor drones and automated turrets with heavy machine guns, according to the ministry. The Air Force command sets each group’s targets based on its weapons and tasks, and, jointly with the company, defines its sector, personnel, and equipment. Who pays, and who pulls the trigger The arrangement splits cost and control. Some weapons the enterprises buy with their own money, holding end-user status, while a company can also ask the Air Force to lend arms and ammunition from military stocks. Private air defense is one layer of a multi-tiered shield, meant to protect industrial capacity, critical infrastructure and civilian staff from systematic drone attacks. The crews began combat work in 2026. title: Gudea leverages AI to help organizations prevent social media crises before they erupt
body:
Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post — whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor — can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy.
Gudea , a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” is using AI to help organizations spot trouble brewing online before it turns into a crisis.
Unlike traditional social listening platforms, which only track metrics such as mentions, hashtags, and impressions, Gudea aims to show organizations who is driving a conversation, how information is moving, how quickly a story is gaining traction, and where it could be headed. Rather than simply tallying posts, its AI analyzes behavior, relationships, and the pathways through which information travels across more than 500 mainstream and fringe websites and platforms, including X, Reddit, and TikTok.
Instead of simply telling a company that mentions are rising, Gudea aims to provide the context behind that growth so decision-makers can determine how and whether to respond.
Gudea pitched its mission Wednesday afternoon on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , where the company made the case that companies need to take a more proactive approach to protecting their reputations.
“These big industries don’t understand that there are things they can do proactively to defend their reputation and their brand,” CEO and founder Keith Presley said. “A lot of the chief communications officers and chief media or marketing officers, they’re using legacy tools to try to figure out what’s happening. Those tools were only ever designed to tell you the number of hashtags or number of impressions.”
Gudea was founded in 2023 by Presley, Jonathan Sperber, and James Thomin. Presley brings more than 15 years of experience spanning political campaigns and defense, including building the infrastructure for Andrew Yang’s presidential campaign. Sperber, the company’s chief strategy officer, has a background in disinformation research. Thomin, Gudea’s CTO, holds a PhD in chemical engineering and has spent roughly two decades working in AI and machine learning.
Presley called the company’s path to becoming a startup unusual.
“We’re one of those weird startups where I never wanted to do a company,” he said.
The team began with the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit established after the 2020 election. The organization adapted strategies and tactics that the intelligence community has used overseas to disrupt online networks tied to groups such as Al Qaeda and ISIS. It applied them to domestic information campaigns.
The goal was to identify the online environments where information campaigns were taking shape and disrupt the pathways that allowed those narratives to reach wider audiences.
However, the team found that existing tools didn’t show how information was actually moving across people, groups, and platforms. That gap became the opening for Gudea.
Three years after its founding, Gudea has nearly 40 clients. According to Presley, its customer base includes a Fortune 50 telecommunications company, a Fortune 50 retailer, “one of the world’s largest AI labs, one of the world’s largest bands,” public relations and crisis communications agencies, and government agencies.
With the rise of generative AI, Presley believes that the need for Gudea’s technology has only grown, as the company looks to expand its customer base.
AI tools have dramatically lowered the cost and effort required to generate content and coordinate online campaigns. What once required a larger organization can increasingly be carried out by a single person with a laptop and access to the right software.
“When we first started in 2021, and then as a company in 2023, we maybe saw one out of four things we looked at have inauthentic activity around it,” Presley said. “Now it’s probably nine out of 10 things that we look at have this inauthentic activity.”
Looking further ahead, Gudea plans to expand its ability to understand where narratives originate and how they spread. One major upcoming initiative is geolocation for narratives. Slated for next year, the technology is intended to allow users to identify where conversations are happening with far greater precision, down to the city-block level, Presley explains.
The company also wants to give customers greater access to the tools behind its analysis. For example, a company could eventually run an advertising campaign through Gudea’s AI model before launching it and get a better idea of whether the strategy is likely to produce a negative outcome or not.
Last week, Gudea announced that it had raised $7 million in seed funding in a round co-led by Mudita Venture Partners and Silicon Road Ventures. The investment brings the startup’s total funding to approximately $15 million.

title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
body:
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B .
LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.
The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.
Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.
Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.
Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.
During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.
This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.
We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.
The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:
All runs were collected on Pipette , the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.
Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.
GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.
We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.
The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.
Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face .
For API inference, you can also sign up for Liquid Console where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.

title: Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies, whose independence EU made condition for membership, have clawed back $5.1 million for state budget
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies just clawed back millions for the state budget. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) and the State Property Fund have returned about $5.1 million to the state budget, the bureau says . NABU and SAPO were created in 2015 after the Euromaidan revolution as independent bodies to fight high-level corruption, and their independence is a core condition for Ukraine's path to the EU. This recovery is the kind of concrete payoff that EU-backed reform was meant to produce. Investigating one case, detectives and prosecutors found that the leadership of a regional branch of the State Property Fund had failed to act. Because of that inaction, the state risked losing millions of dollars. To head off the loss, NABU and SAPO alerted the fund’s central leadership and gave it access to part of the investigation materials. How the agencies turned a case into cash The fix came from sharing what the investigation had uncovered. After working through the data, the State Property Fund took the necessary steps and secured the full budget amount, the bureau says. NABU and SAPO continue to cooperate with other state bodies to protect the country’s economic interests and prevent corruption crimes, the bureau adds. The agencies framed the case as proof that enforcement, beyond investigation alone, can return money the state would otherwise lose. Why these agencies matter beyond one case The recovery lands at a fraught moment for the two institutions. Their independence has been under sustained pressure, and in July 2026 parliament briefly stripped it before mass protests and EU warnings forced a reversal. In 2025, Brussels tied as much as 50 billion euros in aid and the pace of accession talks to the agencies’ autonomy, treating NABU and SAPO as pillars of the rule-of-law reforms Ukraine promised on its way into the bloc. title: Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers
body: Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly. How does OmniParseBench scoring work? The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families: present: a text, number or equation appears (text) order: text A comes before text B (text) repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text) table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables) layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout) Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review. #mtp-opb-embed-wrap{max-width:880px!important;margin:24px auto!important;background:transparent!important;border:0!important;padding:0!important} #mtp-opb-embed-wrap iframe{width:100%!important;border:0!important;display:block!important;background:transparent!important} #mtp-opb-embed-wrap hr,#mtp-opb-embed-wrap p:empty,#mtp-opb-embed-wrap del,#mtp-opb-embed-wrap s{display:none!important} @media (max-width:640px){#mtp-opb-embed-wrap{margin:16px auto!important}} (function(){var f=document.getElementById('mtp-opb-embed');window.addEventListener('message',function(e){if(e.data&&e.data.type==='opb-embed-height'&&f&&e.source===f.contentWindow){f.style.height=e.data.h+'px'}});})(); What are the OmniParseBench launch results? Parser Headline Text Tables Layout Gemini 3.8 Flash* 92.9 91.3 95.2 92.2 Datalab accurate 92.7 90.8 91.8 95.6 Datalab balanced 91.6 90.0 89.2 95.5 Reducto 90.8 85.4 91.2 95.8 LlamaParse 90.4 88.2 92.6 90.4 Mistral OCR 89.5 82.8 91.9 93.8 Claude Sonnet 5.5* 88.7 93.1 95.4 77.5 GPT-5.6 Sol 87.8 85.4 91.6 86.5 Extend 83.3 64.1 92.5 93.4 Azure 83.0 74.6 81.7 92.8 Tesseract none 17.6 0.0 unsupported *Used in creating and verifying at least some tests, per Datalab . Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time. Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It flags the two models that helped build tests, and it tells readers to weigh the fact that it sells a parser. It commits to reporting OmniParseBench scores for future releases. Its advice: the best benchmark is your own documents. How do you run OmniParseBench? Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser uv pip install omni-parse-bench # score(): no network, no API keys uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[harness]' # + vendor adapters, to predict uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[benchmark]' # + dataset access, to run the benchmark opb benchmark --out runs/ --limit 5 --providers datalab openai/gpt-5.6-sol Vendors need keys such as DATALAB_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The CLI shows its plan and asks before calling any vendor. Runs are resumable. The query guide shows how to compare runs by tag, suite or test type. OmniParseBench vs olmOCR-bench vs ParseBench vs OmniDocBench Feature OmniParseBench olmOCR-bench ParseBench OmniDocBench Maintainer Datalab Ai2 LlamaIndex OpenDataLab Scale 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 docs 7,010 tests, 1,403 PDFs 169,011 rules, 2,078 pages, 1,211 docs 1,651 PDF pages Languages 92 English Not disclosed 5 language types Scoring unit Pass/fail test; headline = mean of 3 families Pass/fail unit tests 5 dimensions, each with its own metric Overall from text edit distance, table TEDS, formula CDM Model judge None Not used for scoring None by default (opt-in for charts) Not used for scoring Content tags Per arg: structure, rendering, role, script, language 7 source categories 5 capability dimensions Page, text and table attributes Per-test provenance Yes, derivation on every test Extraction method per category Human-verified pages Not per test Latency and cost Median s/page, $ per 1,000 pages Not in dataset card ¢ per page on leaderboard Not disclosed License Code Apache 2.0; tests CC BY 4.0 with exceptions; page data licensed per source Dataset ODC-BY 1.0 Apache 2.0 Code Apache 2.0; data research only Key Takeaways 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages in 92 languages. Headline = mean of text, tables and layout pass rates. Tags slice results; they never change a verdict. Datalab built it and ranks second: Gemini 3.8 Flash 92.9*, Datalab accurate 92.7. Apache 2.0 code; scoring runs offline without API keys. * used in building some tests Check out the blog post , dataset and GitHub repo . Thanks to the Datalab team for the resources behind this article. Datalab supported and sponsored this content. title: Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian reinforcements are surging toward Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast The Russians have a plan: take Dobropillia and close the southern jaw of a pincer around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk Ukrainian forces aren't powerless to resist, but many of their own best troops are busy attacking elsewhere The Russians are pouring troops into a key sector just southeast of the town of Dobropillia in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, threatening to overwhelm Ukrainian defenses and march one settlement closer to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the last two big free cities in Donetsk. But the Russians' push toward Dobropillia isn't without cost. Russian losses in this sector are "colossal," according to the mapper Playfra . And every soldier the Kremlin deploys along the Dobropillia axis is a soldier it can't deploy elsewhere. And that may help explain why the Russians are falling back in two other key sectors, in northern Donetsk Oblast and in neighboring Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. The Dobropillia axis is the Russians' clear priority. For the Ukrainians, that's an opportunity to attack elsewhere. Dobropillia ORBAT - Summer 2026 Similar to last year, Russia has significantly reinforced the Dobropillia direction, seeking to capture the town itself while simultaneously developing the southeastern approach toward Druzhkivka and Kramatorsk. To that end, the “Center”… pic.twitter.com/pDhRRlfbGW — Unit Observer (@WarUnitObserver) September 10, 2026 Dobropillia, a former mining town with a pre-war population of around 28,000, is now a fortress. It anchors Ukrainian positions along the highway that threads northeast to Kramatorsk. Russia has attacked here before. In August 2025, Russian troops pushed a salient toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk highway, and Ukrainian counterattacks cut it apart. By October that year, President Volodymyr Zelensky put Russian losses on the Dobropillia front at about 13,000. Ukrainian military analyst Kostiantyn Mashovets describes the push on Dobropillia as the southern flank of a Russian operation to envelop the whole Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area. The other approaches are harder going. From the southeast, the Russians are blocked by stubborn Ukrainian forces still clinging to positions in the ruins of Kostiantynivka. From the north, starting this spring, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps rolled back 18 months of Russian gains. For an army that's been struggling to complete its conquest of Donetsk, to say nothing of breaking through in other front-line oblasts, Dobropillia has become the priority. And that's why the Russians are channeling fresh forces into the Dobropillia sector. Part of the 41st Combined Arms Army and units of its 90th Guards Tank Division are now fighting there, Mashovets wrote on 9 October, and the Russian command keeps feeding fresh assault infantry into the sector through the village of Nove Shakhove despite heavy losses. The open-source account Unit Observer tracked the buildup as early as September. Potentially tens of thousands of troops from those formations join the main forces of the 2nd and 51st Combined Arms Armies, according to Mashovets, as well as elements of the Russian naval infantry, facing the Ukrainian 1st Azov Corps and 19th Army Corps around Dobropillia. The reinforcements give Russian commanders more options. Mashovets expects the 51st CAA to push south and southwest of Dobropillia and the 2nd CAA toward Raksha and Sviatohorivka, enveloping the town and cutting its supply routes from Bilozerske before any direct assault. The neighboring 8th CAA is fighting around Kostiantynivka. The Russians' immediate goal is "to maintain this offensive pressure from summer into the fall," Unit Observer wrote, setting conditions for a possible siege of Kramatorsk next year. The outlook for the Ukrainian defenders of Dobropillia is "worsening," Playfra warned on 13 October: The Russians have a seemingly infinite manpower pool here and a clear numerical advantage, which allows them to significantly increase the flow of infiltrators and, as such, the chance of some passing through Ukrainian defenses. This leads to especially deep Russian infiltrations, which in turn slowly but surely destabilize the situation for the Ukrainians, which are progressively forced to abandon their most advanced positions. The Ukrainians aren't without options, Playfra explained. They should double down on their current strategy of saturating the fields around Dobropillia with drones in a ring at least 2 to 3 km deep, forestalling large-scale Russian movements until the winter strips the leaves off the trees, depriving the Russians of their best cover from overhead surveillance. This could buy Dobropillia "much more time," Playfra predicted. Mashovets puts a date on how long Dobropillia has to hold. If it and Druzhkivka, the town just south of Kramatorsk, hold until mid-to-late December, he wrote, the whole Russian plan for Sloviansk and Kramatorsk would collapse and have to be rewritten almost from scratch. ISW’s map of the Dobropillia area on 22 September 2026 shows Russian-controlled and infiltration areas near the city. Source: Institute for the Study of War. Help isn't coming Just don't expect a lot of Ukrainian reinforcements along the Dobropillia axis. Many of Ukraine's best troops are busy attacking. Taking advantage of the surge of Russian manpower in the direction of Dobropillia, Ukrainian forces have counterattacked where the Russians are weakest: in northern Donetsk Oblast and also in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, just south of Donetsk. Map: Euromaidan Press In months of carefully planned assaults supported by ground robots and intensive drone strikes, Ukrainian forces have liberated hundreds of square kilometers in northern Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk. The Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk largely removed the immediate northern threat to Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk. But it didn't do anything to help in the direction of Dobropillia, where the Russians have many more troops, much more firepower, and—equally importantly—a singular focus: closing the southern jaw around the last big free cities in Donetsk. Explore further Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.

title: UNMISS hands over youth empowerment hub in Yambio
body: Western Equatoria State Caretaker Governor Badagbu Daniel Rimbasa and Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), on Wednesday handed over a newly built youth empowerment hub in Yambio. The facility was constructed under the UNMISS Quick Impact Project (QIP) and implemented by LIFT South Sudan to promote youth leadership, skills development and peacebuilding. Speaking at the handover ceremony, Rimbasa said the hub would give young people a space to exchange ideas, develop leadership skills and discuss challenges affecting their communities. He urged young people to use the facility to promote peace, discourage harmful activities and contribute to community development. Gbeho called on young people to take ownership of the centre and use it to develop solutions to problems facing their communities. “Our responsibility as the older generation is to empower them and invest in them. But the actual change has to come from them,” Gbeho said. She said the hub should enable young people to collaborate, exchange ideas and develop initiatives aimed at bringing positive change to their communities. Joseph Ndani, executive director of LIFT South Sudan, commended UNMISS for supporting the project and the state government for creating an enabling environment for youth-focused initiatives. He called for additional support to establish more youth centres and recreational facilities across Western Equatoria State. The hub is expected to provide a venue for youth groups to hold discussions, share knowledge, strengthen leadership skills and develop peacebuilding initiatives. Its long-term impact will depend on sustained use, maintenance and engagement by young people and their partners. title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1694: Starlink cap cripples Ukrainian drone missions as Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, ordered the cut
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US . In three days, Washington sanctioned the court that issued Putin’s arrest warrant, lifted its own sanctions on Russian diesel, called for Zelenskyy to step down, and declared an “energy ceasefire” that asks only Ukraine to stop firing. These are not the acts of an ally. Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won. . Five months in, it has erased 18 months of Russian advances toward Sloviansk. Military Ukraine blocks Russia from outflanking its fortress cities in Donbas, retaking 277 square kilometers and hitting 8,000 Russian troops . “Four seasons of ‘Vivaldi’ are complete. But the music continues. Until we meet again!” the Third Army Corps noted. Intelligence and technology “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine . The ordinary Starlink on drones is capped at about 160 km/h, too slow for some missions, so faster flight needs the military StarShield version. “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones . Ukraine’s air defense leans on Musk’s Starlink. “Trump was looking for any opportunity to undermine our defense capabilities,” top Ukrainian volunteer, who supplied 291,502 FPV drones to front, says of sudden Starlink limit . Ukraine had stopped hitting Russian oil refineries as Trump asked, yet the Starlink limit still landed. NATO country that pays for Kyiv’s Starlink warns Musk as his cap breaks Ukraine’s drone missions: “As your European customers, we are watching you” . “Are you playing politics with your products again?”, Poland’s foreign minister challenges Musk Planned capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, under 100 seconds to target: US firm pitches a low-cost drone killer . The fastest model cruises at 540 km/h, which may be enough to catch Russia’s jet Gerans, a defense news outlet suggests.. Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army . Drone types, areas, time windows: the model was tested on real data. A second tool ranks artillery plans and is now in trials. New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation” . SpaceX may have imposed the restrictions at the Trump administration’s request, activist Serhii Sternenko suggested. Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving . Eight launcher spots, 32 drone-prep pads, and a layout the channel likens to Tsymbulova, a Russian drone base Ukraine keeps striking. Ukraine sent a spiked tank and a Bradley into Russian drone fire. The spikes held, and Ukraine’s own drones got them home . Armored vehicles aren't dead on arrival anymore on the drone-patrolled battlefield. Friendly drones can escort them to the fight. International “He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow . Trump is using aid and intelligence as levers over Kyiv. “It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared . Viktor Yushchenko invokes the Budapest Memorandum and Pearl Harbor days after the US waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. Humanitarian and social impact Russia attacked Ukrainian retailer Epicentr’s warehouse 10 times in one day, destroying about 85% of goods, company says . The Khmelnytskyi hub had been effectively Epicentr’s only surviving large warehouse complex, after Russia destroyed its two largest logistics complexes in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast. 1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says . Kyiv emergency medical teams have responded to 1,920 calls related to Russian attacks since the start of the year, according to the city’s health department head. Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities . Even border and frontline oblasts are further along on resilience plans than the capital, Zelenskyy says. Russia bombs Sloviansk’s warming center as the day’s attacks wound four Red Cross workers . The 250-kg bomb injured eight people and damaged five apartment blocks, and the wounded workers belonged to a Red Cross branch that had relocated from Lyman for safety Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid . Zelenskyy says Russia has never shown America such disrespect. At least 600,000 people lost power, and four died in Kyiv. New developments Russia-linked bot networks kept their weekly rhythm after drone strikes on three Yandex data centers—disinformation monitor LetsData . One network that spread fake Die Welt sites now pushes a fake Ukrinform site about mobilization in Ukraine, its analysts found. Read our earlier daily review here.

title: RNZAF NH90 helicopter crew find missing teenager
body:
