Crew on a Royal New Zealand Air Force NH90 helicopter say it was a great result after finding a missing teenager in the Ruahine Forest Park yesterday and flying him to safety.
The crew from No. 3 Squadron had been in the area conducting mountain flying training when they were re-tasked to respond to the search and rescue operation for the student. The teenager had become separated from his group, prompting a search by New Zealand Police and Land Search and Rescue volunteers.
The NH90 Helicopter crew began their aerial search in the vicinity of Sunrise Hut. They searched tracks in that area along with Top Maropea Hut before conducting aerial searches along the Waipawa River Valley which is where they found the teenager.
They winched the student into the helicopter and flew him to safety, where he was met by Police and re-united with family.
The crew also then extracted ground search volunteers who had spent a long night searching for the teenager after he was reported missing on Tuesday.

title: Sudanese army announces capture of strategic area in West Darfur
body: The Sudanese army has captured the Bir Kelekel area in West Darfur following clashes with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the state’s governor said on Wednesday, in an advance in a region largely controlled by the RSF. West Darfur Governor Bahr al-Din Adam Karama said the army and allied forces had made “significant progress” in Bir Kelekel, in the eastern part of Jebel Moon district. Karama described the area as strategically important because of its proximity to Jebel Moon. He said military operations along the West Darfur front are continuing. Military officers also posted videos on social media announcing that government forces had taken control of the area. The RSF could not immediately be reached for comment. On Oct. 5, the Joint Force of armed groups allied with the army said its forces, alongside army troops, had captured Bir Saliba in West Darfur after fighting with the RSF. The gains come as Sudan remains divided between rival forces. The army controls most of the north, east and centre of the country, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF holds most of Darfur and parts of Kordofan. Front lines remain contested in several areas. Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the army and the RSF following a dispute over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, triggering one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. title: DA looking to interview 2 witnesses in backseat of ICE vehicle in Houston incident
body:
The unidentified persons were picked up before the incident, the DA said.
Two people were allegedly in the back seat of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle when an agent struck a man during a pursuit in Texas on Saturday and are now sought for questioning by local investigators, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said.
DA Sean Teare told ABC News Wednesday that his office identified the two ICE detainees who were in the vehicle when the unidentified agent struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez at a strip mall outside Houston.
"We were not able to interview them at the scene," Teare told ABC News, adding that federal agents had already moved the two persons away to a detention facility.
The DA said his office alleged that ICE had picked up the two people before the incident with Parra-Hernandez earlier in the day.
Teare said he reached out to the federal government to let them know the two men, who are still in a detention center, are material witnesses in their investigation into the incident.
ICE said in a statement that an agent was pursuing Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national who they allege had a criminal record and a final order of removal by a judge, and observed him get in a vehicle with Parra Saturday morning.
The ICE agent attempted a car stop, and Mendoza-Cervantes and Parra-Hernandez, who the agency alleged is also undocumented, fled their vehicle on foot, according to ICE and the Harris County Sheriff's Office.
Surveillance video of the incident reviewed by ABC News appears to show the ICE vehicle moving in the direction of the man running and striking him.
An ICE spokesperson alleged in a statement that Parra "ran in front of an ICE vehicle" when he was hit.
"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct," the spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.
ICE did not comment on Teare's claims that there were two men in the back seat of the vehicle during the incident. Mendoza-Cervantes remains at large as of Wednesday afternoon, according to ICE.
The DA said his office interviewed Parra on Tuesday in the hospital, where he is in stable condition. The DA said he has not been charged with a crime.
The DA said he is also collecting more evidence from the incident and could possibly issue charges against the ICE agent for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Teare said his office will attempt to interview the ICE agent.
"Context is important. We want to see what led up to the confrontation," the DA said.
ABC News' Luke Barr contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine Has Imposed a Kerosene Shortage on Russia
body:
Drained dry: Cars queue at a Rosneft gas station after Ukrainian drone strikes cause fuel shortages across Russia. Image: SOPA Images Limited / Alamy Stock
Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries have caused a Russian kerosene shortage, disrupting flights, draining the budget and pushing Central Asian partners towards other suppliers.
As Russia is gripped for the second year by queues at petrol stations, more than a third of its international airports face fuel supply issues and light aircraft are forced to use car gasoline. Moreover, it is causing past alliances in Central Asia to fracture, as long-term partners who depended on Russian fuel are forced to seek expensive and dangerous alternatives to keep their airlines in the air. Though the Kremlin has sought to dismiss this as a nuisance, the data shows it to be anything but, and refining output has dropped significantly. Revenue streams have been eaten into and long-term costs and damage have been incurred.
Prior to 2025, Russia was one of the world's largest fuel producers. The figures for 2023 and 2024 attest to that : 88 million and 81.6 million tonnes of diesel respectively, and 43.8 and 41.1 million tonnes of gasoline production. Unlike gasoline and diesel, aviation kerosene production rose by 7.3% in 2024 to 11.6 million tonnes, a sufficient amount to cover both domestic needs and export demands. Export volumes have been classified , but are estimated at 500,000â600,000 tonnes, mainly to Kazakhstan to cover its domestic shortage. When it comes to gasoline, the surplus is much more modest, with the country consuming 90% of production , while for diesel, the country was the second-largest exporter, with domestic consumption estimated at close to half of output and exports at 35â40 million tonnes.
These surpluses were crucial for Central Asia. Putin's Russia inherited the Soviet Union's role as guarantor of social stability in the region through subsidised fuel exports. Mongolia , Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan were over 90% dependent on Russian fuel . To a lesser degree, so were Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan . Domestically, Russia also runs a subsidy mechanism known as the âdempferâ, under which the government pays refineries a subsidy, calculated from prices on the St Petersburg Commodities Exchange, to keep gasoline and diesel prices lower for the public. Airlines receive a different subsidy: they are compensated for 65% of the difference between a fixed kerosene price (â½67,300 per tonne in 2026) and the export price, which serves as the market benchmark.
The fuel issues in 2025 started at the edge of the Russian fuel supply network: in remote parts of Khabarovsk Krai , Vladivostok and Crimea . This is typical of a production shortfall, where the far ends of the distribution network run dry first. Part of the problem was that Russia kept low stocks of gasoline and in early 2025 gasoline exports jumped 25% year-over-year , making the country more vulnerable to shortages. By 28 July, Ukrainian drone strikes had forced so many refineries into repairs that the country banned gasoline exports . Estimates at the time were that 10 major refineries had been damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. Later, even diesel exports had to be partially restricted at the end of September. Companies with their own refineries could still export, but the ban for the rest of the market is in place to this day. Even with these restrictions, the Russian fuel market did not stabilise until November and December. The ban on gasoline was only partially lifted on 1 February 2026, at the urging of Russian refiners, who wanted to increase their export profits. Notably, despite all this, aviation kerosene faced no export bans during this period and was not an issue for Russian airlines.
By mid-2026, the shortages caused by Ukrainian drone attacks had spread from Crimea to almost the whole of Russia. From 18 May to 12 July , all but two of Russia's 83 federal subjects saw local news reports of petrol stations running out of some type of fuel. The full gasoline export ban , covering both refiners and traders and introduced earlier on 2 April, did little to stem the tide. By 30 July, the gasoline export ban had been extended to 31 January 2027, signalling the Kremlin's lack of confidence that repairs would be completed by year-end. A ban on diesel exports by refineries was also introduced on the same day, and that measure has been extended month by month since. Based on the ban on diesel exports, and given that Russia consumes only half the diesel it produces, it can be assumed that refining capacity has been degraded by 30â50% through a combination of Ukrainian strikes and necessary maintenance.

By 12 August, Kommersant, citing industry sources , estimated that refining volumes could fall to 3.8â4.1 million barrels per day from 5â5.5 million barrels per day in summer 2024â25; as mentioned earlier, 2024 was already a lower-production year than 2023, and 2025 saw mass shortages. Apart from the massive queues, there were concerns that diesel deliveries to farmers would be disrupted, with reports from Krasnodar Krai suggesting only 50â60% of the fuel needed reached farmers in July. By now the measures have become so drastic that Russia has allowed the production of fuel as low-grade as Euro-2, and such fuel has already been spotted at petrol stations in Russia's regions.
The Russian kerosene market is faring no better. A full ban on the export of kerosene was introduced on 1 June 2026, as domestic prices reached â½110,000 per tonne and export quotes exceeded â½140,000 per tonne. By then, kerosene had not been traded on the St Petersburg Commodities Exchange for more than half a month. The last traded price was listed as â½82,700 per tonne. Moreover, airline sources contacted by Kommersant reported kerosene shortages in the last week of May at the airports in St Petersburg, Yekaterinburg, Ufa and others, with the Ministry of Transport having to manually direct supplies. The kerosene dempfer payment jumped from â½1,770 per tonne in February to â½52,090 in March, easing slightly to â½47,830 in April, at a cost to the Russian budget of â½24 billion in April alone. At time of writing there are standing NOTAMs (notices to airmen) warning about refuelling issues at 32 of Russia's 227 airports and civilian airstrips, and at times the number has been higher. The picture is worse for international airports alone: 11 of Russia's 27 international airports have NOTAMs issued over fuel availability. Russian airlines operating out of the southern parts of the country raised the alarm in late June that they were adjusting their schedules due to fuel shortages; by then, aviation fuel at Makhachkala had reached â½157,000 per tonne excluding VAT, a 64% increase in June alone, and airlines like Azimut were cutting flights. As the government increasingly redirected volumes manually and imposed price controls, trading volumes on the St Petersburg Commodities Exchange fell so sharply that the exchange began cutting staff by mid-July 2026.
Get a weekly round-up of the latest commentary and research straight into your inbox.
The Russian kerosene shortage has also claimed victims in Central Asia, which, as established above, depends on cheap Russian fuel. Kazakhstan, which largely covers its domestic fuel needs from its own refineries, was still waiting on kerosene deliveries from Russia . Of the 300,000 tonnes it contracts annually, it had received only 186,000 tonnes in 2026 by the time Russia imposed its full export ban. Tajikistan was forced to turn to Iran , requesting, among other things, 100,000 tonnes of aviation kerosene. Mongolia, which is also deeply dependent on Russian fuel and needs aviation kerosene for its tourism industry, was forced to ask China for 3,000 tonnes. Tajikistan saw prices for fuels go up by 30% by September, threatening an inflation spike, and official sources in Kyrgyzstan said gasoline prices were up 24% and diesel 30%. In Mongolia, protests by drivers started in the capital against the fuel shortage . Within Russia, the shortage went beyond rationing: light aircraft such as the An-2 were forced to switch to lower-quality automotive gasoline.
Ukraineâs drone campaign has done real and long-lasting damage to Russian refining capacity, finances and political influence. Expanding Russian secrecy as Ukrainian strikes on refineries intensified conceals just how deeply the shortage is affecting civilian and military operations. More data is being classified as a state secret and sources face ever harsher penalties for disclosing the real extent of the damage.
In parallel, subsidies are seriously hurting Russiaâs federal budget. Despite high oil prices, the revenues from oil and gas in September 2026 were among the lowest in the last few years and the highest since April 2022, as they were offset by the record â½306 billion in subsidies paid to refineries and airlines. To offset these losses of revenue, the Russian state is forced to borrow money on the domestic market at astronomical yields of 16.63% per year. There have already been cases of planes forced to land due to a shortage of fuel because they could not make it to the designated reserve airstrip during a drone attack. Fuel is being rationed.
For Russia, a core concern will be that traditional Central Asian allies are actively looking for alternatives for fuel deliveries even if at present such options are limited with China reducing its exports. Russiaâs previous power dynamic with these states is changing rapidly. Recovery of the lost capacity will also be neither cheap nor quick. Russiaâs own governors have said it may take up to six months for some refineries to recover. The symbol of the Russian free-trading fuel market, the St Petersburg Commodities Exchange, is now a shadow of its former self as the state manually redirects fuel in trucks and trains, finding its free-trade principles a hurdle to its plans.

Consulting firm McKinsey & Company is going to ask some entry-level candidates to have a 10-minute conversation with an AI simulation of a client as part of the interview process, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The AI simulation “aims to reflect 80% of the scenarios McKinsey consultants might encounter in their day-to-day work,” the WSJ says, and it isn’t designed to “mimic an unhinged client.” The AI won’t score the candidates — humans will be in the room to assess the candidates and see how well they deal with the simulated situations.
The McKinsey tool will be in testing for undergrads seeking business-analyst jobs in “some” offices in North America this fall, and the WSJ says “hundreds” may use it.
Other companies are also building tools to use AI avatars as part of the job interview process, and my colleague Hayden Field tried some of them out for a video we published in March .

title: Fish Audio Releases Drama 3, a 35B Open-Weight MoE Text-to-Speech Model
body:
This week, Fish Audio released Fish Audio Drama 3 . Drama 3 is a text-to-speech model from Fish Audio that takes plain-language acting direction. It is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B parameters active per token. The weights are on Hugging Face , and the model is also live in the Fish Audio API . For developers, it is a self-hostable option for scripted dialogue, audiobooks and dubbing. TL;DR Size: 35B total parameters, about 3B active per token (8 of 256 experts plus 1 shared). Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU with at least 48 GB in FP8. No CPU, Apple MPS or AMD ROCm. Official benchmarks use 1 H200. Performance: Fish Audio’s highest-scoring model on Artificial Analysis, but still behind several closed APIs on quality Elo. Best: 95.9% on brands, places and technical terms in Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness. Worst: 86.3% on exact sequences (codes, paths, emails), its weakest pronunciation category. Bottom line: Best: directable, multi-speaker speech with open weights. Worst: 48 GB GPU floor and a revenue-capped license. What is Fish Audio Drama 3? Drama 3 turns a script along with bracketed directions into acted speech. Writers place cues like [barely holding it together] before a line. Paired tags such as
change only the enclosed words, per the Drama 3 docs . Directions can be written in any language, independent of the spoken line. The model supports 83 languages . Speaker tags <|speaker:0|> to <|speaker:15|> allow up to 16 characters in 1 request. The API takes 1 voice ID per speaker, so a full scene renders in a single call. How does the Drama 3 architecture work? According to the launch post , the backbone starts from the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B language model. It has 40 layers, grouped as 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per 1 gated full-attention layer. Only 1 layer in 4 keeps a KV cache. DeltaNet layers store history in a constant-size state instead. A new Codebook-MTP decoder replaces the per-frame Fast AR decoder used in S2 . It has 4 shared layers feeding 9 layers, 1 per acoustic codebook. Only codebooks 0 and 1 feed back into the backbone; S2 fed back all 10. The audio tokenizer is unchanged from S2. It is built on the Descript Audio Codec and outputs 44.1 kHz audio. It runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Training ran 3 pre-training stages, then instruction tuning, then reinforcement learning. RL used GRPO without a KL penalty and a single learned human-preference reward model. Fish Audio reports Drama 3 at 93.2% overall on Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness , ranked #1. Its predecessor S2.1 Pro scored 88.1%. Human listeners judge hard English words across 4 categories: Brands, places, technical terms: 95.9% (S2.1 Pro: 87.3%) Context-dependent readings: 95.3% (86.1%) Shorthand such as numbers, dates and units: 93.6% (92.7%) Exact sequences such as codes, paths and emails: 86.3% (79.4%) This benchmark tests pronunciation, not emotional delivery. Fish Audio describes emotive quality only qualitatively. On the Artificial Analysis quality leaderboard , ‘Drama 3 Preview’ holds an Elo of 1242. That beats S2.1 Pro at 1190 but trails Eleven v4 Turbo at 1328. What hardware does Drama 3 need? The Fish Speech install guide lists at least 48 GB of NVIDIA GPU memory in FP8. CPU, Apple MPS and AMD ROCm are not supported. MoE experts ship in FP8, with the remaining weights in bf16. The model card reports streaming results on 1 H200. At 1 stream, median time to first audio is 88.9 ms with a real-time factor of 0.131. At 16 streams, throughput reaches 927.6 frames per second. Serving runs through SGLang-Omni , whose fused kernels are validated only on Hopper GPUs. How do you access Drama 3, and what does it cost? In the hosted API, set the model header to drama-3 on POST /v1/tts . The docs warn that a missing or misspelled header silently falls back to s2.1-pro . List price is $50 per 1M characters. A $10 launch price runs until November 12, 2026, per the launch post . The weights use the Fish Audio Community License v1.0 . Research and non-commercial use are free. Commercial use is free under USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Hosting Drama 3 as a third-party API needs a separate license. Products must display ‘Built with Fish Audio.’ Cloning a real voice without consent is prohibited. Plain-language direction and 16 speakers per request target scripted audio. 93.2% on AA Pronunciation Robustness; exact sequences lag at 86.3%. Self-hosting needs 48 GB+ of NVIDIA memory in FP8. Free commercial use stops at USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Check out the weights on Hugging Face , the technical report , the GitHub repo and the launch post . title: Russian Drones Pound Kropyvnytskyi, Killing Three and Injuring Six
body:
Russian forces launched a massive drone attack on Kropyvnytskyi, the administrative center of the Kirovohrad region in central Ukraine, approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) southeast of Kyiv, and surrounding areas on Wednesday, Oct. 14, killing three people and injuring six, regional authorities reported.
Andriy Raikovych, head of the Kirovohrad Regional Military Administration, confirmed the rising death toll in an update on his official Telegram channel .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Another sad piece of news – a third person has been confirmed dead in the regional capital. My condolences to the families,” Raikovych wrote.
Five injured people were receiving treatment at city medical facilities, while another refused hospitalization.
The Russian assault struck multiple locations across the region, including residential areas and transport infrastructure.
According to Raikovych , one transport enterprise in Kropyvnytskyi district was hit, while private homes were damaged elsewhere in the district.
In Kropyvnytskyi itself, a strike hit the grounds of a multi-story residential building, shattering windows and damaging parked vehicles.
A private house and a vehicle were also damaged in the Oleksandriia district. No casualties were initially reported at those locations.
As the assault continued, Raikovych warned that logistics, transport and industrial enterprises were coming under attack.
“Kirovohrad region and the regional capital are still under a massive enemy attack,” he wrote, urging residents not to publish information about the strikes online and to remain in shelters.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: The Days Of Army Air Defense Systems Firing Just One Type Of Interceptor Are Ending
body: The U.S. Army now has at least five named programs seeking new anti-air interceptors of various tiers to collectively address everything from advanced hypersonic missiles to small weaponized drones . In the process, an important central theme is emerging: the service’s days of fielding air defense systems that can only use one type of interceptor look to be increasingly over. For the U.S. military, the impacts from the war with Iran have made clear that diversifying munitions stockpiles and supplier bases is no longer just valuable, it is critical. Army Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires, highlighted this growing trend yesterday during a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ has been in attendance. Secretary Hegseth, second from the left, seen in front of a launcher for the Patriot surface-to-air missile system during a tour of Redstone Arsenal in Alabama earlier this year. Army Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano is seen at far right. DoW/USN Petty Officer 1st Class Alexander Kubitza To provide some immediate context, with the exception of Patriot, the main ground-based air defense systems in Army inventory today are fielded with just one type of interceptor. In the case of Patriot, the service’s procurement of new interceptors had also been increasingly limited to just one type, the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE). Production of the preceding PAC-3 Cost Reduction Initiative (CRI) missile ended in 2023. Just earlier this year, the Army placed its first order in decades for new PAC-2 Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical (GEM-T) missiles , an older interceptor design for Patriot that has remained in production primarily for U.S. allies and partners. A graphic showing different interceptor load options for existing trailer-based Patriot launchers. Lockheed Martin Separately, the Army is in the process of fielding Enduring Shield , a new middle-tier air defense system designed to handle multiple interceptor types. However, the service is currently only acquiring AIM-9X Sidewinders to load into them. We will come back to this later on. An Enduring Shield launcher. USAF Pfc. Sang Woo Choi “We have the capabilities we need to have to fight and win, but it’s our job to ensure that victory is achievable in the future inside of any dynamic environment scenario fight we might find ourselves in,” Lt. Gen. Lozano said yesterday. “So, it’s incumbent upon Mr. Ingraham [Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology Brent Ingraham] and I to continue to be creative and looking at, well, should we buy GEM-Ts because they’re being produced?” “GEM-Ts are a really good missile in the battlespace within they operate. I mean, they’re being employed today by air defense brigades around the world,” he continued. “So if we have the opportunity, it’s probably something we should take advantage of, and we’re looking at doing that. “We’ve had a lot of discussions about even more interceptors. From a PAC-3 MSE perspective, our goal has always been to get to 2,000 [per year],” he added. “Why we’re running programs like LCI [Low Cost Interceptor], and NGSRI [Next-Generation Short-Range Interceptor], and NGCM [Next-Generation C-UAS Missile], and Second Interceptor, is because I think the easy button answer is just buy more of a great missile. We’re going to buy more [PAC-3 MSEs], but when we start talking about overall missile output, we start looking at numbers like is it 4,000, is it 6,000, is it 8,000, we’re looking at a diverse set of capabilities.” The LCI program is seeking a lower-cost and lower-tier interceptor for Patriot with a unit price of no more than $1 million. PAC-3 MSE’s average unit cost has been around $4 million in recent years. A PAC-3 MSE interceptor seen being launched. US military A Patriot launcher fires a newer PAC-3-series missile during a test. DoD NGSRI is the Army’s program to find a replacement for the venerable Stinger . The new missiles have to be compatible with existing vehicle-based and man-portable launchers. A US Army soldier fires a Stinger from a man-portable launcher during training. US Army The Army is working to field a new counter-drone interceptor through NGCM. Those missiles will be integrated into launchers the service has now for the Coyote interceptor . The Second Interceptor effort is for Enduring Shield, which is also known as the Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 (IFPC Inc 2). The main goal there is to provide increased capability against incoming cruise missiles compared to the AIM-9X. There is also the Army’s Future Interceptor effort , which also came up separately at the panel yesterday, and is also for Patriot. Unlike LCI, the aim here is to acquire a new interceptor with improved capabilities against hypersonic missiles and other upper-tier threats. Historically, Army programs like these would eventually result in the selection of a single winning missile design. Lozano’s remarks yesterday point to the service increasingly taking a very different approach. On “second interceptor, obviously, we just moved into phase two of that program. We’ve got Lockheed Martin competing with Boeing, who was teamed with Anduril,” Lozano said. “But we wanted to turn up the heat on that program. I constantly get frustrated when a funding profile emerges over the FYDP [the Future Years Defense Program], and then magically we lay in a five-year program.” At left, a model of the Boeing/Anduril offering for the Second Interceptor effort. At right, a rendering of Lockheed Martin’s proposed Second Interceptor. Jamie Hunter/Lockheed Martin “I’m like, no, I actually need that capability now,” he continued. “So, have we thought maybe what if we ran a 24-month program or a 36-month program, right? And so, in that vein, what we have decided to do is, while those two companies continue to compete, we’re going to create a shoot-off opportunity in [the] fourth quarter [of Fiscal Year 20]27, and I want to run an in-parallel, what I call an in-stride competition.” “We just held an industry day, and we basically just said, hey, if there’s any other company who didn’t make the first cut in the phase one, but, oh, by the way, who continued to invest in the IFPC Second Interceptor capability, we’d love for you to come out to the range,” he added. “We’ll give you range time, we’ll present targets, and we’ll allow you to recompete with an opportunity to get back into the program folder.” The Army is doing the exact same thing with NGSRI , where Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have been competing face-to-face. That program is also now planning to hold a new shoot-off that will be open to other vendors in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. A picture showing a test of Lockheed Martin’s NGSRI entrant, called QuadStar. Lockheed Martin Raytheon, which is also the prime contractor for Stinger, has previously released this image in relation to work on its NGSRI design. Raytheon There are signs the Army is moving in a similar direction with NGCM, where it previously selected AeroVironment to supply its Freedom Eagle-1 (FE-1) interceptor . The service put out a request for information seeking new NGCM options in August, with a goal of holding an initial evaluation again in the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027. A deeper operational assessment could then follow in Fiscal Year 2028. To reiterate, on top of all this, the Army is also now pursuing at least two new interceptor options for Patriot. “We have to address the threat, and we need to address the threat in a complementary way, meaning we need to fight on a cost curve that’s affordable for the U.S. Army to maintain and sustain that warfighting capability abroad,” Lozano stressed yesterday. This gets to the crux of the matter. It is not at all a new observation that just having a stockpile of any particular munition on day one of a conflict is not enough, especially if the fight becomes drawn out. There needs to be sufficient depth to those stocks at the start and the ability to readily replenish them in line with expenditures. The war with Iran , compounded by other crises in the Middle East and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine , has made clear that these core truths apply to all armed forces, even the U.S. military. Lower-cost munitions are part of the solution, but they also need to be producible at scale on reasonable timelines. The lead time for higher-end munitions today is often measured in months, if not years. Furthermore, being locked into a single vendor has been shown to not just be undesirable, but a potential national security risk in an actual conflict. Lozano’s remarks yesterday, and how the Army is now pursuing new anti-air interceptors, reflect larger trends, not just in the acquisition of larger volumes of munitions overall, but also from a broader array of total suppliers . There has also been a push across the U.S. military to bring in new and non-traditional firms , including in partnership with established prime contractors. An example of this is the Boeing/Anduril team-up for Second Interceptor. This was also underscored by new framework agreements the Pentagon announced back in May regarding the planned purchase of thousands of lower-cost cruise missiles. The @DeptofWar has reached new framework agreements with a slate of disruptive new entrants to aggressively expand the United States military’s lethal cruise missile and hypersonic missile strike capabilities. Low-Cost Containerized Missiles (LCCM) Program: • Anduril •… pic.twitter.com/Fr2xAnBM7y — Department of War CTO (@DoWCTO) May 13, 2026 With regard to the LCI program, specifically, Lozano highlighted an additional aspect of all of this yesterday. LCI has “a unique twist to it because we’re looking for companies who have all-up rounds, but I’m also asking for companies to come in at the component level,” he explained. “We typically don’t do that, right? There’s a lot of risk in managing components and generating all-up round systems. But we’re also looking for weapon system integrators, because I want to be able to create two or three teams who can compete with the all-up round guys to see if we can generate some momentum behind the fact that we need to thicken our inventory with low-cost, affordable munitions.” The U.S. Navy is now pursuing a roughly similar approach with its Naval Modular Missile (NMM) program. NMM envisions an entirely new family of sea-launched surface-to-air missiles that offer very different capabilities, but that all feature certain common components, as you can read more about here . A graphic laying out the Navy’s vision for the different members of the NMM family, and shared components between them. USN The Army is also eyeing a new family of launcher vehicles, as well as containerized options , all capable of firing various types of surface-to-air and surface-to-surface munitions. Autonomy is also an important aspect of what is aptly dubbed the Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) program . It is also important to note here that the underlying aim is not to eliminate more exquisite munitions, or the capabilities that they offer, but to create a more affordable, complementary mix of options. “What I would say is we’re solely focused on delivering on the programs we are executing now,” Lozano said in closing at the end of the panel yesterday. “We have to deliver, and if we deliver on that wide variety of capability, then we can increase and ramp that capacity. And that would be my wish list, that we have enough resources and we achieve programmatic success in the way that we’re planning to, so we can deliver in mass.” All signs point to the diversity in munitions that Lozano is talking about here being particularly pronounced in future Army air defense capabilities full of systems firing multiple types of interceptors. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post The Days Of Army Air Defense Systems Firing Just One Type Of Interceptor Are Ending appeared first on TWZ .

title: Pentagon needs $50B for mass drone production, Hegseth says
body: The Pentagon wants to build its stockpile of autonomous weapons from thousands of units to the millions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed AUSA attendees at the Project Agincourt panel on Wednesday, sharing that the Pentagon is requesting roughly $50 billion in reconciliation funding to support the push to scale autonomous and robotic systems. This request is part of an effort to make the technology available in far greater numbers. The figure is separate from the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 budget request, which includes $53.6 billion for the Drone Dominance initiative . That request covers $16.9 billion for unmanned-system procurement, $14.4 billion for counter-unmanned systems, $13.5 billion for contested logistics, $4.5 billion for collaborative autonomy and $4.3 billion for institutional systems and personnel. The budget request does not establish that the reconciliation funding Hegseth cited is the same money or that it is dedicated entirely to drone purchases Hegseth characterized the funding as a one-time investment rather than a recurring annual allocation, intended to accelerate the development and production of autonomous and robotic systems. “Ultimately we will be dealing with hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come at a pace that this department’s never ever seen before.” The Defense Secretary said the Pentagon must make it easier for new companies to compete in a defense market long dominated by established contractors and costly platforms. Traditional defense firms remain important, he said, but the department also needs lower-cost systems that can be manufactured at scale. The Army’s Drone Dominance program offers a concrete measure of that ambition. In a December 2025 announcement, the Army said a $1 billion initiative would fund approximately 340,000 small unmanned aircraft systems for combat units over two years. The service said it expected to deliver tens of thousands of drones in 2026 and hundreds of thousands by 2027. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the service is broadening access to its programs for companies outside the traditional defense industrial base. The Army, he said, must make room for new entrants while continuing to work with established suppliers. Telle also described plans to coordinate the Army’s autonomous-systems efforts while distributing capabilities to operational units. The service is developing an approach that incorporates drones, autonomous ground systems, autonomous fires and autonomous lift into future combat operations. “We have an MOS in the Army, 390A, where warrant officers could keep the speciality and the skills over the duration to teach our soldiers how to do robotics,” Telle added. Expanding access to Army test ranges is another part of that effort, Telle said. Greater access gives developers more opportunities to test systems and receive feedback from military users. He also described efforts to share lessons across the force rather than have individual units and organizations solve the same problems independently. Hegseth said the department must remove bureaucratic barriers that slow the adoption of new technology, telling the panel, “I want you to tell me which rules can be signed away.” He urged officials to identify rules and directives that could be changed without involving new legislation to accelerate progress.

That request covers $16.9 billion for unmanned-system procurement, $14.4 billion for counter-unmanned systems, $13.5 billion for contested logistics, $4.5 billion for collaborative autonomy and $4.3 billion for institutional systems and personnel. The budget request does not establish that the reconciliation funding Hegseth cited is the same money or that it is dedicated entirely to drone purchases Hegseth characterized the funding as a one-time investment rather than a recurring annual allocation, intended to accelerate the development and production of autonomous and robotic systems. “Ultimately we will be dealing with hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come at a pace that this department’s never ever seen before.” The Defense Secretary said the Pentagon must make it easier for new companies to compete in a defense market long dominated by established contractors and costly platforms. Traditional defense firms remain important, he said, but the department also needs lower-cost systems that can be manufactured at scale. The Army’s Drone Dominance program offers a concrete measure of that ambition. In a December 2025 announcement, the Army said a $1 billion initiative would fund approximately 340,000 small unmanned aircraft systems for combat units over two years. The service said it expected to deliver tens of thousands of drones in 2026 and hundreds of thousands by 2027. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the service is broadening access to its programs for companies outside the traditional defense industrial base. The Army, he said, must make room for new entrants while continuing to work with established suppliers. Telle also described plans to coordinate the Army’s autonomous-systems efforts while distributing capabilities to operational units. The service is developing an approach that incorporates drones, autonomous ground systems, autonomous fires and autonomous lift into future combat operations. “We have an MOS in the Army, 390A, where warrant officers could keep the speciality and the skills over the duration to teach our soldiers how to do robotics,” Telle added. Expanding access to Army test ranges is another part of that effort, Telle said. Greater access gives developers more opportunities to test systems and receive feedback from military users. He also described efforts to share lessons across the force rather than have individual units and organizations solve the same problems independently. Hegseth said the department must remove bureaucratic barriers that slow the adoption of new technology, telling the panel, “I want you to tell me which rules can be signed away.” He urged officials to identify rules and directives that could be changed without involving new legislation to accelerate progress.

title: The best feature of Apple’s HomeView might be its simplicity
body:
I’m just going to come right out and say it. I love the approach Apple has taken with the HomeView. I think it’s the shared, always-available household interface that my family might finally use. Is Apple’s first smart display my dream smart home dashboard? No. But is it the right product for Apple Home at this moment? Absolutely.
A lot of initial reactions to the $299 HomeView (which looks like a giant Apple Watch on a flatter metallic HomePod Mini) ask why you would want it when you can do most of what it offers on your iPhone or iPad. And yes, its features replicate many of the things you already do on the devices you use all the time. But that’s kind of the point. HomeView gives you another interface for those things, but crucially one that is always powered, always unlocked, and always in the same spot in your home, making it easy to walk up to and interact with.
[Image: The HomeView’s footprint is smaller than that of most smart displays I’ve tested. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6046.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: My iPad-in-the-wall experiment lasted several unsuccessful years. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_1308.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
I’ve tried using an iPad to control my smart home, run my family’s calendar, and be a shared device for controlling music. It wasn’t great. I’ll have to test HomeView, of course, but my initial impression is that this could be a much better solution for those use cases.
Most iPads are more expensive, have worse speakers, and do not like to be plugged in all the time (I present my sad, warped iPad Mini as tribute). An iPad can’t be a hub for your Apple Home; HomeView can. An iPad famously isn’t a good multiuser device, and controlling home devices on one requires it staying logged in to your personal iCloud account; HomeView offers Apple’s first crack at easy multiuser switching.
[Image: The HomeView can be wall-mounted. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6036.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
Apple designed HomeView as a communal device that sits in a fixed place in the home. This means it’s always where you expect it to be, which matters when you want to adjust the thermostat or can’t find your phone and want to check your calendar. Not having a battery or detachable screen is a feature for me, because devices that do inevitably wander off and die under a couch cushion.
And while many people are fine using their personal phones and tablets to interact with the digital world when at home, and don’t want yet another device with a screen on their countertop or wall, the millions of Echo Shows, Google Nest Hubs, Skylight Calendars, and the like in homes today are a good indicator that there’s interest in this type of interface.
As Apple’s uncharacteristically chaotic launch video shows, HomeView targets a new demographic for the company: busy, Apple-centric households. One feature I’m most interested in is HomeView’s role as a home video phone. Do you know how many times I’ve tried to call my daughter when I’m not home, and her phone is dead or on silent? Based on Apple’s video, if she’s home, my call can now ring on the HomeView. I’ve occasionally used the drop-in feature on Echo smart speakers to get her attention, further proof of the advantage of always-on home devices.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0420_still-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0420_still.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I see HomeView as filling the awkward space where families don’t want phones at the dinner table or on the kitchen counter, but still want to check what time Zoey’s soccer game is or look up the origin of French toast (yeah, just kidding). This inevitably ends with one person pulling out their phone, which gives everyone else implicit permission to do the same.
Smart displays and speakers from Amazon and Google already help with this to some extent, but Apple’s version comes without ads (see the Echo Show) and may have a longer lifespan (RIP Pixel Tablet). Siri AI’s much-hyped “personal context” capabilities, in which it can scan your text messages and emails and serve up relevant information to up to six members of your household, also give it an edge here.
[Image: The HomeView has a variety of customizable faces. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/LR6B6068.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
I asked Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home at Apple, why Apple chose now for its biggest smart home push yet. She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.
"As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in a natural way.”" - Lilian Rincon, Apple
Siri AI made this possible because it’s “much more capable,” said Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI at Apple. She also pointed to its new conversational abilities. “It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”
Siri AI in the home has another big advantage over the competition: It doesn’t say too much. Based on the demos I saw, and my time using Siri AI on the iPhone, when you ask it to do something, it does it without peppering you with follow-up questions. Rincon confirmed this is by design. “A lot of these assistants out there are always asking questions because they want more information,” she said. “For us, it isn’t about that. We’re there to get it done, take an action for you, show you what you need to get done, and then really get out of the way.”
[Image: The Home control widget on the HomeView can show live views of security cameras. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_0305.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]
My first reaction to hearing about HomeView’s smart home features, which are basically just what the Apple Home app on your phone can do, was disappointment. I had hoped that, along with new hardware, Apple would bring more functionality and deeper Apple Intelligence integration to Apple Home to make the smart home smarter. I’m still waiting on that.
On reflection, I’m okay with this — for now. Apple trying to make the smart home easier for everyone to use can only be a good thing. As always, the smart home’s most important goal is to come up with an easier way to turn on the lights.
HomeView’s simplicity may put off hardcore home automation enthusiasts, but I’d argue it’s perfect for their long-suffering spouses. I’ve tried every version of physical smart home control interface in my home, and you know who hasn’t used any of them? My family.
Because my family all have iPhones, and because the HomeView will always be there and will feel familiar, I can see them actually using it. That means I could set up a full Home Assistant instance and run a detailed dashboard on a tablet in my office, then feed the scenes and devices into Apple Home so my husband and daughter can just tap to control them on a HomeView in the kitchen.
HomeView may not be the smart home computer I want Apple to make, but it is the smart home device Apple needed to make. It doesn’t have to run all the iPad apps or try to be a bigger version of my iPhone; it just needs to make the smart home accessible to everyone in the house. If Apple has pulled that off, it could be more valuable than any new smart home feature I’ve been wishing for.
Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

title: Official: Army Awarding CAML Medium Platform Soon, Plans CAML Light Effort With Australia
body:
The Army is planning an imminent award for its Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) Medium platform, potentially within the next 30 days, a lead official said Wednesday.
“We just finished our source selection effort,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, program acquisition executive for fires, said during a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
The update follows the Army’s decision to focus on a Medium-sized variant as a lead effort. Lozano confirmed the service is planning to initiate a CAML Light effort in partnership with Australia in 2027 before launching a CAML Heavy initiative around the 2028/2029 timeframe.
“We’re looking at a strategy here…where we have every missile [currently] having its own unique launcher and trying to collapse down to a maximum of three. But that generically is the timeline, and we massage and adjust that timeline as we learn more about industry’s capabilities to deliver what we need,” Lozano said.
The Army has previously said CAML is intended to be an “autonomous, optionally crewed, highly mobile, air-transportable, multi-domain (offensive and defensive) fires launcher with the potential to augment or replace existing Army launchers.”
CAML platforms are expected to encompass a launcher platform, a leader vehicle with an autonomy kit and either an automated resupply vehicle or an “inherent autonomous resupply capability,” the Army has said.
The Army has already selected Georgia Tech Research Institute (GTRI) to serve as the weapon systems integrator for CAML Medium, recently awarding the non-profit a $33.4 million deal for the work ( Defense Daily , Sept. 1).
The service described the deal as “the first key step in the development” of CAML, while noting that subsequent awards were scheduled in the coming months covering the autonomous mobility platform and additional components of the program.
Lozano, in a recent media roundtable, described the Army’s process to coalesce around a medium-sized platform as its initial effort for CAML, after having previously planned to concurrently pursue a heavy version as well.
“We issue these RFIs, we issue these requests for solution briefs, we hold capability demonstrations, and industry is learning through the process as well as my team. And so, what we learned was the capabilities that got demonstrated and proposed to us from a CAML perspective, the platforms were heavier than we wanted them to be. And when I interface with the combatant commands and the requirements community, who are part of the PAE, and I look at the different missile and munition mixes that we’re going to place on these CAML systems, we start to define what we might want this system to look like. And so, what we started to see was the formation of a CAML Medium variant,” Lozano previously said.
Lozano has said that a CAML Medium was envisioned to be capable of carrying munitions such as Tomahawk missiles, PAC-3 MSE interceptors, “probably” the future low-cost interceptor, the Lockheed Martin [LMT]-built MLRS family of munitions as well as Indirect Fire Protection Capability interceptors.
“When I started to define the number of interceptors that I wanted this particular system to carry and I started to communicate with the combatant commands to understand how this system would be employed, we started to realize that a 60,000-pound gross vehicle weight platform was just going to be too heavy. And so, what we settled on in talking with everybody involved was a CAML Medium variant that would have a top-end gross vehicle weight rating of 36,000 pounds. And that gave us the right platform with the right munitions mix, with the formations and the employability that we wanted for that particular system,” Lozano said in the recent media roundtable.
On the forthcoming CAML Light effort, Lozano said Acting Army Chief Gen. Christopher LaNeve directed that PAE Fires execute that program with Australia “to help the Australians meet some of their capability requirements.”
“We have a solicitation, an RFI, ready to issue that will be followed up by an industry day,” Lozano said.
The Army could look to make selections for CAML Light prototyping in the spring 2027 timeframe, according to Lozano.
“That could then support a potential live fire demonstration [at the] Talisman Sabre [exercise] in the June/July timeframe. That would then allow us to make a downselected award on that effort,” Lozano said.
On the future CAML Heavy, Lozano said the Army envisions that platform as handling “some of our larger missile systems, potentially a Leviathan and [Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon], maybe a stack of Tomahawk missiles, right, and have a larger capability.”

title: 25 civic educators trained to promote election awareness in Eastern Equatoria
body: The Support Peace Initiative Development Organization (SPIDO), a civil society group, has trained 25 civic educators in South Sudan’s Eastern Equatoria state to raise public awareness of electoral processes ahead of planned elections in December 2026. The training, held in Torit on Wednesday with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), covered democracy, human rights, inclusion, governance and voting procedures. SPIDO programme officer Advocate Morris John Peter said the participants would return to their communities to share the knowledge gained during the training. “We need to equip them with the basic knowledge and principles of democracy and electoral processes so that they understand what is happening and the different stages of the election process,” he said. The participants represented local government institutions, civil society organisations, women’s and youth groups, organisations representing people with disabilities, academic institutions, security forces and the electoral commission. Peter said security personnel were included because of their role in protecting the electoral process and their right to participate in elections as citizens. Noma Samuel, one of the participants, said the training had improved her understanding of her rights and responsibilities as a South Sudanese citizen. She urged civil society organisations to extend civic education to remote communities, saying an emphasis on urban areas could leave rural residents without adequate information about the electoral process. Another participant, Ebul Simon Ohuro, called on the government and development partners to provide resources to expand civic education across Eastern Equatoria, including translating information into local languages and making it accessible to vulnerable groups. Ohuro said rural communities need clear information about voter registration and voting procedures to help eligible citizens make informed decisions and participate in the elections. South Sudan is scheduled to hold elections in December 2026. The country has faced prolonged political and security challenges since gaining independence in 2011, raising concerns about the conditions for holding a credible vote. The extent to which civic education reaches rural communities will be important in ensuring that voters have access to information about electoral procedures before polling day. The post 25 civic educators trained to promote election awareness in Eastern Equatoria appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: NORTHCOM’s JTF-Gold Helping Set Up Defensive Cyber for Golden Dome
body:
Joint Task Force-Gold, which is to help ensure that the planned Golden Dome for America (GDA) missile defense system is ready for operations, plans to have an initial stage of cyber protection and passive anomaly detection in place by the end of the year.
“Our mission continues to grow,” Army Col. Kevin Stonerook, the deputy of JTF-Gold at U.S. Northern Command, told reporters on Wednesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
The task force has about 100 personnel and a headquarters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. “One of the things that has become a new mission set for us is we did have some major involvement in the defensive cyber of the missile defense system,” Stonerook said. “We are helping put together the ‘team of teams,’ all the different stakeholder community, vendors and other government agencies to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA. That’s one of the main things we’re focused on.”
Army Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, the commander of Army Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC) and JTF-Gold, said that SMDC has chosen a unit to help integrate systems, including command and control (C2), for GDA.
“So now, if you array sensors and interceptors and C2 platforms from across the country, you can use any sensor, best shooter, and C2 in that disaggregated way,” he said.
On Sept. 17, Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, the direct reporting program manager for GDA, told the Ohio Space Forum in Cleveland that the first stage of Golden Dome, to be complete by 2028, would focus on protecting against “a coercive decapitation or rogue nation attack against the homeland.” Stage 2, to be completed by 2035, would be the full version of GDA. Aviation Week first reported Guetlein’s remarks.
In May, Guetlein said that a more than $1.2 trillion, 20-year GDA cost estimate by the Congressional Budget Office did not reflect “what we’re building” ( Defense Daily , May 14).
It appears that Guetlein’s comments last month indicate that the 2028 architecture for Golden Dome, which he has not disclosed thus far, would be much less expansive than that envisioned by President Trump in E xecutive Order (E .O.) 14186 . In May last year, the Pentagon said that GDA would be a “system of systems” to protect the United States from “aerial attacks from any foe.”
In many respects, that 2028 architecture could be the existing Ground-based Midcourse Defense at Fort Greely, Alaska with a few alterations, such as the RTX [RTX] and Lockheed Martin [LMT] Patriot system and Lockheed Martin Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and added protection for U.S. Strategic Command and the National Capital Region.
One source said that defense companies are publicly discussing the full up 2035 architecture due to the huge sums involved but know that the 2028 architecture is going to be nowhere close to the Trump advocated concept.

title: Lozano Wants To Have ‘Multiple’ Solutions In Production For Army’s New Munitions Programs
body:
The Army’s top acquisition official for fires said Wednesday his preference is to have multiple solutions in production for new munitions programs, such as the long-range Precision Strike Missile Inc. 4 and the effort to find a second interceptor for the Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) Inc. 2 defeat system.
Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, program acquisition executive for fires, acknowledged it’s an “aspirational” goal, while citing the model as an opportunity to increase competition and bolster the participation of new defense industry entrants.
“We have to take advantage of the fact that there’s a lot of new market entrants who are being very disruptive in this market space, and I have to be able to offer them a competitive opportunity to compete,” Lozano said during a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington D.C.
“At the same time, we have to break the old tradition of doing a competition and going down to one vendor, and then going all in on one single vendor, because then we’ve just created a sole source environment, a choke point and a manufacturing constraint,” Lozano added.
When mentioning an interest in having multiple solutions for a program, Lozano noted the Army’s recent selection of five companies to develop PrSM Inc. 4 prototypes.
“And the intent is we want to be able to have multiple different missile and munition solutions for every type of capability requirement we’re trying to develop so, again, we can maintain a hearty, robust industrial defense industrial base while also providing ourselves magazine depth, buying the right mix of munitions from a high-low perspective and then ultimately doing so in an affordable manner, where I can give the maneuver commander optionality,” Lozano said.
The Army late last month awarded deals to Lockheed Martin [LMT], who builds the current version of PrSM, as well as Anduril , Castelion , RTX [RTX] and Mach Industries to work on their Inc. 4 prototypes intended to fire at ranges 1,000 kilometers or more, with plans for a competitive fly-off and downselect in fiscal year 2027 ( Defense Daily , Sept. 30).
For the current IFPC Inc. 2 Second Interceptor competition, the Army has selected Lockheed Martin and a team of Boeing [BA] and Anduril to move onto the capability demonstration phase, while for the Army’s Stinger missile replacement program, dubbed Next Generation Short Range Interceptor (NGSRI), Lockheed Martin is currently competing against RTX.
“I would love to have two to four [or] three to five competitive, capable, viable producers of IFPC [Inc. 2] second interceptor missiles. It’s early in that effort. I don’t know if we’re going to be able to achieve that, but that’s the end state that we want to create,” Lozano said.
“We have to be very dynamic and flexible in availing opportunities for industry to compete,” Lozano added.
Lozano, in a panel on Tuesday, confirmed the Army plans to give industry another shot at proposing solutions for both IFPC Inc. 2 Second Interceptor and NGSRI, while both programs are in active competition, with plans to seek additional offerings that can participate in shoot-offs in late fiscal year 2027 ( Defense Daily , Oct. 13).
“The thing that really keeps me up at night is I feel like I’m watching a window of opportunity to increase our warfighting capability slowly close on me each and every day, right? So we’re being very aggressive. We’re accepting a lot of risk in the fact that we’re making these opportunities available to industry, and then we’re keeping in mind, ‘Hey, if you can get there, or even if you can get close, we’d be willing to help sustain you into early production and potentially into full rate production,’” Lozano said on Wednesday.
“The bottom line is we need to break the model where we just go to one single material solution against a requirement because there’s a lot of baggage and a lot of evils that come with doing business that way,” Lozano added.
Lozano was also asked Wednesday about the potential for multiple vendors to build the same solution, describing that as more “challenging” than having each provide their own capability.
“Because that relies on me being able to secure the intellectual property that allows me to farm those rights out, right? And, for some these companies, some of that intellectual property are the keys to the kingdom, and [then] I’m neck deep in a fight to ensure we have the right to repair,” Lozano said.
Lozano also alluded to the Army’s new Project Strike initiative to study consolidating budget line items in its munitions portfolio to more flexibly move around funds for promising capabilities.
“So I [would] have multiple different project codes for very similar capability under a program element that I can move money around and buy different capabilities in the year of execution based off of the realities that our Army is facing in any given year,” Lozano said.

title: Iranian leaders believe renewed US strikes are inevitable, warn Washington against attacking
body: Iranian leaders believe that a US strike against the country is inevitable, viewing the question not as "if" Washington will launch another attack, but "when" it will happen.According to several regional diplomats who spoke to The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday following conversations with senior Iranian officials, concerns are growing within Iran's leadership that the current period of relative calm could be short-lived and that hostilities may resume in the near future.One diplomatic source described the mood in Tehran, saying that the atmosphere in the Iranian capital reflects a widespread expectation that further US strikes are imminent. “The atmosphere in Tehran is such that people feel the bombings are going to resume in the short term."Iranian officials warn US against renewing attacksThe growing sense of uncertainty has been accompanied by forceful rhetoric from Iranian officials, who have warned Washington against launching another offensive. On Wednesday, Iranian Army spokesman Mohammad Akrami-Nia accused the United States of seeking to destroy Iran's Islamic civilization through what he described as an illegal war.“America's objective in waging an illegal war is to destroy Iranian Islamic civilization,” Akrami-Nia said.A spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) similarly warned that, although initiating another war against Iran would be strategically irrational for Washington, the possibility of renewed hostilities cannot be ruled out.According to the spokesman, the Trump administration may be seeking a significant political or military achievement ahead of the US midterm elections, potentially increasing the risk of further escalation.The IRGC spokesman stressed that Iran would respond forcefully to any additional military action. “Iran is prepared to respond to any further aggression with greater force than in the past, and the consequences for the United States will be far more painful,” he warned.Iran increases attacks on vessels in Strait of HormuzTensions intensified further on Wednesday as Iran increased its attacks on vessels and oil tankers operating in the Strait of Hormuz. Two tankers belonging to the United Arab Emirates were sunk after being hit by Iran.Since the beginning of the month, Iran has attacked approximately 30 vessels transiting the strait. These attacks are described as part of an Iranian effort to disrupt an operation conducted by US Central Command (CENTCOM) involving the transportation of oil barrels, which has recently been able to transfer 20-22 million barrels per day out of the Straits, reaching the numbers that were there before the war.Earlier this week, Iranian forces conducted a military exercise during which approximately 30 ballistic missiles were launched.

title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
body: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. The hacks that didn't have to happen Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. Read full article Comments

title: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different
body:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up.
Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt , the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection , which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.
Flock’s website says that the company’s audio systems can pinpoint gunfire instantly, while also being able to “detect street takeovers early to stop chaos before it escalates,” and “identify severe crashes in real time so help arrives faster.” It also says they can “expand awareness beyond gunfire with alerts for car crashes, fireworks, and sideshows.”
The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, announced last year, faced immediate pushback. In announcing the feature, Flock said the technology would listen out for sounds of “screaming.” Privacy groups condemned the company for listening for human voices, prompting the company to amend its website to instead say “sounds of human distress.” Flock later said it pulled the ability to detect “distress” altogether from its customers who tried it.
During the interview, Langley pushed back against what he described as misinformation about his product, arguing that many of its critics misunderstand how its products work. The comments come as public opinion continues to shift against Flock and other license plate reading companies amid growing unease about mass surveillance — sentiments that were visible in San Francisco, where protesters gathered to voice their opposition outside the venue as Langley took the stage.
“Most people don’t call 911 when they hear a gunshot, and so that’s why we built the product,” Langley told TechCrunch editor-in-chief Connie Loizos onstage. “And then some of our customers said, ‘Oh, we have these in parking lots. It would be great if we could get alerted if someone was being abducted, if someone was being harmed.’”
Langley said that the idea seemed logical, so the company prototyped it and rolled it out to a couple of customers, but said that some people then had a lot of concerns. Langley conceded to making mistakes but that he was listening to his customers.
“There’s only a couple customers that were prototyping it with us, and we said, ‘OK, great, it’s just going to do gunshots, plain and simple.’ If a gun goes off, we’ll notify, and if not, that’s all it’s going to listen to,” said Langley.
When asked about the contradiction between his remarks and the company’s marketing materials that say the audio systems can detect more than gunshots, he responded, “It’s just gunshots.”
When reached by TechCrunch, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said: “Flock’s gunshot detection technology is primarily used to detect gunfire but is also capable of detecting fireworks, sideshows, and potential car crashes. CEO Garrett Langley’s remarks were intended to emphasize that Flock’s Audio Detection technology is not designed to monitor conversations or analyze speech and does not currently detect human screaming or distress.”
An FAQ section of the website notes that “in addition to gunshots, Flock Gunshot and Audio Detection can detect fireworks, sideshows, and other disruptive community events.” It goes on to state that the company’s “detection library is continually expanding to include emerging threats that are relevant” to customers’ specific needs.
Langley stated that the number of Flock’s microphones is comparable to ShotSpotter, which as of 2024 had about 25,000 microphones, per reporting by Wired .
Langley’s comments come amid mounting scrutiny of Flock from privacy advocates, including the ACLU, and members of the public who are concerned about the misuse of its technology, with some going so far as destroying the surveillance cameras . The remarks also come as Texas and Florida have moved to end their relationships with Flock, and Amazon’s Ring has ended its partnership with the company.

title: U.S. Congressman proposes Sudan minerals deal tied to civilian-led government
body: U.S. Congressman Jim Baird has introduced legislation proposing an agricultural and mining partnership with Sudan, making cooperation conditional on progress towards civilian-led governance, protection of civilians and responsible management of natural resources. The Sudan Investing in Minerals, Partnership, Agriculture, Commerce and Trade (IMPACT) Act, introduced as H.R. 10795, would provide U.S. agricultural and mining equipment, technology and technical assistance in exchange for access to Sudanese natural resources, according to a statement seen by Radio Tamazuj. The bill states that the partnership cannot be established until the U.S. secretary of state determines that a legitimate, civilian-led governing authority in Sudan has taken sufficient steps to demonstrate measurable improvements in civilian protection, political stability and responsible management of the resources covered by the proposal. It also stipulates that the programme would be implemented in agreement with appropriate counterparts in a civilian-led Sudanese government. The proposal comes as Sudan remains engulfed in a war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which erupted in April 2023 and has caused widespread displacement, civilian suffering and damage to the country’s economy. “Sudan’s civil war is devastating lives and holding back its future. Economic opportunity could play a major role in helping the Sudanese people build a more peaceful and prosperous country, but protecting civilians must come first,” Baird said. Baird said Sudan’s mineral resources could help expand supplies of materials used in technologies such as mobile phones and cars, while creating economic opportunities for Sudanese people. The proposed partnership could include farm machinery, precision-agriculture and irrigation technology, agricultural processing equipment, mining machinery, geological surveying technology and technical assistance to improve mine safety and address environmental damage. The bill identifies gold, uranium, crude oil, chromium, iron, copper, manganese, zinc, silver and nickel, as well as gum Arabic, among the resources that could be covered by the partnership. The legislation would link access to these resources with progress towards civilian-led governance and improved protection of civilians. It does not, however, establish that Sudan has agreed to the proposed arrangement or that a partnership is already in place. Baird introduced the bill on October 13, and it was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs for consideration. It has not become law. Baird, a Republican, has represented Indiana’s 4th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives since January 2019. Before entering Congress, he served in the Indiana General Assembly from 2010 to 2018 and as a county commissioner from 2006 to 2010. He serves on the House committees on Agriculture, Foreign Affairs, and Science, Space and Technology. The post U.S. Congressman proposes Sudan minerals deal tied to civilian-led government appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Tree Appreciator
body:
Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with:
Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.
Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play.
