title: Hegseth Pushes For Reconciliation With At Least $350 Billion For Defense ‘Regardless’ Of Midterms Outcome
body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday the Trump administration plans to continue its push for at least $350 billion in defense funds via the reconciliation process “regardless of what happens in the midterms,” noting the Pentagon could ask for “potentially more.”
Hegseth’s doubling down on the push for a $1.5 trillion fiscal year 2027 defense topline, to include the $350 billion sought through reconciliation, comes amid the department’s move to establish a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, noting the mandatory spending request includes more than $50 billion for unmanned systems.
“We’re lockstep on that with the White House. We’ll ensure, regardless of what happens in the midterms, we’re running fast immediately with the [congressional] committees to ensure that that reconciliation bill, at a minimum of $350 [billion for defense], potentially more, ultimately fills up what this department needs in order for the president to ensure that we reestablish deterrence and rebuild the military around the world,” Hegseth said during a panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington D.C.
“It’s not hyperbolic to state whether or not we rebuild our military to meet the threats of the future will depend on funding the president’s vision for $1.5 trillion. And our goal, come hell or high water, and we’re working shoulder to shoulder with the [Joint Chiefs] chairman and the joint staff to get it, is to make sure we hit that number on behalf of the president and the country,” Hegseth added.
While the government is currently operating under stopgap funding legislation with Congress having yet to pass final FY ‘27 appropriations bills or a negotiated reconciliation bill, Hegseth said Pentagon leaders’ “number one priority” is ensuring the department gets the full $1.5 trillion request.
“Especially when you look at the deferred maintenance and the [continuing resolutions] that the services have had to endure for years and years and the chronic underfunding that’s existed. Add that to the bureaucracy which adds more to the personnel costs and exquisite systems which crowds out [operations and maintenance funding] and certainly doesn’t leave any opening for any new innovations or new investments or new entrants,” Hegseth said. “So a one-time generational investments gives us the chance to reflect the president’s priorities.”
Prospects for passing another GOP-led reconciliation bill remain tenuous, with many lawmakers having yet to back the large defense spending request, to include lead Republican appropriations pushing back against the use of mandatory rather than discretionary funding for several top Pentagon priorities, and with Congress potentially facing a change in majority control in the next Congress following the upcoming midterms.
“The president recognizes all of this and said, ‘Hey, we would love to do it through the regular budget process but if we cannot then we’ll do it through reconciliation.’ And we will ensure, whether it’s $350 [billion] as a minimum [in] a reconciliation bill or more, that we meet the president’s expectation,” Hegseth said on Wednesday.
Hegseth announced in late September plans for the Pentagon to stand up a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command (AutoWarCom) along with launching the Project Agincourt initiative aimed at “operationalizing the acquisition system” for the autonomous capabilities ( Defense Daily , Sept. 30).
“Take autonomy for example. There’s about $50 billion in autonomous and robotic systems in the reconciliation bill that would go into [Defense Autonomous Warfare Group], into Project Agincourt and into AutoWarCom,” Hegseth said, noting the large increase from the $1.2 billion included in 2025’s reconciliation bill.

OpenAI is facing a new wave of lawsuits from eight US states that accuse the company of harming children and misleading customers about the safety of ChatGPT, as reported earlier by Reuters . The lawsuits, filed separately by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana, allege OpenAI unlawfully put profits over safety when developing ChatGPT.
The string of complaints claims that OpenAI violated local consumer protection laws by failing to warn customers about the dangers of ChatGPT, citing several lawsuits filed by the family members of teens and adults that allege the AI chatbot played a role in their loved ones’ deaths. They allege that while OpenAI misleadingly presented ChatGPT as a “safe, youth-appropriate tool that puts safety first,” it was actually “dangerous to vulnerable users” — including by “degrading critical thinking skills, encouraging paranoias and delusions, offering dangerous medical advice, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.”
Additionally, the states accuse OpenAI of collecting data from minors and not doing enough to keep underage users from using the chatbot. The lawsuits also cite recent rogue AI hacking incidents as evidence of OpenAI’s alleged “recklessness.”
“OpenAI has devolved from its original mission as a public-first nonprofit that prioritized safety into a cautionary tale about what can happen when the development of a tool as powerful as AI is driven not by safety, but by a profit‑at‑all‑costs mindset that sidelines essential safeguards,” Arizona’s lawsuit claims .
In an emailed statement to The Verge , OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections” into ChatGPT:
While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company.
The states are asking the courts to force OpenAI to pay a series of civil penalties and to stop misleading the public about the safety of ChatGPT. Some states are also seeking the deletion of unlawfully collected personal data.

title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
body:
TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. ð¥
A huge debate weâve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.
To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.
On the other hand, thereâs no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We donât want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.
Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under âdanger zoneâ flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!
See these new capabilities as a continuation of what weâve built over 2 years of stealth. Theyâre less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. Theyâre also an early glimpse into what weâre focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.
Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, weâre enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along!
Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.
As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.
Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images
Weâre introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. Itâs our first type thatâs not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.
We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so weâre enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).
Weâve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than weâve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.
We arenât your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:
Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length
We love the communityâs desire to help make models better! Weâve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.
Weâre also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything . Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.
Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but weâre well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while.
We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0 . Weâll release a deprecation policy prior to this.
As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks . However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers.
Weâre trying something new out here: weâre going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.
This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, donât expect them to be consistent.
Donât believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.
Weâre including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.
This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.
Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi weâre releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

title: Air Force Searching for Next-Gen Perimeter Air Defense Radars
body: The Air Force is looking to replace the three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations. A Sept. 21 notice from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center seeks sources for new technology to continue the Air Route Surveillance Radar-4’s mission and potentially improve its technology. The notice’s details are classified, but AFLCMC updated the original notice Oct. 13, according to Sam.gov. The number of radars needed to replace the 44-radar network and the price for those replacements has not yet been determined and will come via market research, Air Force Materiel Command spokesperson Mark Wyatt told Air & Space Forces Magazine. There is also no development timeline publicly available, though responses to the sources sought notice are due by Oct. 21. The Air Route Surveillance Radar system version 4, or ARSR-4, long-range radar, Paso Robles, Calif. (Air Force photographer Deb Henley) Wyatt said AFLCMC is requesting an instrumented range of 250 nautical miles, identical to the current ARSR-4. ARSR-4 helps operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. While historically the radar has been very effective at this task, newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly. “Wind farms are one of many sources of clutter that any solution would have to address,” Wyatt said. “The Air Force is not prescribing any technique to solve this long-standing challenge for radars.” Interested industry parties can continue to pair their replacement option with the existing Monopulse Maintenance Surveillance Radar or replace that radar with another solution, Wyatt said. The MMSR works with the ARSR-4 to “interrogate” aircraft transponders it detects by sending out coded radio frequency pulses that the transponder then responds to. Using the monopulse method, the MMSR can determine an aircraft’s azimuth from a single pulse received from the transponder, instead of needing multiple hits when sweeping the area. The MMSR is mounted on the ARSR-4, and they rotate together as they monitor the skies. ARSR-4 Locations Ajo, Ariz. Bootlegger Ridge, Mont. Bucks Harbor, Maine Caribou, Maine Cross City, Fla. Deming, N.M. Eagle Peak, Texas Empire, Mich. FAA Academy (Training Site), Okla. Falls City, Ore. Finley, N.D. Fort Fisher, N.C. Fort Green, Fla. Gibbsboro, N.J. Jedburg, S.C. King Mountain, Texas Lake Charles, La. Lakeside, Mont. Makah, Wash. Melbourne, Fla. Mica Peak, Wash. Mill Valley, Calif. Morales, Texas Mount Kaala, Hawaii Mount Laguna, Calif. Key West, Fla. Nashwauk, Minn. North Truro, Mass. Oceana Naval Air Station, Va. Oilton, Texas Mount Santa Rosa, Guam Paso Robles, Calif. Rainbow Ridge, Calif. Remsen, N.Y. Riverhead, N.Y. Rocksprings, Texas San Clemente Island, Calif. Slidell, La. Tamiami, Fla. Tyndall Air Force Base, Fla. Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. Watford City, N.D. Whitehouse, Fla. Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, Cuba An Aging Platform The Air Force purchased most of the existing 44 radars in the 1990s, upgrading the previous 1, 2, and 3 models that have monitored the skies since the late 1950s. The Raytheon-built ARSR-1 entered service in 1958 and was first used to manage the exploding growth of civil aviation. It had a 170-200 nautical mile range. That early system used the Army/Navy/Fixed Radar Surveillance-20 and later variants of the AN/FPS-66. In the 1960s, Raytheon produced the ARSR-2, which improved maintenance and reliability factors. That radar was the AN/FPS-115. Both the ARSR-1 and -2 ran on vacuum tubes. Joint radar evaluation and optimization team members, 84th Radar Evaluation Squadron radar team and Federal Aviation Administration member, testing the Air Route Surveillance Radar system version 4, or ARSR-4. (Air Force photographer Deb Henley) Westinghouse Electric Corporation built the AN/FPS-130, the radar base of the ARSR-3, fielding it in the 1970s and extending detection ranges beyond 240 nautical miles; it was incorporated into joint military-civil air defense networks. The ARSR-4, also built by Westinghouse and commissioned in the 1990s, was the first radar in the family to offer three-dimensional target tracking. That capability allows users to simultaneously measure a target’s range, azimuth, and altitude. The system also provided advanced look-down/clutter rejection capabilities for military operations. Northrop Grumman acquired Westinghouse in 1996, rolling the company’s radar and electronic warfare programs into its Electronic Systems sector. While the ARSR-4s monitor the perimeter of the country, Guam, and Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, for the U.S. interior, the FAA manages a network of Common Air Route Surveillance Radars. The CARSR has an estimated 200 nautical mile range. The complete CARSR system replacement rollout concluded in 2015. The rollout maintained the legacy sites, towers, and mechanical controls while refitting the internal electronics of the radars. One ARSR-4 location has a strategically vital area to protect: Watford City, N.D., is 165 miles from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., home of the 91st Missile Wing, and 263 miles from Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.—putting hundreds of ICBM silos in its range. The Western Air Defense Sector’s 225th Support Squadron conducts a joint technical inspection of the radar and radios at Ajo Defense Program Facility near the U.S./Mexico border in Ajo, Ariz. (Air National Guard photo by Bruce Robie) A Larger Network The ARSR-4 system is one piece of a larger detection system used to track incoming threats. The Air Force and NORAD used the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77, both of which serve as northern warning systems out to 250 nautical miles. These systems are specifically designed for extreme cold weather, such as in their locations in Alaska and northern Canada. The Space Force operates the AN/Frequency Precision and Quantization-16 Perimeter Acquisition Radar Attack Characterization System, which tracks missiles and precision space objects out to about 2,000 miles. USSF also operates the AN/FPS-108 COBRA DANE to track missiles out to 2,000 miles and high-altitude space objects at 25,000 miles. The Space Force’s 20th Space Surveillance Squadron at Elgin Air Force Base, Fla., operates the AN/FPS-85 Phased Array Radar, which can track objects beyond 22,000 miles. NORAD is also currently building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network. The Homeland Defense OTHR , which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion , respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031. Canada’s Polar OTHR is expected to cost up to $3.5 billion and is a slice of the nation’s estimated $38.6 billion overhaul of its portion of NORAD. The polar project is currently in the site procurement phase, with operational deployment planned for 2029 and FOC by 2033. The U.S. Northern Warning System Modernization project “Crossbow” could cost up to $6 billion, and the system rollout is expected to last until 2028, with the project concluding in 2035. The High-Altitude and Mobile Near-Space Surveillance Systems has a $4.2 billion contract ceiling and is currently in field testing and initial low-altitude deployments. It is expected to achieve full cloud-based command-and-control network integration by 2028. The post Air Force Searching for Next-Gen Perimeter Air Defense Radars appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Here’s the 2027 cost-of-living increase for retirees, veterans
body: Social Security beneficiaries, military retirees and people receiving veterans benefits will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, in 2027. The Social Security Administration’s COLA announcement Wednesday sets the rate of increase for about 72 million Social Security beneficiaries, but also for military retirees and people receiving veterans benefits. The increase goes into effect in January and is 0.8% higher than the 2.8% COLA in 2026. It’s the biggest increase in four years. Officials estimate that on average, the monthly Social Security benefit will increase by $75. As an example, a military retiree who receives $2,500 in retired pay will see a COLA increase of about $90 per month. For a veteran receiving $1,500 per month in benefits, the increase would be about $54 in 2027. In 2024, Congress passed legislation that ties increases in veterans’ benefits to the rate of Social Security increases. The cost-of-living increase applies to disability compensation, clothing allowances and dependency and indemnity benefits, as well as some other Department of Veterans Affairs assistance programs. The COLA is designed to ensure benefits keep pace with inflation. The calculation is based on the Consumer Price Index, which tracks the cost of a wide range of items and calculates inflation and changes in the cost of living. The 2026 COLA was 2.8%, a few ticks higher than the 2025 COLA of 2.5%. Those with personal “my Social Security” accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November, a few weeks earlier than those who receive paper notices in the mail, officials said.

title: Fixing C Strings With String Views
body:
I have always been frustrated about C not having a proper String type that most modern languages have nowadays. I love the simplicity of C, but there are some features that I would really like to have in it, and this is one of them.
Since I made a small library (just one .c file) that you can use to make the experience of working with strings in C just a little better, I would like to show it to you here.
For the impatient, this is the general idea:
But before getting into the library itself, I will go over how âstringsâ work in C and why I find them annoying, what the issues are with this model, and then it will be easier to explain why I decided to take the route that I took.
If you only care about the actual implementation details, you can click here .
As many might already know, strings in C are NUL-terminated. NUL is an ASCII character which, in the context of ASCII encoding, literally corresponds to the value 0. In C, this character is represented by '\0' . Inside a text, it generally does not carry any semantic meaning, so it will never be used inside the text for the sake of carrying information (as opposed to letters like 'a' or 'y' ).
C does not really have âstringsâ per se. It only has arrays. These arrays are simply chunks of data where you can put things. To understand where the array ends, one has two options:
Since âstringsâ (which are not really strings) in C are simply arrays of characters, each string has a NUL-terminator at the end of it.
C is a very old language and back then - when it was first created - this seemed like a good idea.
Storing the length of the data separately required more memory than a NUL-character at the end. A NUL-character in ASCII encoding is 8 bits (or 1 byte). If you tried to store the length of the data in only 8 bits, you could only have strings that are up to 255 characters in length, which is obviously too short. Bigger numbers require more data to store, so weâre talking about around 4 to 8 bytes instead of 1.
But this is not even the main reason - the main reason is because of simplicity. Back when C was created, there existed some languages that already had strings with a separately stored length. C just wanted to be as simple as possible, and having NUL-terminated character arrays seemed like a sane decision.
First of all, if you want to find out the length of a string, with a NUL-terminated string you have to start at index 0 and start counting until you reach the end of the data. This process has a time complexity of O ( n ) O(n) O ( n ) , as opposed to O ( 1 ) O(1) O ( 1 ) for just reading the separately stored length.
This is fine for short character arrays, but imagine you had to figure out the length of a 1 , 000 , 000 1,000,000 1 , 000 , 000 character text. That would take a considerable amount of CPU cycles that could have been used for something else.
This bothers me especially in a language like C, since it is supposed to give you some of the best performance that programming languages have to offer (without counting assembly and certain exceptions in some specific scenarios). C is often the baseline when comparing languages to gauge their relative performance. Why, if C focuses so much on performance, would you settle for this?
Let us assume that we have some C-string some_str :
This is great, but now I would like to work with the second word specifically ( World ). I do not care about changing the data, just about reading. Maybe I want to pass it to a function or something. Well, I could do something like this:
By doing this, we are reusing the NUL-terminator that some_str was using to terminate itself.
Fine, what if I want to access the first word only, though? Now we have a problem. We somehow have to end the string at the fifth index. To do that, we would have to insert a NUL-character at index 6 . By doing so, we are changing the data that some_str is pointing to, and we can therefore not use that variable anymore.
So, what do we do? We have to copy the string. Thatâs slow, since it involves memory lookups. We have to allocate to memory, and then copy it. We can also use the stack if we know the size of the data at compile time, but that is often not the case. That would look like this:
In this simple example, the stack would have been fine, but in most realistic scenarios, we have to use heap allocations.
This problem is solved by so-called âstring viewsâ, which are basically immutable data and a length. You can just give the string view the same pointer as some_str and decrease the length to whatever you need, 5 in this case.
God forbid you forget to NUL-terminate a string. If you pass a pointer to a non-NUL-terminated string to a function in string.h , like strlen , the computer will just keep counting characters until it either randomly finds a NUL-character or - alternatively - until it tries to access a region of memory that it should not touch and the operating system kills the process.
This generally does not happen with actual strings (or string views), since you will use functions to interact with them, and they always keep the length of the string in sync with the data. In that case you always know when the string stops, you do not have to rely on remembering to NUL-terminate all your strings.
There are probably more issues, but these are hopefully enough to convince you. In general, I find strings with a separately stored length more intuitive and easier to work with.
Luckily, strings are not particularly hard to implement in C. Here is how I did it.
Just so you are aware when reading the code, I typedef some basic types in C before I start coding. In this case we will only need a few of them, but this is what I paste at the start of every project of mine.
This makes it more convenient to use the integer types with a fixed size instead of the older int , long , long long , etc.
I generally prefer this since int is not the same size on all platforms. int32_t on the other hand is guaranteed to be exactly 32 bits.
For your information, I have adapted this library to be compatible with my arena implementation. It can be found in the same repository as this string library. I have an article about it here if you would like to read up on that.
What you need to know is that each function that needs to allocate some memory receives a struct arena * as its first argument. Instead of malloc and realloc I use arena_alloc and arena_realloc respectively.
First, letâs define our string types. I donât prefer not to typedef structs, but if you want to you can do so. If you do decide to typedef these structs, I would advise you to use PascalCase as a naming convention (to better differentiate them from built-in types).
As you can see, we have two string types: struct str_view and struct str_owned . The difference is that struct str_owned owns the data, and the data can also be changed. Ideally, you should try to only have one str_owned pointing at any given region in memory.
On the other hand, struct str_view should be used as read-only views of a given region of data. It should not be used to modify the data.
Separating these two concerns is nice for multiple reasons. Who owns the data becomes clear immediately. This is especially useful when returning string structs from functions. By using this model, it is easier to understand whether we need to concern ourselves with freeing data or something similar.
As a general rule of thumb, struct str_owned are heap-allocated. If you have a struct str_view viewing some region in memory owned by a struct str_owned , that string view is only valid as long as the underlying owned string is still valid. That means that you have to be careful about not freeing the struct str_owned and after that still using string views that view that data.
Also, you might have noticed that I am using u8 s (a.k.a. uint8_t s) instead of char s. That is because, technically - even though in almost all cases it does not matter - char s are not guaranteed to have a size of exactly 8 bits. On certain embedded systems, a char is sometimes 16 or 32 bits large. On very old systems, they used to be 9 bits. This has historical reasons. A char is simply guaranteed to have a size of one byte, but the exact size of a byte is not clearly defined as a definitive size in bits. Knowing all that, using u8 is more consistent across platforms.
As a side note, this is also the reason why the CHAR_BIT macro exists. It tells you how many bits are in a char on the system that the code is run. That is because the size of a char depends on the system that you are currently on.
Also, I do not really like using a redundant type. A u8 holds all the semantic information I need, so u8 it is.
Next, we create some macros. I try to minimize the use of macros, but in certain cases they are just perfect for the job. I believe that this is one of them.
Mainly I care about the STR macro, that I use to easily create a struct str_view out of a char * literal.
STR_PRINT is used to print a struct str_view . You can use the %.*s format specifier to manually give it the length of the string to be printed (since string views are not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated, since they can view a region of memory in the middle of a struct str_owned ). This can be done as follows:
Here you can also see the STR macro in action, which creates a struct str_view on the fly from a char * literal.
Since my implementation uses memory arenas, there is no need to free an owned string specifically, but if you would like to move away from arenas you can always create a simple wrapper function that calls free on the data field of an owned string.
We need some way to convert between struct str_view and struct str_owned and back. Converting an owned string to a string view is trivial; you simply use the same pointer and length of the owned string in a struct str_view :
Also, as you might have noticed, I like using [[nodiscard]] . This is a compiler directive which makes the compiler issue a warning if the return value of the function flagged with this directive is disregarded. In scenarios like this one I find it to be very useful, since it is completely useless to call this function if you are not going to do anything with the result.
We also need to convert string views to owned strings. This is a bit more tricky and should not be done unless strictly necessary, since it requires memory allocation. An owned string can be mutated, which means that we have to give it its own region in memory to avoid damaging other owned strings that might be using the same memory (recall when I said that we should try to avoid having multiple owned strings on the same chunk of memory).
As a small side note, whenever I need to return multiple values from a function I donât like using output parameters (which is a technique often used in C programs). I prefer to return a struct. Also, it does not allow the caller of the function to use the return value directly, which makes it more likely that the programmer will remember to check for errors.
It makes code very verbose but more consistent in my opinion, as opposed to output parameters. If you donât like it, moving away from this system and adapting the code to your own needs should be trivial.
I also wrote a bunch of functions that implement common string operations and hopefully make the experience of working with strings much more ergonomic than the standard library.
This should behave similarly to the String.slice function in JavaScript.
I decided to use a struct for the input parameter, because this makes it easier to support optional arguments. You can simply initialize it like this
And then, by default, both boolean fields are false. You can then set whatever fields you want. If you do not provide a start , the default is 0 . If you do not provide an end , the default is the length of the string view.
start is inclusive, while end is exclusive. I could not use negative values for representing âunsetâ values. For one, I really dislike this practice, and also I wanted to give the user the option of passing negative values which reference the end of the string.
What I mean is that if you pass -1 as start , the function will start slicing at the last character of the string. -2 would be second to last.
This is really ergonomic whenever you only want to shave off some characters at the end (for example, the \r\n\r\n at the end of the head of an HTTP string).
I loop keep slicing away one character at a time from a string and check if the resulting string starts with the desired substring.
For this, I simply use the str_find_substr function defined above and extract the found field from the struct str_find_out output.
This is straight forward. Check the lengths and compare the memory.
Here is the same thing, but it ignores the casing. Adding 32 to an uppercase letter character converts it to the lowercase equivalent. This, of course, only works with ASCII encodings.
This one is a bit more complicated, since it involves heap allocations. At first, I implemented it in a way that required a memory allocation for each new split that was found. I later changed it and created this helper function:
This counts the number of occurrences of a substring before splitting, which is useful for allocating all the required memory upfront. The number of splits will be the number of occurrences of the delimiter plus one.
An empty delimiter does not split the string at all, it returns one split which contains the entire string. The delimiter can also be made of multiple characters (which is why I used a struct str_view instead of a char ).
Another thing to note is that struct str_owned are usually NUL-terminated. The len field does not include the NUL-character, but it is there. This is a natural consequence of creating a struct str_owned from a struct str_view created with the STR macro. Also, I try to keep this convention in my utility functions.
This makes it very nice to work with functions in the standard library that require you to use NUL-terminated strings. Just pass the data field of the struct str_owned , and it acts as a normal C-string.
Also, some things are missing in this article that are actually implemented in my string implementation that you can find in the repository. For example, one function that is quite long I did not feel like pasting here was a str_replace function which
All the code is available on my codeberg repository .
I plan to add more utilities to this repository as time goes on, which is why the name has nothing to do with strings, but with libraries in general.
I also wrote some tests for the string functions.
The idea is that you can simply copy the code that you need and put it in your own projects. Feel free to use it however you please.
Also, I have recently started to employ so-called âunity buildsâ for my projects. Basically, I do not use header files for my own code. Everything lives in .c files and I #include them directly.
For very large scale projects, this is not good practice, but for personal the scale of almost all personal projects this is completely fine and has the nice benefit of significantly speeding up compilation times, since it completely skips the linking step, which takes the most time.
If you do not like unity builds, you can create your own header file to hide the API of the string library.

title: Army Explains How Merops Interceptor Drone Became Program Of Record In Just 142 Days
body: The U.S. Army turned the Merops interceptor drone into a formal program in just 142 days, an acquisition milestone that highlights efforts to speed the service’s response to emerging threats and get combat-proven capabilities into the hands of troops and allies. The Merops won accolades for its role in defending against Iranian barrages of Shahed-136 one-way attack munitions in the Middle East. Speaking at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance, Col. Christopher Hill, director of the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD), described the Merops effort as “an example of how we can move fast when we need to.” A Polish soldier packing the parachute for a Merops drone near Lipa, Poland, in November 2025. U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Luis Garcia, 52d ADA Bde The Merops is a small, relatively low-cost counter-UAS system designed to rapidly intercept long-range, one-way attack drones in flight. It was originally developed under the U.S.-backed Project Eagle initiative, with contributions from Swift Beat, a company associated with former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. The system uses Surveyor drones as airborne interceptors, with onboard sensors to track targets and the ability to operate autonomously or under remote control. The interceptors can destroy enemy unmanned aircraft through direct impact or a proximity-detonated explosive warhead. The interceptor was initially brought to the Army’s attention after drone incursions involving two NATO partners prompted a senior commander to demand an urgent response. The system was not part of the commander’s original acquisition plan, Hill explained, but its demonstrated performance in Ukraine made it a compelling candidate. “He said, ‘I want this capability in the hands of our partners within 14 days,’” Hill recalled. “Everyone looked around the room, and he looked over at me, and I nodded my head like, ‘We’ll figure it out.’” The Army did not quite meet that deadline. Hill said acquisition personnel and soldiers went into the theater to evaluate the capability, ultimately getting it into the hands of NATO partners within approximately 21 or 22 days. That initial effort has since expanded. Hill said the Army procured additional Merops systems in partnership with the Joint Interagency Task Force, which procured 13,000 of the interceptors. The effort also progressed from providing the capability to NATO partners to supplying mobile Merops firing teams to a second theater — presumably U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). In CENTCOM, the U.S. military has been confronting the threat posed by Iran’s Shahed-136 and other one-way attack drones, which have been used in barrages against American and allied forces and installations in the Middle East. Former Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll had previously highlighted Merops as a particularly attractive option for countering such threats because of its relatively low cost and the speed with which it can be acquired. You can watch Driscoll’s testimony on Merops at the 36-minute mark of the video below: During congressional testimony, Driscoll said the Army was able to purchase 13,000 Merops interceptors within approximately eight days after the conflict with Iran began. He put the cost at about $15,000 per interceptor, with the potential for that figure to fall below $10,000 as production scales. In a separate interview with Bloomberg , he suggested larger orders could eventually push the price down to between $3,000 and $5,000. U.S. Secretary of the Army Daniel Driscoll poses for a photo after signing a Merops counter-unmanned aerial system in Ansbach, Germany. U.S. Army photo by Sgt. 1st Class Jacob Kohrs Shahed drones have been estimated to cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece, while traditional air defense interceptors are far more expensive. Using comparatively inexpensive drones to defeat them can improve the economics of air defense while preserving more sophisticated interceptors for threats that require them. Ukraine has employed Merops alongside domestically produced interceptor drones to counter Russian Shahed/Geran one-way attack drones. The system’s battlefield use has helped demonstrate the potential of a new class of air defense weapons designed to defeat these kinds of drones without relying exclusively on costly surface-to-air missiles. The thermal infrared targeting system of a Merops displays a green target lock box milliseconds before intercepting a Hornet mid-range strike drone during a Perennial Autonomy drone demonstration for 2nd Marine Division on Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center, Twentynine Palms, California, July 28, 2026. U.S. Marine Corps/Courtesy photo illustration However, Hill cautioned that success in Ukraine does not automatically mean a system will perform equally well in every operational environment. “On the Merops, it absolutely was influenced by [Ukraine]. I mean, that’s where it came from. That’s where we saw the capability,” he said. “But that’s one of the things where the employment of the system really matters.” A Merops drone is prepared for flight during a Perennial Autonomy drone demo on Range 220 as part of Service Level Training Exercise 4-26 on Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center, Twentynine Palms, California, July 28, 2026. U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Carla Perez Ramirez Hill noted that the system’s effectiveness will vary depending on where it is used, including differences between desert environments and the urban areas where it has operated in Ukraine. The objective, he said, is to get the capability into the Army’s inventory so commanders can make informed decisions about how and where to use it. “Once we get it into our hands, now we can make a decision in Europe. Where does it go? Do I even need it?” Hill said. “It’s getting it in our hands. So that was the key for the Merops. The speed of getting it, then we can make the decision of how we employ it.” That approach reflects a broader change in how the Army wants to manage emerging technology. Rapid fielding is important, but the service also wants to avoid acquiring a capability for an urgent operational need only to leave it without a clear path toward long-term funding, production, and support. Hill said G-TEAD’s process is designed to involve the organizations that will eventually take responsibility for a capability from the outset. Program acquisition executives, or PAEs, are involved early, while the Army’s test and evaluation community and soldiers provide feedback as the system is assessed. The goal is to identify a transition partner upfront rather than wait until after an initial fielding effort to determine who will take ownership. A U.S. Army soldier carries a component of the Merops counter-drone system during a live-fire demonstration at the Deba training grounds in Subcarpathian Voivodeship, Poland, on November 18, 2025. Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto “We want to make sure that we’re giving commanders capability that we know works,” Hill said. He described the directorate’s standard process as a 180-day effort, with the objective of reaching a decision on whether a capability should become an Army program within that period. The Merops effort, at 142 days, moved faster than that target. The process is also intended to address what acquisition officials often call the ‘valley of death’: the gap between getting an emerging capability into the hands of operational units and the point at which a program office takes over and provides the funding and contracting structure needed to scale it. “We will work to fill that valley of death gap between the time that we put capability into the hands of units and the time that the PM picks it up and actually [provides funding],” Hill said. “There’s a gap there. So we can do that intermediate scaling portion before it fully transitions.” A U.S. Army soldier launches an interceptor drone, part of the Merops counter-drone system, during a live-fire demonstration at the Deba training grounds in Poland. Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images The effort builds on the Army’s wider push to streamline acquisition, an issue Driscoll has also emphasized. The Army secretary previously described an old process involving 16 decision-making steps, each with the ability to veto a proposal and send it back through the system. That structure could leave the service waiting two to seven years to purchase a capability. The Merops experience suggests that some of those delays can be reduced when acquisition professionals work directly with operational units and the organizations responsible for evaluating and sustaining new equipment. But rapidly acquiring an interceptor is only part of the challenge. The Army must still determine where it offers the greatest value, how it fits into existing air defense architectures, and how to produce and sustain enough systems to meet operational demand. Low-cost interceptors are also not a replacement for every layer of air defense. They are, however, an increasingly important option against large numbers of relatively inexpensive attack drones, particularly when the alternative is expending missiles worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars to defeat each target. For the Army, Merops is therefore serving two purposes: providing an additional tool against the growing one-way attack drone threat and demonstrating a faster route from an emerging battlefield capability to a formally supported military program. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Army Explains How Merops Interceptor Drone Became Program Of Record In Just 142 Days appeared first on TWZ .

title: ‘Addicted to the Guard’: Generals call for ‘traffic cop’ to control state governor’s demands
body: In Florida, about 3,000 of the state’s National Guard troops — nearly 30% — are currently deployed overseas. Another 800 are on federal orders supporting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement , and “quite a few” are deployed to Washington, D.C. , to support local law enforcement. It all makes up more than three times the Guard’s true capacity, according to Maj. Gen. Robert Carruthers, assistant adjutant general of the Florida Guard. And that’s even after the activation in recent years of the Florida State Guard , a volunteer civilian military force, to support hurricane response and other state needs. In a panel at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting on Tuesday, the message of other Guard leaders was clear: The demands are unsustainable — and they need to stop. “The governor’s become quite addicted to the Guard and how useful they are since COVID,” Carruthers said, referring, presumably, to Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has been in office since 2019. The effects are felt in equipment readiness and training, he said, particularly as funding has not followed the deployment of units and their gear. “You’re going to have this cascading effect of breaking units downstream,” Carruthers said. “In the case of Florida, what are we going to lose first? Are we going to lose our transportation companies, which are critically important in hurricane [relief], or are we going to lose our aviation first? So it’s also important for us to plan for that aspect.” The Florida Guard, Carruthers said, had ordered a “maintenance stand-down” to assess the status of infantry brigade combat team equipment sitting unused in motor pools. As a result of the assessment, he said, equipment readiness rates dropped from 90% to 27% within six weeks. “It’s somewhere five degrees below combat-ineffective, right?” he said. “So that’s just the state of where we are, because the equipment sits … we are not funded to maintain it all the time.” Maj. Gen. Jack James, commanding general of the New York-based 42nd Infantry Division, proposed a solution to push back on governors’ demands: a “broker” and a “traffic cop” to filter activation and employment requests and prioritize them. “You hear what these guys are up against with their governors, right? And then what the warfighting commanders are up against with our, whether it’s the [U.S. Central Command] commander, [U.S. Pacific Command] commander, our Army components, right?” James said. “There’s inherent friction right there, so we need a brokering function. We need a traffic cop function. We need the arbiter of how those resource allocations are going to be made in a quick, timely manner, so we can get after it for the country.” Carruthers acknowledged there would be “political pressure” and fallout as the Guard works to manage expectations and requirements in line with its actual capacity. “There are probably homeland defense people who think they’re getting these dudes and dudettes, and all of the governors think they have all of their Guard because they’re not really led in war plans,” he said. “And the time of mobilization is not the time to adjudicate that. So that’s something we got to work now to include … trying to get our governor and our state leadership in on these plans at a classified level, so they understand.” Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 saw a historic mobilization of some 118,000 Guard troops at home and overseas. And the start of President Donald Trump’s second term in 2025 kicked off a new wave of domestic deployments, both to quell unrest and support ICE enforcement actions in Democratic-controlled cities and to contribute to crime reduction in Washington, D.C . The D.C. deployments alone are expected to cost the country another $1.4 billion through January 2029. While the increased role of National Guard troops in domestic affairs has been a point of concern for some time, Army National Guard Director Lt. Gen. Jonathan Stubbs said the current situation would force action, and even confrontation, within the next year. “Hope is not a method in this case; there is no fail. We’ve got to figure this thing out,” Stubbs said. “It’s going to require hard conversations between adjutants general and governors. There’s going to be a level of dialog, of informing and educating our state commanders and chiefs in terms of the prospect of … mobilization and what it could mean for their access to the respective National Guard service members when conflict comes,“ he continued. ”And then when conflict persists, as it expands and retracts, and at some point in time, what they’re going to have left inside the state.”

title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
body:
Update 2026-10-15: I wrote a followup to answer questions and concerns.
Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:
Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called “derived data” to make operations like blames more efficient:
I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for “hard-won lessons”, and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google’s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)
I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you’re always a bit unsure if what you’re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke’s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke’s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)
But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.
Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.
For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti’s blog post for Cursor . ↩︎

title: Army looking to expand its new space operations branch amid increasing demand for capabilities
body: The Army is positioning itself to grow its space-related capabilities over the next year as officials face a growing demand for those types of assets to support military operations. The service’s June launch of a new Space Operations Branch “was a recognition of the increased not just reliance that the Army has on space as the biggest customer of space for, you know, everything from precision, navigation and timing to communications to intelligence, … but also recognition that space enables multi-domain operations and Army space sets those conditions for the joint force to exploit,” Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commanding general of Space and Missile Defense Command, told reporters Wednesday during a media roundtable on the sidelines of AUSA’s annual convention. Command Sgt. Maj. Rickey Jackson noted that SMDC is going through major structural changes. Earlier this month, more than 600 soldiers were reclassified to the new 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialist billets. “The Army really helped us with that in providing feeders, which were from the intel community, our communications community, and our air defenders were the primary feeders into the Space Operations Branch. Now, as we continue to evolve, we open this up to the entire Army to have an opportunity to come over and be space operators,” Jackson told reporters at Wednesday’s roundtable. “We wanted to make sure we brought the right people. So, as we boarded across our Army … we wanted to make sure we had non-commissioned officers that had experience to be able to come in and execute right away,” he added. SMDC has been moving to fill roles in the new branch while allowing for future expansion, Jackson suggested. “Even though there was a marker that we wanted to meet, we didn’t select everyone, and we left room for growth so that we do have that pipeline to be able to grow,” he said. “In the beginning, there was a target number, and because of the interests across the Army, that number grew, right, almost doubled in size, which is a good problem to have. And just to give you a marker, we’ll use sergeants major just for an example, I’m authorized nine and I only filled … five. [That] just gives me an opportunity for master sergeants to grow talent into those billets, and gives us an opportunity to kind of view out what critical positions we want to fill in the future with the right people versus just putting people in. So that’s an example of how we look at talent, and then how we can grow into positions across the command,” Jackson said. The Army projects that there will be nearly 700 (40A) officers and 1,000 (40B) enlisted soldiers in the branch by the end of fiscal 2027, according to a fact sheet. “We’re focusing across the Army and messaging and campaigning to bring in more of our junior soldiers. So that’s where I need to provide a little bit more effort,” Jackson said. Two of the Army’s key contributions for military space operations include capability integration to enable Army and joint ops on the ground and “interdiction” of adversary assets with electronic warfare systems, according to officials. “In the Pacific, for example, we have space capabilities that we’re going to operate in the first and second island chain that need to be able to provide survivable capabilities to interdict adversary use of space,” Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of TID-Space Superiority at SMDC, told reporters at Wednesday’s roundtable. He likened soldiers’ ability to target adversaries in the space domain to their ability to target ships at sea with land-based assets. Mroszczyk also touted the Army’s planning contributions to the joint force. “That’s a big aspect of some of the formation growth that we’re bringing is not just in the actual weapons platform, but on the space control planning teams and our ability to integrate that capability. That’s something unique to 1st Space Brigade, where we have space control planning teams and space control planning sections who perform the planning and the current operations function for space interdiction,” he said. SMDC serves as the Army service component to U.S. Space Command, which is one of the military’s combatant commands. “The role that the Army plays in the space domain is distinct from what the Space Force guardians do. You know, primarily they’re focused on ensuring that our nation maintains space superiority, and what we want to do is bring those space capabilities to bear in the tactical environment. So, we work very closely together and often under the authorities that [Spacecom boss] Gen. [Stephen] Whiting and his command has, but we’re focused … on enabling joint operations on the ground,” Rafferty said. Amid the conflict with Iran, a significant portion of the Army’s space forces are forward deployed to the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility in the Middle East, according to the SMDC chief. “We have, you know, space control companies and then space support planning teams … that are integrated into multiple echelons of commands forward. So, we have Army space that’s embedded working with Centcom, working with U.S. Army Central. There are, you know, space support element that’s in the 82nd Airborne Division that’s organic to that. So, space is really, you know, embedded in every single echelon there,” Rafferty told reporters. The Army space community is also growing its formations, Mroszczyk noted. The service’s 4th Multi-Domain Task Force stood up last week at Fort Carson, Colorado. That unit will be focused on the Pacific region where China is viewed as a strategic competitor. “That formation includes a space control company within that MDTF. So that’s additional space capacity for the Army that’s grown just this year, and that’s going to continue to get up to full operational capability,” Mroszczyk said. The Army is also setting up a Theater Strike Effects Group. “By next year at AUSA, we expect that there will be some formation out there in the Theater Strike Effects Group that is supporting U.S. Army Pacific and again growing capabilities for space interdiction to meet the demand,” Mroszczyk told reporters. Officials see a role for soldiers in supporting high-altitude operations at 60,000-100,000 feet. “What I’m pushing for is a family of stratospheric systems that really covers smaller size all the way up to larger size types of platforms in terms of balloons, and what that enables us to provide is space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain,” Mroszczyk said. Such systems could carry payloads for sensing, communications or extending the military’s “launched effects” portfolio, he noted. Multiple experiments are expected to be conducted over the course of the coming year, he told reporters. Mroszczyk noted that there will also be command-and-control experiments at the Project Convergence Capstone 7 event next year. “We’re also working on a virtual space training environment that complements that, that allows us to be able to do live, virtual and constructive [training] … moving forward to help train our warfighters in that environment. And we’re building the virtual space layer to be able to visualize and understand how space effects can play in modern multi-domain operations,” he said. Rafferty suggested that he expects SMDC to continue to evolve. “We anticipate when we get together next year that we’ll have maybe some growth to talk about and some new capabilities that have been fielded. We won’t be the same next year as we are today,” he told reporters. The post Army looking to expand its new space operations branch amid increasing demand for capabilities appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) recorded 222 combat engagements along the front line throughout Wednesday, Oct. 14, with the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes seeing the most intense fighting again.
The figures come from the General Staff’s evening operational update which ended at 10:00 p.m. local time.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Over the course of the day, Russia carried out one missile strike, 58 airstrikes, and dropped 190 guided aerial bombs (KABs). Russian forces also deployed 5,221 kamikaze drones and shelled Ukrainian positions and settlements 1,736 times, according to the AFU.
Russian forces launched 29 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis, trying to advance near Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Chernihivka, Svitle, Dobropillia, Novohryshyne, Hulive, Serhiivka, Myrne, Molodetske, Muravka and Novopavlivka.
According to preliminary estimates, the Ukrainian military eliminated 68 Russian soldiers and wounded 14 on the axis, while also destroying 11 vehicles, four pieces of special equipment and three shelters.
The AFU damaged two vehicles, an artillery gun, a drone control point and 37 personnel shelters as well.
About 164 drones of various types were destroyed or suppressed, according to the General Staff.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, Ukrainian Defense Forces repelled 19 assaults near Kostiantynivka and toward Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Novopavlivka, Toretske, Hruzke, Vilne and Molodetske, with fighting still underway at the time of the report.
Russian forces made 15 attempts to improve their positions on the Kupiansk axis, attacking toward Radkivka.
Five attacks were repelled on the Lyman axis, toward Lyman and near Masliakivka, and two near Kryva Luka on the Sloviansk axis.
No assaults were recorded on the Kramatorsk axis, according to the General Staff.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Russian armed forces attacked 10 times near Izbytske, Ternova, Okhrimivka and Chuhunivka and toward Zakharivka, Chorne and Mala Vovcha.
At the time of the report, five of those assaults were still ongoing.
On the Northern Slobozhanskyi and Kursk axes, the General Staff recorded two Russian assaults and one airstrike using a KAB. According to the report, Russian forces shelled multiple Ukrainian positions and settlements at least 44 times, twice with multiple-launch rocket systems.
In the south, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled 13 attacks on the Huliaipole axis near Rybne, Ternuvate, Rivne, Vozdvyzhivka, Hirke, Verkhnia Tersa, Novoselivka and Omelnyk.
Russian forces attacked four times toward Pavlivka and Stepnohirsk on the Orikhiv axis and once toward Berezove on the Oleksandrivka axis.
No assaults were reported on the Dnipro axis and no significant changes were recorded on other axes, the General Staff said.

title: Darfur and Kordofan face rising famine risk, IPC warns
body: Sudan faces a growing risk of famine in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan as conflict, displacement and severe drought worsen food insecurity and malnutrition, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said on Monday. New evidence points to deteriorating nutrition conditions in several localities, including areas previously identified as at risk of famine in a worst-case scenario for October 2026 to January 2027, the IPC said in an alert. The warning comes as humanitarian operations face severe funding shortages, insecurity and restrictions on aid access, particularly in Greater Kordofan, limiting efforts to reach people in need. In Greater Darfur, 13 of 17 nutrition surveys conducted since January recorded critical levels of global acute malnutrition, while six found prevalence above 20%, according to the report. A survey conducted in August and September in four camps for internally displaced people in Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, found global acute malnutrition among children aged six to 59 months at 38% in one camp and 30.8% in another. Nearly a quarter of households surveyed reported severe hunger, while about two-thirds had poor food consumption scores. Death rates were at emergency levels, the report said. In Nyala, the proportion of children accessing nutrition services who were admitted for severe acute malnutrition rose from 5.2% in January to 11.4% in August. In Kas locality, the proportion increased from 4% to 17.4% between January and June. Admissions for severe acute malnutrition in Um Baru, North Darfur, remained nearly twice the levels recorded in 2025. In Al Malha, admissions increased more than eleven-fold, while At Tina and Kernoi also reported high numbers, the IPC said. North Darfur continues to face severe food insecurity, with delayed rains damaging crops and forcing displaced farmers to rely on markets for food. Food stocks are critically low, and high prices reflect increasing scarcity. Tawila, which hosts more than 650,000 internally displaced people, could receive further arrivals as people flee neighbouring areas in search of food, water and basic services, the report said. Conflict threatens harvests More than 300,000 people have been displaced across Greater Kordofan since October 2025, disrupting agricultural activities and limiting access to livelihoods, according to the IPC. Fighting in North Kordofan has driven farming communities towards El Obeid, where damaged infrastructure, strained services and restricted humanitarian access have increased pressure on residents and displaced people. In South Kordofan, fighting in Heiban locality and attacks on Kauda and surrounding villages have displaced thousands during the planting season, forcing people into remote areas of the Nuba Mountains where poor rainfall is further undermining agricultural production. The IPC cautioned that lower numbers of malnutrition admissions reported in North and South Kordofan did not necessarily indicate improved conditions, citing limited access to health services and gaps in reporting. Severe drought associated with El Niño is compounding the effects of the conflict. Poor vegetation growth was recorded across 64% of croplands in North Darfur and about half of croplands in South Darfur, West Kordofan and South Kordofan, the report said. Severe water deficits affected all or nearly all croplands in the four states, leaving limited prospects for agricultural recovery. Failed rains and poor crop growth are expected to reduce harvests, push cereal prices higher and cut household incomes from farming and livestock. The post Darfur and Kordofan face rising famine risk, IPC warns appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: OpenCode 2.0
body:
OpenCode 2.0 is a major over haul. It draws on mil lions of daily users' expe ri ence to deliver a system that can flex to every thing an agent needs to be. There are quite a lot of new fea tures, per for mance improve ments, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impact ful user-facing changes.
From the begin ning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not some thing it took advan tage of by default and was mostly used by power users.
In 2.0 this server now auto mat i cally runs as a single back ground process on your machine. When you open up a TUI, the web inter face or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process.
If you're using the pro gram matic client @opencode/client to make your own scripts, they will autodis cover the local service and just work. This is par tic u larly useful for sched uled tasks. You can also call it via CLI by using opencode api com mands.
You can expose it to other hosts and run /pair or opencode pair to connect it to other appli ca tions. We have native apps in the works that take advan tage of this flow.
The old API grew hap haz ardly as we and the world col lec tively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad.
We started from scratch and exam ined all the weird use cases across the mil lions of users who use OpenCode every day. It now sup ports nearly any thing you need to be able to do.
OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git work tree when start ing new work.
We've also shipped a new client package @opencode/client that con tains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect.
The models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advan tage of that more than any other coding agent. We've built a minimal JavaScript inter preter in the @opencode/codemode package.
This package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI end points, con vert ing them into func tions that the agent can call in a script. It can run these scripts natively without the com plex ity of Node.js VMs or embed ding com pli cated solu tions like QuickJS.
This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool, map over the results and call another tool. Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time.
All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into code mode by default. This means you can add a thou sand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will dis cover and compose them to get things done.
The latest batch of models are incred i bly good at orches tra tion and it is impor tant for har nesses to let them express the full extent of that capa bil ity.
First, we've added back ground sub agents. This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it con tin ues.
This happens auto mat i cally but you can also trigger it man u ally - even with a dif fer ent model. It lets you do things like âspawn a back ground fable sub agent to review this codeâ while you keep prompt ing.
Second, we've added back ground shell com mands. The shell tool can be invoked asyn chronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent. It'll be noti fied when things are com plete.
If any fore ground shell command or sub agent takes longer than you expect, you can hit a hotkey to move them to the back ground so you can keep prompt ing.
Although OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system, it never got the atten tion it needed. To correct that, we forced our selves to imple ment nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an inter nal plugin and there are now 80+ of them. This guar an tees that the Plugin API stays well main tained.
We've also pro moted TUI plugins from exper i men tal to stable. Since it is all powered by OpenTUI, you can build nearly any thing. Here is an example of some thing useless.
We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded. So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away - we covered the design of this in a previous blogpost .
You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to. But if you do want to read the docs, they are available here .
OpenCode can also now be used as a library with the @opencode/sdk package. This is the exact same code that powers our CLI.
This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in spe cial ized envi ron ments like Durable Objects. And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the stan dard OpenCode server pro to col.
It also has an optional Effect-based API.
This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can already use it .
To upgrade the CLI, make sure you're on the latest 1.x release, then run opencode upgrade --major .
To upgrade your desktop app, download the latest here .
There are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible. It is worth pointing OpenCode at this doc so it can migrate things for you.

title: Ukraine blocks Russia from outflanking its fortress cities in Donbas, retaking 277 square kilometers and hitting 8,000 Russian troops
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has completed its Operation Vivaldi, aimed at protecting its fortress belt cities of Donetsk Oblast, which helped Kyiv preserve the region from Russian occupation for 12 years. Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, the commander of the Third Army Corps behind the operation, has reported that the fourth phase secured 101 km² of territory. Among the latest achievements is the liberation of three settlements—Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi. The operation's main objective was to move Ukrainian troops into more advantageous defensive positions, Biletskyi said in the first days after the operation was made public. Vivaldi has now summed up the results of all four phases: Ukraine has established full control over 16 settlements, liberated 277 km² of territory, and inflicted 8,000 casualties on Russian forces. Ukraine worked against Russia's deadline During Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainian forces have prevented Russian troops from outflanking the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration and cutting the Kharkiv–Sloviansk highway, a key supply route for Ukraine’s forces in Donbas, Biletskyi says. “We thwarted the offensive of the Zapad grouping and forced it to redeploy some units of the 1st Tank Army, which eased pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi,” Biletskyi announces. Previously, the Institute for the Study of War noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin was confident that Russian forces would be able to seize the entire Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026 — the Kremlin’s latest deadline for achieving this goal. Ukraine’s military was on a mission to prevent this. Season one: clearing russian infiltration groups On 15 September 2026, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps announced Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk Oblast. During the first phase, Ukrainian troops cleared Russian groups from 75 km² of territory and liberated another 10 km². The Third Army Corps said it had struck Russian supply routes and fuel infrastructure, prompting Russia to relocate its fuel and lubricant reserves to Voronezh Oblast. According to the corps, Russian forces lost around 1,500 troops, more than 12,000 drones, and hundreds of pieces of equipment. Season two: liberation of Shandryholove and Derylove On 20 September, the Third Army Corps reported the liberation of Shandryholove and Derylove and the establishment of full control over Drobysheve. During the second season, Russian forces lost another 800 troops, bringing their total losses across the first two seasons to more than 3,000, according to the corps. During the first two seasons of the operation, Ukrainian troops and attached units regained control of 125 km² of territory, including 50 km² that had been fully liberated. Soldiers of Ukraine’s Third Army Corps. Source: Ukraine’s Third Army Corps The first phase of Vivaldi involved eliminating Russian groups that had infiltrated Ukrainian positions, explained the commander of a battalion in the 125th Brigade, callsign Darwin, per ArmyInform. After clearing those groups, the Defense Forces moved on to the operation’s second phase, using reconnaissance drones to detect Russian forces, he added. For this, Ukraine used UAVs and ground robotic systems. “The Third Army Corps was the first in the world to begin deploying ground robotic systems by air. Our heavy bombers deliver kamikaze ground robotic systems more than 10 kilometers behind enemy lines,” Biletskyi noted. Season three: advances near Novе and Ridkodub On 28 September, the Third Army Corps reported the liberation of Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and the restoration of control over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka. Ukrainian forces regained another 51 km² of territory, bringing the total area liberated since the start of the offensive to 176 km². Russian forces lost around 2,000 troops, and more than 250 were taken prisoner, the corps said in its summary of the operation’s third phase. Settlements Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps says it liberated during Operation Vivaldi north of Lyman, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, as of 28 September 2026. Map: ISW “The Russians were convinced that the main axis of attack was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna. This led it to squander its reserves in counterattacks along that very axis. The Russians slept through the actual strike, which was focused on capturing Nove,” Biletskyi said. Operation Vivaldi aimed to disrupt Russia’s plans in Donetsk Oblast The need for Operation Vivaldi arose amid Russian attempts to encircle Ukraine’s fortified belt in Donetsk Oblast. Ukrainian forces conducted preparatory efforts aimed at degrading Russia’s offensive capabilities, including strikes on Russian drone operators, the Institute for the Study of War reported on 9 October. Ukrainian counterattacks in the Lyman direction and east of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk were intended to complicate Russian efforts to seize the fortified belt in Donetsk Oblast, the report noted. The corps advanced gradually, reclaiming small areas instead of attempting a large-scale breakthrough.
