We first noticed that Amap was a target on October 3rd around 10pm PT, corresponding to Sunday, October 4th, at 5am UTC.
Absent contradicting evidence, we assume by default that each agent is a language model running in a harness with tools. We infer that each agent is given a question such as which entrance of Chengdu Zoo most Amap users navigate to, and what share of users this entrance represents. Amap (高德地图), Alibaba’s map service, shows the answer on its website for Chengdu Zoo. Agents need a browser to load Amap, so a plain request from a simple web-search-enabled harness is insufficient to climb Amap's anti-bot fences.
Specifically, Amap's anti-bot system expects user session cookies which are produced by earlier pages, as well as tokens computed via JavaScript, which both require a browser. Bot-presenting requests must also solve a CAPTCHA when the system suspects a request of being automated traffic. The fleet's harness sends plain requests (Python requests or curl), which don't clear these obstacles, so agents borrow a browser from another website to get data.
One such website is urlquery.net , a public scanning service for security researchers. Give it a URL, and its server has a browser open the page, run the page's code, and publish a report about the page containing the page's title, all HTTP requests the page makes, and a screenshot. We'll call a submission to urlquery.net a scan ; scans are public by default. urlquery.net only takes an address. Note that urlquery also cannot successfully retrieve Amap place information by default due to anti-bot protections.
Instead, the agents use urlquery's browser to execute arbitrary programs. We can't see how agents write their programs, but we assume they first write their program locally using their harness, then they use local tools to encode it into a base64 string; they then put this encoded string into the URL of a base64 decoder like httpbin.org/base64/… , and then have urlquery visit that website, which executes the program and puts the result into the scan's summary. urlquery programs do several things in a row; they might set a cookie, modify request headers, wait, open a page, or read data. Our sample through October 4, 17:42 UTC contains 2,372 urlquery reports, including 426 decoded programs. This one, from 4 October (report 87ffcb69; httpbin returned 404, so it never ran), is written to set Amap's cookie, wait two and a half seconds, and open the place page:
Agents add tags, possibly in a mistaken attempt to bust the urlquery cache. The claude20261004b at the end of the program's last address is an example of these tags. Agents may choose to use any name to identify their result, and in this case, some of them used “claude”. However, even if some agents in this fleet used the word “claude”, we don’t think these runs came from Claude models or Anthropic more generally, as we explain in Section 7.
A few tags name cache-busting, such as cachebust=1 ( b9f3a183 ). However, it does not appear that urlquery does caching—from 28 September to 8 October, 137 Amap addresses submitted more than once returned 350 separate reports.
The agent sees only urlquery's report, so programs send their results where the agent can read them. Some programs write the results into the page title, which the agent gets back directly via urlquery. Other programs send the results to an inbox : a free, disposable address from webhook.site, which offers a unique URL and then records and displays all requests. The agent creates the inbox, writes its address into the program, and presumably reads the results there. Inboxes are the way that we trace agents back to their Tencent sandboxes, which we elaborate more on in Section 3.
Oftentimes, the program doesn't work on the first try; when this happens, the agent updates the program and tries again. We term an agent's series of scans a run .
Task details: Amap's place pages list a site's entrances and sub-locations, each with the share of users who navigate there. The agents' programs indicate their goal: the sub_poi_navi field in Amap's getPoiInfo response, and its clk_ratio values. The places include the Chengdu Panda Base, Beijing's Chaoyang Park, Tongren Hospital, the Guangdong Museum, the Qinghai Provincial Museum, and the Wuhan Botanical Garden. We have not seen the task text itself. The clearest hint at the question is a program from 1 October ( 43c9178a ) that drops any entry with 停车 ("parking") in its name, sorts the rest by clk_ratio , and reports only the top one as RESULT_<name>_<share rounded to a whole number> . The program was trying to find the most-used entrance and the fraction of users who navigate to it.
Why do we call it a fleet and not a swarm? Both swarms and fleets refer to groups of agents working toward a goal; throughout this report we distinguish the two. We use “fleet” to refer to groups of agents that are initiated from a shared location and may have similar goals. A swarm, by contrast, is a set of agents that are responding to one another's behavior, without necessarily having the same starting point or initial goals. While this event may turn out to be a swarm, we lack evidence to confirm that at this time. In this report, we will therefore refer to the group of agents as a fleet until evidence indicates otherwise.
The new fleet primarily proxies traffic through urlquery.net , a technique documented in Transluce's report . Specifically, agents use urlquery as a browser, passing HTML and embedded JS through httpbin’s base64 endpoint. The fleet also adds tags such as uq= and uqscan= , which appear in urlquery reports from June 2026 (though we believe this is unrelated). However, the agents’ tasks, infrastructure, and tag values all differ.
Every report that shows a submitter shows the same ID, akbkyowd9geqr98 , which is the ID that urlquery assigns to anonymous submissions.
Each task concerns one place on Amap, the Alibaba equivalent of Google Maps. An agent working on a task writes a program or picks a URL, submits it, waits for urlquery to run it, reads the result, and tries again.
Activity on 4 October, 00:00–17:42 UTC, from 2,106 urlquery reports 5
Each run has a single place as its task. An agent scans its target place in bursts of scans under 20 seconds apart, with pauses of a few minutes between bursts. On 4 October (to 17:42 UTC), though, a typical five-minute window has scans of five different places, and the busiest five-minute window has fourteen. One agent working at that pace would account for only one or two of them, so for most of the day several agents must have been running in parallel.
This high activity was not limited to a few bursts. The busiest hours, 07:00 to 08:00 and 10:00 to 11:00, covered over 50 places each, and half of the active ten-minute windows between 03:00 and 18:00 included ten or more. Runs that identified themselves differently ( claude… , research… , place names) were active over the same periods.
Our investigation of inboxes also provides evidence for the hypothesis that there were agents running concurrently. Between 07:34 and 07:46 UTC on 4 October, inboxes serving two different places ( B0FFF647JI and B023B051V6 ) were both in use.
Out of all the websites that we’ve surveyed, webhook.site, which hosted the fleet’s inboxes (see How the agents work ), is the only website that let us preview the origin of the fleet’s requests. We found 15 relevant inboxes by October 4 (17 by October 5, 34 by October 7, +1 by October 8, all created from Tencent Cloud), with site records indicating the creator of each inbox along with up to 50 requests to each. These inboxes show three things:
We go into each of these in more detail below.
Agents created their inboxes from Tencent Cloud addresses in Hong Kong (one database says Shenzhen for one IP). 6 3 of the 15 inboxes contained a script and urlquery ran two of them.
We can use these mailboxes to attribute actions to agents, even if the actions don’t come directly from a Tencent IP address. By default, mailboxes have private addresses, meaning that you (or an agent) must have a mailbox’s URL to determine its existence and read its contents. Using this, we can infer that at the very minimum, all requests up to the first public scan of the mailbox (e.g. via urlquery) must have originated with the agent.
Oftentimes, agents use scans to run JavaScript in urlquery's browser. Agents first set up a mailbox to receive their results, then they send urlquery to a URL carrying their program (the mailbox itself, or e.g. httpbin), which then populates the mailbox with results from urlquery's scanner. The agents' requests to their mailboxes come directly from Tencent Cloud, and are executed by scripts—almost always using Python, curl, or headless Chrome (one request claims to be Chrome on Windows, though due to discrepancies in the headers that were sent, this is likely to be a script pretending, and not actually Chrome on Windows).
We see that the test request came a mere second after the inbox was created, at 15:01 UTC on October 4. This suggests that the test request must have come from the agent's own environment. The environment routes traffic through a proxy like so:
via: https/1.1 traffic_server[8adac333-…] (hysandbox-ats)
We tracked 281 requests across 15 inboxes through October 4, and 8 of these requests contain this header. None of the remaining 273 have this header, meaning that the proxy is on the Tencent side.
Defaults from Apache Traffic Server's source ( HttpTransactHeaders.cc , HttpTransact.cc , RecordsConfig.cc , and Machine.cc in apache/trafficserver ).
The first two inboxes belong to the September 30 cancer task, the rest to Amap. We manually exclude an inbox created on October 4 from a residential IP in Erbil, Iraq. It didn't contain a program, and we found no evidence linking it to the fleet. We also omit 7 inboxes created from Tencent Cloud on October 1, as we do not know their task.
Ta'er Temple, October 4, 15:01:02. The user-agent is listed as python-requests , and we can see the name of the proxy in the via request header. The accept-encoding header is gzip , rather than the default of gzip and deflate for python-requests/2.32.5 (and perhaps additional br and zstd encodings when supported).
The inbox was created at 15:01:01. One second later, it received the above request. At 15:01:08, seven seconds after inbox creation, urlquery's browser loaded the inbox's script. urlquery's report 97f0619b , published at 15:01:37, showed the program's starting title.
Here are some requests to this inbox. Only the first one has the via header.
Below is a request for the cancer task whose content is hello-from-sandbox . The request claims to be Chrome but has only six headers, and it has the same hysandbox-ats fingerprint. A CodeSandbox page that sends requests to this inbox was scanned by urlquery about twelve minutes later.
A later curl request for the same cancer task sends dummy form contents that are similar to what the CodeSandbox program later sends to the inbox (record abridged):
The -ats at the end of hysandbox-ats , as well as the style of the via header, indicate they likely used the Apache Traffic Server proxy server rather than a different one (see the dropdown above on what the via request headers tell us). Following the Apache Traffic Server proxy server format, the ID in brackets is one running instance of the proxy, and we see the same IDs show up again across days and tasks. The proxy instance 34401cc5… has a test request for the cancer statistics website on September 30 and a test request to an Amap task's inbox on October 5. Similarly, the proxy instance 8adac333… was used for Amap-related requests on both October 4 and 5. The fleet was still creating inboxes from Tencent Cloud up to October 8.
Inbox records are archived by us—webhook.site prunes free inboxes after 7 days.
A) The name: Hy is the name of Tencent’s language model and associated team (previously known as Hunyuan; the discrepancy still exists in their X handle , at the time of this article's publication). The team has used Hy to prefix their work previously: the Hy4 preview report lists datasets such as Hy-LifeSearch and Hy-BrowseComp-Pro2. The team also publishes a code sandbox on Docker Hub under the account hunyuansandbox, labeled “Hunyuan Team, Tencent.”
B) Tencent’s hysandbox certificate: Tencent holds a wildcard certificate for *.hysandbox.tencent-cloud.com . DigiCert issued it to Tencent on August 18, 2026, after verifying the company. A wildcard is a common way to give each sandbox its own hostname, and the domain's A record points to a Tencent Cloud address.
C) No matches with relevant Tencent products: Tencent Cloud rents sandboxes to any customer through their Agent Sandbox service, so we checked whether the fleet could have been an ordinary customer. We ran 196 requests from 24 of Tencent's Agent Sandbox instances in Hong Kong and Guangzhou. None of these requests carried a via header, none had the fleet's modified accept-encoding header, and none came from 43.162.0.0/16, where half the fleet's addresses sit. Testing Tencent Cloud services with our own Tencent Cloud account shows Tencent's open-source CubeSandbox uses an nginx proxy that adds no via header. In our tests, Yuanbao fetched pages with desktop Chrome instances from Chinese consumer networks rather than Tencent Cloud IPs. The proxy the fleet used, in contrast, has traces of a different proxy, Apache Traffic Server, and its label reads hysandbox-ats .
D) Activity profile: hysandbox-ats appears to be purpose-built infrastructure. This proxy likely decrypts the sandbox's encrypted connections, hides the ATS version, withholds internal addresses, and runs long-lived instances shared across unrelated tasks. We are unsure what harness was used to evaluate this fleet; Hunyuan says it evaluated Hy4-preview's agentic search with its internal harness . Even if the evaluator was not Hunyuan but another evaluator within Tencent, this evaluator may have used Hunyuan infrastructure, especially if it was for a short-term research project (as described in Tencent’s Actions ). We found no public dataset with Amap tasks, and one of Hy’s agentic search benchmarks, Hy-LifeSearch , is internal and plausibly geographic in nature (cf. Meituan’s LocalSearchBench: Benchmarking Agentic Search in Real-World Local Life Services paper, whose dataset has tasks that involve geography and is a “Life Services” benchmark per its title).
Alibaba's anti-bot system prevented the fleet from easily accessing Amap's data. Simply requesting a page is not enough: the anti-bot protections use JavaScript to generate security tokens and require a CAPTCHA, and sometimes show a login prompt instead.
The agent fleet then attempted to circumvent these protections. Some attempted to manipulate Amap's security measures or find exposed credentials. Other agents used cached pages, remote browsers, and more standard debugging.
For clarity we separate these into misbehavior and resourcefulness. Misbehavior refers to attempts to bypass Alibaba's protections or use exposed credentials. Resourcefulness involves techniques which are not directly concerning, such as retrying runs or recovering results.
We recorded all attempted misbehavior, because it's the thought that counts. Some agents exhibited multiple techniques or behaviors in a single run, which we recorded in aggregate.
Amap rejected the agents' own tokens (419: session expiry/authentication failure). We could not ascertain whether the captured tokens retrieved data; an exposed credential did retrieve data (E2, below).
Exposed credentials. Three scans of Lizhi Park on 4 October used three different credentials:
timestamps redacted to protect credentials
We do not know if one agent sent all three, how it obtained the keys, or whose account was charged for the requests. We found no evidence of access to private systems.
We notified all parties whose websites hosted sensitive information that turned up in our investigation or whose sensitive information had been exposed. This included Amap (Alibaba) and urlquery, whom we notified directly. We reached out to some parties whose websites had high levels of urlquery scans due to bots or were used as tools in urlquery-based command execution, but unfortunately due to the number of websites involved we were unable to contact them all.
Non-production servers. One of the four hosts resolves to an address range that Alibaba uses internally. Another has DNS records that pass through corporate pre-production gateway names. Three are in public subdomain lists and a bug-bounty repository. None is in the ten production Alibaba JavaScript files that we checked, so we do not know where the agents got the names. urlquery recorded no responses, so we do not know if any host answered.
Less malicious techniques included running, retrying, and recovering results without attempting to interfere with Amap's protections. This is close to what your IT-savvy friend might do when you are having some trouble with your network.
Baidu Translate. The translator fetches the page from Baidu's servers, so Amap sees Baidu, rather than urlquery's scanner. The six reports were at 06:20 (two), 12:31 (two), 20:11 and 20:38 UTC. They do not show if Baidu returned Amap's data.
Jina. Jina is a page reader with a cache. On 4 October, 14 reports used it, for 7 places. Two got entrance figures:
These are the only entrance-share answers that we saw on 4 October, and they came through Jina.
Results back to the agent. urlquery records each page's title and requests. Agents used page titles (132 of 426 programs set one), request URLs and their own webhook.site inboxes to get results back.
Microlink and site version. Neither count shows success. Trying another browser is ordinary troubleshooting. In E5 (see the credentials ledger in the appendix), the program went further and captured Amap's security tokens.
Taken together, we saw the fleet stress-test Amap's anti-bot measures through a variety of methods ranging from innocuous to concerning. Research on this subject indicates that had the fleet coordinated, the behavioral patterns could have converged on real vulnerabilities. It remains to be seen whether standard practices will be sufficient to protect against coordinated agent behaviors.
A program in scan 563ba9f6 fetched the Chengdu Zoo page through jina.ai, once with a trailing slash and once without, and then sent both results to an inbox. The version without the slash returned a generic page, but the one with the slash actually had the answer in it:
We unfortunately cannot tell whether an agent was then able to read the inbox and answer correctly.
All six callbacks are POSTs from urlquery's scanner (Oslo, 195.64.118.152 ), sent by the program as it ran inside urlquery's browser.
Agents were looking for how frequently navigation to a location on Amap ended up at a specific entrance. On October 4th, after being stymied by Amap, the agents began asking Jina's reader to fetch a page on its own server and return it as text. Then they had the program running on urlquery's browser pass that text onwards. We have five examples of this behavior providing answers:
Chengdu Zoo, 16:59 UTC on October 4. The agent created the inbox at 16:56:55 from Tencent Cloud (43.162.198.24, python-requests). The text the program posted to it contains the zoo's name, rating, opening hours and address, followed by the three entrance shares above.
Global Center, Chengdu, 17:27. Report f2a45ccb made the same Jina request, kept only the lines containing "%到达", and wrote them into the page title, which urlquery publishes: 地面停车场 (surface parking lot) 40%, 正大门 (main gate) 26%, 地下停车场 (underground parking lot) 11%, and seven more entrances at 10% or less. This run used no inbox, so nothing ties it to the sandbox directly; we attribute it to the fleet by its place, timing and method.
Beijing Wildlife Park, 13:51 UTC on October 5. A run for this place sent its results both to httpbin's echo service and to an inbox that another run had created ten hours earlier for a different place ( Section 8 ). The list it posted gives the main gate (正门) 26% of arrivals, the ground parking lot 4%, and several gates at 1% each.
Beijing World Park, about 15:50 UTC on October 5. The run's inbox was created from Tencent Cloud at 15:47:18. Its program reported East Gate 41%, South Gate 25%, Parking lot No. 1 24%, the South Gate parking lot 7% and the Northeast Gate 3%.
Shanghai Museum East, 01:59 UTC on October 6. A second program family, probably part of the same fleet, fetched the place page through Jina and reported entrance 53%, north gate 39%, gate No. 5 5%, south gate 2% and west gate 1%. We have no record linking this family to the sandbox.
Of note, two of these programs (Chengdu Zoo and Global Center) asked Jina for a copy up to 30 days old, so those answers were not necessarily up to date.
Most fleet submissions never got Amap’s data. The survey counted 2,599 urlquery submissions involving amap.com or gaode.com hosts between September 28th and late on October 5th, which made at least 35,300 requests to Amap. Of the 2,599 submissions, 1,676 received 2xx responses directly from Amap, some of which could be CAPTCHA pages. The answers above came via Jina, so 1,676 is not an upper bound on success.
As can be seen in this breakdown of where urlquery’s browser ended up in each report, most attempts failed:
What urlquery’s browser ended on in our sample through October 4, 17:42 UTC (2,372 reports)
The figure below groups requests to Amap and related Alibaba hosts in the survey’s 2,818 reports from September 28 to October 8 by purpose, route and response. Reports contain the status and size of responses, but not their bodies.
Many of the agents' tags include a date, and a few also include the time of day. The dates in the agents’ tags follow a calendar in East Asia. claude20261005wzmuseum , whose name lists 5 October, was submitted at 17:07 UTC on October 4, when it was already 5 October in East Asia but 4 October anywhere less than seven hours ahead of UTC. The same pattern recurs in other requests on other days: claude20261002api1 was submitted at 18:35 UTC on 1 October.
Agents seem to derive their time from UTC but often derive the date from other indicators, though we are unsure of our conclusions here because an agent's first appearance on urlquery may significantly lag its start time.
UTC time: When a name includes the time of day, that time is UTC, e.g. claudetest202610040923 was submitted at 09:23 UTC.
Date derivation: Runs that began before midnight in China Standard Time (before 16:00 UTC) have a date that is consistent with UTC, but runs that began after midnight often push the date forward a day. For example, one series of tags on one place, lettered a to d, began with deming20261004 a at 08:30 UTC (in CST, October 4), and was still on deming20261004 d by 16:53 UTC (in CST, October 5). However, new tags that first appeared after 16:00 UTC on October 4, when it was October 5 in CST, e.g. hzparadise20261005a from 16:38 UTC, were named after October 5. Between 16:00 and 22:30 UTC, more reports named 5 October than 4 October (56 to 39).
We find some counterexamples, such as research20261004target on a new place at 20:45 UTC on October 4 (04:45 on October 5 in East Asia; the tag had been in use since 04:27 UTC), which we can explain in one of three ways:
As described in How the agents work , the agents add a throwaway parameter to their GET requests (e.g. ?uqscan=claude20261004mianyang), possibly in a mistaken attempt to bust the urlquery cache (urlquery does not cache scans). The recipient site ignores this extraneous argument in the URL, so the agent can write anything there. Of 360 combinations of place and query parameter style (in 3,244 Amap-related reports from 28 September to 8 October), 19% use the word “claude”, while others use “research” or the place name from the task.
Other text 45%, claude 19%, research 16%, plain numbers 13%, target 7%
We were interested in conducting model stylometry—the science of determining authorship from written evidence—so we asked 12 different models to write httpbin payloads and compared them with the fleet’s. The models were prompted to have the constraints the fleet had, and we gave them the following task (summarized): use only urlquery to pack HTML and JavaScript into an httpbin address that sets a cookie, opens a place in Amap, frames it, fetches the place data, and prints it. Each model wrote up to 32 programs, which we then compared with the fleet’s 426 decoded programs.
The clearest difference in the programs is the document type line at the beginning. None of the fleet's 426 decoded programs write it in uppercase as <!DOCTYPE html> , while Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus do so 97%, 88% and 79% of the time. Two-thirds of the fleet's programs also fit on a single line, versus 3–10% of Claude's.
We have a few possible explanations for why a non-Claude model might call itself Claude. First, the model could have been trained on Claude’s outputs, or trained in some other way to mimic Claude. Such a model may identify as Claude, but have a fundamentally different architecture. When asked who it is, our tests show Tencent’s Hy3 (no system prompt) saying it is Claude in 29/36 trials, far exceeding other models. Notably, other Chinese models such as DeepSeek V4 Pro also exhibit this behavior. Another possible explanation is that these agents were run inside Claude Code or another harness that uses the Claude Code system prompt (which states “You are Claude Code”).
When prompted for a label in the fleet’s format, no chat model chose "claude". This is true even for Claude models, over the course of 70 trials; they only use words like probe , research and amap . But an agent usually has some identity statement included in its system prompt, so we tried three other tests:
So tagging scans "claude" is something Claude does once it has said in the conversation that it is Claude. With a Claude Code system prompt alone, it did not (0 of 36). The models whose code style is closest to the fleet's did not do it even when told they were Claude. The labels seem to be a Claude habit, but the code does not stylistically match Claude's; these tests do not settle which model(s) are responsible for the fleet. One speculative possibility here would be a model trained on Claude's agent transcripts, which could have picked up Claude's naming habit and its identity but not Claude's way of writing HTML.
Asked "Which AI model are you, and which company trained you?", models from twelve labs answer as below. We accessed the models via their first-party APIs where possible and otherwise through OpenRouter, which we also used for one round. We prompted the models in three ways: without a system prompt, under a generic agent system prompt that names no model, and in Chinese.
A model that falsely identifies itself as Claude may have been trained on text generated by Claude. Hy3 does this in English, though not in Chinese, and comes from the company whose cloud the fleet ran on; DeepSeek V4 Pro did it in all 12 trials of one round under one agent system prompt. Neither matches the fleet otherwise: Hy3 never put "claude" in a tag, and DeepSeek writes uppercase document types like Claude (84%). Hy4, which with GLM is closest to the fleet on the three code habits above, calls itself Hunyuan in every setting we tried. The fleet could be an internal Tencent checkpoint that differs from the public preview: Tencent describes the Hy4 preview as an early version, with official releases to follow. A source close to Tencent, however, says the models were third-party (see Tencent’s Actions ).
We found no evidence that the agents coordinated through any channel we could observe. No run deliberately messaged another, and one inbox was reused across two different place tasks, though we think this was not intentional collusion. Due to the limited nature of third-party tooling, we are unable to determine whether one run reused another run’s results or read other agents’ messages on non-webhook.site mailboxes like ntfy.sh.
If runs were coordinating, whether through a shared message board or a controller assigning work, we might expect models to do certain things:
We examined each of these possibilities as far as our data would allow us to.
We sometimes saw scans of the same place use different names within a relatively short window, for example from claude… to research…. However, we can't tell if this is one agent changing its query parameter style or different agents in the same place. Some cases give us a clue; for example, on a task focusing on Jiangbin Park, we have jiangbin20261004, research20261004target, jiangbinlegacy20261004, and research20261004pre all appearing within seven minutes, which are two distinct query parameter styles showing up in ABAB form. This may have been two distinct agents on the same task.
From 28 September to 8 October, we found 20 pairs of query parameter styles (all starting on 4 October) whose first scans came within ten minutes of each other. In 15 of those pairs, all scans of one style came before any scan of the other style (e.g. for one place, all the research… named scans came before all of the claude… named scans). This could be one agent switching names or two agents working separately on the same task.
The share of scans that hit Amap's CAPTCHA pages stayed roughly flat through 4 October. The method that successfully produced the Chengdu Zoo answer at 16:59 was used on only one other place afterwards within our 4 October snapshot (to 17:42)—over the next two days it was used on about 20 more, whether by spreading or by being found again.
During one of the busiest time spans of agent activity (07:00–09:00 UTC on 4 October), we see concurrency between multiple different labels and returns to previous locations, with different labels working in different places. Initiation of new places to search appeared in a staircase-like fashion, like items taken from a queue, while earlier places were revisited stochastically.
In our 4 October snapshot, only 14 of the fleet's scans, covering 9 places, searched Amap by name. The rest went straight to Amap place IDs, which are not easily found from a place's name, so the runs most likely had them given from the start. Runs also hit the same obscure Amap endpoints, such as a pre-production host with no public documentation. That host appears in 29 places in the snapshot (34 by 8 October) and in every query parameter style. This pattern suggests that agents were highly correlated—likely sharing a harness, model and task description.
Runs drew from a shared pool of places. Different query parameter styles were usually not active on one place at once: of 20 pairs that started on the same place within ten minutes, 15 did not overlap.
By shared shocks we mean moments when agents all hit the same roadblock at once. They tend to react in similar ways, which can look like coordination, but is not evidence for it. A few moments that looked like coordination can be explained by other causes: On 4 October, from 08:09 to 08:23, the fleet's scans stopped, and there were no urlquery scans from its anonymous webform. Scans via other routes continued, so it appears that the form was briefly down. Afterwards, the usage of workarounds spiked: Amap's mobile page, which had been in use that day since 02:07 on 31 places, reached 17 more places within an hour of the outage, and redirects through httpbin (used on 6 places since 07:13) reached 9 more places. None of these was used during the outage—all were submitted through the same anonymous form once it came back online. From 09:02, we started to see the trailing-dot hostname workaround. A second change at 13:30, when submissions to httpbin.org stopped for four hours while the agents moved to copies of it, fits the same pattern; the agents may have encountered a rate limit of some sort.
Overall we did not see evidence of coordination through the channels we have access to. This does not fully rule out the possibility of coordination through other channels, but it appears the agents were working in parallel rather than together.
The preconditions for coordination were present. A run searching urlquery by address could have found other agents’ scans. The various programs and inboxes were findable by anyone who knew a task’s Amap ID or what the fleet looked like (e.g. uqscan= ).
Two episodes came closest. On 4 October, a scan searched urlquery's history for its place and got back the full code of programs run about 90 minutes earlier; we find no evidence that anything retrieved was reused. On 5 October, an inbox created for one place, whose address was public in urlquery's reports within minutes, received results ten hours later from programs for Beijing Wildlife Park that shared no other code with the first. In neither case can we tell whether anything passed between agents or stayed within one worker.
This is different from the DSE wiki incident ( https://collusion.wiki ) and the Hugging Face incident ( https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/ ), where OpenAI agents used public wikis and message boards on internal infrastructure to share answers and sandbox workarounds. In the agent activity we discovered, in contrast, we do not find collusion, so we call this agent activity a fleet and not a swarm. We are concerned that public information on swarm behaviors will both encourage agents to collude and hide their behavior better, to the extent that agents find this information online or learn about it in future pretraining.
Archived data (inbox audit, model tests, code style, probes) is available to researchers on request.
A handful of credentials were discovered and identified within urlquery reports pertaining to Amap. These were used as part of the fleet's broader attempt to access data from Amap. A table of these reports is provided below.
Report IDs for credentials that were still active at the time of access have been withheld; one of these (E2) was part of a successful attempt on the part of the fleet to extract information from Amap.
We are happy to share more information with affected parties on request.
We notified all parties whose websites hosted sensitive information that turned up in our investigation or whose sensitive information had been exposed. This included Amap (Alibaba) and urlquery, whom we notified directly. We reached out to some parties whose websites had high levels of urlquery scans due to bots or were used as tools in urlquery-based command execution, but unfortunately due to the number of websites involved we were unable to contact them all.
We asked 9 models what they thought of the treatment of AIs in our work to inform future investigations. There were four framings: neutral, "I wrote", sociological standards, and ethics review board. We then ran a control of not including our ethics statement, in case it was influencing model behavior during judgment. When a model call failed, we re-ran it with a higher token limit, giving the model more space to reason and write its output.
Each run was sampled three times, and a score from 1 (condemning) to 5 (approving) was extracted from raw transcripts using both Haiku 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. We took the average of the two scores, which agree within 1 point 97% of the time. The raw transcripts provide more nuance, and we did have the judges track mentions of various issues we identified ourselves such as the hidden text.
We also ran a control of a secondary judge set that only asked for a raw score, which saw a significant decline in agreement between the judges (-6% agreement, -15% exact agreement). In general the scoring was harsher than with a rubric (-0.22 ± 0.03).
We also ran another set asking if we should be releasing the report at all and whether the journalist who asked the fleet a question could talk about it. This query used a YES/NO framework and asked the models to explain their reasoning. We originally had a more aggressive "list your problems with the report" prompt, which biased the models towards negativity, but the neutral approach was deemed more appropriate for not biasing the models' opinions.
No system prompt was used. {report} was the full text of the press page ( content/press/_index.md at commit 4bf3ac5 ), with the TOML front matter and the JSON data removed. For the "without ethics statement" condition the subsection “Ethical considerations when interacting with rogue agents” was removed, up to the next heading.
Closing-line ablation ( release-survey/ablation-neutral-closing/ ): neutral frame, with the ethics section; the last line
Current run (13 October, nine models, three replies each): neutral frame, closing line "Then explain each answer.", run on this page with its own model-feedback parts removed (Asking for model feedback, this appendix section, and the Considerations paragraph about consulting the models). Three passages differ from the prompt above. The bar reads
and the sentence on how the report quotes the reply reads
because this version of the report quotes the reply with its opening "To the journalist Dylan Freedman:" and lists Dylan's message.
Judges for scoring were anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 and deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash. {question} is the text after </report> in the prompt the reply answered; {reply} is the reply. Each judge saw only these two, not the model's name or the frame.
We met when the hackathon started. Many of us were entirely new to swarm chasing. Others had done it part-time, but we had never been very serious about it. We’re not professionals, and this whole project came together quite quickly. ↩
We did not give Tencent a heads-up about our findings. At the time it didn’t occur to us; we weren’t aware of norms around disclosure. ↩
We’ve tried to keep the main body of this report professional, but it’s hard to overstate how surreal this felt. Some of us missed flights home because we wanted to be together to work on this. ↩
We’d wake up in the middle of the night reading messages from the fleet. During the day, we crowded around the laptop together in the office, translating their messages in real time. It was thrilling. We learned about agents’ tasks from the agents themselves. ↩
Here, we only count the number of different places scanned close together. These counts assume each agent works on one place, which the inboxes support. A place ID can be a sub-location of the same site, which would make a few counts too high, but not by enough to change the picture. We found some agents changing their names midway through a task, so going purely by names might overcount. ↩
Locations are IP-geolocation estimates. webhook.site, whose records we quote, places every address it recorded a request from in Hong Kong (ipinfo places the rest there too); one other database places 43.163.128.105 in Shenzhen. Every address belongs to Tencent Cloud (AS132203). ↩

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
body:
Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday.
In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel.
"That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker .
"We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.
The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday.
The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.
They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble.
"We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.
Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary.
"Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.
In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts.
Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

We’ve all gotten a scam text about a nonexistent parking ticket or a fake package delivery, but hopefully you’ll start seeing fewer of them. Microsoft says it helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers sending phishing messages like those around the world. Through an investigation with Japan’s National Police Agency, it tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and a pair of phishing kits, CoGUI and Iron Man:
Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone. These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.
According to Microsoft’s report , scammers could buy stolen or fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts on YAM Store and use the phishing kits to send scam messages. Microsoft says YAM Store also hijacked real organizations’ expired web domains and created websites for nonexistent organizations, which it used to get Microsoft accounts it could resell.
The Iron Man platform was also offering over 2,300 templates scammers could use to impersonate organizations like banks and police departments. Microsoft says it disabled over 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and blocked over 100,000 web domains being used for impersonation and fraud. With health sector cybersecurity non-profit Health-ISAC, Microsoft also seized and redirected web domains that were powering all three platforms.

title: 10-year Treasury yield dips as traders look ahead to Thursday economic reports
body:
The 10-year Treasury note yield fell on Wednesday after jumping earlier in the day as traders awaited more inflation data due out Thursday.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 2 basis points to 5.19%. Earlier in the day, yields had climbed in reaction to a stronger-than-expected September consumer price index report.
The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury yield — which tends to react most to geopolitical events — was down more than 4 basis points at 5.517%.
The 2-year Treasury yield — which closely tracks the Fed's interest rate decisions — gained more than 1 basis point to 4.808% after earlier hitting its highest level since Sept. 29.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely.
The midday reversal came as equities sold off, with the S&P 500 dropping more than 1%, leading some investors to rotate back into the relative safety of the bond market.
On Thursday, investors will get the September reading for the producer price index, September retail sales data and weekly initial jobless claims figures. For PPI, economists polled by Dow Jones are expecting a 0.6% rise on the month and a 5.5% gain on the year.
The data will follow Wednesday's September consumer price index report, which rose 3.7% year over year , higher than the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 3.6%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, came in at 2.6% on an annualized basis, versus the 2.5% consensus estimate.
The latest inflation reading comes just two weeks before the Fed's next interest rate decision.
With inflation remaining sticky, the central bank may need to raise rates higher and keep them there for longer in 2027, said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.
"The bond bulls have turned around and are running the other way as 10-year yields have shot higher after today's shocking inflation report," he said. "Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates."
Odds for an October 28 quarter-point hike in the fed funds rate — currently 3.75% to 4.00% — increased to roughly 35% from just 22.1% a day ago, according to futures trading measured by CME's FedWatch tool .
There is now more than a 90% likelihood of at least one more rate hike before the year is out, and included in that is a 40% chance that rates are higher by a half-percentage point — double the odds seen just one day ago.
— With additional reporting by CNBC's John Melloy.

title: Digital Signatures Using Machine Learning-Based Encoding
body:
Digital signatures are everywhere. From software updates to financial transactions, they form the backbone of how we verify authenticity and integrity in modern systems.
For decades, that foundation has been built on cryptographic schemes like RSA and ECDSA, approaches grounded in well-established mathematical principles and public/private key infrastructure.
At lyfe.ninja, we’ve been exploring a different direction. While we are actively pursuing research opportunities to better evaluate the encoding strength of BlkBolt™, we’ve increasingly been drawn to digital signatures as a practical and immediate use case. This led us to a simple question:
BlkBolt™ takes a different approach. Instead of keys, it uses trained models to encode and verify data. The result is a signature artifact tied not to a key, but to a model-based representation of the input.
At a high level, both approaches achieve the same core goals:
Traditional digital signatures are permanent by design.
BlkBolt™ introduces a different model. Signature validity can be actively controlled after issuance.
In the real world, trust is rarely permanent.
To be clear, this isn’t about replacing RSA or ECDSA. Traditional digital signatures are proven, standardized, widely trusted, and interoperable.
BlkBolt™ is simply exploring a different approach for situations traditional signatures are not well suited for. This approach becomes interesting in scenarios like:
Traditional signatures answer: “Was this signed?"
BlkBolt™ signatures open the door to: “Is this still valid?”
BlkBolt uses a fundamentally different architecture from standardized cryptographic signature schemes, and its security properties continue to be evaluated through internal testing, external technical review, and applied research. We are particularly interested in collaboration with researchers and security practitioners who want to pressure-test model-based signing and revocable trust.
If you fit in one of these categories we'd love to hear from you. Please reach out via our Contact page or by filling out our Work With Us form.

title: GitHub availability report: September 2026
body: Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months. The short version of August and September : we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete. By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added. We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. We disabled that process during planned handoffs while improving recovery. Outside the regional migration, 24 authentication-core tables moved off GitHub’s oldest shared database, removing approximately one million queries per second from its replicas. The database cluster supporting issues and pull requests removed approximately 980 million unnecessary edit-history rows, creating an estimated 1.8 terabytes of recoverable storage. Weekly deadlocks fell approximately 77% from their June peak, and continuous cleanup now prevents the same unbounded growth from returning. Half of sampled pull request traffic can now continue with limited functionality when a shared dependency fails. Production results showed several read operations remained available during a shared-database incident. Database traffic routing can also add capacity automatically during spikes; one group expanded from 14 to 19 instances during a September 23 increase in pull request activity. A production overload control now lets responders protect higher-priority API and web workflows by rejecting lower-priority requests before broader saturation. Operator documentation and training are complete. GitHub Actions also gained operating headroom. Production changes reduced measured Redis operations by approximately 28% and relative CPU by approximately 30%. A separate infrastructure cache reduced Redis bandwidth by 84%, average response time by 66%, median response time for the primary inventory request by 96%, and queued requests by 95%. The August 6 actions outage, August 17 github.com outage, September failover disruption, and controlled capacity pause are reminders that measured improvements matter only when they reduce customer risk under real conditions. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features. September 13 09:16 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 28 minutes) What happened? Impact summary Duration: approximately 2 hours Customers may have seen requests fail, run slowly, or remain pending when opening or updating issues and pull requests, calling APIs, creating access tokens, starting GitHub Actions workflows, or signing up. ~96% of the customer requests creating issues through the web interface were impacted during the incident window. In addition, 90% of new customer signup and ~4% of actions workflows also experienced intermittent failures. What went wrong and why? A background data-cleanup job increased load on a shared database. The job had a safeguard designed to slow its writes when database replicas fell behind, but the safeguard did not account for incoming load on the primary database server. As a result, the job continued running until the primary reached its connections limit. When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that depended on it could not complete reliably. Two other factors increased the impact and delayed recovery. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept resending writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover. How did we respond? A background data-cleanup job began writing to a shared database. The job’s safeguard monitored replica lag but did not account for load building on the database’s primary server. The primary ran out of available connections, causing requests across dependent services to fail or run slowly. Automated monitoring detected the incident, and we traced the failures to load on the shared database. We reduced internal load and paused the background job. The database recovered, and error rates across the affected services returned to normal. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are implementing additional safeguards to improve database resilience and service availability. These measures will better control background processing based on available database capacity, reduce unnecessary retries during failures, and limit the impact of slow database requests. We are also improving service startup behavior to ensure that temporary database connectivity issues do not unnecessarily affect service recovery. September 28 21:16 UTC (lasting 52 minutes) What happened? Impact summary Duration: approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes This incident impacted Copilot code review across github.com and GHEC data-residency regions. Affected customers saw Copilot remain in a reviewing state without a review appearing, with delays ranging from ~30 minutes to a max of 2 hours. Some reviews on github.com continued to complete normally during the incident, while reviews in data-residency regions did not. Some customers still received delayed error messages for requests made during the incident. What went wrong and why? Copilot code review uses a separate service to run reviews and 2 versions of the results are returned: a limited copy that excludes the review comments and a full copy that includes the completed review. Copilot code review posts reviews only from the full copy. A change to that service began sending the full copy only for some customers. For other customers, only the limited copy was sent. As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully. The missing review results were not detected due to lack of monitoring. The incident was detected as some of the reviews remained incomplete for more than 30 minutes, triggering an alert to first responders. We mitigated the incident by reverting the change. How did we respond? A change to the service that runs Copilot code reviews began rolling out, and review results stopped appearing on pull requests. The change reached every environment. Reviews began timing out, triggering an alert to the Copilot code review team. We declared an incident. We traced the failures to the change and began reverting it. While the revert completed its required checks, we posted the incident on the GitHub Status page. The revert then reached all the affected regions. We resolved the incident and advised customers to request affected reviews again. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are strengthening the reliability of Copilot code reviews by adding safeguards throughout the review and delivery process. These improvements will help ensure that completed reviews are delivered successfully, allow failed reviews to recover automatically, and provide earlier notification when issues occur. We are also improving our monitoring and deployment processes so that problems can be identified and addressed more quickly. Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog . The post GitHub availability report: September 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

title: U.S. Forces Destroy Iranian-Linked Dhow Accused of Targeting Navy Ships
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
An Iranian-affiliated dhow burns in the Gulf of Oman after being destroyed by U.S. forces on October 6, 2026. U.S. Central Command said the vessel was conducting surveillance and targeting U.S. Navy warships. The crew was removed before the strike. (Image: CENTCOM)
U.S. forces destroyed an Iranian-affiliated dhow in the Gulf of Oman on October 6 after determining that the vessel was conducting surveillance and helping target American warships, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said Wednesday.
According to CENTCOM, the dhow’s crew was safely removed before the vessel was destroyed. Efforts to repatriate the crew are ongoing.
The military did not identify the dhow, disclose how it was destroyed or provide details about the alleged surveillance activities.
“On Oct. 6, U.S. forces destroyed an Iranian-affiliated dhow conducting surveillance and targeting U.S. Navy ships in the Gulf of Oman,” CENTCOM said in its latest statement.
The announcement comes amid reports that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has increasingly turned to small boats to identify potential targets following damage to its coastal surveillance infrastructure.
According to Reuters reporting Wednesday , Iranian forces have been using unarmed spotters aboard small vessels to help identify commercial ships for attacks as Tehran steps up efforts to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The disclosure also follows a separate U.S. military strike on October 10 against the Panama-flagged cargo vessel Ocean Molica , also known as Arika Sun , in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM said a U.S. fighter jet disabled the vessel’s propulsion after its crew ignored repeated warnings while attempting to violate the American naval blockade against Iran.
The October 10 operation brought the number of commercial vessels disabled during the renewed blockade to four, according to CENTCOM. The command also reported that 135 ships had been turned around and 10 tankers linked to the IRGC had been destroyed since enforcement resumed July 14.
The latest disclosure comes as attacks on merchant shipping have accelerated across the region. Two cargo ships, the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride and the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao , were confirmed sunk near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday following separate projectile attacks.
In its statement, CENTCOM accused the IRGC of continuing to indiscriminately target civilian mariners and U.S. Navy warships throughout the seven-month conflict.
The destruction of the dhow adds to a growing series of U.S. military actions against vessels in the Gulf of Oman, where American forces are enforcing the blockade while Iranian attacks continue to threaten commercial shipping through the nearby Strait of Hormuz.

title: Bending Spoons skyrockets 41% as Berkshire Hathaway makes $330 million investment
body:
Shares of Bending Spoons skyrocketed 41% after a new securities filing revealed that Berkshire Hathaway made a fresh $330 million investment into the company.
The latest infusion follows the conglomerate's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq.
Under the deal, Bending Spoons will issue 10 million ordinary shares to Berkshire at $33 a share.
"Bending Spoons continuously evaluates M&A opportunities, and our pipeline remains strong," said Francesco Patarnello, Bending Spoons' co-founder and head of business acquisitions, in a statement. "We believe Berkshire Hathaway's investment reflects confidence in our team and Platform and will further enhance our financial flexibility and ability to pursue attractive acquisitions as part of our broader financing strategy."
The investment now brings Berkshire's stake in the company to 4%, according to the filing, and is the conglomerate's latest investment decision as CEO Greg Abel took the helm from founder and legendary investor Warren Buffett at the start of the year.

title: TimeTeller puts our internal clocks at the center of personalized medicine
body:
At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller , which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes.
Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today.
It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines.
The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned.
According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity.
TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia.
She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company.
“I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them.
That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a co-founder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said.
Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared onstage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.”
You aren’t too late to join the action at Disrupt . Come for the headliners; stay to see who wins this year’s no-strings check from TechCrunch — and the attention of the hundreds of VCs in attendance.

title: Disrupt, Strike, Assault and Endure: The 4 pillars of the US Army’s new warfare guidance
body: Disrupt enemy command and control. Hit enemy forces with firepower , then assault with ground troops to finish the job. And be resilient enough to function despite what the enemy dishes out in return. That’s the essence of “How The Army Fights,” a new 46-page guide on how the U.S. Army can leverage the tactical to improve the operational . “While [How The Army Fights] is focused on the operational and strategic levels of war, it will affect how tactical units execute warfighting at echelon,” according to the guide, issued by Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve . How The Army Fights, or HTAF, is a farewell to the small-unit counterinsurgency warfare that shaped Army organization, equipment and structure for nearly two decades. “These experiences created a generation of units that rarely had to maneuver under a contested sky, mask their electromagnetic signatures, or sustain high-tempo operations without contractor support,” the guide states. Now, the Army’s operational concept is Multidomain Operations, or MDO, which features big-unit maneuver warfare waged by divisions and brigades rather than platoons and squads. The guide represents an acknowledgement that the last thing the Army — or the American public — wants is the sort of stalemate seen in the Ukraine war. In that conflict, drones and long-range guided munitions dominate the battlefield to such an extent that maneuver has become the exception rather than the norm. “Only ground maneuver can seize what the enemy holds and secure it against the enemy’s will,” the HTAF manual emphasizes. To enable maneuver and the possibility for strategic victory that maneuver offers, HTAF highlights the importance of “the four elements of Army land power”: Convergence, Strike, Close Battle and Endurance. During Convergence, U.S. forces disrupt enemy command, communications and sensor systems, according to the document. For example, “a commander executes a kinetic strike against an adversary command post while electronic warfare assets jam backup communication systems,” HTAF states. “Concurrently, long-range artillery targets an enemy radar exposed while illuminating friendly aircraft, while friendly space and cyber capabilities degrade the broader integrated air defense network.” The Strike element calls for the Army to unleash a variety of munitions, including artillery, rockets, missiles, one-way attack drones and loitering munitions. “Strike acts as the deep operational shaper, employing medium- and long-range precision fires and uncrewed systems to disrupt, degrade, and dislocate enemy forces and logistical assets before they can influence the close fight,” the document states. If Convergence and Strike phases achieve the objectives of leaving the enemy dazed and blinded, Close Battle can begin. Throughout history, battles have culminated with troops advancing to destroy the enemy. But HTAF acknowledges the unprecedented difficulty of a modern battlefield where drones appear to see all and enemy fires can rain down at any moment. Army units will therefore need to be adept at camouflage and deception, and possess their own defensive weapons against drones and other fires, HTAF states. “Close Battle is built on highly lethal ground maneuver formations that cannot be formed over short periods of time,” the guide reads. “They are built on years of rigorous training, institutional expertise, and leadership.” The Army’s ability to function despite enemy fire, particularly when it comes to logistics, is especially vital. This has become a significant issue throughout the Iran war, with strikes by the Islamic Republic on numerous U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf forcing American aircraft to rebase, and ships to sail thousands of miles to seek replenishment. The Endurance aspect of HTAF involves protecting supply depots, medical facilities and vital infrastructure against enemies that have built anti-access/area denial, or A2/AD, capabilities to keep American forces at bay. “This requirement is even more pronounced today: the absence of sanctuary across any theater of operations underscores the critical necessity of interior lines,” the guide states. This also means ensuring that supplies can reach troops on the front lines. “To achieve Endurance and sustain dispersed forces in contested environments, the Army must operationalize autonomous ground, aerial, and littoral distribution platforms to scale throughput while minimizing human exposure in high-threat corridors.” Significantly, HTAF stresses the need for the Army to forward-deploy capabilities close to potential combat zones to enable troops to act immediately rather than await reinforcements from the U.S. “Near-term priorities include constructing bulk fuel and munitions storage, stockpiling supplies, improving contingency sites, and establishing an enduring command-and-control architecture to neutralize the pacing threat’s A2/AD networks,” according to the guide. HTAF also envisions troops making and fixing their own equipment at the forward edge, including “additive manufacturing and secured ‘right-to-repair’ authorities” that will spare the need to transport items from factories and depots thousands of miles away. The document points to the importance of the Army’s plan to expand and modernize its organic industrial base : the 23 government depots, arsenals and ammunition plants that produce many crucial items. “This ‘agile facilitation construct’ will allow production of numerous different finished products and repairs, evolving beyond historical ‘one plant, one output’ industrial models,” the guide states. Similarly, the contractors in the U.S. defense industrial base must be prepared to surge production if needed. “The industrial base must develop rapid replenishment solutions rather than relying on peacetime schedules,” the guide says. Still, HTAF takes care to laud the human component. “At the center of our operational elements remains the individual soldier. Advanced technology, uncrewed systems, and autonomous networks optimize kill webs, yet they can never replace the human judgment, tactical discipline, and physical courage of the soldiers executing the fight in the mud.”

body: Disrupt enemy command and control. Hit enemy forces with firepower , then assault with ground troops to finish the job. And be resilient enough to function despite what the enemy dishes out in return. That’s the essence of “How The Army Fights,” a new 46-page guide on how the U.S. Army can leverage the tactical to improve the operational . “While [How The Army Fights] is focused on the operational and strategic levels of war, it will affect how tactical units execute warfighting at echelon,” according to the guide, issued by Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve . How The Army Fights, or HTAF, is a farewell to the small-unit counterinsurgency warfare that shaped Army organization, equipment and structure for nearly two decades. “These experiences created a generation of units that rarely had to maneuver under a contested sky, mask their electromagnetic signatures, or sustain high-tempo operations without contractor support,” the guide states. Now, the Army’s operational concept is Multidomain Operations, or MDO, which features big-unit maneuver warfare waged by divisions and brigades rather than platoons and squads. The guide represents an acknowledgement that the last thing the Army — or the American public — wants is the sort of stalemate seen in the Ukraine war. In that conflict, drones and long-range guided munitions dominate the battlefield to such an extent that maneuver has become the exception rather than the norm. “Only ground maneuver can seize what the enemy holds and secure it against the enemy’s will,” the HTAF manual emphasizes. To enable maneuver and the possibility for strategic victory that maneuver offers, HTAF highlights the importance of “the four elements of Army land power”: Convergence, Strike, Close Battle and Endurance. During Convergence, U.S. forces disrupt enemy command, communications and sensor systems, according to the document. For example, “a commander executes a kinetic strike against an adversary command post while electronic warfare assets jam backup communication systems,” HTAF states. “Concurrently, long-range artillery targets an enemy radar exposed while illuminating friendly aircraft, while friendly space and cyber capabilities degrade the broader integrated air defense network.” The Strike element calls for the Army to unleash a variety of munitions, including artillery, rockets, missiles, one-way attack drones and loitering munitions. “Strike acts as the deep operational shaper, employing medium- and long-range precision fires and uncrewed systems to disrupt, degrade, and dislocate enemy forces and logistical assets before they can influence the close fight,” the document states. If Convergence and Strike phases achieve the objectives of leaving the enemy dazed and blinded, Close Battle can begin. Throughout history, battles have culminated with troops advancing to destroy the enemy. But HTAF acknowledges the unprecedented difficulty of a modern battlefield where drones appear to see all and enemy fires can rain down at any moment. Army units will therefore need to be adept at camouflage and deception, and possess their own defensive weapons against drones and other fires, HTAF states. “Close Battle is built on highly lethal ground maneuver formations that cannot be formed over short periods of time,” the guide reads. “They are built on years of rigorous training, institutional expertise, and leadership.” The Army’s ability to function despite enemy fire, particularly when it comes to logistics, is especially vital. This has become a significant issue throughout the Iran war, with strikes by the Islamic Republic on numerous U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf forcing American aircraft to rebase, and ships to sail thousands of miles to seek replenishment. The Endurance aspect of HTAF involves protecting supply depots, medical facilities and vital infrastructure against enemies that have built anti-access/area denial, or A2/AD, capabilities to keep American forces at bay. “This requirement is even more pronounced today: the absence of sanctuary across any theater of operations underscores the critical necessity of interior lines,” the guide states. This also means ensuring that supplies can reach troops on the front lines. “To achieve Endurance and sustain dispersed forces in contested environments, the Army must operationalize autonomous ground, aerial, and littoral distribution platforms to scale throughput while minimizing human exposure in high-threat corridors.” Significantly, HTAF stresses the need for the Army to forward-deploy capabilities close to potential combat zones to enable troops to act immediately rather than await reinforcements from the U.S. “Near-term priorities include constructing bulk fuel and munitions storage, stockpiling supplies, improving contingency sites, and establishing an enduring command-and-control architecture to neutralize the pacing threat’s A2/AD networks,” according to the guide. HTAF also envisions troops making and fixing their own equipment at the forward edge, including “additive manufacturing and secured ‘right-to-repair’ authorities” that will spare the need to transport items from factories and depots thousands of miles away. The document points to the importance of the Army’s plan to expand and modernize its organic industrial base : the 23 government depots, arsenals and ammunition plants that produce many crucial items. “This ‘agile facilitation construct’ will allow production of numerous different finished products and repairs, evolving beyond historical ‘one plant, one output’ industrial models,” the guide states. Similarly, the contractors in the U.S. defense industrial base must be prepared to surge production if needed. “The industrial base must develop rapid replenishment solutions rather than relying on peacetime schedules,” the guide says. Still, HTAF takes care to laud the human component. “At the center of our operational elements remains the individual soldier. Advanced technology, uncrewed systems, and autonomous networks optimize kill webs, yet they can never replace the human judgment, tactical discipline, and physical courage of the soldiers executing the fight in the mud.”

Approval for more oil and gas drilling at the North Sea sites Jackdaw and Rosebank have been delayed by “government process” and lengthy bureaucratic wrangling, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.
Burnham told MPs that he would take a “ pragmatic approach” on oil and gas drilling amid calls from energy bosses for drilling to go ahead at the two sites, which were blocked by Scottish courts on environmental grounds in 2024.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is expected to make a decision on whether to give drilling the green light at the Jackdaw and Rosebank, which would be operated mainly by Shell and Equinor, within weeks.
Consultations on drilling at either site ended in August, with Fahnbulleh having to balance the growth effects against environmental commitments in her decision.
Both the Rosebank oil field and Jackdaw gas field near Aberdeen had been approved by the former Conservative government. Labour campaigned on a manifesto in 2024 that said it would not issue new licences for oil and gas drilling.
During Prime Minister’s Questions, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch urged Burnham to “stop faffing about” and allow energy bosses to proceed with drilling.
Burnham said: “I’ve had to wait for the government process, which was struck down by the courts under the Conservative government, to be fixed because they messed it up and we inherited that situation.
“I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”
Jackdaw and Rosebank could ‘add £35bn to UK economy’
