title: LLM vs. Decision models like Jev and use-cases
body:
I ran a small benchmark on my laptop this week. Eight triage questions, four model rows, one shared ground truth. The general-purpose 4B chat model got all eight right, in both thinking and non-thinking mode. So did the best decision model. The clock is where they split: 1,035 ms with thinking off, 26,783 ms with thinking on, against 176 ms for the decision model and 34 ms for the smallest one.
That is the pitch for decision models like Jev in a single table. It is also why the pitch needs care, because the accuracy row tells a different story than it did a year ago.
A decision model takes a state and a set of questions and returns typed answers: a choice from a fixed option map, a score on an ordered scale, or a boolean with a probability attached. One forward pass handles it. No generation loop, no sampling, output_tokens in the usage block always 0. The probabilities come out of fitted heads with per-type temperatures baked into the GGUF, which is what "calibrated" amounts to in practice.
A chat model can answer the same questions if you write a JSON-only prompt, describe the schema in every request, and parse the reply back into a structured shape. It works. It costs time and plumbing.
Accuracy no longer separates the two camps. A 4B chat model tied the best decision model and tripled the smallest one on these prompts. What it cannot do is answer in 176 ms: 5.9× slower with thinking off, 152× with it on, and it hands you plausible numbers (1.00, 0.90, 2.00) with no fitted temperature behind them.
The smallest model's 3/8 deserves a look too. It filled in every answer field correctly and chose wrong: routed a billing ticket to shipping, called an angry customer not angry, rated a blocking bug as minor, and accepted secure-verify-bank.xyz as a real bank domain. Its misses were knowledge gaps. Worse, its sentiment score flipped from 0.96 to 0.04 on a reworded state alone, which I verified is sensitivity in the small encoder rather than a bench artifact. Fast and fragile are a package deal unless the model knows your domain.
Decision models are input-bound. Latency tracks prompt length: about 0.5 ms per token for vllm-d3, 0.08 for Julia. Chat models are output-bound. Latency follows generated tokens at roughly 54 tok/s plus a prompt-eval term the prompt cache usually erases. Thinking mode explains almost the entire gap in the table: 843 to 2,079 generated tokens per request with the budget on, 29 to 43 with it off, identical answers, 26× difference. The obvious knob ( reasoning_effort: "none" ) silently fails on this template; chat_template_kwargs: { enable_thinking: false } is the one that works.
Caching flips the comparison for long inputs. A bidirectional decision pass renders the whole prompt every request, so warm and cold measurements match within noise. A chat model replays a cached prompt, so the same 1,205-token state costs 807 ms warm and 2,448 ms cold. At 2.2k tokens vllm-d3 always sits at 901 ms; the chat model beats it warm and loses to it cold by 2.7×. A unique long state, which is what production usually sends, is where the decision model wins.
Routing and orchestration is the most cited case: deciding which LLM to call (large model or small), which tool or sub-agent to invoke, and whether a sub-agent should interrupt its parent. When2Call is the dedicated benchmark for that last question.
High-volume classification follows. Support tickets (one report: 49 of 50 correct), email intent (Banking77: 94.5%), sentiment, article tagging, SOC triage, and sorting errors without burning reasoning tokens on each line of a log.
Guardrails sit in front of actions: is this shell command safe to run, is this input a jailbreak, does this text contain PII. One caveat from the threads: with Base64 or hex-encoded commands Jev drops to around 91% accuracy. Decoding first with deterministic code puts it back near 98.4%.
Confidence thresholds work as architecture. Above 95% act automatically, between 70 and 95% escalate to a strong LLM, below 70% hand off to a human. The value used for that comparison is the model's calibrated distribution, which matters because a chat model's self-reported confidence is prose.
Verification is a quieter use: re-checking every fact an LLM claims to have extracted, catching a wrong side or sex in a radiology report template, logging decision ID, model version, distribution, threshold, and the verified outcome afterward.
Micro-decisions inside agent loops are where the savings compound. A stopping decision in DeepSearcher went from 2.23 s to 0.55 s at roughly 7.5× lower cost with unchanged Recall@5. A real-time signal scanner spends about $0.00002 per decision in 80 ms and calls the expensive LLM only on doubtful cases. Retry, stop, escalate, ask a human: each is one cheap classification.
Beyond that: home automation and Kubernetes autoscaling where a wrong free-text answer breaks things, on-device voice agents and robotics (the setting people keep calling the endgame), game AI mapping unit state to options, and the boring long tail such as CV screening, insurance classification, and search reranking. One case study reports the same accuracy as Gemini, faster and cheaper.
Generation, coding, deep reasoning, math, difficult multi-hop retrieval, open-ended answers. On knowledge and reasoning tasks general models still hold the edge: Haiku 5.5 scored 61 against Jev's 58 on the AA Decision Index, at 11× the latency and 4.4× the cost. My bench points the same direction from the other side, since the 4B chat model swept a test full of domain knowledge the small decision model failed.
Calibration holds up on classification and tool-calling and degrades on knowledge and reasoning. Confidence is not permission: 94% means probably right, not authorized to act. Compare against the baseline you would otherwise ship, a rules engine or a small fine-tuned classifier, rather than only against a frontier LLM. And mind the formula: Jev's confidence is (p_max − 1/n) / (1 − 1/n) , which is not the max probability, so thresholds written for one will misbehave with the other.
A cheap decision is not a saving until you check the outcome.

title: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government”: Musk says Trump, not SpaceX, is behind cut hitting Ukraine

His claims come amid a storm over Ukrainian reports that a speed cut had broken their frontline operations. Ukraine’s drones and air defenses rely on Starlink to steer and strike, so a limit on the network hits combat directly. Ukrainian troops reported that overnight into 14 October, the faster military package they depend on was throttled, halting a series of missions. Musk’s answer shifts the decision and the blame from SpaceX to the US government and, ultimately, to the president. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. StarShield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk says. He draws a line between the two services. Ordinary Starlink is a commercial product owned by SpaceX, limited to civilian or defensive use and not for offensive military action, which he called inappropriate for a commercial company. Their conversation took place the same week that Washington pressured Kyiv over its strikes on Russian oil refineries amid US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Moscow. The exchange that forced Musk to answer The statement followed a direct appeal. Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told Musk on X that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and pressed for more. “Removing StarShield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense. Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” Fedorov wrote, framing the cap as a direct constraint on the war. The faster package Ukraine cannot do without The ordinary Starlink Mini mounted on drones is capped at about 160 km/h, which is too slow for some missions, so faster flight requires access to the military version, StarShield, Ukrainska Pravda notes . Ukraine has used StarShield since 2024. title: Ambrosia Energy will build a 10 GWh factory in Texas to make batteries for off-grid data centers
body:
Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco.
“That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said.
The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years.
The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock.
Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX.
Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime.
Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers.
Sections of Ambrosia’s first pilot-scale power plant have been operating continuously for more than 100 days, Longmier said. The pilot is capable of generating 200 kilowatts of electricity 24/7.
To hit its cost targets, Ambrosia has been finding ways to simplify its components, including solar mounts and battery packs. By reducing part counts, and manufacturing many components in a factory, the startup has been able to reduce costs relative to buying from outside suppliers.
“We buy existing cells and we make our own pack in-house, and it has the fewest parts by a factor of about 100 compared to any other competitor we’ve seen,” Longmier said. ”We’ve been able to get to about 1.3x the cost of the bare cell compared to about a 5- or 7x for most stationary storage systems.”

title: Act before El Niño: Expert worries about deepening hunger in East and South Africa
body: El Niño, a naturally occurring climate pattern that involves unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean can alter atmospheric circulation and significantly influence rainfall and temperatures patterns far beyond the ocean, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). The WMO, the United Nations’ weather agency, says this warming is already underway and getting stronger. In an Oct. 8 update, it put the chance of an El Niño continuing through February 2027 at nearly 100%. It expects the event to be strongest in December. Regional forecasters predict a 90% chance of heavier-than-usual rain in southern Ethiopia, central to southern Somalia and northeastern Kenya between October and December 2026. Excessive rainfall could cause flooding, destroy crops, spread disease and make health services inaccessible in some areas, depending on local conditions and the season. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) map illustrates typical seasonal rainfall shifts associated with El Niño, rather than a specific forecast for 2026. Graphic courtesy of NOAA. Action Against Hunger, an international aid organization, says families in southern Madagascar are enduring food shortages earlier than usual following a season of poor harvests. Its teams are treating children for malnourishment, as households continue to endure worsening food insecurity. Cuts in aid are also making help to tackle malnourishment harder to obtain. title: Russia's Biggest Bank Sberbank Wins Approval to Trade Bitcoin
body:
The Bank of Russia has added Sberbank to its register of organizations authorized to exchange digital currencies, clearing the country's largest lender to buy and sell crypto in its own name and with its own money. The decision was posted on the regulator's website, Russian outlet Interfax reported.
The approval landed six days after the central bank put Sberbank on its separate list of digital depositories, the firms that keep the official record of who owns which coins. Holding both statuses lets the bank sit on the other side of a client's trade and also keep the ledger of that client's holdings, without sending anyone to an outside venue.
Sberbank said the depository status would let it offer crypto services in interfaces clients already use. That means SberBank Online, SberInvestments and SberBusiness, where the bank plans to start with Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT on December 1, according to its press service .
The bank has hedged that date, saying it depends on the central bank's decisions and on the secondary regulations being ready in time. Both approvals by the Bank of Russia have now arrived, which leaves the secondary rulebook as the main variable.
Sberbank ended the second quarter with 110.6 million retail clients and 3.5 million corporate clients, per its quarterly results . Plugging crypto into that user base turns a regulated on-ramp into one more menu item inside an app those customers already use for everyday banking.
Deputy Chairman Anatoly Popov has forecast that crypto trading volumes in Russia could reach 4 trillion rubles, roughly $46 billion, in the regime's first year and 7.5 trillion rubles by 2029 or nearly $89.7 billion. The bank also plans to accept Ethereum and USDT, alongside Bitcoin, as collateral for loans once the central bank allows them into public circulation.
Under the law Putin signed in August , non-qualified investors can spend up to 300,000 rubles (about $3,800) a year per intermediary, buyers must pass a knowledge test, and the central bank's draft list of tradable coins includes only Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT.
In January 2022, the Bank of Russia proposed banning crypto use, mining and exchanges outright, citing threats to financial stability. Less than five years later, it is licensing the country's biggest lender to run a crypto desk. As of today, spending crypto inside Russia is still illegal, so Sberbank customers will be able to buy Bitcoin but not pay for products with it.
Firms already on the registers have until September 1, 2027, to bring their operations fully in line with the new law, the central bank said .

title: Supreme Court declines to hear the case of a lobster fisherman who opposes boat tracking
body: PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — The Supreme Court has declined to hear the case of a lobster fisherman who alleged the government requiring commercial fishing boats to use electronic tracking devices amounts to unreasonable search and seizure. Maine lobster fisherman Frank Thompson sued after his state began requiring all federally permitted lobstermen to install GPS trackers on their boats to collect data that will help manage the industry. Thompson appealed to the high court after losing at the appeals court level. The Supreme Court formally denied Thompson’s petition on Oct. 5. The decision allows the state to collect “critically important” data, said Carl Wilson, commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources. “It will inform the lobster stock assessment, enhance offshore enforcement, and support better decision-making in a range of federal management contexts,” Wilson said in a statement. Thompson’s lawsuit raised questions about the limits of government surveillance and the ways commercial fisheries are managed. Pacific Legal Foundation, which represented Thompson, said in a Tuesday statement that “the fight over whether the government can use industry regulations to sidestep Fourth Amendment protections is far from over.” The foundation said in a blog post that the court’s decision means some 1,200 Maine lobster fishermen who hold federal permits can be tracked. However, the legal battle over government surveillance isn’t over, the foundation said. Environmental groups that have called for more commercial fishing surveillance cheered the decision. title: Aboard an icebreaker, a writer got a closer look at the Arctic's 'Sea Change'
body:
Rana Foroohar reports from the USCGC Healy (pictured above) in Sea Change. Crown hide caption
As polar ice melts in the Arctic , shipping lanes are opening up , making the region a new zone of superpower competition. Writer Rana Foroohar got an up-close look aboard the USCGC Healy, a Coast Guard icebreaker. She says that traversing the North Pole by ship — once a "largely conceptual" route — is now becoming a "real possibility" for two or three weeks a year.
"If you are taking one of these Arctic routes, you can save as much as 40% of the time it would take you to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and depending on the price of oil, that's a heck of a lot of money," she says. "China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest."
In her new book, Sea Change: America's New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Foroohar makes the case that the "High North" may become as critical to world shipping as the Suez or Panama canals . But she also notes that beneath the Arctic waters are large deposits of oil, natural gas and rare earth minerals, as well as underwater cables , which carry a large part of the world's intercontinental information flow.
"Undersea cables have become a real touchstone in wars and conflicts around the world," she says. "So you are seeing a race to lay down new cable, and who can get there fastest, and then who can potentially commercialize and even militarize areas where those cables have been laid."
Foroohar describes the Arctic Circle as one of the few areas of the globe where countries and companies can still "hunt" for territory and "duke it out potentially with rivals." And she predicts more conflict in the coming decades as the region continues to warm.
"There is going to be more commerce done through this area. There is gonna be greater military interest in the area, and all of that matters because it really is in America's backyard," she says. "I just think that everything in the High North is going to be higher priority for America in the future."
On increased international interest in the Arctic
China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest. And that's very interesting because it starts to dovetail with something that's happening in U.S. policy, which is more of a sense of we need to protect what's close to home. And so if you look at things that way, then you have the U.S. and China coming into much closer geographic conflict. Whether or not it would ever be a hot conflict, I hope not, but certainly competition in that area.
On the debate over rights to resources in international waters
There's some debate over that. There is something called the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea , which governs maritime activities, including those in the Arctic. It has ... rules about where you can mine, how you can mine, who gets what. But the U.S. never signed on to that convention. Various presidents from Clinton to Bush [to] Obama did support it, but key Republican senators opposed it, basically on ideological grounds, the notion that no international body should have sovereign right over what the U.S. does. ... And so it makes it much more of a free-for-all as to who gets what in the Arctic. And then you throw in the fact that Russians and Chinese don't always play by the U.N. rules either.
On how Arctic power struggles are part of a larger global trend
It's kind of part and parcel of a bigger collapse of international rule and a pendulum shift from globalization to something that is much more about regionalization and spheres of power ... and influence, which is exactly what's happening in the Arctic, which to me is so interesting, not only just for itself, but because it's a mirror into what's happening in other parts of the world. Some of the same conflicts over territory and mineral rights and ports that you see in the Arctic now are also happening in Latin America or West Africa or parts of the South China Sea. So it's a bit of a bellwether for geostrategy more broadly. …
And then there's this — kind of largely theoretical up until now, but becoming more realistic — trans-polar route where right now it might be a couple of weeks that you could consider going right across the pole, but if global warming continues the way it seems to be going in the next decade or two, that could turn into a month, two months, three months. And so who's going to control that area? This is what's up for stake now.
On what it's like to be onboard an Arctic icebreaker
You begin to feel and hear the ice as it is being broken by the ship. And I remember being down on the mess hall, which is a couple floors down from the waterline, and I was sitting eating my lunch and you begin to hear this shhhhhh kind of sound, like something traveling through sound, and then it becomes squeaky, like fingers on chalkboard, and you can kind of feel vibration and it gets louder and louder and you're like, "Wow, there are only 12 inches of reinforced steel between me and death." That's very sobering.
I actually touched base with some of those scientists several months after we had come off of the Healy, and they were starting to go through that data and look at it. And there is some real scientific data showing that these areas are changing. They are warming. They are becoming different than they have been in the past. And that affects all kinds of things. It affects the kind of fish that could live there. It affects wind and wave patterns that you might get, which could in turn affect things like the Canadian boreal forest fires that I experience in my home in Brooklyn, New York. You would think that has nothing to do with the Arctic, but it actually has everything to do with what's happening in the High North.
Therese Madden and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.
The audio of this story incorrectly states that the Coast Guard is part of the Commerce Department. In fact, the Coast Guard is part of the Department of Homeland Security (during peacetime). Additionally, in the audio of this story, as in a previous web version, we incorrectly refer to the Coast Guard Cutter Healy as the USS Healy. The correct designation is the USCGC Healy.

title: U.S. military debuts new Task Force Easy to enable drone tech ‘adaptation dominance’
body: The Pentagon recently established a new task force that’s charged with rapidly iterating and advancing weaponized drones and small uncrewed ground vehicles across the U.S. military. Col. Michael Penn, the Army official who is commanding the team — dubbed Task Force Easy — shed new light on its origin and Defense Department leaders’ overarching vision for it during the annual AUSA conference on Tuesday. “We’re slower, less effective. We don’t outpace our enemy and our threat in how quickly we adapt new technology. So we’re trying to fix that in our task force,” Penn said. Task Force Easy was initiated as DOD personnel have been hustling to solve technical and structural challenges associated with acquiring and deploying affordable drones and other unmanned capabilities en masse for modern combat operations. In September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a set of new policies to fuse the U.S. military’s drone procurements and real-world operational use. They included instructions for senior defense officials to launch a four-star combatant command to lead autonomous warfare , working directly with the office of the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) that was set up earlier this summer. Originally, the new task force was working under the Defense Autonomy Warfare Group . Formed last year, that organization grew out of the Replicator initiative developed under the Biden administration to advance autonomous, unmanned, and AI-enabled systems across the military domains. Notably, Penn said that the DAWG recently transitioned into the new Joint Task Force-Autonomous Warfare that is also now a direct report to the DRPM-UxS. “But, at Task Force Easy, we’re really focused on small unmanned aerial systems [and] unmanned ground vehicles,” Penn said. “Particularly, we’re focused on initially first-person viewer, one-way attack [drones] and how to rapidly iterate on that and make that capability better.” The task force is serving as the department’s lead for pacesetter work on the Chief Digital and AI Office’s Project Swarm Forge to deliver collaborative autonomy at the edge. Penn said Task Force Easy has also been tasked to stand up a drone team that’s focused on training, defining the latest tactics, training and procedures and standards development, as well as assisting combat training centers’ training and combat evaluations for the new equipment. Those involved “really believe the solution isn’t just drone dominance — it’s that adaptation dominance,” he added. “It’s not just about buying 1,000 drones, but it’s really about building institutional and industrial engine that’s going to learn, update, and build better capabilities faster than we have in the past,” he noted. title: Things to know if you get cancer in 2026
body:
I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.
Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings . The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). title: Cairo ‘not serious’ about joining Mecca pact, offer to help Saudis is symbolic, expert tells ‘Post’
body: Cairo has no real intention of joining the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and its offer to send support to Riyadh, though significant, is symbolic and unlikely to be called upon, Jonathan Hessen, a senior fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security (JISS), told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.His comments came a day after Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in an interview with Bloomberg on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting that Egypt was both considering joining the pact and willing to provide whatever support Riyadh requested in its ongoing war against the Houthis.“Whatever is being asked by the Saudis, of course we will respond,” Abdelatty said. “Without any reservation, we are providing all kinds of support.”Hessen explained that on the same day Cairo said it was considering the pact, the defense ministers of Cyprus and Greece held a trilateral meeting in Cairo with their Egyptian counterpart, which “does not necessarily bode well for the Turkish narrative that Egypt would soon join.”Each Mecca pact member focused on combating specific powerBeyond the issue of Cairo navigating the conflict between Cyprus and the Turkish occupation, Hessen highlighted that each member of the Mecca pact had a power they were fixated on, motivating their membership. For Saudi Arabia, it is the Houthis; for Pakistan, it is India and Iran; and for Turkey, it is Israel.Notably, Article 6 of the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty requires Cairo to carry out the peace terms unconditionally, regardless of outside political pressures or external treaties, and restricts it from signing future international agreements that contradict or undermine the peace treaty.Under the Mecca agreement, an attack on one country must be considered an attack on all, which could potentially pave the way for future complications given the state of Ankara-Jerusalem relations, as explained in an analysis by Institute for National Security Studies senior researcher Ofir Winter.“It's about strategic autonomy. On the one hand, it's about hedging against the US-based security architecture in the region. More importantly, it's about having an integrated military-industrial base that can address deficiencies in the West's ability to shore up support for these countries, particularly Saudi Arabia and Turkey,” Hessen said.“I do not think we will see a significant alliance emerge between Turkey and Saudi Arabia. I believe this is a form of alignment aimed at deterrence, with no real intention of implementing long-term strategic goals that could involve deploying entire military divisions to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. I just don't see that happening.”Egypt preoccupied with other challengesThough he maintained such regional alliances could materialize in the distant future, he maintained Egypt was too preoccupied with other challenges to focus on supporting Riyadh.“We will not see a reenactment of the 1950s and 1960s, when Egypt joined Saudi Arabia in the fight in Yemen. This is a new reality in which Egypt sees a whole host of challenges surrounding it,” he said, noting the issues posed by the Muslim Brotherhood, tribal tensions, and disagreements with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which Ethiopia built on the Blue Nile River, potentially threatening water supply.With conflict-rife Sudan sharing a border with Egypt, Hessen reasoned that Cairo's plate was also simply too full to accept any support that would require significant resources being sent abroad.However, he admitted that it was in Egypt's interest to ensure the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains as open as possible, given its potential to impact the Suez Canal, which is now just starting to recover after the Houthis began targeting Red Sea shipping in 2023.“They're talking about a net loss of some $20 billion resulting from Houthi belligerence, which has disrupted freedom of navigation through that very important strategic strait,” he said. “While the Saudis have asked for Egyptian support, and we saw MBS [Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud] travel to Cairo to meet with President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on September 15 – despite the joint statement issued at the time and Egypt's pledges to stand by Saudi Arabia as a founding member of the Saudi-led naval operation to ensure freedom of navigation through the Red Sea and the adjacent strategic waterways – Egypt has yet to send any naval assets in that direction.”

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
body:
A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels.
The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore .
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday.
Containers were floating in the water after the vessel sank, Pakistani maritime authorities warned in a navigational alert . It is the third commercial ship sunk during the Iran war, according to the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations' agency.
A second Singapore-registered container ship, the GFS Giselle, sustained damage to its hull after it was hit by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday. The ship has arrived at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the Singapore maritime authority said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim . But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks.
Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert.
Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait.
More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and more than a dozen injured, according to the IMO.
Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased. Oil prices closed slightly higher Wednesday.
Exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler .
Shipments from the Middle East, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed.
Daily crude flows are very volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

title: Show HN: Run AI-generated logic safely inside your app
body:
Stof is JSON with functions. One document holds data and the logic that works on it, and your app runs it in a sandbox, in-process, in Rust, JavaScript, or Python. Get started Open the playground npm i @formata/stof cargo add stof pip install stof
npm i @formata/stof cargo add stof pip install stof
The discount is a function stored in a field, so new logic goes in the same way new data does.
Any JSON document is already valid Stof. Add types and functions where you need them, and export back to JSON, YAML, or TOML any time.
Animation showing that a JSON object is already a valid Stof document: the outer braces and key quotes are removed, types are added to each field, and a greet function is added alongside the data. data.json { " name ": "Alice" , " age ": 30 , " active ": true } → data.stof { str " name " : "Alice" , int " age " : 30 , bool " active " : true } fn greet () -> str { `Hello, ${self.name}!` } Valid JSON is already valid Stof.
Stof has functions, but it isn't a language for writing apps. It's a document, and every part of it is data, functions included.
Merge two documents, pull one object out with its functions, diff two versions, store it in a database, or send it over the wire as compact binary.
It can parse new fields and functions into itself, or drop them, with no build step.
Your app adds its own functions, types and schemas live in the document, and in Rust you can add your own formats and kinds of data. Instead of designing a rules language or DSL for your product, describe your domain in Stof.
If you can read JSON and a bit of JavaScript, you can read Stof, and so can a model.
Models are good at writing small pieces of logic: a routing rule, a validation check, a transform, a tool. Running code your team didn't write is the hard part.
A library inside your app. No server, container, or extra process.
Editor support comes with the CLI: the VS Code extension gives you errors as you type, go to definition, completion, and rename. To teach an AI model Stof, give it the Stof skill . Read the quickstart View on GitHub

title: Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close
body:
Google engineer Haydn Belfield says self-improving AI remains far off, even as significant automation is already taking hold.
Google Deepmind has seen no measurable acceleration of AI research driven by AI itself, according to Belfield. That doesn't mean significant automation isn't happening already: AI now writes more than 75 percent of production code. But about 88 percent of code changes still need human oversight or review, and every change is reviewed by a human before submission, according to Belfield. The share of code changes fully delegated to AI rose from 7.5 to 11.9 percent.
The more complex and time-consuming a task gets, the less likely AI is to handle it on its own . Across 1,389 internal Argon agent runs, the success rate without human input dropped sharply as complexity increased. Humans remain essential for creative research, novel experiment design, diagnosing subtle training instabilities, and long-term planning, Belfield said . A survey of twelve senior Deepmind researchers confirmed the pattern, with automation running highest for well-defined, verifiable tasks and lowest for open-ended scientific ideation. Ad
On Deepmind's in-house benchmark RE-Bench, which includes 74 realistic ML engineering tasks, Argon solves about half of them. That's a big jump from Gemini 3.7 Flash at 27 percent, but it's still far from the near-perfect performance full automation would require. Ad
To track progress systematically, the team built a General Capability Index (GCI) covering 123 models and 92 benchmarks. Gemini model capabilities are growing at a steady pace of about 0.1 GCI points per month, with no significant change in speed. The team attributes Gemini 4 Argon sitting slightly above the trend line to more compute and organizational investment rather than AI-driven acceleration.
The team currently rates the risk from AI-driven research automation as low but is building the measurement infrastructure to track signs of acceleration going forward. Ad
Belfield's findings align with recent research , but not everyone in the field agrees. More than 20 AI researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and OpenAI's Jakub Pachocki, recently warned of a possible "intelligence explosion" in a research paper. They argued that AI systems could automate all AI research and development within a few years, compressing what would normally be years of progress into just months.

title: Solana Sets a Date for Its Next Major Upgrade
body:
Solana has locked in October 21 for Alpenglow, a full replacement of the system its validators use to reach consensus. The switch is tied to epoch 1064, which the Solana Foundation expects to begin around 15:00 UTC that Wednesday.
Alpenglow retires TowerBFT, the current system the network uses, and aims to make transactions final in roughly 150 milliseconds. Finality is the moment a transaction becomes irreversible, and under TowerBFT that currently takes about 12.8 seconds.
On Solana today, a payment is confirmed pretty quickly, but that’s not a guarantee. Until TowerBFT runs out its 13 second clock, the block could in theory still be dropped.
That small doubt is why anyone handling real money tends to wait out the full window. With finality at around 150ms, the irreversible answer arrives almost as fast as the optimistic one, which is what a checkout counter taking SOL or a DeFI application, or a trading desk settling a position actually needs.
TowerBFT works by having validators post their votes as on-chain transactions, and a block only counts as final once 32 slots’ worth of those votes pile up. Votor, the voting protocol shipping with Alpenglow, takes votes off the chain, so validators message each other directly, package the votes into certificates, and can lock in a block after a single round of voting, or two at most.
When 80% or more of stake backs a block in the first round, it finalizes on the spot. If support lands between 60% and 80%, a second round with 60% thresholds decides whether the block is finalized or skipped, and the Foundation says the design tolerates 20% malicious stake plus another 20% offline.
Alpenglow goes live on mainnet-beta Wednesday, October 21, ~14:50 UTC.
18 months of work for a migration that happens in one slot. Finality drops from seconds to ~150ms.
Make sure to follow us @anza_xyz as we countdown to go-live.
Ordinary users don’t need to do anything, and wallets and apps should behave as they do now. The Solana Virtual Machine, transaction formats, programs, and fees are left alone, while for developers the “confirmed” and “finalized” commitment levels become one and the same.
Each vote account also needs 0.8 SOL on top of its rent-exempt balance to pay the new Validator Admission Ticket, a per-epoch fee of the same size that gets burned. It replaces the roughly 1 SOL per epoch validators spent on vote transaction fees under TowerBFT, and a validator that can’t cover it sits out voting and block production for the following epoch.
The feature gate turns on as epoch 1064 begins, yet TowerBFT stays in charge for another 5,000 slots, roughly 18 minutes, before Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. This assures stability and prevents any issues during transition.
Validators approved Alpenglow in September 2025, when the SIMD-0326 proposal passed with 98.27% of votes cast in favor. In May, Anza Lead Economist Max Resnick told Decrypt the team was looking at a late Q3 or early Q4 mainnet activation, so everything is going according to schedule.
October 21 delivers only Votor, the first half of Alpenglow. Rotor, a replacement for Turbine, the system Solana uses to broadcast block data between validators, comes later and still has no date.

title: U.S. Army Aviation Center of Excellence Wants Recon Drones With Multiple Sensors
body:
In decades past, the U.S. Army would use “pink teams” and “heavy weapons teams” in which Boeing [BA] AH-64 Apaches served as a shield for Bell [TXT] OH-58D Kiowa Warrior scout helicopters. The Army then moved to RQ-7 Shadow drones as reconnaissance stand-ins when the service retired the OH-58D in 2017.
In future manned-unmanned teaming, the Army wants to field en masse drones that have multiple sensors on them.
“When we lost the 58Ds, we put in Shadows–a great platform, but that did not drive the integration and interoperability we need to go out and fight,” Army Maj. Gen. Cain Baker, the commander of the Army Aviation Center of Excellence (COE) at Fort Rucker, Alabama said during a Wednesday panel discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army conference in Washington, D.C. “As we look at the manned-unmanned aspect of that, we need systems that we can deploy in mass and have multiple sensors–not just RF [radio frequency] and EO/IR [electro-optical/infrared].”
“We need collaborative behaviors that we’re able to operate with those systems out in front of us so we know how how they’re going to react, and we can use that to fight with our manned assets,” he said. “We’ve got to have network capability out to the tactical edge.”
The Army has said that it wants replacements for Textron ‘s [TXT] RQ-7 Shadow in the Group 3 unmanned aircraft system (UAS) category and General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. ‘s MQ-1C Gray Eagle drones in UAS Group 4 for Army division and corps-level reconnaissance ( Defense Daily , Aug. 12, 2025).
“At the end of the day, there’s an interdependence we have to have between those [replacement drone systems] and our manned platforms,” Baker said.
Acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve designated Fort Rucker as the UAS Autonomy Center of Excellence ( Defense Daily , Oct. 13).
“I tell people I will feel complete as the COE commander when I walk outside of Fort Rucker, and I see a Group 3 UAS leading out to the training area with an Apache or a Black Hawk,” Baker said on Tuesday.
For all echelons, the Army wants information exchange among drones and manned platforms. Having multiple iPads on helicopters leads to information overload for pilots and is not the right path, Baker said.
“We’re putting stuff in the cockpit today–a lot of generating stuff,” he said. “This is not where we need to have our pilots–multiple iPads, multiple data [feeds] coming in. The radios are increasing…This speaks to the collaborative behaviors we’ve got to have on these platforms. When they’re out operating as teams, they’re talking together, sharing multiple sensor information, they know how to maneuver around a threat when they see a threat without having to go back to a cockpit on every single spot report. On a ‘pink team,’ that 58D crew in front of me was not calling me every two seconds. It knew how to maneuver. It knew the PRI [primary radio frequency] I needed to accomplish my task. Those are the behaviors we’re putting on platforms today. We’ve experimented with them. We have tested them.”

title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
body: Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away. Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page. The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper. Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything . What maintainers need from star history We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators . After the access change, callers without the required permission could receive an empty response or a 403 Forbidden response. That change also cut off tools that had used the old response to calculate star history, often without displaying or otherwise using the usernames it returned. So we talked with maintainers and tool builders to understand what they still needed. They used star history as an approximate signal of interest: to compare activity before and after a release, or to see whether an announcement reached new developers. What they cared about was the curve. The old API response had made identity look like part of that contract because every timestamp arrived attached to a user. In practice, tools such as Star History needed counts and dates, not usernames or other user data. Once identity was no longer part of the requirement, we could design an aggregate endpoint for the actual job: retrieving changes in star counts over time at a useful resolution. When the API change disrupted Star History, users rallied around the project. GitHub’s Community team listened and connected us with product engineering, who dug into our use case and worked alongside us to design a purpose-built endpoint. A difficult situation became a constructive collaboration between GitHub, Star History, and the broader community—ultimately leading to a better solution. Tianzhou Chen, star-history.com maintainer and Bytebase co-founder Why the original endpoint was expensive Once we knew what maintainers needed, the next step was understanding why the original design couldn’t provide it cheaply. The original GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers endpoint was built to answer a simple question: who starred this repository? It returned a paginated list of people, and if the request specified a custom media type, each entry also included when the star was created. The star model was built for the same job. It records the current set of people who have starred a repository, which keeps showing a star count or a list of stargazers simple. It was not designed as a historical event log: when someone removes a star, that record is removed. When tools began using the list as a time series, reconstructing a growth curve meant retrieving individual identities and processing every current star. Because each page held at most 100 people, the work grew with the repository’s popularity: building the full curve for react/react , with about 251,000 stars, took about 2,511 requests, so tools often ran into rate limits or sampled pages instead of reading them all. Serving a page required the database to query the repository’s current stars. Due to a bug in the pagination implementation, every request also counted all of those stars to work out how many pages existed, even though the caller received only one page of up to 100 people. On a highly starred repository, that meant counting many thousands of entries on every request. In the week before we restricted access, nearly 37,000 of these count queries ran slowly enough to be logged, averaging nearly 3 seconds each, and database safeguards killed more than 1,000 of them, which contributed to request timeouts. The chart below shows what all that counting cost. title: The AI race is back on
body:
Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China, impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up.
Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game.
Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China.
A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research.
Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends.
Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier.
That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier.
The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta.
All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long.
If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

title: EU authority classifies Circle’s USDC as ‘significant’ under MiCA
body:
The second-largest stablecoin by market cap will be overseen by French and EU authorities under its classification as a “significant e-money token.“
The European Banking Authority (EBA) has classified Circle’s USDC stablecoin as a significant e-money token under the region’s Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) framework.
In a Wednesday notice, the banking regulator said the e-money token classification, granted to only 45 other projects, effectively means the USDC stablecoin will be jointly overseen by the EBA and France’s supervisory authority, the Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel et de Résolution. The stablecoin is the second largest by market capitalization, at $73 billion compared to Tether USDt’s $184 billion.
The “significant“ classification came as many EU-based token issuers pushed for regulated US dollar-pegged stablecoins in the region. Stable Mint CEO James Bennett told Cointelegraph that while Europe couldn’t “wish away“ dollar stablecoins, regulators could control safeguards and rules for issuers.
“For European corporates to make cross-border payments globally, offering only a euro stablecoin isn’t enough,” AllUnity CEO Alexander Höptner told Cointelegraph.
As authorities and issuers move closer to embracing dollar stablecoins, policymakers at the European Central Bank continue to explore the potential introduction of a digital euro. The EU authority first proposed the central bank digital currency in 2020, with the potential to issue the coin in 2029 after the conclusion of legislation and a pilot program.

title: Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge
body:
A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.
Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia -backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)
Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield . Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren , popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.
Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.
The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.
One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.
"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."
The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.
CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.
"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

title: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico
body:
The Department of Justice said Wednesday it is appealing a federal judge's decision to extend his order blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico.
The notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit came less than a day after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the three outlets targeted by President Donald Trump can keep their access to the White House complex.
That ruling, a preliminary injunction, replaces Kelly's temporary restraining order against the ban that Trump first announced on Sept. 18. It is not a final ruling in the ongoing lawsuit that the three news outlets filed against Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran and White House communications director Steven Cheung.
Kelly, in an opinion filed Tuesday night, said the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claims that Trump and his co-defendants violated their First Amendment rights through unlawful retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.
"It is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," wrote Kelly, whom Trump nominated in 2017 for his current seat.
"In other words, it was 'an effort to suppress the speaker's activity due to disagreement with the speaker's view' ... rather than to vindicate any other purportedly 'compelling governmental interest,' ... including maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security," he wrote.
"Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote.
Kelly was also unmoved by arguments that the decision to revoke the outlets' White House access was partly based on national security concerns.
"There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote.
Trump did not mention national security in his initial Truth Social post announcing the ban, nor did he do so when asked about the move later that same day, Kelly noted.
"All this suggests that 'national security' was merely a post-hoc justification for the decision," the judge wrote.

title: Hiyd is a health tracker that attaches to the watch you already wear
body:
If you’re a watch enthusiast, you probably don’t want to exchange your prized timepiece for a bulky fitness tracker. But Hiyd founder Salah Batroukh doesn’t think people should have to sacrifice fashion for function.
“We don’t think that health tracking needs to be this overly conscious decision where you have to change something about the way you look,” Batroukh told TechCrunch. “That’s the ethos of the entire company. Our plan is to build out this product ecosystem of invisible health tracking.”
Hiyd’s first device to make health tracking look cooler is a small, slim disc that attaches to the back of your watch via microsuction , a material technology that allows the sensor to sit flush under your watch without magnets or adhesive. That way, it won’t leave any residue or mess with the mechanics of watches that keep time using magnets.
“Microsuction is essentially a textured silicone, with hundreds of tiny pockets per square inch molded into a pliable sheet. So when you press on it, it pushes air out of all those pockets, and you end up with a vacuum — just like traditional suction cups but scaled down incredibly,” Batroukh explained. “It works incredibly at stopping shear forces, but a little bit of prying allows it to pop right off, which is ideal for us. It’s also incredibly thin at just 0.3 mm with our manufacturing processes.”
According to Batroukh, the sensor, which measures 2.7 mm thick and weighs 7 grams, collects biometrics similar to those of leading wearables, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep staging, movement, calories burned, and VO2 max estimations, then syncs to an iOS or Android app. In order to fine-tune the sensor, Hiyd’s team is filming themselves doing various activities, then labeling those datasets to train its AI.
“We go for a walk and say, ‘This is somebody walking, this is somebody jogging, this is somebody running,’” he said. “The one thing that AI is really good at is data analysis, so we can basically fit a lot of heuristic analysis into our sets really quickly.”
On its app, Hiyd is also working to incorporate nutrition tracking. The goal isn’t to count calories, but rather to help users glean insights about how their eating habits impact their sleep quality or workout performance.
“What we will do is say like, ‘Hey, on days where you work out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m., your sleep quality is actually worse,’ and that’ll be specific to you,” he said. “Or it’ll say, ‘Hey, we think you had a less deep sleep last night because you had a slice of cake before you went to bed, and the sugar affected it.’”
Batroukh spent about seven years as a manufacturing design engineer at Apple, a company synonymous with iconic hardware. But he wanted to know if he could design something great without the support of a global brand and a multitrillion-dollar market cap.
“One of the reasons I left Apple was a lot of the products became a little bit more about being an Apple product, rather than being something for the customer,” he said. “[Hiyd] gives me the opportunity to do the exact opposite.”
Batroukh is joined by fellow founders Omar Shakir, an experienced mechanical engineer who is the startup’s CTO, and Mahamad Charawi, who is its head of software. (Charawi previously co-led the Y Combinator-backed startup Laudspeaker through its sale .)
Hiyd is bringing its tiny sensor to the big stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where the company is competing as one of the top 20 companies at Startup Battlefield on Wednesday. ( Don’t miss out on the action .) In November, the company plans to launch a Kickstarter. So far, over 16,000 people have made deposits to secure Hiyd’s first units.

title: Saving Lives on the Front Line: Kyiv Post’s Jason Smart Hits €1M Milestone
body:
Along the roads leading into Ukraine’s front lines , safety is measured in sheer speed. Routes that were quiet thoroughfares months ago are now tunneled under makeshift anti-drone netting, where Ukrainian troops must floor the accelerator to outrun Russian FPV operators actively hunting any moving target. Between regular visits, familiar landmarks vanish: cozy roadside cafes where soldiers once shared coffee are flattened into rubble, and bridges are wiped off the map.
In a battlespace where Russian electronic countermeasures shift constantly and transport vehicles are destroyed daily, off-the-shelf military gear often fails to keep troops alive. Bridging that lethal gap , an emergency pipeline spearheaded by Kyiv Post special correspondent Jason Jay Smart and security analyst Sergej Sumlenny has surpassed €1 million. This effort pooled contributions from 8,585 international donors to rush nearly 2,000 custom-engineered drones, replacement vehicles, and electronic warfare systems directly to combat brigades.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We don’t come with a product,” Sumlenny explains. “Instead, we come with the question, what do you need ?”
For the German security analyst , rapid frontline adaptation has rendered cookie-cutter tech supplies ineffective. Traditional military supply chains relied on mass-issuing standardized hardware, but the electronic battlefield moves too quickly for a one-size-fits-all approach. A commercial drone that flies reliably in one sector can be rendered completely useless ten miles away by localized Russian jamming.
Russian forces lean heavily on centralized, mass-produced systems, whereas Sumlenny works backward from a Ukrainian unit’s immediate tactical dilemma. His team engineers drones tailored to distinct radio horizons, flight ranges, and payload weights. Rather than shipping boxes through backline depots, Sumlenny personally delivers the systems to combat zones, running immediate field tests and modifying components based on pilot feedback.
Such constant presence has put him on speed dial for frontline commanders whose survival depends on solving unexpected equipment crises in real time .
This direct lifeline proved critical when soldiers from the 93rd Mechanized Brigade contacted Sumlenny after Russian strikes destroyed both of their transport vehicles. With available campaign funds exhausted, Sumlenny initially had to tell the unit he could not help. Then, while they were still on the phone, an unexpected donation from a supporter, in Germany, flashed across his phone’s screen.
“Oh, actually we have money now,” Sumlenny recalled telling the relieved soldiers.
Thousands of Donors Saving Ukrainian Lives
Behind these shipments are thousands of individual donors, largely drawn from Smart’s YouTube audience across the United States, Europe, Australia, and dozens of other nations.
“The soldiers are incredibly appreciative of all the support they receive,” Smart said, reflecting on his visits to frontline positions.
Sumlenny regularly relays donors’ personal messages to the troops, explaining that teachers, veterans, retirees, and families thousands of miles away are personally backing their survival.
Assistance has reached key fighting formations, including the 1st Azov National Guard Corps, the 4th Rubizh National Guard Brigade, the 47th, 67th, and 93rd Mechanized Brigades, the 225th Assault Regiment, and the 501st Marine Battalion. In many cases, the Ukrainian soldiers have recorded video messages, thanking donors, which were later broadcast on Smart’s YouTube channel. Night behind truck with Ukranian flag: In Kharkiv - with the 225th Assault Regiment.
Night behind truck with Ukranian flag: In Kharkiv - with the 225th Assault Regiment.
Among them, fighters from the Rubizh Brigade thanked contributors after receiving 200 drones, while the 67th Mechanized Brigade’s air-defense unit credited the online community with supplying 22 interceptor drones.
According to Smart , who hosts the largest English-language YouTube channel focused on the inner workings of the Putin regime, reaching his goal of €1 million raised to support Ukraine’s soldiers - more than military medals or other recognitions - is his greatest source of pride from the past four years.
“I am profoundly thankful to all the people who watch the channel and chose to contribute, for keeping abreast of the existential fight in which Ukraine is heroically engaged. The struggle for Ukraine’s future does not stop at its borders; it is one that touches the lives of all of us,” said Smart.
“If the Putin Regime is not crushed now,” continued the American, “we can expect greater wars that will undoubtedly spiral into incalculable costs for countries around the world, especially in the West. By standing with Ukraine today, we are making the world a better place for future generations. This is the fight of our lives.” Standing in front of some drones being delivered: In Sloviansk with the 501st Marine Battalion.
Standing in front of some drones being delivered: In Sloviansk with the 501st Marine Battalion.
Recognition From Ukraine’s Military Leadership
Beyond his public analysis and fundraising, Smart, who first moved to Ukraine in 2015 at the invitation of the Director of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), has collaborated closely with Ukraine’s defense and security apparatus. Formal decorations have followed from the nation’s senior command, including the Armed Forces’ Medal of Merit, the Medal of Valor in Service to the Military, Third Class, and a medal from the Department of State Protection of Ukraine (ODU), the agency tasked with safeguarding the president and top state officials. Jason in front of Pyaterka: Ukrainian-occupied Kursk, Russia
Jason in front of Pyaterka: Ukrainian-occupied Kursk, Russia
Defense Intelligence Chief Kyrylo Budanov issued an official citation recognizing Smart’s sustained assistance in achieving military intelligence objectives. While still Ukraine’s top military commander, General Valeriy Zaluzhny conferred a commendation for his contributions. Separately, the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security formally acknowledged his work in countering Russian state disinformation. Jason in armored personnel carrier: At the zero line entering Ukrainian-occupied Russia.
Jason in armored personnel carrier: At the zero line entering Ukrainian-occupied Russia.
Following Russian strikes on October 13 and 14 that damaged all three of Kyiv’s municipal heat and power plants, the initiative launched a €25,000 drive to supply frontline units with portable power stations, drones, and medical gear before winter.
Building on contributions from 8,585 international donors, this upcoming push focuses on rushing critical equipment to combat units facing freezing temperatures and ongoing grid disruptions.
Smart noted that supporters can contribute directly to frontline deliveries through the initiative’s PayPal link. Contributors donating over €100 are eligible to receive a commemorative military patch produced in Ukraine.

title: Ship Sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran Escalates Maritime Attacks
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy

Iran has quite obviously been surging its attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz in an attempt to wreak uncertainty and economic havoc for the Trump administration ahead of the November midterm elections, undermining a recent recovery in Persian Gulf oil shipments.

title: EU Disburses Another €2.86B to Cover Ukraine’s ‘Most Urgent Needs’ – Drones and Missiles
body:
The European Union (EU) has disbursed another €2.86 billion ($3.1 billion) to Ukraine for air defense, particularly drones and missiles, as the country nears its fifth winter of Russia’s aggression.
The European Commission confirmed the payment on Wednesday, Oct. 14, made under the defense component of the €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) Ukraine Support Loan. The funds will also cover radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Amid intensified Russian attacks on our cities and critical infrastructure, this support is vital,” Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement on Telegram.
“More drones, air defense systems, missiles, and ammunition mean stronger protection for our people and greater capabilities for our defenders on the front line,” he added, noting that Kyiv is working with European partners to secure the rest of the defense funding without further delays.
The disbursement follows one of Russia’s heaviest strikes on Ukraine’s energy system this autumn.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukraine’s Defense Forces recorded roughly 39 missiles and 128 launched by Russia, which left at least 600,000 people without power according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks – cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure,” President of the European Commission Ursula von Der Leyen said.
The defense payments are expected to reach Ukraine in the upcoming weeks.
Ukraine still has €29.64 billion (roughly $33 billion) in EU financial support available for the rest of the year, according to the Commission.
That includes €25.24 billion ($28 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan, split between €12.54 billion (approx. $14 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industry and €12.7 billion (about $14 billion) in budget support, plus €4.4 billion (about $5 billion) left under the earlier Ukraine Facility.
Budget payments depend on Kyiv meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and a memorandum of understanding with the EU.
Ukraine had received €1.2 billion (roughly $1.3 billion) just a week earlier, on Oct. 7, bringing total funding received under the program to nearly €13 billion ($14.5 billion) according to Koretskyi.
Mid-September, Koretskyi warned Ukraine risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international financing if the parliament misses deadlines for required legislation.
The government has moved its deadline for 42 required decisions to Oct. 15 as it prepares for winter pressure on the budget.
According to the European Commission, the Ukraine Support Loan was adopted in February 2026, and it provides up to €90 billion (approx. $100 billion) over 2026-27, with an indicative €60 billion ($67 billion) for defense and €30 billion ($33 billion) for the budget.
The Council approved this year’s allocation on April 23 after Ukraine submitted its financing strategy.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion ($258 billion) in total support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: IPO-Bound Tonbo Imaging Nets ₹255 Cr From Anchor Investors
body: Ahead of the commencement of the bidding for its public issue on October 15, defence tech startup Tonbo Imaging has raised ₹255.4 Cr from anchor investors. According to BSE data , the startup allotted 36.5 Lakh equity shares to 43 anchor investors at ₹700 apiece, the upper band of its IPO price band. Of the total anchor allocation, 21.1 Lakh shares, or 57.7%, were lapped up by 12 domestic mutual funds via a total of 25 schemes. The domestic mutual funds that anchored the round included SBI Infrastructure Fund, Axis Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund, Kotak Mahindra Services Fund, Mirae Asset, Canara Robeco Mutual Fund, among others. Other investors who participated in the round included Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, WhiteOak Capital, Aranda Investments, Allianz, among others. With this, Tonbo Imaging’s public issue will now go live on October 15 and close on October 19. The defence tech startup’s public issue consists entirely of an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares, with no fresh issue component. It has also set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per equity share for its ₹852 Cr IPO, which values the company at ₹4,009.8 Cr (about $480 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The startup had initially filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI in December last year. It then received SEBI’s approval in July this year. However, the company then re-filed a fresh DRHP in August this year . Founded in 2012 by Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza, Tonbo Imaging designs and develops advanced imaging and sensor systems for surveillance, reconnaissance and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, driver-vision systems, targeting equipment, fire-control systems and missile seekers. The startup claims that its expertise lies in blending micro-optics, low-power electronics and digital image processing to produce low-power platforms across visible and infrared spectrums. It counts the likes of NATO, US Navy SEALs, Israeli Defense Forces (IDF), and the defence ministry of Armenia as its customers. At the end of June 2026, the startup claims to have deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries. On the financial front, Tonbo Imaging reported a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27 against an operating revenue of ₹36 Cr. For the full fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), the startup’s revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25. Meanwhile, net profit declined 30% to ₹50.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year.
