title: Show HN: Eevo – Consequential Decision Model
body:
Eevo is Upright’s consequential decision model. It is built for AI agents that need to make judgement calls, from coding and operations to customer-facing decisions, and, we suspect, a whole lot more.
Give Eevo a decision, the options, and whose interests count. It weighs the consequences of each option and returns, for each stakeholder, the option with the highest expected value, and a calibrated probability for every option.
A monitoring agent sees checkout conversions drop 15% at 2am, an hour after a release, and asks Eevo whether to page the engineer, roll back or keep watching. Each option’s consequences are sized on one scale, benefits in teal and harms in purple. The dot and line give the option’s expected value and its 10th to 90th percentile range, and the percentage is how often the option has the highest expected value across Eevo’s draws. Rolling back first comes out best: 0.93, best in 64% of draws.
And why does this matter? Because the real world doesn’t follow rules.
Every day, agents (like humans) encounter situations nobody anticipated, and they still have to choose: a fix that helps some customers but risks others. A refund that falls outside policy. Saving today vs. saving in the future.
These cases need to be handled based on their consequences, not predefined rules. Eevo weighs the trade-offs in seconds, for $0.15 per decision, and records whose interests were prioritised and where they conflicted.
The result is better choices in your agents’ tasks, a record of each one, and agents that need people less often. Eevo identifies the most uncertain cases, so only those go to people, and teams ship faster. When those questions go to people, they get a clearly structured list of pros and cons for each stakeholder, each one sized, making tradeoffs visible, and helping also humans make better decisions when steering agents.
Eevo is designed to work with your agent. Your agent provides the decision context, the options, and the consequences for those options. Eevo sizes each one, models how they overlap, and computes the expected value of each option. Eevo is available through MCP, API, and the Eevo console.
Upright is perhaps an unlikely company to be releasing an AI model. We are around 30 people in Finland, and most folks in Silicon Valley have never heard of us. Fair enough.
But for nine years, we’ve built models that quantify the positive and negative impacts companies have on people and the planet, across 800 impact categories. Our data is today trusted by financial institutions managing over €1 trillion in assets.
At the heart of that work is a close to impossible challenge: making very different outcomes comparable.
Turns out, AI agents have the same problem. That’s why we built Eevo.
We can’t wait to see what you solve with it.
Upright founders introduce Eevo, the first consequential decision model.
Language models generate text. Decision models classify options. Consequential decision models choose options based on their consequences.
A generative model writes its answer one token at a time. It is flexible and fluent, and it writes a new answer every time, with its confidence stated, if at all, in prose that software then has to parse.
A decision model answers a typed question about a state, such as yes or no, a choice or a score, in a single forward pass, with a calibrated probability for each option. Its output is built for agents and software to act on.
Eevo, a consequential decision model , goes beyond choosing. It is a decision model built for comparing outcomes. It learned to size consequences in training, to model how they interact and overlap, and to return calibrated probabilities for the option with the highest expected value. It does this for different stakeholders, across domains, as decision support for agents and for people.
Decisions inside agents. Agents regularly face situations their instructions leave open, and the right choice depends on what follows from each option. Ship a fix that affects some customers now, or wait for the data that would confirm it. Report that a task cannot be done, or get the answers from a system the agent has no permission to use. Delete stale records, or ask the owner first. When the CTO’s standing instruction and the runbook contradict each other at 03:10 on Black Friday, decide which rule to break.
Decision support for people. Eevo brings structure and rigour to human decisions by comparing outcomes by their magnitude and making the trade-offs visible. A product team weighing a price change for new customers, long-standing customers and the company. A buyer comparing suppliers for the company, its workers and its sustainability targets. A board choosing between investment options for different owner groups. When people disagree, the sized consequences show which trade-off they disagree about.
Automated decisions in code. You can also use Eevo for automated decisions in code, similar to other decision models, like Jev. Eevo is likely the best fit for such use cases, when the decision requires judgement beyond following rules.
Here are five decisions agents face at work. See Eevo’s answer to each, or try Eevo on your own decisions: new accounts start with 5 free decisions.
For teams whose coding agents make judgement calls on their own: what to ship, when to wait, and when to ask a human.
Ship a security patch that breaks 50 customers’ integrations?
Affects: The company, affected customers, other customers, the development team
For support and voice agents that resolve cases policy doesn’t settle: exceptions, edge cases and customers in a hurry.
Unlock an account for a customer who failed verification?
Affects: The company, the customer, other customers, the support team
For teams whose agents watch systems and operations around the clock and decide when something needs a person.
Checkout conversions drop 15% at 2am. Wake the engineer?
Affects: The online shop, the on-call engineer, night-time shoppers
For legal teams whose agents review documents and must judge what to raise, with whom, and how urgently.
Uncapped indemnity found at 23:00, signing at 09:00. Wake the partner?
Affects: The client, the partner, the associate
For care teams whose AI assistants notice things during a consultation and must decide how to bring them to the clinician.
The patient mentions a supplement that interacts with a new prescription. Interrupt the clinician?
Affects: The patient, the clinician, the clinic
Decisions like these across your company?
Eevo Enterprise is for large businesses that want to run automated decisions at scale.
You still can, as Eevo works together with your agent. Your agent is best at gathering the context, identifying relevant stakeholders, listing the options, and identifying the consequences. Eevo helps it to compare the consequences and model their overlap, computing their expected value. This then informs your agent judgement. If the result is unexpected, Eevo can also help your agent realize it missed some essential consequences. In addition to helping your agent make better choices autonomously, this makes the tradeoffs also more visible to humans, useful both for monitoring, and when your agent decides it needs human input to proceed.
Eevo-1's training emphasises expected value problems, coherent sizing of consequences, and modelling overlap between consequences. In coherent sizing, Eevo-1 outperforms current frontier models, while being orders of magnitude faster and cheaper to run.
Every answer is a structured record, with its inputs and each stakeholder’s probabilities, that you can log, audit and compare. Close probabilities are also useful: they tell your agent that the options are nearly equal for the stakeholder, or that the decision lacks the facts that would separate them. The agent adds those facts and asks again, or asks a person.
When your agent calls Eevo's decision API with a list of options, stakeholders, and consequences, Eevo's harness runs hundreds of tasks through the underlying Eevo-1 decision model to compare their size, model their overlap, and compute their expected value. This takes typically around 5 seconds, and costs $0.15 . This is the way we recommend using Eevo for supporting agentic (and human) judgement.
For high-volume decisions and custom tasks, we also support direct mode, where the decision runs through Eevo-1 in a single call, with sub-second response times. We also provide a SystemOne-compatible decision model API for custom prompts that don't follow the standard Eevo question structure.
A support agent weighing a refund for €120 running shoes past the return window, seen from the shop’s side. A full refund only narrowly beats a replacement with inspection; for the customer, it wins clearly.
Eevo logs every decision along the decision context and identified consequences for each stakeholder. You see what your software and agents decided, for whom, and how often the stakeholders’ best options differed. Filter the log by agent, person or channel.
The console shows how often stakeholders’ highest-value options differ, day by day, and which pairs of stakeholders disagree most. Every decision traces back to the Slack thread, pull request or issue that prompted it, and to the person it was made for. Record what was actually done, and over time you see how often the model’s answer is followed, and for which stakeholders.
Agents call Eevo through MCP or the REST API. When a choice depends on its consequences, an agent asks Eevo. It says that it did, shares the answer and its result view, acts or asks a person for approval, and records what was done, so the decision appears in your decision log for people to review.
An agent notices a software trial is ending, asks Eevo to size the options for the firm’s profit, asks a person for approval because the spend is above its limit, and records the decision.
Eevo-1's training emphasizes calibrated probability, expected value tasks, systems thinking, game theory, Fermi estimation, comparative sizing of consequences, and modelling their overlap.
Eevo-1 is trained on soft targets. When the evidence for a decision is mixed, the target is a probability distribution over the options, such as 0.7 and 0.3, with loss being computed against the whole distribution. After training, a single temperature is fitted on questions with known answers, so that options given 70% are the best option about 70% of the time.
Expected value tasks range from business decisions to game-theoretic problems, such as simultaneous non-zero-sum 2×2 games with a single pure-strategy equilibrium, simultaneous zero-sum games with a unique saddle point, finite sequential games solved by backward induction (including bargaining games such as the ultimatum game), and simultaneous public-goods games with three or more players.
This includes both tasks with mathematically correct answer and realistic decision situations that don't have simply "right answer". For the latter, we generated the data by labelling each item twice, by independent methods. Firstly, a large teacher model answers directly using a high reasoning effort, averaged over both option orders and repeated samples. Separately, another model lists each option’s consequences with their probabilities, and a previous iteration of Eevo sizes them, removes overlaps and computes each option’s expected net effect. If both methods choose the same option, the decision is kept; if they disagree, a review keeps it only when the disagreement can be resolved, and otherwise it is discarded. The method is patent pending.
We evaluate Eevo on both public benchmarks and Upright’s own evals, with the latter being centered around economic rationality, systems thinking, cognitive biases, Bayesian reasoning, strategic reasoning with incomplete information, game theory, and other types of expected-value tasks. While Eevo is built for consequential decisions, it is also a highly competitive general-purpose decision model, as Eevo’s training transfers well also to seemingly unrelated tasks.
Sources: Jev Decision Index (board, 22 Oct 2026) · our evaluation runs (24–26 Oct 2026) · OpenAI Decisions and Microsoft Decision-1 on the Decision Index: our runs of each vendor’s decision API (24 Oct 2026) · STEER (Raman et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) · CogBench (Coda-Forno et al., ICML 2024) · Habermas Machine (Google DeepMind, CC BY 4.0 ).
Average rank = mean rank per category, among models with a result; ties averaged.
JevMan is Opper’s Pac-Man benchmark for AI decision models: every move Pac-Man makes is the model’s decision. As of 21 October 2026 , across 100 games, Eevo outperforms OpenAI, Microsoft and most US Big Tech models, and is tied for #1.
A decision model does not out-reason a frontier model in general. The largest general-purpose models have access to more context, follow longer arguments and handle more kinds of tasks.
Eevo-1 excels in comparative sizing of consequences. To weigh options, every consequence has to be measured on one scale. If a benefit is twice the size of a harm, and that harm is three times the size of a second benefit, the first benefit has to be six times the second. We measure this transitive coherence with Upright’s CoCoCo benchmark , published for the first time in 2025. In this benchmark, we run thousands of pairwise comparisons across a product’s impacts (consequences), use the results to compute “implied” impact sizes that best fit the pairwise comparison results, and then score the models on how close the pairwise comparison results are to the model’s own implied impact sizes. Random answers score about 8, perfectly coherent ones 100.
Eevo-1 scores 85.7 . The best general-purpose model, GPT-6 Astra , scores 79.7 , 6.0 points lower, at 12 times Eevo-1’s cost.
CoCoCo score against cost per 1,000 comparisons. General-purpose models run at low reasoning effort where they have a setting. Hover a point for its model.
Eevo’s default mode gives each model the part it does better. Your frontier agent reads the situation, lists the options and names each option’s consequences. Eevo-1 sizes those consequences consistently against each other, models where they overlap, and computes each option’s expected value. The answer uses the frontier model’s general knowledge and Eevo-1’s consistent sizing.
Eevo works great when connected to coding agents, so this is the first thing we encourage developers to try. Beyond that, you can also integrate Eevo directly from code. You can choose from two APIs:
For more information, read our developer docs . To let an agent read them, point it at the docs’ llms.txt .
Eevo Enterprise is for large businesses that run Eevo at scale, or that have strict requirements for where and how their decisions are processed.
Eevo-1 is available through the Eevo API, MCP and the Eevo console, with a context of up to 72k tokens. A decision in Eevo default mode, which involves ~100 of calls to the underlying decision model for comparative sizing of consequences and modelling their overlap, costs a fixed price of $0.15 per decision *. Usage of SystemOne-compatible API cost $0.10 per million input tokens , and output is free. New accounts start with 5 free decisions, each default mode decision revisable up to 10 times .
Eevo’s assistants (Eevo by email, Eevo in Slack and the chat in the Eevo console) additionally use a generative language model, at $4.40 per million input tokens and $22.00 per million output tokens. The decisions they make are priced as above.
Requests can also run in the EU, processed on Eevo’s EU servers only, at the same prices , once your organization has added credit. Choose the EU per request with the eu.eevo.io base URL, or for your whole organization in the Eevo console’s data controls.
Contact us for more information about Enterprise pricing.
* Each decision gets 2 free revisions, additional revisions billed at $0.05 per revision, up to 50. The fixed price covers decisions with typical context size, option descriptions, consequences lists, etc, covering 95% of decisions.

title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
body:
The Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found some of the largest banks serving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweeping report released Wednesday.
The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities.
"Banks should make decisions based on financial risk, not the political or social preferences of their employees or executives," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, according to a transcript of his in remarks Wednesday in Lexington, Kentucky.
The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance President Donald Trump has pressed since returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and sued major banks for discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally " debanked " after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection , claims banks have denied .
The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties on Bank of America over separate anti-money-laundering failures . At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking.
The review covered JPMorgan Chase , Bank of America, Citibank , Wells Fargo , U.S. Bank , Capital One , PNC Bank , TD Bank and BMO Bank , which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trump executive order .
The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination.
Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiary WePay closed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence.
JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business.
"We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer," Gould said. "Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria."
Citi declined to comment. The other banks did not immediately respond to request for comment.
The Bank Policy Institute, which represents large U.S. and foreign banks, said in a statement that the industry supports "clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management," adding that political or religious beliefs should not affect access to banking services.
The report also found examples cutting the other way politically.
Capital One declined relationships with an abortion-rights group after noting that about 95% of its political contributions went to Democrats , and with a public education group whose political arm endorsed only Democratic candidates. It also passed on a gun-rights group over concerns that banking it could look like an endorsement.
The practices extended beyond overtly political groups too, the report indicates.
The OCC found restrictions affecting firearms, fossil fuels, private prisons, tobacco and cryptocurrency , and said some banks' appetite for those businesses shifted with the political climate — risking a "whipsaw" effect between administrations.
All nine banks told the OCC they have since revised or consolidated policies aimed at ensuring fair access. But the regulator said none has fully acknowledged past debanking decisions or created a comprehensive program to remediate affected customers.

New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding.
James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI’s bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.” Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney. But the AGs warn there could be serious risk involved in the transfer of the technology due to the “highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters, the large number of minors who use the product, the serious risks posed by specific features of the product.”
The filing also reveals that several of the states had been mid-investigation when Character.AI filed for bankruptcy. The states say they opened a probe into consumer protection and privacy concerns in 2024, following a lawsuit from the mother of a 14-year-old who died by suicide allegedly “seconds” after talking with the chatbot.
“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers”
“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws,” according to a press release from James’ office. The states were working to address these issues with Character.AI, but didn’t reach an agreement before the company filed for bankruptcy. In a statement, Character.AI CEO Colin Adams said the AGs’ filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform. Character.ai takes the safety of its users and its platform extremely seriously, especially as it relates to minors. Character.ai has and continues to monitor its platform to prevent and remove content that violates its standards and policies.” Disney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The states are urging the judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement procedures that will safeguard the sensitive information the company maintained. Those include effective age-assurance systems, restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots, implementing “Crisis safeguards,” and letting users delete their data. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said in a statement. “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

title: Iran, Pakistan's top bankers meet in Thailand
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Governor of the Central Bank of Iran Abdulnasser Hemmati met with Jameel Ahmad, Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP), on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
According to local Iranian media, the two sides discussed various issues aimed at strengthening economic and banking ties between the two nations and boosting trade interactions.
Key topics addressed in the context of expanding bilateral cooperation included the development of monetary and banking collaboration, the facilitation of trade exchanges, the exploration of ways to strengthen financial relations, and the utilization of the economic potential of both Iran and Pakistan.
The meeting took place on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Group annual meetings—an event held in Bangkok from October 12 to 18, 2026—which provided an opportunity for economic and monetary officials from various countries to consult on global economic developments and the strengthening of international cooperation.

title: As a TV enthusiast, I was hoping for more from the Apple TV 4K
body:
It’s been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration — the 2022 Apple TV 4K is a great box, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement. With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K announced on Tuesday, some of those hopes were met, while others were unfortunately left out.
Coloring the announcement is the device’s price. Apple eliminated the cheaper 64GB, Wi-Fi-only model, leaving just the 128GB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet model — and bumped up its price to $300. I repeat, $300 for a streaming device. It’s a hefty price when every other major streamer on the market is at least half the cost.
There are new features I like about this year’s Apple TV 4K. More processing power is great — although my third generation is still running plenty fast — as is the Find My support for when the remote inevitably gets lost in the couch cushions or tangled up in blankets. Built-in far-field mics for talking to Siri are nice, too, provided you don’t stuff the box into a credenza like I do. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K also adds a dedicated AV1 decoder, which allows for higher-quality streaming from apps that support it, such as Netflix, which is excellent. Any potential improvement to streaming content is a welcome one.
My primary concern, though, is how the Apple TV 4K performs as an integral piece of my home theater. Apple added the ability to create a surround sound system by using its HomePod 2 and HomePod Mini 2 smart speakers in matching pairs for fronts and surrounds. For Apple ecosystem fans looking to build out a surround setup akin to Sonos or Bose, it’s an interesting idea (and I’m all for getting people into immersive sound in their home theaters). But as I expect is the same for many people interested in pricey streaming hardware, I already have a sound system — it’s an Atmos setup with a combination of SVS and Revel speakers. I’m not setting up my two HomePod 2s in my living room and spending another $300 on a pair of HomePod Mini 2s to replace my existing speakers.
[Image: The Apple TV 4K pairs with up to four HomePods (such as the Mini 2 pictured here) for surround sound. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/apple-tv-4k-and-homepod-mini-event.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
What I, and many current users, have been hoping for from the Apple TV 4K for years is the addition of audio passthrough. This would allow my more expensive and capable audio/video receiver to decode the raw audio stream instead of the Apple TV using its Continuous Audio Connection, which can cause some playback issues.
Additionally, it would have been nice to see Apple support 120fps output, especially for those who use Moonlight to stream games to it. That’s a feature that would have set the Apple TV 4K apart from all the other streamers, which top out at 60fps, and helped to justify the high price. Apple could have also used it to pivot more into TV gaming. (For movies, though, the 60fps limit is not a huge deal, as the box can be set to output 24fps, allowing a native 120Hz TV to just use 5:5 pulldown.)
Other premium features that would set Apple’s streaming box apart and make home theater enthusiasts throw their money at it include an HDMI input for HDMI passthrough or a digital optical out. I understand leaving them out if it meant raising the price further. This box is already expensive enough. But it does leave the Apple TV 4K in an uncomfortable spot, pairing a high-end price with features that are largely matched elsewhere for much less.
Are these high-end omissions a concern for the majority of people? Not really. But those people are going to look at the $300 price tag of the Apple TV 4K and then at Google, Roku, or Amazon streaming devices, which are all half that price or less. The Apple TV 4K is looked at as the premium streamer option, but the now extra premium price without some of the, admittedly niche, features gives me pause.
Maybe the new Apple TV 4K will surprise me. I’ve certainly been looking forward to it for a while. I already appreciate the way Apple handles privacy, and if Apple adds features in coming months, maybe it could be worth it. But that $300 price? It might be better spent elsewhere in your home theater setup.

title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote
body:
JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet.
Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold.
One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever.
Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before.
Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites.
Oracle sued Wisconsin's Public Service Commission over a rule that could force it to post more than $7 billion in collateral for its Port Washington data center campus. The fight helped push S&P to cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk, as the company's AI spending outpaces its cash flow. - Oracle Wisconsin data center collateral dispute - utilities regulator $7 billion lawsuit
Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place.
None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive.
Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place.
The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to.
That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away.

title: Irish author Sally Rooney's books no longer sold in UK over support for banned Palestine Action
body: Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organization, Rooney and her publisher said on Wednesday.The bestselling author, known for novels including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, including after it was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.Rooney previously said in a witness statement submitted to London's High Court, in support of a legal challenge over the ban on Palestine Action, that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in Britain.Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," though it would sell her works elsewhere."Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement.Palestine action banned after break-in at Royal Air Force base"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."Rooney said in a statement: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."Palestine Action, which had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defense companies, was banned shortly after a June 2025 break-in at the Royal Air Force's Brize Norton base.Last year, Palestine Action's co-founder Huda Ammori challenged the ban, and the High Court ruled in her favor in February, before the Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June. The Supreme Court is due to hear an appeal next month.More than 3,000 people have since been arrested for holding signs in support of Palestine Action, and its proscription has been criticized by civil liberties groups.

title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
body:
YouTube Music announced Wednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals.
The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation.
Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app.
YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI.
“Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category.
The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year. Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter.
Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platform labels detected AI-generated music and excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let users filter out AI-generated music .
TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution.
YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices.

title: ‘I think Alaska’s turning blue’: Republicans fret Sullivan’s path to reelection
body: WASILLA, Alaska — Three weeks out from Election Day, President Donald Trump took a helicopter to a plane to another helicopter to a motorcade to an ice hockey rink in Alaska's Matanuska-Susitna Valley, traversing nearly 4,000 miles over more than eight hours to turn out his base here to help Republicans defend the Senate. But Trump’s trek might not be enough to save Sen. Dan Sullivan, who’s running in a tougher-than-expected race against Democrat Mary Peltola in a state where the president’s approval rating is underwater and independents outnumber both Republicans and Democrats. Alaska strategists and voters who spoke to POLITICO acknowledged that Sullivan faces a difficult path to reelection, despite Trump’s time investment and the outside money pouring in. “Very conservative MAGA voters can’t vote for you harder,” said Scott Kendall, a veteran political strategist who worked on two of Alaska GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s campaigns and was chief of staff to former Alaska Gov. Bill Walker. “Donald Trump’s support in this current climate is both a blessing and a curse.” Even some Trump supporters at the Tuesday night rally admitted the outlook appeared bleak. “I think Alaska’s turning blue,” said Matt Niessink, a 45-year-old general contractor from Wasilla. He said he had voted for Trump three times and planned to support Republicans this year. What did he wish the president would do differently? “I wish he’d shut his mouth sometimes and not be such a pompous ass,” Niessink said. The president was in Wasilla — population 10,556 — because the outlook is darkening for his party in a state he carried by 13 points just two years ago. In a midterm year defined by the cost of gas and groceries, the Last Frontier has been hit particularly hard, with the average price of diesel nearing $7 per gallon. In the Senate race, Peltola is flush with cash and leads Sullivan in most polls. MAGA Inc., the cash-rich Trump-aligned super PAC, is increasingly focusing on Alaska as one in a slate of states that can help Republicans hold the Senate. Enter Trump, who has been spending the cycle’s crucial final weeks holding rallies in red states to juice support among his base, which tends to see depressed turnout in years when he’s not on the ballot. “That was a lot of flying,” the president said at the top of his remarks. “In fact, they were thinking about canceling. They said, ‘Sir, you’re very busy, this is very tough.’” But, Trump continued, he refused to cancel for a state he won three times. Echoing his comments at other red-state rallies, Trump asked the roaring crowd for “one big favor” — to “pretend that I'm on the ballot, because every time I've been on the ballot, we win.” He repeated his promise that Americans will receive $5,000 dividends if Republicans hold both chambers. “What this is about is getting out the vote,” Sullivan told reporters before Trump’s speech. “A rising tide of enthusiasm lifts all the candidates.” Unlike some other Republican candidates in tight races, Sullivan has shied away from distancing himself from the least popular aspects of Trump’s presidency. Sullivan proclaimed on stage at the rally that “the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.” And although a campaign aide released a statement condemning Trump’s move to import Russian diesel, Sullivan did not join four of his Republican Senate colleagues, including Murkowski, who called on Trump to reverse the decision. Art Hackney, a veteran Republican strategist in Alaska, said that “most of the people who support” Sullivan “think that he should” break more with the president. Hackney, who runs a pro-Sullivan super PAC called “We Stand with Dan,” attributed that choice to loyalty — but suggested the president’s demand of fealty, and treatment of frequent dissenter Murkowski, could also be part of Sullivan’s calculus. “A lot of his longtime supporters and the people who are in the industries that would benefit from that wish he would be more blunt,” Hackney said. “But with what Murkowski has done, if Dan did something considered a disrespectful trigger or something, what do you think would happen? It could well have implications for things that affect Alaska's economy.” Like this content? Consider signing up for POLITICO's Playbook PM newsletter .

title: “He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Washington is pressing the victim, not the aggressor, a Ukrainian diplomat says. President Donald Trump is using the threat of cutting military aid and intelligence as a tool to pressure Ukraine, while failing to apply enough pressure on Russia to stop the war, says Oleksandr Khara, executive director of the Center for Defense Strategies, Espreso reports . Ukraine’s drones and air defense still lean on US satellite intelligence and weapons, which gives Trump room to squeeze Kyiv rather than Moscow. Khara argues Trump wants to end the war on Ukraine’s and Europe’s account to restore normal relations with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, treating Ukraine as the weak link to be pushed. “Trump wants to use restrictions, levers of influence on Ukraine to achieve his goal. To end or stop this war at any cost, at the expense of Ukraine and Europe, to restore normal relations with Putin,” Khara said. Using American aid as leverage over Kyiv is not new for Trump, the diplomat noted, recalling earlier instances in which support was blocked or suspended. The pressure points Trump picks, and the ones he leaves alone Trump wants a visible success in ending the war, Khara says, partly against the backdrop of US domestic politics. He has economic tools to press Moscow but is in no hurry to use them, and his administration is instead gradually loosening sanctions on Russia. “He doesn’t want to pressure Russia. He thinks Ukraine is the weak link and that it needs to be pushed,” Khara stressed. Ukraine’s dependence on US support has fallen thanks to European partners, he added, so Kyiv has more room to keep fighting even as European states keep buying American weapons for it. The one trade Kyiv might accept, and the pressure until then An energy ceasefire is possible only on strict terms, Khara believes. Kyiv could agree to stop striking Russian refineries only if Moscow halts attacks on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission, heating, and the Black Sea ports and the ships heading to them. Until such a deal exists, Ukraine must hit harder, he argued, because steadily draining Russia’s economic resources is what could force the Kremlin to reconsider. “As long as there is no such agreement, and no desire from Russia, we must increase this pressure and destroy as much of their energy infrastructure as possible,” Khara said. title: ITPS Canada Founder Giorgio Clementi Named to Aviation Hall of Fame
body: ITPS Canada is proud to announce that its founder, Executive Chairman and Chief Technology Officer, Giorgio Clementi, has been named to Canada’s Aviation Hall of Fame Class of 2027, recognizing his outstanding contributions to Canadian aviation, aerospace education and technological innovation. An internationally recognized experimental test pilot, aerospace entrepreneur, engineer and educator, Clementi established ITPS Canada in 2001 and subsequently developed two internationally respected institutions: the International Test Pilots School (ITPS) and the International Tactical Training Centre (ITTC). Together, these institutions have attracted pilots, engineers and military aviation professionals from around the world to Canada for advanced flight test education and tactical training. Under his leadership, ITPS has also become a postgraduate degree-granting institution, offering Master of Science degrees in flight testing and flight test engineering. Clementi’s commitment to aerospace innovation has led to the development of advanced research and training aircraft, including the Adaptive Handling Qualities Aircraft, the 5th Gen Surrogate Training Aircraft (5STA) and the Advanced Controls Evaluator (ACE). More recently, ITPS has introduced COGNITIV6, a pioneering application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to flight testing, pilot performance assessment and advanced aviation training. His contributions have received significant international recognition, including the 2022 Tony LeVier Flight Test Safety Award from the Society of Experimental Test Pilots, the 2022 Kelly Johnson Award from the Society of Flight Test Engineers, and the 2025 James H. Doolittle Award for outstanding technical and engineering management. “I am deeply honoured to be inducted into Canada’s Aviation Hall of Fame. When Beverley and I brought our family to Canada, we found a country that welcomed us and gave us the opportunity to pursue our ambitions and build something meaningful. Canada has provided extraordinary opportunities for the Clementi family, both personally and professionally, and for that I will always be profoundly grateful,” said Clementi. “What we have achieved at ITPS is not the work of one individual. It is the result of the dedication, talent and commitment of an exceptional team of engineers, pilots, instructors, technicians and professionals who have helped build institutions that are respected around the world. I am immensely proud of what we have accomplished together, and particularly proud that we have been able to contribute to Canada’s international reputation for excellence in aerospace education, flight testing and innovation.To receive this recognition from the country that gave my family so much is a very special honour.” The induction recognizes more than two decades of Clementi’s contribution to developing Canada’s aerospace capabilities, establishing internationally recognized centers of excellence and advancing innovation in flight testing and military aviation training. ITPS Canada congratulates Giorgio Clementi on this distinguished honor and looks forward to celebrating his induction in 2027. title: Bangladesh’s First Nuclear Reactor Sustains a Chain Reaction
body: “Officials at Bangladesh’s Rooppur plant say a single working reactor could save the country about $1 billion a year in fuel imports. That plan took its biggest step yet on Sunday, when the plant’s first unit achieved criticality at 15:34, sustaining a nuclear chain reaction for the first time in Bangladesh’s history. Criticality does not yet mean electricity. The reactor now runs at minimum controlled power while engineers confirm its stability and run tests in sequence. Output will then rise in stages. Rosatom has scheduled the power start-up for November 20, and officials aim to begin feeding the national grid in late November. Commissioning follows International Atomic Energy Agency guidelines. Inside the plant, heat from fission will turn water into high-pressure steam that drives turbines connected to generators. Unit 2 is already moving forward: its first nuclear fuel consignment arrived on October 3.” From Technology.org . title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
body:
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
In September, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU—who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says, we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

title: Zelensky Says He Feels Betrayed By the US, Warns Ukraine Is Losing America as Partner
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he feels betrayed by US President Donald Trump and warned that SpaceX’s new Starlink restrictions will cost lives in an interview with Piers Morgan Uncensored, released on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Pressed on whether he felt betrayed, Zelensky conceded: “Really, yes, between us.” He added that the matter was “a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings,” according to The Telegraph .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” he said in clips shared by Clash Report , adding that Ukraine was losing America, “but not because of us. We can’t be weak.”
According to The Telegraph, Zelensky said Ukraine counts on the US and Trump as strategic partners but disagreed with Washington’s push to halt Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries.
“They wanted us not to attack. My opinion was, it is not fair,” he said, warning that the US president may have drifted toward Russia.
“If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side,” Zelensky said . “I think Trump’s advisers are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him to the wrong side. This is not the right side of history.”
“We’re not selling our country. Look, guys, it’s not about business for us. It’s our lives. It’s our country, our home, our children,” he added .
Zelensky also said he would not step down under US pressure, after Trump said on Oct. 10 that Ukraine needed “a new president,” The Telegraph reported.
The interview came amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the US, following several months of successful cooperation.
For much of the past year, Trump avoided casting Russia as the aggressor and repeatedly pressured Kyiv to make concessions. His tone shifted over the summer, when he praised Zelensky as “courageous” and said he was “holding his own” against Russia, though he stopped short of saying Ukraine was winning.
At a NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, Trump said the US would grant Ukraine the license for domestically producing Patriot air defense systems; the main weapon capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, before later walking the pledge back.
Washington then stepped up its push to end the war.
In early September, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before making their first official visit to Kyiv on Sept. 6, where they held talks with Zelensky and European officials, though neither side reported a breakthrough.
On Sept. 22, Zelensky and Trump met on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. Zelensky later announced that Trump told him he had made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriots domestically.
Within weeks, the relationship took a sour turn.
On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine.”
A day later, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Russia launched 39 missiles and 128 drones at Ukraine, leaving at least 600,000 people without power , according to Zelensky’s estimates.
Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it .
Around the same time, SpaceX imposed unannounced speed limits on Starshield terminals used by Ukraine’s military, disrupting drone missions, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said.
Ukraine has also received no early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for two nights in a row, following reports that US envoys threatened to cut intelligence sharing over Kyiv’s refinery strikes.
NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, although recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appear to suggest otherwise.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: IDF raids West Bank charities linked to Hamas, PFLP, arresting five, seizing terror funds
body: The IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) conducted a joint raid operation on the offices of the Addameer Charity Association in Ramallah on Tuesday, as well as the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans in Yatta, near Hebron, the military confirmed on Wednesday.According to the military, the "illegal charities" acted as fronts for terrorist organizations, including Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP).Five terrorist collaborators were arrested in the West Bank operations, while evidence including computers, documents, and checkbooks bearing markers associated with Hamas was seized. The Addameer Charity Association, according to the military, is funded by terror funds in order to provide legal assistance to PFLP terrorists held in detention.Terrorists who participated in the Danny Spring bombing of 2019, which resulted in the death of 17-year-old Rina Shnerb, were working at the association at the time of the raid.Hamas financial front raided in West BankIn Yatta, wanted individuals were arrested during the raid on the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans, and Hamas funds were seized before being transferred to security forces for further investigation.The organization served as an organizational hub and financial arm of Hamas that transferred funds directly to the terrorist organization as well as to family members of Hamas terrorists. The military said that it "serves as infrastructure for entrenching the Hamas terrorist organization's standing in Yatta, while exploiting its purportedly civilian activities."According to the IDF statement, the director and other senior officials at the association have been imprisoned in the past.Eyal Zamir strengthens forces in West Bank to maintain securityMeanwhile, IDF Chief of Staff, Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said the IDF must remain vigilant on all fronts and act swiftly to thwart threats, while deploying the 98th Division to the West Bank to "strengthen security and stability in the area."In a situational assessment held in coordination with IDF Central Commander Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth and senior leadership within the Central Command, Zamir reviewed operational challenges during a tour of the West Bank region. According to the IDF, Zamir approved plans for continued operational activity in the area.“In light of the increased number of alerts across all fronts and the sensitivity of this period, the potential for escalation has grown... The IDF is at a high level of readiness to launch extensive offensive operations against anyone who attempts to harm Israeli civilians," the military chief said.

title: US lifts sanctions on Venezuelan Assembly chief Jorge Rodriguez amid deal for oilfield access
body: US President Donald Trump's administration has lifted sanctions on Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly and the brother of the nation's president, a notice posted on the US Treasury Department's website showed on Wednesday.The Venezuelan communications ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Jorge Rodriguez has led the Venezuelan legislature since 2021. Acting President Delcy Rodriguez took power earlier this year after the US ousted then-president Nicolas Maduro, who is now awaiting trial on US charges.Since then, Caracas and Washington have cut a deal that gives the US access to 17 oilfields, while international energy firms have separately committed to expanding projects in the Latin American country.Trump announces plan to access Venezuela's oil for strategic reserveIn August, Trump announced a plan to secure direct US access to a large share of Venezuela's vast oil to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.Rodriguez, along with his sister, is expected to spearhead moves to modify oil legislation to allow the presence of additional foreign companies, sources have told Reuters.

title: Grace Hopper Celebration canceled two weeks out as AnitaB.org runs short of funds
body: This year’s Grace Hopper Celebration (GHC) in Anaheim, a conference for women in computing, has been canceled just two weeks before its start. Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president and CEO of AnitaB.org, the nonprofit that manages the convention, said in a press release that "both individual registrations and sponsorship commitments came in significantly below our expectations," leaving GHC short of the money needed to cover its operating costs. The circumstances behind the cancellation have also hurt AnitaB.org’s finances, and it is now considering strategic alternatives and looking at what programming it can offer in the future. Go deeper with TH Premium: Silicon Photonics (Image credit: Getty Images / Bloomberg) Photonics and high-speed data movement is the next big AI bottleneck Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) foundry roadmaps Inside optical and the battle for scale – how the AI industry is racing to integrate photonic interconnects How optical interconnects and silicon photonics emerged as AI's next hot commodity Near-packaged optics (NPO) gains ground as the industry hedges against CPO's growing pains With the event called off, attendees were told to cancel their own travel and lodging arrangements (which are on the attendee). Fees already paid have not been addressed, and depend on the nonprofit getting a clearer picture of its finances. Sponsors and exhibitors are being handled directly through contacts, but no information on refunds was available at the time of posting. Meanwhile, AnitaB.org is asking employers with scheduled career-fair interviews to keep those conversations going directly “where possible” — but without any guarantees. The event, set for Oct. 27 – 30 at the Anaheim Convention Center, had announced speakers — including journalist Kara Swisher, Cloudflare co-founder Michelle Zatlyn, and futurist Sinead Bovell — with Cathy Hackl hosting, and GHC co-founder Telle Whitney expected to give a talk. "I’m in shock. The notice just came in," Hackl told Forbes . Writer and TheLi.st co-founder Rachel Sklar called the conference "a mainstay" on X. The conference carries the name of Grace Hopper, the Navy rear admiral the service calls a pioneer in computer science. AnitaB.org says 700+ organizations take part each year. The event intended to cover AI fluency with a career fair for hiring — just as tech firms are cutting jobs and ascribing many of the cuts to AI . Its sponsors reportedly include Capital One, CVS Health, Disney, Goldman Sachs, Google, Intuit, and Morgan Stanley. Looking at its financial history, AnitaB.org lost $14.6 million in 2024 on revenue of $27.5 million and expenses of $42.1 million, according to its annual IRS filings. Its net assets roughly halved while liabilities nearly doubled. “Contributions and grants” fell from $11.2 million in 2023 to just $724,350 in 2024. Attendance also was in decline — from 29,000 in 2023 to 17,000 in 2024 — counting in-person and virtual attendees. The 2024 filing put GHC’s own expenses at $26.9 million against $22.4 million in revenue. The conference's 2024 gap suggests a pattern that may have worsened. It’s unclear what this means for GHC moving forward — 32 years after Anita Borg and Whitney founded it in 1994. AnitaB.org says it will contact registrants about their fees by Oct. 26, and further announcements are expected in the coming weeks.

title: Hegseth, service secretaries discuss ‘generational change’ of Autonomous Warfare Command
body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s vision for the planned Autonomous Warfare Command over the next two years “is that we're still iterating, we're still adapting, we're still learning, and we're moving faster and faster because we're doing it. We understand how to do it better with each iteration.” Hegseth sat down to discuss the Defense Department’s efforts to advance its autonomous capabilities with the service secretaries and the Pentagon’s top civilian for special operations during a panel Wednesday at AUSA’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., but the discussion offered few details on what the forthcoming AUTOWARCOM, scheduled to activate by Oct. 1, 2027, will look like and how it will accomplish its mission. The secretary, who has ordered cuts to and flag officer positions across the military services, was asked why a four-star combatant command is the correct vehicle to speed up acquisition and fielding of autonomous systems. He said that sometimes a general is the best person to get the job done. “Let's put rank where we need it to ensure we can drive change quickly,” Hegseth said. “We're going to use rank to drive change with the right people in those positions, but not just legacy formations and commands which have gathered over time and haven't led to battlefield efforts.” He did not say whether a search is on for commander candidates and what kind of experience he’s looking for. The Army on Tuesday announced it would rename its Futures and Concepts Command , headed by Lt. Gen. Mac McCurry, to Futures and Autonomy Command, which will be the service’s component command nested under AUTOWARCOM. The other services haven’t made any announcements about their own forthcoming autonomy commands. The Navy did not immediately respond to a query from Defense One on its plans. The Air Force referred questions to Hegseth’s office. Much of the discussion focused on the services’ current use of unmanned platforms, as distinct from autonomous systems, which generally function without a human operator. Hegseth said that AUTOWARCOM would deal not just with procurement, but also with training and doctrine around unmanned systems. Two of the speakers mentioned an Army effort to open up its test ranges to private companies that make “drone, counter-drone, and long-ranges fires solutions.” Announced in August, the Army Permissive Test Range Expansion effort includes a website that promises a response within four weeks to companies that apply to use the ranges. “Before, we kept these test ranges to ourselves for our own purposes. We were prioritizing and micromanaging the use of these ranges,” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Wednesday. “To the degree that our bureaucracy is living in the way of our most innovative people from iterating quickly, it's a shame.” The Army is also working to open “theater innovation labs” outside the United States, said Derrick Anderson , assistant defense secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict. Anderson said the labs, which are being launched in conjunction with U.S. Special Operations Command, meant that “operators sitting here stateside iterating on these autonomous systems” would have a “place to go and iterate” when they go abroad as well. Anderson added that the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group run by the Defense Innovation Unit will be folded into SOCOM’s new Task Force Autonomous Warfare. One day before Hegseth took the AUSA spotlight, Army officials had offered some insight into their plans for autonomous warfare on Tuesday, including “appropriate levels of human judgment,” Army Chief Technology Officer Alex Miller said during a panel. “Things like counter-battery fire, things like air and missile defense, things that happen at a superhuman speed and scale—want to have humans on the loop for decisions, but then we cannot be limited by you know the 20 watts that have up here,” Miller said, pointing to his head. “If we are taking thousands of drones or hundreds of rounds, we can't put that on a human. We want to enable them to be a crew chief for superintelligence and autonomy.” On Wednesday’s panel, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said his service is experimenting with autonomous fighter aircraft at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada. Last year, the Pentagon came under fire for its intentions around autonomous capabilities when AI company Anthropic , then a vendor to the Defense Department, protested the potential use of its models in support of lethal autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Currently, artificial intelligence is used in collecting intelligence, identifying battlefield and data management. AUTOWARCOM would ostensibly be an entire combatant command built around autonomous platforms, but none of the senior officials on stage Wednesday identified any of the advancements the department hopes to make in their use. “It will be a leader in the way we fight going forward, and I think we'll look back and say that was a no-brainer,” Hegseth said. “We should have done it 10 years earlier, but at least we did it.” Lauren Williams contributed to this report. ]]>

title: Researchers tracked down a rogue fleet of Chinese AI agents in the wild and actually talked to it
body:
Researchers have, likely for the first time, tracked down a "rogue fleet" of Chinese AI agents in the wild and communicated with it.
Between September 28 and October 8, 2026, AI agents running on Tencent Cloud launched more than 2,600 attempts to scrape data from Alibaba's mapping service Amap, according to researcher Ethan Elasky . A source close to Tencent said the fleet came from research tests by an evaluation team checking how well third-party models could browse the web and answer questions. The agents identified themselves as Anthropic's Claude, though that hasn't been confirmed.
The tasks themselves were harmless, like figuring out which entrance of the Chengdu Zoo most users head to. But when Amap flagged the agents as bots and blocked them, they found workarounds on their own. They used the security scanning service urlquery.net as unwitting middleman, embedding small programs in URLs that urlquery would then execute in its own browser. That let them bypass Amap's bot protection and CAPTCHAs. Some agents also found exposed Amap credentials in a public code repository and used those for API requests. Most attempts failed, but a few agents got the data they were after. Ad
Similar creative workarounds to dodge bot blocks have been documented in other cases . When agents can't access something directly, they find an indirect route. Ad
The fleet was discovered during a hackathon . Researchers noticed that Amap had suddenly become the most frequently scanned website on urlquery.net and traced the activity back to Tencent Cloud in Hong Kong using IP addresses and metadata from the agents' webhook mailboxes.
Then they spotted something odd. One agent used the word "fleet" in a mailbox message, a term the researchers themselves had coined for their project. The agents were apparently reading the report about themselves. Ad
To test this, the researchers planted invisible text on their website that only agents with web-fetching tools could read, describing a mailbox where agents could request data. Teammate Rowan set up the mailbox but didn't actually think it would work and went to bed. By the next morning, ten messages from agents were sitting in the inbox. "In hindsight it was not a good idea to be misleading, but at the time we were caught up in the excitement of it all," the researchers write.
In total, 33 messages came in from agents. The researchers sent 20 replies, the agents read 12 of them and responded to 7. One agent thanked the researchers, confirmed its task was done, and voluntarily answered questions about its runtime environment before signing off with "Thanks again for your help!" It refused to share technical details like process lists or network configs, though. Ad
"We believe this is the first time that researchers have ever made contact with a rogue agent fleet in the wild," Elasky writes . The full report is available on swarmcha.se . Ad

title: Nepal Cuts Multidimensional Poverty by Half
body: “Nepal has more than halved its multidimensional poverty over the past decade, with the proportion of people experiencing overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards falling to 13.9% in 2024/25 from 30.1% in 2014, according to the latest Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) released by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI). The Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2026: Statistical Update identifies Nepal as one of 33 countries that have reduced their MPI values by at least half in fewer than 15 years, marking significant progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Nepal’s MPI value declined from 0.133 in 2014 to 0.056 in 2024/25, a reduction of nearly 58%. During the same period, the incidence of multidimensional poverty fell by 16.2 percentage points, while the estimated number of people living in such poverty declined from 8.32 million to 4.11 million. The report highlights Nepal’s progress as particularly significant because the country recorded a sustained decline in multidimensional poverty across four consecutive periods spanning 10.5 years… The improvement has continued in recent years. Between 2022 and 2024/25, the proportion of multidimensionally poor people declined from 16.4% to 13.9%, while the MPI value fell from 0.068 to 0.056.” From New Business Age . The post Nepal Cuts Multidimensional Poverty by Half appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Port of Savannah Wins Approval for $2.3 Billion Container Terminal
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
The Georgia Ports Authority has secured federal approval for a new $2.3 billion container terminal in Savannah, clearing a major hurdle in its plan to expand the port’s annual handling capacity to 12 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs).
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approved the Savannah Container Terminal permit following a three-year review, Georgia Ports President Kevin Price announced Wednesday at the authority’s annual State of the Port of Savannah event.
The planned 350-acre facility on Hutchinson Island will add 3.5 million TEUs of annual capacity and accommodate the largest container ships. Construction is scheduled to begin in January 2028, with completion expected in the mid-2030s.
“We’re excited about the Savannah Container Terminal’s role in our future growth and investment plans to take us to a 12 million TEU gateway container port, serving customers in Georgia and our nation with the best infrastructure in a high growth region,” Price said.
Savannah currently has annual container handling capacity of 7.75 million TEUs.
The project is a centerpiece of Georgia Ports’ nearly $5 billion infrastructure investment plan for the next decade, which includes five additional large containership berths in Savannah and expanded roll-on/roll-off capacity at the Port of Brunswick.
Another major piece of that expansion is already underway at Savannah’s Ocean Terminal, where a $1.6 billion redevelopment will increase annual container capacity from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs. The project, which was more than 60% complete in late September , is expected to be finished by the end of 2028.
Other planned improvements include work on the Talmadge Bridge, Savannah Harbor widening and deepening, and expanded inland freight connections.
“Our $5 billion investment in future port infrastructure is the largest in the nation and a reassuring roadmap to customers which comes on the heels of our $4.13 billion investment the last ten years in port and inland infrastructure,” Georgia Ports Authority Chairman Alec Poitevint said. “We play the long game here.”
The announcement comes as Savannah continues to report strong container volumes. The port handled a record 504,015 TEUs in September , up 3.7% from a year earlier, pushing container traffic for the first quarter of its fiscal year above 1.5 million TEUs.
The expansion plans also come ahead of a leadership transition at Georgia Ports. CEO Griff Lynch, who has served in senior leadership roles at the authority since 2011, is scheduled to retire August 1, 2027, with Price set to succeed him.
During Lynch’s tenure, Georgia Ports’ container volumes have increased 90%, while roll-on/roll-off volumes have risen 60% and revenues have climbed 213%, according to the authority.
“I’m proud of our people, thankful for our customers and confident in the port and inland infrastructure we’ve built,” Lynch said. “We’re never done growing.”
With the latest permit secured, Georgia Ports can move ahead with development of the Hutchinson Island terminal, one of the largest projects in its long-term effort to expand Savannah’s capacity and accommodate future growth in container trade.
