title: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'
body:
An attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump 's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective.
The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook.
Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel.
No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted.
The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires.
Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September.
"She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.
White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve."
"The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.
An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.
Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.
But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.
The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts.
Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns."
"With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.
Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook , an appointee of former President Joe Biden , from the central bank's board of governors.
The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.
Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."
But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.
Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025 .
Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.
The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'"
"A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

title: Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
body: The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW . State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away. Some also note that federal workforce departures have weakened cooperation with outside partners, including social media platforms, to track false information online. While the federal government continues to gather intelligence on foreign threats to U.S. elections, some of those who lean on those findings say federal agencies are less reliably sharing information with non-federal researchers and state officials responsible for countering those campaigns. That cooperation began to weaken before President Donald Trump returned to office, and his administration has since dismantled several programs dedicated to countering the problem. This story is based on interviews with current and former federal officials, state election officials and specialists in cybersecurity and influence operations. Several people spoke on the condition of anonymity to be candid about their views and for fear of retribution. Their concerns come as fast-evolving AI tools now allow foreign influence operators to do more than just generate fake images or audio, instead helping them produce plausible-sounding messages, find audiences to target and autonomously adjust campaigns at a scale not seen before. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions about foreign malign influence to the Justice Department, saying that influence operations fall outside CISA’s mission. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration, DHS, and CISA,” a CISA spokesperson said. “CISA works closely with intelligence and law enforcement partners to monitor threats to U.S. critical infrastructure, including election infrastructure.” The spokesperson added that the agency is committed to supporting state and local election officials “to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy.” The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to a request for comment. Foreign influence operations aim to shape what people believe and how they act, often without revealing who is behind the message. Around elections, that can mean spreading false voting information, stoking political divisions or casting doubt on results. Such messages can be harder to question when they appear to come from or be amplified by fellow Americans and reinforce views people already hold. One election nonprofit official told Nextgov/FCW that, during the November 2024 election, they received an early-morning text from a colleague in Georgia asking about bomb threats at voting sites, which U.S. officials later deemed may have been tied to Russia . The official was sitting in CISA’s election operations room. Finding out whether other jurisdictions were facing similar threats meant simply walking across the room and asking federal personnel. “Any time you have federal support to help connect the dots, it’s a game-changer,” the official said, noting that they have not been alerted to or invited to a CISA elections operations room for the coming midterms. The CISA spokesperson said that, before and during Election Day, the agency will “activate an Incident Coordination Group to establish a unified operational picture, rapidly share critical information, coordinate essential services for stakeholders in the field and strengthen incident response within its mission and authorities.” Bret Schafer, senior director of policy and research for information operations at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, said efforts to bring government, technology companies and researchers together grew during Trump’s first term, after Russia’s interference attempts in the 2016 election exposed gaps in their understanding of foreign campaigns. Each could see activity the others could not. Sharing those findings helped them recognize operations that might otherwise go unnoticed, Schafer said last week on a panel at a national-security law conference hosted by the American Bar Association. Those routine exchanges with the government have become harder to sustain. Now, “civil society is out on both sides,” he said, adding that he had gone at least two years without an information-sharing conversation with a relevant technology company, and a couple of years without one involving the government. Much of that cooling began in the Biden administration, when GOP litigation over federal interactions with social media companies made participants more cautious . The Trump administration has gone further. It shuttered CISA work focused on election disinformation, disbanded the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force and closed the State Department’s office for countering foreign information threats, all largely on censorship grounds. The ODNI Foreign Malign Influence Center also faced a similar fate last August under then-director Tulsi Gabbard. An office can retain its responsibilities while losing the relationships that helped it do the work, according to a person familiar with U.S. efforts to address influence operations. But someone who once knew exactly whom to call may find that their counterpart has departed, or that the people still there are unsure whether leadership supports exchanging information. One current U.S. official described an environment that puts less public emphasis on election security at CISA and across the Department of Homeland Security than in previous cycles, with greater attention to other critical infrastructure matters, including water systems . The official speculated that employees could hesitate to highlight their election security work after seeing others who worked on elections lose their jobs, though they noted they had not heard staff express that fear directly. The official also acknowledged that midterms generally receive less attention than presidential elections. The administration has maintained that federal support continues. ODNI has assigned officials to coordinate election threat intelligence, while CISA outlined election support plans last month. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also directed Cyber Command and military intelligence agencies to prioritize foreign election threats and coordinate with the Department of Homeland Security last month. A current Defense Department analyst argued that closing offices focused on tracking influence operations does not necessarily erase expertise, because personnel can continue the work elsewhere in government or as contractors. But it’s unclear how much of that work has continued, or whether those who left government still have access to relevant information and federal contacts they once relied on. The analyst recalled a strong working relationship with Meta, which operates Facebook and Instagram, when they worked on those issues around two years ago. The analyst could not say whether those exchanges continue today. Similarly, one former U.S. official recalled preparations for the 2020 election beginning roughly a year before Americans went to vote, with coordination growing more frequent as Election Day approached. Some calls included 80 to 100 participants, including private companies, discussing topics that included ballot security and broadcasting accurate voting information. “Our nation’s security is best protected when private individuals, private sector, industry and government work together toward a common goal to protect our freedom and way of life, and that includes reporting suspicious and illegal activity and leveraging legal access and authorities to protect the American people and interests,” Erin Joe, special counsel at Wiley Rein LLP and a former senior FBI executive, told Nextgov/FCW in an interview. At the ABA conference, former DHS Secretary Michael Chertoff argued that the government still has a role in helping people recognize deception. Officials can explain where a message came from or show that a supposed recording was generated by AI, without telling people which political views to accept. “It is fighting bad speech with good speech,” Chertoff said. A TikTok spokesperson referred Nextgov/FCW to a webpage outlining steps the company is taking to prepare for midterms and disrupt covert influence operations on its platform. Several other social media companies and AI firms — including Meta, X, Anthropic and OpenAI — did not respond to requests for comment. Two state election officials described how their offices are responding to misleading information while receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles. One said identifying who is behind false messages can be difficult. Their office often focuses on information that could confuse people about when, where and how to vote, as well as threats to election workers. When a misleading claim surfaces, communications staff and leadership decide whether responding would help voters or draw more attention to something that might otherwise fade away. Threats to election officials are referred to law enforcement, the official said. The same official said they had not received an election-specific federal briefing “in quite some time,” although they attend regularly held CISA calls about software vulnerabilities and known flaws being exploited by hackers. Those discussions offer little information that is specific to elections, the official said. Monthly meetings through the state’s fusion center still bring together state, local and federal law enforcement to discuss threats to election officials. The second official said their office sends a representative to federal election-threat briefings whenever they are available, but those briefings have occurred less frequently than in 2024. That official nevertheless described their election offices as better prepared than in past years, with multiple backup plans, in case disruptions occur. “We hope that we don’t have to use them. But if we do, they’re there,” the official said. Those preparations come as AI has lowered the cost and effort required to conduct influence campaigns. AI has played a key role in helping to run these operations, from writing posts and distributing them to studying how people respond, said Snehal Antani, CEO and co-founder of cybersecurity company Horizon3.ai. Operators can test different messages and use the results to adjust their approach, and AI agents can automate much of that work, reducing the time and expertise it once required, he said. “AI has dramatically reduced the skills required and dramatically accelerated the speed at which this cycle can be executed,” Antani said. Another former U.S. official added that increasingly capable, downloadable open-source models allow smaller actors to undertake work that once required substantial investment and specialized engineering. “The barrier to entry is much lower,” the former official said, adding that AI-generated text can blend into everyday online conversations and make it harder to spot than a manipulated image or video with visible flaws. Russia is more likely to pursue more obvious inflammatory messaging this cycle, while China’s efforts may be more covert to serve longer-term objectives, said another current official, adding that both are expected to make greater use of AI. Pro-Iran outfits have especially leveraged AI more overtly in recent months amid the war that began in late February. But the official cautioned that more powerful AI tools and more convincing content do not necessarily mean a foreign operation is changing how people vote. An image or video getting lots of views does not mean people believe it or will vote differently because of it, they added. In some cases, an influence campaign may not even target eligible voters. For instance, content aimed at younger Americans could sway their political stances, but they may not be of legal age to cast a ballot. And in other settings, a foreign influence operation may not be needed for an American to vote a certain way. “If I see gas is $7 a gallon, I don’t necessarily need a lot more to go vote blue,” the official said, referring to California voters who have faced record-high fuel prices in some parts of the state. These foreign threats come as political campaigns at home have increasingly used AI in their advertisements. The growing use of AI-generated political videos could also make it harder to distinguish real footage from fabricated material, according to research released Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Check Point. “Video is one of the easier ways to make a claim feel real, since people tend to trust what they can see and hear for themselves,” the company’s findings say. As AI-generated political content becomes more common, it becomes harder for voters to “trust that a video of a candidate is real” and easier for anyone “to dismiss a real video as fake.” The scale and sophistication of false information today “makes our sensitivity to it a little bit more dull than perhaps in years past,” said Kimberly Kearney, a former CIA case officer. “We as individuals have to have the desire to know whether what we’re consuming is true or false, or if it feeds into a narrative that is convenient or more comfortable for us,” she said in an interview. “So it starts with that cognitive honesty and awareness to want to know whether what you’re consuming is accurate or if it could have a bias to it.” ]]>

title: Putin Fights to Preserve Russia’s Fading Influence in Central Asia
body:

Eurasianet is an independent news organization that covers news from and about the South Caucasus and Central Asia, providing on-the-ground reporting and critical perspectives on…
Back in 1991, the formation of the Commonwealth of Independent States placed the final nail in the Soviet Union’s coffin. Since then, the CIS itself has proven mostly moribund, falling far short of fulfilling the aims outlined in its 1993 charter .
The results of the recent CIS summit in Turkmenistan, marking the 35th anniversary of its formation, offered more of the same, featuring lots of empty rhetoric about the organization’s relevance and happy talk about its future. Russian leader Vladimir Putin was perhaps the CIS’ biggest cheerleader at the conclave, held at the Avaza resort on the Caspian seashore.
At odds with the organization’s lengthy record of inactivity and dysfunction , Putin’s pumped up the CIS for “having come a long way, establishing itself as an influential regional integration association.”
Economically speaking, there is little justification for keeping the CIS around. But Putin has a very good reason to keep it alive. Despite its shortcomings, the CIS is a regional vehicle that the Kremlin can use to combat the erosion of Russia’s cultural and historical legacy in Central Asia and the South Caucasus.
Underlying Putin’s speech at Avaza was a fear that Russia is losing its cultural grip over its erstwhile empire. He noted the CIS had enabled member states to “preserve, and in many areas even broaden … social, cultural and humanitarian ties our peoples forged over centuries of living together within a single state.”
He also cast the Russian language as “a powerful unifying force throughout the vast space of the CIS.” He went on to mention a Kremlin initiative launched this year to “preserve the common Russian-language cultural and humanitarian legacy, and to promote and popularize Russian.”
The Russian language is under growing pressure across Central Asia. It remains the primary means of interstate communication for business and diplomacy, but English is gaining ground. The same holds for a growing number of young people in major cities in the region, including Almaty, Astana, and Tashkent, who seem to prefer to speak English or their local languages, rather than Russian. Meanwhile, outside major urban centers, many under 35 show only a rudimentary grasp of Russian.
Central Asian governments are likewise legislating the erosion of Russian. Kazakhstan’s new constitution, for example, downgraded Russian’s status. Also this year, Uzbekistan introduced a revised Latin alphabet, although Cyrillic also remains in use. Kazakhstan is also moving towards the Latinization of its alphabet.
Moves to reduce Russia’s cultural influence extend to interpretations of history. Soviet historiography tended to cast Russian political, cultural and economic influence in Central Asia as a “civilizing” force. A revisionist trend now views Moscow’s legacy as oppressive, rather than beneficial.
Underscoring this change in attitude is the Uzbek State Museum Devoted to the Memory of Victims of Repression during Tsarist and Soviet rule. Kazakhstan and other Central Asian states have also scaled back celebrations commemorating the Red Army’s triumph over Nazi Germany in 1945.
The historical revisionist movement in Central Asia strikes at a central pillar of Putinism, which views the Soviet collapse in 1991 as a calamity and the defeat of the Nazis as an eternal achievement reaffirming Russia’s greatness.
It is noteworthy, then, that among the 15 mostly perfunctory documents signed at the conclusion of the Avaza CIS gathering, one stands out for articulating an aim to “preserve historical memory.” That document was highlighted in a readout of the summit’s proceedings issued by the Kremlin. It is specifically intended to “preserve the memory of the Victory of the Soviet peoples in the Great Patriotic War of 1941–1945.”
In pondering whether such a document can help the Kremlin reinforce Russia’s cultural influence in Central Asia, one might recall a phrase uttered by then-Russian prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in 1993 when talking about Russia’s reform process: “We wanted the best, but it turned out as usual.”

title: Apate sends AI agents undercover to get scammed so they can gather fraud intelligence
body:
Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed.
Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.
The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned only after a victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running.
Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The company will pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt , which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.)
It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. The FBI received more than 22,000 complaints of AI-related crimes in 2025, which resulted in about $893 million in losses. More than $632 million of that came from investment scams, in which the FBI says fraudsters use AI to run conversations, and deepfake the voices and appearances of celebrities, executives, and trusted figures.
For a long time, people have made a hobby out of deliberately stringing scammers along — sometimes hilariously, like getting scammers to read aloud entire books , or even to get ridiculous tattoos . Now, with AI growing increasingly capable, the tables are turning.
Curiously, the idea behind Apate was sparked by a real scam call.
Several years ago, Apate’s founder and CEO Dali Kaafar was at a family picnic when he got a call from an unknown number. Realizing it was a scammer on the line, he decided to play dumb for the benefit of his kids and managed to keep the call going for 44 minutes.
Everyone had a laugh, but Kaafar noticed that those were 44 minutes the scammer had not spent calling a real victim. It was also 44 minutes of his wasted time, which led him to wonder: Could he automate it, and in the process, learn something useful?
That idea eventually led to research work at his job at Macquarie University, where Kaafar and his colleagues used machine learning and natural language processing to uncover the content of scam calls, and develop better ways to detect and prevent scams.
“Most of the industry works after the fact. Telcos block numbers, but scammers just get new ones. Banks watch transactions, but by then the scammer has already reached the customer. We go to the scammer directly and get the information before anyone gets hurt,” Brad Joffe, co-founder and chief commercial officer, told TechCrunch. “Our AI agents talk to tens of thousands of scammers every day across calls, messages, email, and the web. What we offer our customers is what comes out of those conversations, and what they can do with it.”
Joffe said Apate uses both frontier models and its own fine-tuned models to power its agents and analysis. The company trains its models on conversations its agents have had with scammers, as well as the research Kaafar did at Macquarie.
In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get access to an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. Customers can even assign these agents particular missions, such as obtaining a bank account number or crypto-wallet address. Its text agents can search forums, investment groups, and social platforms for potential scam activity, and can then enter conversations with a fabricated identity to surface scammers’ details.
The startup’s customers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia, TPG Telecom, as well as other utilities, telcos, and government agencies. Joffe said TPG has diverted nearly 590,000 calls to Apate’s agents, Commonwealth has seen a 76% drop in publicly reported scam losses, and an unnamed Australian bank the startup works with has used its outbound agents to disrupt 22 scam campaigns.
Investors are betting there is money to be made from fooling scammers, too. Apate raised $8.15 million in seed funding in August from Lobby Capital, OIF Ventures, Investible, Concept Ventures, and Baobab Ventures. Joffe said the 20-person company has raised just under $10 million in total and plans to spend the latest round on its product and international expansion, including opening an office in London and building a larger presence in the U.S.
“Apate is named after the Greek goddess of deception, which felt appropriate given what our agents do,” Joffe said, adding that the startup even features scammers swearing at the bots in its pitch material.
“We track that as a sign of frustration and every swear word gets celebrated by us at Apate. We are probably one of the only businesses in the world that celebrates when people swear at our product.”

title: European officials weigh mix of high-tech drones and heavy armor
body: WARSAW, Poland — European governments are encouraging their defense industries to jointly develop and produce unmanned systems with Ukrainian companies, while cautioning to simultaneously new keep tanks and armored vehicles on hand for defending NATO’s eastern flank, officials said at the Warsaw Security Forum. Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius, the deputy prime minister and defense minister of the Netherlands, highlighted the Dutch defense sector’s ties with Ukraine in the field of drones. “Our armed forces are really training, as we speak, every day with the knowledge the Ukrainians have, because … they have the most innovative Army in Europe,” Yeşilgöz-Zegerius said on Oct. 12. “And what we are doing at the same time … is investing in our own defense industry. Because it was also, of course, due to a lack of spending, not that strong anymore. And in Europe we have that issue.” Meanwhile, while investing in drone and counter-drone systems, NATO allies bordering Russia are also procuring heavy gear for their land forces and seeking to secure a significant share of manufacturing work for their domestic defense industries. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told Defense News at the forum that the country’s planned acquisition of six-wheel-drive armored personnel carriers from Finland’s Patria is an example of how allies can work together on major purchases for their land forces. The vehicles are to support the Baltic state’s National Division, its main combat unit. “One of our intentions is not only to assemble, but also be involved in the R&D process,” Kaunas said. “The National Division is important because, together with our allies, including the United States, Germany, Poland, we can block our adversaries near the front line, near our borders, and then, of course, use drones, modern types of weapons to break them.” Kaunas said that combining the two categories of military assets is crucial, as demonstrated in Ukraine. “Ukraine adapted tanks with additional defense anti-drone capabilities and used them as a great source of protection for their soldiers, pushing Russians back near the front lines,” the Lithuanian minister said. Dovilė Šakalienė, a Lithuanian lawmaker and the country’s former National Defence Minister, told Defense News that European allies must sign “smart contracts” that reflect the rapidly changing battlefield reality in Ukraine, as exemplified by Lithuania’s 2024 deal to buy 44 Leopard 2A8 tanks for the country’s military, which she signed while in office. “We need to sign smart contracts which give us the delivery of the newest technology,” Šakalienė said. “In the Leopard agreement, we also included in a very clear way a condition that the newest version of anti-drone defense systems is going to be included. Not the ones which would be ready in 2024, but the ones that will be ready at the time of the assembly of these tanks. For the development of such technology, three years is eternity.” Despite European nations’ rapid expansion of drone procurement, allies should continue to invest in heavy equipment such as tanks and armored vehicles for their land forces, Šakalienė said. “Massive land maneuvers cannot be completed only with drones,” she added. Meanwhile, as Poland, the forum’s host, is making efforts to increasingly shift from the role of a buyer of foreign military gear to exporter of such goods, foreign defense groups competing for major orders are investing to expand their manufacturing footholds in the country. For U.S. companies, Poland’s drive to expand its domestic production capacities comes as many industry players are already planning to boost their capabilities in the country. “One of the things I can say about Poland is that the workforce here is exceptional. We’ve already got 1,000 employees here in Poland. And we’re looking to have much more than that,” Vince Logsdon, vice president for international business development at Boeing Defense Space and Security, told Defense News. Building on the 2024 deal to sell 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters to Poland under a deal worth around $10 billion, the producer is now offering its CH-47 Chinook aircraft to the country’s armed forces, pitching it as a complementary platform to the Apaches that can support troop movements and battlefield logistics. “The Chinook is our offering, it has proven itself throughout the world as a vertical lift, heavy lift helicopter. It has lots of operators throughout the world, and one of the things I have seen with our CH-47 offering is that most operators that acquire the Apache, they ultimately also acquire the CH-47,” Logsdon said. “It’s a perfect combination in terms of extending the battle space for the Apache.

title: Larus Receives $800K from NRC IRAP to Advance ScenarioGPT
body: Larus is pleased to announce that the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is providing advisory services and up to $800,000 in funding toward a $1.7M research and development project to further advance ScenarioGPT, an LLM-powered assistant that transforms natural language into executable military scenarios for command and control, simulation, and training. ScenarioGPT addresses one of the most persistent challenges facing military planning and training: the time and labour-intensive process of developing realistic operational scenarios. Current workflows rely on specialized expertise and manual effort, making it difficult to rapidly adapt scenarios as missions evolve or produce them at the scale required for modern training and planning. By enabling users to generate executable scenarios through natural language, ScenarioGPT reduces scenario development time from weeks to minutes, allowing organizations to prepare for a broader range of missions with greater speed and flexibility. Through the NRC IRAP-supported project, Larus will build on Canadian and NATO operational doctrine, tactics, techniques, and procedures to further refine ScenarioGPT while introducing a modern online interface, standardized APIs, and validating interoperability with partner systems. Together, these enhancements will improve integration readiness across defence organizations. “Preparing for today’s missions requires planning tools that can keep pace with an evolving operational environment,” said George DiNardo, CEO of Larus Technologies. “This project advances ScenarioGPT’s readiness for integration while enhancing its core capabilities. ScenarioGPT gives defence organizations a faster way to develop realistic scenarios while supporting the modernization priorities of the Canadian Armed Forces and our NATO partners.” Beyond defence, ScenarioGPT has broad dual-use applications for civilian markets including logistics, supply chain, route planning, emergency management, procurement and other areas, where organizations face similarly complex planning challenges requiring rapid evaluation of multiple courses of action. “ScenarioGPT combines large language models with military doctrine to simplify one of the most complex parts of operational planning,” said Dr. Rami Abielmona, Chief Technology Officer at Larus Technologies. “Instead of requiring specialized technical workflows, users can generate executable scenarios through human language, making advanced planning capabilities faster, more intuitive, and easier to integrate into existing defence systems.” ScenarioGPT works in tandem with Larus Foresight including combining rapid and dynamic scenario generation with other capabilities including fusion, analysis, simulation, and optimization, to improve the reliability and traceability of AI-based outputs. This project, with NRC IRAP support, marks another step in Larus’ mission to equip the Canadian Armed Forces and allied defence organizations with AI-powered decision intelligence that strengthens preparedness, accelerates planning, and supports mission success. The post Larus Receives $800K from NRC IRAP to Advance ScenarioGPT appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: US authorities dismantle crypto scam network that stole tens of millions
body:
Brooklyn prosecutors and the FBI seized 112 servers and shut down 241 websites linked to investment scams that targeted Russian-speaking Americans.
Prosecutors in Brooklyn, New York, working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have disrupted an Eastern European cryptocurrency scam network accused of stealing tens of millions of dollars from Americans, primarily Russian-speakers.
The operation, carried out last week and announced on Wednesday, resulted in the shutdown of 241 websites and the seizure of 112 servers hosted by companies in Eastern Europe and the United States, according to the Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office. No arrests were made.
“These criminals stole many millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims through an elaborate investment scheme, then tried to exploit them again with false promises to recover their money,” Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement. He credited the office’s Virtual Currency Unit and the FBI with uncovering the network’s infrastructure.
Seizing the servers was key to the operation because it disrupted the scammers’ ability to create new websites and contact victims. “We disabled the back end of the operation,” Assistant District Attorney Alona Katz, who led the investigation, said , according to Bloomberg.
The operation comes amid a rise in cryptocurrency-related fraud across the US. Americans reported $11.4 billion in crypto fraud losses in 2025, a 22% increase from the previous year, according to FBI figures cited by Bloomberg.

title: Russian Strikes Destroy Epicentr K’s Last Major Logistics Hub
body:
Epicentr K has lost its last remaining major logistics hub after Russian forces hit the distribution centre in Khmelnytskyi 10 times, destroying some 85% of the stored goods and igniting five major fires, according to an official company statement. The devastating blow capped a brutal week of relentless shelling that also hit the chain’s shopping centres in Chernihiv and Dnipro.
While no employees were injured in the Khmelnytskyi attack, emergency response efforts were hindered by approximately 30 Russian drones operating overhead. The company’s Facebook post stated that with this latest destruction, Epicentr K has lost its last major operational warehouse complex, as its primary distribution hubs near Kyiv were destroyed earlier in the war.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The loss directly affects 520 employees at the site, many of whom had previously been relocated to safer areas after earlier Russian strikes destroyed or damaged company facilities in Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa. In the same post, the company wrote that the cascading destruction of supply chains and retail infrastructure poses a serious risk to maintaining jobs and paying the salaries of thousands of workers.
The destruction of the logistics centre followed a series of attacks on the retailer’s stores throughout the week. Earlier, Russian forces virtually destroyed a new shopping centre in Chernihiv - a facility the company had painstakingly rebuilt, larger and more modern, after it was completely destroyed in 2022, according to press secretary Yulia Chundovets’s Facebook post. Shortly afterwards, a strike hit one of the chain’s oldest shopping centres in Dnipro, a site that had been in operation for almost 20 years and was of particular importance to local residents, she wrote.
Reflecting on the unprecedented toll of recent weeks, Chudnovets wrote on Facebook that “the past two months have brought the company more grief, losses, and terrifying news than all the preceding years of the full-scale war,” adding that “it feels as though the relentless destruction has no end, and honestly we are running out of strength”
Founded by Oleksandr and Halyna Hereha in 2003 with the opening of their first home improvement store in Kyiv, Epicentr K has grown into a major national retail network. The chain currently operates 72 shopping centers across Ukraine, with a total retail area of more than 2 million square meters (21.5 million square feet) and around 38,000 employees. Approximately 4,600 of its employees are currently serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. According to financial statements registered in YouControl , the company generated Hr. 81.2 billion ($1.9 billion) in 2025.

title: Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
body:
The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment will be 3.6% in 2027, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, provides an annual inflation adjustment to both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits.
Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, the agency said.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.
Around 72 million Social Security recipients will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. About 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries will receive higher payments starting Dec. 31, the agency said.
The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is in line with Social Security experts' projections , which last month forecast an increase of 3.5% to 3.6%.
The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. That year, beneficiaries received an 8.7% benefit boost — the highest in four decades — in response to rising inflation.
New government inflation data released Wednesday shows consumer price increases are accelerating. The consumer price index rose 3.7% over the past 12 months, as gas prices jumped.
About 40% of Social Security beneficiaries ages 65 and over rely on the program for at least half of their income, according to AARP .
A recent AARP survey found 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA would not be enough .
The Social Security COLA is "critically important" because it helps millions of Americans cover rising everyday costs, including groceries, routine bills and health care, AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement.
"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," Minter-Jordan said.
Beneficiaries can multiply their current monthly benefit amount by 3.6%, or 0.036, to estimate the increase to their checks for 2027.
However, keep in mind that increases to Medicare Part B or Part D premiums for 2027 — which may be deducted directly from benefit checks — can affect the size of beneficiaries' monthly payments.
Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B are projected to be $209.50 in 2027 , up from $202.90 in 2026, according to a report from Medicare trustees. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, or IRMAAs, if they have higher incomes. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary and preventive services.
Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to an analysis by KFF , a nonpartisan health policy research group.
The Social Security Administration will send beneficiaries notices about the COLA changes. The notices will include specific information about their 2027 benefits, including exact payment dates and dollar amounts as well as any deductions.
Individuals who have created online My Social Security accounts can access that information starting in late November, according to the agency. Beneficiaries without an online account who want to see their COLA notice online must create an account and opt into paperless notices by Nov. 18.
Beneficiaries who have not signed up to receive online notices will get mailed COLA statements in December. Those individuals should make sure the address the agency has on file is up to date, according to SSA.
Medicare premium amounts for 2027 will also be available online through the My Social Security message center starting in late November, the agency said.
The COLA is based on the percentage increase of one specific government inflation measure — the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W — from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year.
The CPI-W is a subset of the consumer price index that tracks the average change in prices for goods and services purchased by urban households.
The CPI-W rose 3.9% over the past 12 months, according to September data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Wednesday.
Policymakers and advocates have proposed alternatives to the CPI-W for calculating the annual COLA. One alternative is the chained CPI, an index that accounts for changes in buying habits as prices rise. However, a recent AARP analysis found that switching to that measure would "substantially lower benefits over time."
Others have proposed using the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, an experimental index that tracks spending for individuals ages 62 and over. However, some experts say the CPI-E does not necessarily grow much faster than the current measure used to calculate benefit increases.
Switching to a different COLA measure is among the changes lawmakers may consider in upcoming Social Security reform.
"Social Security's future is on the ballot this November, and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments," said Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group focused on expanding Social Security.

title: “Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); US Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the Russia sanctions law named after Lindsey Graham, has issued a sharp statement on the latest developments in Ukraine. He says that President Donald Trump and SpaceX chief Elon Musk should be held accountable for reported Starlink failures that could cripple Ukraine’s defense. On 14 October, Ukraine’s military reported a Starlink disruption that halted its operations. It happened at the same time the country’s air defense stopped receiving intelligence on a Russian ballistic strike that killed three people in Kyiv. Both failures came right after the US struck a diesel deal with Russia, letting low volumes of fuel into global markets and America while pressure grew on Ukraine to stop hitting the Russian oil refineries that raise the cost of the war. "Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," he says. When the network falters, the war feels it The alarm rests on how completely Ukraine leans on the system. SpaceX has reportedly throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use, with connections dropping once the drones move at speed, and breaking a series of missions. Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the latest limits revived long-running fears that its battlefield lifeline can be dialed down from outside the country. Blumenthal’s demand sits inside a broader revolt in Congress. A bipartisan group of 12 senators wrote Trump on 13 October urging him to rescind his deal letting Russian diesel back to market, calling the Treasury’s General License No. 135 a gift to Moscow that should be withdrawn. They pressed him instead to use the Graham-Leach-Bliley Act he signed in September to squeeze Russia and its enablers, above all, China. "If there's one lesson from Trump's mindless warmongering, it's that we need to break our dependence on foreign imports of fossil fuels & embrace alternate sources of energy," he said.
