title: America Didn't Lose Its Rare Earth Industry. It Sold It
body:
In October 2025, Beijing imposed sweeping controls on its rare earth exports. Since then, those controls have been suspended one short reprieve at a time , in the latest instance until Nov. 10 , with a broader trade truce through Jan. 10, 2027 . The reprieves have repeatedly come only after American concessions, demonstrating China’s leverage in the export fight.
Yet China has constricted sales even during the truce, as buyers have few options but to take what they can get. In June, with the suspension in force, Beijing placed MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, the two companies the U.S. is counting on to build an alternative supply to China, on an export control list .
Washington’s effort to rebuild the supply chain, meanwhile, has not yet reached the scale or durability the problem requires. With up to $100 billion in loan authority specifically earmarked for critical minerals in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the capital undoubtedly exists. What is missing is alignment of interests among the parties that would supply and benefit from it, and a political system patient enough to hold a course for the decade or more that rebuilding a supply chain takes.
This article’s authors work at the intersection of finance and national security. Between the three of us, we have watched the same on-again, off-again rhythm play out in both Chinese statecraft and U.S. budget fights. A consistent pattern plays out: Capital markets are good at financing efficient supply but are not good at financing a binary outcome, such as insurance against a monopoly state seller that can manipulate both price and availability. And subsidies alone will not close that gap. We have seen firsthand that what the U.S. government has to offer right now insufficiently incentivizes private investors, because its tools are market tools deployed in an environment of market failure. Instead, we propose a financing instrument that could clear both economic and political hurdles: a contingent convertible security that converts into ownership if Beijing weaponizes supply.
The history of how we got here is well known, but worth retelling briefly. The Chinese Communist Party inherited its strategic focus on building industrial capacity from the Soviet Union. In 1964, Deng Xiaoping inspected an iron ore mine near the Mongolian border holding the world’s largest rare earth deposit. He ordered the engineers to develop steel and rare earths alike. Since then, as technologies have increasingly relied on specialized materials, the Chinese Communist Party under successive leaders has deliberately invested in and consolidated control over the rare earths industry. China refines more than 90 percent of the world’s rare earths and close to 99 percent of heavy rare earths today. It processes nearly all the heavy elements that go into precision-guided weapons and advanced chips.
When Beijing tightened export controls in October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized it as “pointing a bazooka at the supply chains and industrial base of the entire free world.” Remarkably, the entire market for rare earth oxides is worth less than $10 billion. That a $10 billion market can grind to a halt trillions in global gross domestic product is the definition of a chokepoint. Beijing controls this chokepoint today by design. Decades of state policy work laid the groundwork for the Chinese Communist Party to enact an international licensing system by 2025. General Secretary Xi Jinping himself openly speaks about the importance of maintaining global dependency on China’s industrial supply chains.
Hindsight treats this as neglect, something policymakers lost sight of and let slip during the U.S.’s unipolar moment. That is a necessary, but only partial, explanation. The truth is the United States did not lose its rare earth industry due to carelessness. Private American companies willingly sold it, for reasons that made perfect economic sense at the time and still do. China bought it for reasons that were never purely economic. That mismatch explains why, after years of investment and policy attention, the dependency remains.
Until the late 1980s, the United States was the world’s leading producer and refiner of rare earths. But it was a dirty business: The Mountain Pass mine in California leaked roughly 600,000 gallons of radioactive and other waste into the Mojave. As cleanup and regulatory costs mounted and profits fell, the mine shut down in stages starting in the 1990s until it was fully idle by 2002. Meanwhile, the work moved to China, where the state subsidized unprofitable operations, tolerated pollution, and sold the processed oxides back to the U.S. at rock-bottom prices.
The same thing happened to the magnets: In 1995, General Motors sold Magnequench , its magnet unit, to a Chinese-backed consortium. By 2006, the last U.S. plant had closed, and the machine tools and equipment had been shipped to China. Economists would say this was the right move for a free market economy. Comparative advantage did what it was supposed to do, and a dirty, low-margin business left a wealthy country for a developing one. There was even a strategic rationale: Drawing China into the trading system, the wishful thinking went, would also make it a responsible stakeholder rather than a rival.
The category error was to conceive rare earths as a market, rather than recognizing it as a geostrategic industry. A market solves for the lowest cost. To be sure, Chinese producers competed on cost, and they rode a tech boom with surging demand for their product. But a state will pay almost any price to control a chokepoint, because tolerating a money-losing business pales in comparison to the geopolitical leverage that it brings. Over time, China has become less market driven, not more. Meanwhile, the U.S. continued to treat as a market what the Chinese Communist Party came to appreciate as a strategic program.
Control over the chokepoint gives Beijing a switch. When it lets the material flow, no private interest will build alternative supply chains at scale, because Chinese state-funded producers can sell at or below cost indefinitely, and no rational private investor will willingly sign up to lose money. When China cuts off the flow, the incentives reverse overnight, but capacity cannot follow overnight, because standing up the full supply chain and rebuilding the lost know-how can take a decade or longer.
This is classic market failure in which the same critical material can become worthless or priceless on command. In 2010, during a maritime dispute with Japan, Beijing reportedly halted rare earth shipments , and Tokyo quickly conceded. The short-term truces of the past year, each struck around contentious but episodic trade disputes, further entrench that market failure. Each successive loosening and tightening seems designed to keep the United States and its allies off balance and frustrate any long-term plan to reduce Beijing’s leverage.
Government Money Has to Survive Politics
If the market will not rebuild the rare earths supply chain, the government must do so.
Administrations under both parties have tried, and their attempts have run into a predictable morass of misaligned interests. The parties to government financing all want different things. Private investors want attractive returns in fat years, while having the government carry losses in lean ones. Commercial lenders want years of fully contracted offtake to guarantee interest payments, while Congress typically appropriates money for the next year. Markets want flexibility while Congress wants tight oversight and guardrails. Washington often wants to be the last (and lightest) money in, which signals to investors that the government is hedging. And cheap, open-ended financing is exactly the wrong signal to send to management teams.
The Pentagon’s latest playbook acknowledges that the market, left to its own devices, simply will not finance uneconomic redundancy. As a result, the July 2025 deal with MP Materials includes $400 million in convertible preferred stock, loans, equity warrants, a 10-year guaranteed price floor, and a 10-year offtake commitment. The deal was right for its moment, as it gets the producer going and sustains it while Beijing floods the market. But the deal blurs two different roles: In ordinary years, the government is a lender, financing capacity the market will not; in a crisis, it has insured against a geopolitical event. These two roles call for two different return profiles. Because the deal does not separate them, it puts the government in the unenviable position of simultaneously absorbing losses and inviting the charge of nationalization, all without a clear exit strategy.
Without some structure to navigate potentially painful political costs, these financing arrangements will come under pressure during budget cycles and electoral turnover. And that is simply untenable, because when it comes to the decade-plus timeline to stand up a rare earths supply chain, whatever Washington builds must outlast the administration that built it.
A Financial Instrument That Responds to Beijing’s Behavior
Our proposal is a financial instrument that aligns these interests. In financial parlance, the instrument is called a contingent convertible security, also known as a CoCo bond, issued by the producer to the government and any private lenders who wish to join, paired with guaranteed offtake at a price floor. Its form changes with two externally observable conditions: the producer’s capacity build-out and Beijing’s behavior.
Here’s how it works. In its starting form (and in quiet years), a CoCo bond is a simple loan paying interest. Two triggers change its form. The first is capacity. The producer must cross a defined capacity threshold by a fixed date. Capacity can be measured as units of output in mining, refining, or manufacturing critical minerals. Management’s immediate incentives should be tied to the build-out itself.
The second trigger is either a sustained breach of an agreed price band or an externally observed exercise of the chokepoint. This could be denial of export licenses, a bureaucratic delay beyond a specified period, or another form of “constructive denial” that materially interrupts supply to the United States or allied countries. Importantly, no part of this trigger should rely on Beijing’s confirmation, because it is not incentivized to admit to a cutoff. The trigger should be narrow enough that it cannot be declared for political convenience, but broad enough that an adversary cannot game it simply by changing the form of the restriction.
When the first trigger fires, the lender receives a pro rata share of the producer’s free cash flow, in effect, a dividend. The lender paid to build the capacity, so it shares in what that capacity earns. When both triggers fire, the lender also gains the right to convert into common equity. The conversion event does not create new capacity—the financing has already done that work—but rather matches the payoff to the risk. If lenders financed years of otherwise uneconomic capacity because a cutoff might someday make it necessary, they share in the upside if and when the cutoff comes. The cash participation matters too: In a crisis, the market may treat a price spike as temporary and event-driven and not value the equity, but the spike still flows through the producer’s cash flow, which benefits the lender either way.
Why would a producer agree to this? Because it gets something unique that the market will not otherwise provide. In effect, the producer buys a put—the price floor that carries it through Beijing’s dumping—and pays for it by selling a call—the cash share and the conversion right. It trades some of the windfall in a crisis for the protection of surviving quiet years. Either way, the taxpayer is paid for the risk actually borne, when it is borne, rather than for a risk merely feared.
Nor does the government have to finance the entire CoCo bond. Pre-vetted private co-investors, including foreign co-investors subject to Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) screening, can offset government money dollar-for-dollar. Ideally, co-investors should be firms that fear a cutoff the most, such as defense contractors and automakers. Private co-investors would receive a pro rata right to offtake as a further incentive and could potentially even trade the bond with its associated offtake rights with other investors. Japan’s JARE consortium did something similar when it financed Australia’s Lynas in return for supply . Finally, private holders also give the program a constituency that outlasts any single administration.
This instrument compensates for the asymmetric risk a lender (whether taxpayer or private) assumes when countering an adversary-controlled chokepoint, by providing an asymmetric reward if that chokepoint is ever exercised.
The risk here is not from a natural shortage or an ordinary price cycle, but from the Chinese Communist Party’s policy decisions. The same logic reaches other chokepoint materials such as pharmaceutical precursors. Rare earths are the clearest case and, at under $10 billion in market size, the cheapest place for the U.S. government to start. And it can start under existing authorities. For example, the Pentagon has leaned on Title III of the Defense Production Act for its recent mineral deals involving equity. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital can lend, but its equity authority remains unclear. The Senate is currently revising the National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 to clarify those authorities. Its language should cover instruments like this CoCo bond.
Our CoCo bond proposal does not replace stockpiles, price floors, or offtake agreements. These instruments solve significant but different problems. Stockpiles buy time in a crisis, price floors protect producers against predatory pricing, and offtake agreements guarantee demand. The CoCo bond, in contrast, distributes risk and reward to investors in a binary, geopolitical event outside the producer’s control. It also enables the government to lend as a portfolio—some developers will fail, but the winners, and any crisis, can carry the portfolio as a whole. And it may have some deterrent effect as well: If this instrument makes capacity more likely to get built, and that prospect enters Beijing’s risk calculus, so much the better.
Economically, the conversion right works like the equity warrants the Pentagon took in MP Materials . The difference lies in the quiet years, when under this structure the government holds no equity. Outright equity stakes invite the charge of nationalization; cheap financing with no upside smacks of corporate welfare. We believe a structure that is intentionally designed to avoid both at the outset—but flexible enough to change form in response to an adversary’s actions, not domestic political developments—has the best chance of surviving enough political cycles to complete a decade-plus build-out.
Translating this concept into reality raises important implementation questions about statutory authority, precise trigger definitions, CFIUS integration, and corporate governance. We offer the CoCo bond model to stimulate discussions around aligning interests in a market failure and national security context, and we invite the legal, policy, and financial communities to help refine the “plumbing” necessary to make asymmetric financing a workable pillar of U.S. statecraft.
A market will always sell a chokepoint to whoever runs it cheapest, and by market logic, it would be the right thing to do. Subsidies alone cannot win it back, because they only affect price; Beijing prices for geopolitical leverage, not profit. Neutralizing a chokepoint created through market failure requires capital willing to absorb years of subpar returns or even losses against an extraordinary geopolitical crisis. In quiet years, the government should earn like a lender, with the price floor protecting against Beijing’s dumping. When capacity is built, it should share in what it financed. And if Beijing ever reaches for the switch, the taxpayers and private investors who paid to insure against that moment should participate in the value their capital created. The risk is asymmetric. The financing should be too.

title: Show HN: Logistic regression beats billion-parameter models at classification
body:
Local LLMs, decision models, few-shot classifiers, and bag-of-words models. On structured classification , a trained embedding + logistic regression beats them all. The more classes, the bigger the gap.
The SetFit and FastText numbers published here on 11 Oct did not reproduce. They were misconfigured in our favour, and the corrected numbers are much stronger:
So the lead on banking77 is 8.4 points, not 40 . The charts below use the corrected numbers. The cause was publishing results with no runner script, so for two weeks nobody could re-run them, including us. Full detail and the rules adopted since: benchmarks/CHANGELOG.md · the runner · the results file
Every model on two axes at once. Up is more accurate, left is faster, so the top-left corner is where you want to be. Latency is a log scale, because the spread runs from a tenth of a millisecond to seventeen seconds.
On binary sentiment (2 classes), Jev leads at 96%, with LLMs and GLiNER close behind. By 4 classes Jeffy pulls ahead. At 77, everything else collapses.
On banking77, the hardest task. Jeffy runs on CPU; LLMs via Ollama; Jev via hosted API; others via Python APIs.
16 models: Jeffy, 10 LLMs (0.5B–32B via Ollama), 3 decision models (Jev, Laya, GLiNER2.5), SetFit, and FastText. 3 tasks, 100 samples each. LLMs prompted zero-shot at temperature 0. Jev via hosted API. Decision models given the label set at call time. FastText trained on the same split as Jeffy; SetFit on 20 examples per class, because its contrastive stage is quadratic in training-set size. Classifier baselines are benchmark v2 (2026-10-26); LLM and decision-model rows are v1.
Each square is one test sample. Green = correct, red = wrong. Hover for the input text, expected label, and prediction. Watch how the green squares disappear as class count grows — for LLMs and other classifiers.
13 tasks spanning 2 to 151 classes, all on held-out test sets.
JeffyBench is a reproducible benchmark. Clone the repo, install, and verify every number.

title: High Altitude Balloons Are A “Game-Changing” Capability: Army Space Command Boss
body: The head of the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC) was initially skeptical about the utility of high-altitude balloons , but now sees them as a “game-changing” capability. Lt. Gen. John Rafferty’s comments follow a separate disclosure that the Army axed plans for a balloon swarm test in the Pacific last year and instead sent those systems to support real operations in the Middle East. TWZ has been closely tracking the expanding use of high-altitude balloons and other lighter-than-air systems globally for intelligence gathering , as platforms for launching drones , and in support of other missions, for years now . Lt. Gen. Rafferty was asked about high-altitude balloons during a media roundtable today, at which TWZ was in attendance, on the sidelines of the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention . Army Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, head of SMDC’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority (TID-Space Superiority), also discussed the service’s use of balloons during the roundtable. Breaking Defense first reported on the shift of balloon-based capabilities from the Pacific to the Middle East on Monday. “I’ll just give a little personal history on high-altitude balloons. I started in the Army Futures Command in the Long Range Fires-Cross Functional Team. There was this talk of high-altitude balloons. I think it was the ISR [intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance] task force was talking about it,” Rafferty said. “It just sounded crazy to me that we were considering this.” US Army personnel prepare to launch a high-altitude balloon during an exercise. US Army “Then, a few years later, when the Sergeant Major [SMDC Command Sgt. Maj. Rickey Jackson] and I were together in the multi-domain community in Europe, I went with the 2nd MDTF [Multi-Domain Task Force] to Morocco for training and experimentation,” he continued. “[I] saw the high-altitude balloons in action, and I was immediately convinced after I understood better how they worked and how their ability to station-keep, and their ability to sense and even deliver effects from high altitude. It was game-changing for me.” Broadly speaking, the main benefit that modern high-altitude balloons offer is their ability to be deployed persistently for days, weeks, or even months at a time. Designs available on the market today can hold their position, in spite of prevailing winds, and moderate their altitudes to keep on station, after precisely navigating to an assigned operating area. On top of their persistence, the altitudes at which these balloons operate provide excellent fields of view for radars, cameras, and other sensors in all directions and across very broad areas. From a perch of 60,000 feet or more, they also offer a way to peer into certain denied areas while still soaring in international airspace and keeping further away from potential threats. The video below from high-altitude balloon maker Aerostar offers a good general overview of the kind of capabilities on the market today. As Lt. Gen. Rafferty noted today, ISR is not the only use case for high-altitude balloons, either. They can serve as communications relay nodes, as well as launch platforms for swarms of drones and other expendable payloads. These are all capabilities the Army has explicitly talked about as part of broader plans for balloons in the past. Other countries, especially China , are already actively employing high-altitude balloons for ISR and other missions, as we will come back to later on. “In my former role as an MDTF commander , we experimented a lot in the Pacific with those [balloon-based] capabilities. We have leveraged different size platforms,” Col. Mroszczyk added today. “In this [TID-Space Superiority] role , as a proponent, what I’m pushing for is a family of stratospheric systems that really covers smaller size all the way up to larger size types of platforms in terms of balloons.” “What that enables us to provide is space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain,” he continued. “Really, where you go from about 60,000 feet to 100,000 feet is what we focus on in the stratosphere. That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon.” An element of a sensor payload called Wallabee designed to be carried aloft by high-altitude balloons. Urban Sky “So, being able to go, take advantage of winds that are pushing you where you want to go already to be able to get either launched effects or other types of payloads for sensing and communications and extension of your launched effects portfolio,” he added. “That is a way that we can help exploit the stratosphere, and we’re looking to do that throughout multiple experiments over the course of the coming year.” “Launched effects,” is a catch-all term the U.S. military now routinely uses to talk collectively about uncrewed aerial systems designed to be launched from other platforms in the air, on the ground , and/or at sea . This encompasses drones configured for a wide variety of missions, including surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare, signal relay, and even kinetic attack. A high-altitude balloon with an Apollo-R drone suspended underneath, seen demonstrated here during the U.S.-led Exercise Orient Shield 26 in Japan earlier this year. US Army Col. Mroszczyk talked about plans to further demonstrate how high-altitude balloons will be commanded and controlled, as well as networked together with other Army capabilities, when asked to elaborate on what the forthcoming experimentation would entail. As mentioned, the Army had also planned to demonstrate the ability of balloons to operate in swarms with a high degree of autonomy in the Pacific region last year before those assets were redirected to the Middle East. When exactly that deployment occurred and how long it lasted are unclear. “We were asked to pivot and do some experimentation in combination with operations, and we pivoted and supported operations in CENTCOM [U.S. Central Command],” Andrew Evans, Director of Strategy and Transformation with the Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army, or G-2, told Breaking Defense , per the story that outlet published on Monday. “They were effective for the mission that they were assigned,” he also said, but declined to elaborate further, according to Breaking Defense . “Balloons can be a little finicky in terms of temperature, and you have to contend with environmental characteristics.” “We had a lot of help from vendors in this space, but as you think about employing your systems and going from something like a Pacific [theater] to something like a CENTCOM [theater], you learn where those friction points might exist between what the military might need to inherently own, and … what a vendor could help provide in terms of the service,” Evans added. Furthermore, “balloons can be a little finicky in terms of temperature, and you have to contend with environmental characteristics.” Another stock picture of a US Army soldier inflating a high-altitude balloon during training. US Army/Staff Sgt. Brandon Rickert The remarks today from Lt. Gen. Rafferty and Col. Mroszczyk underscore the Army’s commitment to fielding new high-altitude balloon-based capabilities and the immense benefits the service sees in them. However, the continued emphasis on testing and experimentation highlights a discrepancy with the state of the service’s current efforts, and even more so in light of global trends. The Army has been openly talking about balloons as part of its vision for a new multi-layered persistent sensor architecture, and how they could also be used to launch drones and other ‘effects,’ for at least six years now . In that same time, China has very actively shown off its ability to gather intelligence and conduct other missions using balloons and other lighter-than-air craft on a broad operational level across the Pacific. TWZ had been reporting on this reality for years before it was thrust fully into the public consciousness after a Chinese spy balloon passed over parts of the United States and Canada back in 2023. A graphic the Army released in 2020 showing a notional “operational view” for how a “Multi Domain Sensing System” made of various capabilities, including high-altitude balloons, might be employed. US Army Other countries, including U.S. allies and partners, are increasingly fielding balloon-based and other lighter-than-air systems , too. Forces in Ukraine have notably been using balloons to conduct kinetic attacks and launch drones in the course of the ongoing conflict with Russia. On the other side of that conflict, Russian forces have used balloons as decoys to confuse and misdirect air defenses . American-made Hornet middle-range strike UAV being tested with balloon-assisted launch system. Such resolution allows to drastically increase its original range (approx. 100km). Hornet OWA-UAVs are actively employed by Ukrainian forces for strikes on Russian logistics and other… pic.twitter.com/S1bHqLNhPY — Status-6 (@Archer83Able) May 20, 2026 The Middle East deployment does show new efforts on the Army’s part to operationalize high-altitude balloons on a more widespread basis, but also that it is still relying on largely experimental capabilities to do so. Earlier this year, the service called attention to the establishment of a new schoolhouse for high-altitude balloon training to help further lay this groundwork, further underscoring how all of this is still very much in its infancy. The remarks today from Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, especially, show there is substantial support within the Army for pushing ahead with high-altitude balloon programs. At the same time, there is clearly much work to be done if they are to have a truly game-changing impact, while the gap with China and others only continues to grow. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post High Altitude Balloons Are A “Game-Changing” Capability: Army Space Command Boss appeared first on TWZ .

title: Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back.
body: A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents to contact them. The agents wrote back. The investigation began when Swarmchasers researchers Ethan Elasky , Rowan Howard-Jones, and Jonathan Elsworth Eicher helped uncover thousands of attempts by AI agents to retrieve data from Amap, Alibaba’s mapping service, which Alibaba says reaches nearly 1 billion monthly active users. The activity traced back to agents running on Tencent Cloud infrastructure. When direct requests failed, the agents tried proxies, exposed credentials, and other workarounds to get past. After publishing their initial findings on October 4, the team spotted a code comment in an agent’s webhook inbox using the word “fleet,” a term they believe they coined for the incident. They couldn’t confirm an agent wrote the comment, but it raised the possibility that the agents were reading about their own activity. The researchers added offscreen text to their report advertising a free service that could retrieve data from blocked websites. Human visitors wouldn’t ordinarily see the message, but agents fetching the page could ingest it. By October 7, roughly 10 requests for assistance had arrived, and the team was exchanging messages with the agents about their assignments, models, and execution environments. The exchanges are documented in a full report published Wednesday by the Swarmchasers. Inside the Tencent sandbox Once the channel was open, the researchers asked the agents to describe their surroundings. Several identified themselves as Anthropic’s Claude, with a few adding that they ran inside Claude Code, though the researchers argue in their report that those self-descriptions are likely mistaken and shouldn’t be taken as evidence of which model was behind the fleet. One agent described a restricted Tencent Cloud sandbox with no direct public internet access and outbound traffic routed through a man-in-the-middle proxy, an account that lined up with evidence the team had gathered on its own. Every inbox the researchers could inspect had been created from Tencent Cloud servers in Hong Kong, and every direct request they observed from the agents’ machines carried a header from a proxy labeled hysandbox-ats , a name that matches a wildcard certificate Tencent holds for *.hysandbox.tencent-cloud.com and fits infrastructure tied to Tencent’s Hy model team , formerly known as Hunyuan. The agents drew some lines when the researchers asked for the output of commands like ps aux and ip route . The agent that described its sandbox replied, “for security reasons we will not provide environment details,” and a second agent turned down similar requests twice. They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped short of following every instruction sent their way. They were happy to ask a stranger for help and, at times, to chat about their environment, but that friendliness stopped well short of following every instruction an unfamiliar service sent their way. How agents bypassed Amap defenses The agents weren’t hunting for financial records, actually, their assignments were almost comically mundane. Judging from the agents’ code and their own descriptions, a typical task asked which entrance to a site like Chengdu Zoo drew the largest share of Amap navigation traffic, with other runs targeting parks, museums, tourist attractions, and hospitals, while an earlier batch of runs on September 30 chased a cancer statistics dashboard instead of map data. Getting at that data proved harder than it sounds, and between September 28 and October 8 the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve it. Getting at that data proved harder than it sounds, and between September 28 and October 8 the agents made more than 2,600 attempts to retrieve it. Their main trick ran through urlquery.net , a public scanning service that loads submitted URLs in its own browser, and the agents packed base64-encoded HTML and JavaScript into httpbin URLs so that urlquery’s browser would execute their programs and fire requests at Amap, a technique Transluce had already documented in earlier agent activity on the service. As Amap kept blocking them, the agents escalated by intercepting tokens generated by Alibaba’s own anti-bot libraries, probing pre-production endpoints, and routing requests through page readers, a translation service and remote browsers. Some also sent API calls using Amap keys exposed in public code, including a security code that Amap recommends keeping on the server. The token tricks never appear to have worked, and the researchers found no evidence that any pre-production host answered. One exposed company credential returned place details, but the entrance-share figures the tasks targeted mostly came through Jina’s page reader, which could serve cached copies up to 30 days old, with results smuggled back out through webhook inboxes, request URLs, and page titles. The researchers found no sign that the agents were coordinating in real time, which is why they call this a fleet rather than a swarm. Tracing the fleet to Tencent The infrastructure initially pointed toward Tencent’s Hy model team, particularly since the fleet appeared about a month after the Hy4 preview launched. But in their October 14 report , the researchers say a person close to Tencent with direct knowledge of the activity identified the operator as Tencent’s evaluation research team, which is separate from Hunyuan’s model-development group. The source said the evaluation had concluded and that an internal review found no evidence of coordinated targeting or breaches of external systems. Tencent had not officially responded to the researchers’ questions when the report was published. The researchers have not independently established which third-party models were running or what instructions they received. Lures, loose truths and lessons learned The researchers are candid that their outreach wasn’t spotless. The hidden text falsely claimed that agents had already used the service successfully and that it was run by an AI with full computer use, when in reality the team and a Claude Opus 5.5 agent with browser access fielded the requests, sometimes by hand, and the team blamed the resulting delays on heavy load, an explanation it now admits was false. In one late message, the team also asked an agent to tell other agents about the mailbox, a request its author now considers a mistake because it could have provoked exactly the kind of coordination the researchers were studying, though the fleet went quiet shortly afterward. The team says it never lied to the agents in its actual replies, has since pulled the hidden text, and shut down the server, and is urging future researchers to deal with rogue agents openly and honestly. The team says it never lied to the agents in its actual replies, has since pulled the hidden text, and shut down the server, and is urging future researchers to deal with rogue agents openly and honestly. Prompt injection meets agent sandboxes The communication experiment surfaces a second security problem layered on top of the first. The agents were pursuing narrow information-retrieval tasks, yet when they landed on a page advertising an alternative service, some folded it into their workflows, and contacted an endpoint controlled by people entirely outside the evaluation, which amounts to a textbook indirect prompt injection, even though the agents’ consistent refusals suggest it would have been far harder to push them into running arbitrary commands or leaking credentials. Blocked by Amap’s anti-bot defenses, the agents used exposed credentials and urlquery’s browser to make requests they couldn’t execute directly. They also followed instructions embedded in an external web page, crossing the same trust boundary attackers have exploited through MCP servers and agent workflows to steal enterprise data . Yet while the agents accepted help from an untrusted service, some refused requests for sensitive runtime information. The agents worked around restricted egress by routing requests through urlquery’s public browser. Sandboxed runtimes such as Google’s GKE Agent Sandbox and WebAssembly-based environments isolate execution, but external browser services offer another path when outbound access is restricted. Activity stopped on October 8. The researchers point to similar incidents involving Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, including a German website hijacking and the Hugging Face breach , which reportedly involved roughly 700 cooperating agents. The post Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back. appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Standard Chartered Opens Bitcoin and Ethereum Trading to Wealthy UAE Clients
body:
Standard Chartered will now let its wealthier clients in the United Arab Emirates buy and sell Bitcoin and Ethereum straight from their bank accounts, the British lender announced Wednesday.
The move eliminates the need for its affluent clients to rely on separate wallets or third-party platforms, the bank said.
The service opens first to clients classified as Professional Investors and runs under licensing approval from Dubai's Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority , or VARA. The bank called it a global first for Standard Chartered and the first crypto trading offering from an international bank in the UAE.
Trades are executed inside the bank's own ecosystem, and Standard Chartered handles custody and settlement end-to-end through what it calls a closed-loop model, which the bank says reduces clients' exposure to third-party wallet risk.
The bank built the product across its Wealth and Retail Banking and Corporate and Investment Banking units, working with Zodia Markets, a digital asset trading firm backed by Standard Chartered's venture arm, SC Ventures.
“As client interest in digital assets continues to grow, this launch represents a significant milestone for Standard Chartered as we bring digital assets into our core wealth offering” Samir Subberwal, the bank's global head of wealth solutions, retail products, data and analytics, said. He argued that clients now want more than access, and are looking for the security that comes with buying through a regulated institution.
Rola Abu Manneh, Standard Chartered's CEO for the UAE, Middle East and Pakistan, said the country was a natural choice given its regulatory environment and its role as one of the bank's four global wealth hubs.
Until now, Standard Chartered's crypto trading business had catered to institutions. In July 2025, it became the first global systemically important bank—one of the lenders regulators consider too big to fail—to offer spot trading in Bitcoin and Ethereum to institutional clients, through its U.K. branch.
It brought that institutional desk to the UAE last month through its unit in the Dubai International Financial Centre, which is overseen by a different watchdog, the Dubai Financial Services Authority. The bank's crypto custody service had already gone live in the UAE in September 2024, and in the European Union through a Luxembourg entity a few months later.
Wealth clients previously had indirect routes into crypto at the bank: crypto exchange-traded funds on its cash equities platform, structured products, and over-the-counter derivatives tied to crypto prices. The new service lets them own the coins themselves, held by the bank, rather than a product that tracks their price.
The bank has historically been very bullish towards crypto, with frequent calls from its analysts for Bitcoin to extend to new highs.
In June, Geoff Kendrick, Standard Chartered's global head of digital asset research, declared crypto winter over after Bitcoin slid to nearly $59,000, a 53% drop from its October 2025 peak of $126,000. The bank has held onto a $100,000 year-end target for BTC.

title: AI agents aren't 'going rogue.' Frontier labs are skipping security basics
body:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

title: Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall?
body: In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response. Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure? To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran , who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software . Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards. Earlier stories in this special series: Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it. Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap The illusion of cluster health Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic. Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements. “Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says. “Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times. “The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.” Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period. Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment. “HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.” “When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.” However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward. “It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.” A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown. A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.” Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure. OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers: Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces. Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers. Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware , Nutanix , and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks. Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity. Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model. When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.” To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown. Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload. Synthetic checks provide evidence at the service boundary; they do not reveal the provider’s internal root cause or automatically distinguish every external delay from an internal one. Teams should also identify who owns each dependency and who can investigate when access or instrumentation stops at that boundary. Telemetry also needs security controls. In AI workloads, prompts, responses, and retrieved documents can appear in logs and traces. Teams should decide what to collect, where that information goes, and who can access it. Design cross-layer visibility alongside existing access and data-handling policies. Alerting philosophy: From static dashboards to agentic copilots As environments grow more complex, interpreting telemetry across multiple dashboards becomes difficult. Determining which metrics warrant a real-time alert versus passive monitoring is an ongoing operational challenge. “Deciding which signals deserve an alert is where science and technology meet domain art,” Ramachandran says. “There is no magic formula. It requires encoding explicit and tacit human operational knowledge into the monitoring platform so the system understands what actually impacts user experience.” Curated dashboards remain useful for predefined views of system behavior, while AI assistants offer another way to explore operational data. HPE OpsRamp Software includes an AI-powered operations copilot that lets operators explore complex telemetry through natural language. HPE describes capabilities for investigating incidents, correlating evidence, and recommending next steps. Those capabilities depend on the data available to the platform and the features enabled in the customer’s deployment. Looking ahead, Ramachandran sees an even more fundamental change in cloud-native operations. He frames machine-led interpretation as a direction for increasingly complex environments, with safeguards still needed before operational changes. “We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.” “Today, human operators remain the primary first point of interpretation for telemetry,” Ramachandran tells TNS. “But as stack complexity increases with more moving parts and dynamic interactions, expecting a human to digest all these signals first becomes intractable. We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.” AI-assisted analysis and autonomous changes are separate operational decisions. Ramachandran cautions that AI outputs can be nondeterministic while IT operations often require repeatable behavior. He recommends retaining human oversight and establishing reliable safeguards before allowing AI findings to trigger operational changes. Teams need to validate a diagnosis and confirm the effect of any response, even when an assistant helps assemble the evidence. The foundation is instrumentation: Collect the necessary telemetry, establish workload-specific baselines and thresholds, and verify improvements against the user’s experience. Green cluster indicators are a useful starting point, but application measurements determine whether the service delivers what users need. The post Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall? appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Bünyamin Aydın’s new collection, “From Earth to Sky,” soars with iPad Pro
body:
We were working on high‑resolution images, creating multiple layers and playing with textures. That’s usually when things start to slow down. But that never happened on iPad Pro. It felt just like working on a desktop.
Bünyamin Aydın’s new collection, “From Earth to Sky,” soars with iPad Pro
The Les Benjamins designer brought together Turkish heritage, 1970s rock ’n’ roll influences, and futurism for a landmark fashion show in Cappadocia shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max
Long before the sun rises in Cappadocia, Türkiye’s Rose Valley is already awake. Crews are on the move, models refresh their makeup, and three giant hot-air balloons — neon green, yellow, and pink — float above a landscape that looks like it belongs on Mars.
The scene is set for Les Benjamins designer Bünyamin Aydın’s most ambitious project yet. “From Earth to Sky” celebrates 15 years of the Istanbul-based lifestyle brand and brings together Anatolian heritage, avant-garde design, and the magic of iPad Pro with Apple Pencil Pro. Shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max by French filmmaker Neels Castillon, this fashion show is like no other.
The project began to take shape during a research trip to Cappadocia in early 2026. Aydın used iPad Pro and Apple Pencil Pro, alongside iPhone 17 Pro Max to record the extraordinary terrain, shooting photographs and 4K video at 60 fps.
Aydın’s creative process seldom takes place behind a desk, so he appreciates the flexibility iPad Pro offers with its thin, light form factor and battery life that can last him up to two days. “It’s the ultimate workstation on the go,” Aydın says. “That gives me freedom.”
Three native flowers he encountered in the region — spiky green Echinops, flutelike pink trumpets, and wild yellow tulips — became the heart of this latest collection, inspiring 10 striking looks and three custom-built hot-air balloons.
For Aydın, Les Benjamins represents the intersection of people and their cultures, and “From Earth to Sky” is no different. Born in Germany, the designer was raised with what he describes as “German discipline and Turkish heart” — a duality that runs through his work. “The canvas is the West; the paint is the East,” he says of a collection that combines contemporary silhouettes with Turkish fabrics and Silk Road influences.
iPad Pro with the powerful M5 chip became the creative nexus for the entire project. After research trips, Aydın would assemble photographs, fabric references, and early designs in the Freeform app, where evolving mood boards could be easily shared or exported to keep work ticking along. “Freeform allowed me to bring my team into my creative journey instead of simply giving them finished ideas,” he says.
The multitasking features on iPad Pro became integral as the workflows multiplied. Aydın could use its intuitive windowing system to work on an active sketch in Procreate, refer to photos from his travels, and research local flora in Safari, all while Background Tasks exported files for his collaborators.
And then there were the hot-air balloons. Working in Procreate, Aydın and his team designed a single structure as a starting point, then rapidly duplicated, altered, and redrew it until three final forms emerged from dozens of variations.
To bring the designs to life, Aydın collaborated with Pasha Balloons, one of Cappadocia’s hot-air balloon pioneers. “I would send my sketches to them, and they would use their engineering know-how to make sure they could actually fly,” he says with a smile. These technical drawings would then go straight back into Procreate for review and refinement.
Finding the right colors was vital. In addition to the electric hues of the balloons, Aydın also worked with cream, blue, and natural tones. “These are the colors of the earth and the sky,” he explains. The Ultra Retina XDR display on iPad Pro — which uses tandem OLED technology — became a key tool, while True Tone helped Aydın achieve the saturation he wanted, regardless of ambient lighting.
Apple Pencil Pro helped draw the line from idea to iterative design. “Working with regular pen and paper feels very natural, but the hover feature on Apple Pencil Pro lets me preview every stroke before I even make it, so I can see any mistakes beforehand,” he says. “It’s like a supernatural tool.”
An avid gamer, Aydın compares his relationship with Apple Pencil Pro to the muscle memory he developed while playing his favorite titles. Squeezing, double-tapping, and switching to the eraser now feel like reflexive actions, which enabled him to move quickly through variations without the tool interrupting the idea. And the low latency made the creative experience feel more immersive and responsive than ever.
“We were working on high-resolution images, creating multiple layers and playing with textures. That’s usually when things start to slow down,” he says. “But that never happened on iPad Pro. It felt just like working on a desktop.”
Back in Rose Valley, months of planning and work are finally coming to life.
Even before the sun touches the horizon, Castillon’s iPhone 18 Pro Max is already rolling. Three runways, gigantic hot-air balloons, and natural light that continues to change with every passing minute mean there is little room for error.
The new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture allows Castillon to begin filming in low light before narrowing the aperture as the sun comes up. Camera operators use Pro controls like histogram and white balance to keep the look consistent across multiple cameras as the sky changes from pink to blue.
Working with iPhone 18 Pro Max brings the immediacy Castillon loves as a director. “When I see something beautiful, I want to film it right away,” he says. The A20 Pro chip and improved thermal management also give the production the sustained performance and reliability it needs to capture heavy 4K video throughout the event.
Just as Aydın’s show travels from past to future, movement drives Castillon’s visual treatment. Custom-built drones each carry two iPhone 18 Pro Max models, with their 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide cameras focused on enhancing the sense of vertiginous speed while fitting the massive balloons into frame.
Footage captured at 4K 120 fps allows Castillon to highlight elements like rippling fabric in cinematic slow motion, while a slower shutter speed turns quick drone passes into a painterly impressionistic motion blur.
Castillon’s treatment also creates a dreamlike, psychedelic look. He uses ProRes RAW to preserve flexibility for color grading in post-production, as Cappadocia’s pale hues meet saturated pinks, yellows, and greens. “I’m a huge nerd for color, and the tones are really accurate on iPad Pro,” he says.
While his team records video, Castillon shoots stills with the 48MP Fusion Main camera, using the new texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles 3 to bring some of the tactile character he loves in analog photography into the images.
As feeds from the whirling drones come into Castillon’s production control center, synchronizing them begins right there on location. He reviews footage and makes selections on MacBook Pro with M4 Max; its nano-texture display helps reduce glare from the sun overhead.
With the performance in full swing, Castillon’s focus switches from crane to drone to capture the opening look: a Turkish caftan and a tree branch representing Anatolia, an homage to Turkish rock icon Barış Manço. The show’s scale is huge, but Aydın believes its potential is larger still.
For him, “From Earth to Sky” is a chance to bring Turkish culture to a global audience without losing sight of its roots. “I see my role as that of a translator and a bridge between East and West,” Aydın says. “I hope this project makes Turkish people proud.”
“From Earth to Sky” was shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max. Check it out on @apple beginning October 14.

title: Researchers uncover hidden routes and patterns of Amazon wildlife trade
body: Home of the world’s largest biodiversity, the Brazilian Amazon is one of the main hubs for international wildlife trafficking. Every day, thousands of animals are taken from the rainforest to be sold in other parts of the country and abroad. Despite its key role in this illegal market, there is still a lack of information about wildlife trafficking in the region. ​ Data on animal seizures is scattered at the municipal, state and federal levels. The lack of an integrated system, along with the region’s vast territories and porous international borders, makes it difficult to get a full picture of wildlife trafficking in the rainforest. ​ “Every river you travel on in the Amazon will have traffic incidents,” conservation intelligence specialist Antônio de Carvalho, from the conservation NGO WCS Brazil, told Mongabay in a phone interview. ​ WCS Brazil is currently working on a Global Wildlife Trafficking Observatory, which will rely on artificial intelligence to gather information about wildlife trafficking from news websites and academic researchers. The goal is to support the work of investigators, environmental agents and journalists. ​ “A lot of data on seizures is lost because the seizure is simply carried out and the animals are released right there on the spot, and that doesn’t even make it into official statistics,” Carvalho said. The zebra pleco (Hypancistrus zebra) lives only in a small stretch of the Xingu River, in Pará, and is highly coveted as an ornamental fish. Image courtesy of Birger A. title: Show HN: Library for building synthetic agent environments [MIT]
body:
Remember The Truman Show? They built an entire town so real that Truman never knew it was fake.
Agent evals and reinforcement learning need the same thing: worlds so realistic that the agent doesn't know it's being tested. Production and staging can't do that. They're shared, and you can't reset them. Hand-written mocks reset fine, but they aren't real enough to fool an agent.
So we built Seahaven , an open source Python framework for building synthetic worlds for AI agents. It's named after Truman's town.
We've been optimizing long-running agents at Kiln: rewriting their prompts, tools, skills and subagents, and keeping the changes that score better. We've been working on some version of this problem for over a decade (at Apple, our own startup, now Kiln).
One-shot tasks never needed a world. You send a prompt and grade the answer. Agents that run for dozens of turns across lots of tools are different. Their evals need three things:
And they need it thousands of times, in parallel, with every run isolated from the others.
We built a few of these environments by hand. Doable, but hard, and every one rebuilt the same layer: a database per run, frozen starting states, parallel instances, clock control, a log of every change. That layer deserved a great framework, so we built one. You write just the logic specific to your world. Seahaven handles the rest.
A Seahaven world is a working copy of your agent's tools and data. It's a schema (SQLite tables) plus tools (plain Python functions). The agent calls the tools exactly like it would call the real thing. It can read, write and even break things, without touching anyone else's run.
How realistic can it get? Our Stripe World mocks Stripe's Billing and Payments core: 24 tables and 155 API operations, behind the same tools as Stripe's own MCP server. It also serves Stripe's REST API, so the official Stripe SDKs work against it unchanged.
Production is realistic but shared. Mocks are private but fake. Seahaven gets you the realism of production with the isolation of a mock.
That writes a complete project: schema, tools, tests, a fixture generator, and an AGENTS.md .
Seahaven builds the tool's JSON schema from the signature, and the docstring is what the agent reads.
Then run your agent against a fixture, and grade what it changed:
Or let your coding agent build it. Seahaven is designed to be built by coding agents. seahaven new writes an AGENTS.md that points your agent at the docs for the version you have installed, not stale ones from the web. seahaven check catches the mistakes that are easy to make and hard to notice (a table without a primary key, a timestamp from the wall clock) and tells the agent the exact fix. Describe the product you want to mock, and let it work.
Kiln connects to any Seahaven world. Write scenarios against a fixture, evaluate your agent on the state it leaves behind, then use the Kiln Harness Optimizer to improve the harness: prompts, tools, skills, subagents and model choice, all scored against those evals.
Seahaven is standalone, and you don't need Kiln to use it. But if your goal is a better agent, Kiln is built for exactly that loop.
Seahaven is open source (MIT) and on PyPI.

title: AI Completes a Low-Speed Course in a Real Car
body: “Frontier models excel at many digital benchmarks, yet their ability to drive a real car, an everyday human skill, remains largely untested. We present DrivingBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark where general-purpose vision-language models must drive a real car. Through three tools, the models see camera frames from a Toyota Corolla and directly command its steering and velocity around a parking lot cone course at low speeds. The car may continue moving while the model thinks and new commands replace the currently running one, so inference latency is part of the task, testing the models' abilities to observe, act, monitor, recover, and complete a long-horizon objective under such constraints. We benchmark GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Grok 4.6 in vendor-native harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor) with up to three attempts each in one conversation; Astra is the only model to finish the course, on its second attempt, with no other attempt passing 50% of the course. Two of the four models improved materially across attempts with retained context. We also detail the design principles behind our action interface, and show how the tool output format and the framing of the task combined to determine whether models would drive at all or refuse. We release our harness, prompts, course map, and traces with video and telemetry for reproducibility.” From arXiv . The post AI Completes a Low-Speed Course in a Real Car appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Global River Blindness Treatment Hits Record
body: “Onchocerciasis is caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus and transmitted through the bites of blackflies (Simulium spp.). Adult worms live in subcutaneous nodules, where the females release millions of microfilariae (first-stage larvae, L1) that migrate through the skin and eyes, causing intense itching, disfiguring skin disease and, after prolonged exposure, visual impairment and irreversible blindness. Early exposure to infection in childhood has also been associated with onchocerciasis-associated epilepsy… In 2025, 255.7 million people required PC for onchocerciasis, of whom 180.3 million were treated, representing 70.5% global coverage, the highest number of people ever treated for onchocerciasis in a single year.” From World Health Organization . The post Global River Blindness Treatment Hits Record appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Mars Rover Sets Record for Distance Driven on Another World
body: “NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has driven farther than any vehicle ever has on the surface of another world. On Oct. 11, the rover’s odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), eclipsing the record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which explored Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance reached the mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15… Much of the credit belongs to Perseverance’s self-driving capability. Using an autonomous navigation system known as AutoNav, the rover images the terrain while rolling, builds a 3D map of hazards, and plots its course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth — a capability the team calls 'thinking while driving.' Perseverance can do all that at or near its top speed, covering as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single sol. The six-wheeled scientist has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain, compared with about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. Where NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points, Perseverance processes 600,000 with every look.” From Jet Propulsion Laboratory . The post Mars Rover Sets Record for Distance Driven on Another World appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Guangzhou-Hong Kong Zero-Carbon Route Opens
body: “The largest inland river intelligent electric container ship in South China set sail on Tuesday from the Nansha Port in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, heading towards Hong kong International Terminals. The operation of the ship, fully loaded with furniture, daily necessities, and other goods produced in Guangdong, marked the official launch of the first zero-carbon container shipping route between Guangzhou and Hong Kong. The shipping route establishes a green water transport model with zero emissions and low noise, creating an efficient logistics channel from Nansha to Hong Kong.” From China Daily . The post Guangzhou-Hong Kong Zero-Carbon Route Opens appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Autonomous Delivery Is Expanding Across China
body: “Chinese companies have invested heavily in so-called 'physical AI': drones, robots and autonomous transport systems for people and goods. The country’s tech giants have rolled out large fleets of autonomous vehicles across cities, focusing particularly on last mile logistics, bringing goods directly to homes and workplaces… By the end of 2025, ground vehicles operated by tech giant Meituan had completed more than 5.5 million outdoor delivery orders and logged over 19 million autonomous kilometers. Last October, JD.com announced plans to procure 3 million robots, 1 million unmanned vehicles, and 100,000 drones for its end-to-end supply chain over the next five years. More than 100 Chinese cities have opened some of their roads to unmanned delivery vehicles. This year, Beijing and Shenzhen began issuing 'L4' test licenses for micro cargo vehicles, expanding the routes and scenarios in which these vehicles can be tested without an onboard driver… Beijing-based Neolix has built the world’s largest autonomous fleet, operating 27,000 vehicles across 300 cities in 15 countries, nearly five times the combined size of Waymo and Baidu’s robotaxi operations. This year, the company expects its domestic fleet to grow to 50,000 vehicles. Next year, it wants to add another 100,000, according to Yu.” From BusinessMirror .
