title: Houthis Vow More Attacks After Strike on Aramco Headquarters
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they will resume attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities "in the coming days," after Saudi authorities reported a limited fire at Aramco's office complex in Dhahran during a Houthi missile attack Tuesday night. The Houthis claimed strikes on Aramco facilities in Dhahran, an Aramco refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis called the sites legitimate targets and urged international shipping companies, civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, said a ballistic missile aimed at Dhahran on Tuesday was intercepted and destroyed , and that debris from the interception fell on a residential area. Three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters the fire at the Dhahran complex spread across several floors. Two of them said operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home. Two regional officials told the Associated Press that the top three floors of a building used by senior Aramco executives were damaged. One official said the CEO’s office was among those hit .
Earlier on Wednesday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh, and several loud booms were heard in the capital, Reuters reported. A witness told Reuters that authorities issued an alert for a possible aerial threat and then lifted it. Saudi Civil Defence said debris from two missiles intercepted Tuesday injured four people, including a child, and damaged 15 homes in Riyadh, according to the AP.
In response, Saudi-led forces have struck oil sites in western Yemen that the coalition said supply the Houthis. The Houthi-run Health Ministry said two people were killed in a Tuesday airstrike on the Ras Isa port area in Hodeida province. Yemen Petroleum Co. said its Al Sabah facilities and a refueling station in Sanaa were hit.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been attacked four times since the start of the war. Saturday's strike killed 13 people. AP put the toll from multiple strikes at the airport in the past week at least 18 killed and more than 300 hurt. Authorities have closed the airport until Oct. 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
U.S. President Donald Trump posted Tuesday that "The Houthis are behaving very badly" and wrote, "I'll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!" Bloomberg reported that the post said the group was "purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices" at Iran's direction before the Nov. 3 midterms. The AP reported that Trump has said he is evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

title: Canada Invests $11.1M in 16 Canadian Space Technology Projects
body: The Honourable Mélanie Joly, Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions , announced $11.1 million in funding for 16 innovative space projects led by 15 Canadian organizations. Recognizing space as a strategic national asset, this investment will help ensure that the Canadian space sector is fully equipped and ready to advance national priorities. Several of the funded projects will help advance capabilities that are increasingly important to Canada’s security, sovereignty, economic prosperity and leadership in space. Among these are cutting-edge satellite imaging technologies to improve access to critical information for emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, environmental stewardship, and security applications. Other supported projects are strengthening secure communications capabilities and improving Arctic sea ice and maritime activity monitoring, contributing to enhanced connectivity and situational awareness across Canada’s North. This funding is also supporting artificial intelligence technologies to enhance satellite autonomy and efficiency, alongside improved communications and power systems for future lunar exploration missions. Together, these innovations position Canadian companies for opportunities in the emerging lunar economy. The funding announced today helps drive the Government of Canada’s broader ambitions for a strong and innovative space sector. It will enable Canadian organizations to seize new commercial opportunities and respond to emerging national priorities as Canada charts its long-term vision for space. “Canada’s future in space depends on our ability to develop and sustain world-class capabilities. Through these investments, we are empowering Canadian companies to advance cutting-edge technologies, strengthen our highly skilled workforce, and seize new opportunities in the growing global space economy. By supporting innovation today, we are helping reinforce Canada’s economic prosperity, security, sovereignty and leadership in space for years to come.” The Honourable Mélanie Joly, Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions ADDITIONAL INFO This investment is made through the Canadian Space Agency’s Space Technology Development Program (STDP). This flagship funding program for early-stage innovation helps Canadian companies develop and test space technologies to bring them closer to market and enhance the competitiveness of Canada’s space sector. Since 2012, the STDP has invested over $130 million to support the pre-commercial development of 266 space-related technologies. Canada’s space sector supports over 28,000 jobs and generates $5 billion in revenues each year. Canadian space companies invest close to $1 billion annually in research and development, with R&D intensity approximately 17 times higher than the manufacturing-sector average. The post Canada Invests $11.1M in 16 Canadian Space Technology Projects appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Hezbollah cannot buy back Shia support as group promises $14,000 to displaced families
body: Hezbollah's financial assistance to displaced families in southern Lebanon, capped at $14,000, is only the first step in a long process if the Iran-backed group hopes to regain the trust and support of Lebanon's Shia community, Lieutenant-Colonel (res.) Moran Levavoni, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.Levavoni spoke with the Post a day after Hezbollah announced it would provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes were destroyed during this year's war with Israel.Under the plan presented by Hezbollah Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will reportedly receive $14,000, namely $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will reportedly receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent. The amounts maintain the same rates as in 2024.The assistance is not extended to families who lost their homes during war in 2006The assistance has not been extended to those families who lost their homes during Hezbollah's 34-day war in 2006 and have still not been compensated, Levavoni noted. The war, triggered by a Hezbollah cross-border raid, displaced around one million Lebanese. The Lebanese government estimated direct war damage at $2.8 billion and lost output and income in 2006 at $ 2.2 billion.While there may have been anger toward Hezbollah at the time, Levavoni argued that the “rift” between Lebanon's Shia community and Hezbollah widened in 2023, when the terror group decided “to support Gaza on the back of the local population.”Majority of Lebanese support a deal with Israel, poll saysAccording to a poll conducted by Statistics Lebanon, a Lebanese public opinion research organization, and published last week, Hezbollah's standing among the country's Shia population has weakened significantly. Of the 800 Shia adults surveyed in September, 42.1% expressed disappointment, anger, or concern over Hezbollah's leadership and conduct.A majority of respondents, 67.4%, also said they did not believe Hezbollah had achieved any or all of its objectives in the war. Reflecting this apparent lack of confidence, 63.3% supported some form of agreement with Israel, whether through direct negotiations, mediation, or a comprehensive regional deal to end the conflict. Meanwhile, 71.1% said decisions on war and peace should be made solely by Beirut.Most respondents, 66.4%, also said they would support Hezbollah transferring its weapons to the state, while only around a third said the terrorist group should retain its arsenal.Hezbollah's first step toward rebuilding trust should be to compensate those affected by the war, Levavoni said.“They can try to minimize [the damage] by starting to pay refunds to the population, the people, the families that were away from their homes, and for the damaged villages,” he said. “And only after that, they can start thinking about regaining the trust.”Despite the damage to Hezbollah's standing, the organization retains some support among Lebanon's Shia population. The poll found that 37.1% of respondents still had a high level of trust in Hezbollah, while another 22.4% expressed some trust. Meanwhile, only 38.5% admitted there was some level of distrust.Reuters contributed to this report.

title: OpenAI’s Sachin Katti to leave infrastructure role, stay on as advisor
body:
OpenAI's infrastructure lead, Sachin Katti, announced on Wednesday that he is departing his role after roughly a year at the artificial intelligence company.
Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new," and he'll continue to support OpenAI as an advisor after his last day on Nov. 15. Uday Ruddarraju, who has been serving as OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson.
"Building AI infrastructure at this scale has given me an incredible view into every dimension of the compute world, from silicon and systems to datacenters, energy, supply chains, financing, and the economics of AI," Katti wrote. "I'm enormously proud of what our teams accomplished together and grateful to the partners who helped make it possible."
OpenAI's compute organization is crucial to its overall strategy; it's tasked with developing the company's infrastructure roadmap and ensuring that it can train and serve its models. OpenAI is targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and it's involved with massive, multi-billion-dollar data center projects in states like Ohio , Texas and Georgia .
The latest leadership shakeup lands during a tense moment for AI infrastructure in the U.S., where backlash against data centers has mounted over concerns about noise, electricity rates and water consumption. The issue has become a flashpoint in the upcoming midterm elections, where both Republican and Democratic candidates have campaigned against the facilities.
"I'm proud of what we've built and have total confidence in Uday and the team to carry it forward," Katti said in a statement. "I'm a builder at heart, and I'm looking forward to building something new."
Ruddarraju joined OpenAI in July of last year, according to his LinkedIn. He previously served as the head of infrastructure engineering at Elon Musk's xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX earlier this year.
Katti's exit is the latest in a string of executive departures at OpenAI this year. In July, Fidji Simo , OpenAI's product and business chief, said she would move into an advisory role to focus on recovery after a "severe exacerbation of a chronic illness." The following month, Brad Lightcap , a longtime OpenAI executive, and Denise Dresser , who served as revenue chief, also left the company.
OpenAI President Greg Brockman told CNBC at the time that he doesn't believe the wave of departures is atypical for a young company. He said since OpenAI is in the spotlight, "every departure gets scrutinized in a way that it doesn't otherwise."
"There have been different eras where we have different sets of, of leaders in place," Brockman said. "I'm a constant, Sam [Altman] is a constant, and I think that we are stronger because of that resilience and diversity."

title: ‘You’re a coward’: Protesters heckle Hegseth during AUSA panel
body: Protesters derailed a Washington, D.C., panel featuring U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, calling him a “war criminal” and a “Nazi.” Six people interrupted the speakers at various points during the beginning of the roughly hour-long panel, which was part of the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting . They shouted condemnations of the U.S. war with Iran and referenced the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. “You’re not a warrior, you’re a coward,” one person yelled, adding, “Children in Gaza are starving!” Another shouted, “You’re killing my family.” The final protester yelled, “The world f—--- hates you.” “You’re a f—--- war criminal. You’re a Nazi. We’ll see you at the goddamn Hague. You should be ashamed of yourself,” as security pushed him outside of the packed ballroom. Hegseth made a handful of quips addressing the initial interruptions, saying, “She thinks highly of me,” in response to the first protester. He appeared to get more irritated as they continued. “Appears we have a bit of a tactic,” he said. The panel was intended to be a conversation about Project Agincourt, a Pentagon initiative to accelerate the development and acquisition of autonomous systems. At one point, after a protester interrupted, a handful of spectators chanted “USA, USA, USA,” before quieting as the panelists continued speaking.

title: Child, 10, killed after dumpster fire triggers explosion in Beitar Illit
body: A dumpster fire broke out near a residential building in Beitar Illit on Wednesday, killing a 10-year-old child, ZAKA confirmed.The child was initially unconscious following the incident and was transferred to Hadassah-University Medical Center in Jerusalem's Ein Kerem for medical treatment, where he was pronounced dead, ZAKA and Magen David Adom said.Paramedic Yinon Bar Nachman, who was at the scene, said, "When we arrived at the scene, we noticed a 10-year-old child who was unconscious, pulseless, and not breathing, suffering from severe injuries and burns across his body."We provided him with life-saving medical treatment that included stopping bleeding, chest compressions, artificial ventilation, and administering medications, and evacuated him to the hospital in critical condition while continuing resuscitation efforts."The cause of the injuries is currently unclear, but it is suspected that children lit the garbage on fire, causing an aerosol can to explode.Authorities and emergency services are investigating the circumstances.This is a developing story.

title: The steel stock that has the shorts and options traders on edge
body:
Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. That seems to be the refrain for Cleveland-Cliffs investors as the steel giant prepares to report earnings.
Cleveland-Cliffs steps into the earnings spotlight on Oct.19, and options traders are bracing for impact. After a massive, nearly 16% one-day price jump following its July quarterly report — nearly double its long-term historical average move of slightly over 8% — short-term implied volatility (IV) has been aggressively bid up as traders fear a repeat. And who could blame them? Short interest is running close to 14%, and the CEO is famous for fighting the naysayers, noting that he likes boil them "like frogs" and that they are "messing with the wrong guy."
With rhetoric like that, it's little wonder options traders are bracing for big moves.
For strategic premium sellers, this inflated near-term fear creates a compelling opportunity to deploy what I call a "strangle-swap." You'll sometimes see traders or strategists refer to this as a "double-diagonal" spread. This structure allows traders to capitalize on the anticipated post-earnings decline in implied volatility (aka "vol crush") without taking on the unlimited risk of a naked short strangle.
To execute this strangle-swap, you sell a shorter-dated strangle and buy a longer-dated strangle to define your risk.
The key to this trade is the differential in IV decay between the shorter-dated November expirations being sold and the longer-dated January options being purchased. Traders are heavily bidding November options on concerns that the sharp move from the last quarterly earnings release may repeat. Whether it does or doesn't, that binary uncertainty vanishes after CLF reports on the 19th, causing November implied volatility (IV) to collapse, a phenomenon commonly known as "vol crush."
Because the January options have significantly more days to expiration, they are less sensitive to this immediate IV crush and suffer much slower time decay (theta).
This trade is most profitable if CLF stays between $11 and $17 after the report. In this scenario, the November short strangle rapidly bleeds value. A trader can then buy back the short legs for a fraction of the $0.80 initially collected, or let them expire worthless. This leaves the trader holding a long January 10/18 strangle for virtually nothing, providing "free" exposure to future price swings through year-end.
This strategy loses money if CLF repeats or exceeds its explosive July fireworks. Because the short strikes (11/17) are narrower than the long strikes (10/18), a massive directional move will cause the short options' intrinsic value to expand faster than the long options can offset it in the short term.
However, the risk/reward profile is highly asymmetrical. The long January wings strictly define catastrophic risk.
Maximum Downside Risk: The width of the put spread ($1.00) plus the net debit ($0.24) = $1.24 ($124 per contract).
Maximum Upside Risk: The width of the call spread ($1.00) plus the net debit ($0.24) = $1.24 ($124 per contract).
By risking up to ~$124 to capture elevated front-month premium, the double-diagonal offers a cheap, defined-risk vehicle to fade the market's recent earnings trauma while maintaining long-term optionality.

LONDON, Oct 14 (Reuters) – A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride , a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait , according to maritime security sources.
“GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported,” the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday.
In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday.
One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said.
Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment.
The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data.
“MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz,” the Singapore authority said.
“Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law.”
GFS Pride’s United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment.
“The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday.
“The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage.”
A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilized or sunk.
The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.
(Reporting by Jonathan Saul and Renee MaltezouEditing by Ros Russell and Philippa Fletcher)

There’s an entire cottage industry of iPod mods out there, but Sprout Pi and Sprout Pico are two of the few full motherboard replacements that combine many of the most popular mods into a single upgrade. Both versions add Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB-C, a microSD card slot, FLAC playback, and more. And while cracking open an iPod will never not be intimidating, at least the Sprout doesn’t require any soldering.
The firmware allows audio over USB for wired headsets, as well as over the original 3.5mm jack. Plus, Bluetooth support lets you connect to your AirPods or favorite UE party speaker . Wi-Fi enables Google Cast and AirPlay streaming, as well as podcast downloads, which is a nice touch. The higher-end Sprout Pi also supports streaming via Spotify and Apple Music, plus apps, which, honestly, kind of misses the point. iPods are popular again exactly because they get you away from the algorithm and limit distractions.
Sprout Pi will only work with 3rd- and 4th-generation iPods and iPod mini, which will limit its appeal somewhat. The project will launch a crowdfunding campaign soon through Crowd Supply , but it has yet to announce a price.

title: Qatar Rewrites Its Gas Playbook With Old Tankers and New Tactics
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
LNG carrier file image (c) Oleksandr Kalinichenko/shutterstock.com
By Stephen Stapczynski, Priscila Azevedo Rocha, Salma El Wardany and Sing Yee Ong (Bloomberg) —
Six months into a war that sowed upheaval in the Persian Gulf, Qatar found itself stuck. By late August, even limited shipments from the gas heavyweight had all but stopped following a projectile attack on one of its tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz. Pressure was growing, not only from energy-starved clients but also from inside an economy built on regular deliveries.
Then senior executives at QatarEnergy saw a potential fix — Al Rayyan, one of the oldest vessels in the fleet.
Out in the calm waters of the Gulf, a few hours from the country’s coast, Al Rayyan’s captain had been idling for days when the order came through. With security assurances from the US Navy in hand, he was given the green light, but was told to sail out quietly, without transponders or lights. At the helm of a 29-year-old gas tanker — a dinosaur in a flotilla that includes some of the most expensive vessels in the world — the shipmaster would be testing a vital workaround.
It worked. The tanker slipped through and headed toward the port of Sohar in Oman on Sept. 10. A few days later, it was met by another Qatar-controlled vessel, the Al Mas’habiyyah, a state-of-the-art carrier built in 2025. The second ship would now carry the cargo of liquefied natural gas on to its final destination: China.
Al Rayyan headed back through Hormuz, for its next load.
Bloomberg News interviewed more than two dozen traders and officials to piece together Qatar’s efforts to steadily restore its position as a leading LNG exporter — until the war began, it was second only to the United States — even without a clear end in sight for the conflict between the US and Iran that has destabilized the region. Their accounts, provided under condition of anonymity given the sensitive nature of the issue, offer a glimpse into how a gas powerhouse has begun to adapt to a new and uncertain reality.
Qatar provided nearly a fifth of global LNG last year and so is closely monitored by traders and rival producers. A sustained recovery could ease strain in the market at a time when winter is approaching and prices are at their highest in years.
“It has to adapt in the near term. Its entire model is based on shipping huge volumes through the strait,” said Toby Copson, China-based managing partner at Davenport Energy, which trades oil and gas. “If Qatar can establish a more regular export route, it would start to ease one of the biggest constraints on the global LNG market.”
QatarEnergy did not respond to Bloomberg queries.
Since the US war with Iran began disrupting shipments, all energy producers in the Gulf have been forced to find new ways to get fuel to customers across Asia and Europe. Large oil exporters and traders have increasingly turned to shuttle runs, which send laden “mother” vessels through the waterway — often older vessels, traveling without lights or transponders that usually aid navigation — to be met by “daughter” vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman, ready to take the cargo, typically crude, to any destination.
Transfers at sea are far harder and costlier for LNG, a fuel that needs to be chilled to minus 162C (-260F) and pressurized. Moving it requires special, cryogenic hoses and trained crews. But with oil shipments flowing through the summer, executives around Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, an industry veteran who serves as Qatar’s energy minister and QatarEnergy’s chief executive officer, were growing concerned, according to people with knowledge of the company’s strategy. They could see gas cargoes from the US replacing shipments for major clients like India, while China was stepping up efforts to diversify away from the Gulf.
With an economy built around LNG, Qatar’s needs are pressing. Every week that Ras Laffan’s operations are not exporting costs the country roughly $1 billion in lost sales, according to Bloomberg calculations based on current long-term deliver prices, a significant sum for a $200 billion economy. The International Monetary Fund estimates Qatar could suffer an contraction of 15.6% this year.
There was no alternative but to restart shipments, Al-Kaabi’s team decided — though other levers would be pulled simultaneously, including an expansion of trading operations in an effort to profit from the same dislocation that was hobbling the company.
After Al Rayyan’s run, exports through Hormuz cranked up. Over the four weeks that followed the first crossing, roughly 20 tankers carrying Qatari LNG exited Hormuz, according to ship-tracking data and people familiar with the operations, racing back once empty. Deliveries approached a third of prewar levels by the end of September, a speed that caught even customers off guard. Buyers, particularly in India, had written off Qatari deliveries after the difficulties of the first months and now had to scramble to make room for arrivals.
“It is absolutely a cornerstone for global energy security,” said Peter Clarke, senior vice president for LNG at ExxonMobil, which has a stake in the Ras Laffan export plant’s production trains, speaking in September around the time the country was ramping up its shipments. Qatar, he told an industry conference, would “continue to play a really important role.”
Still, attacks have not stopped — a new wave last week targeted a tanker linked to QatarEnergy — testing the country’s resolve almost daily.
Qatar’s recovery effort began back in March, in the first days of the war and immediately after the vast Ras Laffan complex was struck. Missile and drone attacks forced the first interruption to supply in three decades of operation, pushing customers to scramble for replacements.
The upheaval posed an unprecedented threat for a producer that preferred to lock buyers, mostly in Asia and Europe, into decades-long contracts with strict terms and rigid pricing. Qatar’s reliability — until this year, it had never declared force majeure — meant it had been able to command a premium. But exports for the period between April and the end of September plunged almost 90% compared to the same six months last year.
From the start, the senior team was all too aware of the challenge, according to people familiar with the company. Al-Kaabi began marshaling different segments of the company, all while accelerating efforts to trade and source gas far beyond the Persian Gulf. In the meantime, contract managers kept in constant touch with customers even when there were no updates, according to people involved in the calls, in an attempt to preserve the link between buyer and trusted long-term supplier.
The first part of the plan was to lean on QatarEnergy Trading. Established in 2020, QET has long had a mandate to buy and sell LNG on the spot market and build supply positions outside the country. With prompt prices in Asia surging, the unit began accelerating purchases of American LNG — not simply to replace lost Qatari supply and keep up deliveries, but to sell to buyers at a profit.
Bangladesh, struggling with energy shortages since the war began, was one such client. The trading arm, which has a long-term contract with Petrobangla, agreed to deliver shipments to help fill the gap left by Ras Laffan. Under the arrangement, Bangladesh paid a small discount to prevailing spot prices — driven to sky-high levels by the war — but the cargoes still sold at roughly twice the price of its much cheaper long-term contract.
The same conversation is playing out across Europe and Asia, with QET hunting down supply and keeping itself in the equation — even if market conditions push prices higher. The unit is on track to handle more than 15 million tons of LNG this year, according to a person familiar with its operations. That’s a fraction of the more than 70 million handled last year by Shell Plc, the world’s biggest LNG trader and a benchmark for Qatar’s ambitions, but a jump from the annual 10 million tons the company estimated it was handling in the middle of last year.
“QatarEnergy has what it takes to become a trader,” said Jean-Christian Heintz, a former trading executive who’s now an independent consultant at Wideangle LNG. “They have the talent, the financial reputation and the rationale — sourcing replacement volumes to mitigate Hormuz.”
QatarEnergy is in advanced discussions with export projects in Louisiana and Texas to purchase millions of tons of LNG for years in order to expand its portfolio of supply, according to the people familiar with the matter. QET already sources gas from the US Golden Pass facility, primarily owned by QatarEnergy, which began operations this year and has been steadily ramping up output.
This week, in a rare move, it offered Bangladesh a long-term LNG deal tied to its “international portfolio” — and not simply Ras Laffan.
“We are building our position,” Al-Kaabi told the Qatar Economic Forum in New York in September, laying out the company’s ambitious goals for itself. “In the very near future, we will be the largest LNG trader in the world by far.”
The prime aim, however, was still to sell Qatar’s own gas. Even in the early months, the company had tested the water with occasional crossings — until the LNG tanker was attacked in July while traversing Hormuz. The engine room was hit and caught fire. Al-Kaabi took the incident as his personal responsibility and suspended plans to increase exports and send more fuel through Hormuz, said people familiar with discussions at the time. Another tanker loaded with Qatari gas was struck at the end of that month.
But as weeks passed, executives watched neighboring oil producers shipping cargoes through Hormuz, and began to worry that Qatar would be left behind. To make matters worse, increasing flows from the US were replacing shipments for some of its major clients like India, and top buyer China was stepping up efforts to try and diversify away from the Gulf.
Storage was also becoming a concern, as the country tried to keep the world’s largest LNG export plant in working order so that it could rapidly expand if the situation around Hormuz stabilized. Two of its 14 production trains were damaged by the March attack and could take about three years to fix. But that still left 83% of its operational capacity available to resume rapidly, and QatarEnergy had mobilized staff to make repairs within days, navigating around struck facilities with shrapnel still strewn about, according to people with knowledge of the situation.
To ensure a rapid ramp-up once Hormuz reopened — LNG need for extremely low temperatures makes restarts slow — Ras Laffan was already producing just enough, sending cargoes to Kuwait every month to allow three to four production trains to keep running at low rates. But exports still needed to pick up, and that meant testing shuttle runs.
The first step was to begin recalling the vessels that it had leased out early in the war, when crossings seemed impossible. Top of the list were those aged 15 years or more, according to people familiar with the planning — tankers for which insurers would charge more manageable premiums, compared to brand new vessels that can cost more than $300 million to replace.
But there were not enough. Short of the vessels required to meet its target — loading around a shipment a day for delivery as far afield as China and Japan — Qatar began chartering tankers from third-party LNG shipowners, including Greece’s Maran Gas Maritime Inc., at freight rates about 10 times the market price at the time, according to sources involved in the trade.
That left a second problem: willing crews. Several countries, including the Philippines, have pushed back against allowing the use of their citizens to ferry cargoes through Hormuz. QatarEnergy worked instead with recruiters in Indonesia, offering double and sometimes triple the usual monthly pay, plus bonuses for sailing through the strait.
Qatar now needs to manage a final and far more challenging headache — the unpredictable nature of crossings and an unstable security situation. Since the attack last week, transits have slowed. All of that will mean different relations with the country’s clients.
“Qatar’s ability to demand premium pricing and terms diminished,” said Saul Kavonic, senior energy analyst at MST Marquee. “Gulf states are rapidly looking to build pipelines and other avenues. Qatar is in the most difficult position as they have no avenues to bypass the strait for their LNG.”
It is possible that not all customers, for example, will wait for Qatar to ship in sufficient quantities. Extended force majeure can eventually give buyers the right to walk away, typically after a prolonged period of canceled deliveries. Some may well seek more flexible terms and conditions, according to people involved in the trade, forcing an LNG powerhouse to consider how far it will go to fit a new reality.
“There is no turning back,” said Anne-Sophie Corbeau, a researcher at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy and former head of gas analysis at BP Plc. “QatarEnergy will have to adapt, either through lower prices, or more flex or a combination of both.”

Anbernic shared a new video of its upcoming dual-screen handheld it announced last week showing the device playing 3DS, Xbox, and PS3 games through emulation. While competitors like Ayaneo have been making dual-screen handhelds for a few years, Anbernic only recently introduced its own dual-screen devices including the RG DS and RG DS Plus . Those handhelds are designed to be modern replacements for the Nintendo DS, but the new RG DDS, short for “Dream Dual Screen,” has a faster processor and displays with aspect ratios optimized to replace the Nintendo 3DS — although Anbernic isn’t trying to recreate the glasses-free 3D effect.
Full performance details aren’t yet known, and Anbernic has yet to reveal the RG DDS’ price or how aggressively it plans to compete with devices like the Ayaneo Pocket DS which currently starts at $579. Both the Anbernic RG DS and DS Plus start at under $100.
What we do know is that the RG DDS will feature a 4.7-inch, 1,200x720 top screen and a 4-inch, 960x720 bottom display that match the aspect ratios of what the 3DS used. Those displays also both feature triple the resolution of the 3DS’ screens allowing emulated games to be easily scaled up. The RG DDS will be powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon G2 Gen 2 chipset with a 6,000mAh rechargeable battery and will include built-in vibration feedback and an extendable stylus stashed inside.
The RG DDS’ design looks nearly identical to the 3DS although you’ll find an additional analog thumbstick on the lower right for playing 3D games that require a pair of them. It also carries forward the small button found next to the top right corner of Nintendo’s New 3DS’ touchscreen. But instead of functioning as a camera controller the RG DDS will use the button as a shortcut for accessing AI features that have yet to be revealed.

title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
body:
Saudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom.
The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Ministry of Energy.
The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday.
Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war.
Iran Revolutionary Guard chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media.
"If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview.
"We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens."
CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3.
On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.
Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile."
In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control.
"IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."
Correction: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election. An earlier version misstated the day.

title: Scimplify Bags $25 Mn To Scale Its Semiconductor Chemicals Business
body: Speciality chemical manufacturing startup Scimplify has raised $25 Mn (around ₹238 Cr) in a fresh funding round led by Hitachi Ventures, the venture capital arm of Japan’s Hitachi Group. The round also saw participation from existing backers such as Accel, Bertelsmann India Investments, 3one4 Capital and Omnivore. New investors including Teknor Apex, Henkel and an undisclosed Japanese chemical company also joined the round. The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its research, processing and manufacturing capabilities across rare earth and critical metals purification. The funds will also go towards scaling its semiconductor chemicals and battery chemicals businesses. A chunk of the capital will also be used to strengthen SciNode, Scimplify’s agentic AI platform that connects research, process development, control and physical manufacturing. Founded in 2023 by Sachin Santhosh, Salil Srivastava, Dheeraj Dhingra and Hersh Manek, Scimplify is a B2B platform that specialises in end-to-end sourcing and manufacturing of speciality chemicals. It also offers contract research and commercial chemical manufacturing for agro-chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients and fragrances. The startup currently operates R&D facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with its SciNode software platform supporting its manufacturing operations. Its network comprises more than 500 manufacturing partners and thousands of scientists and technical partners. Prior to this, Scimplify had secured $40 Mn in its Series B funding round, co-led by Accel and Bertelsmann Investments, in March last year. “In the 18 months since our initial investment, Scimplify has grown from serving 600+ customers across 16 countries to building a global platform with 1,000+ customers across 40+ countries,” Accel partner Rachit Parekh said. Scimplify’s customers include Henkel, Coromandel, Dr Reddy’s, Coherent, Holcim, BASF, Sanyo, Marubeni, among others. The startup claims to operate across five countries and serves more than 1,000 customers across over 40 countries. Going forward, Scimplify plans to expand its presence in the US, initially focusing on sectors where domestic processing capabilities remain limited. These will include rare earth and critical metals purification and processing as well as high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals. Scimplify’s latest fundraise comes as India looks to strengthen its position in the global chemicals value chain. Earlier this week, Bengaluru-based speciality chemicals startup NuSynth Technologies raised ₹36.5 Cr in a seed round co-led by Avaana Capital and Shastra VC. Scimplify operates in the broader Indian deeptech sector, which continues to draw investor attention on the back of regulatory push, subsidies, innovative local solutions, a thriving talent pool and growing local demand. Overall, Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026 , a 176% increase from $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago period. The sector outpaced the broader Indian startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. title: Residents of South Africa’s Limpopo province hold breath amid fears of repeat floods
body: TSHAKHUMA, South Africa — Divhani Rashaka moved up and down the yard of the homestead he has looked after for 26 years, looking toward the Tshamugwana River. He recounted experiencing several floods in the time he has lived here. The riverbed, a few meters from his house in the Tshakhuma area of Limpopo province in the north of South Africa, is now covered with tall grass and bushes. Channels carved into the ground during the January floods show where water found its way toward the house. Rashaka, who is a resident of Tshiswiswini village, has placed stones along some of the channels in an effort to slow or redirect the water if heavy rains return. Farther up the yard, between his house and his neighbor’s, the grass had also grown thick, but Rashaka and his neighbor cleared the area to allow water to pass through more easily. Beyond these small measures, Rashaka has no formal plan for protecting his homestead, should it flood again. In January, floods affected communities across Limpopo, killing people, damaging homes and infrastructure, washing away food and disrupting schooling and access to some areas. Tshakhuma was among the communities badly affected. During these floods, 21 families whose homes were badly damaged were relocated to temporary accommodation at a lodge in Nkuna village, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) away, while temporary residential units were being prepared. title: F-35C Makes First Arrested Landing Aboard A Ford Class Carrier
body: A U.S. Navy F-35C has made the first arrested landing for the type aboard a Ford class aircraft carrier, with the milestone taking place aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79) in the Western Atlantic on October 13, 2026. The milestone marks a major step in testing the Navy’s stealth fighter aboard its newest carrier class, following years of challenges integrating advanced launch and recovery systems. Two F-35C test pilots assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 (VX-23), part of the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD), flew to the carrier as part of an ongoing Aircraft Compatibility Testing (ACT) campaign. A team from the Patuxent River-based F-35 Integrated Test Force (ITF), detached to the ship, is conducting the evaluation using a specially instrumented example of the carrier-capable stealth fighter. The imagery released shows two jets, although only one is seen landing on the flattop. The other is seen carrying inert Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM) bombs externally. An F-35 test pilot from Air Test and Evaluation Squadron Two Three (VX-23), Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD), flies an F-35C overhead the PCU John F. Kennedy in the Western Atlantic on Oct. 13, 2026. U.S. Navy The Navy took preliminary acceptance of the carrier from Newport News Shipbuilding on September 29, following successful acceptance trials in August. That development allows the ship and its crew to conduct at-sea testing and build underway proficiency while the shipbuilder completes final systems testing ahead of formal delivery, scheduled for spring 2027. Two F-35 test pilots from VX-23 fly F-35Cs to the PCU John F. Kennedy in the Western Atlantic on Oct. 13, 2026. U.S. Navy The test is an important step in validating the integration of the F-35C with the Ford class. The Navy’s newest carriers use electromagnetic catapults and advanced arresting equipment , replacing the steam-powered launch systems and conventional arresting machinery found aboard the preceding Nimitz class. Aircraft Compatibility Testing assesses the operational capabilities of a ship’s aircraft launch and recovery equipment with U.S. Navy aircraft. The process helps engineers evaluate how the carrier’s systems interact with individual aircraft and collect data needed to validate their performance. A U.S. Navy F-35C of VX-23 makes an arrested landing on the flight deck aboard PCU John F. Kennedy . U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey A U.S. Navy F-35C of VX-23 catches the wire on the flight deck aboard PCU John F. Kennedy . U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey The F-35C is specifically designed for carrier operations, with larger wings, reinforced landing gear and a beefier tail hook compared with the Air Force’s F-35A. Its ability to launch from a carrier and recover through an arrested landing is central to its role in the Navy’s carrier air wings, which also include F-35Cs operated by the U.S. Marine Corps . The use of a specially instrumented aircraft is particularly relevant to the test campaign. Instrumentation allows test teams to record data during flight-deck operations, helping them assess system performance and identify any issues requiring further evaluation. A U.S. Navy F-35C of VX-23 with its airframe liberally adorned with telemetry markings — these act as precision visual references used during flight testing to capture exact spatial data. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey A close-up of one of the U.S. Navy F-35Cs of VX-23 reveals a full set of underwing stores pylons and a load of three inert 500-pound JDAM-series weapons. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey The first arrested landing aboard John F. Kennedy demonstrates that the ship has reached an important F-35C compatibility milestone. It does not, however, establish that all testing, certification, or operational qualification requirements have been completed. The milestone comes against the backdrop of the Ford class program’s difficulties integrating some of its advanced aviation systems. The lead ship, USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78), introduced the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), technologies intended to improve aircraft-launch flexibility, recovery performance, and overall sortie generation. Development and reliability challenges with both EMALS and AAG have contributed to delays in the class’s progress. In a 2019 report, TWZ highlighted concerns that Ford class carriers would not be ready to operate the F-35C for years. A U.S. Navy F-35C makes an arrested landing on the flight deck aboard PCU John F. Kennedy for the first time. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey USS Gerald R. Ford was designed and built before the F-35C’s full carrier-integration requirements were sufficiently mature, so the Navy deferred several upgrades to a later modernization period rather than delaying the ship’s delivery. Following congressional pressure, the Navy adopted a single-phase delivery approach for USS John F. Kennedy , incorporating these modifications during construction instead. The USS Gerald R. Ford completed its Aircraft Compatibility Testing in January 2020, following 16 days at sea, during which the crew launched and recovered 211 aircraft, testing five different airframes — but the F-35C was not included. A U.S. Navy F-35C, attached to VX-23, after an arrested landing on the flight deck aboard PCU John F. Kennedy . U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Kaitlyn Bailey Beyond EMALS and AAG, integrating the F-35C on Kennedy requires modifications to the carrier’s maintenance infrastructure and support systems. These include specialized spaces for handling the aircraft’s sensitive mission systems and classified data, computer networks and interfaces linking its maintenance and logistics systems with the Navy’s existing infrastructure, and facilities and equipment to support the upkeep of its low-observable coatings and materials. The Navy has also identified the need for more robust jet blast deflectors (JBDs), which protect flight-deck personnel and equipment from the F-35C’s intense engine exhaust. Earlier F-35C integration work aboard Nimitz class carriers included JBD modifications to improve heat resistance and cooling, while planning for John F. Kennedy explicitly included both JBD upgrades and changes to maintenance spaces and information systems. An F-35 test pilot from VX-23 flies an F-35C to the PCU John F. Kennedy in the Western Atlantic on Oct. 13, 2026. U.S. Navy The latest test represents progress toward resolving the compatibility question, although the full scope of the remaining work will depend on the results of the ongoing evaluation. The development also comes as China advances its own carrier aviation capabilities. Unlike the U.S. Navy, its Fujian aircraft carrier has demonstrated electromagnetic catapult launches and arrested recoveries involving several aircraft types, including the J-35 stealth fighter. A J-35 is prepared for takeoff on Fujian . via Chinese internet In contrast to the U.S. Navy, which accumulated decades of experience with steam-powered catapults before adopting electromagnetic launch technology, China chose electromagnetic catapults for its first catapult-equipped carrier . Although China’s demonstrations aboard Fujian and the F-35C compatibility testing aboard Kennedy involve different aircraft, ships, and stages of development, both underscore the technical demands of integrating advanced aircraft with modern carrier launch and recovery systems. For the U.S. Navy, the immediate priority is to demonstrate that the Ford class can reliably support its intended aircraft. The F-35C’s first arrested landing aboard Kennedy is a significant step in that process, with further testing — not least an EMALS takeoff — needed before the milestone can begin to translate into an operational capability. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post F-35C Makes First Arrested Landing Aboard A Ford Class Carrier appeared first on TWZ .

title: Republicans say they don't like the war but not how they'll stop it
body:
In tight Iowa and Maine races, voters want to know if incumbents will actually challenge the president on Iran if re-elected
The Iran war was a central point of tension in Senate debates Tuesday night. As the issue becomes harder to avoid, Republican candidates in Iowa and Maine have signaled a break with President Donald Trump and his war.
Now, they are being pressed on something tougher than whether they want the conflict over: what they would actually do to end it.
Iowa is one of the typically red states now playing host to a razor-close race in 2026. The war’s economic fallout has been a particularly potent political issue in Iowa, perhaps because the state’s gas prices have jumped 69% — tied for the nation’s largest increase , according to AAA data from late August — and because it is among the country’s most farming-dependent states. Two of the state’s Republican U.S. representatives, Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, recently became the sixth and seventh members of their party’s House caucus to support Iran war powers resolutions, which would limit Trump’s ability to go to war without congressional approval.
Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), the GOP nominee for an open Senate seat, once supported the war but has changed her tune, saying Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.” But she has not joined her colleagues in voting to pressure the president to end the war.
Shortly after her pivot last month, one Iowa voter told MS Now that he had noticed the contradiction. “Hinson is all of a sudden portraying herself as the person who's always opposed the war and who wants all these good things,” he said . “But you check her votes and she doesn't.”
Challenged on her voting record Tuesday by her Democratic opponent, Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, Hinson said “we don’t need another resolution on the House floor” in order to end the war. Instead, she said, “the president and the U.S. military can bring it to the end.”
Turek blamed the war, and his opponent’s continued support for it, for the increase in gas prices, along with diesel and fertilizer prices that affect Iowa’s farmers as they go into harvest season.
In Maine, the Republican candidate, incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, has voted in favor of nine of the 14 Senate efforts to constrain Trump’s ability to continue the war. Collins defended her five earlier votes against war powers resolutions because they fell within the first 60 days of conflict, during which, she said, the commander-in-chief has “widespread discretion” to conduct war.
However, her challenger, former President of the Maine Senate Troy Jackson, still pressed her for not doing enough from her perch as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee to bring the conflict to a swift end.
“Senator Collins would like to school us on how this all works,” Jackson said . “I know very well how appropriations works. If she wants to stop the funding for it, she has the ability to.”
Some Democratic Senators have stated that, if they reclaim the Senate in November, they will leverage their majority to block future funding to the Defense Department until the war is over.
A Democratic takeover of both chambers of Congress is looking increasingly possible. Dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and its economic ramifications have played a meaningful role in shifting the midterm landscape toward the Democratic Party.
As Washington Examiner executive editor Jim Antle wrote in RS this week, the GOP could face a “ major wipeout ” in November because of the war’s fallout. Politico reported Wednesday that House Republicans have “privately concluded” that holding on to their majority in the lower chamber is “ likely impossible .” In his latest projections, political analyst Nate Silver gives the Democrats a 73% chance of taking control of the Senate.
This leaves Republican candidates in tight races, like Hinson and Collins, in an uncomfortable spot of trying to distance themselves from the war’s costs while resisting the tools Congress could use to constrain it.

title: Fannie Mae sharply raises mortgage rate forecast for 2027
body:
Economists at Fannie Mae are now predicting much higher mortgage rates through the end of 2026 and into 2027. It now puts the average rate on the 30-year fixed at 7.4% for the fourth quarter of this year and 7.5% through all of next year. It previously forecast 6.8% for the fourth quarter and 6.7% for all of next year.
The average rate on the 30-year fixed stood at 7.46% Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, but will likely move higher today. Bond yields are rising after a hotter-than-expected inflation report.
Mortgage rates have been rising sharply since the start of September, as inflation remains stubbornly high and bond markets sell off due to several factors. The Federal Reserve also raised its benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years. Mortgage rates do not follow the Fed's rate exactly, but they do react to how the central bank sees inflation going forward.
Mortgage rates loosely follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which has been rising sharply on higher oil prices and growing concerns in the global economy.
CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.
Higher rates have already put the housing market in an early deep freeze this fall. Pending sales, counted by signed contracts on existing homes, were down 8.5% in September year-over-year, according to Zillow. Mortgage demand continues to drop sharply, as buyers face higher prices and weakening affordability. Not only can fewer buyers now afford a home, but fewer can qualify for a mortgage.
Fannie Mae did not respond to requests for comment on its latest forecast.

title: BAE Systems Unveils Prototype High Power Microwave System For Killing Drone Swarms
body:
BAE Systems this week introduced a high-power microwave (HPM) system designed to defeat swarms of small drones that it has been developing and testing for four years under a contract with an undisclosed Pentagon customer and is ready for operational testing in a theater command, a company official said.
BAE’s HPM, a large array designed to knock down Groups 1 and 2 drones, has been hardware ready for two years and undergone testing at military ranges against drones and has generated “really good results” in terms of performance versus existing HPM systems, range and frequencies to cover threats as they evolve, Chris Laski, director of business development for weapon systems at the company’s Combat Mission Systems business, told Defense Daily on Wednesday.
BAE showcased its HPM system at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C., including the power management system. The company said its directed energy system is made with more than 99 percent commercial-off-the-shelf components.
Laski said BAE’s HPM system can also defeat fiber optic-linked drones that have been widely used by both sides in Ukraine’s war against Russia. Epirus , which has three first generation prototype HPM systems operating in the U.S. Central Command area of operations, has also demonstrated its ability to defeat fiber optic-controlled drones.
BAE’s HPM system is modular and scalable and could be integrated for use on Navy ships, trailers and fixed-site defenses. The company has one prototype currently.
BAE is self-funding some critical technology efforts of the development effort to mature and prepare the system for production, Laski said. Those investments include areas to weaponize the HPM system so that it can be integrated and operated as part of large battlefield command system, he said.
The demand signal for the technology is “now,” Laski said. If a combatant commander wanted the HPM system, BAE’s prototype is ready to go, he said.
As for building additional prototypes, Laski said he didn’t want to get ahead of customers’ decisions. There will be more to come, he said.
Previously, BAE was under contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory for an HPM development effort called Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR. The new system is a “unique design separate from” THOR, Laski said.

title: Equinox gold output jumps 34% after Orla merger
body: Equinox Gold (TSX, NYSE: EQX) increased third-quarter gold production by 34% following its merger with Orla Mining , as stronger Canadian operations helped the company advance towards its annual output target. The company reported production of 237,019 oz in the September quarter, up from 176,836 oz in the previous three months. The results included two months of output from the Musselwhite mine in Canada and Camino Rojo in Mexico. Gold sales rose 39.6% to 248,484 oz from 177,959 oz. “The third quarter was transformational,” Equinox president Jason Simpson said. “We completed our combination with Orla, bringing together a portfolio of assets positioned to generate significant free cash flow and long-term value for shareholders.” The merger, finished in late July , created a larger North American producer anchored by three Canadian gold mines and a pipeline of development projects. Equinox expects the combined company to produce 1.1 million oz annually, with growth potential exceeding 1.9 million oz. Canadian growth Equinox produced 611,483 oz in the first nine months of 2026, leaving it on track to meet its full-year guidance of 870,000 to 920,000 oz, the company said. Achieving that target would require fourth-quarter output of about 258,500 to 308,500 oz, above the September quarter’s total. “Our combined Canadian operations delivered solid production in Q3, led by strong performance at Musselwhite and steady improvements at Valentine and Greenstone,” Simpson said. Equinox-Orla merger wins approval, creates Canada’s No. 2 gold miner At Valentine, the average gold grade of material fed to the mill exceeded 1.8 grams per tonne during the quarter, reflecting improvements in mining operations. Equinox expects both Valentine and Greenstone to deliver stronger production through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027. Nevada expansion The company also advanced its South Railroad gold project in Nevada, securing a federal record of decision and final federal permits while beginning early construction work. A 2026 feasibility study completed by Orla outlined average annual production of 130,000 oz during the first five years at all-in sustaining costs of about $1,500 per oz. The project is expected to produce more than 100,000 oz annually over an initial 10-year mine life. First gold production at South Railroad is scheduled for 2028, adding another potential source of output as Equinox works to expand its North American portfolio. The company’s near-term challenge is to translate its enlarged asset base into higher production, with operational improvements at Valentine and Greenstone critical to meeting its 2026 targets.

title: OCC report finds debanking efforts tied to crypto activities
body:
The report from the US banking regulator did not include specific examples of debanking related to crypto, but mentioned it alongside ties to oil, gas and firearms.
The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on debanking efforts, including ties to digital assets as activities that influenced banks to limit financial services.
In a report released Wednesday, the OCC said certain banks had “public and nonpublic policies” restricting services for many industries, including oil and gas, tobacco, firearms and digital assets. According to the banking regulator, the report was in accordance with an August 2025 executive order from US President Donald Trump to prevent what he called “unlawful debanking.”
“Many institutions also placed restrictions on banking digital asset activities, including on issuers, exchanges, or administrators, often attributed to financial crime considerations,” said the OCC.
In November 2024, more than 30 tech and crypto executives claimed to have been denied access to banking services. Many in the crypto industry unofficially dubbed the effort as “Operation Chokepoint 2.0” after the Obama-era initiative to fight fraud and money laundering facilitated by banks.
However, Wednesday’s 47-page report did not include specific examples of debanking relating to digital asset activities. The OCC said it had been “unable to quantify on a comprehensive basis the full extent of debanking or alleged debanking actions” based on a review of nine major banks, and the agency’s head, Jonathan Gould, focused largely on the report’s claims around debanking due to ties to coal and firearms.
“These decisions were not based on financial risk,” said Gould, referencing the debanking due to connections to coal. “Instead, banks cited concerns about negative headlines, public protests, and the perceived reputational consequences of supporting the industry.”
The 2025 executive order from Trump followed calls from many in the industry surrounding claims -- including “Operation Chokepoint 2.0” -- that the US government under former President Joe Biden may have influenced financial institutions into cutting off crypto firms from certain services.
