title: Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox
body:
Infinite inboxes, so nobody ever gets your real address. Give every company its own — when one leaks, you delete it, not your life.
Every account comes with permanent addresses that anyone can write to and that never expire. If one starts getting spam, delete it and make a new one.
That works, but it's manual work. The solution? Three specialty inboxes, each for a different kind of sender:
Give it to one company. Once they write, only their mail gets in, and you can let in more senders, up to five in all. Anyone else is turned away, so a sold or leaked list is worth nothing.
Set a lifetime — an hour for a download link, a month for a trial. When it's up the inbox turns mail away, and can wipe what it holds.
Create a prefix once, like “maryann”. Then hand out variations of it, like maryann.vet or maryann-party. A new inbox is created the first time someone writes to one of them, locked to that sender at first.
* Limits are 100 messages per day in the Free plan and 1000 in Pro and Business. Limits subject to change.
Connect Claude, Cursor or any assistant that speaks MCP, and hand it the inbox chores: a fresh address for a sign-up, the code that just arrived, every receipt from March. It gets only the permissions you give it.
Make me an address for the gym trial, and tell me the code they send.
We don't sell it, we don't read it and we don't track you. You can export your entire dataset at any time, on any plan.
How the three inbox types work together in one mailbox.
Check out our documentation , or contact us and a real human will reply.

title: Iran's 'soft war': How Tehran turned antisemitism into a weapon against the West
body: Antisemitism and anti-Israel rhetoric across the Western political spectrum are being amplified by a decades-long Iranian campaign designed to erode trust in American institutions and forge alliances across ideological divides, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Simon Wiesenthal Center (SWC).The report, titled “The War on Western Minds: Iran's 30-Year Campaign to Divide the West,” said that the Islamic Republic has weaponized antisemitism in its ideological “soft war” against the West, exploiting nationalism, religious narratives, and anti-imperialism to spread anti-American and anti-Israel rhetoric.Unable to match US military power, particularly under decades of sanctions, Iran has instead focused on undermining Western social cohesion and trust in democratic institutions, the report said.Antisemitism predates the Islamic Revolution, but the SWC said that it provides Iran with a narrative that crosses ideological boundaries. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has exploited this by presenting the regime as an ally against the “Antichrist,” an anti-imperialist force resisting Western hegemony, or a nationalist partner opposing alleged Jewish and Israeli manipulation.Iran brought conspiratorial claims to the mainstreamThe report said Iran has helped accusations of Jewish control over American foreign policy become mainstream, allowing such narratives to spread without continued Iranian involvement. It compared this strategy to methods first developed in the Soviet Union.Using narrative intelligence (NARINT) to track Iranian influence campaigns, the SWC found that the objective was not simply to spread false information but also to shape how audiences interpret events, assign blame, and identify enemies. Once established, narratives of Zionist conspiracy, Jewish financial control, or Israeli manipulation of US foreign policy can become resistant to conventional fact-checking, the report said.Iran tailors these narratives to different audiences.Among religious Christians, it uses apocalyptic language and biblical prophecy to frame geopolitical conflicts as battles against the Antichrist, hoping to manufacture Christian-Muslim religious convergence, weakening the perceived Judeo-Christian affinity that underpins American support for Israel.The report cited Russian political philosopher Aleksandr Dugin, who consulted Athonite monks before Russia's 2012 intervention in Syria. According to the report, the monks encouraged Moscow's participation in the civil war as part of a “final battle” against the Antichrist. Dugin later credited Russia and Iran with saving Syria from destruction allegedly sought by the West and Dajjal, an Islamic term associated with the Antichrist.Iran has also sought to exploit grievances in other communities.The report highlighted the January 1996 World Friendship Tour by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, a prominent antisemite who visited countries hostile to the United States. The SWC said Iran recognized an opportunity to capitalize on Pan-African grievances while presenting itself as a defender of the mustad'afin, or oppressed and dispossessed.In February 2001, Tehran hosted a regional preparatory meeting for the United Nations World Conference against Racism, culminating in the Tehran Declaration. The declaration accused Israel of committing “a new kind of apartheid, a crime against humanity, a form of genocide and a serious threat to international peace and security.”The report said that these forums enabled Iran to combine anti-imperialism, left-wing anti-Americanism, Black internationalist organizing, and antisemitism under the banner of international legitimacy.Iranian-linked media apparatus amplified 9/11 conspiraciesIran also used its media apparatus to amplify conspiracy theories. In the weeks following the September 11, 2001, attacks, the Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese television network al-Manar promoted the false claim that 4,000 Jewish employees had been warned to stay away from the World Trade Center that day.Although initially confined to fringe circles, such claims helped attract conspiracy theorists and anti-establishment figures who could carry Iranian narratives into Western media, the report said.It cited former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and political writer Michael Collins Piper as examples of Western voices aligned with Tehran's messaging.In 2007, Iran launched Press TV to reach Western audiences directly. The report highlighted programming such as Zero Degree Turn, which portrayed Iranians as saviors of Jewish victims of Nazism while comparing Zionism to Nazism and delegitimizing Israel's founding.Iranian filmmaker Nader Talebzadeh helped develop programming designed to influence international audiences through polished, emotionally engaging storytelling, the report said.The SWC also identified MintPress News as an example of an American-facing outlet that presents itself as an independent progressive watchdog but allegedly relays Iranian and Russian narratives.The outlet's mix of left- and right-wing contributors, the report said, helps it mimic progressive investigative journalism while promoting positions aligned with Iranian foreign policy. The United Kingdom-based Institute of Contemporary Islamic Thought was cited as another platform promoting Iranian narratives while presenting itself as an intellectual hub for the global Islamic movement.The report said that this media ecosystem can have real-world consequences. It pointed to the manifesto of Payton Gendron, the perpetrator of the May 2022 Buffalo supermarket massacre, which referenced a 2016 MintPress News article titled “Thousands of Israelis Take to the Streets Calling For Palestinian Genocide.”By 2026, Iran's influence operations had expanded to include fake news websites mimicking American media, fabricated online personas posing as American activists, and campaigns designed to simulate grassroots support.The report said these operations use wire-service material and plagiarized articles to appear credible and embed Iranian narratives within broader coverage. Additionally, they manipulate Wikipedia, which, by extension, manipulates the majority of AI algorithms and allows the network to exploit social media algorithms.IRGC used cyberattacks to target US institutionsIran has also conducted hacking operations targeting American institutions. During the 2024 US presidential campaign, an IRGC-linked group sent spear-phishing emails to a senior campaign official using a compromised former adviser's account, attempting to infiltrate county-level government accounts in swing states, according to Microsoft's Threat Analysis Center.OVER THE past year, the SWC identified over 340 influencers, media outlets, organizations, and affiliated entities that it said formed an interconnected influence network with shared amplification channels and consistent information flows.The report named Dugin, Jackson Hinkle, Max Blumenthal, The Grayzone, and the account GodivaGoddess97 among central figures. It also identified CODEPINK, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), and the Party for Socialism and Liberation.The SWC outlined a six-stage cycle through which these narratives spread.First, humanitarian organizations publish legitimate reports with appropriate caveats.Second, academics and credentialed figures provide intellectual frameworks that, according to the report, delegitimize rather than merely criticize Israel.Third, alternative media outlets such as The Grayzone and MintPress remove caveats, add inflammatory framing, and cite the original organizations as authorities.Fourth, commentators, such as Andrew Napolitano, Candace Owens, Jackson Hinkle, and Jimmy Dore, repackage the content for left- and right-wing audiences.Fifth, activist organizations translate online rhetoric into campus organizing and direct action, creating environments hostile to Jewish students.Finally, conspiracy theorists cite The Grayzone and MintPress as evidence of alleged Jewish conspiracies.Jewish-affiliated voices and organizations, including JVP and Norman Finkelstein, are also invoked to deflect accusations of antisemitism, the report said.Several recommendations were offered to combat this threat: mandatory coordinated-threat disclosure for platforms; mandatory AI-generated-content labeling; a congressional review of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to remove immunity for content that can be attributed to designated foreign adversaries or their proxies.“For more than 30 years, Iran has been building an infrastructure designed to exploit the divisions within American society,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “What makes this campaign so dangerous is that Iran doesn't need Americans to support its regime to succeed. It only needs Americans to lose trust in their institutions and in one another. Antisemitism has been central to that strategy, giving a hostile foreign government a way to turn existing grievances into deeper divisions. This is a threat not only to Jewish communities, but to the foundations of American democracy itself.”“This is not about the Jews. It has never been only about the Jews,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “Antisemitism is the tool. The real target is Western civilization itself: the Judeo-Christian values, democratic institutions, and shared sense of citizenship that hold free societies together. Jewish communities are simply where the attack shows up first. That is why we called our report The War for Western Minds. Iran's goal is to break the West's confidence in its own foundations, and every American, whatever their faith, has a stake in stopping it.”The full Simon Wiesenthal Center report can be found here: https://wiesenthal.org/iran-report

title: Mosqitter is turning its mosquito traps into an AI-powered surveillance network
body:
Mosquitoes and the diseases they carry are expanding into new territory. Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and global travel are reshaping where disease-carrying mosquitoes can thrive, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cases of dengue, a viral illness spread by mosquito bites, more than doubled in a year, from 6.5 million reported globally in 2023 to a record 14.6 million in 2024, the WHO says.
A 30-person, Pennsylvania-based startup, Mosqitter , thinks fighting that problem requires more than killing mosquitoes. The company started by building chemical-free devices that lure and trap female mosquitoes by mimicking the heat, scent, and breathing cues of humans.
Anastasiia Romanova, co-founder and CEO of Mosqitter, told TechCrunch that the company set out to bring more sustainable mosquito-control products to a market still heavily reliant on chemicals. Romanova says it now has more than 5,000 devices operating across five continents, up from just over 250 when TechCrunch last covered the company in 2022. The startup now wants to turn its traps into an AI-powered monitoring network that can identify mosquito species, track changes in their numbers, and give earlier warnings about emerging disease risks.
Mosqitter began its R&D in Ukraine in 2019 and launched business operations in 2021, which the company considers its official go-to-market year. The company started by examining mosquito behavior. Female mosquitoes, the only ones that bite, seek blood before laying eggs. They lay eggs on a roughly three-week cycle, typically 100 to 200 at a time.
“We saw an opportunity: If we could catch the female mosquito at the point when she is about to lay eggs, we could potentially reduce the mosquito population and prevent it from growing,” Romanova said. “That’s why we combined elements such as heat, similar to the temperature of human skin; scent that imitates human skin odor; and light. In the Grand model,” which is the company’s highest-end offering, “we also use CO 2 to imitate human breathing.”
Mosqitter, presenting Wednesday as part of TechCrunch’s storied Startup Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco, is using AI to identify the mosquitoes its devices catch. Its computer-vision system analyzes biological characteristics to distinguish between species, Romanova told TechCrunch.
To identify a mosquito, Mosqitter runs an image through its neural network, checks the result against external datasets, and has entomologists validate the findings. It then assigns a confidence score based on how closely those assessments align.
“You can think about it as three judges analyzing a case and producing a verdict,” Romanova said.
Mosqitter also feeds environmental data, including weather, wind, and humidity, into its system. The company says that as it collects more data, it plans to use those inputs to forecast changes in mosquito populations and potential health risks.
Mosqitter’s product portfolio currently centers on two devices. Mosqitter Grand, its flagship product, is designed for larger areas and public spaces, while Mosqitter Mini targets smaller residential spaces and can also be deployed as a portable monitoring device. The startup plans to officially introduce its Febris Monitoring System next month, adding a data layer to monitor mosquito populations and assess the potential spread of mosquito-borne diseases.
“It’s very important to understand that Febris does not diagnose disease,” Romanova said. “We can’t say with certainty that a particular mosquito carries dengue. What we can say is that a particular mosquito species is present, and knowing that can help indicate an increased potential risk associated with diseases that species can transmit.”
The company is looking for B2B partners globally, particularly distributors with established sales networks and relationships with governments and retailers, Olga Diachuk, COO and co-founder of Mosqitter, said. Unlike Mosqitter’s hardware products, Febris targets institutional customers, including governments, public-health and mosquito-control agencies, airports, municipalities, and universities that need continuous mosquito monitoring.
Brazil, which has a high burden of dengue , is one example of Mosqitter’s expansion. Mosqitter has built local manufacturing and sales operations there, according to the co-founders. The startup also considers the U.S., Greece, India, Ukraine, and Nigeria key markets, and it uses a different sales approach in each.
In Greece, Mosqitter works with a long-established pest-control company. In the U.S., it sells its Mini device directly to consumers through Amazon and its own website. The company is also working with the U.K. Health Security Agency to deploy Febris at locations including Heathrow and Gatwick airports. International travel can bring in mosquitoes and mosquito-borne diseases from other regions, and Romanova says this highlights the need for more continuous monitoring.
“We think this part of the business could grow substantially with the Febris Monitoring System because governments are major buyers of mosquito-surveillance data,” Romanova said.
Mosqitter Mini retails for $199, while its professional Grand system costs $1,999. The company makes money from hardware sales, while Febris adds a recurring revenue stream from monitoring, dashboards, analytics, and data services.
Mosqitter is on track to generate more than $1 million in revenue in 2026, Romanova said. Revenue from Febris has only recently started coming in, but the company projects the data business could bring in more than $3.5 million next year, based on the value of contracts it is currently bidding on.
Mosqitter is raising a $5 million round in two tranches, starting with $1 million and followed by another $4 million. The startup said the split is tied to milestones it plans to reach with its Febris Monitoring System. To date, Mosqitter has raised $1.9 million.
There’s also a story behind the name. Despite what most people assume, “Mosqitter” isn’t a mashup of “mosquito” and “quitter,” Diachuk said. It combines “mosquito” and “eater,” a name that made more sense when the company was focused primarily on catching mosquitoes.

title: US Army generals propose larger-footprint, more frequent military exercises in Korea
body: A month after President Donald Trump intervened to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing a desire not to upset his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, the commander of Army forces on the peninsula said he’d like to go bigger – both in exercise frequency and geographic scope. Speaking at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting here Monday, Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there. “I think what we recognize is that largely the two big exercises every year in Korea focus on large command posts; we’ve got to move away from that,” Brunson said, in response to a question from a Korean journalist. “So, what we intend to do is take advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight,” he continued. “We’re trying to say how might we train differently, and so [Gen. Kim Sung-min, deputy commander of the Republic of Korea–U.S. Combined Forces Command] and I talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion.” In light of the distributed fight and scope of battle in Ukraine, Brunson suggested a training exercise that spanned from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province — a distance of nearly 300 miles across nearly the full span of the Korean peninsula. “Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say, ‘You can’t utilize the things that you’ve learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learn the same lessons and we’ve distributed ourselves in such a way that we don’t make ourselves the target,” he said. “We won’t be moored in place, and that’s what I’m talking about when I talk about positional advantage. It might not be the same place through the continuum. It might not be the same place when you’re in a crisis or conflict or competition; we might have to change that, and that’s what we’re learning.” His remarks acknowledged ongoing collusion and information sharing between U.S. adversaries, including Russia, China and North Korea, as Russia continues its war of aggression in Ukraine. Also on the table, Brunson said, were additional exercises, or a different schedule. “For a long time, we trained for two big exercises every year. What would happen if we trained in between those exercises?” he said. He cited a recent exercise conducted without troops that drilled, on a small scale, on what a mass garrison evacuation would look like in light of a major threat. “We’re there to protect the Korean people on the peninsula, and so we’re there to defend both homelands, the United States of America and the Republic of Korea. But what would it look like … if our environment changed?” Brunson said. While Trump’s Aug. 16 Truth Social post suggested a broad reduction in exercises with Korea, another general, Lt. Gen. Joe Hilbert, said earlier Monday that the order pertained to only one exercise in August, Ulchi Freedom Shield. Hilbert, who commands the Korea-based Eighth Army, said the live portion of that exercise was reduced by half and some elements that had been joint became unilateral. He maintained that joint training writ large “We continue to train on the peninsula. We continue to train with the Koreans,” he said, adding that troops from the Army’s 2nd Infantry Division were currently training on South Korean ranges in a rotational deployment. “So we’ll continue to train and we’ll continue to build readiness for U.S. forces on the peninsula throughout the year, except from that particular timeline and that particular exercise,” Hilber said. “As we all are observing and watching how the war is changing in Ukraine and in the Middle East, the North Koreans are absolutely doing that too. So rest assured, we pay attention to that, and we work to stay ahead.”

title: 5 Challenges Facing South America’s Copper Boom
body: Supervisors at BHP's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, said they would strike at 8 a.m. local time Wednesday after government-led mediation failed to produce a contract. The union represents about 1,020 workers at a mine that supplies roughly a quarter of Chile's copper, and the stoppage follows a walkout at Antofagasta's Centinela that began Oct. 7. Both land as governments across the Andes ask miners for far more copper, not less.  Demand will not wait  S&P Global projects that copper demand will climb from 28 million metric tons in 2025 to 42 million tons by 2040, with AI data centers and defense each roughly tripling their consumption, and it warns that supply could fall 10 million tons short. The IEA still sees primary supply about 25% short of requirements in 2035, down from a 30% gap in last year's edition.  Copper runs through grids, electric vehicles, wind and solar farms and the AI data center buildout, which S&P says could account for 14% of U.S. power demand by 2030, so a shortfall in the metal reaches well beyond mining. BloombergNEF has warned that a tight market could bring cost inflation or delays for electrification projects. Peru is targeting at least $33 billion in mining investment over five years, and Chile's pipeline tops $100 billion over the decade.  Chile keeps losing output  Chile's copper output fell 12.8% in August from a year earlier to 369,500 tons, the lowest monthly figure since February 2011, according to national statistics data reported by Bloomberg. On Sunday, heavy rain triggered a landslide at Codelco's El Teniente mine that killed two contractors and led the company to partially suspend operations, and El Nio could bring more rain to Chile and Peru in the months ahead.  [RegisterBanner]  Cochilco expects national production to fall 2.6% this year to 5.27 million tons before recovering to 5.55 million in 2027. TD Securities analysts said strike votes, worker fatalities and operational disruptions have helped "maintain a supply-risk premium," and copper has held close to its September record high.  China's acid squeeze  Morgan Stanley estimated in April that 1.1 million tons of Chile's annual leached copper output, more than half its refined production, could be exposed to a Chinese ban on sulphuric acid exports. Miners use the acid to leach metal from ore, and Chinese customs data showed shipments to Chile fell to zero in March, with Beijing reportedly planning a full halt from May.  Permits and protests  Permitting in Chile can take as long as 12 years in some cases, according to GlobalData, and President Jos Antonio Kast ordered ministers in March to clear 50 pending claims tied to about $16 billion in projects. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori's government wants to authorize 240 exploration and extraction projects this year, yet the Observatory of Mining Conflicts counts nearly 200 social conflicts nationwide, 64 of them tied to mining and other environmental disputes, and says most of the main mining regions voted against her.  Argentina starts from zero  Argentina has not produced copper since the Alumbrera mine closed in 2018, which makes Vicua, the BHP and Lundin Mining venture, its biggest test. The project received the top tier of RIGI benefits this year, and its backers are targeting a final investment decision on a $7.1 billion first phase before year-end, with first copper planned for 2030.  In April, a judge in neighboring La Rioja ordered a 30-day suspension and blocked machinery from using an access road through the province, saying the province had been left out of the environmental assessment. A San Juan court allowed work to continue days later.  By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com

title: My AI doppelganger tells me what to eat
body:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here.
For the past 100 days or so, my mornings have had a new rhythm. When I wake up, the first thing I have to do is feed my digital twin. It consumes my metabolic data, and its first “meal” of the day is my body composition data, sent straight from a smart scale.
Once that’s logged in the app, I scoot over to the kitchen to fill an Owala with lemon water to take my medications with. That, too, gets logged in the app. On Mondays, I’ll follow that up with several calming breaths, measure my blood pressure, and offer that to the digital twin as well. Then it’s time to consider breakfast. I consult my digital twin.
My digital twin isn’t so much a robotic clone as it is an AI-powered, color-coded food database that predicts how my glucose levels will react to everything I eat. Red is not so good. Orange is so-so. Green is ideal. It’s built based on the data I feed it, as well as data collected from a continuous glucose monitor.
A bowl of protein Cheerios and milk? My digital twin tells me this is orange if eaten alone, but green if I take my daily walk after. So that’s what I decide to eat and do. When that’s all done, I log it in the Twin Health app. In a few hours, the app will generate an insight based on how my glucose reacted, and my “twin” will become more accurate. For now, my twin is fed.
Rinse and repeat for roughly another 99 days.
Digital twins are a relatively new concept in physical health, both in medicine and sports. It’s a virtual model of a person built from various data points — labs, wearable data, images, genetic profiles, etc. — that is continuously updated over time. Once built, clinicians can then use AI to see how a patient might react to specific medicines or treatments by first “testing” them out on their digital twin. Theoretically, this could also help healthcare providers assess injury risk, predict disease progression, and implement preventive care while minimizing adverse effects for the actual patient. The thought is that this could one day help realize the dream of personalized medicine. Metabolic coaching is perhaps the lowest-stakes, highest-reward version of this technology that can be tested in the real world now.
[Image: The white scale is my Twin Health scale. When not building a digital twin, I sometimes use it to help me keep Pablo’s weight in check. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268664_Pablo_pet_tech_AKrales_0030.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
My metabolic twin was “born” in June with a giant box from Twin Health delivered to my doorstep. Twin Health is a digital twin program to help people “heal” their metabolisms (e.g., lose weight, manage diabetes, sleep better, etc.). It’s not available for widespread download just yet. Digital twins are still experimental, and currently, this service is only accessible through corporate or private health plans. It’s typically aimed at people with chronic metabolic issues. Twin Health provides everything you need to build a digital twin. Building mine would require 90 days’ worth of Dexcom G7 CGMs, a smart scale, a smart blood pressure cuff, three bottles of multivitamins and magnesium glycinate, and my Apple Watch. That was followed up with a trip to Quest Diagnostics, where a phlebotomist stuck a needle in my arm and sent vials of my blood for further analysis.
A few days later, I hopped on Zoom with my Twin Health coach Amanda — a human — and a doctor to review my lab results. Several numbers and formulas were thrown up on a shared screen. As it turns out, my liver? Inflamed, but understandable considering I’ve been diagnosed with a moderate case of nonalcoholic fatty liver. Insulin resistance — definitely there despite ideal HbA1c and fasting glucose tests. My pancreas is apparently working overtime, but my insulin-producing beta cell count seems fine. For now. My triglycerides were also high, though the rest of my lipids looked normal.
I knew going in that I inherited a bunk metabolism. A year of testing CGMs as a non-diabetic made that abundantly clear. But after the doctor logged off and Amanda asked me to define my goals, I launched into a spiel about my vague desire to reduce the number of medications I needed to keep my middle-aged metabolism functioning. Could a digital twin help me do that?
Maybe. For now, Amanda logged my goal, set up a follow-up call in two weeks, and encouraged me to try logging as many of my meals as possible for the first 30-day period. Once I hit the 90-day mark, I’d be scheduled for another blood draw.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/IMG_2894.png?quality=90&strip=all]
In many ways, I’m relieved my digital twin doesn’t have its own avatar. At least, not one that I can see. I’m glad for the abstract color labels. There’s novelty in going to see what color a cup of pineapple or a turkey hot dog with ketchup and relish might be. (Orange and green, respectively.) At times, I am reminded of Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian novel Never Let Me Go, in which clones are raised as organ donors. The scenario isn’t a one-to-one comparison. An AI-powered digital twin can’t actually eat, die, or feel pain. I’m probably anthropomorphizing my discomfort with the idea of “testing” food on a virtual version of my metabolism, as if it were a jester-like food taster in a medieval court.
Still, as the months ticked by, I couldn’t help noticing how hungry my digital twin was. And how much that took from me, almost like I was getting drained each time I “fed” my twin. Building this thing takes an immense amount of personal data — even for me, someone who’s used to tracking and reviewing a ton of health data. In my bimonthly check-ins with Amanda, she noted that tracking fatigue was frequent feedback from Twin Health users.
My behaviors did change. Both in unexpected and expected ways. Anytime I have to log food, I end up avoiding unhealthy treats more often than not; I don’t feel like getting scolded by apps. That didn’t result in any meaningful weight loss, however. And despite my stated goal of tapering off medications, that ended up not working out quite as smoothly as I’d hoped.
I also didn’t learn too many surprises from my digital twin’s metabolic predictions. Though it was validating to see that for me, a bowl of soondubu jjigae and white rice is a solidly green or orange meal, depending on if I’m active after eating. (Take that, low-carb diets. You can pry rice from my cold, dead hands.) I’ve tested far too many CGMs and AI nutrition apps to feel surprised by these insights, though I think it’d be useful for people new to metabolic issues.
Twin Health’s bimonthly check-ins did motivate me to get back to training. I’ve always been disciplined in my fitness routines, but the extra accountability of having to state my progress aloud to another human — one who isn’t family — kicked my inner overachiever into gear. After months of feeling too weak from medication side effects, I recently felt strong enough to run an uninterrupted 5K. I’ve also gotten back to strength training with some cajoling from Amanda.
[Image: This is an orange food because protein bagels are still bagels. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/04/268422_Victoria_CGM_continuous_Glucose_Monitor_AKrales_0288.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
But most importantly, after 100 days, my follow-up labs came back with marked improvements. Amanda says my metabolic health score has jumped by nine points since joining. A year after my doctor’s eyes bugged out at my liver enzymes, all but one are back to normal. These numbers were slowly improving before I tried this whole digital twin business, but they fell faster while trying this whole thing out. My triglycerides dropped by 70mg/dL. There’s been a significant drop in my hs-CRP, which is a biomarker for overall inflammation. I’m still insulin resistant, but less so.
I can’t really argue with results like that, can I?
I can, actually. The concept of a digital twin is founded on trust. As I said, metabolic use cases are high-reward and low-stakes. If you feed a twin an immense amount of data for losing weight, diabetes management, or more nebulous goals like “better energy” or “better sleep,” failure isn’t immediately life-threatening. There are medications and other avenues to try.
Personalized medicine is a different beast. Researchers are looking at digital twins for things beyond metabolism. One area currently being explored, for example, is cancer care and research. There’s massive potential there, particularly when you consider how grueling chemotherapy can be, but also huge challenges. The burden of trust for data privacy, for one. Digital twins are hungry for data, and their accuracy depends on a continuous stream of high-quality and sensitive information about you. That then informs future decision-making. If I felt overwhelmed by three months of logging in a low-stakes environment, how will that translate to higher-stakes scenarios? How does a digital twin exist once treatment is concluded? How does that data “live on” if treatment is unsuccessful?
[Image: The CGM experiments continue, as my digital twin hungers for this data. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25575447/247217_Dexcom_CGM_AKrales_0166.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
As for me, I’ve decided my digital twin will get to “live” for another three months. Despite my lack of success so far, I haven’t given up on the idea of tapering off some medications. I could also use all the help I can get in getting my liver labs all the way back to normal. Amanda also says I don’t have to be as militant with the data for my twin now that I have a solid foundation. Again, lower stakes mean more flexibility.
So, today, I’m asking my digital twin what it thinks about a protein waffle with a tablespoon of peanut butter and some honey, with a side of pineapples. Orange, but again, I can turn it green with a walk.

title: Linus Torvalds's first LLM-assisted patch series
body:
The fairly short series of ten patches basically enhances folio lookup by noticing when folios are hot, and setting a "delay releasing this folio until after a RCU period", and then using that RCU delay it does not just the folio lookup itself under RCU (which we've done forever), but also the actual folio data accesses themselves under RCU. No refcount taking needed for the fastpath where we can just read the data from the folio entirely in an RCU-protected region when the user copy doesn't cause page faults. The end result is an order-of-magnitude speedup for a read() -heavy benchmark. I actually think they have gotten a lot better in very specific ways: namely, peripheral automation. USB and Bluetooth have helped ordinary users enormously with all peripherals. Obviously we still have problems with them all the time, but _relatively_ speaking, computers are vastly easier to use, network and share files when compared to the 80s PC era with PS/2 keyboards/mice, video cables, parallel ports etc. Now we have hot-pluggable auto-detected KB/mice, monitors, storage, cameras, speakers and so on. A huge improvement in the typical usability of the plumbing layers, even if people still have problems all the time. In lots of other ways we haven't advanced much, but IMO that is hugely due to the inertia and requirement for backward compatibility. There is barely room for two major consumer operating systems in each category (Windows/macOS in PCs, Android/iOS in mobile phones), a third is always doomed by the lack of apps. That third entrant will always fail to get native apps, either because: a) they require apps to be ported/rewritten and developers have no time, budget or motivation to do so for minimal customer base b) they have a compatibility layer which supports running apps from one of the incumbents, in which case developers figure again no need to take the risk of porting to the new OS for minimal gain and a tiny customer base

title: Mangroves gain ground globally, marking turnaround after decades of loss
body: After decades of losses, new data show the world’s mangrove forests are beginning to rebound. It marks a modest but significant turnaround for the salt-tolerant coastal trees and shrubs, which provide vital ecosystem services, including carbon storage, habitat for thousands of species and protection from storms and erosion. Global mangrove cover increased by 477 square kilometers (184 square miles) between 1985 and 2025, according to the latest Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) data released in July. Restoration and stronger protections drove the modest net gains, which represent a 0.3% increase over four decades. The new assessment follows a separate study, published in June, that reached a similar conclusion about overall growth in mangrove cover. GMW, a mapping initiative of the NGO consortium known as the Global Mangrove Alliance, has tracked mangrove gains and losses since 2011. In this third update, researchers used 10-meter (33-foot) resolution satellite imagery and machine learning to map changes in mangrove cover across 108 countries. It’s the first of the updates to span a 39-year period, from 1985 to 2024, according to Lammert Hilarides, the GMW program lead at the Netherlands-based NGO Wetlands International. The previous version only tracked changes in the data since 1996, covering about 24 years. “The importance of tracking changes in mangroves lies in the need to have accurate information if you want to successfully halt loss, protect and restore mangroves,” Hilarides told Mongabay by email. He added that the new data show significant differences between regions, countries and the timing of gains…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Oshkosh adapts JLTV for Dutch military patrol vehicle
body: Wisconsin-based Oshkosh Defense has begun production of the first prototype of the Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle, or DXPV. According to the company, the new vehicle, also called the “Kaaiman,” was derived from the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle , or JLTV, and adapted for the Netherlands Ministry of Defence . At the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition, Pat Williams, the company’s chief program officer, described the “production” as “an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands.” Compared to a standard JLTV, the DXPV has been enhanced for mobility, corrosion protection, mission systems and suspension for increased off-road performance. “Just as importantly, it demonstrates the strength of an active production base and our ability to continuously evolve proven vehicle technologies to address the changing needs of our customers and their missions,” Williams said. Beyond the DXPV prototype, Oshkosh officials at the show are emphasizing the company’s renewed approach toward “rapidly delivering mission-ready solutions.” The company added that it has delivered more than 200,000 tactical wheeled vehicles to U.S. and allied forces. The Oshkosh AUSA booth also featured other platforms like its Family of Medium Tactical Vehicle A2 Low-Velocity Air Drop, or FMTV A2 LVAD, and the hybrid electric JLTV, or simply eJLTV. With that, Williams added that “production readiness matters,” referring to how quickly Oshkosh was able to develop the DXPV. The Dutch MoD signed an agreement with Oshkosh for the vehicles last summer and then placed an order valued between $25 and $30 million in January. “Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development,” Williams said.

title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
body:
Diesel prices are surging as midterms approach – and they are likely to stay high in the near future, according to analysts.
The International Energy Agency's monthly report for October, released Wednesday, was the latest to predict that constraints on the diesel market will likely keep prices elevated into next year. The group warned that even if refineries step up production of diesel into the year-end, inventories will likely remain strained until the second half of 2027.
Last Friday, President Donald Trump unexpectedly paused sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and announced that he reached a deal with President Vladimir Putin in which the Kremlin would release 4.8 million metric tons of diesel , or nearly 36 million barrels, to the global market.
Over the weekend, he took to Truth Social to announce an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine , but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later accused Russia of attacking the country's energy facilities .
The foreign policy developments come as rising fuel prices — particularly skyrocketing diesel — have become a major flashpoint ahead of this year's midterm election. But releasing Russian diesel to the global market is unlikely to drop prices in the near term. A note from Goldman Sachs last week even predicted that diesel prices will remain high through 2027 as refineries struggle to meet demand.
Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply.
Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22.
However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making that tightening of supply feel that much more acute.
Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.

The filing, reported earlier by Reuters , is tied to a legal battle between Apple and OpenAI over trade secrets — but this time, OpenAI is doing the accusing. It alleges that the files in question contain images of at least one unreleased device, along with supplier information, engineering data, project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports about the “coating and sealing of hardware components.”
OpenAI also links Apple’s new HomeView smart display and the range of other devices it revealed this week to the former employee’s presentation. “That presentation appears to have happened months ago — and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI claims, while citing an article and a company announcement about Apple’s new product releases.
Apple’s product plans typically operate on a very long timeline, and its smart display has been rumored for years . Conversely, Apple accuses OpenAI of stealing confidential documents and spying on hardware prototypes to help build its own products.
“OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work,” OpenAI claims. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

title: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure
body:
Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.
It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire."
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions. The restrictions apply to the sister service Starshield, which supports national security.
Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday.
"There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday.
He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said.
The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel.
Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Zelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the Starshield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post.
SpaceX and the White House didn't respond to requests for comment.

title: Yemen’s Houthis Vow More Attacks on Saudi Airports, Oil Facilities After Aramco HQ Hit
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
General view of Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura oil refinery and oil terminal in Saudi Arabia May 21, 2018. REUTERS/Ahmed Jadallah
RIYADH/DUBAI, Oct 14 (Reuters) – Yemen’s Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Tuesday night’s attack on Saudi Aramco’s base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom’s backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn’t immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The Saudi government media office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.
In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
In a broad threat, they urged “international shipping companies,” civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations center for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday’s attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.
The UN World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.
“WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children,” WFP said in a statement.
(Additional reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin in Geneva; Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

title: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
body: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container. The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure. The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance. It comes as the U.S. military seeks to expand its inventory of uncrewed systems and distribute capabilities across more dispersed operating locations, particularly in preparation for a potential large-scale conflict with China in the Indo-Pacific. Rendering of the Nomad 100 Fast Pack in action. Courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company Rendering courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company “Military commanders are asking for capability that enables them to deploy worldwide into austere environments,” said Ramsey Bentley, director of Sikorsky Advanced Concepts, speaking at AUSA. They want greater situational awareness, the ability to conduct targeting and deliver effects at range, and the capacity to control multiple assets simultaneously, he added. A rendering of soldiers preparing Nomads for launch in a typical Indo-Pacific operating environment. Sikorsky screencap The Nomad 100 Fast Pack is built around a standard 20-foot ISO container housing four aircraft, mission-command equipment, communications, power systems, and sustainment supplies. The aim is to deliver a self-contained package that can be transported to a forward location, brought into operation, and moved again quickly. A promotional video shows the Fast Pack being transported into a combat theater by one of the company’s Black Hawk helicopters as a slung load. Sikorsky says two Nomad 100s can be prepared for flight “out of the box” in less than 15 minutes and that the other two aircraft — stored on the upper shelf of the container — can be made available within four to six hours. The package is designed to support runway-independent operations from locations including naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas, and improvised landing zones. “We no longer require a ground control station,” explained Sikorsky Vice President and General Manager Rich Benton. “We no longer require a large group of soldiers or operators.” Beyond the containerized package, Bentley said Nomad can be transported by truck or trailer, or potentially self-deploy in a smaller package. Sikorsky is also developing containerized deployment concepts for larger members of the Nomad family. As we have discussed in the past , the Nomad 100 combines vertical takeoff and landing with the ability to transition to fixed-wing flight, bringing airplane-like range and endurance to a compact, runway-independent package that can operate from confined locations. “What is very unique about this aircraft is it’s able to roll over on its wing and also fly like an airplane,” Bentley said. “So you’re getting the vertical takeoff and landing capability, along with the endurance, range, and speed of a fixed-wing aircraft.” Sikorsky cites an endurance of 10 to 14 hours, depending on payload, a range exceeding 800 nautical miles, and a cruising speed of 70 miles per hour, with a dash speed of 90 miles per hour. Its hybrid-electric drivetrain uses combustion engines to drive a generator that supplies power to the aircraft’s rotors and mission systems. Nomad is designed to operate on multiple fuels, including JP-8, JP-4, and Jet A. “Ten gallons of fuel provides over 10 plus hours of operation, so it’s a very efficient system,” Bentley said. He added that the hybrid-electric design reduces maintenance requirements, emphasizing line-replaceable units over more extensive traditional aviation maintenance. The aircraft can carry a 60-pound mission payload, including supplies such as medical equipment. Bentley said its modular center fuselage can be configured as a cargo bay or adapted for other mission equipment. Sikorsky says the Fast Pack can support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and targeting (ISR-T), light attack, and contested logistics missions, depending on customer configuration. On display at AUSA is a Nomad configured with a forward-looking infrared (FLIR) sensor turret with laser designation capability and four small Northrop Grumman Hatchet glide munitions. Other potential payloads include electro-optical and infrared sensors, synthetic aperture radar, launched effects, and electronic warfare systems for jamming. A launched effect is released from a Nomad drone in an earlier Sikorsky rendering. Sikorsky screencap The combination of a small logistical footprint and long-range flight could be particularly useful for supporting expeditionary forces . The aircraft could deliver supplies without relying on a runway or crewed helicopter, while sensor-equipped variants could provide reconnaissance and target designation. Other configurations could carry weapons or deploy additional uncrewed systems. The Fast Pack also relies on Sikorsky’s MATRIX autonomy technology to reduce operator workload. Rather than continuously piloting each aircraft, an operator can assign a mission through a tablet-based interface and let the aircraft execute it autonomously. A drone operator uses a tablet to control a Nomad. Sikorsky screencap “Now, Matrix autonomy is a very mature autonomy capability. We’ve had over 1,000 flight hours on Matrix,” Bentley said. An operator selects a mission, designates a location on a map, and initiates the flight. MATRIX then manages engine start, preflight checks, launch, navigation, and mission execution. “For the operator, very simply, he pulls up the display. He selects a mission, say reconnaissance, and then the operator would select a point on the map where he wants that reconnaissance to occur, and then he hits start,” Bentley explained. “The aircraft Matrix autonomy takes care of everything else along the flight.” Bentley said the system can adapt to changing environmental and tactical conditions, using onboard sensors to navigate and avoid obstacles, including hazards around landing areas. “Our whole approach here with the advanced Matrix autonomy is: How do we take the workload off the operator?” he said. “This is not remotely piloted, although you could do that. Our approach here is that this is fully autonomous.” Communications are designed to be network-agnostic. Bentley identified Starlink or Starshield for beyond-line-of-sight connectivity in the current configuration, alongside tactical mobile ad-hoc networking (MANET) equipment for line-of-sight communications. MATRIX is also used in other Sikorsky autonomy efforts, including the fully uncrewed U-Hawk drone , seen in the video below, and the company’s optionally piloted Black Hawk concept . A common tablet interface could help operators manage different autonomous aircraft without needing a separate control system for each. Nomad 100 originated under DARPA’s EVADE program, which sought to develop a vertical-lift uncrewed aircraft capability. Bentley said two customers associated with the program had placed initial orders, with additional interest from domestic and international customers. Sikorsky has a contract for three Nomad 100s under EVADE. The company announced in July that the first had been delivered to the customer, while a second was entering flight testing at the time of the interview. The U.S. Marine Corps is also buying two Nomad 100s, Bentley told Army Times . Sikorsky is developing the larger Nomad 500, which will offer greater payload capacity, longer range, and increased power output. One Nomad 500 can fit in a 20-foot container, while three can be transported in a 40-foot container, according to Bentley. The largest member of the family, the Nomad 1000, requires a 40-foot container for a single aircraft. A rendering shows how the Nomad family of VTOL drones can be scaled for a variety of sea- and land-based missions. Sikorsky The Fast Pack concept reflects a broader effort to make autonomous aircraft easier to deploy and sustain as military forces disperse across larger operating areas. Its appeal lies not just in the Nomad 100’s combination of vertical takeoff and long-range flight, but in packaging multiple aircraft and their supporting equipment into a single, relocatable system. That could be especially valuable in the Indo-Pacific, where long distances, limited infrastructure, and the vulnerability of fixed operating bases pose major challenges. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment appeared first on TWZ .

title: Copper price forecasts lifted for 2026 but tariff “collapse” still on the table
body: Copper pulled back from a three-week high on Wednesday after US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table, and word of a preliminary deal to avert a strike at BHP’s Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, took some of the supply premium out of the price. Comex copper for December delivery traded at $6.6695 a pound (about $14,704 a tonne) late morning in New York, down 0.8%, after touching $6.7890 earlier in the session. The most-active contract’s record settlement of $6.89 was set on September 9 , the day before a report that the White House tariff plan had stalled knocked more than 5% off the price. In London, three-month copper climbed as far as $14,700 a tonne, its highest since September 23, before easing to $14,532 by early afternoon. Cash copper settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and $14,741 on Tuesday, and LME inventories have fallen for seven straight sessions to 229,650 tonnes. US consumer prices accelerated in September on a surge in gasoline costs, and the CME’s FedWatch tool put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s late-October meeting at about 44%, double the day before, Reuters reported. New York Fed President John Williams said he still sees one more hike this year. Two sources told Reuters that Escondida’s supervisors’ union and the company had reached a preliminary agreement , which members were voting on Wednesday morning, and a union leader told Bloomberg a deal was “virtually done”. Unions at Antofagasta’s Centinela returned to talks on Tuesday after a week-long stoppage, while the open pit at Codelco’s El Teniente remains shut after a deadly landslide . Click on chart for live prices. Copper’s 2026 advance has forecasters raising their numbers for the second time in three months, and with the metal averaging $13,471 a tonne for the year to date, the 2026 revisions mostly bring the sheet into line with the tape. Macquarie now has copper averaging $13,573 this year, BMO Capital Markets $13,619 and BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, $13,500, up from the $12,700 it moved to in July . The differences open up from next year, and they come down to how much of the 1.5 to 2 million tonnes of copper now sitting in the United States is counted as surplus. “The great copper gamble” Macquarie, which in July called the rally “running ahead of reality” , has lifted its 2027 average by 14% to $12,750 and pushed the cycle low to $12,000 in the fourth quarter of next year from $11,000 a quarter earlier, while its long-term price rises to $10,500 a tonne in 2025 dollars. Prices “have disconnected from the fundamentals and could arguably move higher or lower depending on the outcome of the Section 232,” the bank’s strategists write in a quarterly compendium whose copper chapter is headed “The great copper gamble”, listing the metal among its preferred commodities for the next six to nine months “but very binary”. The fundamentals as Macquarie counts them are a 223,000-tonne surplus this year after a 531,000-tonne disruption allowance, and surpluses averaging more than 700,000 tonnes a year from 2027 as mine supply grows 4.9% next year and 4.3% in 2028, with Collahuasi, Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula and Centinela ramping up, Tia Maria starting and Cobre Panama back in full from mid-2027. Global demand growth slows to 1.5% in 2027 on its numbers, with none at all in China, where construction-related copper use is shrinking 9% a year and air conditioner makers are “again looking at aluminium substitution.” Visible stocks worldwide are up 300,000 tonnes this year, but that is the US build; everywhere else they are down 168,000 tonnes, and Macquarie says sentiment will not turn until LME and Shanghai inventories start rising again, either quickly on a tariff decision or gradually as its forecast surpluses feed through. Macquarie’s four tariff scenarios run from a January 1 that passes with no announcement at all, which it rates most likely, to a definitive decision against a duty, which it rates least likely: “the CME price will most likely collapse, taking the LME price with it, and the arb will invert,” with surplus US stocks reappearing in LME warehouses in the US and Asia. A tariff announced six to eight weeks ahead of implementation would pull a last wave of metal into the US and leave the rest of the world “very tight”, while a formal six-month delay would see the spread fade as it did for platinum and palladium after the critical minerals decision. Expectations are also growing that a scrap export ban will be folded into any decision; an immediate ban would take about 600,000 tonnes a year of contained copper off the world market. “Has the market misread US inventory?” BMO Capital Markets arrives at a very different place from a similar starting point. Its quarterly price deck, published two days before Macquarie’s, raises its long-term copper price by 47% to $16,000 a tonne in real terms, or $18,000 nominal by 2030, with $14,675 for 2027 and $16,000 for 2028, and the bank puts itself 46% above consensus on the long-term number. Its market balance is close to balanced throughout: an 83,000-tonne surplus this year, then small deficits from 2027. The argument turns on what the US hoard, now close to 2 million tonnes on BMO’s estimate, or about a year of American consumption, actually represents. China’s refined copper imports have run below trend and its exports above trend since the tariff trade began, a cumulative swing of about 1.6 million tonnes on a net basis, which BMO reads as Beijing allowing its strategic reserve to run down while Washington built one. “Instead of there being a build in above ground inventory over the last 2 years, there has been a geographical redistribution from ‘not visible’ to ‘visible’, meaning today’s price of ~$14,500-15,000/t is fundamentally supported,” the bank writes. Had China bid for metal alongside the US, “copper prices today would in fact be much, much higher,” and at some point China will want to restock. BMO expects no tariff decision before the US midterms in November, which may see copper “pause for breath” and keep the Comex-LME spread narrow, but says investors it talks to are coming around to the view that the US stockpile “could simply stay in situ for many more years.” Rising dependence on scrap, with China’s secondary refined output heading for 3.3 million tonnes this year from 2.8 million, is the other leg of its case: scrap is the marginal unit, and it only comes out at higher prices. BMI sits between the two. It still views the rally “as having extended beyond what fundamentals alone would suggest” and has the market in a 43,000-tonne surplus this year, but has cut its 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.1% from 2.4% with Chilean output down 4%, and expects a deficit from 2027 that widens to 1.7 million tonnes by 2035 as demand grows 3% to 4% a year on grids, EVs and data centres. Its 2027 forecast is $12,900, rising to $15,000 in 2029 and an unchanged $17,000 in 2035. The International Copper Study Group, meeting this week, lifted its 2026 surplus to 104,000 tonnes and kept 2027 at 368,000 tonnes. The arb has gone, the metal has not The spread that built the US stockpile has all but disappeared on a spot basis. Comex October copper at $6.62 a pound trades below LME cash, which at Tuesday’s $14,741 works out to $6.69, and John Gross of The Copper Journal calculates the month-to-date average has flipped to an 85-point LME premium from a 17-cent Comex premium in June. Most of that is London’s doing: the backwardation that put cash $164.50 over three months at Monday’s settlement, since narrowed to $115.50, reflects how little spot metal is left outside the US. Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has offered customers a record premium of $347 a tonne for 2027 supply, 10% above this year’s level, Benchmark Minerals reported, and a company spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a lot of material has relocated to the US, leaving warehouses quite empty.” Further down the curve the premium survives. December Comex at $14,704 a tonne sits about $170 over LME three-month, which Macquarie read at the end of September as the market pricing a 10% chance of a 15% duty (on Wednesday’s prices the same arithmetic gives about 8%). That is too little to pull fresh shipments across the Atlantic, but enough to keep what is already there in place as long as the Comex curve pays traders to hold it. The tonnes still arriving are cargo booked months ago: Comex stocks rose another 6,500 tonnes last week to 713,000 tonnes, with 100,000 tonnes of African and South American copper due through October. Deutsche Bank takes the stockpiling argument furthest. Daniel Ghali, the bank’s new head of metals research, told the Wall Street Journal that with China adding to its strategic reserve for decades and the tariff threat pulling metal into American sheds, the two countries could be sitting on 71% of the world’s supply by the end of the year. On that trajectory copper “simply won’t be available” to users elsewhere by the end of 2028, an outcome averted only by prices high enough to force substitution into aluminium. He sees $10 a pound, or $22,050 a tonne, in the second quarter of 2027, almost 50% above current levels. Even a decision against tariffs may not free the metal, he told the paper, since the LME has warehouses in the US and copper may simply be shuffled between American sites rather than leave the country. Gross points to copper’s premium over aluminium, which hit a record $5.08 a pound in September, more than double its July 2022 low. “Clearly, this rising premium cannot continue indefinitely, but who among us will step forward to say it’s at the top?” he writes. His September monthly report makes the longer point: China consumed 58.9% of the world’s refined copper last year, up from 12.4% in 2000. “There are too many copper eggs in China’s basket.” Miners still pricing $5 copper Copper producers fell with the metal on Wednesday, Lundin Mining down 3.9%, Freeport-McMoRan 3.7%, Southern Copper 3.3% and Teck Resources 2.9%, but the year has been kind. Southern Copper is up 44.1% in 2026, taking its market value to $169 billion, with Glencore ahead 38.6%, BHP 38.0% and Freeport 37.4% at a $100 billion valuation. Teck has gained 36.1% and Anglo American 29.2%. Lundin has managed 13.0%, Antofagasta 7.5% with Centinela on strike, and First Quantum 3.0%. RBC Capital Markets calculates that North American copper producers at 1.0 times net asset value imply a copper price of $5.03 a pound, from $5.98 for Freeport down to $3.96 for Ivanhoe Mines, against a futures price near $6.70. The group trades at 0.9 times net asset value, in line with its 10-year average. Comex copper is up more than 18% in 2026. title: Kraken Parent Company Payward to Buy Saldo Bank in European Banking Push
body: Bitcoin Magazine Kraken Parent Company Payward to Buy Saldo Bank in European Banking Push Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Saldo Bank, gaining an EU banking license and a footprint across five European markets. Payward is buying Saldo Finance Oy, a Finnish holding company whose subsidiary, Saldo Bank UAB, is a digital-first specialized bank licensed in Lithuania. The bank operates in Lithuania, Finland, Sweden and Germany, with a passport into the Netherlands. Payward did not reveal the financial terms of the deal, which is expected to close in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. It comes as Kraken, like other crypto exchanges, pushes further into the traditional finance world, allowing users to trade stocks, bonds and other assets. The company has sold its app as a “primary account for everything.” “A regulated EU bank is the piece that lets us serve European clients the way a primary financial institution should: one place to hold assets, move them freely, and put them to work,” said Arjun Sethi, Payward’s co-CEO. “We are starting in the EU, and the ambition is global.” Payward said that once completed, the acquisition is expected to let Payward Banking offer interest on deposits, SME and consumer loans, credit cards, and banking-as-a-service tools such as card issuance, SEPA payments access and embedded lending for partners. Saldo already offers retail term deposits in all four of its operating markets, consumer lending in Lithuania, Finland and Sweden, and a credit card in Finland. Payward says it already holds a Federal Reserve limited-purpose master account in the U.S. and an e-money license from the Central Bank of Ireland, and has originated more than $2 billion in loans. The deal comes shortly after Payward this week announced plans to launch in the UAE following full approval from Dubai’s Virtual Asset Regulatory Authority. In September, Bloomberg reported that Nasdaq Inc. was investing $100 million in Payward at a $21 billion valuation, citing people familiar with the matter. Payward and SoFi Technologies also recently agreed to route SoFi customers’ crypto orders through Kraken Prime, Kraken’s prime brokerage arm. This post Kraken Parent Company Payward to Buy Saldo Bank in European Banking Push first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: Forterra partners with Hypercraft on autonomous vehicle for high-risk missions
body: Defense companies Forterra and Hypercraft have collaborated to produce a contested-environment-ready autonomous vehicle, which they showed off for the first time at the Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C. Forterra installed its AutoDrive autonomy software platform that powers unmanned maneuverability onto Hypercraft’s Razorback ground vehicle, yielding a product that can withstand the punishing logistics of combat without putting soldiers at risk. “The point of an autonomous military vehicle is to deliver payloads to the point of friction,” Forterra Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders said. “Razorback has the power, power generation and capacity to carry a wide variety of weapons systems without modification.” Forterra’s AutoDrive autonomous driving system has become an industry standard, integrated on more than 200 vehicles in active service. Meanwhile, the Razorback weaponizes 300 horsepower, 4,0000 volumes of payload range, a 500-mile range and up to 38 kilowatts of distributable power. Forterra was the first U.S. ground autonomy company to be actively deployed in Ukraine and has completed 88 casualty evacuation missions to rescue Ukrainian soldiers from the front lines, according to Forterra spokesperson Kelsey Szablowski. That mission to not put military personnel in harm’s way is part of Forterra’s mantra. “Robots don’t bleed,” Szablowski said. The Army has taken notice of the company’s approach. In August, the service selected Forterra as a prime contractor for its Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability program, a larger effort to field autonomous vehicles during mine-clearing missions. The company outfitted a Ford F-250 with its AutoDrive technology and named it the Mobile Autonomous Uncrewed Lanemaker, or MAUL. The MAUL, which hosts no human in the driver’s seat and can drive autonomously or be controlled by an operator, is made for reconnaissance, planning and clearing in mine-contested environments. The autonomous vehicle deploys a rocket-propelled mine-clearing line charge, or MICLIC, to detonate explosives in an area before driving through. In mid-August, Forterra demonstrated the MAUL’s capabilities during Project Sandhills at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, in which drones attacked the vehicle as it attempted to mine-detect and clear. The MAUL fought off and destroyed the drones with an onboard automated turret, while it navigated through the area autonomously. The exercise took place from Aug. 17 to Aug. 28 and demonstrated the Army’s ability to tackle a myriad of mission sets using attributable autonomous systems that reduce risks to soldiers. “Instead of relying solely on high-value, crewed assets, we can field semi-autonomous F-250s, sUAS swarms and autonomous c-UAS systems that are adaptable, scalable and resilient,” said Capt. Denny Drummey, Sandhills Project operations officer, during the exercise.
