title: Peskov: Russia Did Not Break Trump’s ‘Energy Truce’ Because Terms Were Never Set
body:
The Kremlin claimed that Russia cannot be accused of breaking US President Donald Trump’s abrupt energy truce because its terms were never set, hours after Russian strikes cut power to at least 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov made the remarks on Wednesday, Oct. 14, when asked about Russia’s overnight attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified, so it cannot be said that Russia is not complying with it,” Peskov said according to the Russian news outlet Astra .
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces used ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against energy and communications facilities it claimed were serving Ukraine’s military and defense industry.
The ministry listed the Darnytsia CHP-4 and CHP-5 combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, as well as CHP-6, the Trypillia thermal power plant and a major electrical substation in Kyiv region.
In the Kharkiv region, the ministry named the Kharkiv CHP-5 and the Zmiiv thermal power plant.
It also claimed to have hit an Ukrssibbank data center, alleging without evidence that it was used to gather intelligence on Russian forces.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed tha t Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building late Tuesday, Oct. 13, killing at least three people and injuring 26, including an eight-year-old child.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia launched 39 missiles and 128 drones in the attack, which began at 6 p.m. local time. Air defenses downed four missiles and 115 drones.
Zelensky called the strike deliberate, saying it damaged 26 sites in Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities, and warned of further outages.
“Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong,” Zelensky said.
He urged Trump to impose “STRONG sanctions” on Moscow under the sanctions law named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, and asked for more Patriot interceptors; the only weapons system that can successfully deter Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Strains between Kyiv and Washington have continued to grow throughout this week.
For the second night in a row, Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming ballistic missiles.
The lapse followed reports that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation at talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9 that Washington could cut off intelligence sharing if Kyiv kept striking Russian refineries.
Trump’s administration reportedly also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
Meanwhile, Trump has denied that the US stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that cooperation with Washington continues , although neither disclosed whether the scope of intelligence sharing had changed.
Following a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, Oct. 9, Trump announced that the US struck a diesel arrangement with the Kremlin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department issued a license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
On Sunday, Oct. 11, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, without an official response from neither Ukraine nor Russia.
Although Ukraine signalled willingness to abide by the truce and refrained from striking Russia’s facilities, Russia continued its attacks on Ukraine nationwide.
Trump insisted that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire because he told them to , despite neither government confirming such a deal. “They agreed. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ – that’s why,” he told reporters on Monday.
On Tuesday, 12 US senators – six Republicans and six Democrats – signed a joint letter urging Trump to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which grants him the power to sanction Russia and buyers of its energy with tariffs of up to 500%. The senators called the deal “a betrayal” of Ukraine and argued it only helps Russia’s aggression.
The bill was signed into law by Trump just three weeks before he struck the deal with the Kremlin leader.
On the same day that Trump announced the deal, a bipartisan US delegation was in Kyiv, backing expansion of Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urging an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk.
However, Musk did the opposite and imposed speed restrictions on Starshield , the military version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s military, without prior warning overnight on Oct. 13-14. The cap cuts connections for terminals moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour).
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Container ship sinks near Hormuz after being hit by projectile, sources say
body: A container ship has sunk near the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by a projectile, while a separate dry bulk carrier damaged in an earlier attack is also reported to be sinking, maritime security sources said on Wednesday.The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride container ship, with a small 2,824 TEU (20-ft equivalent unit) capacity, had sunk, the sources said."Commercial vessel 'GFS PRIDE' reported sunk with floating containers ... mariners cautioned," the Hydrographer of Pakistan said in a navigational warning to ships dated October 14.The vessel's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment.The loss of the GFS Pride marks the second vessel to sink since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.Separate container ship reportedly sinking after failed rescue attemptIn a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao was reported to be sinking close to the strait after being struck by a projectile on September 23, the sources added.The vessel's UAE-based manager, Peonies Shipmanagement FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment."The Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier CAPE DAO, originally hit on 23 September, is reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt," British maritime risk management group Vanguard said in a note on Wednesday.Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

title: OpenAI will reportedly ship at least one model this year but its flagship still needs alignment work
body:
OpenAI is racing to finish its next flagship model, which uses the same looped transformer technique as Astra. The approach boosts math and coding performance but makes safety monitoring harder. Employees say one or two new models will likely ship by year's end.
OpenAI will likely release "one or two new models" before the end of the year, according to employees, though it's unclear whether "the major upgraded model" the company is currently working on will be among them. That's according to The Information , citing people familiar with the projects.
The new flagship could still be a ways off. The model needs alignment work so its goals match what OpenAI's researchers and customers expect. The company also has to shore up the testing infrastructure around the model before it can move forward. Ad
After leadership is satisfied with safety evaluations, there's another hurdle. Under an executive order from President Trump governing evaluations of advanced AI systems, OpenAI agreed to give the US government access to new models up to 30 days before they go to outside partners and longer still before a public launch. Ad
The new flagship also uses looped transformers, according to a person familiar with the situation. OpenAI already runs this technique in production, where it goes by "Recurrent Depth." It's central to how Astra works , the company's current top model. Instead of passing a token through the transformer layers once, the model loops it through the same layers multiple times before outputting the next word. That drives up performance on math and coding and brings down costs, since a smaller model can punch above its weight.
But the looping also moves some of the model's "thinking" out of readable text and into internal numerical representations that human reviewers can't inspect. That undermines chain-of-thought monitoring , where safety researchers trace a model's reasoning to spot bad behavior. OpenAI deliberately capped how many loops Astra runs to keep its chain of thought readable, The Information reports. Ad
After the Hugging Face incident , OpenAI moved roughly ten percent of its total compute toward alignment and safety, according to a person familiar with the figures. The Information reports that amounts to hundreds of megawatts worth of data center capacity, though it's unclear how much was allocated to safety before or what the current split looks like. At market rates, the compute OpenAI shifted would cost billions of dollars a year to rent. AI researcher Noam Brown said in a mid-September podcast that about ten percent of his team also works on security and safety.
How OpenAI actually uses this technique came to light through a slip-up at Microsoft. The major investor, which has access to OpenAI's intellectual property, published a technical write-up on GPT-6.1 Sol , a cheaper Astra alternative that OpenAI launched earlier this month. Ad
In a now-deleted section, Microsoft described GPT-6.1 Sol as using "looping inference," where the model works through the same problem in multiple "passes" before producing an answer. GPT-6.1 Sol "uses the same base model weights as GPT-6 Sol with two inference passes instead of three," The Information quotes from a cached copy of the page. Ad
A person with direct knowledge confirmed that the write-up matched what OpenAI had told Microsoft in private. Microsoft took the section down after realizing it wasn't meant to be public. Looped transformers remain a sensitive part of OpenAI's model development, both during training and at inference, The Information reports.
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has already acknowledged that chain-of-thought monitoring is growing "fragile" and "unfortunately trending in a negative direction." He also warned against an industry-wide race toward models without readable reasoning.

title: Abilene Christian University is giving Ivy League endowments a run for their money in the market
body:
While universities like Harvard and Yale carry around endowments that are larger than some small countries' economies, this bull market has provided an environment in which their market performance can be rivaled by nimble collegiate counterparts lacking their vast resources and donor networks.
Yale University's $44 billion endowment, a close comp to Nepal's GDP, has returned 9.4% over the past decade through June 2025 — good, but not good enough to beat Abilene Christian University, a private Christian university in Abilene, Texas , and its 11.4% over the same period, which recently led it to surpass the $1 billion in assets milestone .
Through June 2026, ACU's 10-year return climbed to 13.6%, against 9.1% for a benchmark of 70% global stocks and 30% bonds, according to data provided by the school. But it's more than just a good year: ACU's 20-year 10.9% average through June 2026 is well above its 6.8% benchmark.
For many schools, this is the period (September to November) when fiscal year investment performance is released, but not all information is released at the same time. Yale, for instance, has yet to publish its 2026 numbers. The most-cited annual study of hundreds of endowments, the NACUBO-Commonfund Study of Endowments , will be published in February 2027 for FY 2026 performance data.
Joe Lee, president and chief investment officer of ACIMCO (Abilene Christian Investment Management Company), a university-controlled investment company that manages the school's portfolio, said that many small, but good, sound decisions early on, years ago, have compounded over time.
"We do the standard stuff that other endowments do," Lee said, pointing to a philosophy that is equity-oriented, incorporates super long time horizons, and employs good managers and diversification techniques.
But he also said being small can be an advantage, "if you lean into the advantages of a smaller endowment," Lee said. Larger endowments have fund-sized thresholds below which they are not worth their time.
"We can look at a $100 million fund and get excited about it and get something material," Lee said.
ACU's endowment of a little over $1 billion, as of the end of its most recent fiscal year on June 30, 2026, compares to a Yale endowment valued at $44.1 billion in Yale's most recent disclosure (FY 2025).
Yale did not respond to requests for comment.
ACIMCO, while not unique in higher education, is an asset to portfolio management.
"We have a great structure," Lee said, adding that having a separate university-owned management company — as opposed to an outside firm — manage the school's portfolio allows it to have a much longer time horizon.
It also lets the school move faster, Lee said, crediting a dedicated investment committee and a board he described as forward-thinking and open-minded, with critical thinking at the right moments. Good governance matters, he said, as does not going after short-term results.
Despite the advantages to which Lee speaks, the shift to the outsourced CIO model which picked up a decade ago has accelerated over the past five years, according to Anna Dunn Tabke, founder of Leita Advisory, which runs searches that help colleges and foundations pick outsourced chief investment officers. "An in-house CIO is expensive, and even if a school can afford one, that one person can't do everything. They need a team and often outside manager research and due diligence," she said.
Hiring an OCIO can also allow schools to pool their money with other institutions and help to invest competitively alongside larger endowments.
Lee said after interviewing 20 outside managers of investment funds, they all sound smart, aligned and insightful, and "at the end of the day you are betting on people."
It's a pattern-recognition business, he said, with skill, high integrity, alignment and earning their fees all table stakes.
The ACU portfolio is not simply stocks and bonds. A little more than half of the endowment is in private investments and a little less than half is in public markets, Lee said. Privately held equity and publicly traded equity returned similar amounts for ACU in fiscal 2026, he said, adding that it's hard to credit the return to one side or the other because the public portion includes cash, which earns very little.
The endowment also comes with strings attached. The university has a mission of drawing upon the endowment to benefit current and future students, and there are also many stipulations on the money, as some is bequeathed by donors with certain conditions, such as funds that go only to chemistry majors or underprivileged students.
ACU isn't the only small school outperforming far larger rivals in terms of portfolio performance.
Reed College , a Portland, Oregon liberal arts school with an endowment of $885 million, reported returns of 7.5%, 12.4% and 11.6% over the past three fiscal years through June 2025, ahead of Yale's 1.8%, 5.7% and 11.1% in the same years, according to each school's reports. Reed says it has also beaten a traditional 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio and the median college endowment, as tracked by Cambridge Associates, an investment consulting firm, over the past five and 10 years.
Colby College , a liberal arts school in Waterville, Maine, reported an 18.2% return for the year ended June 30, 2026, and a 10.5% annualized return over the past 10 years, net of manager fees, according to data provided by the school. Its endowment was $1.4 billion as of June 30, 2026. A year earlier, Colby's 10-year annualized return was 8.5%, below the 9.4% Yale reported for the same period but ahead of Harvard's 7.7% and Columbia's 7.8%. Colby said no single company contributed more than 1% to last year's return.
Deborah Shufrin, associate vice president and chief investment officer of Colby College, credits the school's long-term relationships as being a factor in its competitive returns.
"Colby's returns have been competitive with much larger institutions in large part due to early/long-standing relationships with premier private fund managers as well as the ability to identify and access newer emerging top-tier private funds," Shufrin said, adding that these relationships enable Colby to take advantage of its perpetual life and long-term investment horizon.
Donors also play a role. Matt Proto, senior vice president at Colby, said the school's Dare Northward fundraising campaign has paid for new academic programs and facilities, financial aid, athletics and the redevelopment of downtown Waterville. "Many gifts enhanced the endowment, several launched new programs and facilities, and others supported annual operations," Proto said.
Not everyone agrees the edge is as clear as the numbers suggest.
Tabke said comparisons between small endowments and giants like Yale need care, because the time periods may not match. She noted the fact that some schools have already reported results through June 30, 2026, while Yale's 10-year figure runs only through June 2025. She says that one-year gap matters a lot right now.
Using a database from Confluence, an investment data provider of 259 small and mid-sized endowments and foundations, with an average portfolio of $220 million, she said the bar for ranking among the top 5% over 10 years was about 8.45% a year as of June 2025, a level Yale topped. A year later, it had jumped to roughly 10.5%, with the middle of the pack at 8.65%. In other words, the typical 10-year return rose almost two points in a single year. Last year's results were also unusually scattered: the best-performing 5% of schools earned nearly 19.5%, while the bottom 5% earned under 4%, roughly double the gap of the year before.
Despite Abilene's CIO noting that its returns from private funds — which comprise a little over half of its investments — were on par with returns from public market investments, Tabke said that private equity, a favorite of big-endowment investors, has paid out little and returned little for about three years, while schools with simpler, stock-heavy portfolios, especially large U.S. tech companies, pulled ahead. Then a few schools that invest like Yale, some through outsourced managers, held shares in SpaceX when it went public in June, which lifted their returns. One year like that, she said, can move a 10-year number noticeably.
Smaller schools will also more frequently run up against illiquidity issues which limit the risks they are able to take across markets.
"Smaller schools generally can't take on Yale's level of illiquidity. Yale's endowment is the product of more than 300 years of gifts, and Yale and peers like Princeton can also draw on fundraising and debt alongside endowment spending and tuition," Tabke said.
"Concentration is a risk at any size: a stock-heavy portfolio can depend on a few large tech companies, and a large SpaceX position is a concentration of its own," Tabke added, noting that resources are the other constraint.
Timing is a big part of the story, according to R. Keith Sauls, CFA, who heads the higher-education endowment and foundation group at Farther Finance, a wealth management firm and the immediate past chair of the College of Charleston Foundation, where he also chaired the investment committee.
The recent edge for small schools is real, Sauls said, but he added that staying out of investments that are hard to sell quickly can help make them look nimble and contribute to beating bigger peers recently. Over time, though, he said larger endowments generally come out ahead by about one to 1.5 percentage points a year, which he described as the payoff for tying money up in those investments.
Sauls said big endowments hold a lot of venture capital and private equity, which aren't revalued often, while the stock market surged, and some of the smaller schools' lead was timing, not a better model or better access. For example, when a fiscal year ends, and whether it catches a crash or a rally, can swing three-, five- and 10-year results, he said.
In the meantime, one might want to head to Abilene Christian University and sign up for FIN 411, Principles of Investment.
"The model being used matters because it can override the limitations of being a smaller endowment," Sauls said.

title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
body:
In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”
Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points , from 63% to 38%.
But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.
In a new survey , Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.
This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026 .
The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).
A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).
Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.
One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.
Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.
The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.
There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.
This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.
The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail.
In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting.
There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.

title: Israel Allies Foundation launches parliamentary caucuses in Greece, Cyprus to build trilateral ties
body: The Israel Allies Foundation (IAF) launched two new parliamentary caucuses in Greece and Cyprus this week, seeking to strengthen ties with Israel and expand cooperation on regional security, energy, and technology.The Greek Parliamentary Israel Allies Caucus was inaugurated at the Hellenic Parliament in Athens on Tuesday, followed by the launch of the Cyprus Israel Allies Caucus at the House of Representatives in Nicosia on Wednesday.The new caucuses aim to build on the existing trilateral partnership between Israel, Greece, and Cyprus, with a particular focus on security challenges in the Eastern Mediterranean, including tensions with Turkey.“The new Israel Allies Caucuses in Greece and Cyprus will help translate these commitments into parliamentary action,” said Leo van Doesburg, executive director of IAF Europe.“Turkish threats must be met with solidarity, not silence. Ankara has no veto over our partnerships or our security,” he added.Cyprus, Greece, Israel ties 'more vital than ever'In Greece, parliamentarians Konstantinos Tsiaras and Harris Theoharis will co-chair the caucus. The launch ceremony was attended by IAF President Josh Reinstein, van Doesburg, and Irini Karipidis, CEO of Amani and president of Aris FC, who will serve as the caucus's acting director.Tsiaras said the initiative comes amid growing regional security challenges and proves the three countries' shared strategic interests and historical ties.In Cyprus, the new caucus will be chaired by Democratic Party MP Chrysis Pantelides and will include six lawmakers from three political parties.The launch followed a meeting between the IAF delegation and Cypriot President Nicos Christodoulides at the Presidential Palace. The delegation was also hosted by House of Representatives President Annita Demetriou.Pantelides emphasized the importance of strengthening relations between Cyprus and Israel in light of regional security threats.“The strengthening of relations and the development of alliance ties between Cyprus and Israel is more vital than ever,” he said, citing the security challenges facing both countries.Israeli ambassadors attended the launches in their respective host countries, while the US ambassador to Cyprus also attended the ceremony in Nicosia.Reinstein welcomed the establishment of the two caucuses, saying they would help strengthen parliamentary cooperation and support for Israel.“Through faith-based diplomacy, we are building a bridge between parliamentarians who understand that Israel's security, and the security of the free world, depend on strong alliances rooted in shared Judeo-Christian values,” he said.

title: 2027: Opposition parties consult Atiku, Obi, Makinde, others on framework
body: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Six opposition political parties have opened consultations with five presidential candidates, among them Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, Mr Peter Obi and Governor Seyi Makinde, on a framework for cooperation ahead of the 2027 general elections. The National Chairmen and National Secretaries of the parties met the candidates as part of what they described as “ongoing strategic consultations and deliberations ahead of the 2027 general elections.” Promoter of G100, Salihu Moh. Lukman in a statement on Wednesday on behalf of Coalition Parties, said the engagements followed the resolutions of the G100 Opposition Summit. The summit, he said, “called for sustained dialogue, stronger cooperation and a coordinated approach among opposition parties in defence of multiparty democracy and the interests of the Nigerian people.” The participating parties are the African Democratic Congress ADC, Allied Peoples Movement APM, Nigeria Democratic Congress NDC, Social Democratic Party SDP, Peoples Democratic Party PDP and Peoples Redemption Party PRP. The candidates consulted were Atiku of the ADC, Makinde of the APM, Obi of the NDC, Prince Adewole Adebayo of the SDP and Mr Donald Duke of the PRP. According to the statement, “the consultations represent a practical step towards giving effect to those resolutions. They provide an opportunity for party leaders and presidential candidates to deliberate on the framework for opposition cooperation, identify areas of common ground and consider the steps necessary to advance a shared democratic agenda ahead of 2027.” The statement said the process is driven by a conviction that “the challenges confronting Nigeria demand serious engagement across party lines.” “Nigerians deserve political leaders who are prepared to place the country’s future, the wellbeing of its citizens and the credibility of its elections above narrow interests,” it said. It said the consultations were still going on and would build on the commitment to “an opposition that is organised, responsible and capable of working together in the national interest. “Nigerians will be informed of substantive decisions and agreed next steps as the deliberations progress,” the statement added. The post 2027: Opposition parties consult Atiku, Obi, Makinde, others on framework appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Jio Platforms Sets Stage For India’s Largest IPO At ₹10.3 Lakh Cr Valuation
body: Telecom giant Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065-₹1,119 per share for its IPO, which is set to open for public subscription next week. The company is seeking to raise ₹30,213 Cr at the upper end of the price band, overtaking Hyundai Motor’s ₹27,870 Cr IPO in 2024 to become the largest public offering to hit the Indian equities market till date. At the upper end of the IPO, RIL’s telecom arm is seeking a valuation of ₹10.3 Lakh Cr for the IPO. Jio filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) earlier today for its IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares. Post anchor bidding on October 19 (Monday), the IPO will open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. The telco has reserved ₹500 Cr worth shares for eligible employees, who can avail a discount of ₹54 per share. Additionally, up to ₹2,500 Cr will be reserved for eligible shareholders of RIL. The company intends to utilise ₹27,500 Cr of the fresh capital raised via the IPO for prepayment, in full or in part, of certain outstanding borrowings availed by its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). The remaining proceeds, ₹2,713 Cr to be precise, will be allocated for general corporate purposes may fund strategic initiatives, growth opportunities, capital expenditure, working capital, marketing and other business requirements. The issue has no OFS component, meaning existing shareholders will not sell shares through the IPO. RIL currently holds a 66.43% stake in Jio Platforms, while Meta and Google own 9.98% and 7.73%, respectively. The post Jio Platforms Sets Stage For India’s Largest IPO At ₹10.3 Lakh Cr Valuation appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
body:

New open-source software could make AI-enhanced weather forecasting more affordable.﻿
New open-source software could make AI-enhanced weather forecasting more affordable.﻿
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning.
Researchers with the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance — allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature , and the tool is now open-source software .
Microsoft joins Google , Nvidia , and other companies developing AI tools for weather forecasting. Instead of creating a new standalone weather model, Microsoft’s latest research in this realm uses machine learning to correct bias in existing models. It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI, the researchers hope.
It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI
While physics-based modeling is a resource-intensive endeavor running on supercomputers and generative AI depends on powerful GPUs , Microsoft Research New England senior principal researcher Lester Mackey says the new tool can run just on CPUs. “I have a lot of hope both for the increased resource efficiency of weather forecasting and the extended reliability of forecasts, especially for extreme weather,” Mackey tells The Verge .
Physics-based and AI-based models run into similar problems when they start predicting the weather two weeks or more in advance. Traditional models attempt to simulate the complex physics of Earth’s atmosphere, while AI models look for patterns in historical data to make forecasts. In both approaches, models rely on approximations to fill data gaps, whether from regions with sparse weather stations or complex atmospheric phenomena that scientists are still working to understand. The ways in which these models make up for those gaps in data can become a type of systematic bias. The resulting errors compound when making forecasts further ahead in time, making these predictions less precise.
Microsoft calls its method Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC). The tool uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections. One example Mackey gives is to correct for changes in climate. Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are heating up the planet, but a weather model might make predictions based on historical records that can bias it toward colder temperatures than the world is actually experiencing today.
The researchers found that PBC improved the accuracy of a leading physics-based weather model by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for 98 percent of precipitation and 92 percent of temperature targets. The machine learning framework also doubled the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis. Before the paper was published, the ECMWF had already awarded the authors’ research on PBC in its AI Weather Quest competition .
The new paper on PBC published by researchers at Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF, and other institutions “is a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” Matthew Chantry, ECMWF’s strategic lead for machine learning, said in an emailed comment to The Verge .
“As always, turning ideas into reality [in] an operational process is a most challenging step,” Chantry added.
The amount of compute and infrastructure needed for weather forecasting has often left technological advances out of reach for many agencies in economically developing countries. The paper’s authors, however, think PBC can be different. “One of the things that’s really exciting to me about models like PBC is how lightweight they are, how easy to train, that scientists without huge pools of resources can work on trying to configure [these] models and make them perform better in specific localities,” says Genevieve Flaspohler, one of the authors of the paper.
Flaspohler worked on PBC as an intern at Microsoft with Mackey, and now she’s the executive director of the nonprofit Rhiza Research, which is working with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority — with funding from the Gates Foundation — to see whether AI can help get more accurate early warnings out to people. PBC is one of the methods they’re testing ahead of what’s expected to be a more extreme rainy season during a record-breaking El Niño .

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
body:
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in Germany in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

WhatsApp’s new guest calling feature allows you to invite anyone to a call, without needing them to make an account first. They won’t need the app, either, since Meta also added support for calls on the web version of WhatsApp earlier this year. You can invite guests just by sending them the call link, and guests still have access to call features like hand raising, screen sharing, and emoji reactions, complete with end-to-end encryption.
However, you still need an account to start a call, and there are a few restrictions for guests:
Anyone joining as a guest always needs the call host’s approval. Guests will enter a waiting room until the host lets them in and guests can be removed from the call at any time. Guests can’t see other participants’ phone numbers, send messages, or add anyone else directly to the call.
Meta also says it’s launching Google and Outlook calendar integrations for WhatsApp calls later this year. After installing a WhatsApp plugin and connecting your account, you’ll be able to send a WhatsApp call link with your calendar invites.

title: Russia plans a new pretrial detention center outside Moscow. With room for 4,000 detainees, it would be the largest in the country.
body: Russia’s largest pretrial detention center will be built in the Solnechnogorsk district of the Moscow region. The regional office of the Federal Penitentiary Service has put the construction contract out to bid. The center will hold up to 4,000 detainees. The complex will cover more than 42 hectares (about 104 acres). It will include multistory buildings for men and women, as well as separate buildings for people with tuberculosis and criminal gang leaders deemed a harmful influence on other detainees. The complex will also include three buildings with apartment-style accommodations for Federal Penitentiary Service employees. The complex will be built near the 71-kilometer (44-mile) marker on the M-11 highway, between the villages of Shapkino and Ozhogino. The starting price for the construction contract is 37.8 billion rubles. Construction is scheduled to be completed in October 2031. Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin signed an order in 2022 to build a pretrial detention center for 4,000 people in the Moscow region. The project received final approval from state expert reviewers this past winter. “Kolpino,” known as “Kresty-2,” is currently considered Russia’s largest pretrial detention center. It was built in a suburb of St. Petersburg in 2017. Construction took 10 years.
