title: The Undercurrent: Three European Artists on Making Money Visible
body: Bitcoin Magazine The Undercurrent: Three European Artists on Making Money Visible Amsterdam helped lay the foundations of modern finance, but its artists were among its earliest critics. When speculative bubbles burst across Europe in 1720, Amsterdam printers and satirists responded with The Great Mirror of Folly , a collection of engravings and plays exposing the excesses of financial speculation. Nearly three centuries later, the city hosted another monetary experiment. David Chaum, the cryptographer whose work on anonymous communication helped lay the groundwork for the cypherpunk movement, came to Amsterdam in the 1980s to work at CWI, the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science. Around 1990, he founded DigiCash to develop private electronic cash. The company went bankrupt in 1998, a decade before bitcoin, but the dream of digital money was already taking shape. Last year at Bitcoin Amsterdam, BMAG exhibited The Waterworks of Money , in which Dutch artist Carlijn Kingma, working with financial journalist Thomas Bollen and researcher Martijn Jeroen van der Linden, depicted the monetary system as a vast irrigation network, with some areas flooded by liquidity while others remain dry. The drawing makes a complex financial system legible, exposing the mechanisms through which money is created, distributed, and concentrated. The Waterworks of Money, Carlijn Kingma (2022) This tradition of questioning money and making its hidden dimensions visible continues in the work of three European artists exhibiting at Bitcoin Amsterdam this November. ZETRA, RYR, and Cypherpunk Now draw from graffiti, political printmaking, hacker culture, and early bitcoin communities to explore the changing meaning of money. Martin Fischer joined the Prague art collective Ztohoven in 2003, a group known for inserting a fictional nuclear explosion into a live Czech Television broadcast. In 2014, the collective opened Paralelní Polis, a hackerspace whose café accepted only bitcoin, and Fischer designed its logo. As he told Bitcoin Magazine’s Aaron van Wirdum in 2020, the arrival of a screen-printing press the following year prompted him to produce his first prints. Since 2020, he has worked under the name Cypherpunk Now, developing a visual record of bitcoin’s evolving culture. RYR and ZETRA both emerged from Germany’s graffiti scene but approach money from different directions. RYR uses currency itself as material, making paper from shredded banknotes, pigment from their ashes, and concrete grenades filled with shredded cash that he calls “artifacts from the future.” ZETRA, who began painting in the early 1990s and discovered bitcoin in 2017, examines what money can buy. His TOMATOSOUP paintings revisit Andy Warhol’s iconic Campbell’s Soup Cans to chart changing prices in dollars and bitcoin, while THE BIP39 SERIES explores the 2,048 words used in bitcoin wallet recovery phrases, including 1206/NOTE , a collaboration with Polymerbit. Bitcoin has shaped these artists’ practices, their livelihoods, and the communities around them. Its growing acceptance by banks, investment funds, and corporations has also prompted some difficult questions about the movement’s original ideals and where its culture is heading. From left: RYR, Cypherpunk Now, ZETRA BMAG: Andy Warhol turned Campbell’s soup into an icon of consumer culture, taking an ordinary commodity and elevating it into fine art. Your TOMATOSOUP series returns to that image but introduces something Warhol largely left outside the frame: the changing value of money itself. How did the idea of reworking Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans first come about, and do viewers immediately recognize the commentary on inflation? ZETRA: We frequently see iPhones and houses in our bitcoin Twitter timelines, showing how they become cheaper in BTC terms. I thought it would be fun to take something from art history instead, something more visually appealing, like Warhol’s iconic Campbell’s Soup Can. For my TOMATOSOUP painting, I used real stickers placed on the can to show how the price of soup has increased in USD over the past decades, compared with the lower prices we might expect in BTC terms in the decades to come. Bitcoiners looking at TOMATOSOUP generally understand it immediately. They know they’re in a better position as the purchasing power of fiat money continues to decline through inflation. Other viewers usually need a bit of explanation, and I’m always happy to help them understand. TOMATOSOUP series at Bitcoin Asia, ZETRA (2025) BMAG: In THE BIP39 SERIES, you draw from the 2,048 words used to generate bitcoin wallet recovery phrases, turning ordinary words into artworks with a deeper significance for bitcoin holders. Can you unpack the different layers of inspiration behind the series and what they reveal about bitcoin, language, and the ownership of money for someone unfamiliar with these concepts? ZETRA: Everyone who moves their precious sats into cold storage encounters 12 or 24 of these significant words, often early in their journey as a bitcoin newcomer. As mentioned, there are 2,048 words in a carefully curated list representing the power of self-custody. I started going through the words one by one, imagining how each could be visualized in a physical form: the key visual for the word, its corresponding number, the style, and the medium I would choose. There are millions of possibilities for bringing these words to life through bitcoin art. 1044/LIST was the obvious choice to kick off THE BIP39 SERIES. Naturally, it features all 2,048 words presented as a list. As an ’80s kid, I had to choose 1638/SMILE as the second piece: a proper yellow smiley face, with the number 1638 in place of the eyes. It’s a fine art print on Alu-Dibond beneath a 6 mm acrylic glass cover. So clean. Another work in the series is 0388/CORN , an obvious homage to Warhol once again. THE BIP39 SERIES will be an ongoing project for many years to come. 1206/NOTE (THE BIP39 SERIES with Polymerbit), ZETRA (2026) BMAG: You shred banknotes into paper and burn them to produce pigment. Artists have long manipulated currency to question where its value resides, but your work goes a step further by making destruction part of the creative process. Is there a contradiction in destroying money to create an artwork that may ultimately be worth much more? RYR: Money is essentially a narrative system built on collective belief and obedience. It has worked for hundreds of years because we collectively agree on the story it tells and the value it represents. I’ve always been fascinated by that idea, particularly how something as ordinary as a banknote can carry so much meaning, authority, and perceived value. I was looking for a different way to tell that story, both conceptually and physically. Back in 2017, I had an exhibition title in mind: To Cut a Long Story Short . I liked the cheekiness of it, especially in relation to money and the stories we attach to it. Shredding banknotes became a very literal interpretation of that title, but it also opened up an entirely new artistic medium for me. Ultimately, I’m not simply destroying money. I’m taking an existing story, cutting it into pieces, and using those pieces to tell a new one. Satoshi Nakamoto, RYR (n.d.) BMAG: Your concrete weapons are presented as relics from a future in which the fiat wars have already ended. Yet bitcoin is increasingly held through the very financial institutions it was designed to circumvent. Is that a victory for the movement, or have the institutions simply absorbed the alternative? RYR: I think that’s precisely what makes the story so interesting. When I created the concrete weapons, I imagined a future in which the traditional financial system had already fought its battle for survival. The weapons had become fossils, archaeological artifacts from a monetary conflict that future generations might struggle to understand. My concrete weapons represent a future in which that battle is already history. Whether bitcoin ultimately wins or becomes part of the very system it challenged remains to be seen. Desert Eagle at Bitcoin Conference Miami, RYR (2023) BMAG: Much of your work is made from the physical remains of money, at a time when currency is becoming increasingly digital and invisible. Do you think people are losing something in their understanding of money as it disappears from everyday physical experience? RYR: I think we’re losing a physical connection to money, but not necessarily our understanding of it. Money has always been a narrative built on collective trust, whether printed on paper or represented by numbers on a screen. What fascinates me is how something as abstract as value can be represented by a physical object. I don’t necessarily believe that art has to be authentic or entirely original. Almost everything has been done before. To me, art is a wonderfully human, almost plebeian way of expressing an opinion and giving ideas a physical voice. Bitcoin will likely evolve into a much broader and increasingly regulated financial asset, but I hope its grassroots culture and artistic identity remain visible. That’s something my fellow artists and I will continue to contribute to, preserving the spirit of a movement that was cultural long before it became institutional. Bitcoin Amsterdam, Cypherpunk Now (2025) BMAG: Paralelní Polis wasn’t just a place to discuss alternative monetary systems or a hacker meetup; its café was one of the first to adopt bitcoin as money. What were the early years of Paralelní Polis like, and what has your own experience been selling artwork for bitcoin? Martin Fischer: Paralelní Polis was founded in 2014, during a bear market. The funny thing is, none of us who founded it even knew what a bear market was. We didn’t think of bitcoin as something that could make us rich. We saw it as uncensorable money and understood the changes it could bring to society. There was no speculation involved, and that’s what made those early days so great. I sold my first screenprint for bitcoin in 2017, almost ten years ago, and many more since then. But practically every sale was a matter of survival. I spent most of the bitcoin I earned financing my next projects and continuing to make art. I never managed to accumulate much bitcoin, but looking back, it gave me something far more valuable than investment returns: the freedom to remain an independent artist. HODL series (Peace, Resistance, Pain), Cypherpunk Now ( 2024) BMAG: Political printmaking has a long history in Europe, from Amsterdam’s financial satires of 1720 to twentieth-century protest posters. Your work emerged from Ztohoven, a collective that famously hacked a live television broadcast to show a fictional nuclear explosion—an audacious intervention, even by today’s standards. Ztohoven challenged institutions through disruption, while bitcoin uses game theory and economic incentives to create an alternative. Do you see bitcoin as a continuation of that same spirit of intervention, and your prints as an extension of it? Martin Fischer: I think there’s a connection, but I wouldn’t say it’s exactly the same thing. With Ztohoven, we used art to question authority, challenge institutions, and expose how easily reality can be manipulated. Bitcoin doesn’t need to make a statement or provoke anyone. It simply offers an alternative that works without asking anyone for permission. That’s a much more interesting form of disruption to me. But today, bitcoin has become so corporate and so intertwined with traditional banking that it’s hard to still see it as an anti-establishment movement. I don’t see this as a betrayal of its original ideals, but rather as a natural consequence of its success. That doesn’t mean I like where things are going. What’s strange is that bitcoin’s fundamental principles haven’t really changed, but the way people perceive and use it certainly has. And my screenprints? I still work with the original idea of separating money from the state while exploring the myths, memes, and legends of the bitcoin age. That’s what I enjoy most. Out of Order, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, Bitcoin Is Energy, Cypherpunk Now (2023) BMAG: Your Amsterdam presentation brings together more than a decade of work documenting bitcoin’s evolution from an underground movement to an increasingly institutionalized financial system. Looking across those prints today, has the movement changed more than you expected, or has your own perspective changed? Which of your prints are your favorites? Martin Fischer: I like remembering the old days, when we were all part of the same tribe and our main enemy was Faketoshi. Today? We have culture wars over JPEGs, Ordinals, BIPs, OP_RETURN, over what’s spam and what should or shouldn’t belong on bitcoin. What makes me saddest is that people who once fought together against censorship and for freedom now spend enormous amounts of energy fighting each other over what others should or shouldn’t be allowed to do with bitcoin. Maybe it’s a natural consequence of bitcoin’s success. The bitcoin community has changed enormously, and so has my perspective on it. I’m definitely much more skeptical today of the idea that technology alone can automatically change society for the better. As for my favorite works, Bitcoin Meteorite is definitely one of them. In this piece, I reworked the meme of banking dinosaurs watching their own extinction, incorporating the abstract from the Bitcoin white paper. It gave me my fifteen minutes of fame when Max Keiser and Stacy Herbert brought it into the spotlight. Cypherpunks of the World, Cypherpunk Now (2021) Then there’s Cypherpunks of the World . This project is important to me not only as a celebration of the cypherpunks and their legacy, but also because of its complexity. It started as a series of original collages, continued through handmade screenprints, and eventually evolved into animated NFTs and a virtual gallery. It’s one of my most elaborate projects, connecting different techniques and media while staying true to the original idea. Among my more recent works, I really like Out of Order from 2023. It’s an incredibly detailed screenprint, and the first one where I finally managed to make absolutely no printing mistakes. That alone makes it special to me. I also love St. Satosius Contra Draconem (2025), which is inspired by the classic depiction of Saint George fighting the dragon, reimagined through bitcoin mythology. Lazar Eyes, Cypherpunk Now (2022) Works by ZETRA, RYR, and Cypherpunk Now, alongside other European artists, will be presented at Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 4–6, 2026, as part of the Bitcoin Museum & Art Gallery (BMAG) programming. Additional artworks and editions will be available through https://shop.museum.b.tc . Explore more work by the featured artists at ZETRA , RYR , Cypherpunk Now , and www.martin-fischer.cz . The Bitcoin Museum & Art Gallery (BMAG) organizes international exhibitions, auctions, and artist collaborations exploring bitcoin and its cultural implications. Learn more at museum.b.tc . Join us at Bitcoin Amsterdam, Get your tickets here and use code BA26-BMAG20 for discounted admission. This post The Undercurrent: Three European Artists on Making Money Visible first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Dennis Koch .

title: Government working to address economic challenges driving youth into galamsey – Mahama
body: President John Mahama says the government is working to address the economic challenges driving young people into illegal mining, as part of efforts to provide alternative livelihoods and curb the menace. He says the implementation of the New Economy Agenda by his government, which seeks to invest in job-rich sectors of the economy, is expected to create opportunities for young people who might otherwise turn to illegal mining,galamsey. Speaking during a courtesy visit by the Western North Regional House of Chiefs at the Jubilee House, President Mahama said the government is aware of the economic circumstances pushing some young people into the activity and believes that creating alternative sources of income must complement law enforcement. “Often, when enforcing the fight against galamsey, we find even Senior High School students in illegal mining pits,” he said. “When you ask them why they are there, they say their fathers could not give them money to go to school, so they have come to work and earn some money. It is a major issue we need to confront.” He said that the government’s enforcement efforts have resulted in the arrest of several young people, with hundreds awaiting trial and others on bail while their cases remained pending. President Mahama stressed that the government must address the circumstances that lead young people into galamsey while ensuring that the law is enforced. “The question we must ask is, what alternative do we have for them? Alongside enforcing the law against illegal mining, we must provide alternative livelihoods. That is why we are implementing the New Economy Policy,” he said. He expressed confidence that investment in sectors capable of generating significant employment would help reduce the attraction of illegal mining. “I believe that if we invest US$10 billion in job-rich sectors of the economy, including tourism, one of the nine pillars, it should provide alternative livelihoods for our young people and discourage them from going into galamsey,” he said. The Government’s New Economy Policy is a planned US$10 billion investment programme aimed at moving Ghana from economic stabilisation to job creation, wealth generation and sustained economic growth. The idea is to channel investment into productive sectors that can expand businesses, increase local production and create employment, particularly for young people. The President also called on traditional authorities to support the fight against illegal mining, particularly in forest reserves and water bodies. He said the National Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Illegal Mining (NAIMOS) has made efforts to tackle the menace, but some communities continued to resist the task force. “The National Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Illegal Mining (NAIMOS) is doing a good job, but in some communities, sometimes the youth, traditional authorities and others fight back against the task force,” he said. He further disclosed that the Minister of Finance has provided an additional GH¢400 million in the 2027 Budget to recruit more Blue Water Guards to patrol water bodies. On efforts to protect forest reserves, he said the government has cleared all nine reserves previously classified as red zones because of extensive destruction and the danger posed by heavily armed illegal miners. He said soldiers have been deployed to clear the affected areas and will remain stationed there to prevent illegal miners from returning. The President also disclosed that the Goldbod has started working with the military to replant destroyed forests and reclaim degraded land. Under the programme, bulldozers will be used to level the land for the planting of economic trees, while the Forestry Commission would support the reclamation exercise.

title: Domestic Capital Africa campaign targets US$600bn pension funds for SME growth
body: Africa’s more than US$600 billion in pension assets could play a greater role in financing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), infrastructure, and climate solutions if investors, regulators, and policymakers address the structural barriers limiting domestic investment. Stakeholders made the call at the official launch of the Domestic Capital Africa (DCA) campaign, organized by Impact Investing Ghana (IIGh), the Africa Impact Investing Group (AIIG), Ghana Venture Capital and Private Equity Association GVCA, the Growth Firms Alliance (GFA) and regional partners on October 8, 2026. Held under the theme “ Mobilizing African Capital for Africa’s Prosperity ,” the webinar brought together pension trustees, asset managers, impact investment advisers and regulators to explore ways of directing more African savings towards productive investments on the continent. The campaign seeks to address the disconnect between the growing pools of institutional capital available in Africa and the financing needs of businesses, particularly SMEs, which continue to face limited access to long-term, appropriately structured funding. The Board Chair of Impact Investing Ghana, Kwabena Boamah, said the initiative offered an opportunity to bring together stakeholders to develop practical solutions for financing Africa’s development with its own resources. “Across our continent, institutional investors manage growing pools of capital. The opportunity before us today is to harness more of these resources to finance African businesses, infrastructure, innovation, climate solutions and sustainable development,” he said. Mr Boamah said the campaign was more than a launch, describing it as a call to action for asset owners, fund managers, entrepreneurs, policymakers, regulators, and development partners to work towards a common goal. Closing Africa’s SME financing gap The campaign comes against the backdrop of a significant financing gap facing African businesses despite the substantial resources held by the continent’s institutional investors. Data presented at the launch indicate that SMEs account for 92 per cent of enterprises in Africa, employ 80 percent of the workforce and generate 70 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP). Yet these businesses face an estimated US$331 billion financing gap, with many unable to access the patient capital needed to expand operations, invest in technology and create jobs. At the same time, African pension funds hold more than US$600 billion in assets, while Ghana’spension assets are estimated at about US$7 billion. Less than one percent of Ghana’s pension assets is invested in alternative assets, according to the presentation. Stakeholders believe that mobilizing even a greater share of these funds into carefully structured investments could help bridge the financing gap while supporting long-term economic growth. Esther Ndeti, Vice Chair of the Africa Impact Investing Group, said the challenge was to create the market infrastructure, investment vehicles, policy alignment, and trust required to connect available capital with businesses and development priorities. “Domestic capital mobilization cannot be solved by any single institution. It requires collaboration among different partners and learning from the experiences of different African markets,” she said. Amma Lartey of Impact Investing Ghana also highlighted the importance of mobilizing domestic capital to support African businesses and development priorities. Her contribution aligns with the campaign’s objective of connecting institutional investors with investment-ready enterprises, particularly SMEs, to expand access to long-term financing, create jobs and promote sustainable economic growth. The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Venture Capital and Private Equity Association (GVCA), Amma Gyampo, said Africa needed to move beyond the aggregation of capital towards addressing the underlying risks that discouraged institutional investors from financing businesses. She noted that the continent’s development challenges, including limited economic opportunities for young people, required a more deliberate approach to deploying domestic savings. “We cannot solve some of these structural issues and crises within our borders by parking the vast majority of our retirement savings in sovereign paper. We need to evolve,” she said. Ms Gyampo said recent developments, including the launch of the Ci Gaba Fund of Funds, had demonstrated that domestic institutional capital could be successfully aggregated to support businesses. However, she said the next phase of the effort must focus on developing risk-sharing arrangements and investment structures that meet the requirements of pension trustees and other institutional investors. “We are ready to invest. They keep telling us this, but they also tell us that they need to see the risk structures and the deals they can actually back,” she said. Ci Gaba offers a model for replication A key example highlighted at the launch was the Ci GabaFund of Funds, a US$75 million blended-finance initiative designed to mobilize Ghanaian pension capital into SMEs. The initiative was presented as the first pension-backed fund of funds in West Africa and a potential model for other African markets seeking to channel domestic institutional savings into businesses. Its target investment areas include agribusiness, healthcare, education, clean energy, financial technology, and enterprises led by women and young people. The Chief Executive Officer of Ci Gaba Venture Capital Limited and founder and CEO of Savannah Impact Advisory, Hamdiya Ismaila, who manages the Ci Gaba Fund of Funds, said collaboration had been central to the initiative’s development. She stressed that fund managers must begin by understanding the market’s needs rather than designing investment vehicles before identifying the problems they are intended to solve. “Collaboration is very important, but you also have to start with validated market needs, not a predetermined fund vehicle,” she said. Ms Ismaila explained that listening to pension funds and understanding their requirements had informed the design of the Ci Gaba model. “When you understand the market and validate its needs, you can develop a structure that is fit for purpose,” she said. She added that investor confidence would depend on demonstrating the ability to manage investments effectively and generate returns. “Pension money is not charity. It has to be returned, and it has to be returned in style,” she said. Stakeholders called for regulatory flexibility, technical support, catalytic funding and stronger investor coordination to mobilize domestic capital. They said lessons from the CiGaba Fund could guide similar initiatives across Africa, helping channel pension savings into businesses, job creation and sustainable economic growth while protecting investors’ returns. The DCA campaign builds on the pioneering work of Impact Investing Ghana and the Ghana Venture Capital and Private Equity Association (GVCA), which showcased insights from Ghana’s private capital and impact investment ecosystems at the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year.

title: 2027: Nigerians won’t renew a mandate of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu
body: Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has described the APC’s revised Presidential Campaign Council as “a crowded confession of Tinubu’s fear”, saying Nigerians will not renew “a mandate of hardship”. He said the length of the list revealed a President more eager to count politicians than answer for what Nigerians have endured. “Only a man afraid of his record would think he could bury it under hundreds of names. Tinubu can gather every governor, minister and political defector in Nigeria. None of them can erase the hunger in people’s homes, bring back those killed by violence or free Nigerians still held captive. Their families are waiting for answers, not another campaign list.” In a statement issued by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said: “Tinubu has room for an army of ministers and a stadium full of campaign officials, but no room in his plans for Nigerians crushed by the cost of living. He feeds his political machine and tells hungry families to sacrifice. He may surround himself with elite friends and fill his campaign schedule with endorsements, but the list of Nigerians determined to vote against him is much longer. On January 16, Nigerians will answer with one question: Are we better off under Bola Tinubu?” Atiku said Tinubu’s campaign council exposed the same appetite for political excess that produced one of Nigeria’s largest federal cabinets. He also condemned the decision to inaugurate the APC Presidential Campaign Council inside Aso Rock Villa. “The Presidential Villa belongs to the Nigerian people. It is not a campaign venue or the private property of any political party. Using it for an APC political event is a gross breach of public trust and a troubling abuse of public office. “Abuja has no shortage of halls and public spaces large enough to host a campaign gathering. Why, then, did Bola Tinubu choose to inaugurate his campaign council at night, behind the gates of the Presidential Villa? “Nigerians may draw their own conclusions. But a president confident in his record should be willing to face the public in daylight and ask for another mandate. Tinubu cannot expect Nigerians to renew a mandate built on a promise of renewed hope when, for millions, that promise has given way to hardship and disappointment. “For the political class, there is always another seat. For Nigerians struggling to survive, there is always another sermon about sacrifice. Tinubu’s government grows more comfortable while the people it governs grow poorer. “When the first list drew criticism, Tinubu had a chance to show that he understood the country’s anger. Instead, he returned with an even longer list, reaching into other parties for more names. He is collecting politicians like shields against public judgment. Let him collect them all. Not one of them can cast a vote for the mother who can no longer feed her children or the family still waiting for a loved one taken by kidnappers. “The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index recorded an increase of 17.9 million Nigerians living in multidimensional poverty. Three and a half years of Tinubu’s leadership have left millions in deeper hardship and thousands more traumatised by insecurity. Tinubu can write all the names he likes on his campaign list; his record has given millions of Nigerians a reason to vote against him. They are the automatic volunteer wing of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council. “He may have assembled an army of politicians, but the list of Nigerians determined to reject his re-election is much longer. No campaign council, however crowded, can make food affordable, restore a worker’s purchasing power or explain why the sacrifices demanded of ordinary Nigerians never seem to reach Tinubu’s own political circle. “The ADC has assembled a focused campaign team to take its case to Nigerians. Tinubu can keep adding names to his council. He cannot add a name that will make life affordable again for the families struggling under his government. “On January 16, the ballot will contain no column for the size of a campaign council. Nigerians will judge Tinubu by the lives they have lived under his government: the mother who cannot afford enough food for her children, the worker who spends most of his wages getting to work, the parents who cannot pay school fees, and the families afraid that loved ones may not return safely from a journey. “Families face hunger, hardship and fear every day. No crowd of politicians can stand between a President and his abysmal record. Tinubu can surround himself with every political heavyweight in Nigeria; on election day, he will still face the people who lived through his failures and their list is much longer.”

title: HMCS St. John’s Completes Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR 26-2
body: His Majesty’s Canadian Ship (HMCS) St. John’s concluded participation in Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR 26-2 in Scotland and the North Atlantic approaches, strengthening Allied warfighting readiness, interoperability, and collective defence. The Royal Canadian Navy (RCN) ship operated with maritime, air and land forces during the United Kingdom (UK)-led multinational exercise, training in a complex multi-domain environment. Throughout the exercise, HMCS St. John’s operated alongside Allied naval forces as part of a multinational maritime task group. The ship contributed to anti-submarine warfare training, maritime security operations, air-maritime integration activities, warfighting scenarios, and command-and-control exercises. The participation of HMCS St. John’s demonstrates Canada’s enduring commitment to collective security and interoperability with Allied navies while maintaining combat-ready maritime forces capable of operating effectively alongside Allies and partners anywhere in the world. “Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR demonstrated the strength of the collective approach to security. By training alongside Allies and partners in a demanding multinational environment, Canada reinforces its commitment to collective defence, contributes to regional stability, and ensures our forces remain ready to respond alongside like-minded nations wherever required.” Rear-Admiral Pascal Belhumeur, Commander, Maritime Forces Atlantic and Joint Task Force Atlantic “Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR tested our ship’s company in a demanding, realistic environment and demonstrated what can be achieved when Allied forces operate as one team. HMCS St. John’s leaves this exercise sharper, more integrated, and ready to contribute wherever Canada and our Allies need us.” Commander Kyle Aubrey, Commanding Officer, HMCS St. John’s ADDITIONAL INFO Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR 26-2 brought together personnel and capabilities from Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, and the United Kingdom to enhance multinational cooperation and prepare forces for realistic, high-end warfighting operations. Canadian participation included operations alongside surface ships, submarines, maritime patrol aircraft, and amphibious forces, reflecting the RCN’s ability to contribute across the full spectrum of modern maritime operations. The HMCS St. John’s completed Intermediate Multi-Ship Readiness Training (IMSRT) on conclusion of Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR 26-2, which is the final all-ship readiness training to complete prior to deploying as the flagship of Standing NATO Maritime Group 2 (SNMG2) under Operation REASSURANCE in 2027. The post HMCS St. John’s Completes Exercise STRIKE WARRIOR 26-2 appeared first on Canadian Defence Review .

title: Azerbaijani government websites hit by cyberattack allegedly originating in Turkey
body: Cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites More than 100 government domains in Azerbaijan were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted access to several government agencies’ websites. According to the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security, the attacks began at around 22:00 Baku time on 13 October. The agency said a foreign hacking group was behind them. The agency said technical measures had helped limit the impact of the cyberattack and keep the websites running reliably. However, it has not disclosed detailed information about how the attack was carried out, who organised it or what motivated it. As Meydan TV reports , one theory under discussion is that the cyberattack may have links to Turkey . The incident has prompted debate about the resilience of the country’s digital government infrastructure and the possible political motives behind the attack. Available information confirms that the websites experienced disruptions, but it is not yet possible to assess the full scale of the cyberattack or its consequences. Clarify the agency’s responseTighten the final paragraphUse more cautious attribution Expert: Russia may be behind attack on Delta Telekom in Azerbaijan The expert says Russia often uses cyberattacks as a tool in its dealings with other states Which websites were targeted? According to initial reports in local media, users experienced access problems with the websites of the Cabinet of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Health and the State Examination Centre. An official statement confirming a cyberattack followed simultaneous disruptions affecting several government websites. According to official figures, the attack targeted more than 100 domains. However, this does not mean that the attackers managed to disrupt all these websites or gain unauthorised access to their systems. The number of resources targeted must be distinguished from the number of systems that actually suffered damage. The official statement does not specify which websites became unavailable or how long the disruptions lasted. It is also unclear whether the outages affected only information pages or disrupted electronic services as well. The State Service for Special Communications and Information Security says it is continuing its cybersecurity measures. The nature of the cyberattack remains unclear Disrupting a website and gaining unauthorised access to its database are two different types of cybersecurity incident. In the first case, users lose access to the resource. In the second, the confidentiality and integrity of data may be at risk. One common method of disrupting websites is a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. This involves sending a large volume of requests to a server simultaneously from different sources. The resulting traffic overloads the servers or network infrastructure, leaving legitimate users’ requests unanswered. Such an attack can disrupt a website without anyone gaining unauthorised access to its database. There is no official confirmation that the latest cyberattack in Azerbaijan used this particular method. Authorities have also published no findings from checks for possible data leaks. The available information therefore does not establish either that personal data belonging to citizens were stolen or that the authorities have fully resolved all the consequences of the attack. The restoration of websites indicates that users have regained access to them. However, determining whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to the systems or whether any data leaked requires a separate technical investigation. Phishing attack by cyber fraudsters posing as members of Armenia’s ruling party Civil society representatives receive emails posing as messages from the Civil Contract party. Experts say the goal is to obtain confidential information. Possible motives and speculation about links to Turkey Cyberattacks on government websites may aim not only to disrupt online services but also to express political views, attract public attention or undermine trust in state institutions. In its report on denial-of-service attacks, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) lists political and ideological objectives, as well as financial interests, among the possible motives behind such attacks. The specific motives behind the latest cyberattack on Azerbaijani government websites remain unknown. The fact that the incident occurred amid political tensions has prompted speculation about a possible link between the events. However, further evidence is needed to substantiate such claims. According to Meydan TV, social media users are discussing a possible link between the cyberattack and Turkey. The outlet examines this speculation against the backdrop of protests by members of some religiously conservative groups in Turkey against restrictions on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools, as well as Baku’s relations with Israel. Protesters gathered outside the Azerbaijani embassy in Ankara and the country’s consulate general in Istanbul. However, no evidence has established a link between the cyberattack and these protests or any groups in Turkey. The Azerbaijani authorities have also refrained from naming specific countries or organisations in their official statement. The phrase “foreign hacking group” used in the official statement does not, in itself, indicate that any foreign state was involved. Identifying those who organised and carried out the attack, establishing their motives and determining whether they have links to state institutions will require a separate investigation. Warning about cyber threats issued five days before the attack On 8 October, five days before the cyberattack, Azerbaijan’s Electronic Security Service published a warning about active cyber threats targeting several information systems. The statement noted that some attacks involved outdated database management software and default login credentials that administrators had failed to change. The warning also said that attackers who gained access to inadequately protected systems could use them to launch attacks against other resources. The service advised administrators to update their software, change default passwords, restrict access to systems and monitor suspicious activity. The service did not report any possible connection between this warning and the cyberattack that began on 13 October. There is currently no evidence to suggest that the two incidents formed part of the same operation. Nevertheless, the warning highlights that cybersecurity depends not only on responding to attacks but also on regularly updating software and controlling access to systems. Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev's statement As always on Thursdays, Armenia’s prime minister answered journalists’ questions for exactly one hour. Questions left unanswered after services were restored One of the key criteria for assessing the impact of a cyberattack is the extent to which it disrupts government electronic services. The temporary unavailability of an informational website can have very different consequences for users from disruptions to systems for submitting documents, registering applications and processing requests. No specific data has yet been published on whether the latest cyberattack interrupted users’ transactions, caused people to miss deadlines for submitting documents or applications, or resulted in data loss. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the actual damage caused by the incident based solely on the number of domains targeted. Future official statements will be particularly important in clarifying which services were affected, whether the attackers gained unauthorised access to internal systems, and what the security checks found regarding personal data. The restoration of the websites demonstrates that the authorities have taken steps to respond to the cyberattack. However, a fuller assessment of how resilient the country’s digital government infrastructure proved to be against such threats will only be possible once more detailed information becomes available. title: Dublin hotel cancels 70 rooms booked for antisemitism conference delegates
body: The Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin canceled a reservation for 70 rooms intended for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after learning the purpose of their visit, according to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.In his speech at the opening event at the Irish Foreign Ministry – sent to The Jerusalem Post – Cohen recalled meeting with hotel management after the booking was completed, and being questioned about whether the gathering was connected to the Israel Defense Forces.Cohen also remembered the manager's demeanor changing and becoming tense after he mentioned that the delegates would be Jewish leaders.“There is an uncomfortable irony in organizing an international conference to discuss antisemitism and finding that, before the conference has even begun, you have already encountered something that forces you to ask exactly the questions the conference was created to address,” he said.“How quickly does the word 'Jewish' change a conversation? How easily does a gathering about antisemitism become associated with the Israeli army?”He noted that the question about the IDF was not an innocent misunderstanding, as it instead “revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel, how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion, and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination because contemporary antisemitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past.“It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat, or a placard. Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification. It begins by treating Jewish identity as evidence of political allegiance,” he said.Resetting the conversation between Jewish groups and governmentsThe European Jewish Congress called the incident “deeply disturbing.”“That a hotel would cancel accommodation for participants in a conference dedicated to combating antisemitism, while raising questions about supposed links to the Israeli military, reflects precisely the kind of prejudice and suspicion that such gatherings seek to confront,” the EJC noted.“It is profoundly troubling that those working to combat antisemitism should themselves encounter such treatment. Jewish organizations and those standing against hatred must never face exclusion or discrimination because of their work,”Israel's Foreign Ministry said. “The Irish government cannot use the fight against antisemitism as a diplomatic PR exercise while failing to confront it at home.”The conference in question was the 15th meeting of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum, organized by the World Jewish Congress in partnership with the European Commission, and convened as an Associated Event under Ireland's rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.Jewish community leaders from across the world joined government envoys, representatives from international organizations, and technology company executives in Dublin from October 12 to 14.Leaders representing the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism – connecting the Delegación de Asociaciones Israelitas Argentinas, Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Canada's Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Board of Deputies of British Jews, alongside the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations from the United States – also joined the forum following a series of high-level meetings in London earlier in the week.Statements, condemnations only go so farThe gathering included a meeting with Ireland's Taoiseach or government leader, Micheál Martin; visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta; and other discussions.“Our meeting in Dublin is a much-needed opportunity to reset the conversation between Jewish organizations, governments, and technology companies,” Maram Stern, WJC executive vice president, said. “Statements and condemnation of antisemitism only go so far. Practical solutions must urgently be put in place to protect Jewish life globally.”The delegates were officially welcomed by Irish ministers despite the current Ireland-Israel tensions.At the start of Tuesday's agenda, Colm Brophy, a member of the Irish parliament, said he was “very pleased to welcome Jewish community leaders” and was particularly happy to see that the event has a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms, given the “troubling increase in antisemitism and other forms of racism online in recent years.”The incident comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ireland and Israel, with Jerusalem accusing Dublin of fostering an increasingly hostile environment toward the Jewish state.Tensions have escalated following Ireland's recognition of a Palestinian state, its legal and diplomatic moves against Israel, and controversy over Dublin City Council's proposal to remove the name of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog from Herzog Park in Rathgar and replace it with “Free Palestine Park.”The attempt was eventually condemned by Irish officials, and the J7 representatives visited the park for a photo-op this week during the conference.

title: 100-year-old Yakasai wishes Tinubu success in 2027 election
body: Sekinat Osundiji Elder statesman Alhaji Tanko Yakasai has wished President Bola Tinubu success in the 2027 presidential election. Yakasai, who said he was born in 1925, spoke on Wednesday at the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council inauguration in Abuja. The elder statesman expressed gratitude to Tinubu and the party leadership for inviting him to the gathering, describing his attendance as an opportunity to reconnect with old friends and political associates. “I would also like to convey my best wishes to Mr President, President Ahmed Bola Tinubu, and wish him success in the coming election,” he said. Yakasai thanked God for keeping him alive to this day and thanked the president for giving him the opportunity to address the gathering. He also thanked the APC leadership for recognising him and inviting him to participate in the event. “I know that at the moment, being born in 1925, I don’t have anybody that I can call my age-mate among you here,” he said. The elder statesman concluded his remarks by wishing the gathering well and praying for God’s blessings. Also speaking at the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council in Abuja on Wednesday, Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke said he could already feel victory coming for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 election and declared himself ready to lead the campaign movement. Adeleke, who recently aligned with the APC, said no one could stop the movement and promised that Tinubu’s supporters would celebrate their way back to Aso Rock. Known for his dancing at public events, he said the campaign would be marked by singing and dancing. He urged Nigerians to give the president more time for his reforms to work, admitting that the policies have not been easy. He said he was joining the campaign because he wants action, not too much talk and added that he has already begun work on his end. The post 100-year-old Yakasai wishes Tinubu success in 2027 election appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Prismm helps banks keep inherited money in-house
body:
Meet Prismm , a startup that helps banks keep families’ money in-house after an account holder dies. It does this by building beneficiary and estate planning into accounts from day one, which makes the transfer of assets to heirs less complicated. Prismm is presenting its mission today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 .
Prismm was founded in 2020 by sisters Martha Underwood and Shella Sylla, who each have decades of experience in banking and finance. The pair came up with the idea for Prismm based on their own experience of seeing firsthand how difficult it can be to manage a family’s affairs in an emergency.
Their father was hospitalized in 2017 after he fell while helping clear a tree from a neighbor’s roof following Hurricane Irma in Miami. Their mother, who had always relied on him to handle the family’s finances and paperwork, didn’t know where all the important documents and financial information were, and neither did they. Their father recovered, but the experience of not knowing how to access critical information stuck with them.
That was the starting point for Prismm, but the idea really took shape three years later, when Underwood was working at a bank during the COVID-19 pandemic. She saw families come in after a loved one had died, scrambling to find accounts, understand bills, and figure out how to support the surviving spouse.
“That’s when it hit us that this is an infrastructure problem, and as I started to dig deeper, we’ve created all of these platforms for wealth growth and tracking, but almost nothing for transition,” Underwood said in an interview with TechCrunch. “It’s still very much all manual. And that’s when we said, ‘We can digitize this process.’ We were like, ‘We can solve it because we see that there’s other families that are going to have this issue,’ and that’s when we really doubled down.”
With Prismm, account holders can give designated family members access to their accounts and documents ahead of time. When the account holder dies, the designated person can log in, see the assets and documents in one place, and start eligible beneficiary transfers digitally. Because identity, consent, and supporting documents are all already on file, the process can be completed remotely, even when family members live in different states.
“What’s on the market is consumer-based,” Underwood said. “What we found is when you’re asking the consumer to do something with everything else on their list, that’s going to be the last thing they do, especially women. Women are the ones that are typically going to be handling these issues when there’s a death. We’re typically the caregivers, and so asking me to manage the documents for my mom and dad while I take care of my kids, my husband, everyone else, it just becomes too much. And so, this needs to be built as infrastructure, and there needs to be as little friction as possible to allow people to get to the information that they need to execute on a decision, and so that’s why we integrate directly into bank cores.”
The company has two central products, with a third in development. The first, Prismm Designate, lets banks offer customers a simple, digital way to update their own beneficiaries. The goal is to make keeping beneficiaries up to date faster and easier for both customers and banks.
The second, Prismm Anchor, gives account holders a secure place to keep track of their accounts, documents, property, and other assets across multiple institutions, with controlled access for designated people. It’s offered through financial institutions, so users can manage everything without needing a separate consumer app.
The third product, Prismm Continuity, is coming soon. It will guide staff and families through the transfer process step by step. The startup says this will keep the hardest part of the process within the institution rather than putting the burden on families.
Underwood and Sylla describe Prismm as infrastructure that helps banks handle what happens when a customer dies. They say financial institutions lose billions in deposits to “estate attrition” every year, which is when heirs move inherited money to other institutions, because banks have no system for managing the transition of accounts after a death. Instead of losing those accounts, banks can use beneficiary information and simpler inheritance processes to keep assets, and potentially the next generation of customers, within their institution.
“We will be the infrastructure that financial institutions use to move money to the next generation, because we don’t only understand that you execute on the back end,” Underwood said. “We understand that you need to be proactive and build relationships with the next generation of consumers on the front end.”
Check out Prismm and the dozens of other startups and investors who are gathered in San Francisco this week for TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield competition ; the lucky winner will be announced on Thursday, October 15.

title: US Army taps 9 companies to build next-gen command and control software
body: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software. The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software. “While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig. Gen. Shane Taylor, portfolio management executive for the Command and Control Information Network. The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield. The chosen companies include General Dynamics Mission Systems, Air Space Intelligence Federal, Immersive Wisdom, LMI, Mente Systems, Stilman Advanced Strategies, Onebrief, Rune Technologies and AIR. The applications will be hosted on the common data baseline, or software foundation, that Anduril Industries, Palantir, Raft and Striveworks have built in collaboration with the Army. The NGC2 system, in conjunction with the applications the companies build for it, will allow information sharing that streamlines mission completion across the Army’s six warfighting functions of command and control, fires, intelligence, movement and maneuver, sustainment and protection, the service said. The Army is currently in the process of delivering the NGC2 software to the I Corps, which commands service members in the Indo-Pacific. The move will further test NGC2 software’s ability to host technologies and devices separated by thousands of miles, some in communication-contested environments. The Army has spent the last year moving from the experimental phase to the fielding phase of NGC2, going from prototype development to placing software in the hands of soldiers at the 4th and 25th Infantry Divisions. In July 2026, the Army hosted a 10-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6, that asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2. The service conducted a joint force exercise shortly after in May at Fort Irwin that marked the end of the NGC2 prototype phase and came away stating that the new platform was ready to be scaled up. The Army awarded Anduril Industries a $162.8 million contract on Sept. 30 worth up to 1.8 billion to continue refining the NGC2’s common data baseline, or software foundation.

title: Big Tech Pushes Back Against Paying for America's Aging Power Grid
body: When Big Tech signed President Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March, promising to pay for all the new grid infrastructure upgrades required to service their data centers, we cautioned that "voluntary pledges from trillion-dollar tech giants have a habit of evolving."  Seven months later, the hyperscalers are pushing back on how much of the grid's bill is theirs to pay.  The past week brought a Democratic Senate report and a North Carolina utility settlement, and FERC is expected to rule on whether new data centers must bring their own power.  But before anyone grabs a pitchfork, ask the question none of them answers how much of this bill is really AI's, and how much is the cost of decades of grid neglect  On Friday, Senators Elizabeth Warren, Chris Van Hollen and Richard Blumenthal released Power and Profits, the result of a nearly yearlong investigation into seven data center operators including Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. The headline finding is as you would expect the companies' promises to cover their full costs apply to infrastructure serving only their own facilities, not the full cost of shared grid upgrades their arrival triggers.  The companies broadly opposed the "but-for" standard consumer advocates are pushing, under which a data center pays for any shared upgrade that "would not have been built but for the data center." One hyperscaler told Senate staff that such upgrades often provide a "system benefit which should be shared among all ratepayers."  They also balked at minimum bills, which advocates want set at 80% to 90% of contracted demand whether the power gets used or not. One Big Tech firm called a 90% floor "insanely high." Another called 85% to 90% "unreasonably high," since facilities often don't use all of their projected demand.  Two days earlier, Duke Energy announced a settlement, signed by Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft and North Carolina's utility consumer advocate, that it says ensures data centers "will pay upfront for all costs to connect to the grid."  The settlement itself is more nuanced. Data centers prepay the full cost of equipment that serves only them, such as a dedicated substation. For shared transmission upgrades, they post a letter of credit covering the estimated cost, collateral that starts shrinking once the facility consistently draws 75% of its contracted demand.  Whether data centers get directly charged for any slice of those shared costs is punted to a Duke study due a year after approval, and would apply only to future contracts.  Bring Your Own Power... Or Else  Then there's PJM, which wanted new data centers of 50 MW or more, starting in June 2027, to bring their own new capacity or be first in line to be cut off when the grid is strained.  PJM asked FERC to sign off by October 12. The Data Center Coalition urged FERC to reject the plan, and Google, which just contracted for 890 MW of new nuclear uprates from Constellation, has warned it would "chill investment." FERC rejected most of PJM's proposed large-load framework.  With Goldman now expecting behind-the-meter power to supply a quarter of all data centers by 2030, more of them may decide that building their own plants beats arguing over the grid's bill.  "But For" What, Exactly  The but-for test only works if everyone agrees on what the grid would have needed anyway, and the senators' own report suggests that is quite a lot. Tucked into its opening pages is an admission that roughly a third of US transmission and half of distribution infrastructure is operating "near or beyond its useful life." Nowhere does it estimate how much of that needed replacing with or without AI.  No case makes the point better than Three Mile Island. As we reported in March, Constellation's restart of Unit 1, a reactor that fed this same grid until 2019, ran into a "four-year-tall roadblock" when PJM said full deliverability could take until 2031.  Full output hinges on 765-kV and 500-kV transmission upgrades not expected until December 2030, and Constellation needed a FERC waiver to shift 760 MW of interconnection rights from its Eddystone plant just to try to work around them.  A reactor that can't fully reconnect to a grid it was plugged into seven years ago is a grid problem, not a data center problem.  None of this means the hyperscalers deserve a free ride. They signed the pledge, and they should honor it. But "but for the data center" is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a grid that, by the senators' own account, was already wearing out.  Then again, sending Big Tech the bill is a lot easier than explaining why the grid was falling apart before anyone had heard of ChatGPT.  By Zerohedge

Android is introducing new scam defense features that aim to make it easier for users to evade mobile fraud, including bolstered protection in Google Messages and additional safeguarding tools. Building on the Scam Detection feature in Google Messages, a new “enhanced protection” setting will be rolling out in the coming weeks that taps into cloud-based Gemini AI models to quickly evaluate a potential scammer’s intentions in conversations with an unrecognized sender.
“Scammers often disguise their true motives behind slow-burn conversations,” Google said in its update announcement . “This secure cloud analysis augments and extends our existing on-device detection, allowing us to identify novel and sophisticated attacks, actively uncovering and stopping abusers who try to hide their tracks.”
User data is encrypted during this AI analysis and “processed in a secure dedicated space” that Google (and anyone else besides the user) can’t access. The enhanced protection mode will be opt-in, and also uses on-device Gemini Nano AI to inspect real-time web signals in unfamiliar URLs sent to the user before they’re opened to determine if the links are malicious.
Additional security features announced today include blocking apps from enabling call forwarding, and notifying the user when someone attempts to do so, along with automatically concealing sensitive information while screen-sharing in Chrome and Android WebView. The scam detection feature for chat notifications Google introduced on Pixel phones last year is also expanding to devices from Honor, Motorola, Oppo, OnePlus, Realme, Tecno, Vivo, Xiaomi, and more. Google says it plans to bring it to “hundreds of millions of additional users later this year.”

Square is launching new hardware: a big kiosk for ordering things that has a touchscreen and lets you talk to an AI. It’s called the Square Kiosk.
Square says the Kiosk, which has a large pill shape, has an “agentic, conversational voice layer” that “fully understands a seller’s menu and listens and responds in real time, enabling customers to order the way they’d naturally talk to staff.” While talking with the AI agent, you can do things like ask questions and request modifications and substitutions.
The touchscreen on the Kiosk is 21.5 inches, and the device can welcome you as you approach thanks to presence detection, Square says. When it’s time to pay, you can use the contactless payment reader or card slot.
The Square Kiosk is available starting today at $1,999 for businesses with a Square Plus or Premium subscription and will also have a $99-per-device monthly software fee.
